title: Birdbuddy’s budget feeder foiled my squirrels
body:
Birdbuddy’s next-generation smart bird feeders have finally arrived. After spending a few days with the BirdBuddy Nook (from $99) and longer with the flagship Birdbuddy Home ($219), there’s a clear winner: The Nook is the perfect all-rounder, just the right blend of technology, nature, and value to bring you delightful scenes from the lives of your backyard birds.
But — and this is a pigeon-sized but — the new camera on both the Nook and the Home is a bit of a downgrade compared to the Birdbuddy Pro ($339, but often on sale for less). It has slightly worse viewing angles, the 2K HDR image quality isn’t as crisp or bright, and you now have to remove the whole feeder to charge it.
On the plus side, you can now rotate the new camera to capture a wide-angle 135-degree landscape view. The live feed loads much faster in the Birdbuddy app thanks to a new instant wake-up feature. In testing, the livestream appeared in under eight seconds, compared to about 30 on the Pro. That’s the difference between seeing a bird up close in real time and watching its tail feathers fly away.
[Image: The Birdbuddy Nook (left) with optional perch extender ($43), and the Birdbuddy Home (right). https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6279.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
For those unfamiliar, smart bird feeders use an AI-powered camera to capture photos and videos of visiting feathered friends (and the occasional unwanted furry beast). First announced at CES in January under different names, the Birdbuddy Nook and Birdbuddy Home follow the company’s hugely successful Birdbuddy (2022) and Birdbuddy Pro (2024).
They have completely new designs featuring the new camera, but the headline feature is that both are more affordable than the Pro, which Birdbuddy has now discontinued. (It’s currently selling for $239.99 on Amazon.) New tech that’s cheaper? In 2026? Bravo, Birdbuddy.
[Product: Birdbuddy Nook | https://mybirdbuddy.com/product/birdbuddy-nook/, https://mybirdbuddy.com/product/birdbuddy-nook-solar/]
[Product: Birdbuddy Home | https://mybirdbuddy.com/product/birdbuddy-home/]
[Product: Birdbuddy Pro (solar) | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0DHY6B9GY?tag=theverge02-20]
Birdbuddy’s new camera is the biggest change, but it comes with some compromises. As you can see in the videos below, the new portrait mode has a slightly narrower view of the feeder than the Pro, so while you get close-ups, the bird’s face can get cut off if it’s standing on the edge of the feeder.
In the new landscape mode (which the Pro doesn’t offer), the view cuts off the seed tray. So, while you get a wider view that’s better for seeing more bird activity, you no longer see the feed tray — resulting in more feathers but fewer up-close faces.
[Video: BirdBuddy Testing 1]
[Video: Bird Buddy Testing 2]
Despite the reduced angle and less vivid color, the camera is still very good; the images are clear and colorful, with plenty of detail, and the company says it’s optimized for better action and low-light shots — though I haven’t seen that in my testing.
I also really like the landscape option; it’s one of the reasons I enjoyed the Coolfly model I tested earlier this year. While portrait gives you an intimate up-close look, landscape captures more of the scene, including birds in flight and interacting. (You have to manually change the angles by repositioning the camera; you can’t do it through the app.)
[Media: https://youtube.com/shorts/LfTvM9DII3U?feature=share]
A montage of videos from the Home (blue tray/red perch) and the Nook (green tray/white perch) in portrait and landscape views.
Birdbuddy’s excellent app shows you the videos and photos the camera captures in a fun “feed,” where you can scroll through all your backyard visitors and manually initiate free, AI-powered species identification.
To have the app automatically identify birds, you need a subscription ($7.99 a month or $69.99 a year), which also lets you name returning visitors and put silly augmented-reality hats on them, which was a lot more fun than I expected.
Birdbuddy’s identification has been very good overall, though I’ve noticed the new camera struggles to identify some smaller, faster birds compared to the Pro.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0639.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0640.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0641.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0642.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-21-at-6.40.26-PM.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-21-at-6.40.44-PM.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0644.png?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0645.png?quality=90&strip=all]
While the camera is the same on the Home and Nook, the feeders differ. The easiest way to sum this up is maintenance. The Home is more hands-off: it holds six cups of seed compared to just under four on the Nook, has built-in solar, so you won’t have to take it down to charge as often, and supports 5 GHz Wi-Fi, while the Nook is only 2.4 GHz. The Home is also slightly bigger, with a larger seed tray, so it may attract larger birds.
In addition to the $99 base model, the Nook has two models with add-ons that bring it closer to the Home feature-wise: Nook Solar for $159 (with only one panel compared to two on the Home), and the Nook Extended Edition for $199, with solar and a perch extender to accommodate more visitors (you can buy the perch separately for $43). That’s the model I’m testing, but it’s just $20 less than the Home. If you’re tempted by those upgrades, I’d stick with the Home for its larger seed capacity and two solar panels.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6229.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6178.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6182.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6187.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
The Nook is pitched as better for balconies and small spaces, whereas the Home is better for bigger yards. And I get that. The Nook is smaller, with a smaller perch and a smaller seed tray than the Home. But in my few days with it in my big backyard, the Nook’s better value beats out the Home’s convenience upgrades.
Also — and this could be its killer feature — the Nook fully foiled my squirrels. Its smaller seed tray and perch seem to make it harder for them to balance (even harder if you don’t add the extended perch). I have a video where you can hear them trying to clamber onto it and giving up, whereas they got down to dinner in the Home with its deeper seed tray. (However, your squirrel mileage may vary!)
Birdbuddy had a strange rollout for the Home (originally called Birdbuddy 2), releasing it to existing customers through its app a few months ago in what felt like a beta test. It seems there were a lot of kinks to work out.
When I installed the Home earlier this year, I initially had trouble with Wi-Fi connectivity and battery life. But firmware updates seem to have fixed most of it. This summer, after one update, the Home’s battery lasted around three months; I only had to recharge it after a period of overcast days.
[Image: The Home (blue) holds almost twice as much seed as the Nook (green) and uses two solar panels to keep the battery charged. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6299.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
I had no Wi-Fi connectivity issues with the Nook, and both models paired to the app much faster than the Pro. I’ve only had the Nook for a few days, so it’s too early to judge battery life. However, recharging both devices is more involved than with the Pro because you have to remove the entire camera housing, which sits inside the bird seed compartment. It’s easier to just remove the whole feeder and take it inside.
The good news is that the Home is much easier to refill with birdseed without spilling it everywhere than the Pro is, thanks to a wider mouth and larger reservoir. The Nook is even easier, since you take the entire roof off to add seed — though, again, this requires removing it from its perch. You can pole-mount or hang both devices using the included hardware.
One problem I have noticed with the new designs is that the roof on both no longer fully covers the seed tray, as it does with the Pro. This lets in more light for the camera, but it also means the seed gets wetter when it rains.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6203.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6291.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
If you are looking for your first smart bird feeder, or for a great holiday gift for your nature-loving friend or family member, the Nook is an easy buy. Upgrade to the Home if you really don’t like refilling seed and recharging batteries. If you want to add solar to the Nook, buy that up front — you can’t currently purchase the solar roof as an accessory.
If you’re an existing Birdbuddy user, there are two reasons to upgrade from the Pro. First, if you’re having any issues with missed videos or slow livestream loading. Both new models load faster and capture video more reliably. Second, battery life. I had to charge the Pro every couple of weeks, even with solar. The Home got three months.
Today, I wouldn’t recommend buying a Pro, even if you can find one. While I prefer its portrait camera angle and it has slightly better video quality, the connectivity and battery life of the new models are worth those compromises. I’d rather see more birds more often than a bit more of a bird less often.
Birdbuddy Home ($219), Nook ($99), and Nook Solar ($159) are available now at mybirdbuddy.com and ship next month. The Nook Solar and Nook Extended Edition ($199) will be available at Target, Best Buy, and Walmart later this month.
Photos, video, and screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

title: Googlebooks just aren’t ready
body:
Every Googlebook laptop we’ve tested so far has great hardware. The problem is the software. While Googlebook OS has exciting ideas for how a laptop and phone can work together, right now it’s mostly a frustrating experience filled with annoying bugs and lackluster app support. It often feels like using an Android tablet with a keyboard and trackpad grafted on, rather than a cohesive laptop OS. It’s too bad, because those keyboards and trackpads — and pretty much all the laptops’ hardware components — are great.
Frankly, they should be. The cheapest is $900, a price where you start to expect quality processors, metal builds, higher-quality displays, good speakers, and great keyboards and trackpads (even haptic ones in some cases). The Googlebooks have those covered, and they also have very good battery life and at least 16GB of RAM.
Google wanted Googlebooks to feel premium, and HP, Acer, Lenovo, Dell, and Asus all delivered. It’s Google’s software that needs to catch up. In their current state, we don’t recommend you buy any of them. But it’s worth reviewing the hardware to determine which shows the most promise if the software one day improves — or if crafty modders manage to install other operating systems. Since the software is the same on all Googlebooks (save for some preinstalled manufacturer apps), and we’ve already covered that software at length, we’re strictly talking about Googlebook hardware here. The scores, however, cover hardware and software as they stand today. Brace yourself — the scores are bad.
If you’re a dedicated Google user or Pixel fan and you really want to be an early adopter / paying beta tester — or if you’re just here for some schadenfreude — here are our collective thoughts on each and every Googlebook.
[Product: Acer Googlebook 14 | https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://store.google.com/product/acer_googlebook, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Facer-googlebook-14-laptop-14-3k-oled-120hz-touchscreen-intel-core-ultra-5-series-3-2026-16gb-memory-512gb-storage-elemental-blue%2FJJ8V8HLZP2%2Fsku%2F6690085, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://www.acer.com/us-en/laptops/acer-googlebook/acer-googlebook-14]
The Acer Googlebook 14 is the only 2-in-1 convertible of the bunch, and it’s one of the nicest-feeling and -looking Acers I’ve ever used at this price. It’s light, with a sturdy metal chassis and a great 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz OLED touchscreen with stylus support. I find 2-in-1s pretty handy, even if they look clunkier than tablets like a Microsoft Surface Pro or an iPad with a keyboard case, but Googlebook OS doesn’t yet support portrait orientation, which limits the Acer’s stylus potential. Like all Googlebooks, the Acer has an Auto-Rotate toggle in settings, but it only flips the orientation 180 degrees — a strange oversight.
The speakers don’t have a lot of bass, and they can get muffled in tablet mode depending on how you hold the laptop, but they’re decent and sound balanced overall. The webcam is a slight weak point, as colors and contrast are a touch drab. But nothing here is bad. This isn’t like some of the Acer Aspires or Swifts I’ve tested in the past where you had to deal with a terrible screen and shoddy build quality for the sake of a good chip. It’s just an all-around nice package. That extends to the battery life, which lasted me eight to nine hours of light-to-mixed usage.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0005.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0010.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_Acer_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0013.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
If this was running Windows or a proper Linux distro with the same hardware and price, it’d be a rare bright spot in our ongoing RAMageddon hellscape. But thanks to Googlebook OS, it’s not. And an Acer rep told us its $900 launch price is only available for a limited time. That might sound like an incentive to buy one before a price increase, but please allow me to tap the “Don’t buy it now for what it might do later” sign. Actually, picture me tapping it as you read this whole article.
— Antonio G. Di Benedetto, Laptop Reviewer
[Product: Dell XPS Googlebook | https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://store.google.com/config/xps_googlebook, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fdell-xps-googlebook-13-4-2-5k-touchscreen-laptop-snapdragon-x-elite-x1e-80-100-2024-16gb-memory-512gb-storage-shimmer%2FJ3K4L6QQFC%2Fsku%2F6690181, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://www.dell.com/en-us/shop/laptop-computers/spd/xps13dx13267]
Here’s my theory: If Googlebooks are going to work anytime soon, they’re going to work as secondary computers. Maybe they don’t need to replace your primary work machine if they can instead be light, fast, simple, and fun to use. (Yes, I agree that $900 or more is a lot to pay for this kind of device, but hey, iPads pull it off!) I already see glimmers of possibility here, even through the bugs of Googlebook OS. “A Chromebook, but also it runs all my apps” is not a bad pitch for an off-day computer.
That’s why, of all the available Googlebooks, the Dell XPS Googlebook makes the most sense to me. At 2.2 pounds, with a 13.4-inch screen, and starting at $999, it’s one of the smallest and lightest Googlebooks available. (And unlike the cheaper Acer Googlebook 14, it doesn’t offer a bunch of flippy tablet modes that don’t really work.) Like the other models we’ve tested, it’s a lovely piece of high-end hardware; I love the keyboard and trackpad, I appreciate that I can open the thing with one hand, and the Qualcomm chip inside does its job fine for all my practical purposes. The battery got me through a full day of travel and then some.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Dell_XPS_Googlebook_ADiBenedetto_0004.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Dell_XPS_Googlebook_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Dell_XPS_Googlebook_ADiBenedetto_0006_1bfdbe.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Dell_XPS_Googlebook_ADiBenedetto_0005_95774a.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
My only real complaint is with the anti-glare coating on the display, which does help tamp down reflections but also creates that slight rainbow-shimmer effect that makes the screen appear a little less sharp and clear. The coating also dims the screen a bit — I’ve used the XPS Googlebook mostly at max brightness, just to get it up to normal. I am generally extremely in favor of these matte displays, but I’d trade the XPS Googlebook’s for a glossy one in a heartbeat.
As we keep saying, there’s simply no way around the fact that Googlebook OS isn’t ready. Google is fixing and improving it quickly (adding the ability to run any website as an app was a big win), but I can’t get past the apps that don’t work properly with a keyboard, don’t work on this size screen at all, or simply don’t exist on Googlebook OS (bring back Linux apps, now!). If you’re in the market for an overpriced second computer and you want easy access to Google Messages and your Drive files, a Googlebook might be exactly what you need. Someday. Maybe by then Dell will have fixed the screen.
— David Pierce, Editor at Large
[Product: HP Googlebook 14 | https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fhp-googlebook-14-3k-oled-touchscreen-snapdragon-x-elite-16gb-memory-512gb-ssd-atmospheric-blue%2FJ3PPHVH9QX%2Fsku%2F6687893, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://www.hp.com/us-en/shop/pdp/hp-googlebook-14-cj7x9av-1]
HP’s Googlebook 14 is more proof that of all the problems facing these early Googlebook models, the hardware isn’t one of them.
Starting from $1,199.99, this Googlebook is about the same size and weight as a MacBook Air 13, despite fitting in a larger 14-inch display. It’s a great panel, too: a 2880 x 1800 resolution, 120Hz, OLED touchscreen with a slim bezel, good viewing angles, and punchy brightness. The Snapdragon X Elite chip has proved reliable so far (and for what it’s worth, my Asus model with an Intel chip has been solid too, despite early concerns), with 16GB of RAM and the option to bump memory up to 32GB and storage as high as 1TB, but I haven’t pushed it through anything more demanding than image editing in the infuriating mobile versions of Lightroom and Photoshop.
The body is mostly metal, so the whole thing feels tough and solid. The keyboard’s comfortable and the haptic trackpad expansive, and the privacy shutter on the webcam is always a welcome touch. There are only two USB-C ports and a headphone jack, so grab one of the other Googlebooks if you know you need HDMI or USB-A.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0004.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0010.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268755_HP_Googlebook_14_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I’m a fan of the Googlebook-specific hardware touches too, which you’ll find across the lineup. I’m already building the habit of using the Caps Lock key for its Quick Insert function instead, with easy access to features like the clipboard, emoji, and Rambler dictation — though the latter gets its own dedicated function key too. It’s joined by keys for the classic Android navigation buttons and a shortcut for some flexible screenshot and screen recording options. The Glowbar is a little less impressive; it’s a cute design but doesn’t actually do very much, and since it’s on the lid you’ll rarely see it in action anyway.
From the hardware side this feels like a $1,200 laptop through and through — it’s the software where we still have questions.
— Dominic Preston, News Editor
[Product: Asus Googlebook 14 | https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fasus-googlebook-14-3k-oled-touchscreen-laptop-w-gemini-intelligence-intel-core-ultra-5-325-2026-16gb-ram-512gb-ssd-dusk-ash%2FJJGHGST42S, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=87443X1797501&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Feshop.asus.com%2Fus%2F90cb0a71-m003d0-asus-googlebook-14.html]
Asus’ entry in the first slate of Googlebooks was able to keep up with me better than I expected, with solid hardware that helped soften the blow of software frustrations.
At $1,299, the Asus Googlebook 14 is the priciest of the first five Googlebooks. The base configuration has an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 CPU, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage (you can also get the 512GB model for the same price at Best Buy). I rarely felt like I was pushing those specs to their limit — the Asus got pretty toasty when I was running games on it, but that’s true of just about any laptop. It breezed through things like managing a dozen or more Chrome tabs and hopping between a few different apps at once. Asus says the 70Wh battery lasts up to 18 hours, and while I didn’t get quite that long, I didn’t have trouble getting through a typical day without charging.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/asus-googlebook-android-19.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/asus-googlebook-android-11.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Asus_Googlebook_14_ADiBenedetto_0005.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Asus_Googlebook_14_ADiBenedetto_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268755_Google_event_Asus_Googlebook_14_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
One major plus is the Asus’ wealth of ports: two USB-C, two USB-A, a headphone jack, and even HDMI. That’s more than most of the other Googlebooks have, or my MacBook for that matter. I was able to hook up the Asus to my monitor, keyboard, mouse, and a wired controller without needing a USB-C hub or a docking station.
I mainly used the Asus without my external monitor, though, largely because it has a fantastic keyboard — it’s satisfyingly clicky with good key travel and tactile feedback. The 14-inch OLED (2880 x 1800) display doesn’t disappoint, either. It has a 120Hz refresh rate and a nice matte finish. The few games that ran well on the Asus, like the Android version of Dredge, looked great.
The Asus Googlebook 14 has some real highs, but the current Googlebook OS experience makes it a tough sell at $1,299. For the same price, you could get the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with similar specs or, for $100 more, you could also get Asus’ new Windows ExpertBook A7.
— Stevie Bonifield, News Writer
[Product: Lenovo Googlebook 15 | https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/101881227/type/dlg/https://store.google.com/product/lenovo_googlebook, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Flenovo-googlebook-15-3-3k-120hz-oled-touchscreen-laptop-intel-core-ultra-5-processor-325-2026-16gb-memory-512gb-storage-cloud-grey%2FJ3PT7KJYXG%2Fsku%2F6687176, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=87443X1797501&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.lenovo.com%2Fus%2Fen%2Fp%2Flaptops%2Fgooglebook%2Fgooglebook-series%2Flenovo-googlebook-15%2F83w6cto1wwus1]
The $1,099 Lenovo Googlebook 15 is the largest of the launch lineup, and it’s low-key my favorite. I love a bigger screen, especially in a lightweight laptop. At around 2.8 pounds / 1.27kg, the Lenovo Googlebook is nearly half a pound lighter than Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air. It’s not as thin or nice as a MacBook Air, but it makes up for that with more ports (HDMI 2.1, two USB-C, and one USB-A). It also has a bright 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz OLED display and a large haptic trackpad that feels and sounds like a tight drum when you click it. Despite that sizable OLED, the battery easily lasted me an eight-hour workday of navigating Chrome tabs with a handful of extra apps like Apple Music and Signal running. And its light gray color and satiny finish is just charming.
Of the three Googlebooks I’ve tested (I tried the HP as well), this has been the one I used the most because of that larger screen and satisfying trackpad. The speakers are good too, with a touch of stereo separation due to the laptop’s size, and they get surprisingly loud. On the other hand, the keyboard is only fine. It’s got a nice clacky feel, but the keycaps are slightly wobbly, and overall it lacks the tight, satisfying tactility of other Lenovo laptop keyboards (like ThinkPads). And while I love this laptop’s off-white color, the bright white keyboard backlight sometimes makes the legends harder to see unless you’re actually in a dark space (this is one place RGB backlighting would actually help).

Also included with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 (at least, if you buy it directly from Lenovo or Google) is an AI Mouse. Uhh. It’s a Bluetooth mouse. It’s got a light-up button for launching Gemini. That’s about all that makes it an “AI Mouse.” Having a Glowbar that actually faces you seems like a nice idea, but just like the ones built into the lid of every Googlebook, the one on the mouse doesn’t do much. You can pick different lighting colors and patterns in the preinstalled Lenovo Vantage app, and the Glowbar does a brief colorful flourish when you summon Gemini — but that’s about it. It’s just a fine ergonomic mouse that matches this fine laptop hardware.
And that’s the story with every Googlebook so far: The hardware is fine, and even great. But until the software is worthy of the hardware, that’s just not good enough.
— Antonio G. Di Benedetto, Laptop Reviewer

Birdbuddy is finally launching the new smart bird feeders it originally announced at CES 2026 earlier this year, but with new names. The Birdbuddy 2 Mini is now called the Birdbuddy Nook, and it is designed to be a smaller and more affordable option the company describes as its “most accessible smart bird feeder yet.” The flagship Birdbuddy 2 has been renamed the Birdbuddy Home and delivers upgrades like a redesigned camera with a wider field of view and integrated solar panels. Both models are now available through Birdbuddy’s online store while some configurations will be available at other retailers later this month.
The Birdbuddy Nook starts at $99 and features a redesigned circular 2K HDR camera with a 135-degree field of view. The camera wakes up the moment a bird lands to help ensure visits are captured. The camera can shoot in landscape or portrait orientations, making it easier to share videos and images on social media, while the AI-powered Birdbuddy app identifies exactly what species is visiting.
The Nook’s 3.8-cup seed reservoir may need frequent refills if a lot of birds regularly stop by, but you can avoid frequent battery charges by upgrading to the $159 Nook Solar , which adds a solar panel to the roof. For an extra $40 on top of that, the $199 Nook Extended Edition includes a larger perch to accommodate more birds.
The $219 Birdbuddy Home uses the same 2K HDR camera with a 135-degree field of view as the Nook, but in a larger feeder designed to require less maintenance. It has a six-cup seed reservoir and comes with a pair of solar panels on top to help keep the battery charged, assuming the feeder’s installed somewhere with adequate sun exposure. The Home also has a built-in perch extender to accommodate more visitors, dual-band Wi-Fi, and an upgraded mic that can help the mobile app more accurately identify a species through its birdsong.

title: Insta360 launches a cheaper version of its wireless mics with color screens
body:
Following the launch of its wireless Mic Pro system last May featuring built-in color E Ink screens for custom branding and an array of three microphones to emulate different pickup patterns, Insta360 has announced a cheaper alternative that skips a few features many content creators might not miss.
The new Insta360 Mic sits between the company’s Mic Pro and the budget-friendly Mic Air, which uses much smaller screenless transmitters. While the Mic Pro is priced at $329.99 for a kit that includes two microphone transmitters, one wireless receiver, and a charging case, the Insta360 Mic costs $249.99 for a similar bundle. Insta360 sells the microphones individually since they can directly connect to smartphones and many of the company’s cameras (including the X6, X5, and Luna Ultra) over Bluetooth. The Mic Pro transmitter on its own costs $99.99, while the new Insta360 Mic is $79.99.
[Image: The Insta360 Mic is available in bundles that include two transmitters, a wireless receiver, and a charging case. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/insta360_3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The design and functionality of the Insta360 Mic is very similar to the Mic Pro. It has the same 1.22-inch, six-color E Ink display on the front that can be customized with logos, photos, or solid colors to help it blend into clothing. The transmitters have a range of up to 400 meters when paired with Insta360’s wireless receiver that can connect to professional cameras, laptops, or other recording devices using a built-in USB-C connector. The Insta360 Mic also features AI-powered noise canceling to reduce background noise and automatic gain control modes that adjust recording levels on the fly to help prevent clipping if things suddenly get too loud.
[Product: Insta360 Mic | https://www.amazon.com/Insta360-MC120-Mic/dp/B0HKJ4DZGN/?tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=87443X1797501&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fstore.insta360.com%2Fproduct%2Fmic-pro, https://www.amazon.com/Insta360-MC120-Mic/dp/B0HKJ7Y4CG/?tag=theverge02-20]
So what are you missing out on when choosing the cheaper Insta360 Mic? The biggest downgrade is that the transmitters have just a single mic instead of the triple mic array in the Mic Pro, so you cannot select from multiple pickup patterns; omnidirectional is the only option. However, that simplified hardware makes the transmitters slightly lighter than the Mic Pro’s — 19.4 grams compared with 19.7 grams — and battery life increases from up to 10 hours to up to 13 hours, which can be boosted to 34 hours with the charging case.
The Mic Pro’s transmitters come with 32GB of built-in storage for creating a backup recording. The Insta360 Mic transmitters don’t have any built-in storage, but you can enable backup recording by sticking a microSD card inside each one. As with the lighter design and improved battery life, the microSD option also feels like an upgrade for the Insta360 Mic if you want more than 32GB of storage.

title: UFC 333 predictions: Volkanovski and Dvalishvili to leave Abu Dhabi as champions
body: Abu Dhabi will host two title fights as the UFC returns to the UAE this weekend. Alexander Volkanovski puts his featherweight championship on the line while Petr Yan makes his first title defence as bantamweight champion. There are nine fights on the card at Etihad Arena. Below are our predictions for UFC 333. Main event Alexander Volkanovski v Movsar Evloev Alexander “The Great” looks back to his brilliant best following two polished wins over Diego Lopes. He will need to be on top form against the unbeaten Russian. Evloev boasts a perfect 20-0 record in pro MMA. Volkanovski (28-4) has the edge in experience. Saturday will be his 12th successive title fight and the sixth time he has defended the UFC featherweight title. He is in the conversation as the greatest 145-pounder of all time and is looking to add to his legend against Evloev. UFC 333 build-up - in pictures If Volkanovski has the advantage in striking, Evloev has it in grappling. The Russian is a master wrestler; the way he dominated Aljamain Sterling is a testament to that. He tried to venture away a little in his win over Lerone Murphy, before reverting to type to secure the victory. Volkanovski warned Evloev to “not try to be exciting” and to “bring your best game”, saying he didn't want to hear any excuses if things don't go the Russian's way on the mat. “People want to see how I handle that wrestling anyway. I think that's a part of the story,” he told The National . Prediction: Volkanovski to win on the judges' scorecards. Co-main event Petr Yan v Merab Dvalishvili Yan fought the perfect fight to end Dvalishvili's three-fight run as bantamweight king. Ripping body shots took the wind out of the Georgian's sails when they met last December. Yan's takedown defence was textbook too. It was Dvalishvili's fourth fight of 2025 and, by his own admission, accepting the Yan fight was a mistake, coming only two months after his victory over Corey Sandhagen. “I'm not blaming that because of my loss, but I know why I lost,” Dvalishvili told The National . His loss to Yan ended a 14-fight win streak and necessitated a long-overdue break for Dvalishvili. Neither has fought since their last meeting. UFC 333 will be the third time they have met, with Dvalishvili taking the first fight on the judges' scorecards. Many admire Yan's skill set, not least because he is an underrated ground technician too. But with Dvalishvili well rested, “The Machine” should be too much for his Russian opponent this time around. Prediction: Dvalishvili to reclaim the title. Rest of the main card Lone'er Kavanagh v Ramazan Temirov Flyweight prospect Lone’er Kavanagh will look to protect his top-six ranking and potentially move into the title conversation when he faces Ramazan Temirov. A win over former champion Brandon Moreno put the rest of the division on notice, but a late submission at the hands of Brandon Royval has some questioning whether the likeable Londoner has the all-round game to challenge for championship gold. In Temirov, he faces a fearsome puncher, one who separated Steve Erceg from his consciousness the last time he was in Abu Dhabi in July . It was his 13th first-round knockout. Prediction: Temirov by KO. Alexander Volkov v Rizvan Kuniev Alexander Volkov's victory over Jailton Almeida in Abu Dhabi 12 months ago put him next in line for a shot at the heavyweight title. By the end of UFC 321, those hopes lay in tatters. Ciryl Gane’s wayward fingers changed the heavyweight landscape. Tom Aspinall is still recovering from his injuries. Gane, meanwhile, has been promoted to undisputed king of the division. Volkov, a fighter more methodical than mesmerising, needs to put on a show against Rizvan Kuniev if he is to convince his UFC bosses he deserves a crack at Gane. Prediction: Volkov by decision. Aaron Pico v Losene Keita Losene Keita was drafted in at short notice following an injury to Arnold Allen. The Belgian featherweight became a viral sensation following his spectacular walk-off KO over Muhammad Naimov at UFC Paris in September. The celebration will take some topping, too. After being stopped by Lerone Murphy, Pico returned with a flawless performance over Patricio Pitbull, taking a unanimous decision over the feared Brazilian. Prediction: Keita to deliver another highlight reel KO.

title: Nile University of Nigeria Inducts 75 New Medical Doctors at 5th MBBS Attestation Ceremony
body: Nile University of Nigeria has inducted 75 new medical doctors into the medical profession at its 5th MBBS Attestation Ceremony in Abuja, bringing the total number of doctors produced by the University since the inception of its MBBS programme to 257. The graduates, members of the University’s Class of 2025/2026, took the Physician’s Oath on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, following years of academic study and clinical training at the University’s College of Health Sciences. The ceremony marked a significant milestone for the graduates as they prepare to apply their training in professional practice. Four graduates stood out for their academic performance, recording multiple Pass with Distinction results across key medical disciplines. Abubakar Dahiru Bobo achieved seven distinctions, Shuaib Sanni Farida recorded five, while Sadi Abdu Fatima and Hafsa Awwal Abubakar each earned four. Delivering the attestation lecture, the Medical Elder, Professor Ahmed Ahidjo, former Chief Medical Director of the University of Maiduguri Teaching Hospital, drew on his professional experience to emphasise the importance of discipline, mentorship and continuous learning in medicine. He also discussed advances in interventional radiology and the role of innovation in medical practice, highlighting the need for doctors to keep abreast of developments in their field. The Registrar of the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN), Professor Fatima Kyari, administered the Physician’s Oath and commended the University’s contribution to medical education. She urged the graduates to look beyond individual achievement and consider how they could mentor others and contribute to national development through their profession. “Start to think about today. How you will make others grow, in this profession and in the country at large,” she said. The Vice-Chancellor of Nile University of Nigeria, Prof. Dilli Dogo, FNAMed, DFMC, reminded the graduates that completing their training was the beginning of a career that would demand dedication, accountability and service. “The journey starts now. It’s a journey of service, dedication, commitment and delivery,” he said. He urged them to honour the commitments they had made in taking the Physician’s Oath, stressing the responsibility that comes with the trust placed in medical professionals. “You are called to a profession that does not tolerate excuses. I urge you to stand by the oath you’ve taken,” he added. The Vice-Chancellor also highlighted the University’s international academic links, noting that it has partnerships with 126 universities worldwide. As the graduates prepare to begin the next stage of their careers, they also received medical starter tools to support their transition into professional practice. The induction of this fifth cohort reflects Nile University of Nigeria’s continuing contribution to medical education and the development of healthcare professionals in Nigeria.

title: Turkey waiting for sale contract from Qatar for Eurofighter Typhoon jets, defense ministry says
body: Turkey is waiting for Qatar to send it a sale contract and a draft training program as part of its deal with Britain to procure Eurofighter Typhoon jets, the Turkish Defense Ministry said on Thursday.NATO allies Turkey and Britain signed the deal for 20 jets last year to deepen bilateral ties and bolster Turkish air defenses. Ankara has also said it is seeking 24 more jets from Qatar and Oman, though progress on that procurement has been limited.Under the deal with Britain, Qatar and Oman can supply Turkey with some of its own Typhoons, though that requires a separate sales contract.At its weekly press briefing, the ministry said that talks on the procurement were continuing and that Turkish and Qatari delegations discussed technical and logistical matters in August and September.These included the scope of jets and ammunition to be procured, as well as training for pilots and maintenance teams."It is expected for Qatar to prepare the draft training program and the sales contract to be sent to our country," it said.Turkey signs defense accord with Qatar, Pakistan, IndonesiaTurkey signed an accord with Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia on Wednesday to boost defense cooperation and strengthen defensive capabilities, including through joint development and production.The ministry added that its defense budget was increased for 2027 due to ongoing domestic defense industry projects for air defenses and platforms, Turkey's indigenous KAAN fighter jet program, drone development, and shipbuilding.

title: Court Seeks Speedy Trial For Five Suspected Kidnappers Of NYSC Members, Others In Imo
body: A State High Court sitting in Owerri, Imo State, has called for speedy trials in the ongoing cases involving five suspected kidnappers, urging prosecution and defence counsel to cooperate with the court to ensure judgments are delivered before January 2027. Presiding Judge, Justice Emeka Orafu, made the appeal during proceedings in the cases involving three defendants accused of abducting prospective National Youth Service Corps members and two others facing charges over a separate kidnapping case. During the hearing, a Department of State Services (DSS) investigative officer, Ikem Emmanuel, testified on the investigation that led to the arrest of the three defendants in the NYSC-related case. Emmanuel told the court that the investigation involved intelligence gathering, phone data analysis, record checks, interviews and statements obtained from the defendants, victims and witnesses. He said an identification parade was conducted, during which victims and witnesses identified the defendants as alleged members of the criminal gang. The officer further told the court that one of the defendants, Usman Aliyu, admitted in his statement to participating in the operation and allegedly disclosed that 11 people were involved. Emmanuel maintained that the defendants’ statements were obtained in the presence of their legal representatives and DSS legal officers. In a related proceeding involving two other defendants, the DSS officer also gave evidence on the investigation, stating that their statements were taken in the presence of their lawyers and DSS legal officers. Following the proceedings, Justice Orafu adjourned the cases to October 27, 28, 29 and 30 for continuation of the hearing. The judge reiterated the need for all counsel to work with the court to facilitate the speedy determination of the cases and ensure judgments are delivered before January 2027. The five defendants are to remain in the custody of the Department of State Services (DSS) as proceedings continue. On October 1, 2026, 20 corps members were abducted by gunmen near Umunoha in Mbaitoli Local Government Area, while travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to their assigned NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states. However, the prospective corps members and a civilian were rescued from the Amakohia-Ubi forest in Owerri West Local Government Area six days later. The DSS later arrested five suspects in intelligence-led operations conducted between October 10 and 14 in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, and Aba in Abia State. title: Africa CDC, Nigeria target 2m community health workers by 2030
body: By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), in collaboration with the Nigerian government and continental partners, is set to convene a high-level forum in Abuja to accelerate efforts to recruit, train, deploy and retain two million community health workers across Africa by 2030. The forum, scheduled for October 28 to 30, is expected to secure political commitments, sustainable financing and concrete national action to address the continent’s health workforce shortages and strengthen preparedness for disease outbreaks. According to an advisory issued by Africa CDC on Thursday, the meeting will take place at the Transcorp Hilton Hotel, Abuja, under the political leadership of President Bola Tinubu, the African Union Champion for Human Resources for Health, and the Community Health Delivery Partnership. It will bring together African ministers of health and finance, senior government officials, African Union institutions, development partners and community health representatives to discuss strategies for strengthening the continent’s health workforce. Africa CDC said an adequately trained and equipped health workforce was critical to strengthening health security and sovereignty, particularly as recurring public health emergencies highlight gaps in the continent’s capacity to detect and respond to disease threats. The advisory noted that ongoing Ebola outbreaks and other health emergencies had underscored the importance of investing in community health workers, who play vital roles in early disease detection, surveillance, community engagement and rapid response. Despite progress in expanding community health services, significant workforce gaps persist across Africa. The continent had an estimated 1.15 million community health workers in 2024, while the projected shortage across the broader health workforce could reach 5.85 million by 2030, according to the advisory. The forum will examine strategies for closing these gaps through sustainable financing, workforce development, harmonised standards and costed national plans to accelerate the recruitment and deployment of community health workers. A major highlight will be the launch of the Continental Community Health Acceleration Plan, alongside the Continental Community Health Programme Scorecard and the next cycle of the Continental Community Health Landscape Survey. Participants are also expected to develop costed national acceleration plans for community health workers covering the 2026–2030 period. Discussions will focus on domestic financing, employment, deployment and retention, as well as establishing continental priorities for workforce investment and accountability. The meeting will further examine how community health workers can strengthen primary healthcare, improve maternal and child health outcomes, reach children who have not received any routine vaccine doses, and enhance preparedness for and response to disease outbreaks. The high-level ministerial session, scheduled for Friday, October 30, is expected to secure political and financial commitments from participating governments and advance continental initiatives to accelerate the development of Africa’s community health workforce. title: ‘Our problem with Ghana sports is long-term planning’ – NSA boss Osei Sarpong advocates sports development
body: The Acting Director-General of the National Sports Authority (NSA), Prof. Emmanuel Osei Sarpong, has stated that hiring top-tier coaches alone will not solve Ghana’s recurring sports challenges urging a shift in focus toward long-term development and athlete development. His comments come amid a difficult period for Ghanaian football, with both male and female national teams struggling on the international stage to qualify for or win major tournaments. Speaking in an interview with Citi Sports, Sarpong emphasized that without long-term planning, the root causes of Ghana’s sports dip in form will remain unresolved. “Our problem with Ghana sports, not football alone, has been long-term planning, long-term development of athletes,” he said. The NSA chief’s assessment reflects the recent decline across various national teams. The Black Maidens, currently competing at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, sit at the bottom of their group with just one point from two matches. They trail third-placed Canada and second-placed Norway by two points, and group leaders Brazil by three. The Maidens will have to secure a victory against Canada in their final group match to keep any hopes of advancing alive. Meanwhile, the male U-17 team, the Black Starlets, missed out on qualifying for the U-17 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), which doubles as the qualification path for the 2027 FIFA U-17 World Cup. At the senior level, the Black Stars recently suffered back-to-back set-backs, falling 2-0 to Côte d’Ivoire in Bouaké before enduring a disappointing 4-2 defeat against The Gambia. These collective struggles have intensified public calls for structural reforms within the Ghana Football Association (GFA) and a complete restructure of the nation’s football development framework. “As we speak now, there is no Ghanaian who is qualified as a fitness trainer, strength and conditioning coach, specifically for football,” he added. “Why can’t you use that money to develop some coaches in Ghana so that they will become multipliers of their knowledge?” He advocated for a stronger partnership between the NSA, the Ghana Olympic Committee (GOC), and various sports federations to build a structured talent-identification system. He pointed to the establishment of the Grassroots Sports Secretariat as a vital first step toward creating a sustainable pipeline. According to him, talent identification must be backed by consistent investment and structured training. He proposed a target model of identifying promising athletes at age 12 and nurturing them through a six-year program to prepare them for world class competition by age 18.

title: West’s aggression, need to respond: key remarks by Russian defense chief
body:
MINSK, October 22. /TASS/. The West’s aggressive actions against Russia and Belarus are intensifying, with NATO, the European Union, and the Kiev regime deliberately pursuing a path of escalation, Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov said during a joint board meeting of the Russian and Belarusian Defense Ministries.
He emphasized that the North Atlantic Alliance’s military preparations require the armed forces of Russia and Belarus to respond promptly to changes in the military-political situation.
TASS has summarized the defense minister’s key statements.
Aggressive actions by the West against Russia and Belarus are on the rise: "Today, the military-political situation surrounding our countries remains complex. We are observing a rapid increase in tensions and aggressive actions by the West against Russia and Belarus."
NATO, the European Union, and the Kiev regime are deliberately pursuing a path of escalation: "NATO, the EU, and the Kiev regime are deliberately pursuing a path of escalation. <…> The accelerated militarization of Europe poses a particular danger, as it is shifting industry toward military production and preparing infrastructure for the rapid deployment of armed forces."
NATO countries are increasing their military presence near the borders of Russia and Belarus: "The coalition’s military presence near our borders is growing."
In 2027, the North Atlantic Alliance plans "to bring eight multinational battalion tactical groups on its ‘eastern flank’ up to brigade strength in 2027."
NATO is also conducting exercises to rehearse offensive scenarios against Russia and Belarus: "The Alliance is conducting drills rehearsing offensive scenarios against our countries."
The North Atlantic Alliance’s military preparations require the armed forces of Russia and Belarus to respond promptly to changes in the military-political situation: "All of this requires us to respond in a timely manner to changes in the military-political situation - to strengthen cooperation in ensuring security and to build up our military capabilities. To this end, we are refining our approaches to the joint use of armed forces."
As part of this response, military personnel from both countries regularly conduct "combat coordination exercises for formations and units assigned to the regional grouping of troops (forces)": "We give priority to joint practical exercises based on best practices from the special military operation."
In September-October, the Center 2026 strategic command and staff exercise took place alongside the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) Rapid Reaction Forces’ Interaction maneuvers held according to a unified plan, the Search intelligence forces and assets exercise, and the Echelon logistical support exercise: "I would like to note the active participation of the Belarusian side in these events."
Belarus and Russia are close allies and partners with shared cultural and moral values: "Belarus and Russia are strategic allies and partners, bound not only by treaty obligations but also by shared values, a shared history, and a shared responsibility for security within the Union State."
Russia and Belarus are developing cooperation between the defense-industrial complexes of the two countries: "We continue to pay special attention to cooperation in the military-technical sphere. We are establishing cooperation between the defense-industrial complexes of the two countries."
Russian military universities, he reported, continue to train Belarusian military personnel at the Russian Defense Ministry’s educational institutions: "Currently, 418 Belarusian military personnel are studying at 24 military universities under unified curricula and programs."
Training in the most sought-after specialties is organized at Russia’s joint-force combat training center in Mulino: "Since the start of the special military operation, 1,315 people have undergone training there on behalf of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Belarus."
"We are developing cooperation in the field of culture. In May 2027, we will organize the Avanpost International Festival of Army Culture and Creativity, featuring ensembles from the armed forces of Russia, Belarus, and other friendly nations."
The extensive cooperation achieved between the military departments of Russia and Belarus ensures the prompt fulfillment of tasks aimed at countering the full spectrum of modern challenges and threats to the security of both countries.

title: Chief of Staff calls for more transparency in delivery of public private partnership projects
body: The Chief of Staff, Dr. Julius Debrah has called for more transparency in the delivery of public private partnership projects. He disclosed this when Ghana took center stage on October 16 as host of the 7th Africa Public Sector Conference and Awards (APSCA 2026), an evening that brought together some of the continent’s most influential public leaders in Accra. Speaking at the summit, Dr. Debrah said this is critical to safeguard expenditure and ensure timely delivery of infrastructure for citizens. “We need transparency and fairness in our partnerships as government agencies and I must assure you that Africa can develop rapidly if we pay attention to this” he said. Speaking on the topic, Leadership, Coordination and Institutional Resilience: Building Public Institutions That Work.”, the Chief of Staff, he urged public servants to share knowledge among themselves as another step in enhancing economic transformation. Under the theme; “Governance 2030: Resilient Institutions for a Digital, Green & Secure Africa, the event brought together delegations from Nigeria, Sierra Leone and other African countries to share a common platform to discuss growth in the public sector. In total, 67 honours were awarded, recognising 22 public agencies and 45 individuals whose work is reshaping how government serves its people. Winners came from Kenya, Ghana, Nigeria, Botswana, The Gambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), among others, proof that the drive for excellence in public service runs across Africa. “These winners prove that Africa’s public sector can deliver,” said Akin Naphtal, Group CEO of InstinctWave Group and Group Publisher of Public Sector Global (PSG) Magazine. “Behind every award is a citizen better served. We celebrate leaders and institutions whose results can be measured.” Continental Leadership: Presidential and Executive Honours William Samoei Ruto, PhD, CGH, President of the Republic of Kenya and Commander-in-Chief of the Defence Forces, received the APSCA 2026 Continental Leadership Award for Visionary Governance & Human Capital Transformation. Dr Julius Debrah, Chief of Staff, Republic of Ghana, won the Distinguished Leadership in Governance & Public Service Excellence Award.

title: Just because Tesla’s Optimus is in production doesn’t mean it’s actually ready
body:
On Tesla’s earnings call Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk announced that the company had begun early production of its humanoid robot on its high-volume line in Fremont, California. Then he laid out what still needs work: the robot’s hands, its safety, reliability, and durability, and the artificial intelligence needed to make it a productive tool.
“There’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks,” Musk said.
"“At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans.”" - ELON MUSK
These are substantial caveats for a product slated for volume production. Musk expects the pieces to come together around the end of 2027, when Tesla could begin delivering Optimus to outside companies, but didn’t say which or what exactly the robots would do for them. In the meantime, Tesla needs to build a fleet of robots that can practice tasks and generate training data, then feed what they learn back into the system. It also needs to integrate a new chip that Musk says will give the robots far more computing power.
Tesla called the machines coming off the Fremont line its first “production-quality bots” and said its manufacturing process was suitable for a commercial product. But the company did not disclose how many robots it has produced, what tasks they can currently perform autonomously, or how often they can complete the tasks without human intervention. The announcement marks a step toward manufacturing Optimus at scale, not evidence that Tesla has a robot ready to do even the initial jobs Musk envisions — dangerous, repetitive industrial work performed around the clock — let alone become the general-purpose household machine he ultimately imagines.
“You can produce them, but the software is lacking,” Ken Goldberg, a robotics professor at the University of California, Berkeley, told The Verge. “If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that’s a big problem.”
Musk himself spent much of his discussion of Optimus explaining why investors shouldn’t expect finished robots to immediately pour out of the factory. Production will follow an S-curve, he said, with a slow, bumpy beginning. “There’s like 10,000 things that have to go right for production of the robot,” Musk said, “and it will move as fast as the slowest.”
Most of the equipment for a line intended to produce a million robots annually is already in Fremont, according to Musk. But reaching a rate of 20,000 robots a week will take “at least a year, maybe a little longer,” he said.
“There’s still parts of the design that are changing,” Musk said. “You’ve got to basically build up an entire gigantic global supply chain and have domestically a very, very big factory, and everything has got to work.”
"“If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that’s a big problem.”" - KEN GOLDBERG
Those production challenges are only one part of the unfinished work.
A robot that can repeatedly perform a carefully defined task has a different job from a general-purpose humanoid expected to adapt to varied objects and surroundings. Musk described industrial applications as the first market for Optimus, with at-home purchases coming as the robot develops a much wider range of capabilities.
Optimus is “going to do like 1,000 times more things than a car would do,” Musk said.
Some of Goldberg’s more pessimistic colleagues think a truly useful humanoid robot is still 25 years away, he said. Goldberg believes the field will solve its hardest problems — including reliability, speed, and dexterity — sooner than that. But even he doesn’t expect them to be solved on Musk’s timeline.
Robots have become adept at walking, running, and jumping, Goldberg said, but dexterity remains much harder. Manipulating flexible materials, such as wires and fabric, or assembling products is incredibly difficult; doing it quickly and reliably enough for real work is harder still.
“I’ve been working on these problems for 40 years,” Goldberg said. “I don’t think they’re going to be solved in the next year or two.”
Musk acknowledged that Tesla is ramping production before resolving Optimus’ main hardware problem: its hands. “We’re building robots that do not have perfected hands,” he said.
Unlike human hands, robot hands can’t heal themselves. Yet they must withstand repeated use while remaining soft enough to handle delicate objects without damaging their sensors. “What an incredible thing the human hand is at the end of the day,” Musk said.
Durability is a challenge for the rest of the robot, too. “It can’t, like, wear out after a month,” Musk said.
Closing the software gap will require training data Tesla doesn’t yet have. Unlike its cars, Optimus has no vast installed base from which the company can gather information. Musk said Tesla therefore needs to build roughly 10,000 to 20,000 robots to practice tasks at what he called “Optimus Academy.”
“With Optimus, we have to bootstrap it by making the robots and having them do self-play, which is really how a human learns to navigate the world,” Musk said. He compared the process to a toddler gradually mastering increasingly complex skills. “Eventually, they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone,” Musk said. “And then they learn to read and do all sorts of things.”
Goldberg described learning through self-play as a hypothesis whose success in software doesn’t establish that it will work as well in physical hardware. “When you get into hardware, it’s not so clear,” he said.
Tesla is also waiting on hardware that has yet to be integrated. Musk said he hopes to put the company’s AI5 chip into Optimus around April 2027, providing roughly 10 times the computing power of AI4. He expects the new chip, improved software, and mechanical refinements to come together before customer deliveries.
If all that works, Musk expects Optimus will eventually have a hand in its own production. “The Optimus robots will build the future Optimus robots,” he said, describing a self-reinforcing production loop that would grow “extremely fast.”
“At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans,” Musk predicted.
Before then, Musk promised a video within a month or two showing Optimus performing tasks that aren’t preprogrammed. He criticized humanoid demonstrations that look impressive but wouldn’t translate into useful real-world performance. “If you actually try to use that humanoid robot in the real world, you would have a lot of trouble,” he said. “It wouldn’t work, basically.”
Goldberg calls the problem “video emptor.” A video might show the one successful attempt out of a thousand, he said, hide a person controlling the robot offscreen, or depend on a precisely arranged setting. In robotics labs, task success rates have stalled at around 70 to 80 percent, Goldberg said. “That’s not acceptable for real industry.”
Musk remains convinced Optimus will become “the biggest product on Earth.” While Tesla’s announcement brings it closer to manufacturing Optimus in large numbers, building a robot customers can depend on – and actually use – remains a separate milestone.

title: EU grudgingly admits sanctions failed to cripple Russian economy — Polyansky
body:
VIENNA, October 22. /TASS/. European politicians are being forced to grudgingly acknowledge that EU sanctions have failed to bring about the collapse of the Russian economy or inflict significant damage on its defense industry, Russian Permanent Representative to the OSCE Dmitry Polyansky said at a regular meeting of the organization’s Permanent Council.
"Since February 2022, 22 packages of so-called sanctions have been adopted. Each new package is proclaimed the ‘largest in history.’ Russia’s economy has not collapsed, as the architects of the sanctions promised, but has adapted and is developing quite successfully. Russia’s military-industrial complex has not ground to a halt. On the contrary, it is actively ramping up production of the most advanced weapons systems, something Europe is being forced to acknowledge through gritted teeth," he said.
Polyansky added that sanctions against Russia have dealt a blow to the EU economy from which it has yet to recover.

title: Ebola: Africa CDC seeks full travel history of Nigeria’s patient to trace source of infection
body:
The Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Jean Kaseya, has called on Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola patient to disclose her complete travel history and possible contacts during a recent visit to Uganda to help health authorities establish how she contracted the virus.
Mr Kaseya said the woman, who was born in Uganda but resides in Abuja, spent several days in her home country before her husband, a diplomat, travelled to join her. The couple subsequently returned to Nigeria on 3 October.
Speaking during an interview on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday, Mr Kaseya said investigators were seeking additional information about the woman’s movements, including whether she travelled outside Kampala and had contact with anyone who might have been exposed to the virus.
He said the information was necessary to support investigations by Nigerian and Ugandan authorities and prevent disagreements between countries over the possible source of infection.
“What we want is collaboration from this person, the lady. She has to disclose to the authorities,” he said.
Mr Kaseya explained that the Africa CDC was working with authorities across the region to establish the circumstances surrounding the infection and determine whether the patient might have been exposed elsewhere during her trip.
He stressed that the woman needed to provide accurate information about her movements and contacts to enable public health officials to identify possible transmission links.
“I need this information, Nigeria needs this information because we need also to support Uganda,” he said.
“She needs to tell us if she flew to the DRC; if she went out of Kampala; if she was in contact with someone who came from the DRC.”
He added that obtaining the information would help strengthen cooperation between countries responding to the outbreak.
“I think these are informations we are looking for, and it will help all of us and avoid a crisis between African countries.”
Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola patient is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, for a holiday.
Mr Kaseya had earlier disclosed that the woman, originally from Uganda but resident in Abuja, developed symptoms three days after returning to Nigeria on 3 October.
Providing details of her medical history during an interview with the BBC’s Newshour programme, he said she first developed symptoms on 6 October and initially sought treatment at a private hospital, believing she had malaria.
She subsequently visited another private hospital, where she was admitted on 11 October after her condition failed to improve.
“She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th,” Mr Kaseya told the BBC .
Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, confirmed that the 42-year-old woman spent two and a half weeks in Kampala before returning to Abuja through Ethiopia, where she had a two-hour stopover in Addis Ababa.
Mr Pate said the patient, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, was stable and responding to treatment.
He said health authorities had identified 44 people who came into contact with the patient and were taking measures to prevent further transmission.
“Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible,” he told the BBC .
The Africa CDC chief’s latest appeal comes amid differing accounts of the patient’s movements before arriving in Nigeria.
Uganda’s Ministry of Health had earlier described the patient as a Nigerian national who travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for business and only passed through Uganda while returning home.
Ugandan authorities maintained that the country had no active confirmed Ebola cases and that the woman’s transit through Uganda did not establish that she contracted the virus there.
Mr Pate said Nigerian authorities were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the patient’s complete travel history and determine where she might have contracted the infection.
“We respect our sister nation of Uganda,” he said. “We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together.”
Nigeria’s case comes amid a continuing Ebola outbreak in the DRC and recent cases in other countries.
According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the DRC had recorded 9,552 confirmed cases and 4,602 related deaths as of 19 October, based on data available up to 18 October. The outbreak has affected eight provinces.
Kenya had also reported nine confirmed cases, including one death, as of 20 October, following an imported case involving a person who had travelled from the DRC through Uganda.
Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus between May and June. 15 of the cases were imported from the DRC, while five were locally acquired among contacts and health workers linked to the imported cases. In August, the World Health Organisation (WHO) declared the outbreak in Uganda over after 42 days without a new confirmed case.
WHO has also urged Nigerians to remain calm, saying that one imported case does not by itself mean Nigeria is experiencing an Ebola outbreak.
WHO Regional Director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the organisation is supporting Nigeria with case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, and protection of health workers and communities.
Nike Adebowale covers the health beat. She holds a degree from Ekiti State University, Ado Ekiti. Twitter : @nikeadebowale1

title: Zelensky Did Not Expect Russia to Launch Full-Scale Invasion
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he did not believe Russia would launch a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, explaining that the absence of preventive sanctions and other measures by Kyiv’s partners had shaped his assessment before the attack.
Speaking on The Diary of a CEO, Zelensky recalled the moment he learned Russian troops had crossed the border on Feb. 24, 2022, and described his visit to Bucha after its liberation as the hardest day of the war.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I didn’t think there would be a full-scale invasion,” Zelensky said. He questioned why partners had not taken stronger preventive action if they knew an invasion was coming.
Zelensky said he was with his family when a call from his office brought news that Russian forces were crossing the border and missiles were approaching.
“I got ready and told my wife and children that the war had begun,” he said.
Asked about the most difficult day he had experienced during the war, Zelensky recalled traveling to Bucha, outside Kyiv, after Ukrainian forces regained control of the town.
He described seeing the bodies of children, adults, and elderly people, some with their hands bound and evidence of torture. Others had been buried in pits.
Ukrainian authorities have started to exhume the bodies found in a mass grave in Bucha, to identify each of the victims pic.twitter.com/wuyQb7oyhW
“If such a mass grave were found today in the US or Britain, God forbid, containing 500 tortured people. How could anyone forgive that?” Zelensky asked.
Bucha became a symbol of atrocities committed during Russia’s occupation of areas around Kyiv in the opening weeks of the invasion.
After Russian troops withdrew, journalists documented civilian bodies lying in streets and shallow graves, including victims with bound limbs and apparent execution wounds.
On Feb. 25, 2022, Russian forces broke through Ukrainian defenses and advanced on the city of Bucha accompanied by overwhelming artillery bombardment which destroyed much of Bucha’s infrastructure.
Fighting continued for two more weeks before Moscow declared it had gained complete control of the city on March 12. A Ukrainian counteroffensive was then mounted and by March 29 Ukrainian forces regained control of the city.
At the time, Ukrainian authorities found bodies laying in the streets with mass graves being discovered in parks and wooded areas around the city.
The number of those killed was given to Ukrainian authorities at the end of 2024.
The records showed that 554 civilians for the city had been killed, and another 636 from the surrounding areas, all died from violent shootings, torture, or artillery strikes.
At least 43 bodies currently remain unidentified, with more than 38 more civilians still unaccounted for, of which more than 30 are suspected of being held in Russia.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Senate Orders Probe Of Tansian University Over Alleged Regulatory Violations
body: The Senate has ordered an immediate investigation into the operations and management of Tansian University, Umunya, Anambra State, over allegations of administrative excesses and concerns about the institution’s compliance with the NUC regulatory requirements. The directive followed a motion raised by Sen. Victor Umeh, who questioned the university’s alleged disregard for established regulatory procedures, particularly in the appointment and dismissal of personnel. President of the Senate, Sen. Godswill Akpabio, directed the relevant committee to investigate the circumstances surrounding the university’s operations and report its findings to the Senate. Senate President, who harped on the need to strengthen the regulatory authority of the National Universities Commission, NUC, to ensure that both public and private universities operate within the confines of the law, further noted that the National Assembly has an oversight responsibility to support the Commission in enforcing standards across the university system. The Senate President added that where an institution is found to have violated the law, the National Assembly could recommend appropriate action to the President, including the proscription of such a university. The investigation comes as the Senate considers an executive bill seeking to repeal the National Universities Commission Act 2026 and establish a more comprehensive legal framework for regulating university education in Nigeria. The bill, read by the Senate Chief Whip, Senator Tahir Munguno, seeks to strengthen the NUC’s enforcement powers, update minimum academic standards, improve accreditation processes and ensure that Nigerian universities meet global best practices. It also proposes appropriate sanctions for regulatory violations and reinforces the Commission’s position as the apex body responsible for academic programme accreditation. Lawmakers again argued that a stronger regulatory framework is necessary to improve quality assurance, promote research and innovation, and ensure that Nigerian universities remain competitive internationally. The Senate has referred the investigation into Tansian University to the Senate committee on tertiary education and TETFund, to report back within two weeks as the NUC bill scales second reading. The post Senate Orders Probe Of Tansian University Over Alleged Regulatory Violations appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Africa faces ‘complex’ Ebola outbreak after virus spread to Nigeria – WHO
body: The World Health Organization’s Africa chief warned on Thursday that the continent now faced a “complex” Ebola outbreak after the virus crossed from east Africa to Nigeria, which has reported the first case in the west of the continent. “We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape. Nigeria has confirmed an imported case of Ebola virus disease,” Mohamed Janabi, the regional director for WHO in Africa, told an online media briefing. Nigeria on Tuesday announced an imported case of the Bundibugyo strain behind a major DR Congo outbreak, in a woman, a diplomat who had a history of travel to Uganda. The continent’s most populous nation is the fourth African country affected by the outbreak, which this week came to span the continent, with Kenya in the east reporting nine cases since October 6. The case reignited memories of a widespread outbreak in 2014 that struck several countries in the region and killed more than 11,000 people across west Africa between late 2013 and 2016. Nigeria’s experience in successfully containing the Ebola outbreak in 2014 raised confidence that the country can respond effectively to new public health threats. The DRC’s Ebola epidemic has become the deadliest in the country’s history, killing 4,381 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since mid-May, according to the health authorities. The post Africa faces ‘complex’ Ebola outbreak after virus spread to Nigeria – WHO appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russia, US football authorities discuss holding friendly international match
body:
KRASNOYARSK, October 22. /TASS/. The Russian Football Union (RFU) is in talks with the United States Soccer Federation (USSF) about the possibility of organizing a friendly match between the national teams, RFU Secretary General Maxim Mitrofanov told TASS on Thursday.
