Also Read: 20/04/2026 – Georgia in Freedom House Report Among Six New Countries Using ‘Tactics of Transnational Repression’ 09/07/2025 – Activist Jailed for Five Days Over “Insult” in Facebook Comment 14/07/2026 – Court Fines Formula TV GEL 10,000 Over Report on Pro-Government Film Director Goga Khaindrava 09/07/2025 – Activist Jailed for Five Days Over “Insult” in Facebook Comment 12/04/2024 – Freedom House: Georgia on its Way to Becoming Semi-Consolidated Authoritarian Regime

title: Russia-Europe energy cooperation will always continue — Novatek CEO
body:
ISTANBUL, October 22. /TASS/. Energy cooperation between Russia and Europe cannot come to an end and will always exist in one form or another, Novatek CEO Leonid Mikhelson told reporters on the sidelines of the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum.
"I believe it cannot come to an end. It will always exist in one form or another," Mikhelson said.
Earlier at the forum, the Novatek CEO said that it was impossible to exclude Russian LNG volumes from the global supply-demand balance. "Most likely, if the EU’s decision to stop Russian supplies [from January 1, 2027 - TASS] remains in force, the situation will only worsen. LNG production facilities around the world are currently operating at full capacity," he noted.
Mikhelson also pointed out that global energy agencies’ forecasts for gas demand growth could only be revised upward due to rising energy consumption by data centers.

title: Ukraine Reports Record Russian War Losses in a Day
body:
Attacking Kremlin troops suffered record-breaking single-day losses for the entire Russo-Ukrainian War, two Ukrainian military sources said on Thursday.
During the 24-hour period between Oct. 21-22, Russian forces suffered at least 2,250 men killed or seriously wounded in combat across the war’s 1,000-1,250 km (about 600-800 miles) fighting front, according to morning figures published by Ukraine’s General Staff.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The numbers broke the previous wartime record of 2,200 set in December 2024, and exceeded the most recent record-setting day for casualties – Oct. 18, 2026 – by at least 150 men, General Staff records showed.
Russia does not publish casualty figures from combat in Ukraine, but its state information outlets insist Russian assaults are successful and suffer moderate but acceptable casualties, while accusing Ukraine of inflating claimed kill counts. Practically all units in the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) say their estimates of Russian losses are accurate because engagements and images of dead and wounded Russian soldiers are recorded in real time by drones. Some but not all of that content is made public.
The commander of Ukraine’s drone forces, Maj. Robert Brovdi, in a Thursday statement announced his pilots and maintainers had, over the same 24-hour period, “eliminated” 680 Russian soldiers in strikes with first-person view (FPV) and bomber drones, a single-day wartime record for the country’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF).
The record Kremlin losses were likely the result of heavy Russian infantry attacks in the eastern Donetsk region aiming to break into the fortress city of Dobropillya, according to Ukrainian milbloggers.
According to statements published by the overall command headquarters in that sector, Ukraine’s 1st Army Corps “Azov,” the preferred Russian assault tactic has been to send small groups of infantrymen into open fields on foot to infiltrate Ukrainian positions and dig in.
Dense Ukrainian observation and strike drone coverage of fields, woodlines and villages into which the Russian foot soldiers have been attempting to advance has at times eviscerated Russian assault units, said Ihor Oboliensky, commander of Ukraine’s 2nd Army Corps “Khartiia,” in a Thursday statement.“We are neutralizing the enemy’s numerical superiority and conducting meticulously planned operations that strengthen the front line,” Oboliensky said, citing observations of his troops deployed to the northeastern Kharkiv region and southern Kherson region.
“Over the past few days, the enemy has suffered record losses in manpower; in some sectors, irreversible losses have reached as high as 74 percent. This is the price the Russian Federation is paying for the war it launched against Ukraine,” he added.
Ukrainian milblogger Vasyl Pekhno, in a Thursday analysis , estimated that Russian total combat losses for October 2026 had reached 35,950 soldiers and were on track to approach or exceed 50,000 permanent losses – a figure exceeding Russia’s capacity to recruit or conscript new soldiers to replace them.
Ukraine’s military, thanks to its powerful drone forces, is holding its defensive lines well and conducting effective counterattacks. But those successes, Pekhno said, come from strong USF drone support for conventional formations along the front. He called on Ukraine’s military to beef up its frontline infantry and tank units with more drones and pilots, so that USF-run unmanned aircraft strikes can hit deeper behind Russian lines.
“Our military needs to undergo further transformation: the USF should be conducting deeper operations – hunting down enemy pilots, striking logistics, and so on – rather than chasing after individual ‘f*ckers’ [low-level targets],” Pekhno wrote.
“That task should fall to the line brigades. Yet, it is currently quite clear that not all brigades are fully prepared to take complete responsibility for the sector of the front entrusted to them. Consequently, the USF is stepping in to cover the gap,” he added.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday claimed , inaccurately, that AFU forces are unable to stop Russian attacks and that Russian manpower reserves are effectively bottomless. According to the US leader, Ukraine’s attempts to defend itself are futile.
Speaking to reporters in Oslo on Monday, President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected the idea that Ukraine is losing the war to Russia and said his government was looking for a ceasefire to reduce Ukrainian citizen deaths and injuries, and to allow his country to move towards reconstruction.
Effective Ukrainian combat operations are shutting down Russian attacks and inflicting heavy casualties, directly assisting him in peace talks, he said.
“Of course, we are not losing this war. But we are losing people. Because of the Russian attacks, we’re losing people and time,” Zelensky said.
“It’s such a pity, because our children don’t have a real life and childhood. Not only children, but all people. That’s why we need to end this war as quickly as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us,” he continued.
“God bless, our strong soldiers stay strong on the battlefield. It helps me stay strong during any kind of negotiations.”
Stefan Korshak is the Kyiv Post Senior Defense Correspondent. He is from Houston Texas, is a Yalie and since the mid-1990s has worked as correspondent/photographer for newswire, newspapers, television and radio. He has reported from five wars but most enjoys doing articles on wildlife and nature. You can read his weekly blog on the Russo-Ukraine War on Facebook, Substack and Medium. His new book on the 2022 Siege of Mariupol is available on Amazon UK and Amazon US .

title: NAPharm Proposes 10-point Plan to Strengthen Ebola Preparedness
body: Uchechukwu Nnaike The Nigeria Academy of Pharmacy (NAPharm), has called on the federal government to strengthen Nigeria’s preparedness for Ebola Virus Disease and other emerging infectious diseases through a coordinated national epidemic-readiness framework. The academy said preparedness measures should be institutionalised, regularly assessed and made functional across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. In a statement signed by the President and Chairman of the Governing Council, Prof. Lere Baale, the academy said the country must move beyond outbreak awareness to measurable national readiness. The call follows the academy’s policy report titled ‘From Awareness to Readiness: Strengthening Nigeria’s Preparedness for Ebola and Emerging Infectious Disease Emergencies’. The report draws on discussions at its national webinar on Ebola Preparedness held on August 20, 2026, and the work of its multidisciplinary Task Group on Ebola Virus Disease Resurgence, chaired by Prof. Fola Tayo. Baale stated that Nigeria’s success in containing Ebola in 2014 should serve as a foundation for stronger preparedness rather than a reason for complacency. “Nigeria demonstrated extraordinary leadership, professional competence and national coordination in containing Ebola in 2014. However, yesterday’s success does not automatically guarantee tomorrow’s preparedness. “Our responsibility is to ensure that the capabilities that protected Nigeria in 2014 are institutionalised, continuously strengthened and demonstrably functional across the country,” he said. The stressed that epidemic preparedness should no longer be treated as an emergency intervention activated only when an outbreak threatens the country. It proposed a continuous national system built around seven interconnected capabilities: anticipate, prevent, detect, respond, recover, learn and improve. It added that the approach would strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to manage Ebola, Lassa fever, cholera and other emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. It commended the federal government, Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention for existing preparedness measures, including surveillance, laboratory readiness, infection prevention and control, point-of-entry monitoring, intergovernmental coordination and public communication. It however said that further action is needed to ensure that existing systems remain functional and effective. The academy outlined10 priority actions for urgent policy consideration and implementation: Nationwide epidemic-readiness audit; mandatory epidemic simulation exercises; community pharmacy surveillance integration; diagnostic and laboratory turnaround standards; strategic emergency health-commodity reserves. Others are: multidisciplinary epidemic-readiness teams; healthcare worker protection framework; risk communication and misinformation management; survivor rehabilitation and reintegration; and annual national epidemic preparedness scorecard. It identified community pharmacies as an important component of Nigeria’s proposed early-warning system for infectious disease threats, adding that community pharmacists are often among the first healthcare professionals consulted by people experiencing fever, weakness and other symptoms that may resemble common infections. “Under the proposed NCDC–PCN–NAPHARM Community Pharmacy Sentinel Surveillance Pilot, participating pharmacists would receive appropriate case definitions, surveillance protocols, referral pathways and reporting procedures,” it said. The academy noted that the initiative would not authorise pharmacists to diagnose Ebola, but would strengthen their role in recognising possible warning signs and notifying the appropriate public health authorities. It summarised the proposed approach as: “Recognise. Protect. Refer. Report.” The academy also stressed the need to protect healthcare workers to sustain an effective epidemic response. It added that doctors, pharmacists, nurses, medical laboratory professionals, community health practitioners, rehabilitation professionals and other frontline personnel should receive continuous preparedness training, appropriate protective equipment and institutional support. According to the academy, effective preparedness requires collaboration across professional boundaries and healthcare institutions. It therefore recommended multidisciplinary readiness teams, coordinated training and periodic simulation exercises reflecting real-life outbreak scenarios. Beyond the 10 priority actions, the academy proposed an immediate 90-day implementation framework to support government consideration. The proposed activities include a national functional-readiness audit, laboratory referral mapping, an inventory of emergency health commodities, a community pharmacy surveillance pilot, healthcare worker preparedness programmes and the development of a national epidemic-readiness scorecard. Longer-term recommendations include preparedness education, stronger surveillance networks, improved supply chain visibility, One Health collaboration and annual public reporting on epidemic readiness. The academy said that preparedness funding should be tied to measurable outcomes, verified operational capabilities and corrective action rather than procurement alone. It expressed readiness to collaborate with the NCDC, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, state health authorities, professional regulatory bodies, healthcare associations, academic institutions, pharmaceutical manufacturers, development partners and community organisations. It added that the proposed collaboration would support surveillance, pharmaceutical supply security, professional training, public communication, policy research and preparedness measurement without duplicating the statutory responsibilities of existing public health institutions. The academy urged Nigerians to remain vigilant without panic, rely on verified public health information, disclose relevant travel and exposure histories to healthcare professionals, seek medical attention promptly and avoid spreading rumours or stigmatising suspected patients. It said that public trust, responsible communication and community cooperation are essential to successful epidemic preparedness. Baale said Nigeria must translate its experience in containing Ebola in 2014 into lasting institutional capacity. “Our greatest tribute to the healthcare professionals and institutions that protected Nigeria in 2014 is to build a stronger, more resilient and permanently prepared healthcare system. We must not wait for the first imported case to discover whether our surveillance systems, laboratories, emergency supplies, healthcare workforce, and response structures are ready,” he said. “Preparedness is not panic. Preparedness is foresight, competence, coordination and national responsibility. Above all, preparedness saves lives.” The academy reaffirmed its commitment to advancing pharmaceutical sciences, strengthening interprofessional collaboration, supporting evidence-based public health policy and contributing to a more resilient Nigerian healthcare system.

title: IMI Media Academy and Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation to prepare 29,000 young people for careers
body: IMI Media Academy and the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation have announced a five-year partnership to develop Arab media talent, aiming to reach 29,000 young people and train them for careers in the field. Under Al Ghurair Voice Lab, the partnership will connect education and skills development with practical experience and professional opportunities. It will also help create pathways into the media sector by offering access to internships, placements, employment opportunities and other forms of professional development. Seven connected programmes will cover the foundational media skills, advanced professional upskilling, university curriculum integration, storytelling for school pupils, national youth initiatives and regional programming across the Arab region. These will provide young people with technical and professional skills, practical learning, mentorship and direct exposure to media professionals and workplaces. The agreement was signed by Ali Al Hammadi, chief operating officer at IMI, and Dr Sonia Ben Jaafar, chief executive of AGF, in the presence of Dr Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and chairman of IMI, and Abdul Aziz Al Ghurair, chairman of AGF’s board. The partnership comes as rapid changes in technology, audience behaviour and media production reshape the skills required across the industry. It brings together IMI Media Academy’s industry expertise, professional training capabilities and access to a media ecosystem with AGF’s regional experience in education and youth empowerment and its learning-to-earning approach, connecting skills development with pathways to meaningful professional opportunities. The partnership builds on the organisations’ existing collaboration through the Nomu Al Ghurair Siraj programme, which has equipped 450 graduates with future-ready media skills and provided opportunities to engage directly with the media industry. The five-year plan expands that work in scale and ambition, with a greater focus on connecting learning to tangible professional opportunities. “Media has an important role in how our region sees itself and how others see us. That makes investing in the people who will shape its future especially important,” Dr Ben Jaafar said. “Young people will have the chance to learn within a real media environment, develop their skills alongside professionals and see a clearer route into the industry. We want young people across the Arab region to have the skills, the access and the space to contribute their perspectives and tell the stories of their communities.” Khalid Al Hosani, director of operations at IMI Media Academy, said: “This partnership is about building a stronger pipeline of Arab media talent – not simply delivering training. By connecting education directly with practical experience, mentorship and professional opportunities, we will help thousands of young people move from learning about the media industry to actively contributing to it. Our ambition is to create a model that delivers measurable outcomes in the UAE and can be expanded across the region.” Chantal Saliba, director of media and training at IMI Media Academy, said: “Media cannot be learnt from a classroom alone. Young people need the opportunity to work with experienced professionals, understand how newsrooms and creative teams operate, and develop their own voices through practice. This partnership will give them that exposure – helping them build not only the technical skills required by today’s industry, but also the judgment, confidence and curiosity needed to shape its future.” The partnership will launch in the UAE and is expected to expand across the region over the five-year period. AGF and IMI Media Academy aim to strengthen the pipeline of skilled Arab media professionals and create clearer pathways for young people to move from education and training into the industry.

title: B.C. NDP Leader Eby campaigns in Vancouver, while Tories heads to Surrey
body:
British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby campaigns in Vancouver and Richmond Thursday after wrapping his swing through the vote-rich city of Surrey with a rally.
Hundreds of people attended the gathering near City Hall on Wednesday.
Eby made six stops in the Surrey-Delta area throughout the day to meet with seniors and visit a trucking company.
Meanwhile, interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is set to make an announcement in B.C.’s second-largest city, where 10 ridings are up for grabs.
He’s also expected to hold a rally in Surrey later tonight.
Advance voting also wrapped up on Wednesday, ahead of Saturday’s election.

title: Abu Dhabi currently considered as venue for Russia-US-Ukraine meeting — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Abu Dhabi is now being considered as a venue for trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"At this point, we are talking about Abu Dhabi," Peskov said, when asked whether the UAE capital was being considered as the main venue for trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine.
"Wait, you are getting ahead of yourself, do not do that," the Kremlin spokesman said, when asked to comment on whether Russia’s negotiating team was preparing any written documents or proposals.

title: NITDA DG to Media: Deploy AI for fact-checking, not replacing journalists
body: The Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, has urged media organisations to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) to verify information and strengthen public trust. Abdullahi spoke on Thursday at the official unveiling of the Media Trust Group’s converged newsroom, where he emphasised the need for ethical and responsible use of AI in journalism. He said the greatest contribution of AI to newsrooms should not be the speed of breaking news but its ability to help journalists authenticate information and combat the growing difficulty of distinguishing genuine content from fabricated material. “We should make sure we are not using AI to replace people. AI is a tool that can enhance what we do. Therefore, for us, the greatest contribution AI can give to the newsroom is not generating faster breaking news, but helping people believe what they see,” he said. The NITDA director-general noted that advances in AI had made it increasingly difficult for members of the public to determine the authenticity of images, videos and other digital content. He said manipulated content could make people appear to say or do things they had never said or done, creating challenges for journalists and media organisations seeking to provide credible information. “Today, it is difficult to believe anything you see. People can take anybody’s picture to get him speaking or doing things, which makes it difficult for people to believe what they see,” he said. Abdullahi urged journalists to make verification a priority before publishing or amplifying information, noting that the media had a critical role to play in helping the public navigate the growing volume of digital content. “What people are looking for from people like you in the media, journalists, is to make sure you authenticate everything before amplifying it,” he said. He expressed confidence that the Media Trust Group would deploy AI tools to improve verification, clarify information and strengthen the credibility of its news reports. “I believe you are going to use AI in your newsroom for clarification, for amplifying authenticity, and for letting people trust what they see,” he said.

title: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as conflict flares
body:
Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.
He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.
Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.
Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said that a wary Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it has learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. In recent days, Tehran has indicated that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran still promotes its latest proposal that would end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions. Those conditions, which include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, echo ones in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.
In late September, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected that seven-day proposal, but both sides have acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.
A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.
Now the landscape of the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.
The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.
The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.

title: Claude did not invent scorpion antivenom
body:
An investment research firm wanted to prove AI could revolutionize drug development. So they teamed up with Anthropic to see whether an unreleased version of Claude could make scorpion antivenom. It couldn’t. It came up with some promising starting points, but nothing close to an actual drug, experts tell The Verge.
Citrini Research, the firm behind the experiment, admitted that “none of us could claim to know anything about AI as it related to biology.” That didn’t stop it from trying to make a drug from scratch — or publishing a blog post titled “We Wanted to Use Claude to Create a New Drug. Here’s What Happened.” The account came complete with rhetorical questions like “Why don’t we try to use AI to create a new drug?”, a blow-by-blow account of its amateurish scientific adventures, and a quote from Charles Darwin.
If the name Citrini sounds familiar, that’s because the firm was behind a widely circulated piece of fiction imagining an AI-induced economic catastrophe that gained traction on social media and rattled real-world markets. It also claims to have visited the Strait of Hormuz in April to get a firsthand perspective on what was happening in the volatile region.
For its latest venture, Citrini enlisted the help of Anthropic, which, mere weeks out from its hotly anticipated IPO, has a few reasons to talk up AI’s potential in drug development and the life sciences — two areas it’s actively pursuing.
The collaboration came about after Citrini ran into Claude’s biosecurity guardrails while trying to get the model to research drug candidates. The post’s author said they “spam called anyone in my contact list who worked at an AI lab,” eventually finding a willing partner in Anthropic. The AI lab agreed to drop the restrictions and give the team access to a more advanced, unreleased model on the condition that they work from its offices. “Luckily,” Anthropic also agreed to foot the hefty compute and token bill, which came just shy of $50,000.
After weighing a few options, the team settled on scorpion antivenom, a costly treatment that can be difficult to produce, often involving injecting venom into horses. The goal was to use Claude to design proteins that could bind to the toxins in scorpion venom. Armed with a 35-page prompt, they set the AI to work, unleashing some 300 subagents to discover suitable proteins.
In its own more sober account of the experiment, Anthropic said Claude generated nearly 320,000 candidates, whittling them down to 180 designs after discarding those that resembled known toxins or existing proteins. The entire process took 64 hours. Anthropic said the team worked “with Claude” to add another 31 designs, bringing the total to 211.
Citrini then sent the designs to two outside laboratories — Swiss biotech company Adaptyv Bio and US-based Twist Biosciences — to test whether the proteins could actually bind to their intended targets, a key step for developing an effective antivenom. That cost another $150,000, give or take. It’s unclear why Anthropic could not have conducted these tests in-house at its biology wet lab in California. Seventeen of the proteins passed muster, collectively binding to four of the five scorpion toxins the team had hoped to target. Not one of the proteins bound to more than a single toxin, Citrini said.
Even if they had, Citrini would still be a very long way from a working antivenom. Binding to a toxin does not mean a protein can actually neutralize it, let alone function as a safe and effective treatment. Citrini acknowledges this itself, noting that “no experiment has yet tested whether they actually stopped the toxin working.”
In other words, the experiment had not succeeded. Citrini set out to make a new drug, but experts tell The Verge it had only accomplished the relatively “easy” part of the process. “It is easy-ish to discover a good binder against snake and scorpion toxins,” said Andreas Hougaard Laustsen-Kiel, a professor of antibody technologies at the Technical University of Denmark. “The hard part is to translate it into a medicine.”
Melisa Benard Valle, an assistant professor, and Anne Ljungars, a senior researcher, both at the Technical University of Denmark, agreed. “The results are technically promising, but some of the excitement is premature,” they wrote in a joint email, describing the findings as “far from a medicine and hyped.” Much remains unknown about the proteins Claude designed, they said, including their safety, stability, how they behave in the body, and whether they can be developed into viable treatments. “Translating these binders into an actual medicine is likely still a long and challenging process.”
The most novel aspect of Citrini’s experiment, they said, was the “autonomous discovery process rather than the biological results.” AI has huge potential to accelerate discovery, they added, but warned “turning promising molecules into effective medicines remains a much greater challenge.”
Nor is the underlying approach particularly new. Andreas Bender, a professor of machine learning in medicine at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, told The Verge existing methods like high-throughput screening “are often able to find a multitude of hits at manageable cost,” even without any AI. Designing proteins that bind to targets is “kind of” a solved problem, said Bender, who is also a visiting professor at the University of Cambridge. The much harder challenge is turning those results into treatments that actually work in living systems. “It’s exactly this translation that lacks.”
While it failed to make a drug, Citrini declared the experiment a success of sorts. The firm argued it offers a glimpse into the investment opportunities emerging in the upcoming era of AI-enabled drug discovery. As for why it didn’t bother to take the research further? Citrini accused critics of “nitpick[ing]” and added, “Not to beat a dead horse, but we are an investment research firm - not a biotech startup.” Citrini and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.
But it still made a bullish case for companies that might benefit. Naturally, the specifics were reserved for paying subscribers, though Bloomberg reports the firm highlighted companies involved in the testing side of drug development, including Charles River Laboratories, which supplies primates for animal research. In a video discussing the experiment, Citrini described the AI portion as “free,” conveniently overlooking the tab picked up by Anthropic.

title: As the Kremlin Seizes Control of European Companies, U.S. Rivals Remain Largely Spared
body:
Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing U.S. firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russia n officials and U.S. businesspeople said.
Of the 20 foreign-owned firms President Vladimir Putin has placed under temporary administration since U.S. President Donald Trump's inauguration in January 2025, only three were linked to the United States, with the rest controlled by European companies, a Reuters analysis of official data shows.
A person close to Russia n financial regulators said that it is not in Moscow's interest to take a tough line on American companies while business negotiations with Washington are underway.
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for talks aimed at resolving the war in Ukraine. Russia n news agencies reported that Putin told Witkoff he was interested in restoring economic ties with the United States.
Ukraine and its allies have voiced concerns that the U.S. is backing away from its support of Kyiv, and Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russia n oil refineries even as European leaders have lined up behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russia , citing Europe's wartime support for Ukraine and involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities," has taken control of the local units of Swiss food group Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro since last month.
Last week, the Kremlin seized control of the local assets of four smaller companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russia n property."
Nestle, which said in September it would take steps to protect its rights in Russia , declined to comment further. The other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs said that the available information supported the perception that more European than U.S. firms were being targeted.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Commenting on the report after its publication, the Kremlin said that U.S. companies were better treated than their European rivals because of Trump's efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine.
"The American administration is doing a lot to help bring about a peaceful settlement. The European capitals are doing nothing to help while doing a lot to prolong the military action," Peskov told reporters.
Russia 's relations with the Trump administration, meanwhile, have warmed. The U.S. announced a deal this month to buy Russia n diesel, and other deals, including those on gas, have been discussed at meetings in recent months.
Trump also signed an executive order on Saturday waiving key sanctions and tariffs on Russia n goods.
Russia n negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, a U.S.-educated investment banker who heads the Russia n Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and has pushed in talks for the return and expansion of American firms, hailed the move as a "historic moment."
Trump's envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner have used the prospect of multibillion-dollar deals with Russia as an incentive to push Putin toward a peaceful settlement since the start of peace talks in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in February 2025.
Dmitriev said last week that Russia and the U.S. would soon announce new joint initiatives that could move ahead before the war ends. The U.S. has previously signaled that deals are unlikely while the conflict continues.
One person familiar with the situation said that some Russia n officials who do not support peace efforts could still push for the Kremlin to seize more American firms.
The RDIF's only current partnership with a U.S. company is a joint investment with New York-listed Titan International in a tire factory in Volgograd.
Another person familiar with the situation said Dmitriev has in private highlighted this as an example of a thriving U.S. business in Russia .
Titan did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump's commitment to economic cooperation with Russia and ongoing talks have helped protect the interests of American companies, two U.S. businesspeople in Moscow said.
American Chamber of Commerce Russia President Robert Agee said in December last year that European firms in Russia were less optimistic than American ones, citing European foreign policy. The chamber estimates there are around 300 U.S. firms remaining in Russia .
"We have Trump, and they don't, and our hopes are linked to him," Agee told Russia n media last year. Agee and the chamber declined to comment further for this story.
Russia did target some mid-sized U.S. firms during its property redistribution drive after the start of the war. One report estimated that the Kremlin seized more than $50 billion worth of private property from both Russia n and foreign owners.
The European Commission in Brussels declined to comment on the number of EU firms being targeted relative to U.S. ones, but said the recent asset seizures were without due process and amounted to "forced expropriation in all but name."
"This follows a clear pattern of economic retaliation," a Commission spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the moves showed " Russia is not a safe environment for business."
"The EU has measures in place to respond. We can sanction those profiting from forced expropriations," the spokesperson added.
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help .
