By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.

title: Kazakhstan Expands Middle Corridor Fleet as Caspian Sea Levels Fall
body: Containers are piling up on Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast as they await shipment to Azerbaijan. A shortage of vessels and weather-related restrictions are delaying cargo along the Middle Corridor, a trade route connecting China and Europe while bypassing Russia. Kazakhstan plans to acquire five vessels and has ordered another six to expand maritime freight capacity. At the same time, falling Caspian Sea levels are limiting how much cargo existing ships can carry and complicating port operations. Yerkin Nygmetov, CEO of KTZ Express Shipping, described the container backlog at the New Silk Way international transport forum , held in Astana on October 15–16. According to Nygmetov, adverse weather conditions can restrict operations at Kazakhstan’s ports for a total of up to 75 days a year. Freight Volumes Rise as Vessels Face Delays The Middle Corridor, officially known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, runs through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. From there, cargo continues to Turkey and Europe, including via the Black Sea. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the route attracted increased interest from companies seeking to reduce their dependence on transit through Russia. According to Kazakhstan’s national railway company, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), container traffic along the Middle Corridor reached 44,200 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in January–August 2026, an increase of 58% from a year earlier. A TEU is a standard measure of container capacity equivalent to one 20-foot container, approximately six meters long. During the same period, 419 container trains departed China along the route, compared with 228 a year earlier. The maritime section requires containers to be transferred from trains onto vessels in Kazakhstan and then back onto railcars in Azerbaijan. Waiting for an available ship increases delivery times, particularly during periods of heavy cargo arrivals. The World Bank has assessed the corridor’s potential for growth. According to a study published in September, investments in transport infrastructure and better coordination of logistics procedures could more than triple trade volumes along the Trans-Caspian Corridor by 2040 and cut delivery times in half. The bank also projects that implementing the proposed measures could increase the combined GDP of nine countries connected to the route by 3.3% and create two million jobs. Kazakhstan Orders Vessels from China and Azerbaijan KTZ Express Shipping, a subsidiary of KTZ, plans to acquire five container vessels in 2026. Another six multipurpose dry cargo and container ships have been ordered from shipyards in China and Azerbaijan. By 2028, the company aims to expand its own fleet to 13 vessels with a combined deadweight tonnage of 96,000 metric tons. Deadweight tonnage refers to the maximum weight a vessel can carry, including cargo, fuel, supplies, and other variable loads. On October 15, Kazakhstan’s Samruk-Kazyna sovereign wealth fund confirmed that two dry cargo vessels would be built at the Baku Shipyard under contracts signed in April 2026. Another four vessels have been ordered from China’s Jiangsu Haizhongzhou Shipping Industry. Each is designed to carry up to 537 TEUs, with a deadweight tonnage of 9,900 metric tons. The river-sea vessels are intended for operations on the Caspian Sea and inland waterways. The company is also considering deploying its own fleet on Black Sea routes. Kazakhstan aims to increase annual container traffic along the Middle Corridor to 300,000 TEUs by 2029. KTZ Express Shipping also intends to charter vessels from Azerbaijani partners if necessary. Kazmortransflot, the national shipping company within the KazMunayGas group, is also expanding its fleet. Together with AD Ports Group of the United Arab Emirates, it is building two container ships at the Baku Shipyard. Construction of the first vessel began in June 2026, with both ships scheduled for completion by the end of 2027. Each new vessel will have a capacity of 780 TEUs, compared with 350 TEUs for existing container ships serving a similar purpose. Their length will increase from 113 to 149.5 meters, while deadweight tonnage will rise from approximately 5,200 to 9,400 metric tons. Carrying larger shipments on each voyage could reduce costs per container, provided the vessels operate with sufficient loads. Falling Caspian Sea Levels Limit Vessel Loads The declining water level of the Caspian Sea is reducing depths at berths and in approach channels. Shipowners must account for vessel draft when selecting routes and determining how much cargo to load. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has noted that falling water levels have already restricted vessel loading at Kazakhstan’s Aktau and Kuryk ports, increasing costs for freight operators. In September, a representative of the Azerbaijan Caspian Shipping Company reported that one of its ferries could carry only about 80% of its full load from Kazakhstan because of falling water levels. Transporting the same volume of cargo therefore requires more voyages. Dredging work has been carried out at Kuryk, while modernization of port infrastructure continues at Aktau. As The Times of Central Asia previously reported , the combined cost of several projects to deepen channels and reconstruct Kazakhstan’s ports is estimated at approximately $179 million. Ports Prepare for Higher Freight Volumes The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), together with the European Union, has announced a financing package of up to €45 million for the modernization of Aktau port. The project includes expanding container-handling capacity, upgrading berths, and purchasing cargo-handling equipment. Average container-handling time is expected to fall from four minutes to two and a half minutes. In October, transport companies from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and China said they had introduced a unified schedule for container trains and automated exchanges of cargo information. These measures are intended to reduce delays when transferring containers between rail and maritime services. Kazakhstan is ordering larger vessels in anticipation of growing transit traffic between China and Europe. But the Caspian Sea is getting shallower, and existing ferries are already having to sail with reduced loads. Even the newer vessels, designed for shallower waters, will face constraints if the sea continues to retreat.

title: London’s prime properties take a 10% hit but new super homes emerge
body: Sellers of properties in prime London postcodes were forced to accept discounts of 10.1 per cent in September, as overall sale prices fell by 7.1 per cent compared with a year earlier. The number of sales was the lowest in any September since 2016, according to property analysts LonRes, with 16.8 per cent fewer transactions than September 2025 and 13.9 per cent fewer than the 2017-20129 pre-pandemic average. There was slightly better news for properties worth more than £5 million , with transactions falling 12.5 per cent but new instructions increasing by 32.5 per cent. Buyers continued to pay well below asking price. Compared with pre-pandemic levels, prices were 8.2 per cent lower in September. For homes above £5 million, there was 0.8 per cent more discounting, but 88.8 per cent above the levels from 2015-24. The founder of London taxi company Addison Lee sold a mansion overlooking London’s Regent’s Park for little more than half the price he paid 13 years ago. John Griffin, who sold his business to the Carlyle Group for about £300 million ($464 million) in 2013, offloaded the property on the park’s western perimeter for £11.5 million at the beginning of October, down from his purchase price of £20.7 million. It had been discounted a number of times over recent years but failed to sell. LonRes said that, in the context of a weaker market, it was important to set a competitive initial asking price “as the longer a home is on the market, the bigger the discount needs to secure a sale”. Between July and September, the average discount for homes selling in under three months was 3.8 per cent, but increased to 11.1 per cent for homes taking six to 12 months to sell. There appears to be movement at the top end of the market, with 32.5 per cent more new £5 million-plus instructions compared with the same month last year, and 63.6 per cent higher than the 2017-2019 average. LonRes said super prime sales continue to be “impacted by news and speculation, resulting in a stop-start market”. Nick Gregori, head of research at LonRes, said: “September typically sees the market pick up after the summer lull, and this year this was partly true. Activity across prime London – from both buyers and sellers – improved relative to the summer but remained sluggish for the time of year. Achieved prices continued to slide downwards, reflecting buyer hesitancy.” He said borrowing costs and a perceived lack of future growth were the two factors driving lower demand, combined with global uncertainty and fears of inflation. He believes there are unlikely to be any giveaways for prime property buyers in Chancellor John Healey’s budget on October 28, “so the best that can be hoped for is no further damaging changes”. Reports that dropping the mansion tax threshold from £2m to £1.5m is not going ahead would probably be welcomed by a market seeking certainty, he said. “The £5 million-plus market continues to be most impacted by uncertainty and weaker sentiment, with a higher proportion of discretionary buyers and sellers meaning less urgency to do deals,” he said. Super properties Knight Frank’s latest Residence Report highlighted the growing scarcity of larger new build apartments, with fewer than 3 per cent of completed homes across Westminster and Kensington & Chelsea exceeding 200 sq m, making super prime residences rare. One of the luxury properties released on to the market in recent weeks is a £15.5 million, 3,100 square foot, four-bedroom duplex penthouse with a private roof terrace at 100 George Street in Marylebone. Developers Native Land said the 41-residence development was one of the fastest-selling in prime central London. The trophy penthouse has been designed by Eloisa Cuturi of design studio Cuturi Cameto. It includes bespoke furniture and commissioned artwork including paintings by Joanne Yulan inspired by the neighbouring Regent’s Park. Nicholas Gray, executive director at Native Land, said: “Opportunities to acquire a newly built home in Marylebone of this calibre, with this quality of interior design and scale of private outdoor space, are exceptionally limited.” Rupert des Forges, head of prime central London developments at Knight Frank, said: “We are seeing sustained demand from buyers for larger, turnkey homes in prime central London.” A £20 million ($26.4 million) penthouse has also gone on sale at Southbank Place , the final launch of a £1 billion development delivered by Braeburn Estates, a joint venture by Qatari Diar and Canary Wharf Group. The development is on the site of the former Festival of Britain, and has taken more than 10 years to complete.

title: Show HN: Whybook, tackling the gap between AI notebooks and human understanding
body:
[?] Whybook, an open-source JupyterLab extension
Whybook is a view of a Jupyter notebook with no chat box. Point at a column, a plot or a value, and pick one of the questions it offers, or type or say your own. Whybook writes and runs the cell, and shows each choice it finds behind the result.
Watch a 4-minute demo, or a whole analysis
Drag IL6 onto the model cell. Or click IL6, then the button that appears on the cell.
IL6 lives in olink: joined on patient_id first.
Runs on pick, no confirmation. Shift+drop always branches. Alt+drop explores in parallel.
Language models now finish well-defined programming tasks that take an engineer hours, and they beat the best students at programming contests. They can also run a complete statistical analysis that experts judge sound in most cases. Software development went through this change first. Engineers now spend more of their time reviewing and fixing code they did not write. Projects that adopted coding agents show more complex code and less stable releases, and developers who hand the coding to an AI assistant understand it less . Data analysis is going through the same change now . Tim Hanewich calls the result the understanding gap : a divide "between what is being produced and our understanding of what was produced". In data analysis the gap opens in four ways.
A chat that is asked to "analyse this data" returns an analysis. It does not build insight and it does not exercise curiosity. The analyst no longer decides what to ask next . Asking a chat is the lowest-effort route. Under pressure , analysts default to it, unless their tools make a question-driven exploration fun and fast.
Generated code carries modelling choices that the analyst never sees. In the demo cohort, a constant in prep.py leaves out 27 of 318 patients, and no cell of the notebook sets it.
Even before language models, analysis code moved from notebooks into modules. A default set in a module does not show in the notebook that uses it.
Models reason before they answer, and the analyst does not read that reasoning. Claude never returns its raw chain of thought, and by default its newest models return not even a summary . A trace that is shown does not always report what the model used.
There is no point in analysing data if no one asked the question.
Mathematics has the same debate: is mathematics about solving problems, or about the understanding gained on the way to the solution? OpenAI's AI-made proof that the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up revived the debate in September 2026. An answer has little value when no one understands why it holds.
Whybook opens any .ipynb file as a second view, in JupyterLab or in Jupyter Notebook 7. Both views share one notebook model and one kernel, so an edit in one shows in the other. Agents do most of the work, under one rule: the result is an ordinary notebook, and the questions, choices and assumptions go into its metadata. The analyst chooses how deep to go on each cell: its question, the choices on its chips, or its code.
Anything in the Variables and Contents panels can be dragged onto a cell, a variable or a column, and so can files and database tables. Whybook lists up to 12 ranked questions of five types , each with a place in the notebook.
Questions from templates show at once, and most of them run code with no model call: a template is code written in advance, with the selected names filled in. For those marked needs AI , an AI writes the code. A connected model adds up to 5 questions of its own a few seconds later. Above the questions, a box takes a question of one's own .
Dragging is optional: in Click mode the analyst clicks the source, then the target, or uses the keyboard. The Wonder, Do and Report modes change which questions rank first: Wonder is for finding what else is in the data, Do for carrying the analysis on, and Report for building what goes into a report.
What the prototype offers when the analyst drags, selects or clicks
After a cell runs, Whybook reads its code against the live kernel and lists the values that the result depends on. Each value becomes a short chip, its name and its value, such as MIN_DAYS 14 , or inner join Ã2 for two merges that keep pandas' default. The colour shows where the value comes from, and the tooltip describes what the value does. Constants defined in imported files are shown on the cell that uses them.
MIN_DAYS = 14 is set in prep.py . It leaves out 27 of 318 patients, and no cell sets it. Drop MIN_DAYS onto cell [4] and Whybook re-runs [4] with 7, 14 and 21 in a branch.
The prototype's output. With 14 or 21 days, 27 of the 318 patients are left out. With 7 days, 11 are.
Every mark of a plot drawn by Whybook's helpers maps to rows of its data frame. A selection on the plot shows how many rows it holds, what differs there, and questions about it. The analyst can keep the selection as a variable and drag it like any other.
Try it: drag across the plot. This is the plot of the demo's cell [4], weekly pain per patient by treatment arm, with bootstrap intervals. The numbers next to the plot are computed from the plot's data the way the prototype computes them.
Drag across the plot to select weeks. Every mark maps to rows of weekly .
A minus B is +1.86 here and +1.33 elsewhere.
Keep selection as a variable: sel_week14_24
The text of a markdown cell shows in each of Whybook's views of the notebook, and it can be questioned like a result. Whybook first lists each number the text states, with the outputs that show it, rounded as the text rounds it. A number that no output shows stands out. Then come the questions, which an agent answers with the cells they need after the text. Words selected in the text are the subject of the questions instead.
Try it: the panel shows the questions about the words "by 0.32 points more per month", marked in the summary. Select other words to question them instead, or press Question this text. This is the summary of the demo after six more hours of analysis, and the matches are the ones the prototype finds in its outputs.
Pain falls over the six months in both arms, faster in arm B, by 0.32 points more per month , and the difference holds without site east and for each value of MIN_DAYS. More patients stop keeping the diary in the first 12 weeks in arm A (26%) than in arm B (9%), so the patients who stay are not a random half of either arm. Of the 4,812 proteins, only NGF tracks how fast pain changes once the false discovery rate is controlled.
Shift+drop turns any question into a branch. Alt+drop starts several branches at once. Whybook calls each one a parallel run: underneath, each branch runs in its own kernel subshell (Jupyter Enhancement Proposal 91, in ipykernel 7), so branches run in parallel on the same data without copying it.
The notebook stays a single list of cells. The Code view shows the cells as the notebook does, branches included. There is no reactive execution: an edit to a cell does not re-run the cells after it.
When a question needs AI and its answer goes into a new cell, an agent answers it in the notebook. It adds and runs the cells that the question needs, reads what each one shows, and compares choices side by side as branches that run in parallel, such as another model or another subset. It ends with an answer of a few sentences that links the cells that show it, and with follow-up questions. When one cell is enough, it writes one, and code too long for a cell goes into a module next to the notebook.
Each cell goes into the notebook as it runs, marked as written by AI, with the choices in its code on chips. Stop ends the run, and one click removes its cells, with an Undo. With the data kept on this machine, the agent reads what local models wrote about each table, and only the kind and size of other outputs, never their values.
A run answered by the screenshot script: the cells ran in the kernel, and the script wrote the steps and the answer.
Whybook shows one notebook in three views. The map draws the cells and the data frames they use as a graph. The bench shows each cell as a card with its title, its chips and its outputs, and Show code opens its code. The Code view shows every cell as the notebook does. Within each view, the Detail slider sets how much of each output shows, down to a tile with its size and a label.
An agent, Whybook's or any other, does not tire after a hundred cells. The analyst still has to understand those cells, and chooses what to understand, and how deeply . The map shows the whole analysis, the bench each step, and the Code view each line. This is the order of Ben Shneiderman's Visual Information-Seeking Mantra : "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand".
In a long notebook, the analyst finds a cell on the map: a double-click on its card shows the cell on the bench. With the setting Minimap on, a minimap in the corner of the bench opens the map again.
Try it: switch between the views, each in a box of the same size, move the Detail slider, and double-click a card on the map.
Does treatment arm B change how pain evolves over the first six months? The data is synthetic, made for the Whybook demo.
Does treatment arm B change how pain evolves over the first six months? The data is synthetic, made for the Whybook demo.
Analysis tools have to be fun to use, or analysts take the lowest-effort route of Â§1. In web design, language models gave people new room to explore, and many of them are happier for it.
Work in progress always has a progress bar. The Exploration panel counts each question by type once its answer has run, apart from those that failed. It also counts guesses: while a cell about a relation or an effect runs, the analyst can say with one click what they expect, such as higher or lower. The panel fills a square for each column, Series or array that the analysis has used, and suggests what to ask next, with the reason. Once a causal question is asked, and while fewer than 15% of the questions are causal, the panel shows the note "Few causal questions so far: the effect estimate rests on untested paths."
The panel rewards questions of one's own. A question the analyst types counts in a darker shade than one picked from the offers, and a column reached only through offered questions gets a lighter square. The box for a question of one's own sits above the suggestions, and the setting "Offered questions per request" at None hides the offers, so that every question is typed.
Across 26 studies, students taught to write questions about what they read understood new texts better. 1 In a tool for data, a display of the columns already covered doubled the questions that analysts asked, and raised their main findings from 5.2 to 7.6 each. 2 The kind of question counts more than their number: in tutoring, students who asked a larger share of "why" and "how" questions had higher exam scores, and students who asked more questions did not. 3
A count on screen makes people do more of what it counts, and the extra work is not always better, 4 so we weigh four designs before any reward grows.
Try it: type a question of your own, or press Ask on a suggestion, and watch the counts change. The panel starts from the demo notebook's state after Run all.
Darker: questions you typed. Lighter: questions you picked.
Several choices in Whybook follow from user studies. Each finding names the choice it supports and links to its source.
In a study of 22 analysts who checked analyses an AI wrote, participants "often noticed errors faster in tasks where the AI clearly stated its assumptions about the data". Gu et al., CHI 2024
With 20 users, a copilot that guided each step did better than a fully automated one in user control, software utility and learnability, "especially for exploratory and creative tasks". The automated one saved time on simpler visual tasks. Khurana et al., CHI 2025
AI agents given the same dataset and hypothesis reached different effect sizes, p-values and conclusions, from different choices in preprocessing, model and inference. Another model or persona gave other results. The authors ask for multiverse-style reporting of AI analyses. Bertran et al., PNAS 2026
Against a chat, two systems that showed editable assumptions and steps gave 18 participants significantly more control, and made intervention, correction and verification easier. Task success and completion time did not differ. Kazemitabaar et al., UIST 2024
Offered questions can take the place of the analyst's own. In the Voyager 2 study, recommended views made one participant "start thinking less" , while the tool that adds them cut the share of fields that people overlooked from 20% to 7%. Handing the whole task to an AI costs more: developers who let an AI write all the code understood it less than those who asked it only about concepts. Offered questions sit between the two. Studies of overreliance suggest two safeguards : a guess before each result, and a question back in place of an answer.
The prototype is an extension for JupyterLab 4.4 and later, on a laptop or on JupyterHub, with a Jupyter server extension. Its demo is a synthetic clinical cohort: a daily pain diary, patient characteristics, a protein panel and a SQLite database of clinic visits. A second copy of the demo shows the notebook after about six more hours of analysis, with 28 cells, larger tables and a written summary.
Each video is one recorded session in JupyterLab, on public data, with a live AI model. Start with the 4-minute demo: a validator checks a notebook that someone else wrote. Or watch a whole analysis, from the raw file to the answer.
A model developer hands over a credit scorecard notebook (today, often written with an AI agent), and a validator checks it in Whybook. The chips on the model's cell show the settings that the code never wrote. A click on a chip reruns the cell with another value, in a branch. An agent writes the same model in R, and Whybook compares every estimate with R's. The data are 30,000 card holders of a bank in Taiwan; the scorecard notebook was written for this video.
A whole causal analysis of 1,629 US smokers weighed in 1971, and 1,566 of them again in 1982: the codebook, a question about a plot, an agent's comparison of who quits and who does not, the adjusted effect checked by three methods, the 63 people with no weight in 1982, and the same models in R.
A whole analysis of the CDC's 2025 survey of 10,710 high school students, with the survey's weights: shares checked against the CDC's own tables, the assumptions drawn as a causal diagram, an adjusted ratio, and a negative control: a check that should not find a link.
A second example, from another field: 360 homes, their electricity meters, and a time-of-use tariff that a quarter of them chose. Nothing in Whybook is specific to either example.
Whybook is one Python package with two parts: an extension for JupyterLab in the browser, and an extension for the Jupyter server. It needs no kernel and no file format of its own: the notebook's kernel runs the cells, and the sandboxed kernel that it adds is ipykernel in a sandbox.
When the analyst drags a column onto a cell, the browser part asks the server part for questions. Once the analyst picks one, the server part writes or edits its code, the browser part runs that code in the notebook's kernel, and the result is saved in the .ipynb file.
Three ways to show a notebook: Code, Bench and Map. The panels Variables, Contents, Questions, Exploration and Cell details. Cell details shows all that Whybook knows of one cell, in one place: the cell that the analyst worked on last, or the one picked on the map. A Databases panel sits under the file browser.
Questions from templates, ordered by the rules and a small learned ranker, or by a model of the analyst's choice. Code edits on the syntax tree. Local models through llama.cpp, and the review guard. Calls to the models of the AI provider that the analyst connects, with a default cost cap of $0.50 on each call and $2 on each run of an agent, where the price is known. SQLite files, read-only.
The main shell runs the cells. Subshells run branches at the same time, and list variables while a cell runs.
Cells and outputs, as in any notebook. The whybook metadata keeps each cell's question, assumptions, decisions and branch, so the notebook opens as it was left, and the version of its layout, so later releases can migrate it.
Whybook builds on these parts of Jupyter and adds its own, such as the questions, the AI models and the kernel sandbox: Â§9 shows what each part of Jupyter gives it.
The roadmap puts this work on the path to v1, through an alpha and a beta, and lists what waits for v2.
Clinical, financial and other personal data should not leave the analyst's machine. Most of the model work in Whybook is small: order up to 12 questions, label a table, title a cell. A small open model of the analyst's choice can do this work in the Jupyter server: label tables, summarise frames, title code cells, suggest more questions, sort a user question and order the offered questions. In the settings, the analyst chooses the model of each task and can add any other model ( Â§7 lists each use , and Â§8 compares the methods for each job ).
A hosted frontier model reads what each task needs and writes the code.
Local models read the tables and describe them. A frontier model writes the code from those descriptions and the names, kinds and sizes of the variables.
Local models read the data and write the code. Nothing leaves the building, and the work goes on with no internet.
When the first notebook opens, Whybook asks which of the three ways to use. Later, one setting, "Keep data on this machine", switches from the first way to the second. Here "this machine" is the machine that runs the Jupyter server, with any model server in its network that the analyst connects as local. c.Whybook.keep_data_local in the server's configuration turns it on for every user, and the setting then shows as fixed. c.Whybook.way_to_use_models sets the way for every user, and with "all-local" the server refuses every model outside this machine and its network.
Connecting a model. The AI models panel finds the model servers that answer on this machine, such as Ollama, and lists their models. There the analyst signs in to OpenRouter, for Claude, GPT, Gemini and open models, or pastes a Hugging Face access token, for open models served by a company that the analyst picks, such as OVHcloud or Scaleway in Europe. It also takes an API key of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or Mistral AI. A model connected at a provider in one of these ways is the remote model. Each key is the analyst's own, stays on the server and never reaches the browser. A model on this machine reads the data as the small local models do. The calls go through Pydantic AI , which reaches any server with an OpenAI-compatible API.
Marked as written by AI. Every cell, label and question that a model writes carries a mark in the notebook's metadata: which model wrote it, and when. Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act asks providers of AI systems that generate text to mark it "in a machine-readable format", from 2 August 2026. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 50
An analyst who lets AI write and run code needs to know two things: what goes out, and what the code can read, change or send. Whybook checks both before either happens, on the analyst's machine. The privacy guard reads every prompt before it goes to a model on another machine, and looks for patient and household IDs, names, ages, dates, health details, small counts and keys. The execution guard reads every cell, set of branches and module that a model wrote, before it runs, and asks about more while the notebook's kernel runs outside the sandbox. In ask mode the guard shows what it flagged and waits; in reject mode it masks the flagged parts, or holds the cell back, and the work goes on.
The rules run first, on the analyst's machine, in at most a few hundredths of a second. A guard model, also on the analyst's machine, can read each prompt or cell as well, and the stricter answer wins. Whybook offers three guard models that read a policy written in the analyst's words: IBM's Granite Guardian 4.1 , DynaGuard and Mistral AI's Shieldstral . For admin-level enforcement, c.Whybook.review_guard in the server's configuration sets ask or reject for every user and keeps both guards on, and no user can turn them off. c.Whybook.keep_data_local does the same for "Keep data on this machine".
AI in a notebook ranges from full agentic control to full user control. Full agentic control gives the fastest results and costs the analyst understanding. Full user control keeps data safe and private but is slow. Whybook keeps the control with the analyst, and one setting keeps the data on the analyst's machine. The analyst still gets results quickly, though not as fast as with full agentic control: the analyst asks the questions, agents write the code, and every choice stays in sight. Each job that Whybook gives to AI: what starts it, what the model reads, where it can run, and what changes when the data must stay on the analyst's machine.
Whybook gives AI a few small jobs, such as ordering the offered questions and labelling a table. For each job we tested rules built into Whybook, open models on the analyst's machine and remote models, on what analysts asked in real notebooks. Whybook's default is the simplest method that did the job.
Each share comes from the tests below. The columns "On this machine" and "Remote" list up to three models that an analyst can pick in Whybook, best first, with their distance from the default in percentage points. A grey line names better models that Whybook does not offer yet. For table labels, the column lists the five models that the settings offer, by the memory of the laptop that each one suits.
Whybook's default Named in the plot Another method tested No method: random order, or a new cell every time
A table too large for the bench shows as a tile with a description of one to three words and a headline. A small model on the analyst's machine can write them, so that the table stays on the machine.
300 examples from public notebooks. The score is the share of examples where the first question offered had the same type as the question that the notebook's author asked next, a proxy for a good question .
300 examples made from public notebooks, as in the demo at the top . The score is the share of examples where the first question offered had the same type as the question that the notebook's author asked next.
276 questions from public notebooks. The score is the share of questions that a method gave the same type label as a reader who labelled them without seeing any method's labels.
360 questions, each written for one of the four places. The score is the average, over the four places, of the share of questions that a method put where their writer meant.
650 public notebooks. When the analyst drags something, the rules choose the place of the answer, and no model does.
More research is needed on traces of real use. The tests replay saved notebooks, which keep only the questions that their authors asked. They do not show which offered questions an analyst picks, skips or undoes. That needs Whybook's own logs, shared with consent.
The future of the notebook as an interface is a common topic in the Jupyter community , and Jupyter has the parts to build it from.
A notebook is JSON with room for metadata. Whybook keeps there the question that each cell answers, the model that wrote it, its cost and its assumptions, so the file records how each result was made.
The variables of the analysis stay in memory while the analyst works. Whybook lists them in the Variables panel. The analyst drags one onto a cell to ask about it, and a chip on a constant offers other values to try.
An output carries a result in rich forms, such as an HTML table, a picture or a plot with its data. The analyst asks about a picture or a region of a plot, whose marks keep their rows. JEP 129 proposes _ai_repr_ , a form of an object written for a model.
Kernel subshells (JEP 91, in ipykernel 7) run several branches of an analysis at the same time, on the same data in memory.
The notebook reaches its kernel only through messages, so the kernel can run in a sandbox with access to one folder of files . Whybook runs it under bubblewrap on Linux and Seatbelt on macOS.
Users, universities and companies add an extension to the JupyterLab they already run. A new application costs far more to adopt. A standalone app can come later.
The awesome-jupyter-ai list has over 100 AI extensions for Jupyter. The largest group, nearly 30 of them, are chat panels and agents. We found none built around the analyst's questions about the data. The closest tools each share one part of the idea:
Many AI tools for notebooks have stopped. Forks fell behind the project they copied. Extensions stopped when the company behind them changed course or closed. Results turned into errors when the service that made them shut down. Each of these projects tried something early, and each left a lesson for the community. Several also gave back to Jupyter. Most of the cases come from a survey of more than 100 AI extensions for Jupyter .
Pretzel forked JupyterLab 4.2 in 2024 and licensed its changes under AGPLv3, which JupyterLab's BSD licence cannot take in, so they could not go upstream. Its development stopped the same year, and its last release lacks the fixes for 11 security advisories that affect JupyterLab 4.2, 5 of them rated high. Whybook is an extension for JupyterLab 4.4 and later. It uses the extension API that has been stable since JupyterLab 4.0, so users update JupyterLab as usual.
Kite's JupyterLab extension started in 2020 as a copy of jupyterlab-lsp. Kite also contributed improvements to JupyterLab's completer. The copy was last updated in 2021 and Kite shut down in 2022, while jupyterlab-lsp is still maintained, and so are Kite's improvements in JupyterLab. What Whybook needs from other packages goes to those packages as changes, and the roadmap lists them.
Tabnine's JupyterLab client had its last release a week after its first, and Einblick's extension still installs but calls a server that no longer exists. IBM ended its Qiskit Code Assistant service in 2026 and archived the extension, but the models are open on Hugging Face, and the archived extension still supports Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Whybook names no provider: templates need no model, over ten open models run in the Jupyter server and the settings can add others, and the remote model and decision models of several makers, such as Jev of TypeSafe AI, are choices in the settings.
Excel's COPILOT function stopped working on 14 September 2026, and a cell that recalculates now shows #NAME?. Each answer in Whybook is code and outputs in the .ipynb, and the questions, assumptions and labels are in its metadata. Any Jupyter frontend opens it, with no model and without the extension. Microsoft Support
Posit retired Databot, its agent for exploratory analysis, and explained why in public: it was "too narrowly scoped", and "EDA does not happen in a vacuum". Whybook puts each answer in the notebook that the project already has, next to its code and its modules. Posit, June 2026
Observable no longer develops Canvases, where cells sat anywhere on an open board ( August 2026 ). The bench and the map are drawn from one linear notebook, in the order of its cells, so the notebook stays usable if the views change or go.
Whybook reads what libraries already produce, and its own helpers are optional. Widgets, tqdm bars and Plotly charts show as in the notebook. The analyst can draw a box on a Plotly scatter chart or a matplotlib figure to ask about the rows in it, with no change to the code that makes them.
Whybook comes from long-time maintainers of JupyterLab and its extensions, at a company that builds and supports open-source software. They have reviewed and released JupyterLab for years, so they know which of its parts stay stable, and they can make the changes that the extension needs in JupyterLab itself.
Analysts will ask by dragging and by clicking. The study measures the time to the first question, the questions that go to the wrong cell, and keyboard use.
Whybook will log picks, changes of place and Undo to a local file. A placement model will be fitted to the rules first and then to those corrections, and the learned ranker to the picks.
Whybook offers decision models for the type and the place of a user question. On 276 questions from public notebooks, Decider V1.2 of Perplexity and Jev 1.13 gave the right type for 89%, against 67% for the keywords. For the place, on 360 questions written for a given place, Clef of Cloudflare put 82% right by balanced accuracy, against 43% for the first words on the Ask button. The places that analysts pick in Whybook will test the classifiers on the questions that matter.
The sandboxed kernel will install a package when the analyst asks for one. Whybook will show in its toolbar which kernel runs in the sandbox, as the AI models panel already does.
Templates and questions about plots in R, kernels of other languages such as Julia, JupyterLite, and _ai_repr_ in libraries.
The roadmap sets out the path to v1 through an alpha and a beta, and what waits for v2.
Whybook is on PyPI, and its code is at openteams-ai/whybook . Install it into the environment of your JupyterLab:
Add local for the models that run in the Jupyter server: pip builds llama-cpp-python with the system's C++ compiler, in about 4 minutes, and each model is a download of 1.6 to 7 GB.
The second command writes three files of the installed release into the folder pain_diary : the notebook, prep.py and clinic.sqlite . The notebook imports its helpers and data from prep.py . In JupyterLab, choose "Open Notebook in Whybook" in the command palette. The first time, Whybook asks which of three ways to use models: pick one, or press Decide later. Then press Run all. The run takes under a minute. The demo after six more hours of analysis is on GitHub, and it opens with its map and panels before anything runs. Questions marked "needs AI", and questions that the analyst types, need a model connected in the AI models panel: OpenRouter after a sign-in, a Hugging Face access token, an API key of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or Mistral AI, or a model server on this machine. Until one is connected, Whybook greys those questions and shows what to set up. With the setting "Keep data on this machine", no tables, printed outputs or pictures leave the machine.
Whybook is a research prototype, open source under the Apache-2.0 licence. Taking it to v1, along the roadmap , needs people as much as code: research with analysts, reviews of its statistics and its security, and maintainers. We are looking for partners:
Talk to OpenTeams about a trial with a team, funding or sponsorship, or contribute on GitHub.
Ask a question or share an idea where others can join in. Mike, who created Whybook, replies on GitHub and on the Jupyter forum. No GitHub account? Use the forum.
Send Mike an informal message on LinkedIn or in Jupyter's Zulip chat. On LinkedIn, add your question to the connection request.
[?] Whybook, a research prototype created by MichaÅ Krassowski ( LinkedIn , GitHub ) and incubated at OpenTeams , updated on 22 October 2026. The prototype was built in spare time, largely with Claude Code, under MichaÅ's direction and review.

title: Rheinmetall opens Telford factory to restore UK tank and artillery gun production
body: At peak capacity, the 11,500-square-metre facility can produce up to 245 barrels across both calibres and more than 50 breeches a year. Breech and breech-block production began in May 2026, followed by barrels in June. Rheinmetall said it converted the empty building into an operational manufacturing facility in eight months. The work included installing and commissioning equipment, training British employees and transferring specialist knowledge from Germany. “Britain is back in the business of making the weapons that our Armed Forces need to defend the nation against our adversaries,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting. “From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action.” Domestic production and supply chains The factory provides a British manufacturing source for components needed by tank and artillery programmes. Rheinmetall intends to introduce steel from Sheffield Forgemasters into production and develop long-term supply relationships with British small and medium-sized businesses. The Gun Hall forms part of more than £200 million the company has invested across its UK operations over the past five years. Its wider British activities include the Boxer mechanised infantry vehicle and Challenger 3 tank programmes. “Today’s opening is an important milestone for Rheinmetall and for the United Kingdom,” said Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger. “In a remarkably short period of time, we have turned our commitment into a sovereign manufacturing capability that will strengthen Britain’s defence industrial base for decades to come.” Workforce to grow with output The Ministry of Defence said the facility supports 100 highly skilled jobs. Rheinmetall said 35 people currently work at the Gun Hall, with more than 100 expected as production develops. British employees trained at Rheinmetall’s Unterlüß plant in Germany in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production. The company also recruited workers from Telford’s engineering sector and plans further hiring as output increases. “The official opening of our UK Gun Hall is a landmark moment for Rheinmetall UK and for Britain’s defence industrial base,” said Rebecca Richards, managing director of Rheinmetall UK. “In just eight months, we transformed an empty facility into an operational manufacturing capability by investing in British people, British skills and British industry.” Cooperation under Trinity House Agreement Streeting opened the factory alongside Chief of the General Staff General Sir Roly Walker and Papperger. The project combines Rheinmetall’s German manufacturing expertise with production capacity and a trained workforce in Britain. Both the company and the ministry linked the investment to the UK-Germany Trinity House Agreement, signed in October 2024. The agreement seeks closer bilateral defence cooperation and stronger NATO collective deterrence. The ministry also placed the opening within the government’s wider industrial and defence spending programme. It cited a £298 billion commitment over four years under the Defence Investment Plan.

title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge mass shooting conspirator set to enter plea in U.S. court
body:
The alleged co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge , B.C., has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. court and is set to go on trial in December, accused of aiding one of the worst school shootings in Canadian history.
James Bryant entered the plea in a brief arraignment appearance in Seattle on Thursday, after a grand jury last week indicted the 30-year-old Bellingham, Wash., resident for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.
The criminal complaint against Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, alleges she colluded with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar online, helping set up an attempted livestream of the murders.
Bryant, who appeared in a tan prison jumpsuit and dark-framed glasses with her hair down to her waist, has been denied bail.
Her trial is scheduled to begin before U.S. District Judge Kymberly K. Evanson in Seattle on Dec. 21.
Bryant also allegedly advised 18-year-old Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.
Van Rootselaar killed eight victims last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before she fatally shot herself as police closed in.
The accusations against Bryant remain unproven.
Magistrate Judge Michelle Peterson presided over Thursday’s arraignment hearing, where Bryant was told she faces penalties of up to life in prison and US$25,000 in fines.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s complaint against Bryant says that on Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she had dressed for the mass shooting.
The document shows a photo of someone from their shoulders down, holding a rifle and wearing black fishnet stockings and a black miniskirt.
“A few moments later, Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she went live with the stream and had just killed her family members at their residence,” the complaint said.
Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant, “I’m going now. (for real). Live. I shot them,” after killing her mother and brother at their home.
Bryant is alleged to have helped Van Rootselaar start the family car — she did not know how to drive — before she headed to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

title: Ghana’s fiscal consolidation in 2025 largely driven by expenditure restraint, not revenue growth – ISSER
body: Ghana’s fiscal consolidation in 2025 was driven largely by expenditure restraint rather than increased revenue mobilisation, the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER), has disclosed in its State of Ghanaian Economy Report 2025. According to the economic research firm of the University of Ghana, though smaller deficits and lower debt reduce pressure on government financing and create conditions for greater macroeconomic stability, fiscal adjustment achieved through sharp reductions in capital spending may constrain infrastructure development and future growth. It therefore advised that sustaining fiscal consolidation requires not only expenditure discipline but also stronger domestic revenue mobilisation and improved spending efficiency. Ghana’s fiscal position improved substantially in 2025, with the overall deficit narrowing from 7.9% to 1.0% of GDP on a commitment basis and the primary balance returning to surplus. The World Bank similarly estimates a general government deficit of 1.2% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Total revenue and grants amounted to 16.1% of GDP, while capital expenditure declined from 2.5% to 1.4% of GDP, raising concerns about public investment. The public debt also fell from 62.7% to 46.0% of GDP, reflecting fiscal adjustment and the effect of cedi appreciation on the domestic currency value of external debt. ISSER said Ghana’s fiscal consolidation was substantial, but sustaining it will require stronger revenue mobilisation without sacrificing productive public investment. Policy Priorities On policy priorities, ISSER wants the strengthening of revenue mobilisation via the broadening of the tax base, improve compliance and reduce revenue leakages. Again, it called for the protection of productive investment through improve expenditure efficiency while safeguarding priority infrastructure and social spending. It also emphasise on sustaining fiscal discipline, calling for improved commitment controls, the prevention of arrears accumulation and the management of debt refinancing risks.

title: Naftogaz has 24 scenarios for getting through winter, company chief says
body:
Naftogaz Group has prepared 24 scenarios for navigating the 2026/2027 autumn-winter period, taking into account Russian attacks on gas infrastructure, temperature conditions and domestic gas production, Naftogaz CEO Serhiy Fedorenko said.
"We have calculated 24 scenarios for getting through the winter, taking into account the intensity of Russian attacks, temperature conditions and our own gas production volumes. We have solutions and a defined action plan for every scenario," Fedorenko wrote on Facebook on Thursday after an online briefing with Ukrainian ambassadors attended by Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.
He stressed the importance of intensifying work with international partners in several areas: restoring damaged infrastructure, strengthening protection of energy facilities, supplying critical equipment and specialized machinery, and securing financial instruments to contract additional gas volumes in advance.
Fedorenko added that Naftogaz had a successful example of cooperation with Norway, which provided substantial grant assistance for purchasing additional gas. The company continues to work with international partners to secure additional resources for infrastructure protection and restoration.
As reported, Naftogaz Group received a EUR 270 million loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) in April 2025 to purchase gas, backed by a state guarantee. Norway supplemented the loan with a EUR 139 million grant. In August, the Norwegian government allocated NOK 1 billion ($98.3 million) to Ukraine for natural gas purchases. In February 2026, Naftogaz and the EBRD signed an agreement for an EUR 85 million grant from the Norwegian government.

title: ‎‘We Are Proud of You,’ Barau Hails Media Trust
body: ‎Deputy Senate President Jibrin Barau has commended Media Trust Group for its investment in journalism, newsroom innovation and media diversification, declaring that the organisation has made the government proud through its contribution to the Nigerian economy. ‎ ‎Barau gave the commendation on Thursday in Abuja at the launch of the Media Trust’s Converged Digital Newsroom, where he praised the media organisation for embracing technology and adapting its operations to changing trends in the industry. ‎ ‎“We are proud of you. Really proud of you,” he said, noting that Media Trust had demonstrated the entrepreneurial qualities required to sustain and grow a business. ‎ ‎The Deputy Senate President described the organisation as a trailblazer, citing its transition from a weekly publication to a daily newspaper and its subsequent expansion into television, radio and digital platforms. ‎ ‎“Before I came in, I told the chairman that this outfit is a game changer. You have broken the jinx,” he said. ‎ ‎According to Barau, Media Trust’s willingness to take risks, innovate and diversify its operations offers valuable lessons for other media organisations and businesses seeking to remain competitive. ‎ ‎He said the launch of the digital newsroom demonstrated the organisation’s commitment to modernising its operations and keeping pace with technological developments, including artificial intelligence. ‎ ‎“Do not remain where you are. Try to move with the trend. Try to innovate. Try to be proactive. You don’t win, because if you remain where you are, the world will move and leave you behind,” he said. ‎ ‎Barau urged businesses to embrace innovation, describing it as essential to their survival and long-term success in a rapidly changing business environment. ‎ ‎He also highlighted Media Trust’s contribution to the economy through employment generation, increased business activity and tax payments. ‎ ‎According to him, the organisation’s expansion has increased its workforce and patronage, enabling it to contribute more to government revenue. ‎ ‎“You are not only helping your enterprise, you are helping the entire economy. Because you are growing. As you grow, you are contributing to the economy,” he said. ‎ ‎The Deputy Senate President added that the private sector remained the engine of economic growth and commended Media Trust for playing its part in strengthening the economy. ‎ ‎He said the organisation’s achievements showed that media businesses could combine professional journalism with sound entrepreneurship and effective management. ‎ ‎Barau also cited his own investment in technology education as an example of the importance of anticipating future trends. ‎ ‎He recalled sponsoring about 200 students to study artificial intelligence and robotics at universities abroad approximately two years ago, saying the students had completed their studies and were expected to return to Nigeria. ‎ ‎He expressed optimism that their expertise could contribute to the country’s technological development and potentially benefit organisations such as Media Trust. ‎ ‎Barau congratulated the management and staff of Media Trust on the launch, saying the Senate recognised and appreciated the organisation’s efforts to improve its operations and advance journalism in Nigeria. ‎ ‎“I congratulate you, and I commend you on behalf of the legislature,” he said.

title: US Embassy issues health alert to Americans in Nigeria amid Bundibugyo Ebola case
body: The United States Embassy in Abuja has issued a health alert following Nigeria’s report of a case of Bundibugyo virus disease, a form of Ebola, on October 20, 2026. In the alert published on October 21, the US Mission Nigeria said health officials were conducting contact tracing after the case was reported. According to the alert, the Nigerian Ministry of Health said the affected individual had travelled by air from Uganda. The embassy described Ebola as a serious health concern, stating that “Ebola is a rare, severe, and often fatal hemorrhagic fever illness.” The US Embassy urged travelers to consult health guidance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and take precautions against possible exposure to the virus. It advised people to visit the CDC’s Ebola information page and its travel health page for Nigeria for relevant information. The embassy also advised people who may be at risk of Ebola to alert their healthcare providers if they experience symptoms consistent with the disease, so they can receive guidance before presenting for medical care. Travellers were further advised to continue taking malaria preventive medication as recommended by their doctors, noting that malaria symptoms can resemble those of Ebola and trigger avoidable health scares. The alert also urged people returning from areas experiencing an Ebola outbreak to monitor their health for 21 days after travel. The US Embassy advised travellers to consult the US Department of State’s Nigeria country page for general health information. It also directed them to the embassy’s list of medical providers and encouraged them to contact their travel insurance providers to understand available medical evacuation options if they become ill while overseas. Vanguard News The post US Embassy issues health alert to Americans in Nigeria amid Bundibugyo Ebola case appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: UK orders dozens of official websites offline after flaw warnings
body: British government official websites were taken down on Thursday as administrators rushed to safeguard against two critical ​security flaws in PHP, ​a programming language that powers a large share of the internet. Baroness Lloyd, parliamentary undersecretary of state at the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, told the House of Lords the decision to protect data was made after the flaws emerged. “The principle impact on government digital services has arisen from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates are applied,” she said. “The government continues to monitor the situation closely and work with departments to maintain the security, resilience and availability of public services.” Government, school and hospital websites across Europe and beyond were taken offline on Wednesday as cybersecurity ⁠agencies across the world warned fixes were needed. Organisations unable to apply fixes in ⁠time were told to consider taking affected sites offline. PHP's developers said a ​set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was available. The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki mark one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running, exposing how deeply governments and companies depend on code that few people understand. "I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at an event in Germany on Thursday, ⁠saying the incident showed the importance of building software that can be maintained securely as systems grow more complex. "It was a long day and a long night, I ​know, for all ⁠the IT and security folks." Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, said the discovery appeared to be the most serious vulnerability detected for five years. Felix Kuhlenkamp, head of security at German digital industry association Bitkom, said that many larger operators had already carried out updates, but that for complex IT systems and smaller organisations it could ​take longer. "They may run a website using PHP but don't really keep a close eye on it," he said. "If a website is based on an old version of PHP for which there is no security update, the entire system must be updated." UNITED KINGDOM The British public service broadcaster BBC said it had taken down some web portals on Wednesday. The broadcaster also reported several municipalities taking down their web services, including the city of Edinburgh. GERMANY A representative for the German Digital Ministry said on Wednesday the federal IT service provider ITZBund had taken several websites offline due to the discovery of PHP vulnerabilities. The temporary deactivation was purely preventive and no security incidents were known to have occurred, they said. FRANCE The Interior Ministry said it ⁠had temporarily taken offline the websites of prefectures, which are local government administrative offices, while awaiting a security fix for ​the PHP framework ⁠they use. It said the move was ‌a precaution pending a patch from the framework's publisher. BELGIUM Belgium's Foreign Ministry said it had temporarily taken its websites offline after reports ​of cyber attacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, although the country's cybersecurity centre said it had not recorded any attacks on Belgian websites. NETHERLANDS Many organisations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and preventively took their public-facing sites offline. They included the Port of Rotterdam, government site Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites of the five largest political parties and numerous hospital websites across the country. FINLAND State IT centre Valtori shut down the government's public web services on Wednesday as “a precautionary measure”. Valtori said it had not identified any attempt to exploit the flaws and that the services being taken down was not the result of a data breach. CZECH REPUBLIC The Czech government took its website offline on Wednesday at 7pm (1700 GMT) at the recommendation of the country's cyber watchdog to “allow for the implementation of necessary security patches”. “The measure aims to ensure the secure operation of the website. During the shutdown, the site and its content will not be accessible to the public. Services will be restored once the recommended security updates have been applied,” the government office said. JAPAN Japan's Ministry of Finance and Meteorological Agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan's National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service. Several Japanese companies, including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA and East Japan Railway said ​on Thursday they were also temporarily suspending some internet services as part of emergency measures. ORANGE SA The French telecoms group temporarily suspended access to a number of websites ⁠and applications using the PHP programming language as a precaution. The measure affects websites, services and applications across several subsidiaries and entities.

title: Carney lands in Turkey for meetings with Erdogan, business leaders
body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is forming a “strategic partnership” with Turkey aimed at securing a free-trade agreement.
Carney arrived in Ankara overnight for the first official bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey.
In a joint statement with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan , the two leaders said they’re also looking to ratify an “air transportation agreement” which could lead to more direct flights.
The agreement also commits to deeper people-to-people ties with Turkey, something Carney also has sought with the European Union to offer more flexibility to tourists, workers and students.
The statement said Canada and Turkey have shared values, including “human rights, individual liberties, democracy and the rule of law.”
The Erdogan government is under heavy scrutiny internationally right now over reports of official persecution of LGBTQ+ organizers in the country.

title: NATO to Open Centralized Arms Purchases for Ukraine
body:
NATO will let Ukraine buy weapons through the alliance’s centralized arms procurement agency, the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), under an upcoming partnership.
The partnership would let Kyiv buy weapons, ammunition and other military supplies through NSPA.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The Financial Times (FT), which reported the new partnership on Thursday, said the decision would help Kyiv obtain supplies faster and provide a new channel other than bilateral deals.
“It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services and access to established industrial base,” Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA director of support to operations, told the FT.
Borsboom explained that Kyiv can order supplies such as uniforms, and the agency can help it obtain them.
The outlet said the latest decision followed the NSPA’s April decision to allow Ukrainian arms makers to compete in tenders, and another industry event in Kyiv during the past week for 150 Ukrainian arms makers on how to register for the tenders.
Alyona Getmanchuk, the head of Ukraine’s Mission to NATO, told the FT that she hopes the deal will give Ukraine “expanded access” to the alliance’s supply network and an “important gateway into NATO’s defense industrial ecosystem.”
Kyiv has long appealed for additional air defense systems as Russia ramps up attacks across Ukraine for the winter campaign, with Kyiv saying that Moscow aims to cripple 90% of Ukraine’s utility networks .
Chief among the requests are the US-made Patriot air defense systems and the associated PAC-3 missiles capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles, whose stockpiles in Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, have been exhausted .
The NSPA partnership also coincides with the latest rift between Kyiv and the White House, with the alliance’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program, through which NATO members bankroll US weaponry for Ukraine, under threat.
Zelensky has accused the US administration of delaying Patriot missiles already paid for via PURL after the latest rift, though the latter has maintained that supplies continued as usual .
But it’s unclear whether the new partnership would cover the Patriots, as the Pentagon must approve their procurement and transfers.
On Wednesday-Thursday, Kyiv was hit by three waves of ballistic missiles overnight, damaging metro infrastructure on the capital’s South Bridge and a medical facility in the Pechersk district, killing at least one and wounding 24.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Francesca Albanese calls for Indonesia to reconsider involvement with Board of Peace
body: Indonesia should reconsider its involvement in US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan because it is being shaped by Israel and the US and lacks a Palestinian voice, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories told Reuters on Thursday.Trump unveiled the "Board of Peace," of which Indonesia is a key troop-contributing member, in January to address global conflicts ​typically handled by the United Nations. The world's largest Muslim-majority nation has also pledged troops to be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilization force.Francesca Albanese, a prominent human rights lawyer known for her vocal criticism of Israel, said in an interview in Jakarta that Indonesia has historically supported the Palestinian cause, but joining the board was dangerous.Indonesia's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Board of Peace discussions remained on hold, reiterating its earlier position.Albanese has drawn the ire of several Western capitals. The US has imposed sanctions on her, and others, including her own native Italy, have called for her resignation."I understand (Indonesia's) good intentions. I still think that it's very dangerous, because it risks to normalize a very abnormal mechanism," she said.Albanese rejects Israel having a role in determining Palestinians' futureAlbanese said that, legally, Israel could not have a role in determining the future of Palestinians.Rights experts have criticized the board for not including a ​Palestinian representative even though it is meant to supervise the ​temporary governance of a Palestinian territory.The Board of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside US business hours.Indonesia, which backs a two-state solution and has repeatedly condemned Israeli violence, has drawn criticism from domestic Muslim groups for agreeing to join the board, which also counts Israel as a member.President Prabowo Subianto has vowed to quit if it does not bring benefits to Palestinians, his office has previously said, adding that joining the board would allow Indonesia to push for cessation of violence.Indonesia risks ties to Palestinians over Board of PeaceAlbanese said Indonesia risked compromising its close ties with Palestinians. "It's very risky to do so when the rules are set by Israel," she said.Albanese recommended that Jakarta join the Hague Group of countries, which includes South Africa and Indonesia's neighbor Malaysia, and seeks to uphold international law and processes, including at the International Criminal Court, regarding Israel's actions.Trump's Gaza plan has stalled. A 2025 ceasefire secured the release of the remaining hostages held by Hamas and hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees, but efforts to disarm Hamas and secure an Israeli withdrawal have faltered, while Israeli forces continue near-daily attacks in Gaza.

title: Diesel deal may be clinched with Europe, Dmitriev says
body:
ISTANBUL, October 22. /TASS/. The more transactions will be made between Russia and the United States, the more European companies will have the desire to join them, Russian Presidential Special Envoy for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev said at the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum.
TASS has collected the key statements of the Russian presidential envoy.
Deliveries of Russian fertilizers are very important for the global and the US markets. "We see that supplies of Russian fertilizers for the American farmers - it is utterly important," Dmitriev said.
Russia has the world's cheapest electric power for artificial intelligence development. "I spoke yesterday, for example, about a joint datacenter project. Because Russia boasts the cheapest electricity for artificial intelligence across the globe and we see that we can cooperate in the technology sphere," Dmitriev noted.
Energy cooperation between Russia and the United States will evolve and European countries will join it over time.
The diesel fuel deal with Europe if possible if there is a need for it.
Russia is "breaking the media wall" and continues interacting with other countries in a number of projects.
Russia wants to interact and will interact with Europe and historical ties cannot be severed at once.
All the businesses in Europe are affected by the rejection of Russian energy resources and the policy pursued by the EU. "All the business in Europe suffer from very high energy prices. These are the attempts and the results of rejecting Russian energy resources," Dmitriev said.
European businessmen thanked Russia for the continuation of the dialogue.
The Nord Stream gas pipelines will inevitable become operational again at a certain moment of time.

title: China Moves to Lock Its Own Top AI and Chip Designs Behind Export Controls
body:
China proposed adding large AI models, agents, computing clusters and advanced AI chip designs to its export control list, and made pre-export registration mandatory from October 16 while the draft is open for comment.
For years the story ran in one direction. Washington cut China off from advanced chips, and American officials accused Chinese labs of copying US models. On Friday Beijing drew a border of its own. China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology proposed putting the country's biggest AI models, AI agents, computing clusters and advanced chip designs on its list of technologies whose export is prohibited or restricted.
The rule is still a draft. But one piece of it is already live: a temporary pre-export registration requirement that took effect the same day.
The draft adds 40 technologies to the export catalogue. Artificial intelligence takes 23 of them, covering large models, agents, computing clusters and information processing. Biomedicine gets five, including cell and gene therapy and small nucleic acid drugs such as siRNA. Photovoltaics gets 12, from polysilicon to wafer and cell manufacturing and the key equipment behind them.
For large models, the curbs would reach the weights, source code and other core technology of models trained on "important data" that have at least 2 trillion parameters, or that rank among the world's top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety, according to Bloomberg . The draft names no model. Bloomberg pointed to Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max as examples already above that size.
Chips are in it too. Design technologies for AI chips made at 14 nanometers or more advanced, or built with 2.5D or 3D advanced packaging, would be covered, along with design know-how for certain advanced memory chips.
Beijing is not slamming every door. AI technology already public through open source or academic papers is excluded. So is access through APIs, websites, apps and software-as-a-service platforms, which means overseas users can keep using Chinese models through apps and APIs, TNW reports . The ministry said most AI technologies would remain freely exportable.
The tricky part is what counts as an export. Deploying a covered model on servers abroad would qualify. Chinese companies running their own computing centres overseas would get simplified or automatic licensing, and open-source exports would get simplified licensing as well. In biomedicine, transferring IP ownership of some novel cell and gene therapies and siRNA drugs would be banned outright, while licensing deals that keep ownership in China would be eased.
The comment window runs from October 16 to November 15. Until the catalogue is formally revised, the temporary registration rule applies, and it reaches back into deals already underway but not completed. That includes IP transfers, overseas licensing and changes that would put Chinese technology owners under foreign control, the Wall Street Journal reports .
That is the immediate catch for deals already in motion, from overseas licensing of Chinese technology to a foreign buyer taking control of a Chinese tech owner. The paperwork applies today, before the final rule exists.
A ministry spokesperson said the rules aim to "prevent misuse and abuse" and "ensure that AI remains under human control." The ministry pointed to risks such as AI capable of generating and deploying autonomous malware against critical civilian infrastructure, and said the plan does not target any country or company.
The geopolitical reading is hard to miss. Reuters framed the move as Beijing's latest effort to limit transfers of tools it sees as vital to national security and its competition with Washington. The Financial Times had reported in July that Beijing was weighing controls on AI models and chips. PCMag called it an ironic twist : after years of US curbs and complaints about copying, China is now restricting access to its own AI.
The timing sharpens that irony. Last month US security agencies accused DeepSeek, Alibaba and four other Chinese AI firms of industrial-scale distillation of American frontier models. Now Beijing is the one treating model weights as strategic assets that cannot simply walk out the door.
For Chinese labs, the draft adds another layer of uncertainty to an industry that already works under strict content controls, Bloomberg noted, and it lands just as those labs keep training ever larger models. The bigger they get, the more of them will cross the 2 trillion parameter line and fall under the state's export gate.
