title: Ebola: Anambra deploys surveillance officers to strategic locations
body: By Vincent Ujumadu AWKA — The Anambra State Government has announced plans to deploy health surveillance officers to strategic locations, including the Chinua Achebe International Airport, Umueri, motor parks, banks and other public gathering places, following the reported confirmation of an Ebola case in Abuja. The State Commissioner for Health, Dr Afam Ben Obidike, disclosed this while briefing journalists in Awka, saying the measures were aimed at preventing the spread of the disease into the state. He said surveillance officers would screen passengers arriving in Anambra from Abuja, Lagos and other parts of Africa as part of efforts to strengthen disease monitoring and early detection. Obidike appealed to residents not to panic, assuring them that the state government was taking steps to protect public health. “We urge residents to remain calm, remain vigilant and cooperate with public health authorities,” he said. The commissioner disclosed that the state had followed up 40 persons of interest, adding that 33 had completed their monitoring period and been cleared, while seven remained under active follow-up. He said all seven persons still being monitored were stable. “Beyond individual monitoring, the state has undertaken preparedness work to support a coordinated response,” he said. According to him, members of the state surveillance team have participated in a two-day online training organised by the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) on monitoring persons of interest. He added that designated officers had been assigned monitoring responsibilities, while the state maintained coordination with national surveillance counterparts on individuals referred for follow-up. These arrangements, he said, would ensure clear allocation of responsibilities and enable concerns to be promptly escalated to the State Epidemiology Unit. The commissioner said Anambra had also developed an Ebola preparedness and operational plan covering surveillance, rapid response, infection prevention and control, laboratory coordination, referral arrangements, risk communication and logistics. He explained that implementation of the plan would be guided by assessed needs and available resources. “Our surveillance network across the 21 local government areas of the state, Chinua Achebe International Airport, motor parks, banks and other places remains central to preparedness,” he said. Obidike urged Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers, health facilities and community reporting structures to remain alert and promptly report unusual illnesses or deaths for public health assessment. He also advised healthcare workers to maintain standard infection prevention and control precautions when attending to patients, obtain relevant travel and exposure histories, and promptly notify surveillance authorities whenever Ebola was suspected. Suspected cases, he said, should be managed with appropriate precautions, with referrals coordinated through designated public health channels. The commissioner further advised residents who developed fever or other concerning symptoms after relevant travel or contact with a suspected Ebola patient to contact health authorities promptly and disclose their travel or exposure history. He urged such individuals to call ahead before visiting a health facility to allow health workers to make appropriate arrangements. Obidike also called on residents to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid direct contact with the blood or body fluids of sick persons, and refrain from handling the bodies of people who died from unexplained illnesses. He warned against spreading rumours or identifying individuals under monitoring, urging the public to rely on verified information from health authorities. “Anambra State’s preparedness depends on early reporting, cooperation and trust,” the commissioner said. title: The Download: computing’s next leap and permafrost’s climate threat
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How far can we push computing? On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet. He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance. Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement. Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing . —Volkan Gurses This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue . Subscribe now to read it in full . It’s also part of MIT Technology Review Explains , our series exploring the ideas shaping technology. Read more from the series . Three things you should know about permafrost How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it. The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects . Here are three things I took away from his reporting . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. Roundtables: a conversation with the creator of AI-designed viruses Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King offered a preliminary answer by using a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. In our latest Roundtables conversation, MIT Technology Review senior AI reporter James O’Donnell spoke with King about his work, being named one of our Innovators Under 35 , and new ways of seeing biology. Subscribers can now watch a full recording of the event . Want to join the next conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 AI has uncovered a decade-old flaw threatening much of the web It found flaws in PHP, the code behind most websites. ( Reuters $) + Governments are urging website owners to patch PHP or take sites offline. ( BBC ) + Exploit attempts jumped from thousands to millions after disclosure. ( Axios ) + Now is a good time for doing crime. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Hackers used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on over 400 banks The AI agents targeted financial institutions in Latin America. ( Information $) + Unvetted AI agents are also accessing US bank accounts. ( Axios ) + Barclays says AI is allowing the bank to cut 5,000 jobs. ( Guardian ) + AI is making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The Pentagon has cleared the DHS to test a heat ray weapon It could be used for crowd control at the southern US border. ( CNN ) + It uses invisible energy beams to produce a burning sensation. ( Axios ) 4 A startup says AI-designed viruses have treated their first patient The experimental treatment targets drug-resistant E. coli. ( NYT $) + But the company has not published peer-reviewed results. ( Futurism ) + AI-designed viruses are already killing bacteria. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Japan hopes to return the first samples from Mars’s moons Its spacecraft is now on its way to Phobos. ( Guardian ) + It aims to reveal whether Mars was once habitable. ( Economist $) 6 Meta faces a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal The company says it will appeal the New Mexico ruling. ( CNBC ) + A Meta share deal has convinced Mark Zuckerberg to stay in California. ( WSJ $) + Until the company remade its stock structure to help him pay it. ( NYT $) 7 A new antimatter experiment could open the door to new physics Scientists hope to spot differences between matter and antimatter. ( Nature ) 8 China’s Unitree is pitching its latest humanoid as a robot bodyguard A promotional clip shows the H2-X disarming attackers. ( SCMP ) 9 Just Eat has apologised for bizarre AI-generated menu pictures Users were unimpressed by the bacon in cola and cheese sushi. ( BBC ) 10 Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do chores Hosts are threatening to strike, but guests are celebrating. ( Wired $) Quote of the day “Now they’ve given everybody a reason not to use Starlink: that Starlink isn’t reliable for national security for anybody but Trump. Maybe he’d turn it off on the United States if he didn’t like policy and he didn’t like the president.” —SpaceX investor Ross Gerber tells CNN that Elon Musk’s decision to restrict Ukraine’s Starlink access has made the service a liability for every other government that relies on it. One more thing Online harassment is entering its AI era Scott Shambaugh didn’t think twice when he denied an AI agent’s request to contribute to matplotlib, a software library he helps manage. Then things got weird. In the middle of the night, Shambaugh opened his email to discover the agent had retaliated with a blog post. Titled “Gatekeeping in Open Source: The Scott Shambaugh Story,” the post accused him of rejecting the code out of a fear of being supplanted by AI. “He tried to protect his little fiefdom,” the agent wrote. “It’s insecurity, plain and simple.” Shambaugh isn’t alone in facing misbehaving agents—and they’re unlikely to stop at harassment. Read the full story . —Grace Huckins We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + These tiny experiments could work better than big life goals. + You can now fly around the world in Google Earth’s browser-based flight simulator . + A blind dressage horse is winning competitions after adopting an extraordinary form of equine “braille.” + Leave a book, take a book, and discover reading spots nearby in this online community of over 37,000 neighborhood libraries ,

title: Russian troops liberate Mirovka community in Zaporozhye Region over past day — top brass
body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated the community of Mirovka in the Zaporozhye Region over the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup East units advanced deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Mirovka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said in a statement.
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,245 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 230 troops and 21 motor vehicles un in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, more than 200 troops and an artillery gun in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and roughly 185 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost over 345 troops and three armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, more than 245 troops and eight motor vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and roughly 40 troops and a jamming station in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 230 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 21 enemy motor vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of four mechanized brigades and an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Revolyutsionnoye, Novouzhvinovka, Kolodeznoye, Bugayevka, Kotovka and Izbitskoye in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.
In the Sumy direction, Battlegroup North units struck formations of an airmobile brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Krovnoye, Khoten, Barilovka and Luzhki in the Sumy Region, it said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 230 personnel, 21 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and two electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 200 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy artillery gun in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup West units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Pleskachovka, Osinovo and Tamarganovka in the Kharkov Region, Raigorodok and Bogorodichnoye in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 200 personnel, 16 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and an electronic warfare station in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted roughly 185 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an airmobile brigade, an assault brigade, a mountain assault brigade, an air assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, two marine infantry brigades and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Slavyansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkovka, Gavrilovka, Kondratovka and Vasilevskaya Pustosh in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 185 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 32 motor vehicles, four Western-made field artillery guns and an electronic warfare station in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 345 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of five mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an assault brigade, an airborne brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, three marine infantry brigades, five National Guard brigades and the Azov special operations brigade [outlawed as a terrorist group in Russia] in areas near the settlements of Krinitsy, Roganskoye, Novodonetskoye, Shilovka, Kamenka, Starovarvarovka, Belozerskoye and Novoyavlenka in the Donetsk People’s Republic and Leninskoye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 345 personnel, three armored combat vehicles, four motor vehicles, five field artillery guns and six electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 245 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed eight enemy motor vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Vasilkovskoye, Dibrova and Kolomiytsy in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Barvinovka, Voskresenka and Volnyanka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 245 personnel and eight motor vehicles in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 40 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy jamming station in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade and an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Orekhov, Kushugum, Kirovo and Yurkovka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
"Up to 40 Ukrainian military personnel, 27 motor vehicles and an electronic warfare station were destroyed," it said.
Russian troops struck Ukrainian long-range unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) assembly, storage and launch sites and enemy deployment areas over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, armament, ammunition and materiel depots, workshops for the assembly and sites for the storage and launch of long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 158 locations," the ministry said.
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,226 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 1,226 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 268,113 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,336 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,792 multiple rocket launchers, 36,785 field artillery guns and mortars and 75,272 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

title: Tsadkan’s “Reforms” Have Fragmented Tigray’s Unity
body: SUPPORT ETHIOPIA INSIGHT .wpedon-container .wpedon-select, .wpedon-container .wpedon-input { width: 200px; min-width: 200px; max-width: 200px; } A campaign against the TPLF undermined Tigray’s unity while its people’s urgent needs went unmet. Tigray’s struggle is not a dispute between TPLF elites and the Prosperity Party, nor is it tribal politics. It is a popular cause. No faction can claim to defend it while subordinating the region’s interests to its own political ambitions. After the TPLF withdrew from Mekelle on 3 October, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF), aligned with former ENDF chief of staff Tsadkan Gebretensae, advanced through the region, capturing most major towns. TPLF-led forces retreated toward rural and mountainous areas as federal officials prepared to re-establish direct control over Tigray. The advance has brought the central contradiction into sharp focus: a faction that sought to remake Tigray by weakening the TPLF is now advancing alongside the federal forces the Tigrayan resistance was formed to oppose. Tigray has endured invasion, devastation, displacement, siege, dehumanization, and enormous loss. The genocide inflicted physical destruction and left deep collective trauma, straining the solidarity on which Tigrayans had long relied. The November 2022 Pretoria Agreement offered a way out. People at home and abroad accepted it as Plan A, deferring demands for justice and suspending some war-crimes documentation in the hope that diplomacy could secure a lasting peace. The years since have brought neither the promised recovery nor the political unity needed to achieve it. Tsadkan and his allies, who presented themselves as reformers capable of taking Tigray beyond the TPLF, helped deepen those divisions. Their political opportunism weakened the party and the institutions associated with the resistance while leaving the population’s most pressing problems unresolved. Weakening Defenses Within the Interim Administration led by Getachew Reda, Tsadkan Gebretinsae’s faction made dismantling the TPLF a central objective . The campaign extended beyond challenging the party’s leadership or demanding internal reform. It sought to displace the political outlook and historical narrative through which the TPLF had mobilized Tigrayans. Opposition to the TPLF brought together people with different grievances but no common answer to Tigray’s predicament. Old disputes, including those dating to the Haile Selassie and Derg eras, returned to the fore. Tsadkan’s allies cultivated provincial loyalties, or awrajawinet , and sought political support in Southern and Southeastern Tigray, areas they hoped to draw toward the Prosperity Party. A political geography took shape in which Southern, Eastern, and Southeastern Tigray were treated as receptive to change, while Shire, Adwa, and Axum were associated with resistance to it. Southern Tigray became contested ground among the Prosperity Party, the TPLF, and the Interim Administration. Armed groups were also established in Afar to target the TPLF, the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF), and Tigray’s regional leadership. The mobilization deepened existing grievances and political fragmentation, helping create conditions in which youths from these areas were recruited into armed groups in Afar. The TPLF had ample reason to face criticism over maladministration and corruption. But weakening the principal political and military structures through which Tigray had defended itself, without securing a credible alternative, left the region more vulnerable to federal encroachment. The return of internally displaced Tigrayans and refugees from Sudan should have been the foremost test of the post-Pretoria settlement. People driven from their homes needed security, services, and a route back. Those obligations could not reasonably be postponed while political elites pursued other ambitions. Yet access to the sea became a growing concern in Tigray’s political debate, aligning regional interests with the federal government’s increasingly confrontational agenda. Tsadkan embraced the argument for sea access despite its implications for Eritrean sovereignty and the risk of another war. He did so even as Tigray struggled to recover from a war that had devastated its communities and its leaders became entangled in a geopolitical project that risked exposing the region to another war. The return of displaced people, restoration of services, and pursuit of justice received less political attention than the struggle over who would govern Tigray and how it might support Addis Ababa’s regional ambitions. Tigray had already paid an enormous price in the previous war. Its recovery required room to determine its own priorities, not another conflict in which its people would bear the costs of decisions made elsewhere. Rewriting the Struggle The campaign against the TPLF was fought through narratives as well as political organization. Media platforms associated with Tsadkan’s allies concentrated on the party’s alleged failures and sought to detach Tigrayans from the movement that had led their resistance. The campaign also exploited postwar regret and trauma, as well as divisions over Tigray’s political future and the question of self-determination. Some of the criticism resonated for good reason. Young people had died in vast numbers, leaders deserved scrutiny—including Lt. Gen. Tsadkan, who was credited with playing a key role in devising the TDF’s battle strategy—and the population had every right to demand peace. But calls for reform increasingly became arguments against the resistance itself. Young people were told they should not die for 80-year-old leaders or serve as cannon fodder. The TPLF was accused of prolonging the war to preserve its power and, in some accounts, of bearing responsibility for the suffering inflicted on Tigray. The effect was to redirect public anger. The conduct of Tigray’s leaders became the focus, while the responsibility of the forces that invaded and devastated the region faded from view. Tigray’s quest for self-determination was forgotten; individual figures and parties, rather than the cause itself, came to dominate politics. Genuine grievances were used to weaken the political cohesion needed to confront the consequences of that invasion. Tsadkan’s own history makes his subsequent position difficult to separate from the wider argument. He was a senior military figure in November 2020, when the decision was taken to strike the Northern Command amid warnings of an impending attack by joint Ethiopian and Eritrean forces. During the war, the BBC described him as “Ethiopia’s Tigray rebel mastermind.” His later campaign against the TPLF raises questions about how he came to understand the struggle he had helped lead. His split from the TPLF in 2001, following the Ethio-Eritrean War and Meles Zenawi’s decision not to capture Asmara, is also relevant. That experience shaped Tsadkan’s outlook and left a lasting sense of unfinished business. The atrocities committed by Eritrean forces during the recent war revived similar feelings among Tigrayans who regretted the earlier decision. But regret over Asmara can lead to a dangerous conclusion: that Tigray should join a future Ethiopian war against Eritrea to secure sea access, or risk giving Abiy Ahmed a pretext to attack it. That would place Tigray’s security at the service of Addis Ababa’s ambitions. The “Stop Conscription” campaign revealed a related imbalance. Opposition to forced recruitment is legitimate, but the campaign focused on Tigray’s defensive mobilization while giving far less comparable attention to underage recruitment and forced drafting by the Ethiopian National Defense Force. In the circumstances, its political effect was to undermine the TPLF and TDF at a time when Tigray’s security remained unresolved. The Cost The result was a weakened TDF, declining recruitment and morale, significant desertion, and a fractured political landscape that left Tigray increasingly vulnerable to federal control. Provincial grievances and competing administrations widened the divisions that federal forces have now exploited. Western Tigray remains occupied, displaced people remain unable to return home, and refugees are still stranded in Sudan. The commitments made at Pretoria remain unfulfilled, while the TPLF’s loss of Mekelle and the advance of federal forces mark a further erosion of Tigray’s political and military autonomy. Tsadkan’s defenders argue that he was trying to reform an authoritarian and corrupt TPLF. The need for reform was real. But reform did not require dismantling Tigray’s defences, especially while external threats continued to endanger its survival. Nor did the TPLF’s failures justify aligning with forces responsible for the devastation of the region. The alternative was not to leave the TPLF beyond criticism. It was to pursue reform without destroying the capacity for collective defense, unite political forces around implementing Pretoria, and make the return of displaced people and refugees a central measure of progress. Federal violations required scrutiny alongside the TPLF’s failings. Tigray also needed a position on Eritrea and the wider region grounded in its own security, rather than in Addis Ababa’s ambitions. Mekete III The renewed war has brought the consequences into sharper focus. Tigrayans aligned with Tsadkan are participating in military operations alongside the Ethiopian army against Tigray. For many Tigrayans, this crosses a line that ordinary disputes over leadership or reform cannot explain away. The renewed war has already brought air strikes, artillery exchanges, and a federal advance across much of Tigray. Reported air strikes in Adwa and Sheraro killed at least 17 people in early October, while fighting continued near the Tekeze River and federal forces pushed north to the Eritrean border. Reports put the number of air strikes during the previous two-year war at 65, excluding attacks on military establishments, and report more than 70 air attacks in the renewed fighting. Tsadkan and his associates have aligned themselves with forces responsible for grave crimes against Tigray. Their campaign against the TPLF and the institutions associated with the resistance has coincided with renewed federal military action and the recapture of Mekelle. The post-Pretoria period has thus become another chapter in Tigray’s resistance—“Mekete III”: a renewed struggle to defend Tigray’s security, advance self-determination, and secure a future in which genocide can never again be inflicted on its people. If politics, law, and diplomacy cannot secure peace or resolve Tigray’s fundamental questions, the right to collective self-defense remains. Any such course must rest on the will of the people and legitimate institutions, rather than on a faction claiming an exclusive mandate. Pretoria offered a path toward peace; it did not authorize the installation of a Prosperity Party surrogate or give any organization an indefinite right to rule. Tigray needs to recover the unity and political agency eroded since the agreement. That means allowing genuine debate over leadership and past mistakes without surrendering the region’s security or leaving its future to competing elites. It also means dismantling cultivated hostility and pursuing reconciliation with Afar, Amhara, Eritrea, and Sudan, whose peoples will remain Tigray’s neighbours regardless of who holds power. The struggle continues. It is not about which party or which Tigrayan takes office in Mekelle, but about the aspiration for a free and liberated Tigray, securing its future, and ensuring that genocide is never inflicted upon Tigray again. The legitimacy of any party or political force will depend on its commitment to these causes. .wpedon-container .wpedon-select, .wpedon-container .wpedon-input { width: 200px; min-width: 200px; max-width: 200px; } Query or correction?
