title: Evolver DFR Debuts a Complete Drone as First Responder Program for Public Safety Agencies
body:
The solution, powered by Drone Nerds, combines Parrot ANAFI UKR aircraft, DBOX autonomous docking station, and SkyfireAI software, with implementation support and training.
Evolver DFR, powered by Drone Nerds, a division of XTI Aerospace, Inc. (NASDAQ: XTIA), today launched its Drone as First Responder (DFR) program, which gives police, fire, and emergency agencies everything they need to confidently send a drone to an emergency call. The solution debuts this week at the International Association of Chiefs of Police (IACP) Annual Conference and Exposition in Orlando.
Evolver DFR integrates the Parrot ANAFI UKR GOV aircraft, the DBOX PRT autonomous docking station, and SkyfireAI’s FlyAura public safety software into one purpose-built emergency response system. Within minutes of a call, the Evolver DFR solution puts real-time aerial video and data in front of dispatchers and commanders, improving situational awareness, protecting responders, and helping departments send resources where they are needed most.
“Launching a DFR program involves more than purchasing a drone. Agencies need the aircraft, software, infrastructure, training, and ongoing support to make the system part of their daily operations,” said Jeremy Schneiderman, Interim CEO of XTI Aerospace and CEO of Drone Nerds. “Evolver DFR brings those pieces together through a single solution.”
Parrot ANAFI UKR GOV, Blue UAS approved, carries wide and telephoto cameras with 35x zoom and a 640 thermal sensor, uses AES-256 encryption on its radio links, and is FIPS 140-2 compliant. It launches from and returns to the DBOX, a climate-controlled docking station, built specifically for the aircraft, that recharges it between flights and operates in heat, cold, and rain.
FlyAura software lets authorized users fly missions, stream live video, and share a common operating picture from a web browser, with TAK integration and a searchable record of every flight.
“The ANAFI UKR GOV was designed to deliver mission-critical aerial intelligence in demanding operational environments. Through our collaboration with DBOX, SkyfireAI and Drone Nerds, agencies can now deploy a fully integrated DFR solution that combines secure autonomous operations, thermal imaging, and long-range visual capabilities in a streamlined platform built specifically for public safety,” said Chris Roberts, Senior Vice President & Chief Revenue Officer of Parrot.
“We know a dock is only valuable if it is ready every time a call comes in,” said Dr. Linas Gelazanskas, CEO at DBOX. “We engineered the DBOX PRT around the ANAFI UKR so the two work as one system in any weather. Together, we called it Evolver DFR.”
Evolver DFR goes well beyond buying equipment. The solution team guides each agency from the first needs assessment through coverage planning, site selection, installation, system integration, and training. It also supports agencies through FAA approval processes, including
Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) authorizations, so new programs are ready to operate safely and in compliance.
Built around proven public safety workflows, Evolver DFR gives departments automated dispatch, remote operations, live video streaming, advanced imaging, and real-time information sharing. Incident commanders can assess threats earlier, coordinate personnel more effectively, avoid unnecessary deployments, and make better-informed decisions before responders arrive on scene.
Every program includes Always Flying TM by Drone Nerds, which provides expedited replacement aircraft when equipment is damaged, along with dedicated technical support, maintenance resources, and operational help. Always Flying minimizes downtime so departments can count on aerial response when their communities need it most.
Unlike traditional DFR offerings built around ongoing subscriptions, Evolver DFR lets agencies buy a complete, multi-year program covering multiple locations on a single purchase order. With no recurring subscription fees for the contracted solution, departments gain predictable budgets, simpler procurement, and the flexibility to expand coverage while keeping long-term costs under control.
“The future of Drone as First Responder isn’t just about getting an aircraft in the air. It’s about what happens before, during, and after every mission,” said Don Mathis, CEO of SkyfireAI.
“With FlyAura, we’re bringing AI-assisted mission planning, remote flight operations, and real-time intelligence together in one platform. Combined with SkyfireAI’s operational expertise, Evolver DFR gives agencies the flexibility to manage their own programs or rely on our team to operate them. That’s how we move DFR beyond individual deployments and make it a scalable, everyday public safety capability.”
Evolver DFR will be on display at IACP 2026 in Orlando from October 24-26 at Booth 2761, where representatives from SkyfireAI and Drone Nerds will be in attendance.
Agencies can schedule a demonstration at www.evolverdfr.com .

title: Kyrgyzstan Economic Growth: Government Targets 8% Annually
body: Kyrgyzstan has set a target of average annual real GDP growth of at least 8% and a 20% annual increase in foreign direct investment inflows through the end of 2030. Bishkek aims to achieve these goals by developing export-oriented industries, expanding transport routes, and attracting international capital. While recent international forecasts suggest growth could exceed 8% this year, sustaining that pace through 2030 remains a challenge. The government outlined the priorities at a meeting in Bishkek on October 21. Its plans include expanding production of export goods, modernizing trade and customs procedures, strengthening private property protections, and improving businesses’ access to long-term financing. Positive Momentum Set to Continue The targets are set out in the National Development Program through 2030 , adopted in June 2025. The program calls for nominal GDP to reach at least $30 billion and GDP per capita to rise to $4,500. International forecasts suggest Kyrgyzstan’s economy will maintain strong growth in the near term, although a slowdown is expected. Following 11.1% growth in 2025, the IMF forecasts 9% growth in 2026 and 7% in 2027, while the World Bank projects 9.6% growth this year. However, both institutions have highlighted risks to the country’s economic momentum, including a potential slowdown in re-export trade, weaker growth in Russia and China, rising energy prices, and tighter sanctions restrictions. To maintain rapid growth, Bishkek intends to support food processing, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, light manufacturing, machinery production, and mineral processing. The goal is to increase exports of domestically produced goods. Infrastructure-led Growth One of the country’s largest infrastructure projects remains the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. Construction began in December 2024, with completion scheduled for 2030. The project is estimated to cost $4.7 billion, including $2.3 billion in loans from Chinese banks. China holds a 51% stake in the joint project company, while Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan each own 24.5%. The railway is expected to give Kyrgyzstan its first direct rail link to China and provide Uzbekistan with an alternative route to the Chinese market. For Bishkek, it offers an opportunity to generate transit revenue and develop logistics centers. However, the route’s commercial viability will depend on freight volumes, tariffs, and the efficiency of border crossings. Another major project is the Kambarata-1 hydropower plant, which Kyrgyzstan is advancing jointly with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Additional electricity generation capacity is needed, among other purposes, to support industrial expansion. On October 14, Kyrgyzstan’s ambassador to Switzerland presented both projects to potential investors in Geneva. Bishkek also plans to encourage state-owned companies to issue Eurobonds, expand long-term financing through state banks, and develop the Tamchy special financial and investment zone to attract international capital. Logistics, information technology, tourism, and financial services have been identified as promising sectors. Risks At the same time, Kyrgyzstan’s close economic ties with Russia create additional risks for its banking sector and foreign trade. The IMF has warned that exposure to international sanctions and weaknesses in financial oversight could disrupt banking relationships and cross-border trade. A further challenge is ensuring that major infrastructure projects benefit the wider economy. As The Times of Central Asia noted in its analysis of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, without the development of industrial zones, warehousing infrastructure, and workforce training, a substantial share of the economic benefits could accrue to transit operators and large companies rather than the broader local economy.

title: Ukraine Receives 252 Bodies From Russia, Identification to Follow
body:
Ukraine has received the bodies of 252 people whom Russia claims were Ukrainian servicemen, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War announced on Thursday, Oct. 22.
The headquarters said in a Telegram statement that law enforcement investigators and forensic specialists would carry out the procedures needed to establish the identities of those returned.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“According to the Russian side, the bodies belong to Ukrainian military personnel,” the statement says.
In June 2025, Ukraine said Russia mixed in bodies of deceased Russian troops during repatriations.
The latest operation involved the coordination headquarters, the Joint Center under the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), the interior ministry and the parliamentary human rights commissioner’s office.
The Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Missing under Special Circumstances, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) and other security and defense institutions also participated.
The headquarters thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for its assistance and support in carrying out the repatriation.
It separately acknowledged personnel from the Armed Forces’ Joint Center for Civil-Military Cooperation Support, who transport repatriated remains to specialized state institutions.
Their work includes arranging the transfer of the bodies to law enforcement representatives within the interior ministry system and forensic medical institutions within the health ministry system. Military civil-military cooperation structures oversee the broader coordination.
The return of remains is one stage in a process that can leave families waiting months or years for definitive information about missing relatives.
Ukrainian police have described complex forensic and safety procedures required after repatriation , including mandatory checks for dangerous objects before identification work begins.
Taras Tarasenko, a senior police investigator in the Kirovohrad region, said explosive objects and grenades had been discovered in repatriated bodies on several occasions.
After safety checks, specialists look for documents, mobile phones, military identification tags and bank cards. They also photograph clothing, tattoos and other distinguishing features that may help establish a person’s identity.
Investigators have sometimes received the remains of several people mixed in a single bag. Forensic experts must separate them for examination and DNA analysis.
Tarasenko said batches of 200-250 bodies could arrive at once, while his team aimed to examine around 10 a day to preserve the quality of its work.
A DNA match becomes possible once both the relative’s sample and the profile from the returned remains are entered into the database.
Earlier in October, Ukraine announced plans for an interagency group to accelerate identification , with a significant share of more than 26,000 repatriated bodies and remains still unidentified.
Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov outlined the initiative on Oct. 2 following a meeting on the rights of veterans, prisoners of war, missing persons and their families.
The proposed measures included reviewing the work of forensic medical examination bureaus, particularly in the regions, and seeking additional international capacity for DNA testing.
Budanov criticized bureaucratic delays and violations of forensic procedures, saying families needed reliable information about their loved ones as quickly as possible. He did not specify how many of the returned remains were still awaiting identification.
Ukraine previously received 252 bodies in a separate operation on Sept. 17. In that case, Russia said the remains belonged to Ukrainian citizens, including military personnel, pending Ukrainian identification procedures.
Other returns this year included 522 bodies in June and 1,000 in April.
The larger repatriation process followed agreements reached during talks in Istanbul in June 2025, when Ukraine and Russia committed to returning thousands of bodies.
Under that arrangement, each side agreed to return the remains of 6,000 fallen soldiers, according to then-Defense Minister Rustem Umerov. The agreements enabled successive repatriation operations despite the continuing war.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Ghanaian actor and media personality, Kwame Dzokoto of Edziban fame, dies
body: Ghanaian actor, comedian and media personality Seth Kwame Dzokoto has died. The entertainer, widely known for his portrayal of Judge Koboo in the popular Ghanaian television series Efiewura, died on Thursday, October 22, 2026. Reports say he collapsed during a radio show at Owass Radio in the Tarkwa Nsuaem Municipality of the Western Region, where he lived. He was rushed to a hospital in Tarkwa, where he was pronounced dead on arrival, according to a source in the National Democratic Congress (NDC), to which he belonged. He was 51 years old. His death comes barely weeks after images of him looking unwell went viral on social media. His reported death marks the loss of a familiar face in Ghanaian entertainment, where he built a career spanning television, radio broadcasting, comedy and voice-over work. A household name through Efiewura Dzokoto became widely recognised for playing Judge Koboo in Efiewura, one of Ghana’s well-known local television productions. His performance helped establish him as a recognisable figure in Ghanaian homes, with the character becoming one of the defining roles of his entertainment career. Beyond acting, Dzokoto demonstrated his versatility as a television presenter, particularly through TV3’s food and tourism programme Edziban. The programme explored Ghanaian cuisine and local food culture, introducing audiences to different meals and culinary experiences across the country. His work in television, alongside his comedy and advertising voice-overs, helped build his profile as an entertainer who could connect with audiences across different formats. Broadcasting and voice-over career Dzokoto also had a career in radio, working with stations including Skyy Power FM in Takoradi and Hello FM in Kumasi. His broadcasting work complemented his television appearances and voice-over assignments, making him a familiar voice as well as a recognisable face. His career reflected a range of interests within the media industry, from comedy and acting to presenting and broadcasting. Entry into politics Outside entertainment, Dzokoto ventured into partisan politics under the banner of the National Democratic Congress (NDC). He contested the Tarkwa-Nsuaem parliamentary seat in the 2016 general election, taking his public profile beyond the entertainment industry and into electoral politics. Although his political career did not result in a parliamentary seat, his participation reflected his interest in public affairs and national development.

title: One or two Russia-US joint projects could be launched by year-end — AmCham chief
body:
ISTANBUL, October 22. /TASS/. One or two joint projects between Russia and the United States could be launched before the end of the year, President and CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce in Russia (AmCham Russia) Robert Agee told reporters on the sidelines of the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum.
"We discussed some projects and what our joint actions would be. <…> They (the projects - TASS) are being prepared. I hope one or two could be ready," he said when asked whether joint Russian-US projects would be ready before the end of the year.
Agee stressed that these projects would not require the lifting of temporary or permanent sanctions. "Even if they did, as we can see, President Trump has the authority to change this policy very quickly. We are very pleased about that," he said.

title: Popoola: Africa Must Connect Capital to Build Business Champions
body: Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX Group) has called for a more integrated approach to capital formation across Africa, connecting businesses with appropriate sources of financing at every stage of their growth to build globally competitive enterprises. Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of NGX Group, Temi Popoola, made the call at the Financial Times Africa Summit 2026 in London on Wednesday, October 21, during a panel session titled ‘Building African Champions – The Investment Case for Scaling SMEs.’ Popoola noted that capital markets have traditionally focused on large, mature companies ready to list, while promising businesses often require several rounds of financing before they can access public markets. “Historically, we have taken a sort of a top-down approach to look for big companies ready to go public,” he said, explaining that businesses typically progress from founder funding and support from friends and family to venture capital, private investment and, ultimately, public-market financing. He observed that the growing availability of private capital, alongside fewer new listings and an increase in delistings across several markets, underscores the need for a more connected capital formation ecosystem. Rather than waiting for businesses to mature before engaging with them, capital market institutions must find ways to support promising enterprises earlier in their development. This requires stronger connections between public markets and the broader investment landscape, including private equity, venture capital and institutional investors. Such linkages can help businesses access financing as they grow while creating potential exit opportunities for private investors through public listings. Popoola also highlighted family-owned enterprises, describing them as “hidden champions” that could make significant contributions to African capital markets if supported to scale and access appropriate sources of capital. He identified receivables and invoice financing as another way capital markets can help ease funding constraints facing smaller businesses. By enabling companies to leverage invoices, receivables and purchase orders linked to larger corporate customers, these financing structures can help SMEs unlock working capital and sustain growth. In Nigeria, the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) Growth Board provides small-cap and growth-oriented companies with a pathway to raise long-term capital through the public market, supported by more flexible listing requirements. The Exchange is also working with institutions such as the Bank of Industry (BoI) to strengthen SME investment readiness through targeted engagements, capacity building and greater awareness of capital market financing opportunities. These efforts support the development of a stronger pipeline of businesses capable of accessing public markets as they grow. Popoola’s remarks underscores the importance of a connected financing ecosystem in enabling promising African businesses to transition into established enterprises, attract institutional investment and expand beyond their domestic markets. Achieving this requires collaboration across public and private capital providers, supported by capital markets equipped to facilitate sustainable business growth and broader economic development. The Financial Times Africa Summit 2026 brought together business and financial sector leaders to examine investment opportunities and the conditions required to support Africa’s next generation of business champions.

title: Congressmen urge Trump, Musk to give Ukraine ability to destroy missile launchers in Russia – media
body:
American congressmen, including 16 members of the Democratic Party and seven members of the Republican Party, have signed a letter urging U.S President Donald Trump and SpaceX founder Elon Musk to grant Ukraine access to Starlink satellite systems to detect missile launchers on the territory of Russia.
"We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," reads the text of the letter sent on Wednesday, as cited by The Hill.
Among the Republicans who signed the letter are Joe Wilson (South Carolina), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), Don Bacon (Nebraska), Carlos Gimenez (Florida), Jeff Hurd (Colorado), Andy Harris (Maryland), and Max Miller (Ohio).
"Mr. President, we all share the goal of ending the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused... If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian arrows, it must be able to strike the archer. The Starlink system, operated by Mr. Musk's SpaceX, could help with this," the letter states, with the congressmen noting that Vladimir Putin "currently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed."
As reported, Ukraine began using StarShield in 2024. Standard StarLink (Starlink Mini), installed on drones, has a limited speed of up to 160 km/h, which is insufficient to perform certain missions. To make an aircraft fly faster, it is necessary to gain access specifically to the military version of StarLink – StarShield.
SpaceX, without warning the Ukrainian Defense Forces on the night of October 14, unilaterally restricted the operation of StarShield terminals; this complicated the work of UAV missions, in particular interceptors and middle strikes. By the end of that same day, the operation of terminals at speeds of 160 km/h resumed, but Ukraine received confirmation that the 160 km/h restriction applies only within its territory.
On the same day, Musk stated that decisions regarding restrictions on the operation of military StarShield systems are made by the U.S military and the president, and commercial StarLink cannot be used for offensive military actions. However, Trump later stated that Washington was not involved in slowing down StarShield for Ukraine, and U.S Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that StarShield was allegedly unavailable to Ukraine and the White House had nothing to do with disruptions in StarLink's operation. U.S Secretary of War Pete Hegseth reported that his department refrained from issuing any directives regarding restricting StarShield's operation. Later, the British newspaper The Telegraph, citing its own sources, reported that Musk personally appealed to Trump with a proposal to limit StarLink's operating speed for the Ukrainian military.
Following this, a number of senators and congressmen stated the unacceptability of such actions, Musk's influence on the course of the war in Ukraine and U.S security, and that they would demand an investigation into the restrictions on the operation of StarShield systems in Ukraine and hold those responsible accountable.
On October 20, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the American side had restored the operation of Ukraine's early warning system for Russian ballistic missile launches and announced a conversation with Rubio, while Rubio himself stated that he had nothing to do with decisions made by Musk and SpaceX regarding the operation of StarLink and StarShield.
The European Commission stated that SpaceX's restrictions on StarLink services for Ukraine contradict agreements, and the company must ensure full access for Ukraine.

title: BAS Finance: SME Lending Requires Better Risk Assessment, Not Just More Capital
body: * Firm disburses N55bn to over 120 businesses in nine months, expands invoice-backed financing Sunday Aborisade in Abuja The Managing Director of BAS Finance, Adnan Kayode, has said that expanding access to credit for Nigerian small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs) requires better risk assessment and a deeper understanding of businesses’ transactions rather than an exclusive reliance on conventional collateral. Kayode said lenders could improve access to financing by assessing verifiable invoices, buyers and delivery records to determine the repayment capacity of businesses that might otherwise struggle to secure credit from traditional banks. He spoke as BAS Finance emerged SME Lender of the Year at the 2026 BusinessDay Banking and Financial Institutions (BAFI) Awards held on October 9 at The Civic Centre, Lagos. The company’s sister subsidiary, BAS Capital, also won the SME Investment Bank of the Year award, recognising its role in structuring and raising capital for businesses seeking to expand beyond conventional borrowing. Explaining the company’s lending philosophy, in a statement on Thursday in Abuja, Kayode said the challenge facing many businesses was not necessarily the absence of viable commercial opportunities but the difficulty of satisfying the requirements through which financial institutions assess creditworthiness. “Lending to a small business well is an underwriting problem before it is a capital problem,” he said. “If you can see the invoice, the buyer and the delivery record, you are not taking the risk the market thinks you are taking. What we have built is the ability to see those things quickly enough for the financing to still be useful.” BAS Finance said it disbursed N55 billion to more than 120 businesses over nine months, with an average transaction size of N2 billion and a median disbursement period of seven days. The company focuses on financing businesses that fall outside conventional banking criteria, particularly through arrangements linked to receivables and productive assets. Its approach places emphasis on identifiable commercial transactions and repayment sources, offering an alternative for businesses whose financing applications may be constrained by collateral requirements or lengthy approval processes. Through Zuvy Technologies, acquired by BAS Group in 2025, BAS Finance has also expanded its invoice-backed financing services to suppliers of large corporate organisations. The model enables suppliers to seek financing against invoices arising from completed or verifiable transactions, potentially easing the pressure on working capital while they await payment from corporate buyers. Kayode’s position highlights a broader challenge in Nigeria’s SME financing market, where the cost of borrowing is only one of several obstacles confronting business owners seeking formal credit. Lengthy application procedures, collateral requirements and difficulties demonstrating creditworthiness have also constrained access to financing, particularly for enterprises with limited fixed assets but identifiable customers and commercial transactions. Estimates of Nigeria’s SME financing gap vary according to the methodology used. However, a figure of approximately N13 trillion was presented at the 2025 Annual Directors Conference of the Chartered Institute of Directors, underscoring the scale of the challenge. Micro, small and medium enterprises account for a substantial share of economic activity and employment, yet many continue to face difficulties obtaining financing suited to their operational needs. BAS Group’s position is that addressing the challenge requires lenders and investment institutions to match financing instruments to businesses’ circumstances, rather than treating every funding request as a conventional loan application. Group Chief Executive Officer, Abdulateef Hussein, said businesses required different forms of capital depending on their activities and stages of development. “The question is not only whether capital exists. It is whether anyone has done the work of matching it to the business in front of them,” Hussein said. He explained that a manufacturer seeking funds to fulfil a confirmed order might require short-term working capital, while a company pursuing an acquisition or major expansion might need structured growth capital. “Most of what gets called a funding gap is a translation failure,” he added. The group’s approach combines lending with investment banking and capital-raising services through its subsidiaries. While BAS Finance provides working capital and transaction-linked financing, BAS Capital advises companies that have outgrown conventional lending but remain below the threshold that typically attracts larger investment banking institutions. BAS Capital’s Managing Director, Yinka Adetuberu, said many growing businesses needed financial institutions willing to undertake the structuring required to attract institutional and development finance investors. “The companies we work with are not short of ambition or of a market. They are short of someone willing to do the structuring work at their size,” Adetuberu said. The company reported closing more than 25 transactions valued at over N50 billion in 2026. The recognition of both subsidiaries at the BAFI Awards highlights the two financing approaches pursued by the group: providing credit to businesses with identifiable commercial transactions and structuring investment capital for companies seeking to finance their next stage of growth. Founded in 2020 and headquartered in Abuja, BAS Group operates across lending, investment banking, wealth and asset management, insurance and financial technology. Its subsidiaries include BAS Finance, BAS Capital, BAS Wealth, BAS Financial Services, BAS Technologies, ALLY Healthcare and ALLY Microinsurance. The group said the latest recognition marked the second consecutive year its companies had received awards at the BAFI ceremony. BAS Capital was previously named Emerging Investment Bank of the Year.

title: International situation continues to deteriorate, says Russian defense minister
body:
MINSK, October 22. /TASS/. The international environment keeps worsening calling for preventive steps, Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov told Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, according to BelTA news agency.
"You are absolutely right. The international situation continues to deteriorate. It remains extremely complex. Not only is it complex, but it is becoming increasingly unpredictable. We can see what is happening in Europe and the Middle East. And this requires preemptive actions," he said.
Belousov said this was among the key topics on his agenda for discussions with Belarusian Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin.

title: Russia set to hold inaugural international laser tag sports competitions next year
body:
KRASNOYARSK, October 22. /TASS/. International laser tag competitions will be held in Russia next year, Head of the Russian Laser Tag Sports Federation Dmitry Solodov told TASS on Thursday.
TASS reported earlier that laser tag competitions have been recognized and registered as an official sport in Russia.
"We are holding international competitions with the participation of athletes from various countries," Solodov said.
"We are pioneers in the official recognition of this sport. Now we have also set the task of forming and establishing an international federation for this sport. As of today, we plan to organize international competitions in 2027 with the participation of 15 countries."
The 14th Russia: Country of Sports annual international sports forum is taking place in Russia’s second-largest Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk on October 21-23 with the support of the Russian government and the Sports Ministry. The event is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Krasnoyarsk Region government. TASS is the official information partner of the forum.
The annual forum was established in 2009 by a decree of the Russian president to promote physical culture and sport, international sports cooperation, and a healthy lifestyle.

title: Ebola: ‘They’ll Be Blacklisted,’ Africa CDC Warns Aid Partners Against Lack Of Transparency
body: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has warned that it will blacklist partners who fail to account for funds received to combat disease outbreaks on the continent. ﻿ It also warned that the era of organisations operating without transparency is over. The Director General of the Africa CDC, Dr. Jean Kaseya, stated this during an interview on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday. He expressed displeasure that, out of the $962 million already disbursed from the $3 billion pledge made on the margins of the UN, the G20 meeting in September, some partners claimed they received around $220 million. “There was a practice in many African countries, I say many, not all, but many. Partners will get money from donors. They will implement their activities without disclosing how much they got, without even sending a report to the government,” Kaseya. “And when the outbreak is over, we’ll hear from some capitals that billions of dollars were invested to stop this outbreak. I said, enough is enough. It will never happen again on this continent. “We managed to fundraise. We got figures from all donors. Out of $3 billion pledged, based on the last meeting that the US organised in September on the margins of the UN G20 meeting, we got a total pledge of $3 billion.” “Out of that, $962 million was already disbursed. We went to work with the DRC government. We organised a meeting with partners. Only 19 out of 92 partners attended. These 90 partners who attended one night disclosed that they received around $220 million. “If I see, out of $962 million disbursed, the government knows only about $220 million, what kind of government can accept to lead a response without knowing even how much they have, without knowing who’s doing what and where? “Then I said, stop. I need first to know: where is the $700 million? For now we are not talking about mismanagement. For now we are not talking about fraud. No, for now we are talking about traceability; we want to know where is money? “This is why even in Nigeria, I already instructed Professor Aliko Ahmed, who’s working closely with Professor Mohammed Pate. His role will be to coordinate all partners who will be working in Nigeria and to provide the updates to the minister on a daily basis,” he added. Asked whether he could rule out fraud or mismanagement, the Africa CDC DG said, “You know we are working with donors. The US, they are sending me today the list of partners who got money, how much they got. “The European Union, they already shared with me. I know exactly who got what. Other partners they are sending to other donors; they are sending to us. “If today a partner got money from a donor, and the partner is unable to tell us what he did with this money, then I will start talking about fraud. Then I will start talking about mismanagement. “But let me tell you, it’s not a threat. Partners who don’t want to comply with this rule, I will make sure that I will send a letter to all African countries, and I will go to the AU Assembly where they will be blacklisted in Africa.” The post Ebola: ‘They’ll Be Blacklisted,’ Africa CDC Warns Aid Partners Against Lack Of Transparency appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Saudi strike hits Indian boat off Yemen coast
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – Saudi Arabia targeted an Indian boat carrying 14 Indian nationals near Zuqar Island off western Yemen, and Yemeni forces rescued those aboard, armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree said.
Yemen's armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree said the Saudi army targeted an Indian pleasure boat near Zuqar Island off western Yemen, with 14 Indian nationals aboard, according to initial reports.
Saree said in a social media post that Yemeni armed forces rescued those on-board.
He warned that the Saudi action threatens international navigation in the Red Sea and said the international community must deter the Saudis from such irresponsible actions.

title: Kazakhstan Opens $15 Million Rare Metals Research Center with South Korea
body: Kazakhstan is seeking to turn more of its mineral wealth into high-value materials for electric vehicles, electronics, and other advanced industries with the opening of a Korean-backed rare-metals research center in Almaty. The center, which opened on October 21, is supported by a five-year funding program worth approximately $15 million. Based at the Institute of Metallurgy and Ore Beneficiation at Satbayev University, the center will develop technologies for processing and refining rare metals. The project is being developed under South Korea’s official development assistance program, with the participation of the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology (KITECH) and the Korea National Institute of Rare Metals (KORAM). South Korea has outlined a five-year funding plan worth 19.8 billion won (approximately $15 million) for the Almaty center between 2026 and 2030, including 2 billion won ($1.5 million) for 2026. Kazakhstan has substantial mineral resources, but extracting metals and producing finished materials require different technologies. The most challenging stages involve separating individual elements, purifying them, and producing materials suitable for industrial use. These are the processes the new center will focus on. The research is expected to be tested in cooperation with Kazakh mining and metallurgical companies. According to Satbayev University Rector Meiram Begentayev, research priorities should be determined by the needs of industry. “We expect our industrial partners to take an active role in the center’s work. Their specific production challenges will help identify priority areas for research, while joint testing will allow us to prepare scientific developments for implementation in industrial production,” Begentayev said. At the steering committee’s first meeting, participants discussed laboratory equipment, specialist training, and cooperation with industrial enterprises. The Almaty center was established as Kazakhstan seeks to develop its own capacity to process critical minerals. The country is holding talks with foreign partners interested in raw materials for batteries, electronics, and energy equipment. The Times of Central Asia previously reported on plans for the Almaty center in July. Kazakhstan has also proposed cooperation with Belgium on rare-earth metals processing. Authorities also plan to establish an internationally accredited laboratory in Astana to analyze mineral samples.

title: Defence spending in Northern Ireland hits record high
body: Ministry of Defence expenditure with industry in Northern Ireland rose by sixty-three per cent in a single year to reach £464 million in 2025-26, the highest level since records began, according to an answer given in Parliament. Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what recent assessment he had made of the geo-strategic importance of Northern Ireland. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Northern Ireland has a growing and strategically important defence sector, founded on a strong engineering heritage and backed by robust research competence, collaboration, and world-leading academic institutions. Recent figures show that MOD expenditure with UK industry in Northern Ireland rose by 63% compared to the previous year. In real terms this equates to £464 million in 2025-26, the highest level since records began. “In recognition of its geo-strategic importance and huge potential to support Defence meet its national objectives, the Northern Ireland Defence Growth Deal was launched earlier this year. It is a £50 million investment aiming to strengthen and grow NI’s defence ecosystem by supporting SMEs to scale capability, access opportunities and contribute to a more resilient UK supply chain.” Thales in Belfast carries most of that figure, and the Castlereagh site builds Starstreak and the Lightweight Multirole Missile, the weapons that have been fired in quantity in Ukraine and reordered repeatedly since, and the plant has taken contracts worth more than a billion pounds across the past three years while taking on hundreds of staff. Northern Ireland’s defence spend stood at around £190 million in 2023, so the figure has more than doubled in three years. Harland and Wolff’s Belfast yard sits in the same picture, now under Navantia ownership after the company’s collapse, with a share of the Fleet Solid Support ship programme that will see blocks built in Belfast and Appledore. Spirit AeroSystems, Denroy, Survitec and a substantial cluster of aerospace and engineering small firms feed into the wider total. The Northern Ireland Defence Growth Deal was launched this year, and this publication reported when Northern Ireland was to be boosted by the defence growth deal . Fifty million pounds aimed at small and medium firms is intended to let the supply chain around the large manufacturers scale up out of its dependence on single contracts. The post Defence spending in Northern Ireland hits record high first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: FCT Police intercept SUV with concealed presidency number plate
body: By Kingsley Omonobi FCT Police Command operatives have intercepted a Lexus LX570 SUV with a concealed number plate in Maitama District of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). According to the Police, officers intercepted the SUV on 20th October 2026, at about 8 pm, and promptly arrested the occupant for investigation and subsequent prosecution. Spokesperson of the command, SP Josephine Adeh, said, “Preliminary investigations revealed that the concealed number plate bore the inscription ‘PRESIDENCY’ and registration number 10B218 FG. “Following the suspect’s claim of being the legitimate holder of the number plate, further investigations revealed that the plate’s registration documents were forged and that the suspect was impersonating a Permanent Secretary attached to the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation. “Investigations are ongoing, and the suspect will be charged to court upon their conclusion. “The FCT Police Command urges residents to remain law-abiding, cooperate with police operations, and promptly report suspicious persons or activities to the nearest Police Station or through the Command’s emergency numbers: 08032003913, 08061581938.” The post FCT Police intercept SUV with concealed presidency number plate appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Seplat Energy appoints Effiong Okon as chief executive officer
body:
Seplat Energy Plc has appointed Effiong Okon as its chief executive officer, making him the first Akwa Ibom indigene to occupy the top executive position at the Nigerian energy company.
Mr Okon, an engineer with more than 35 years of experience in the oil and gas industry, was appointed by the company’s board of directors in June 2026 and assumed office on 1 August 2026, according to information published on Seplat Energy’s website.
Onofiok Luke, a former member of the House of Representatives and former speaker of the Akwa Ibom State House of Assembly, commended the appointment, describing it as a significant milestone for the state.
In a Facebook post , Mr Luke congratulated Mr Okon, saying his emergence reflected years of professional dedication, competence and service.
He said the appointment should inspire young people from Akwa Ibom to pursue leadership positions in the oil and gas industry and other globally competitive sectors.
“For years, we have consistently clamoured, advocated and hoped to see our sons and daughters rise to the apex of International Oil Companies, particularly those operating within our communities and drawing substantially from our natural endowments,” Mr Luke wrote.
He also called for greater opportunities for local professionals and host communities, arguing that communities where oil and gas are extracted should participate not only in resource production but also in industry leadership, value creation and prosperity.
Mr Luke cited Udom Inoyo, a former vice chairman of ExxonMobil’s Nigerian affiliates, as one of the Akwa Ibom professionals who had previously attained senior leadership positions in the industry.
He wished Mr Okon a successful tenure and described the appointment as a source of inspiration to aspiring professionals from the state.
Mr Okon joined Seplat Energy in 2018 and has held several senior positions, including executive director of operations, director of new energy, and director of projects. He also served as managing director of ANOH Gas Processing Company Limited, a joint venture between Seplat Energy and Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC).
According to his biography, he oversaw the development of the 300-million-standard-cubic-feet-per-day ANOH Gas Processing Plant, which achieved its first gas in January 2026.
ANOH is an acronym for Assa North-Ohaji South, a major natural gas development project located in Imo State, Nigeria
Before joining Seplat, Mr Okon spent 26 years at Shell, where he held senior positions in Nigeria, Europe, the Middle East and the Americas. His assignments included vice president of cost leadership and continuous improvement in the Netherlands, general manager of deepwater and offshore assets in Nigeria, and deputy vice president technical and manager of the North Field at Qatar Shell.
He also participated in the commissioning and early production phases of Qatar’s Pearl gas-to-liquids project and QatarGas LNG Trains 7 and 8, according to his biography.
Mr Okon studied at the University of Benin and attended IMD Business School in Lausanne, Switzerland, and Harvard Business School in Boston, United States. He is a fellow of the Nigerian Society of Engineers and the UK Energy Institute, and a registered engineer in Nigeria.
He is married to Bertha Okon, and they have four children.
Seplat Energy was established in 2009 through a partnership between Shebah Petroleum Development Company and Platform Petroleum Joint Ventures. The company has since expanded its operations in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry, with interests spanning hydrocarbon production, gas processing, and energy transition initiatives.
A major turning point came in December 2024, when Seplat completed its acquisition of Mobil Producing Nigeria Unlimited (MPNU), the Nigerian shallow-water oil and gas business formerly owned by ExxonMobil. The transaction followed an agreement announced in February 2022 and regulatory approvals for the deal.
Following the acquisition, Seplat renamed the business Seplat Energy Producing Nigeria Unlimited (SEPNU). The acquired assets include interests in four oil mining leases — OMLs 67, 68, 70 and 104 — operated under a joint venture with NNPC, as well as associated infrastructure, including the Qua Iboe Terminal and interests in the Bonny River Terminal and gas processing facilities.
Seplat said the acquisition more than doubled its production and expanded its portfolio across onshore and shallow-water operations. The enlarged business has interests in oil and gas fields, gas processing facilities and export terminals, strengthening its position among Nigeria’s indigenous energy producers.
The company is listed on both the Nigerian Exchange and the London Stock Exchange. Its operations contribute to Nigeria’s oil production and domestic gas supply, with gas serving as an important fuel for electricity generation and industrial activity. The company has also identified gas-led growth and the development of cleaner energy solutions as priorities in its strategy.
Mr Okon takes over the leadership of the enlarged company following this expansion, with responsibility for overseeing its operations, project delivery, production growth, and gas development strategy.

title: Maksim Stepanenko’s Path from Kyrgyzstan to Silicon Valley
body: Maksim Stepanenko’s career has taken him from Aydarken in southern Kyrgyzstan to Silicon Valley. After co-founding Operator, an artificial intelligence startup acquired by OpenAI , he chose to step away rather than join the buyer. Stepanenko told The Times of Central Asia that he is now taking time off and working on new projects. From Aydarken to MIT Stepanenko was born in Aydarken, in Kyrgyzstan’s Batken region. Before entering university, he represented the country at the International Physics Olympiad . He received an honorable mention in Singapore in 2006, a silver medal in Iran in 2007, and a bronze in Vietnam in 2008. His route to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology was not immediate. After his first application was unsuccessful, he spent almost a year studying in Germany before entering MIT in 2009 to study computer science. While there, he worked as an undergraduate research assistant at the MIT Media Lab. Early Engineering Roles Stepanenko graduated in 2012. His early experience included two summer internships at Google and a role as one of the first software engineers at Locu, a startup founded by MIT graduates. Locu helped local businesses manage their online listings. A business could update its information once and distribute the changes across services including Yelp and Facebook. GoDaddy acquired the company in August 2013 for a reported $70 million. In 2014, Stepanenko joined cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase as employee number 21 . Over five years, his work included Coinbase Commerce and the USDC stablecoin, as well as Coinbase Ventures. “I graduated in 2012 and moved to [San Francisco] to work here, at a different startup. Around 2013-2014, I started spending more and more time on crypto – Bitcoin Talk was the popular forum at the time. I was finding it more and more interesting. And then, at some point, I decided I wanted to explore working full-time in this space. At that time, there wasn’t really any legitimate company in the space. Coinbase was the only company that was already relatively well known, at least here in Silicon Valley. So, I ended up joining Coinbase,” Stepanenko previously told Compound. Co-Founding Primer In 2019, On Deck’s Erik Torenberg introduced Stepanenko to Ryan Delk. The two co-founded Primer, an education startup offering online learning activities and, later, small in-person schools. Ryan Delk (left) and Maksim Stepanenko (right) Primer initially focused on homeschooling. During the COVID-19 pandemic, it developed online clubs where children could pursue shared interests and work together on projects. The company later allowed children to create and run their own clubs. It then developed microschools, combining small groups of students with in-person instruction and digital learning tools. The company’s history records expansion to Alabama in 2025 and Texas in 2026 . Primer raised a $3.7 million seed round in 2020, led by Founders Fund. In April 2022, it announced a further $15 million round , led by Founders Fund and co-led by Khosla Ventures. Stepanenko left Primer in November 2022. “I decided to step away from the company after we launched Microschools to explore some new ideas. My co-founder Ryan continues to run Primer, and the company is doing great,” Stepanenko told TCA. Building Operator In March 2024, Stepanenko co-founded Operator with his MIT classmate and friend Usman Masood. Masood had worked as an engineering manager at Stripe and vice president of engineering at Pipe. Initially named Dot Product, the startup built a platform for AI agents operating across voice and messaging channels. In its introductory post, the company described software designed to help operations teams handle workloads without increasing staffing at the same rate. Its first product was a voice agent for customer support. Michael Dong (left) and Usman Masood (right) The startup raised $6 million from investors including Index Ventures, Lachy Groom, and Conviction, before OpenAI acquired the business. Stepanenko chose not to join OpenAI following the deal. His personal website currently describes him as being on sabbatical. “I decided not to join OpenAI as part of the acquisition, and instead to take some time off and work on new projects,” Stepanenko told TCA. “More on this soon, hopefully.”

title: Putin will not risk using nuclear weapons because he would lose allies – Zelensky
body:
The head of state made the remarks on The Diary of a CEO podcast, hosted by British entrepreneur and investor Steven Bartlett, Ukrinform reports.
"I don't think they [the Russians] will risk using nuclear weapons, because then they definitely won't have any allies, I'm sure of that," Zelensky said.
According to him, if nuclear weapons were used once, this would open the door to their use in other conflicts as well, which would be catastrophic.
"That is why I think Putin will not risk using nuclear weapons," the president said.
In June, the Center for Countering Disinformation under Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council said the Russian regime had stepped up its nuclear threats, once again demonstrating the Kremlin's complete unwillingness to pursue a diplomatic settlement of its war against Ukraine. In particular, an opinion piece published in the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta openly advocated using tactical nuclear weapons on the battlefield to break through the Ukrainian Armed Forces' defenses.

title: Google Open-Sources Harness²: Self-Improving AI Agents Without Retraining
body:
Google's Harness² lets AI agents improve their prompts, tools, memory, and scripts through two recursive loops without touching model weights. Learn more, including how to run the free demo yourself.
Google Research has open-sourced Harness² (or Harness2 ), a framework that lets AI agents improve themselves without retraining the underlying model. Instead of touching model weights, Harness² rewrites the harness around the model: its prompts, tools, memory, skills, and scripts. Then it carries what it learned into the next task.
The code ships under the Apache 2.0 license , alongside a research paper, Harness²: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World , and a project site . The release is already being discussed on X .
This article explains how Harness² works and what its benchmark results show, then walks you through Google's free demo and a real benchmark run on Vertex AI. If you're looking for an open-source agent framework for self-improving AI agents, start here.
A harness is everything around a model that lets it act as an agent: prompts, tools, memory, skills, and orchestration. Harnessing is the work of optimizing it. Today, most teams do it by hand: an engineer watches the agent fail, tweaks the prompt, adds a tool, and tries again. That works for tasks you planned for, but breaks down in what the paper calls an open world , where agents meet tasks nobody anticipated.
Harness² automates that tuning "while keeping model weights fixed" (README). There's no fine-tuning and no new training data; only the model's surroundings change. It can edit eight components :
From the README, the first four build the model's context; tool guidance and scripts define its tool interface, subagents handle delegation, and plugins control middleware. Together they cover nearly everything about how an agent behaves except the model itself.
The superscript "2" in the name refers to two loops. One improves the harness for the current task; the other improves how harnesses get improved across tasks.
The top loop runs on every task. The highlighted improvement harness persists between tasks and shapes the next round of edits.
The key detail is that Harness² learns "from behavioral contrasts between executions, without ground-truth feedback." It never needs the correct answer, only the difference between two runs of the same task. That matters because in the open world, nobody hands an agent an answer key.
After each task, an experience reflector stores the adopted harness and "evidence-supported lessons" in a persistent improvement harness , which guides refinement on the next task. So the first loop makes the agent better at this task, and the second makes the framework better at improving agents on future tasks. You'll see both loops leave files on disk in the demo below.
You can spend more compute on Loop 1 with a budget, k , and a mode ( experiment guide ):
The budget drives cost. Each task takes 4k executor rollouts and 3k improver sessions ( run_sweep.py ), so --k 3 means 12 rollouts and 9 improver sessions per task. LAB alone has 1,143 tasks ( experiment guide ), which is why every example here starts with one.
Google tested GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash across four model—harness configurations on three benchmarks. A single step ( k = 1 ) improved both over their base harnesses:
These are best-case "up to" figures, not averages, and LAB's is on its Partial score — the fraction of grading criteria passed. The README adds that a larger k "brings further gains," and the paper has per-configuration numbers. These are Google's own results, so independent reproductions will matter.
The usual way to make a model better at a job is to train it further, which needs training data, GPUs, and access to its weights. Most teams using a model through an API have none of these. Harness² keeps every improvement in plain files instead: a rewritten prompt, a fixed script, a new guardrail. That has three practical upsides.
Google's demo runs both recursion modes with " deterministic editors and real Python executions " and " requires no model credentials ", so it's free.
curl downloads Astral's installer script. The flags make it follow redirects ( -L ), stay quiet ( -s ) while still showing errors ( -S ), and fail cleanly on a bad response ( -f ). The | sh part pipes the script into your shell, which installs uv into your user directory. Open a new terminal and run uv --version to confirm. pip install uv also works.
git clone downloads the full repository from Google Research's GitHub into a new harness2 folder, and cd moves you into it. Run every later command from this repository root.
uv venv creates an isolated Python 3.12 environment in .venv , downloading Python if needed. source activates it, so python and installed commands now come from .venv . Your prompt usually shows (.venv) once it's active. Rerun the source line in any new terminal.
-e installs in editable mode, using the source files in place. The [render] extra adds openpyxl and python-pptx for spreadsheet and slide outputs ( pyproject.toml ), and the quotes stop your shell from misreading the brackets. Installing registers the commands used below: harness2 , harness2-demo , harness2-setup , harness2-check , harness2-judge , harness2-report , and harness2-bridge .
The demo runs the real recursion and library workflow, with scripted editors in place of a model. --output sets the results folder and --k 2 sets the recursion budget. Without --mode , it runs both parallel and sequential modes. It finished in about two seconds for me:
There's one domain, accounting , with two tasks. Both succeeded, and demo.json holds the summary.
The starting harness ships with a bug, and Harness² has to find it on its own. Here's the base harness's helper script:
The script reads the amount column of a CSV as exact Decimal values and adds them up. The if amount > 0 filter is the bug: it silently drops negative entries.
Now run the original and the adopted script on the same ledger:
The first command prints the ledger: three entries, one of them negative. The base script ignores it and reports 105.25; the adopted script reports the correct 85.15 (100.25 − 20.10 + 5.00). Harness² removed the filter without ever being told the right total.
This is the experience reflector's note. adopted: c1 names the winning harness; sequential compositions are named c1 to ck and parallel ones agg1 to aggk ( ledger.py ). "What each edit did" records the probe evidence: the edit from invariant candidate inv1 "helped." The "Transferable lesson" pairs a cue with a lesson, evidence, and confidence — and it's what carries forward.
Next, check how the lesson reached the second task:
library_entries_before counts stored lessons when each task started, with agg for parallel mode and seq for sequential ( library code ). The first task started with none; the second started with one per mode — the lesson from ledger-1 . That's the improvement harness growing between tasks.
The runs/demo folder has four parts worth knowing:
A real run uses models in every role: executor, improver, and judge. We'll use LAB, the legal benchmark the README uses as its example. Model-backed runs cost money , so every command here is limited to one task. I verified each command up to the first paid model call; your model output will vary.
You'll also need Node.js 20+ for the OpenCode executor, the Google Cloud CLI , a Google Cloud project with Vertex AI enabled, and Pandoc and Poppler for LAB's documents. Docker is only needed for WorkBuddy-Bench.
apt-get update refreshes the package list, and the second line installs the tools, with -y skipping the prompt. pandoc converts documents and poppler-utils reads PDFs; setup uses the rest to download code and data.
The README says to copy .env.example , but that file isn't in the repository at the time of writing (it returns a 404). Create .env in the repo root yourself, using the settings from the setup guide and config.py :
Harness² loads these KEY=VALUE lines at startup.
Replace each YOUR_GEMINI_MODEL_ID with the exact model ID from your Vertex AI console. Values set in your shell override .env , which is handy for quick experiments.
This signs you in through the browser and saves Application Default Credentials, which Harness² uses to call Vertex AI. On a headless server, add --no-browser .
Setup downloads pinned versions of LAB (from Harvey's harvey-labs ) and the OpenCode executor, applies Google's patches, installs Bun, builds LAB's own Python environment, and fetches the tasks into dependencies/ . Add --dry-run to preview the plan first. Keep your main .venv active; Harness² finds LAB's interpreter itself.
This verifies dependencies, credentials, and settings without calling a model, and prints a FAIL: line for anything missing. For example, without a .env you'll see FAIL: HARNESS2_SOLVER_MODEL is required for executor rollouts . It can't confirm your account can use the models; that only shows on the first real call.
--dry-run prints the selected task and makes no model calls. --bench lab picks the benchmark, --k 1 --mode parallel sets one parallel step, --only-domains limits the run to one practice area, and --max-tasks 1 caps it at one task per domain.
Without --dry-run , this runs the full loop: 4 executor rollouts and 3 improver sessions at --k 1 . It re-checks your configuration, including the judge, before spending anything. It then runs the base harness, proposes edits, probes them, composes a refined harness, and reflects on the result. If it stops partway, rerun the same command to resume.
The judge grades the refined harness's outputs against LAB's rubric, and the report summarizes Partial and All-pass scores. Use the same benchmark, --k , --mode , and task selection as the run so both commands find its results.
To compare against the unimproved harness:
--bases scores the original harness's runs into base_judged.json , next to judged.json .
Results land in runs/lab/ . Before changing models or task selection, point Harness² at a new folder with export HARNESS2_RUNS_DIR=runs/my-new-experiment . To run Steps 4 to 7 in one go:
run_lab.sh chains the check, refinement, judging, and reporting, passing your flags to the refinement step. Put K=3 MODE=sequential in front of it to change the budget or mode.
Harness² hints at a future where agents improve by building up experience rather than by retraining: lesson libraries grown over weeks of real work, and harness changes that teams review like code. The open questions are how well lessons transfer across domains, how costs compare with fine-tuning, and how to keep self-editing agents safe. With the code open, the community can now find out.
For the full method, read the paper on arXiv . Then clone the repo and run the demo yourself.
Shittu Olumide is a software engineer and technical writer passionate about leveraging cutting-edge technologies to craft compelling narratives, with a keen eye for detail and a knack for simplifying complex concepts. You can also find Shittu on Twitter .

title: Financial performance as collateral: First National Bank expands access to unsecured business finance
body: First National Bank has reintroduced its unsecured, system pre-approved business loan facility to help eligible businesses access financing for working capital requirements and business expansion. Access to finance remains one of the biggest challenges facing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), often due to limited collateral and inadequate financial records. In response, First National Bank is making it easier for qualifying businesses to obtain funding through pre-approved unsecured loans and overdraft facilities. According to Mark Achiampong, Head of Commercial and Business Banking at First National Bank, the initiative reflects the bank’s commitment to making financing more accessible, affordable, and convenient for businesses. “We want to support entrepreneurs who are ready to grow, create jobs, and invest in their businesses. Maintaining accurate financial records and consistently banking revenue is more than an administrative responsibility. It is a powerful way for businesses to demonstrate their creditworthiness and unlock access to finance. Our ambition is to make access to credit faster, fairer, and more accessible for the businesses driving Ghana’s economy,” he said. Mr. Achiampong explained that the bank’s pre-approved unsecured lending solution allows businesses to leverage their own banking and financial performance when seeking funding. “With our pre-approved unsecured loan offering, a business’s financial track record does the work. Our assessment model evaluates transactional behaviour, financial performance, and overall credit risk profile to determine eligibility. Businesses that maintain disciplined records, bank their revenue consistently, and manage their accounts well build a track record that works in their favour. In many ways, strong financial performance becomes a form of collateral, helping businesses access the funding they need to scale and succeed.” The offering forms part of First National Bank’s broader commitment to supporting SME growth and providing innovative financing solutions that help businesses unlock their full potential.

title: Czech president: Trump's diesel deal derails peace progress between Ukraine, Russia
body:
Czech President Petr Pavel stated that a truce between Russia and Ukraine was "very close" until President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. He said this in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which includes Politico.
"It will be much harder now. Russia uses this momentum to get out of pressure, and it’s kind of a moral boost for them," Pavel said, pointing out that coordinated U.S and European sanctions on Russian oil, oligarchs, and other industries had placed Russia "in a difficult position." However, the deal announced by Trump earlier this month, under which Russia was to supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel fuel to the U.S, gave Russia "time to breathe."
Pavel expressed support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who criticized the deal, stating that it "plays into Russia's hands" and allows Russia to "kill more people, conduct war longer, respect America even less, and cause the world even greater loss and damage."
"I believe that President Zelensky and the whole of Ukraine is a victim of a conflict. So, I would be probably the last to blame Ukraine for being guilty of the conflict. It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia. It was not Ukraine who was threatening Russia," Pavel said.
He added that Trump demonstrates a more open approach to Russia than any European leader.
"To some extent, he may be attracted by Vladimir Putin as a leader with authority, but I don’t think that … President Trump sees it from a position of a struggle between democracy and autocracies because he’s looking at it simply from the point of view of economic prosperity for the United States," he added.
Although Pavel expressed concern over the diesel deal, he declined to assert that the U.S had betrayed Ukraine or other European partners.
"I don’t know yet if we can call it betrayal, but I would call it a mistake. Because … it’s now giving Russia a new hope: New hope that they can disregard Europe, they can disregard Ukraine, they can focus on making a deal with the United States, potentially with China, and arranging all things up to their priorities and strategies. I believe that it’s clearly against our interest in Europe," he explained.
Pavel also did not rule out that European countries might buy Russian oil in the future, but added that "it will still take time."
"If one day Russia is a country respecting other countries’ sovereignty and borders, why not have regular business with such a country? But Russia is not there yet," he said.
