Another pregnant woman, blogger Mariana Vishegirskaya, was photographed descending debris-covered stairs in a polka-dot pajama set after the attack. She gave birth to a daughter the following day.
Russian officials claimed the hospital had been taken over by Ukrainian forces and dismissed images of the victims as staged.
In March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova , Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights, over the alleged war crimes of unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied areas to Russia.
The issue is not simply that children crossed a border. Investigators have documented children separated from parents or guardians, taken from occupied territory, placed in Russian institutions or foster families, and subjected to efforts to reshape their national identity.
The circumstances differ. Some children were transferred from institutions, others from occupied communities, and some have relatives who have struggled to locate and bring them home. Each case requires its own evidence.
On June 6, 2023, the destruction of the Kakhovka dam on the Dnipro River sent floodwaters across communities in southern Ukraine, inundating homes, streets, and farmland, forcing thousands of residents to flee.
The death toll remains disputed and incomplete. Ukrainian authorities reported at least 34 deaths in territory under Ukrainian control.
But an AP investigation found evidence that 200-300 people may have drowned in Russian-occupied Oleshky alone – far more than the number reported by Russian occupation authorities. The UN has said it could not fully assess the impact in occupied areas because Russia denied it access.
The flooding also damaged water supplies and irrigation systems and caused extensive environmental harm.
On July 8, 2024, a Russian missile struck Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt children’s hospital , Ukraine’s largest pediatric medical facility.
The attack destroyed the hospital’s toxicology building, where children were undergoing treatment, including hemodialysis. Patients and staff were forced to evacuate. Medical workers and volunteers dug through rubble while parents tried to keep their children safe.
The Ukrainian government said 627 children were inside the hospital during the attack. Patients who needed urgent care were moved outside, with some receiving treatment on benches while emergency teams worked among the wreckage.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission examined the strike and said the evidence indicated a direct hit by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile. Russia denied targeting civilian facilities.
The attack damaged a hospital whose patients were already seriously ill or injured. Some children had to continue receiving care amid the destruction and uncertainty of evacuation.
Ukrainian prisoners of war returning from Russian captivity have described beatings, electric shocks, sexual violence, threats of execution, and mock executions.
The UN has documented widespread torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) held by Russia. In interviews published in March 2024, almost every Ukrainian POW interviewed by UN monitors described torture, and more than half reported sexual violence. Read the UN findings .
One of the deadliest incidents occurred at the Russian-controlled penal colony near Olenivka , in the occupied Donetsk region, on the night of July 28-29, 2022.
An explosion in a barrack holding Ukrainian prisoners killed at least 50 POWs and injured 151 others, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
Russia blamed Ukraine, claiming its forces had struck the barrack with HIMARS rockets. But the UN concluded that the explosion was not caused by a HIMARS rocket.
It could not establish the precise weapon or its point of origin, in part because Russian authorities denied investigators access and the site was not preserved for an independent examination.
The UN also found that injured prisoners did not receive prompt medical care. Some reportedly died from blood loss while waiting for help – survivors were taken to hospitals hours later. The full circumstances of the explosion and accountability for the deaths remain unresolved.
In February 2026 , Kyiv Post published testimony from a former Ukrainian POW describing torture, mock executions and two years without sunlight. In May 2026, Kyiv Post reported on a Ukrainian documentation project that identified nearly 200 detention sites and compiled evidence of abuse.
Torture and cruel treatment of prisoners of war are prohibited under international humanitarian law. POWs must be protected, not subjected to violence or denied necessary medical care.
Ukrainian soldiers have been shot after surrendering, with some executions captured on drone footage and later examined by investigators.
In October 2024, footage circulated showing 16 Ukrainian soldiers being executed after surrendering in the Pokrovsk district of the Donetsk region.
The video appeared to show Russian troops opening fire on the men after they emerged from a trench and lined up. Ukraine’s Prosecutor General described it as the largest reported case of its kind on the front line at the time.
In another case, Human Rights Watch examined drone footage from near the village of Ivanivske in Donetsk region. The footage showed Ukrainian soldiers emerging from a dugout, removing some of their protective equipment and lying face down.
Russian soldiers then shot them. Human Rights Watch said at least three of the clearly surrendered soldiers were killed in the incident. Its investigation documented several other apparent executions of Ukrainian soldiers attempting to surrender.
The killings have continued. On April 12, 2026, Ukrainian military officials reported that Russian forces had captured and executed four Ukrainian servicemen near Vetarynarne in the Kharkiv region. Ukrainian authorities said they were investigating the incident as a war crime.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has also documented a sharp rise in reported executions.
In a report covering the period from late August 2024 to May 2025 , it said it had recorded credible allegations that 106 Ukrainian soldiers captured by Russian forces had been executed.
The UN assessed the allegations using video and photographic material and witness interviews. It had verified 88 executions of people who were no longer participating in hostilities since Russia’s full-scale invasion began, while continuing to investigate additional cases.
Under the laws of war, soldiers who surrender or are otherwise hors de combat must be protected. Executing captured or incapacitated combatants is prohibited and may constitute a war crime.
Russia has repeatedly modified its Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones, including by introducing different warhead configurations.
An AP investigation confirmed that Russia has begun to deploy modified attack drones carrying thermobaric warheads against Ukraine.
The report indicated that a production plant located in Alabuga, in the Tatarstan region, has been equipping the Iranian / Russian Shahed drones with these devastating payloads since at least the summer.
The thermobaric warheads produce intense heat and pressure, and fragmentation warheads, which scatter metal fragments when they detonate.
The consequences depend on the weapon, where it detonates and who is nearby. Fragmentation warheads can send metal pieces into surrounding areas, while thermobaric weapons can cause severe blast and heat injuries.
When such weapons hit populated areas, civilians can be caught in the blast even if they are not at the point of impact.
Russian missile and drone strikes hit residential buildings and civilian neighborhoods across Ukraine every day, from cities near the front line in the east to communities in the west. The scale of the attacks and the number of people killed make it impossible to list every incident in a single article.
As of June 2026, Ukrainian law enforcement data recorded at least 17,596 civilian deaths , including 705 children, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. The figure is not a complete count.
In Mariupol alone, Ukrainian authorities have documented 12,500 individual civilian deaths, while President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine believes the actual toll there may be around 20,000 . The full number of civilians killed across Ukraine remains unknown.
During the 2008 war in Georgia and the subsequent occupation, the European Court of Human Rights found Russia responsible for violations including killings and ill-treatment of civilians, looting and preventing people from returning home.
In Syria, UN investigators found that Russian airstrikes on civilian areas included attacks that amounted to war crimes . The pattern predates the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Alisa is the Head of News and a correspondent at Kyiv Post, where she leads the newsroom’s coverage of breaking events and global developments. With over seven years of experience in TV journalism, Alisa has reported on international and Ukrainian politics, making complex stories easier to understand. Back in September 2022, Alisa joined the Kyiv Post team.

title: Mozambican/South African defence chiefs talk security in Pretoria
body:
Southern African regional security was a priority when SA National Defence Force (SANDF) Chief, General Rudzani Maphwanya, hosted his Forças Armadas de Defesa de Moçambique (FADM) counterpart, General Júlio dos Santos Jane, Chief of the General Staff, at Defence Headquarters in Pretoria earlier in October.
Following a welcoming parade at Armscor sports ground, adjacent to the Armscor Building housing SANDF Headquarters, Captain Jacques de Vries from Maphwanya’s Communication Office reported Maphwanya saying when faced with “…interconnected challenges, it is imperative that both our nations continue to collectively formulate and execute integrated solutions”.
“In modern defence management, security in Maputo translates directly to security in Pretoria; insecurity in Cabo Delgado reverberates across the entire Southern African region,” the Mozambican general heard before replying in prepared remarks “…challenges remind us of an inescapable reality: the security of Mozambique and the security of South Africa are deeply interconnected”.
“The stability of one of our countries contributes to the stability of the other and, consequently, to the peace and security of the entire region,” Jane told his host, adding his visit allowed both defence force chiefs to continue a dialogue that started in March with an official visit to Mozambique by Maphwanya. The Pretoria meeting was an opportunity to assess implementation of understanding reached earlier in the year and identify new opportunities “to give greater dynamism and effectiveness” to co-operation between the Southern African Development Community (SADC) neighbours.
Presentations highlighted ongoing collaboration in training, border security, and regional stabilisation efforts, emphasising the strategic importance of co-ordinated defence approaches between South Africa and Mozambique.
The goodwill visit, as per De Vries, reinforces the priority both nations place on defence diplomacy as a tool for advancing collective security. As neighbouring SADC members, South Africa and Mozambique continue to rely on strong bilateral defence ties to address shared challenges and promote stability across the region.
Jane’s concluding remarks reinforced these sentiments when he stated “in closing, I reiterate my sincere thanks for the invitation and fraternal hospitality and I wish you every success in the work we are now beginning”.

title: NACOC strengthens ties with Ivorian counterparts to combat illicit drug trafficking
body: The Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) has engaged border security authorities in Côte d’Ivoire to strengthen cross-border cooperation and intensify efforts to combat illicit drug trafficking along the Elubo–Noé border. The engagement forms part of the Commission’s strategic measures to curb drug trafficking and related criminal activities along the Ghanaian border. During a working visit to the Elubo Border on Wednesday, October 21, NACOC Director-General, Major General Maxwell Obuba Mantey, called for closer collaboration and a strong working relationship between the security agencies of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire to address the threat. NACOC’s Deputy Director-General, accompanied Maj Gen Obuba Mantey, the Director-General, and Lawyer Alexander Twum-Barimah, who is in charge of Enforcement, Control and Elimination, along with other members of the Commission’s management team. He appealed to the Ivorian border security authorities to sustain their cooperation with their Ghanaian counterparts in pursuit of the shared goal of suppressing illicit drug trafficking and related activities. The Director-General also assured the Ivorian authorities that NACOC and other state security agencies operating under the Elubo Border Security Committee (BORSEC) would continue to uphold the professional and ethical standards governing their work. “We appreciate the existing working relationship among both BORSEC authorities. For NACOC, we are committed to ensuring that the drug trafficking network is curtailed,” he said. Maj Gen Obuba Mantey stressed the importance of maintaining effective cooperation between the two countries, noting that coordinated efforts among border security agencies were essential to tackling cross-border drug trafficking. In response, the Commissioner of Customs at the Ivorian Border Post, Avon Tah Felix, commended the NACOC delegation for the visit, describing the engagement as an opportunity to build and maintain a constructive working relationship between the two countries. He assured the delegation that the Ivorian border authorities would continue to provide support in various ways to protect the interests of both countries.

title: Formulate anti-sexual harassment policies to ensure zero tolerance in hospitality sector – Prof Christopher Mensah
body: The Pro Vice-Chancellor of Ho Technical University, Prof Christopher Mensah, has advocated for hotels to formulate strict policies to ensure zero tolerance for sexual harassment and maltreatment in the hospitality sector. He asserted that these vices may lead to a shortfall in human resources and compromised working and educational environments, among other consequences. He said that failing to curb these unfortunate behaviours, which are bred mostly in training institutions, would affect the sector’s productivity and growth. Prof Mensah was speaking at his inaugural lecture at the G.M. Afeti Auditorium of Ho Technical University, themed “Hidden curriculum toxic socialisation in Ghana’s higher education and hospitality sectors”. Academic portfolio Prof Christopher Mensah, a professor of Hospitality and Tourism Management, obtained his Bachelor of Science in Tourism in 1999 and his M.Phil. in Tourism in 2007 from the University of Cape Coast. He joined Ho Technical University in 2008, rose through the ranks, became an associate professor in 2020 and was subsequently promoted to the rank of professor in March 2025, with 65 peer-reviewed publications, among other achievements, to his credit. Sexual harassment and maltreatment are global phenomena In his inaugural address, Prof Christopher Mensah indicated that sexual harassment and maltreatment are global phenomena, with recorded occurrences in educational institutions and tourism and hospitality facilities. He said that date requests were the most common form of sexual harassment and maltreatment recorded, followed by uncomfortable touching, sexual conversation, requests for sexual favours, attempts to kiss or fondle, rewards promised for sex, faster promotion in exchange for sex, and threats of dismissal. He further indicated that records showed that guests were most likely to sexually harass workers in the hospitality and tourism sector, while co-workers and supervisors were also responsible for a proportion of harassment cases. He asserted that individuals begin learning the habit of using power to bully or coerce their subordinates into doing their bidding in training institutions. He used the lecturer-student relationship as a case study, recounting how some lecturers use their authority to make sexual demands, coupled with threats of academic failure, among other forms of coercion. Recommended approach for universities Prof Christopher Mensah called on lecturers to cultivate the habit of teaching authoritatively, without verbal abuse, aggression or excessively high standards, among other harmful practices. He also entreated university management to reform examination guidelines by introducing transparent marking schemes, providing options for second marking and establishing a fair appeals system. He called for guidelines to restrict lecturers from requesting personal services from students, establish robust reporting, investigation and accountability structures, and ensure “regular climate surveys; counselling; staff development.” “Mistreatment and harassment are common in Ghana’s universities and hospitality workplaces, and are sustained by power, dependency and silence rather than by a few individuals. Hospitality students meet them earlier and more often, mostly from those who teach them. Universities carry a double responsibility: to prepare students for the industry, and to stop passing on its worst habits”, he said. Recommended approach for hotels Prof Mensah advocated that hotel management introduce and display policies emphasising the facility’s zero tolerance for sexual harassment and maltreatment. “The hotel management must adopt and display a policy that states the hotel’s position on zero tolerance with posters and leaflets in all areas”, he said. He also suggested training complaints-handling staff to act on complaints, including those from and about guests, while protecting young women working in reception and food and beverage areas, as they are more vulnerable to harassment. He said another essential measure was to reduce reliance on tips by paying approved minimum wages to provide workers with financial security. Recommended approach for the Ghana Tourism Authority Prof Mensah entreated the Ghana Tourism Authority to make anti-harassment policy a requirement for licensing or renewals, urging it to support lower-star hotels in developing such policies. He also called on the authority to enforce the payment of the minimum wage to hotel staff and train staff in how to prevent and report sexual harassment and maltreatment. Call to students He entreated students not to let anyone trample on their rights, to use trusted channels to report sexual harassment and to keep records of such incidents, including dates, places and witnesses. “Support your peers; speak up when you see mistreatment/sexual harassment. Break the cycle; when you hold power, do not repeat what you suffered”, he counselled. The Vice-Chancellor of Ho Technical University, Prof Ben Honyenuga, eulogised Prof Christopher Mensah for his contribution to shaping hospitality and tourism education and the sector. “Prof Mensah has made significant contributions to advance fields including Tourism Development, Hospitality Management, and Human Resource Management, academic integrity, and sustainable tourism management, employee well-being, student development and industry resilience”, he listed, among other contributions.

title: Montenegro plans to join EU in 2028, Russian ambassador tells TASS
body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Podgorica plans to join the European Union (EU) in 2028, Russian Ambassador to Montenegro Alexander Lukashik told TASS in an interview.
"The introduction of a visa regime [for Russian citizens] indicates that the Montenegrin leadership is continuing its policy of severing ties with our country, which are already close to zero at present. It explains this course by its desire to align itself with the European Union’s foreign and security policies, which Montenegro plans to join in 2028," the diplomat said.
He emphasized that Podgorica’s full support for the EU’s anti-Russian restrictions was another reflection of this approach.
Earlier, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stressed that the EU integration process, in connection with which Montenegro had decided to introduce visas for Russian citizens, "no longer implies in any way that new members can retain neutral status."
According to the diplomat, Podgorica’s new measures will reduce tourist flows from Russia, deal a blow to Montenegrin businesses and lead to a deterioration in the country’s investment climate. At the same time, the Montenegrin authorities "should not expect Brussels to compensate them for the inevitable losses," she warned.

title: Terrorist propaganda outpacing global efforts to stop it – UN
body:
Terrorist groups recruit, raise money and even plan operations through propaganda “embedded” in every stage of their work, a new United Nations (UN) report warns as governments struggle to keep pace.
The report by the UN Security Council Counter-Terrorism Committee secretariat tracks the movement of terrorist propaganda to what is said to be “far beyond messaging”.
“It has become part of the operational structure of these groups, shaping how they recruit fighters, raise funds and govern territory,” as per the UN report which notes “an especially alarming trend”. This is an increase in the numbers of children and young people targeted “not just on social media but through gaming platforms and online communities built around shared interests”
“The speed at which terrorist groups adapt propaganda strategies has created an acceleration gap between their strategies and the legislation and policies of [UN] member states,” the report warns.
“Propaganda,” it continues “has long been integral to terrorist strategies but the deployment and scale have evolved significantly and its function is now more central, integrated and adaptive than in earlier phases”.
“Groups such as Al Qaeda – which carried out the seismic terror attacks on the United States (US) 25 years ago – relied on centralised messaging distributed mainly through physical media. The emergence of ISIL, also known as Da’esh, in the mid-2010s brought a switch to ‘high-volume, multi-lingual, digitally distributed propaganda ecosystems’.”
Among emerging trends identified by the report are the use of artificial intelligence (AI), exploiting gaming platforms as well as alternative online spaces including Discord, Twitch and Stream.
Terrorist recruitment targets young people through gaming, with many groups designing violent extremist themed first person shooter games and modifying existing games to embed violent extremist narratives in familiar entertainment formats, as per the report, which adds “graphic violent content or ‘gore’ – execution footage and images of mass casualties, as examples – and nihilistic online sub-cultures are increasingly important for radicalisation”.
Another trend is the growing convergence of violent extremist ideologies across the digital space. In this case, content produced blends narratives, symbols and grievances from various contexts to maximise resonance and reach numerous audiences.
Among the report’s recurring themes is the growing intersection between propaganda and other core terrorist group functions, with the focus on Al Qaeda affiliate JNIM in the Sahel, Al Shabaab in Somalia, ISIL K in Central and South Asia and TTP in Pakistan.
Analysis shows these groups use propaganda “to reinforce governance activities, exploit local grievances, build legitimacy, facilitate fundraising and shape perceptions of authority.”
The report also notes while terrorist groups adjust tactics quickly, “policy responses and implementation have longer legislative and operational timelines.”
It stresses effective responses must address propaganda not only as content, but as a core operational enabler of terrorism, while ensuring counter-terrorism measures remain in line with international human rights law.

title: Human Shamonda Virus: Reported Case Has No Health Risk, Says France
body: There was “no health risk to the general public identified at this time”, France’s health and agriculture ministries said in a joint statement on Thursday after the country detected the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, in a human for the first time, in a severely immunocompromised patient who died earlier this month. It added that the human infection appeared to be “an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient” hospitalised for a serious medical condition. “Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans,” the ministries said. The virus, which belongs to the Orthobunyavirus group and is typically transmitted to animals by small biting insects, was first detected in Europe this summer, they said. At this stage in the investigation, the patient was believed to have contracted the virus through the bite of a midge in eastern France, where the virus was circulating in animals during the spring and summer, the ministries said. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death are very likely linked to infection with the Shamonda virus,” they added, citing preliminary findings. But “clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are still ongoing”, they said. In 14 European Countries The virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported in cattle in several parts of Africa and in Japan. The virus was detected in Europe for the first time at the end of July, including on cattle farms in France. It has now been detected in 14 western European countries, according to an epidemiological bulletin from France’s national research institute monitoring animal health. Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although sporadic infections in smaller livestock and horses have also been identified in France this summer. In cattle, the main symptoms are acute diarrhoea, fever, lethargy and a drop in milk production. An investigation is ongoing, and both the World Health Organization and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control have been notified. AFP The post Human Shamonda Virus: Reported Case Has No Health Risk, Says France appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Kabiru Yusuf: Media must uphold fairness
body: The Chairman of Media Trust Group, Mallam Kabiru Yusuf, has urged journalists to uphold fairness, accountability and independence in their reporting. Speaking on Thursday at the official unveiling of the company’s converged newsroom, the chairman described journalism as “history in a hurry,” noting that journalists must strive to report accurately and fairly despite the pressures and complexities of the profession. “If you choose journalism, you will be misunderstood and you will misunderstand others,” he said, adding that Media Trust recognised the possibility of errors and the need to address them responsibly. According to him, the organisation provides opportunities for people to respond to reports through its right-of-reply column and issues apologies when mistakes are established. “We have a column where we give people a right to reply because we know that in this business, there is nobody who is always right or who is always wrong. So, when we make these mistakes, we apologise,” Yusuf said. He stressed that journalists must remain committed to asking questions, listening to different perspectives and correcting inaccuracies where necessary. He maintained that fairness required journalists to listen even to people they regarded as opponents or those who considered them adversaries. “Fairness demands that we should listen to even people we consider enemies, or they consider us enemies. That’s what fairness demands,” he said. He acknowledged that maintaining professional standards could be difficult in an environment where attempts to influence media coverage were widespread, but said Media Trust remained committed to the principles of neutrality and accountability. He said the organisation was not perfect but continued to strive towards the standards expected of a responsible media institution. “At Media Trust here, I would say that we aspire, we are not perfect, to live up to this standard, at the risk of being misunderstood,” he said. The chairman added that journalists must remain conscious of their responsibility to the public and avoid allowing external pressure to compromise their independence.

title: Cobra Aviation Group: Powering Africa’s aviation future
body:
Africa’s aviation future will not be built by ambition alone. It will be built by companies with the capability, technical expertise and determination to turn opportunity into reality. Cobra Aviation Group is stepping into that space with purpose.
Proudly South African and 100% black female owned, Cobra Aviation Group is emerging as a dynamic force in Africa’s aviation landscape, delivering safe, compliant and innovative aviation solutions while helping to build a more capable, inclusive and competitive industry.
At the recent Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD 2026) exhibition, the Group put its capabilities, vision and transformation agenda firmly on the industry stage. Its presence at Africa’s premier aerospace and defence exhibition signalled a clear ambition to participate meaningfully in the growth of African aviation and to help shape an industry in which excellence and transformation advance together.
Cobra Aviation Group’s integrated portfolio spans Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO), scheduled and non-scheduled flight operations, cargo and passenger services, VIP and executive charter solutions, serving commercial, government and private sector clients.
It is a member of the South African Aerospace, Maritime and Defence (AMD) industries association and has vast experience working with defence and other governmental entities, with its services ideally positioned for military and state customers.
At the heart of the Group’s approach is a commitment to operational excellence. Safety, regulatory compliance, technical capability and service reliability are not simply business priorities. They are fundamental to building trust and sustainable aviation capability.
But Cobra Aviation Group’s ambition extends beyond aircraft and operations.
As a 100% black female owned aviation enterprise operating in a highly specialised and technically demanding sector, Cobra Aviation Group represents a powerful dimension of South Africa’s transformation story.
The Group is committed to creating pathways for black professionals, women and young people through employment, skills development, mentorship and inclusive leadership.
It recognises that Africa’s aviation growth depends ultimately on the people behind the machines: the pilots, engineers, technicians, aviation specialists, entrepreneurs and leaders who will carry the industry forward.
Developing this talent is therefore central to Cobra Aviation Group’s vision. By investing in people while expanding operational and technical capability, the Group is working to create an aviation business that delivers immediate value while contributing to the industry’s long-term resilience.
AAD 2026 offered Cobra Aviation Group a powerful platform to engage with government, aerospace and defence stakeholders, aviation leaders, technology partners and potential clients.
It was an opportunity to demonstrate capability, build strategic partnerships and identify opportunities that can accelerate localisation, skills development, job creation and African participation across the aviation value chain.
One of Cobra Aviation Group’s Boeing 737 aircraft took part in the AAD Air Show with a spectacular flyby on Saturday 19 September, giving a practical illustration of Cobra’s charter and freighter services, which have been used by the South African Air Force, amongst others.
Cobra Aviation Group believes the continent has both the demand and the talent to build a stronger aviation industry. Unlocking that potential requires investment, collaboration and bold African participation.
The Group’s message at AAD 2026 was therefore unequivocal: Africa’s aviation future must be built in Africa, powered by African capability and strengthened through meaningful transformation.
With a vision grounded in excellence, innovation, safety, compliance and empowerment, Cobra Aviation Group is ready to play its part.
This is more than a flight path. It is a commitment to the future of African aviation.

title: GPL 2026/27: Hearts boss Kapor wary of ‘difficult’ Holy Stars encounter
body: Hearts of Oak head coach Nebojsa Kapor has cautioned his side ahead of their Ghana Premier League game against Basake Holy Stars. The two teams face each other on matchday eight of the league, with both teams hoping to continue their winning run from last weekend. The Phobians have won all of their last two games against Port City and Vision FC, while Holy Stars have won one and lost one in the same period, losing to Bibiani GoldStars and claiming victory over Bechem United. Each team has claimed one win in the last four meetings between Hearts and Holy Stars, and despite two points separating the two teams on the league table, Kapor has warned his side not to be complacent. “We are not going to say we are a better team and we will win. No, never. We are really going to approach them very deep from every single department and from every single individual player,” he said. “Every game here is very difficult. Especially from the mentality side, we have to face this game very tough.” The fixture is scheduled to take place at the University of Ghana Stadium on Friday, October 23.

title: Show HN: Return Ledger free portfolio TWR/XIRR tracker with AI PDF import
body:
Log contributions, withdrawals and valuation checkpoints; get an approximated time‑weighted and money‑weighted return, computed entirely in this page.
Upload a buy/sell confirmation, a coupon or dividend notice, or a position statement from your bank or broker. An AI model reads it and proposes one row for this ledger; nothing is added until you confirm.
Experimental (alpha): tested mainly on Italian broker documents and a few synthetic English ones, so other formats may be misread or flagged for review. Always check every figure against the original before confirming. This is not financial or tax advice.
No access code? Questions, bugs or a document that doesn't read correctly: write to Giorgio Bozio .
Privacy: the PDF contains personal data (name, address, account numbers). It is sent to this site's server and to Anthropic, the AI provider, only to read it, and is not stored or logged by this site.
"Value after" is only required for Valuation rows and the last row (today's value) — leave it blank on a Deposit or Withdraw row if your bank doesn't give you a historical value for that date. The first row's value defaults to its deposit amount if left blank. Fees and Tax withheld are optional costs deducted from a Deposit or Withdraw — leave them at 0 if none applied. Amount stays the gross figure (what actually moved in/out of the account, matching your statement); fees/tax only affect the separate net-of-cost XIRR below. Note is a free-text label purely for your own reference (e.g. "rent", "principal", "interest") — it never affects the calculations, and the filter above only changes which rows are shown here, never what's used in the results.
Time-weighted return (TWR): the ledger is split into sub-periods at each row where a value is actually known (a valuation row, or a deposit/withdrawal you also priced). Between two known values, Modified Dietz estimates the sub-period return from the start value, end value, and the dated flows in between, weighted by how long each was invested — no value is required at every single flow. The sub-period returns are chain-linked, then annualized over the full span. With only an opening and a closing value, this collapses to one Modified Dietz estimate for the whole period.
Money-weighted return (XIRR): every deposit and withdrawal is treated as a signed cash flow on its date, with the final value as a closing inflow; the annual rate that makes their net present value zero is found numerically (Newton‑Raphson with a bisection fallback). XIRR never needs interim values — only dated flows and the current value. If the first row is a valuation carrying a pre-existing balance rather than a deposit, that balance is treated as if it were invested on that date, since XIRR has no way to know when it actually went in — skipping it would understate the invested capital and wildly overstate the return.
Fees, tax, and gross vs. net: the Amount field always stays the gross figure — what actually moved in or out of the account, matching your broker statement. That's what TWR uses, so it keeps measuring market performance on its own, undistorted by what you paid in costs. Fees and tax you log on a Deposit or Withdraw only feed a second, separate figure: XIRR · net , computed on the amount minus fees and tax (what actually reached your pocket, or cost you extra on the way in). The gap between gross and net XIRR is the cost drag tile — roughly how many percentage points a year fees and tax are costing you. Tax withheld on unrealized gains inside valuation checkpoints isn't captured this way; only tax you actually record against a withdrawal is.
Ledgers aren't summed into a total: their valuations fall on different dates, so a combined figure would be mostly interpolation. Compare XIRR for "which did better for my money", TWR for "which asset performed better".

title: 14 EU Countries Affected As France Reports First Case Of Human Shamonda Virus
body: The Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, has been detected in 14 European countries, according to an epidemiological bulletin from France’s national research institute for animal health, as reported by AFP. The virus was detected in Europe for the first time at the end of July. It was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported in cattle in several parts of Africa and in Japan. However, French health authorities said Thursday that the virus had been detected in a human for the first time, in a severely immunocompromised patient who died earlier this month. Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although sporadic infections in smaller livestock and horses have also been identified in France this summer. In cattle, the main symptoms are acute diarrhoea, fever, lethargy and a drop in milk production. An investigation is ongoing, and both the World Health Organization and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control have been notified. While responding to the outbreak, France’s health and agriculture ministries said in a joint statement that there was “no health risk to the general public identified at this time”. It added that the human infection appeared to be “an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient” hospitalised for a serious medical condition. “Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans,” the ministries said. The virus, which belongs to the Orthobunyavirus group and is typically transmitted to animals by small biting insects, was first detected in Europe this summer, they said. At this stage in the investigation, the patient was believed to have contracted the virus through the bite of a midge in eastern France, where the virus was circulating in animals during the spring and summer, the ministries said. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient before his death are very likely linked to infection with the Shamonda virus,” they added, citing preliminary findings. But “clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are still ongoing”, they said. AFP The post 14 EU Countries Affected As France Reports First Case Of Human Shamonda Virus appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Hensoldt SA’s Argos-15 gimbal offered on Do228 NXT special mission aircraft
body:
The Do228 NXT twin turboprop aircraft being developed General Atomics AeroTec Systems (GA-ATS) will be offered with Hensoldt South Africa’s new Argos-15 electro-optical/infrared gimbal as an additional mission-system configuration.
This was revealed by GA-ATS on 22 October. The company said the option of the Argos-15 expands the platform’s capabilities for a broader range of operational requirements.
The Argos-15, the successor to the operationally proven Argos-II, is mounted in front of the retractable main landing gear and therefore provides a clear 360° unobstructed view for the camera operator.
The new export-friendly, single Line Replaceable Unit (LRU) Argos-15 has a smaller footprint, combined with a new generation smart payload, GA-ATS said. “It is equipped with next-generation multi-spectral sensors and built-in AI-powered object detection, classification and tracking capabilities. These enable sharper images in diverse environmental operating conditions, reduce operator workload and improve mission efficiency.”
The Argos-15 is available with a variety of payload options, including long-range multi-spectral cameras, as well as a laser pointer, illuminator, range finder and designator for military missions.
The Do228 NXT can patrol the mission area for eight hours, flying as slowly as 78 kts (144 km/h) and up to 260 kts (481 km/h) to allow short ferry times. This enables the tactical flight officer (TFO) to maintain the optimal position for the mission and maximize the mission effectiveness, GA-ATS said.
“The Do228 is a field-proven design, serving customers for many years all around the world in versatile missions. The Do228 NXT continues its legacy and defines a true multi-mission aircraft with cutting-edge sensors to extend the mission capabilities to the next level.”
“Due to its unmatched short take-off and landing (STOL) capabilities in its class, the Do228 NXT can operate from short grass or unpaved runways, allowing it to access locations in especially harsh environments. These areas are beyond the operational reach of many aircraft in its class. This rugged and smart design is reflected in the Argos-15 as well, making the two a perfect match for ISR missions that require enhanced capability and performance. Combined, the Do228 NXT special mission aircraft and Argos-15 offer operators new, unprecedented mission capabilities,” GA-ATS said.
Built originally by Dornier between 1981 and 1998, licensed production of the Do228 has continued in India by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. While GA-ATS acquired the rights to the aircraft from RUAG in 2021, it later announced its intention to start production of a modernised version of the aircraft, formally launching the Do228 NXT at Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany, in June 2026.
GA-ATS hopes to capitalise on the aircraft’s previous success across Africa. Having seen service in approximately 20 countries across more than 30 operators, the Do228 has been a mainstay of African civil and military aviation for decades. About 145 Do228s remain in service worldwide, with a significant number in Africa.
The Do228 NXT is designed to perform a wide range of roles. These include passenger and cargo transport missions, search and rescue missions, medical evacuations, reconnaissance flights, and border surveillance operations.
Powered by twin Honeywell TPE331-10 turboprop engines producing 579 kW each, the Do228 NXT is capable of a maximum cruise speed of approximately 444 km/h. The aircraft has a 16.97 m wingspan, is capable of carrying up to 19 passengers or a maximum useful load of 2 700 kg, and has a range of up to 2 450 km, payload depending.
Notably, GA-ATS has already secured the Do228 NXT’s first sale, signing a contract with an undisclosed non-governmental humanitarian organisation earlier this year, with delivery slated for some time in early 2027.
Benjamin Schuhmann, Head of Sales at GA-ATS, told Defensehere at the recent Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) exhibition that GA-ATS is also exploring new configurations intended to broaden the aircraft’s mission capabilities, including a signals intelligence (SIGINT) version incorporating electronic intelligence (ELINT) and communications intelligence (COMINT) systems, a counter-unmanned aerial system (C-UAS) variant, and an armed version.

title: Akwa Ibom Assembly adopts recommendations to establish state police
body:
The Akwa Ibom House of Assembly has approved the recommendations of its committee on Inter-Governmental, Political and Special Matters to support the proposed establishment of state police in Nigeria.
The approval followed a unanimous vote by the assembly members during the sitting on Wednesday.
Presenting the report, the committee Chairman, Emem Udom, said the committee had examined the provisions of the National Policing Bill, and recommended its approval without amendment.
The Speaker, Udeme Otong said the bill sought to establish a constitutional framework for state police services.
“It also sought to retain the federal police service and its responsibilities for federal policing functions,” he said.
Mr Otong said the proposed framework would promote cooperation between federal and state police services through information sharing and mutual assistance.
The speaker said that state police would bring policing closer to the people, improve responses to security threats and enhance crime prevention through local intelligence and community engagement.
He further said that establishing state police services would create employment opportunities for the youth.
In another development, the assembly commended President Bola Tinubu for establishing the Federal University of Agriculture and Technology, Obio Akpa, in Oruk Anam Local Government Area of the state.
The commendation followed a motion by the Deputy Whip, Bernard Idiong, which Eric Akpan supported.

title: WGES 2026: Dubai’s green economy summit puts waste, water and AI on the agenda
body: Thousands of delegates gathered at Dubai's World Trade Centre on Wednesday for the opening day of the World Green Economy Summit (WGES), with speakers pressing the case that the transition to a green economy requires change not just from governments and industries but from every individual consumer. The summit brought together figures from waste management, artificial intelligence and environmental finance, among many other sectors. The conversations ranged from the contents of a Dubai rubbish chute to the future of AI-powered desalination, and most confirmed that solutions exist, but we still need incentive structures and out-of-the-box thinking from entrepreneurs looking to scale them. Waste as a resource For Timothy Clarke, chief executive of Dubai's Warsan Waste Management Centre (WWMC), the single most important shift in thinking is linguistic. "We need to stop talking about ‘waste’," he said. "It is a hugely valuable ‘resource’. We have a resource which, at the moment, we destroy, we throw away. But actually what we need is for people to look at that and say, ‘I can use that part of it for something else’." WWMC receives 6,000 tonnes of unsorted waste every day from Dubai Municipality, burning it to generate electricity. The plant works, but Mr Clarke argues it is the last resort, not the goal. "If nothing comes to the energy-from-waste plant, that is a success for me, because it means we are recycling everything." Getting there requires a policy environment that makes recycled materials economically competitive with virgin ones. "Everybody always goes for the cheapest product that meets their requirements," he said. "If cost is a major driver, we have got to make sure that the green alternatives are economic, so that people make the wiser, sustainable, recycling choice." Cleaning rivers before the plastic reaches the sea Sitting alongside Mr Clarke on a morning panel about driving the circular economy was Anssi Mikola, co-founder of River Recycle, a company that operates cleaning and recycling operations on rivers in the developing world. He argues that the ocean plastic crisis starts inland, where inadequate waste infrastructure leaves communities with rivers as their only disposal option. "The rivers are the only place where nobody comes after you," Mr Mikola said. "It is out of sight, out of mind. Nobody is responsible for it. Once you get it in the river, it moves to the next municipality." River Recycle is now operational on 20 rivers and is expanding to 30, a milestone Mr Mikola described as significant because it opens the door to larger, city-scale solutions rather than individual waterway interventions. "It has taken a long time to prove that the cleaning works and that the recycling part works." The company's challenge – and its reason for attending WGES – is funding. Scaling a circular economy in developing nations requires capital those nations do not have. "We exist to save the oceans," Mr Mikola said, "and the oceans have been destroyed by developing countries. You need funding to scale up a circular economy in those countries." Blended finance instruments – combining philanthropic seed funding with impact investment – are the vehicle he is seeking. The connections made at events like WGES, he said, matter as much as the panel discussions. AI's place in a green summit AI was also, naturally, integral to the conversation. Darren Kimura, chief executive of AISquared, delivered one of the morning's keynote addresses. "A summit, by nature, brings together leaders in an area – people that can actually create policy, laws, guidance, thought leadership," Mr Kimura told The National . "And then it allows you to bring different perspectives in and hopefully change the way people are thinking or what they are doing." His keynote included what he called the Dubai AI Challenge: a call for the UAE's technology community to stop measuring AI by headline-grabbing capabilities and start measuring it by concrete environmental outcomes. "Rather than having AI just create interesting things that are cool, like a headline, why don't we try to quantify it with things like metrics that show how much we are actually saving? How much money we are saving and how much water we are saving?" Mr Kimura's presence at a green economy summit raised an obvious question, given the volume of criticism directed at AI's water and energy consumption. He argues the technology's footprint depends entirely on how it is designed and deployed. New liquid cooling approaches – immersing processors in nano-material fluids rather than relying on water evaporation – can significantly reduce data centre water use, for example. And AI applied to resource management can drive efficiencies that offset its own demands, he said. "Using AI to actually get to those new technologies will help us to reduce it in the grand scheme of things over time," he said, "and I think that is something that is not necessarily talked about in the common conversation." His company's focus is on sovereign, democratised AI; models small enough to run within a single company or household, keeping data private and computation local. A new family of such models is due imminently. "Giving the power to the consumer – I think that is really what we are trying to do now." The challenge of getting everyone involved Across the morning sessions, it was agreed that the green economy cannot be built by summits alone. Mr Clarke said: "Everybody needs to be involved in this. It is not something that governments or industries can do. A lot of it is the individual person – about your choices when you go into a supermarket." He was particularly pointed about packaging. Around 15 per cent of the waste arriving at WWMC each day consists of single-use items – packaging that consumers did not want, bundled around the product they did want. The solution, he said, requires both consumer pressure and business leadership. "What we need is for more people to be influencing people directly to make the right choices." Mr Mikola is thinking in similarly collective terms. For example, he noted that River Recycle turns electricity into heat in its processing operations, while WWMC turns heat into electricity. "Why don't we just work together?" he asked. “And take the heat once it is there, rather than getting all the losses that it takes to turn it into energy?" That kind of lateral thinking, he suggested, is what a summit like WGES is designed to produce. "I hope [the event] leads to people thinking a bit more outside the box – looking at the bigger picture rather than just your own,” added Mr Mikola. “The solution may not be inside your focus, but there may still be a very good solution out there." This page was produced by The National in partnership with WGES

title: Russian missiles and drones kill one and injure 24 in Kyiv, splitting its metro line in two
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian missiles and drones killed one person and injured 24 in Kyiv overnight on 22 October, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office said . Damage spread across six of the city’s districts, the city military administration reported . The strike came hours after Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Putin had told Witkoff that Russia was “in principle” ready to resume three-way talks with the US and Ukraine in mid-November. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy read the overnight attack as a sign that Russia’s attitude has not changed . A day earlier, Russian drones killed two people in a 24-story Kyiv apartment block. 21 ballistic missiles in three waves Russia fired 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv overnight, Zelenskyy said . The barrage came in three waves, around 22:00, at about 02:00, and around 03:30. Aftermath of Russia’s overnight attack on Kyiv. Photo: Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine Across Ukraine, air defenses downed or suppressed 181 of 210 Russian drones, the Air Force said. Its report did not mention any ballistic missiles shot down. One killed in the Dniprovskyi district The only death in Kyiv came in the Dniprovskyi district, on the city’s left bank. There, Russian strikes destroyed 13 detached houses on several streets, prosecutors said. Police said the man killed was 48 and that six people were injured in the district, four of them children, the youngest aged five. Of the injured, five are minors and two are young children, and prosecutors reported acute stress reactions among them. A 16-year-old boy is in hospital with a closed head injury, prosecutors said. Sixteen of the injured were hospitalized, the city military administration said. The final number of injured is still being established. Explore further Not just the grid: Russia struck a 24-story block, a university, and warehouses overnight, and four people are dead Ambulance station and monastery damaged In the Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, and Sviatoshynskyi districts, the attack damaged eight apartment buildings, prosecutors said. It also damaged a building-supply hypermarket, a restaurant, a monastery building, a post office, and office premises. In Pecherskyi, Russia damaged an ambulance station and six ambulances, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote . The State Emergency Service said eight people were injured in that district, three of them children, and reported damaged transport infrastructure in the Darnytskyi district. Aftermath of Russia’s overnight attack on Kyiv. Photo: National Police of Ukraine Bridge closed, metro line split The strikes damaged metro infrastructure on the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge, Kyiv Metro said . As of the morning, green-line trains ran in two sections, Syrets–Vydubychi and Osokorky–Chervonyi Khutir. Inspections and repairs would continue after the all-clear, the metro said. Oleksii Biloshytskyi, head of Ukraine’s Patrol Police Department, announced that traffic across the bridge toward the left bank was temporarily closed. The city is adding buses on routes 22 and 91, the city administration said . Russian drones had already hit the bridge repeatedly in early October.
