title: PRP alleges plot to weaken opposition coalition ahead of 2027
body: The Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) has alleged a plot by some members of the ruling party to destabilise it and weaken efforts to build an opposition coalition ahead of the 2027 general election. The party also warned against attempts to recruit polling agents in its name by individuals it said were not authorised to do so. In a statement released at the wee hours of Thursday, October 22, and signed by its National Chairman, Dr Hakeem Baba-Ahmed, the PRP alleged that some former members and serving party officials were being used to create divisions and undermine its grassroots support. The party further claimed that senior members of the ruling party were being persuaded to finance the alleged scheme with hundreds of millions of naira. INEC records 313,115 new voters in Zamfara NIMASA detains four vessels in fresh cabotage crackdown It urged its members and the public to resist attempts to recruit polling agents without authorisation, alleging that money could be used to influence party members to support opposition candidates. The PRP also warned serving officers allegedly involved in the scheme that they would face disciplinary action. “The party hereby alerts its members and the public to these attempts and warns against the temptation to support these subversive elements,” the statement said. The party urged individuals in the ruling party allegedly involved in the plot to distance themselves from what it described as efforts to create a fictional PRP with their funds and names. Baba-Ahmed assured the party’s candidates and supporters that its leadership would not abandon their commitments and loyalty. He said the party remained committed to challenging the continuation of the present administration beyond 2027 and contributing to the formation of a potentially winning opposition coalition. The PRP however did not name the individuals or ruling party members allegedly involved in the scheme in the statement.

title: Millions of hacking attempts as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws
body: Companies and governments worldwide rushed on Thursday, October 22, to patch critical flaws in the widely-used PHP programming language , as a cybersecurity company reported millions of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. The push came after governments in Europe and elsewhere took websites offline as a precaution on Wednesday while website operators scrambled to secure systems running the software. The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki showed how much public and corporate systems rely on the software, and how hard it is to fix such flaws quickly once they are made public. “It was a long day and a long night, I know for all the IT and security folks … I’ve not seen anything like this in a long, long time,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at a company event in Cologne, Germany, on Thursday. He said the episode underscored the importance of building digital systems that can be maintained securely. PHP developers released urgent fixes on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, urging users to “update immediately”. “Details of these flaws became public before fixes were ready, and attacks have since been reported,” said Madeline Lawrence, co-founder of Belgian cybersecurity firm Aikido Security. “So companies are racing to update against attackers who can use AI to exploit them. That’s the whole race.” As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended websites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, according to cloud services firm Cloudflare. “In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday. “That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.” From Japan to Finland Japanese companies including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA, and East Japan Railway said on Thursday they were temporarily suspending some internet services as part of emergency measures. Insurer Tokio Marine Holdings said it had suspended the website of a group company. Japan’s Ministry of Finance and Meteorological Agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan’s National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service. The precautionary shutdowns underscore growing concerns over cybersecurity in Japan, which recorded more cyber incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI. French telecoms group Orange said it had temporarily suspended access to certain PHP-based websites and applications across several subsidiaries as a precaution. Tencent Cloud, one of China’s largest cloud-computing providers, urged customers to install updated PHP versions but stopped short of calling for widespread website shutdowns. Finland’s state IT services provider Valtori said it had continued installing PHP security patches overnight and was gradually lifting precautionary service blocks after shutting down government public web services a day earlier. “Restoring services can take days or even weeks, as in addition to updates, the systems need to be carefully tested,” Valtori Director General Hannu Naumanen said in a statement. Valtori said the outages were not caused by exploitation of the vulnerabilities or by a cyber breach, and that it was not aware of any active exploitation of the flaws. Several Asian governments ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP vulnerabilities on Thursday. China’s industry ministry urged organizations and users to inspect systems immediately and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP. It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary. South Korea raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks. – Rappler.com

title: Sultan Haitham renews centuries-old trade links with London on state visit
body: Oman has renewed its historic links to the City of London with pledges by Sultan Haitham to grow joint investment and keep trade flowing under the shadow of the Iran war. Sultan Haitham, who is on the first Omani state visit in 44 years to the UK, used a banquet address in the finance, shipping and insurance hub to pledge that ties dating back to 1647 would blossom. Referring to how the London merchants signed a deal in that year to access Oman's ports, Sultan Haitham said: “Not for the last time the private sector got there first.” “We can see that bilateral investments and trade are moving in a positive direction, with concrete efforts being made to encourage investment and building stronger partnership in sectors such as sustainability, financial services and technology.” Speaking at the City's Guildhall, Lady Mayor Susan Langley said Oman's role in maintaining free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz was globally important. “We understand that the freedom of the seas, the security of trade routes, and global stability are the foundations upon which prosperity and peace are built,” she said. “Our partnership has helped protect those foundations for generations, allowing trade to flourish.” Further treaties followed in 1798 and 1800, while the UK was involved in a counter-insurgency in Oman as recently as the 1980s. Oman and the UK have signed a series of deals during Sultan Haitham's four-day visit with more than more than £1 billion of investment pledged. One pact was to “secure maritime co-operation through strengthened information-sharing and knowledge exchange with the Omani Maritime Security Centre”. Sultan Haitham met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street before the banquet, where the UK leader “gave his thanks for the Oman’s work to reopen the Strait of Hormuz”. “Both leaders agreed on the need to keep the Strait open to reduce the pressure on global supply chains and ease the impact on people at home,” the Prime Minister's Office said in a statement. Sultan Haitham acknowledged that the situation facing his country had “not been great” for more than 40 years but that his country was committed to doing whatever it could to normalise tensions. “We have great relations with Britain and we are all the time co-ordinating our moves and also getting help sometimes,” he said. Start-up and innovation focus Sultan Haitham visited the former Olympic Park in East London on Thursday, which has been one of the capital’s flagship projects for growth and regeneration. The visit was led by the UK's Minister of State for Trade, Anas Sarwar. At Here East, a cluster of buildings that consists of museums and businesses, Sultan Haitham met with chief executives and founders of British and Omani start-ups working at the frontiers of space, health care and artificial intelligence. “What we're showcasing is the best of British technology in those areas, with a view to catalyse on that deepening of that partnership,” said Saj Huq, chief executive of Plexal, an innovation-focused company at Here East that presented the start-up showcase to Sultan Haitham. Among them is Bio Orbit, founded in 2023 by Katie King and Leonor Teles, which hopes to manufacture drugs in space. The company raised £9.8 million ($13.1 million) as part of their seed-funding round. Mr Huq told the National that BioOrbit is “reformulating medicines by using crystallisation science in space to develop drug forms that can improve how medicines are delivered and used”. “There are really clear benefits to society and they're a real sector leader,” he said. Another Here East business is SAIF Autonomy, a start-up that builds safety layers for autonomous technology and embodied AI. “They are operating across both industry and defence and government” and “helping drive autonomy into complex systems in a responsible way”, Mr Huq added. The Omani climate tech company 44.01, which has also laid foundations in the UK, also played a part in the presentation. The company captures carbon emissions and buries them underground, using a natural process that occurs when the gas comes into contact with peridotite, a rock commonly found in Oman. The company won the Prince of Wales’ Earthshot Prize in 2022. “Part of the showcase is showing that we've already got these ties,” Mr Huq said. “The innovation ecosystems are already collaborating and they're growing in region.” Hormuz talks Iran has claimed a handful of attacks on vessels using a so-called Oman route through the Strait of Hormuz this week alone. Figures from data provider Kpler show that oil shipments out of the Gulf hit a high of 24.6 million barrels a day in the week to October 18. The volumes jump and slump depending on the hostility from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and average figures for October to date remain below levels before the war broke out in February. Ships in the Gulf and Red Sea transit hostile narrow straits with their automatic information systems switched off and there is a further lack of clarity about these journeys due to the military-related withholding of satellite imagery over the region. The UK and Oman signed an agreement to build an artificial intelligence data centre in Salalah involving partners from both nations. Officials said the first phase was expected to exceed £1 billion and would create more than 100 highly skilled jobs across the UK by exporting British expertise and attracting returns for UK-backed investors. The UK first signed a Sovereign Investment Partnership with Oman in 2022, with Oman investing £1.7 billion in the UK since its creation, a Foreign Office statement said.

title: Lockheed Martin raises outlook on F-35 and missile growth, flags funding shortfall
body: Backlog reached a record $292 billion, up 27% from the second quarter. Net earnings rose 14% to $1.8 billion, with sales growth across all four business segments. The company increased its forecasts for sales, earnings per share and free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter. Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet attributed the performance to growth across the portfolio. “In the third quarter each of our four segments posted growth year-over-year, sales topped $20.7 billion and net earnings exceeded $1.8 billion, increases of 11% and 14% respectively,” Taiclet said. “We delivered $3 billion of free cash flow in the quarter, and increased our backlog to a record $292 billion, allowing us to raise our dividend for the 24th year in a row.” Missile production lifts revenue Missiles and Fire Control sales rose 24%, driven by increased production of air defense and precision-strike weapons. PAC-3 and THAAD added $480 million in sales, while GMLRS and Precision Strike Missile programs contributed another $330 million. The segment’s operating profit also increased 24%, primarily reflecting higher volume. Across Lockheed Martin, business segment operating profit rose by $200 million, supported by missile production and Aeronautics growth. Aeronautics sales increased 13%, including $710 million in additional F-35 production and sustainment revenue. Higher C-130 sales partly reflected the recognition of pre-contract costs following an award, while lower F-16 volume and unfavorable profit adjustments offset some growth. Lockheed Martin said costs under the Lot 20 advance acquisition contract began exceeding existing authorization and funding during the quarter. Negotiations with the U.S. government continue on production contracts for Lot 20 and subsequent lots. Without additional authorization and funding, the company said future operating results, cash flows and financial condition would suffer. The warning accompanies higher revenue from the aircraft program. Free cash flow fell to $3 billion from $3.3 billion a year earlier. The company attributed the decline primarily to higher customer receipts in the comparable 2025 quarter. Rotary and Mission Systems sales grew 3%, mainly on higher radar program volume. Space sales rose 4%, with Fleet Ballistic Missile and Next Generation Interceptor growth partly offset by lower national security space revenue. Lockheed Martin spent $439 million on capital expenditure and $599 million on independent research and development during the quarter. Taiclet said the company was integrating artificial intelligence and autonomy into established systems through internal development and partnerships with other technology businesses.

title: Repatriation plans underway for 7 ‘missing but found’ Sekondi fishermen from Benin
body: Efforts are underway to repatriate seven fishermen aboard the canoe Second Chance who were reported missing at sea but have since been rescued in Benin’s territorial waters. The crew’s disappearance prompted a multi-agency search after the canoe failed to return from a fishing expedition off Axim in the Western Region. The canoe reportedly departed Sekondi Fishing Harbour on October 9 but suffered an engine failure, leaving the fishermen drifting offshore. The Western Regional Marine Police Command said in a statement dated October 22 that the seven men were rescued by local fishermen in Benin on October 21 at about 10 pm. The rescued fishermen have been identified as Kofi Emmanuel, 32; Uncle Amoah, 45; Kwamena Nkum, 29; Kofi Aboagye, 36; Doboa, 35; Agya Badu, 42; and Kwamena Akyem, 40. “The coordination is ongoing between the Marine Police Command, Ghana Navy and their counterparts in Benin and Togo to facilitate their safe repatriation to Ghana,” the statement said. The Command added that further updates would be communicated as more information became available. The rescue brings relief to the fishermen’s families as arrangements continue for their safe return home.

title: Protecting Ghana’s Students: Is the Time Right to revisit the case for Comprehensive Sexuality Education in our schools?
body: By Michael Augustus Akagbor, PhD When students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School vented their anger on campus in August this year, damaging property and forcing the school to close, many of us saw only indiscipline. Look a little closer, and a more troubling picture appears: young people who, by several accounts, had been trying for months to be heard. At least 19 female students have accused their headmaster of sexual abuse over the past year, according to an investigation by journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni. The Ghana Education Service interdicted him on 14 th October, and on 20 th October, the Interior Minister told Parliament that he had been arrested and that DNA evidence was being pursued. The headmaster has signalled legal action. The allegations are yet to be tested in court; he is entitled to due process, and I will not prejudge the outcome. A system that did not listen We do not need a verdict, however, to learn from how this case was handled. Teachers responsible for girl-child education and safeguarding reportedly wrote several letters and petitions, and the Municipal Education Directorate was aware of complaints. The president of NAGRAT said 38 teachers were asked to leave the school after speaking out against the headmaster, and that concerns date back to 2025. A district inquiry reportedly heard from only nine of 26 students, and treated one girl’s account of unwanted touching as merely her “definition” of assault. The warning signs were there. The people who raised them were sidelined. Left with no channel they trusted, the students eventually took matters into their own hands. Today, newly posted first-years cannot even begin classes. Sadly, Obuasi is not an exception. The same school saw a housemaster accused of misconduct in 2018. A national survey by the Gender Studies and Human Rights Documentation Center estimated that about one in 11 Ghanaian girls will experience sexual violence from a teacher or other school authority figure. Another study of 490 pupils in public schools found that 11.2% had been victims of rape or defilement, with girls making up 92% of victims, and concluded that our child-protection system was ineffective. Years earlier, a UNICEF survey found that 6% of schoolgirls said teachers had threatened to lower their grades unless they agreed to sex. The conversation we abandoned In 2019, Ghana’s attempt to introduce Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE) was withdrawn after a fierce backlash from religious bodies and others who feared it would bring foreign values into our classrooms. As recently as January this year, the Catholic Bishops’ Conference sought assurances that CSE would not return to the curriculum. Those concerns deserve respect. Parents have a right to shape what their children learn about morality and family life, and many sincerely believe that moral formation and abstinence teaching are the best protection a child can have. But Obuasi forces an uncomfortable question: what has our silence protected? Not the girls who reportedly were summoned alone to a headmaster’s residence. Not the students who lacked the words, or the confidence, to say clearly that what was happening to them was abuse and would be taken seriously. What the evidence tells us At its core, good sexuality education teaches children that their bodies belong to them, that no adult, however senior, has the right to touch them or trade favours for grades, and that telling a trusted adult is the right thing to do. A Cochrane review of 24 trials involving 5,802 children found that school-based abuse-prevention education improved children’s knowledge and protective behaviour and made them more likely to disclose abuse, with no sign that it made them anxious. That matters, because abusers depend on one thing above all else: silence. A Ghanaian way forward Revisiting CSE does not mean importing a foreign curriculum wholesale. It means building our own, with parents, faith leaders, teachers and young people at the table, anchored in values most Ghanaians share: dignity, respect and the protection of children. Whatever we call it, certain lessons should be non-negotiable: bodily autonomy, consent, recognising abuse of authority, and knowing how to report it. And because only about half of our adolescents reach senior high school, these lessons must begin in basic school. Education alone is not enough. Children who speak up need adults and systems that respond. That means confidential reporting channels that do not run through the school head, such as a national toll-free line linked to the Department of Social Welfare and the Police DOVVSU. It means real protection for teachers who blow the whistle, not transfers. It means making the GES Code of Conduct legally binding, as the Education Minister has proposed. And it means counseling, legal support and uninterrupted schooling for the Obuasi students. So, is the time, right? I believe it is. The real question was never whether our children will learn about sex and relationships; they will, from peers, phones and, too often, from those who would exploit them. The question is whether they will learn from us, in a framework we design, that their bodies are their own and that adults who abuse power will be held to account. The students of Obuasi SHTS had to protest to be heard. The next generation should not have to. About the Writer The writer is the Programs Manager for Human Rights and Social Inclusion at The Ghana Center for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana).

title: Godongwana moves R560 million to RFMCF, confirms R823 million Op Prosper allocation
body:
Confirmation of the R823 million National Treasury is making available to the SA National Defence Force (SANDF) for the ongoing Operation Prosper anti-crime deployment came from Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana in his Medium Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS) to Parliament on Wednesday 21 October.
Utilisation of more than two thousand SANDF personnel, the majority from the SA Army, for 12 months to support police efforts to curb gangsterism and illegal mining in five provinces was made public by President Cyril Ramaphosa in his February State of the Nation Address (SONA). He said at the time estimated expenditure for the deployment in the Eastern Cape, Free State, Gauteng, North West and Western Cape provinces would be R823 153 960.
Defence, Vote 23 in the Estimates of National Expenditure, will be welcomed by former SA Defence Force (SADF), SANDF and non-statutory force personnel belonging to the Regular Force Medical Continuation Fund (RFMCF) in that R560 million is to be transferred to it from projected unspent funds in other government departments. This ends speculation the Fund cannot pay healthcare treatment and medical claims submitted to it and clarifies what Department of Defence (DoD) Human Resources Division Chief, Lieutenant General Malungisa Sitshongaye, told the Portfolio Committee on Defence and Military Veterans (PCDMV) late in September.
Military and Public Service Act (PSA) personnel planning to take the early retirement and voluntary exit options from the DoD/SANDF are also provided for by Godongwana. R10.1 million will be moved from other government departments’ unspent funds to fund the departures.
Also on early retirement and voluntary exit, the South African finance minister told the National Assembly (NA) R439 million will be rolled over to cover financial incentives and medical continuation for those approved to end their service. Eight DoD/SANDF programmes will “donate” the funds with air defence and military health support each losing over R97 million. Other contributions to the early retirement/exit mechanism war chest are landward defence (R81.8 million), general support (R62.6 million), maritime defence (R48.5 million), administration (R24 million), force employment (R13.6 million) and Defence Intelligence (DI) (R13 million).
On the credit side of the ledger Godongwana’s MTBPS had it revenue in excess of R2 billion came from reimbursements settled by the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and the United Nations (UN). The income was for personnel and materiel contributions to the SADC Mission in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) – SAMIDRC under Operation Thiba – and the UN Mission in the same country under Operation Mistral. Additional income came from the sale of equipment and spares acquired through the Special Defence Account (SDA).
The revenue, Vote 23 reads, will go to relieve operational expenditure pressures, including shortfalls relating to leases and municipal services and provide for critical requirements identified in the 2015 Defence Review, such as upgrading prime mission equipment (PME). Five DoD/SANDF programmes will benefit with administration receiving the lion’s share – R800 million. Landward defence, referring to the SA Army, is number two with an allocation of R608.8 million followed by force employment (R313.7 million), military health support (R150 million) and air defence (R147 million).
Defence analyst Dean Wingrin noted that the latest MTBPS increases the defence budget by around R3.8 billion, largely as a result of the R2 billion reimbursement from UN/SADC and the R823 million allocation for Operation Prosper.
Defence’s adjusted 2026/27 budget goes from R57.6 billion to R61.46 billion, up R3.85 billion (+6.7%). However, “most of it isn’t fresh Treasury money,” he emphasised, and warned that the Department of Defence will again overspend on cost of employees (salaries) by about R3-4 billion.
The bottom line, he said, is that the R3.85 billion mostly refunds Operation Prosper expenses, retiree health, and exit packages. The Army gets the most, the Air Force a little, the Navy nothing new. “With DRC reimbursements fading and internal deployments increasing, expect the pressure to return. This supplementary mid-term allocation my keep the lights on, but that’s only because many of the light fittings have been removed. SA just does not have the economic growth or GDP to increase the Defence budget meaningfully.” Wingrin said it’s time to be realistic and relook at capabilities.
Vote 23 noted that the Department of Defence had achieved 2 298 863 reserve force person days by mid-year against an annual target of 2 619 960. This high achievement was largely attributable to the deployment of South African National Defence Force members through Operation Prosper.
“Over the same period, the department complied fully with all external and internal operations. This included the provision of support to operations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and participating in efforts to combat piracy in the Mozambique Channel, and executing all of South Africa’s internal commitments such as border safeguarding, police support and humanitarian search and rescue missions,” Vote 23 read.
“Although the department had conducted only two maritime coastal patrol by mid-year against an annual target of four, it remains on track to meet the target by the fourth quarter. Similarly, only 2 954 hours were flown by mid-year against an annual target of 12 000. The underachievement is primarily attributable to delays in sourcing specialised aircraft components, which have affected maintenance and repair schedules. This target is expected to be met in the fourth quarter. Delays in the maintenance and repair of vessels resulted in only 3 297 hours at sea against an annual target of 8 000 hours. Performance is expected to improve in the second half of the year once the maintenance and repair work is completed.”

title: Sharjah Animation and Comics Conference: Pixar veterans, comic book artists and a new focus on Arab talent
body: A character that begins in a comic book can eventually become the star of an animated film, a video game or an entire fictional universe. This increasingly interconnected approach to storytelling is at the heart of this year's Sharjah Animation and Comics Conference (SACC). The event, being held until Sunday at Aljada , is expanding beyond animation to embrace comics, bringing illustrators, writers and publishers into a programme that previously concentrated on filmmakers and animators. Organised by the Sharjah Book Authority, this year's event features more than 150 activities. These include 55 workshops and masterclasses, more than 40 talks and discussions, 10 film screenings and three live orchestral concerts. More than 75 speakers from over 30 countries are expected to participate. Khoula Al Mujaini, executive director of the SACC, says the expansion reflects changes already taking place across creative industries. "Comics felt like a natural next step because the way people tell and experience stories is already changing," she tells The National . "A character may begin in a comic, move into animation, become a game or develop into an entirely different kind of world. After three editions focused on animation, we felt SACC should reflect that wider creative reality." The expanded programme will explore everything from adapting animation into webtoons to transforming books into interactive experiences. Al Mujaini says that bringing these disciplines together will encourage collaboration between creative communities that increasingly share similar skills and audiences. Pixar veterans and international comic book artists Among the headline guests is Andrew Gordon, a former Pixar animator whose credits include Monsters, Inc. , Finding Nemo and The Incredibles . He will discuss the studio's approach to storytelling and lead a workshop examining artificial intelligence in animation. Another Pixar veteran, Doug Sweetland, whose credits include Toy Story and Monsters, Inc. , will share insights into directing animated shorts and developing memorable characters. They will be joined by Shuzo Shiota, chief executive of Japanese animation studio Polygon Pictures, and Terry Notary, a movement coach and performance-capture specialist known for his work on Avatar and Planet of the Apes. Notary will lead a workshop demonstrating how posture, breathing and physical movement can help performers create believable digital creatures. Comic book enthusiasts can meet artists Bernard Chang and Ken Lashley, alongside cartoonist Guy Gilchrist and writer and producer Shannon Eric Denton. Sessions will explore character design, drawing techniques and the development of original comics. Other workshops include traditional animation with Disney veteran Robb Pratt, stop-motion filmmaking with Egyptian artist Dina Amin and lightsaber choreography with stunt performer Lauren Mary Kim, who worked on Star Wars: The Clone Wars. Things to do and see Beyond the talks and workshops, the conference is introducing several attractions for fans and collectors. Artist Alley will show original works by regional artists, while the Comic Wall will feature rare and vintage comic books and collectables. At the Dubbing Corner, visitors can try voice acting by recording dialogue for animated scenes. The Meet the Artist programme offers opportunities to interact with international creators and purchase commissioned artwork. Gaming is another major attraction. A dedicated area will feature arcade machines, board games, racing simulators and trading card games, alongside tournaments in EA Sports FC 27 , Tekken 8 and Super Smash Bros Ultimate. A cosplay competition will take place on Saturday, with a Dh25,000 prize pool. Film screenings include Toy Story and Monsters, Inc. , introduced by Pixar animators, as well as The Glassworker , the Pakistani hand-drawn animated feature directed by Usman Riaz. The programme also includes the regional premiere of Walking with Animators and a selection of animated short films. Three orchestral concerts, scheduled for Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, will celebrate film scores, anime and K-pop music, and Disney favourites respectively. Building careers for Arab creators While entertainment remains a significant part of the event, Al Mujaini believes the conference can help address some of the structural challenges facing the region's creative industries. She says the Arab world already has the artists, audiences and stories needed to establish a stronger international presence in animation and comics. The challenge is developing sustainable careers and businesses around that talent. "A talented artist still needs access to producers, financing, publishers, broadcasters and distribution," she says. This year's expanded business-to-business programme aims to connect creators and publishers with producers, studio executives and other industry decision makers. Dedicated meetings will explore financing, international co-production, rights management and commercial development, while the Book2Screen Challenge will connect publishers and rights holders with producers interested in adapting written works for the screen. Al Mujaini says such initiatives can help regional creators move beyond individual projects towards developing original intellectual property with commercial potential. "We also need more original projects that reflect our own humour, cultures and visual identities," she says. "The opportunity is not to imitate what already exists elsewhere, but to build stronger pathways for Arab creators to make excellent work and give those stories the chance to travel." The conference will also examine how AI is changing animation production, from generating early concepts to streamlining technical processes. Gordon's workshop on Sunday will explore how AI can support visual development and production while allowing artists to retain control of their work. Al Mujaini believes emerging artists should remain open to new technology while continuing to develop their fundamental skills. "AI can be a useful tool for experimenting with ideas and making certain processes more efficient, but creativity, storytelling and artistic judgement remain essential," she says. "Ultimately, technology should support the artist's vision, not define it." Dates, location and tickets SACC will runs until Sunday at Aljada, Sharjah. Doors open at 1.30pm on Thursday, 12.15pm on Friday and 10.30am at the weekend. Tickets cost Dh85 for students, Dh135 for regular passes and Dh280 for business passes. Premium passes are priced at Dh3,000. Saturday passes are sold out.

title: Premium Times publisher, Falana, to headline DevReporting LG documentary screening
body:
Dapo Olorunyomi, publisher of PREMIUM TIMES and Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID), will chair the public screening of “LG Billions in the Dark”, an investigative documentary examining the prolonged local government leadership crisis in Osun State.
The screening, scheduled for Thursday, 29 October, at the University of Lagos (UNILAG), will feature human rights lawyer and Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Femi Falana, as keynote speaker.
According to a statement from DevReporting , Mr Falana will speak on “Accountability, Resources and Citizen Voices: Building Local Governments that Work for the People,” focusing on local government autonomy, public resource management, citizens’ rights and accountability at the grassroots.
“Nigeria’s local governments are constitutionally recognised as the tier of government closest to citizens, with responsibilities that directly affect everyday life, including primary healthcare, basic infrastructure, sanitation and other essential services,” it noted.
“However, concerns over financial control, political interference and the capacity of councils to function independently have remained central to debates about local governance in the country.”
The screening will feature a panel discussion involving public officials, civil society leaders, governance experts, academics and development practitioners.
The panellists include Osun State Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Dosu Babatunde; Executive Director of the Resource Centre for Human Rights and Civic Education (CHRICED), Zikirullahi Ibrahim; and Executive Director of Spaces for Change, Victoria Ibezim-Ohaeri.
Others are Joshua Osiyemi, Head of Tracka at BudgIT; Vera Amaechi, a lecturer in the Department of Political Science at the University of Lagos; and Bukola Adebayo, Senior Multimedia Strategist at DevReporting.
Speaking ahead of the event, DevReporting Team Lead, Mojeed Alabi, said the documentary reflects the organisation’s commitment to public-interest journalism and examining governance issues with direct consequences for citizens.
The event will also feature the official unveiling of the Development Reporting Africa Foundation (DRAF) and a fundraising initiative to support the foundation’s public-interest development reporting work.
“DRAF is a nonprofit initiative established to strengthen development reporting, generate and communicate evidence, promote public engagement and advance accountability on issues affecting communities across Africa,” Mr Alabi said.
DevReporting is also developing a civic education and youth engagement initiative that will take the documentary to tertiary institutions across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones.
The initiative will combine campus screenings, training, mentorship and youth-led accountability projects to deepen students’ understanding of local government administration, public finance and citizen participation.
According to DevReporting, the initiative is aimed at encouraging more young Nigerians to take an interest in how local governments are funded, how public resources are spent and how citizens can demand improved services.
The documentary was produced with support from the Royal Norwegian Embassy through CJID.
DevReporting is a media and cinematic platform focused on development issues across Nigeria and Africa. It produces investigative reports and multimedia stories and undertakes research and media capacity development to promote transparency, accountability and inclusive development.

title: Show HN: Runspace: Disposable cloud sandboxes for humans and AI agents
body:
Your commands run in a throwaway GitHub codespace. You get back the output and a patch, and your host stays clean.
Downloads the latest release and checks it against the release's SHA-256 checksums. Other ways to install
Your host runs one static binary with one GitHub token, and no repository configuration. Everything that binary is asked to run happens on the sandbox, a codespace that exists only until you delete it.
runspace acts only on codespaces whose display name is runspace , so it never touches your other codespaces. Code running inside a sandbox is not bound by that rule; see Limits .
The CLI and the MCP server run the same seven commands, defined once. They accept and reject the same input with the same message, so what works at your terminal works for your agent.
Two steps everyone takes, then the path for you or for your agent. create can take a few minutes, so give it time.
The install script downloads the prebuilt binary for your system and checks it against the release's SHA-256 checksums. It installs into ~/.local/bin on Linux and macOS, and on Windows into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\runspace , which it adds to your user Path .
Set RUNSPACE_VERSION to pin a release, such as v0.1.1 , and RUNSPACE_INSTALL_DIR to choose the directory. RUNSPACE_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 keeps the PowerShell script from changing your Path .
Or build from source with Go 1.26 or later, or download a prebuilt binary yourself.
Caution runspace uses the undocumented codespace connection protocol, which can change without notice.
The token needs the codespace scope. Keep it in RUNSPACE_TOKEN rather than passing -T , so it stays out of your shell history and process list.
Verified with a gh OAuth token that has the codespace and repo scopes.
A sandbox checks out the branch from GitHub, not your working tree. Push your changes first.
run creates a sandbox, runs the command there, passes its exit code through, and deletes the sandbox. Inside a repository whose origin is on github.com, you can leave off -R .
The first win: that output came from a codespace. The only thing that ran on your machine was runspace.
Create a sandbox, work in it, and take the result back as a patch. Read the stat before you apply it.
For a shell inside the sandbox, run runspace exec -t "$name" bash .
The tools carry your full authority. Fence them in before the agent gets them.
Add runspace mcp to your client as a stdio server. Clients that expand variables, such as Claude Code, fill in ${RUNSPACE_TOKEN} from their own environment, so the token never lands in the file.
Run it as the agent user, with no host execution or network tools. In the prompt, ask it to create a sandbox with the repository, branch, and sha , run every command there, then call diff with an output path and delete .
To teach it the workflow, install the Agent Skill ; replace .AGENT with your agent's configuration directory.
Delete any leftover sandboxes. Before you apply the patch, look for symlinks (mode 120000 ) and for changes to .github/ , .husky/ , or .pre-commit-config.yaml .
The first win: every command the agent ran happened in a sandbox, and what came back is a patch you have read.
Flags come before NAME or CMD ; everything after belongs to the remote command. runspace COMMAND --help lists every flag, and the README covers defaults and exit codes.
Read these before you hand runspace to an agent. The README has the full text.
The connection depends on an internal REST query, the codespace agent's gRPC service, and Dev Tunnels. Any of them can change without notice.
A sandbox can reach the internet. Its own GITHUB_TOKEN can read and write its source repository.
Code in a sandbox can use the codespace's GITHUB_TOKEN to run commands in every other codespace of the same identity and repository. Use a dedicated identity and sandbox repository, and one agent session per identity at a time.
Output can carry terminal escape sequences, and patches can add symlinks or edit CI and hook configuration.
cp downloads and diff -o write as much as the sandbox sends. --timeout bounds how long a transfer can run.
The repository's devcontainer must provide one, for example with ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/sshd:1 . The default image has one.
runspace waits for the checkout, not for the repository's own postCreateCommand .
While connected, runspace listens on a 127.0.0.1 port that other local users can reach.
A codespace runs for at most 12 hours at a time and idles out after 5 to 240 minutes. runspace works with github.com only.
A codespace is billed to the account that creates it while it exists. Delete each one you create, and set a Codespaces budget.
Install the binary, export a token, and send your first command to a codespace.
Source on GitHub Releases README SKILL.md Sponsor
runspace v0.1.1 · go.sandbox.ec/runspace · linux, darwin, windows on amd64 and arm64 · MIT License · internal/csconn contains code from the GitHub CLI, also MIT · works with github.com only · not affiliated with GitHub · set in Martian Mono, SIL Open Font License 1.1

title: Dubai pledges Dh150m to support humanitarian campaigns across UAE
body: Dubai on Thursday pledged Dh150 million ($40.8 million) to support humanitarian campaigns across the country, including efforts to deliver life-saving health care and offer a lifeline to war-hit civilians in the Gaza Strip . The Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives will provide the funds to 11 UAE-based charitable groups to strengthen their crucial work both at home and abroad. They include the UAE's Operation Gallant Knight, which was set up in response to the outbreak of the war in Gaza in October 2023 to assist civilians caught up in conflict. Al Jalila Foundation, the charitable arm of Dubai Health and a non-profit organisation dedicated to advancing medical research, education and treatment, will also benefit. The other recipients are: Tarahum Charity Foundation; the Mohammed Bin Rashid Al Maktoum Charitable Establishment; Emirates Health Services; the UAE Food Bank; Beit Al Khair Society; Dar Al Ber Society; Fujairah Charity Association; Noor Dubai; and the Digital School. The major investment was announced in the presence of Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence. Sheikh Hamdan praised the philanthropic vision of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, who established MBRGI in 2015. He said MBRGI “continues to provide all the necessary means to advance charitable and humanitarian work in the UAE” and noted that the latest allocation highlights its commitment to serving the needs of the community. The signing of the funding agreements was witnessed by Mohammad Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and secretary general of MBRGI. The organisation distributed Dh2.3 billion in funding for 165 million people in 122 countries last year. It was established in 2015 to oversee aid and relief operations, and launch projects to tackle issues such as poverty, hunger, health and education inequality. Gaza aid drive The latest funding for the UAE's humanitarian campaign for Gaza will boost continuing aid efforts in the enclave, as communities grapple with the effects of the Israel-Hamas war. The MBRGI launched the Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge initiative in September, aiming to supply more than 10 million meals to Palestinians. It began flying food parcels to Gaza in partnership with Operation Gallant Knight 3 this month. The initiative was named in honour of Sheikh Ahmed , brother of the Sheikh Mohammed, who died on September 21. It brought together volunteers, community members and admirers of Sheikh Ahmed at Dubai World Trade Centre to prepare food and aid packages for Gaza. The humanitarian bridge will operate through air and sea transport in seven consignments. Six flights will carry 450 tonnes of food parcels and one vessel will transport 4,000 tonnes of supplies to meet the basic nutrition needs of people in Gaza.

title: Russia returns bodies of 252 deceased to Ukraine
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War announced this on Telegram .
According to the Russian side, the bodies belong to Ukrainian military personnel.
The repatriation was made possible through the joint efforts of staff from the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, the Joint Center under the Security Service of Ukraine, the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Interior Ministry, the Office of the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Gone Missing under Special Circumstances, the State Emergency Service, and other agencies within Ukraine's security and defense sector.
Law enforcement investigators, together with representatives of expert institutions, will carry out all necessary procedures to identify the repatriated deceased.
The Coordination Headquarters expressed its gratitude to the International Committee of the Red Cross for its assistance.
"Special thanks go to the personnel of the Joint Center for Civil-Military Cooperation Support of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, which transports the repatriated deceased to specialized state institutions and organizes the transfer of the fallen to law enforcement representatives within the Interior Ministry system and to forensic medical experts within the Health Ministry system. Thanks are also extended to representatives of the Armed Forces' civil-military cooperation units, who coordinate the process overall," the headquarters said.
On September 17, Ukraine received the bodies of 252 deceased people whom the Russian side claimed were Ukrainian military personnel.

title: Iran preparing to reveal 'Father of All Bombs,' IRGC spox. warns in wake of Trump's MOAB threat
body: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced on Wednesday that it was preparing to unveil a new weapon, which it dubbed the "Father of All Bombs," in response to US threats to use the most powerful conventional bomb in the American arsenal against Iran's nuclear facilities.The announcement comes amid rising security tensions between Tehran and Washington and the possibility of renewed US strikes on Iranian territory.IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohabi told the Iranian Young Journalists Club news agency that "We are in the preparatory stages of unveiling the 'Father of All Bombs.' This is something new for the enemy."However, the spokesperson declined to provide details on the weapon type, its power, operational capabilities, or when it would be unveiled to the public, according to Turkey's official Anadolu Agency.US reportedly preparing plans to use Mother of All BombsThe Iranian announcement follows US media reports that the Pentagon had prepared plans to use the GBU-43/B bomb, known as the "Mother of All Bombs" (MOAB), against targets in Iran. Weighing approximately 9.8 metric tons (20,000 lb.), the bomb is considered one of the most powerful conventional weapons in the US arsenal.The bomb was first used in April 2017, during US President Donald Trump's first term, against an ISIS tunnel complex in Afghanistan. It is designed to generate an exceptionally powerful blast wave over a wide area but is not intended to penetrate deep underground like specialized bunker-busting bombs.In an interview with Newsmax last Thursday, Trump addressed the possibility of using the weapon, emphasizing that it was not a nuclear bomb. The president ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran but did not rule out a strike using the conventional bomb.Alongside the announcement of the new weapon, Mohabi claimed that Iran's missile stockpile had increased by 50% since the 12-day war against Israel in June 2025.According to Mohabi, Iran has also significantly improved the quality of its missiles, their operational ranges, destructive power, and targeting accuracy. However, the spokesperson provided no figures that would allow the claims regarding the expansion of Iran's arsenal to be independently verified.Strait of Hormuz is not open, IRGC spokesperson saysMohabi also discussed the Strait of Hormuz, denying US claims that it was open."If, under the cover of darkness, a few small vessels manage to slip past us - by switching off their tracking equipment and bribing shipping companies or crews - this does not mean the Strait is 'open'; rather, it signifies piracy and smuggling," he said.At most, he said, the US had been able to smuggle one or two million barrels of oil, at what he claimed was a very high cost."The Strait of Hormuz is definitely closed; however, we must clarify what 'open' and 'closed' mean in this context," he said. "An 'open' Strait of Hormuz implies a waterway where any vessel - regardless of its origin or destination - can freely enter and exit, much like the situation that existed prior to the '40-Day War' [operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion]."The announcement follows the war that broke out between the US, Israel, and Iran in February, during which Tehran attacked targets in Israel and US military bases in Arab countries.Despite a memorandum of understanding signed between Washington and Tehran in June, negotiations between the two countries collapsed over disagreements concerning freedom of navigation and security in the Strait of Hormuz.The latest Iranian announcement adds to the ongoing exchange of threats between Tehran and Washington.Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

title: IRGC threatens invasion of neighbours that attack Iran
body:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has threatened “to invade” any country in the Middle East that attacks Iran as tensions in the region rise.
The IRGC spokesperson, Hossein Mohebi, on Wednesday, said Iran’s security doctrine has become “offensive and asymmetrical.”
Al Jazeera reported that Mr Mohebi said Iran’s defence doctrine was previously defensive but shifted to ‘offensive and asymmetrical’ because of its realities.
“We announced that if a country attacked us, we would respond to it,” he said.
“Now, we say if a country attacks us, we will respond to it, and we will invade. Our doctrine will no longer be only offensive and will become asymmetrical. We will attack the enemy in such a way that it will understand the intensity of our action.”
The US-Iran war, now over seven months, continued to heighten tension in the Middle East, with persistent strike exchanges, negotiations, and diplomatic pressure failing to bring an end to the war.
The US and Iran remain divided over the control of the Strait of Hormuz, sanction relief and Iranian uranium enrichment.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the country is prepared to give diplomacy another chance. But this is dependent on “strong evidence of a sincere desire by the US to build trust and reach a just solution.”
“If the US chooses war over diplomacy, it’ll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure.”
The IRGC has also threatened to attack US bases in the region if tankers continue to pass through the waterway illegally.
The armed forces said it will extend “confrontation to US bases” in the region if Washington continues to urge “vessels to pass through mined waterways illegally.”
It also declared that its navy struck four ships involved in oil transfers in the Gulf, and that three other vessels caught fire after hitting mines near the Strait of Hormuz.
“The US aggressor military must understand that, if this continues, the scope of confrontation will extend to the bases of the aggressors in the region. This is a serious warning,” it said.
Mr Mohebi also taunted the United States over the Strait of Hormuz, saying the repercussions would influence the upcoming midterm elections for President Trump’s Republican Party.
“The Strait of Hormuz has squeezed the economic and political throat of the United States,” he said
Meanwhile, Iran called the US naval blockade of Iran “a flagrant violation” of international law and the UN Charter, in a letter to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and Security Council President Aglaia Balta.
The letter, written by Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations, Gholam Hossein, asked the global organisation to urge the US to immediately cease its military aggression against Iran and lift the maritime blockade.
He asked that the UN recognise that Washington remains internationally responsible for its “internationally wrongful acts, including its military aggression” and any “continuing violations of international law, and that the obligations to cease wrongful conduct and to make full reparation remain applicable in accordance with the law of State responsibility.”

title: HACC extends Halushchenko's duties, removes electronic bracelet
body:
The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) has extended the term of procedural duties for former Minister of Energy Herman Halushchenko, who is a suspect in the "Midas" corruption case, but removed the requirement to wear an electronic monitoring device.
"HACC partially satisfied the motion of the SAPO prosecutor and extended for 2 months the term of procedural duties imposed on the former minister of energy," the HACC reported on its Telegram channel on Thursday.
According to the report, the suspect is required to report to NABU detectives, SAPO prosecutors in this criminal proceeding, and the investigating judge upon every request; not leave Kyiv and Kyiv region without permission from NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors; report any change in his place of residence; refrain from communicating with specified individuals; and surrender all his passports for travel abroad and any other documents granting the right to leave Ukraine to the State Migration Service of Ukraine for storage.
"At the same time, the investigating judge refused to extend the term of the duty to wear an electronic monitoring device," the statement notes.
The reasoning behind the decision, as clarified by the court, will be set out in the full text of the ruling, which will be available in the Unified State Register of Court Decisions.
As reported, the former minister of energy was detained while attempting to leave Ukraine as part of Midas case on February 15, 2026. On February 16, he was served with a notice of suspicion in the "Midas" case, facing charges of money laundering and participation in a criminal organization.
Halushchenko was taken into custody with an alternative bail set at UAH 200 million; in June, HACC extended the former minister's detention period but reduced bail to UAH 150 million. At the end of June, the bail for Halushchenko was posted, and procedural duties were imposed on him.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search
body:
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.
Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives , a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong.”
The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.
In the interview with MS NOW , Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.
Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation .
Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.
“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I'm sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seams like a leap,” she said in the interview.
The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.
Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite,” logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.
Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: FACT CHECK: Is Uganda Govt Right About Nationality Of Nigeria’s First Ebola Patient?
body: Claim: The Ugandan government said Nigeria’s first Ebola patient was a Nigerian national who travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for business and transited through Uganda on her way home. The Ugandan government, through its Director-General of Health Services, Charles Olaro, described Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola patient as a Nigerian national who travelled to eastern DRC for business before passing through Uganda in early October. In a statement issued following Nigeria’s announcement of the case, the Ugandan Ministry of Health said the woman had not developed symptoms while in Uganda and that her passage through the country did not establish that she contracted the virus there. “Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said. The Ugandan government also maintained that it had no active confirmed Ebola cases at the time of its statement. The account presented the woman as a Nigerian national returning from a business trip to the DRC, with Uganda serving only as a transit point. However, information subsequently provided by the Africa CDC and Nigerian health authorities differed significantly from this description. What the Africa CDC Said The Director-General of the Africa CDC, Dr Jean Kaseya, in a report published by the BBC on Thursday said that the patient was originally from Uganda but lived in Abuja, where she fell ill after returning from a trip to Kampala. Kaseya identified the woman as the wife of a diplomat and said she had travelled to Uganda’s capital for a holiday, contradicting the Ugandan government’s description of her as a Nigerian business traveller returning from the DRC. According to Kaseya, the woman returned to Nigeria on October 3 and developed symptoms three days later, on October 6. Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate, also stated that the 42-year-old woman had spent approximately two and a half weeks in Kampala before returning to Abuja through Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, where she had a two-hour stopover. The accounts from Kaseya and Pate therefore challenge the Ugandan government’s description of both the woman’s nationality and the purpose of her journey. Nigeria’s Federal Government confirmed its first Ebola case since the 2014 outbreak on October 20, 2026, following laboratory tests on the woman. According to Pate, the patient initially sought treatment at a private hospital after developing symptoms but believed she had malaria. She subsequently visited another private hospital, where she was admitted on October 11 after her condition failed to improve. Public health authorities were alerted on October 19, and her Ebola diagnosis was confirmed the following day after three laboratory tests, according to the minister. Pate said the patient was stable and responding to treatment. The government also identified 44 people who had come into contact with her and began measures to prevent further transmission. The contacts were being monitored, and none had developed symptoms at the time of the report. Pate said Nigerian authorities were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the patient’s complete travel history and determine where she might have contracted the virus. “We respect our sister nation of Uganda,” he said. “We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together.” The dispute over the patient’s nationality comes amid an Ebola outbreak linked to the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. According to reports citing the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, the outbreak, which began in May 2026, had recorded more than 9,500 cases and approximately 4,600 deaths in the DRC by October 19. The outbreak has raised concerns about cross-border transmission as infected people move between countries in the region. The Bundibugyo virus belongs to the group of viruses that cause Ebola disease. It is a distinct species from the Zaire ebolavirus, which caused several previous major outbreaks, including the 2014–2016 West African epidemic. Unlike Zaire ebolavirus, for which vaccines and specific treatments have been developed, there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo virus disease, although research and clinical trials have been ongoing. Uganda also recorded Ebola infections during 2026 but subsequently declared its outbreak over in August after its last patient was discharged and the required period without a new confirmed case had elapsed. The Ugandan government has maintained that it had no active confirmed cases when Nigeria announced its latest infection. Kenya has also reported cases linked to the regional outbreak, increasing concerns about the movement of the virus across international borders. Nigeria’s first major Ebola outbreak occurred in July 2014, when Patrick Sawyer, a Liberian-American man infected with the virus, arrived in Lagos from Liberia. Sawyer became ill after arriving in Nigeria and was admitted to a hospital in Lagos, where he later died. His infection led to further transmission among some healthcare workers and other contacts. Nigeria recorded 20 cases, comprising 19 laboratory-confirmed cases and one probable case, with eight deaths. The World Health Organisation declared Nigeria free of Ebola transmission on October 20, 2014, after the country completed the required 42-day period without a new case. The outbreak was contained through contact tracing, isolation, infection prevention measures and the coordination of public health agencies. How Ebola Spreads Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause high mortality, although outcomes vary depending on the virus species, outbreak conditions and access to care. The World Health Organisation estimates that the average case fatality rate across Ebola disease outbreaks is approximately 50 per cent. The virus spreads primarily through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or someone who has died from the disease. Transmission can also occur through contaminated clothing, bedding, medical equipment and other materials. Ebola does not spread through the air in the same way as infections transmitted through ordinary breathing in shared indoor spaces. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days. Infected people do not transmit the disease before symptoms develop, but they can spread it after symptoms begin. These characteristics make accurate travel histories, prompt diagnosis and effective contact tracing essential to controlling outbreaks. Verdict: False The Ugandan government’s claim that Nigeria’s first Ebola patient was a Nigerian national returning from a business trip to eastern DRC conflicts with the account provided by Africa CDC Director-General Dr Jean Kaseya, who said the woman was originally from Uganda, lived in Abuja and was the wife of a diplomat. Kaseya said she had travelled to Kampala for a holiday.

title: Chinese stocks turn biggest losers as global AI trade stumbles
body:
(Oct 17): Chinese firms have emerged as the biggest losers of the faltering global artificial intelligence (AI) trade, a setback for Beijing’s efforts to use stock markets to supercharge its ambition of technological supremacy.
The Nasdaq-style Star50 Index has tumbled nearly 40% in the current half year, becoming the world’s worst-performing major tech gauge. Major chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits Shanghai Co and Moore Threads Technology Co have both shed around half of their value during this period.
The ChiNext index, similarly focused on hardware stocks, has lost 36%.
It marks a reversal of fortunes from earlier this year, when the Star50 enjoyed a stunning rally as investors ignored frothy valuations to bet on Beijing’s policy push and ride the global AI boom. All that enthusiasm has since unravelled as scrutiny of future demand and earnings prospects hit Chinese stocks the hardest, a worrisome development given the heavier reliance on equity financing by the country’s firms.
“It would be much harder for China to achieve its AI ambitions if technology stocks remain under pressure for an extended period,” said Leonid Mironov, a portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital. “If the weakness goes on for more than six months, this will make fundraising difficult and also imply that the market is unimpressed with the technological progress being achieved.”
The Star50 surged around 75% between April and June — beating Korea’s Kospi — on optimism about Chinese firms’ technological breakthroughs and strong state support. The gauge traded at over 80 times forward earnings at its peak on June 30. Yet as sentiment abruptly turned, the sector’s high valuations have become a liability.
“The global AI-hardware sell-off, spanning the Nasdaq and Korea, hit China A-shares hardest after foreign investors crowded into the sector in 2Q,” Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Jason Liao and Marvin Chen wrote in a note, referring to China’s onshore equities.
Outflows from a trading link with Hong Kong that allows foreign investors access to Chinese local stocks totalled an estimated 90 billion yuan (US$13.5 billion or RM54.9 billion) in the third quarter, the biggest in a year and reversing more than half of the inflows between April and June, the note says.
The recent sell-off has also weighed on some of China’s hottest trading debuts. Memory-chip giant CXMT Corp, which went public in July, has fallen 27% from its post-listing peak. Similarly, robotics firm Yushu Technology Co, has lost around 50% from an August high shortly after its initial public offering.
Chinese companies have fetched a combined US$37 billion (RM151 billion) from onshore IPOs this year, lifting annual proceeds to their highest in three years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg . Tech firms accounted for over a third of the funds raised.
The underperformance of China’s tech stocks poses a challenge for authorities that are keen to use capital markets to fuel the firms’ growth. The country’s AI-linked national champions and startups have shown a stronger preference for equity financing over debt, partly reflecting the higher costs for them to issue bonds globally.
Equities are “the default source” of funding for China’s AI firms, according to Mironov. “If the slump is prolonged it will have an impact and Beijing may need to be more proactive in expediting financial sector reforms and potentially deploying the national team more aggressively,” he said, referring to a group of state-backed funds used by regulators to stabilise markets.
To be sure, the tide may shift if the government significantly increases efforts to prop up the languishing market. Financial regulators held a meeting Thursday to discuss stabilisation measures and called on the national team to accelerate stock purchases. Any pleasant surprises from the upcoming third-quarter earnings season may also help brighten the mood.
Still, some investors are sceptical about the outlook because China’s AI-related stocks remain expensive even after the recent sell-off. The Star50 now trades at over 40 times forward earnings. It compares with less than five times for South Korea’s Kospi Index and 21 times for the Nasdaq 100.
“Current levels represent a technical pullback, not a value play,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at Gam Investment Management. “For many high-potential tech names, big bargains won’t appear until they fall another 30%-50%.”
