title: Could Treating AI as Conscious Make It More Dangerous?
body:
Billions are driving a race against Beijing’s decades-long lead
The Baogang Tailings Dam, near the industrial city of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia, is one of the most polluted bodies of water in the world. The 11-square-kilometer artificial lake holds the effluent from decades of rare-earth and other industrial-processing operations.
One of the singular features of Baotou, an industrial city of 2 million people in Inner Mongolia, is a 10-square-kilometer (4-square-mile) lake that is among the most polluted in the world. The artificial lake, referred to by the name of the dam associated with it, Weikuang Dam (or Baogang Tailings Dam), has for decades collected the effluent from minerals processing for China’s globally dominant iron, steel, and rare-earths industries.
Built in the late 1950s, the lake contains a highly toxic stew of industrial chemicals with substantial amounts of radioactive thorium , the latter resulting primarily from the processing of monazite ores for rare-earths . China has since greatly tightened its environmental regulations and restrictions on mining and minerals processing. For example, largely because of the environmental disaster that is Weikuang Dam, the country doesn’t permit the development or operation of stand-alone monazite mines—that is, mines where nothing is mined except monazite ore.
Now, with industrialized nations in North America, Asia, and Europe spending billions to shore up their rare-earths supply chains, and counting on monazite to help them do it, China’s history and experiences with monazite offer important lessons.
This article is a collaboration between Foreign Policy , the global magazine of politics and ideas, and IEEE Spectrum , the flagship magazine of the IEEE.
Monazite ore is a pillar of China’s rare-earths industry because it is a prime source of some less common but extremely important rare-earth elements, notably dysprosium, terbium, yttrium, and erbium. The country mines and processes vast quantities of monazite ore; it also imports huge amounts of monazite ore for processing.
Most of the domestically mined monazite ore comes from a single mine: the mammoth Bayan Obo complex, 150 kilometers north of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia. Bayan Obo, which is primarily an iron-ore mine, also happens to contain the largest known rare-earth deposit in the world. It’s the source of nearly half of all the rare-earth ore mined on the planet in a typical year. Most of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is a type called bastnaesite; it’s the mining of that bastnaesite that makes it legal to mine monazite ore at Bayan Obo as well.
Related: Can a Radioactive Ore Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths?
All told, ore from Bayan Obo was used to produce 170,000 tonnes of rare-earth metal last year, according to David Merriman , research director at the minerals intelligence firm Project Blue . Roughly 30 percent to 40 percent of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is monazite. That amount alone would be enough to make China the world’s largest processor of monazite for rare-earths.
But a more detailed picture of China’s interest in monazite emerges when you consider the country’s imports of the ore. Last year, they amounted to more than 70,000 tonnes, says Thomas Kruemmer , a Singapore-based consultant on minerals and metals. That figure becomes more impressive when you consider the unique challenges of shipping monazite by sea. Because of its radioactivity, concentrated monazite ore is classified as Class 7 dangerous cargo under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code. That means, Kruemmer notes, that the ore can be imported through only four ports in China.
In addition, importation of some kinds of monazite into China is supposed to go through a joint venture consisting of the China National Nuclear Corp . and Shenghe Resources , which are at least partly state-owned. But lots of imported monazite doesn’t go through those organizations, notes Merriman. That’s because heavy mineral sands, which may contain roughly 2 percent or 3 percent monazite by weight, are not subject to the same import controls as concentrated monazite ore. So companies import the heavy mineral sands; separate out various profitable concentrates, including the monazite mineral concentrate; and then process the monazite concentrate to recover the rare-earths.
China has lately stepped up its efforts to secure rare-earth ore around the world. One reason, says Kruemmer, is simply to make up for recently lost supplies. In 2025, the U.S. government invested US $400 million in MP Materials, which operates the Mountain Pass mine and processing facility in California. The deal put an end to long-standing contracts under which MP Materials had been selling tens of thousands of tonnes of rare-earth concentrate annually to a trading affiliate of Shenghe Resources.
But other Westerners speculate that China has strategic reasons for stepping up its efforts to acquire heavy mineral sands or other rare-earth assets abroad. By locking down rights to deposits or projects abroad, Chinese organizations are making them unavailable to non-Chinese developers, according to this reasoning.
Merriman points out that your view of these activities largely depends on where you sit. The U.S. government recently made a conditional loan commitment of up to $725 million to U.S. monazite processor Energy Fuels, which has been aggressively securing substantial monazite supplies in Australia , Brazil , and Madagascar. To a Chinese observer, those moves probably look rather strategic.
China, meanwhile, is doing what it has been doing for decades. “China’s playing its game,” says Merriman.
This article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Radioactive Realpolitik .”

title: Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO
body: Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee. The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry. Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.” Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.” According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion. Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control. The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis. France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. Under the July 2025 Northwood Declaration the two countries agreed to create a Nuclear Steering Group to provide political direction and coordinate across nuclear policy, capabilities and operations, and President Macron announced changes to French nuclear doctrine in March 2026 which included moving towards forward deterrence. That resulted in bilateral agreements with NATO countries including Denmark and Norway in the High North, allowing French nuclear aircraft to deploy temporarily to their territory for exercises and joint missions. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign. The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales. Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO. The post Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Iran, China stress developing Global South cooperation
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, said Tehran and Beijing both emphasize expanding Global South cooperation during talks with China's ambassador.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, said in a social media post that during a meeting with China's ambassador, the two sides consulted and exchanged views on strengthening cooperation and coordination in defending national sovereignty, respecting international law, countering unilateralism, and addressing threats to regional peace and security.
Gharibabadi added that Iran and China both stress the need to expand Global South cooperation.

title: Escalating geopolitical tensions does not contribute to a peaceful Arctic — China’s MFA
body:
BEIJING, October 22. /TASS/. Taking sides and attempts to stoke geopolitical rivalry in the Arctic do not contribute to peaceful development in the region, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning said at a news briefing on Thursday.
"The taking of sides in the spirit of the Cold War and the fueling of geopolitical confrontation does not contribute to a peaceful and steady development of the Arctic region," the Chinese diplomat argued, commenting on the EU’s new strategy for the Arctic and statements from the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas saying that the EU is going to counter Russia and China in the region.
On Tuesday, the European Commission (EC) unveiled its new Arctic strategy focused on military construction for the first time in more than 30 years. A separate provision in the revamped strategy focuses on developing shipping routes in the Arctic and "protecting northern maritime borders."
Although the EU’s executive arm did not mention the Northern Sea Route in the document, one day before the publication Kallas announced EU plans to challenge Russia’s control of the route and seek unrestricted access to it in an interview with The Times. The bloc’s diplomacy chief said the West "must stop Russia and China" from moving toward dominance in the region.

title: Gov Otu Presents N987.8bn 2027 Budget
body: Cross River State Governor, Bassey Otu, yesterday presented a proposed N987.8 billion budget for the 2027 fiscal year to the state House of Assembly, christening it the ‘Budget of Consolidation and Renewed Hope’, and reaffirming his administration’s commitment to sustainable development, fiscal discipline, and inclusive economic growth. Presenting the estimates in Calabar, Otu described the budget as more than an aggregation of figures, characterising it as “a solemn and sacred pact laden with the trust, expectation and aspiration of the people for their improved livelihoods.” He said its successful implementation would depend on prudent resource management, accountability and disciplined public expenditure, underscoring his administration’s determination to translate its social contract with the people into tangible improvements in their living conditions. The proposed budget, valued at precisely N987,808,089,235.92, represents an increase of approximately 2.57 per cent over the 2026 budget. Capital expenditure accounts for N708.43 billion, representing 71.72 per cent of the total provision, while recurrent expenditure stands at N279.38 billion, or 28.28 per cent. The substantial capital allocation, according to the governor, reflects the government’s determination to prioritise infrastructure, human capital development and productive investments capable of stimulating economic activity. Otu explained that the 2027–2029 Medium-Term Expenditure Framework and Fiscal Strategy Paper provided the foundation for the estimates, adding that the budget would sustain ongoing programmes while opening new pathways for investment, employment creation and improved public services. “The imperative of this exercise underscores our collective resolve to chart a sustainable course for the growth and development of our state,” he declared. Addressing concerns surrounding the state’s debt profile, the governor maintained that his administration had refrained from obtaining fresh domestic and external loans since assuming office in 2023. Citing verifiable indices from the National Bureau of Statistics and the Debt Management Office, he said Cross River remained among the few states that had not contracted new loans during the period. He attributed the state’s existing debt burden to obligations inherited from previous administrations, explaining that debt servicing had constrained the pace at which available resources could be deployed to development projects. He further clarified that the naira value of external debt had been affected by currency devaluation and foreign-exchange liberalisation. “I cannot, and will never mortgage the future of our children with unsustainable loans,” Otu declared, pledging to strengthen internally generated revenue, maximise federal allocations and attract development assistance and private-sector investment to finance the state’s development priorities. Reviewing the performance of the 2026 budget, the governor acknowledged the pressures of exchange-rate volatility, rising operational costs, supply-chain disruptions and inherited debt obligations. He disclosed that the administration had collaborated with the legislature to enact a supplementary budget, raising the spending framework to N963.07 billion to accommodate urgent interventions and counterpart-funding requirements. Among the achievements highlighted was the delivery of more than 608 kilometres of interconnected road projects across the three senatorial districts, including the Nsan–Oban Road in Akamkpa, the Adiabo–Ikoneto Road in Odukpani and the Yahe–Ebo–Wanakade Road in Yala. He also reported progress in rural electrification through solar streetlights, mini-grids and network rehabilitation, describing the interventions as essential to reopening economic corridors, improving mobility and restoring commercial activity in underserved communities. Agriculture featured prominently in the governor’s account of the administration’s economic transformation agenda. Otu disclosed that more than 20,000 bags of fertiliser had been distributed to 8,000 farmers, while over one million improved oil-palm, cowpea and cocoa seedlings had been provided to farmers across the state. He also highlighted the establishment of a 50,000-hectare rice project and support for more than 5,300 livestock farmers, alongside loans, grants and agricultural machinery for smallholder and large-scale producers. According to him, an N18 billion offtake arrangement had helped advance the state’s agricultural initiatives, while the cash-crop revolution was strengthening the productive capacity of farmers. “There is no food security without agriculture,” he asserted, adding that the government intended to become Nigeria’s leading cocoa and oil-palm-producing state through expanded cultivation, mechanisation, agro-allied industries and private-sector partnerships. On healthcare, education and public-sector welfare, Otu outlined interventions designed to improve access, strengthen institutions and enhance service delivery. He cited the renovation and rehabilitation of hospitals, the establishment of medical oxygen plants in Calabar and Ogoja in partnership with UNICEF, and the upgrading of state-owned Schools of Nursing and Midwifery to accreditation standards. He also highlighted a reported 95 per cent routine immunisation coverage, implementation of the Consolidated Medical Salary Structure for medical workers and an increase in the retirement age of health workers from 60 to 65 years. In education, he said the state had deployed more than N17 billion in Universal Basic Education Commission intervention funds, supported classroom construction and rehabilitation, paid WAEC examination fees for 43,694 Cross River State indigenes and approved the promotion of more than 14,000 teaching and non-teaching staff. The government, he added, was targeting a literacy rate of 98 per cent from the current estimated 80.7 per cent, while strengthening technical and vocational education to equip young people with employable and entrepreneurial skills. The 2027 estimates also assign prominent roles to aviation, transportation, maritime development and tourism in the state’s economic diversification strategy. The governor disclosed the integration of a new Bombardier CRJ regional jet into the state’s aviation assets, bringing the fleet to five aircraft, alongside accelerated construction work at the Obudu International Passenger and Cargo Airport. He further highlighted the acquisition of 730 electric vehicles, comprising inter-city and metropolitan buses, tricycles and motorcycles, to reduce commuting costs and support cleaner transportation. On the maritime front, he said the Bakassi Deep Seaport had secured the federal government’s approval and Certificate of Compliance, and was awaiting the commencement of construction, with anticipated private investment of approximately $3.5 billion. He also cited the federal government’s formal re-accreditation of Cross River as a littoral state, describing it as a strategic development for the state’s maritime ambitions. “Our overall target in this sector is to transform our aviation business model into a highly profitable and self-sustaining revenue asset for the state,” he said. Infrastructure receives the largest explicitly listed sectoral allocation of N246.1 billion, followed by education with N99.6 billion, health with N85.4 billion, agriculture with N28.2 billion and aviation with N21.8 billion. Other provisions include N20.2 billion for the House of Assembly, N19.1 billion for the judiciary, N16.6 billion for power and N11.3 billion for tourism. The governor said the budget would continue to align with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, ensuring continuity in unfinished projects and directing resources towards the state’s strategic priorities. He pledged continued investment in forest conservation and the green economy, judicial infrastructure, security and youth empowerment. In education, the governor reaffirmed the policy of free and compulsory education from primary to junior secondary school, alongside the payment of WAEC fees for public-school students. On the judiciary, he promised adequate funding for ongoing court projects and further improvements in the working conditions of judicial officers, while urging the institution to pursue reforms that would strengthen public confidence in justice delivery. Concluding his presentation, Otu pledged to sustain a government that is responsive to the needs of citizens, prudent in the management of public resources and accountable to the electorate. He emphasised the importance of harmonious relations among the executive, legislature and judiciary, describing institutional cooperation as indispensable to peace, stability and shared prosperity. The governor formally sought the Assembly’s consideration and timely passage of the proposed N987.8 billion Appropriation Bill, expressing confidence that its implementation would accelerate economic growth and improve the welfare of Cross Riverians.

title: Interdicted Obuasi SHTS head sues Manasseh Azure, MGL for defamation amid sexual abuse allegations
body: The interdicted headmaster of the Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, has sued JoyNews investigative correspondent, Manasseh Azure Awuni and the Multimedia Group Ghana Limited (MGL) over allegations of sexual abuse involving female students in the school. Mr Azure is the 1st defendant, while MGL is the second. The plaintiff is seeking a declaration that the statements made and or/published about him by the defendants are false, defamatory and malicious. He’s also seeking an order of perpetual injunction restraining the defendant from making, writing or any other way publishing any further defamatory statements about him. He’s also seeking GHS2 million for the defamation and other general damages. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Thursday, October 22, Mr Azure said the case was his 12th defamation suit since 2015. “That is defamation suit number 12 since 2015, and I think my lawyers will handle that,” he said. Manasseh Azure’s investigative piece titled Inside The Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow exposed cases of alleged rape involving the headmaster, leading to his interdiction by the Ghana Education Service amid ongoing investigations. Following the investigation, the Headmaster, who also served as Juaben Constituency Secretary for the National Democratic Congress and was seeking to contest for Constituency Chairman, withdrew from the race under pressure from his party. It emerged from the report that some of the alleged sexual cases had been reported to the Police, but investigations were either slow or had stalled. The report also revealed that some teachers, education authorities and political heads had failed to fulfil responsibilities expected of them, resulting in pressure and victimisation against staff members seeking justice for the affected girls. He specifically mentioned the school’s focal person and girl-child coordinator, as well as others he said were determined to pursue justice for the students. “There were things they were supposed to do that they didn’t do, and because of that there was a lot of pressure and victimisation against the focal person, the girl-child coordinator and those who were bent on getting justice for these girls,” he said. Meanwhile, the Police Criminal Investigations Department has confirmed that the docket on the case had been forwarded to the Attorney General for advice.

title: Three configurable prettyprinters (2023)
body:
I gave a fifteen minute talk about this at Zurihac 2023. If you read this essay, I don't think there's much point in additionally watching the video.
I've been exploring a new-to-me approach to stringification. Except that right now it's three different approaches that broadly share a common goal. I call it/them pretty-gist .
The lowest-friction way to stringify things in Haskell is usually show . It gives the user close to zero ability to control how the thing is rendered.
The Show1 and Show2 classes give some control, but only in limited ways. Importantly, they only work on parameterized values; you could use Show2 to change how you render the keys of a Map Int String , but not of an IntMap String .
There are also things that give you some control over layout, but not much control over content. For example, aeson-pretty lets you pretty-print json data, and pretty-simple can pretty-print typical output from show . Both let you configure indent width, and pretty-simple additionally lets you choose some different layout styles (where to put newlines and parentheses) and stuff. But they both operate by a model where you produce a relatively simple data structure that they know how to deal with, they give you a few knobs and render it in full. (For aeson-pretty the data structure is JSON, for pretty-simple it's a custom type that they parse from show output and that's pretty good at reproducing it.)
Here are some use cases where I've wanted more control than I can easily get:
My test suites generate a complicated data structure. Most of the time, most of this data structure is irrelevant to the test failures and I don't want to see it.
A complicated data structure contains JSON values, and I want them rendered as JSON rather than as a Haskell data type. Or it contains floating-point numbers, and I want them rounded to 3dp with underscore separation ( 17_923.472 ). Or strings, which I want printed using C-style escapes rather than Haskell-style, and with unicode rendered.
A list might be infinite, and I only want to show the first ten elements. Or a tree might actually be cyclic, and I want to only show three levels deep.
pretty-gist aims to enable stuff like this. I call the rendered outputs it produces "gists" following Raku's use of that term, where I think the intention is something like "take a guess about what I'm likely to want to see here and show me that". But if pretty-gist guesses wrong, it lets you correct it.
I've come up with several different approaches to this, which all have different things to recommend and disrecommend them. I'm writing about three of them here.
If you're a Haskell user, I'm interested to hear your thoughts. I have some specific questions at the end.
It should pretty-print, with indentation that adjusts to the available width.
As a user, you should be able to target configurations specifically or generally. "All lists" or "all lists of Ints" or "only lists found at this specific point in the data structure". "All floating-point numbers" or " Float but not Double ".
It should be low boilerplate, both as a user and an implementer.
You shouldn't need extra imports to configure the rendering for a type.
If something almost works, you should be able to make it work. No need to throw everything out and start from scratch.
I don't know how to meet all these design goals at once, but they're things I aim for.
Also: I think there's a sort of hierarchy of demandingness for what sort of situations we expect to use the library in. From most to least demanding:
We're generating user-facing output, and we want to specify what it looks like down to the glyph.
We're generating debug output. We probably don't care about the exact layouting, but it would be unfortunate if we accidentally hid some data that we intended to include. We can't simply edit the config and retry.
We're generating output for a test failure. It's not ideal if it stops doing what we expect without warning, but it's not too bad because we can just change it and rerun the test.
We're writing debug code that we don't expect to commit.
In more demanding situations, we probably don't mind being more verbose, and updating our rendering code more often when the data structures we're working with change. In less demanding situations, we're more likely to be satisfied with an 80/20 of "not quite what I want but good enough".
I'm not personally working on anything where I care about glyph-level exactness, so that one isn't a situation I feel like optimizing for. The others are all things I'd like pretty-gist to help with, but of course the best design for one might not be the best design for the others.
Here's how pretty-simple would render a particular representation of a chess game. Next to it is how I'd like pretty-gist to be able to, either by default or with a small amount of configuration on the user's part.
So one difference is that I've gone with a hanging bracket style, with no newline directly after GameState or board = . I don't feel strongly about that. It would be nice to let users control this, but I haven't put much thought into it.
I've also rendered the floats as percents. I haven't put much thought into this either, and haven't implemented it. But it seems vaguely useful and easy enough to have as an option, though it usually shouldn't be default.
It's not visible here, but pretty-simple has the ability to colorize its output. That's another thing I haven't thought about, and don't currently expect pretty-gist to support any time soon.
But the most important is rendering each Maybe Piece as a single character. There are three parts to that: a Nothing is rendering as _ ; a Just is simply rendering the value it contains with no wrapper; and a Piece is rendering as a single character. The combination makes it much easier to see most of the state of the game. You can no longer see when each piece last moved. But if that's not usually useful to you, it's fine not to show it by default.
(At this point, chess pedants may be pointing out that this data type doesn't capture everything you need for chess. You can't reliably tell whether en passant is currently legal. Maybe there are other problems too. Yes, well done chess pedants, you're very clever, now shut up.)
I've come up with several possible designs for this making different tradeoffs. I'm going to talk about three of them that I've actually implemented to some extent.
Perhaps the very simplest solution is just to write a custom renderer every time I need one. I'm not going to do that.
A level up from that, which I've implemented in the module Gist.Classless , is to write renderers for lots of different data types and combine them. We can write
for some data type Doc that supports layout. (I've been using the one from prettprinter , which has a type argument that I'm ignoring here for simplicity.)
The Prec parameters here are needed for the same reason Show has showsPrec . Sometimes we need parentheses, and this lets us choose when we have them. But they clutter things up a lot. We could imagine predence being something that gets put into config types, but then the user needs to specify it everywhere; plus, a renderer might call one of its sub-renderers at two different precedence levels under different circumstances. So that doesn't really work, so we accept the clutter.
But essentially, we've decided that one particular config parameter is important enough that every function accepts it (which means every function expects every other function to accept it). That feels kinda dirty. Is there anything else that ought to be given this treatment?
Anyway, this works, and it has some things to recommend it. It's incredibly simple, a beginner-level Haskell programmer will be able to figure out what's going on. If I, as the library author, make a decision you the library user don't like, you can just write your own function and it plugs in seamlessly. And if you have a type that can't normally be rendered, like a function, you can pick some way to render it anyway.
It also has some things to disrecommend it. Most notably, it's very verbose. You need to specify how to render every type-parameterized node of your data structure. You can have default configs, but there's no "default list renderer" because there's no "default list element renderer". IntMap v can have a default renderer for its keys, but Map Int v can't unless you write a function gistMapInt separate from gistMap .
This also means that changes to your data structure are very often going to need to be reflected in your renderers, which sounds tedious.
Another problem is, I expect consistency to be hard. Whatever design decisions I make, they're not enforced through anything. So someone who disagrees with them, or simply isn't paying attention to them, can easily make different ones, and then users need to remember things. (E.g. I had gistList , gistTuple2 and gistFloat all take precedence parameters, but they'll completely ignore them. So maybe someone in a similar situation decides not to bother with those parameters.)
Those are problems for users. There's also a problem for implementers: roughly speaking, you're going to be allowing the user to pass a renderer for every field of every constructor of your type. For non-parameterized types (like the keys of an IntMap ) that can be in the actual config type, and for parameterized types (like the keys of a Map ) it comes in separate arguments later, but it's going to be there. That's going to be tedious for you.
We can maybe-improve on this with typeclasses. We can use type families to let each gistable type have a separate config type.
This is the foundation of the approach I've implemented in the module Gist.OneClass .
There are a few significant complications. One is, this won't handle String well, because that's just [Char] . Other typeclasses (including Show ) solve this by having an extra method for "how to handle lists of this type"; then you give that method a default implementation, but override it for Char . This seems fine as a solution, by which I mean "I hate it but I don't have any better ideas". I'm not going to bother showing it here. (Also it's not actually implemented for this approach in the code yet.)
Next: the typechecking here doesn't work very well. If we try
we probably mean defaultConfig to refer to defaultConfig @[Bool] . But all GHC knows is that we mean defaultConfig { ... } to have type Config [Bool] . That doesn't even fully specify the type of defaultConfig , let alone its value. (We might be using the defaultConfig of some other instance that shares the same type; or that has a different type until we update it. The second possibility means injective type families wouldn't help much.) So we instead need to write
which is no fun. That extra unnecessary-looking set of parentheses is an added kick in the teeth. So we add functions gistF and gistPrecF , which replace the Config a argument with a Config a -> Config a argument and apply it to defaultConfig . So now we write
But we do keep the existing functions around for the final complication. Some things can't be rendered automatically (e.g. functions), but we sometimes want to render them anyway, or data structures containing them. Like a function Bool -> Int that's equivalent to a pair (Int, Int) . Sometimes we can use newtypes and maybe coerce for this, but not always, and it might be a pain even if we can.
It turns out we can handle this case. Consider the type
A Gister is a renderer for any type. For types implementing Gist , we can create a Gister through Config , but for any other type we can still write our own rendering function.
This lets us have an instance Gist [a] without first requiring Gist a . We can't have a (useful) default config in that case, the only fully general Gister a s we could write would ignore the value they're passed. But we can still have a default when we do have Gist a (assuming it has its own default):
So now you can call gist on a [Bool -> Int] , and you need to write for yourself how to render one of those functions but you can use gist when you do so. There's no defaultConfig @[Bool -> Int] , but you can do a type-changing update of defaultConfig @[Void] or similar. Though this is harder than we might like, because we can't derive a Generic instance for Gister a which means we can't use generic-lens or generic-optics. Fine in this case, annoying for nested structures, might be able to improve.
And that's just about everything for this solution.
So this preserves a lot of the good stuff about the classless solution. It's still reasonably simple as Haskell code, at least according to my judgment. We can still render any type, though it would be even simpler if we removed that option. And the user can still completely override the implementer if they want, though not as seamlessly as before.
And it's usually going to be a lot less verbose, with less need to change when your data structure changes. If the bits you've configured haven't changed, you should be good.
But there's still things not to like. For one, the tedious-for-implementers thing hasn't changed.
For another, if a type shows up at multiple places in the data structure, you probably want to render it the same in all of those places; if you have a [(Float, Float)] you probably want to render the fst s the same as the snd s. But to do that you have to remember every place it might show up and configure them all separately; and if it starts showing up in a new place, it's probably easy for you to forget to configure that one. (Unlike with the classless solution, where you'll get type errors if you forget about it.)
You're also going to be dealing with nested record updates, which I find unpleasant and have a bunch of questions about. That's somewhat the case with the classless solution too, but I think less deeply nested due to the structure of arguments and the lack of Gister . And here, you'll sometimes be doing type-changing record updates, and I think the future of those is uncertain (they're not supported by OverloadedRecordUpdate ).
First, we find some way to store the config for every possible in a single data structure, even though we don't know all the possible configs yet.
Then we make this config store available to renderers. They look up the config that's relevant specifically to them. When rendering their contents, they simply pass down the same config store. A MonadReader helps here.
This makes "update the config of every occurrence of a type" easy. It makes "update the config of just this specific occurrence of a type" impossible. So we also track our location in the data structure, and in the config store we let users say "this option only applies at this location", or "at locations matching …".
(This last bit sounds almost more trouble than it's worth. But without it, it becomes super awkward to handle things like "only show three levels deep of this self-referential data type".)
This is currently implemented in the Gist.TwoClass module. There's also a Gist.Dynamic module which has just the config-data-structure part, and is actually the implementation I've fleshed out the most. But I currently think it's not worth exploring more and not worth discussing in depth by itself.
Somewhat simplified, here's the main stuff going on with this solution:
The separation between Configurable and Gist might seem unnecessary here - why would we configure something we can't render? The answer is that Configurable doesn't specify the kind of its argument. So we have all of
and then users can add configuration for all Map s without needing to specify the exact types. (And they can override that config at specific types, if they want, using the Semigroup instance of the ConfigFor .) We also have instance Configurable Floating , and then the Gist instances for both Float and Double can look that up.
So the flow is that users build up a Config data structure, specifying "for this type, (optionally: at this location in the data structure,) set these options".
Then we walk through the structure. At each point we look up the relevant config values for the type at the current location, and possibly for other types, and combine all these in some way that users will just have to beat into submission if they're doing something complicated. And then we render, passing an updated GistPath and the same Config to any subcomponents.
This isn't very transparent to users. The Float instance looks up config for both Float and Floating , and the Maybe a instance looks it up for both Maybe a and Maybe . But to discover these you have to either try it and see, or look at the source code, or read the instance docs that someone probably forgot to write.
Also, each config option needs to have a Monoid instance that distinguishes between "this value hasn't been set" and "this value has been set to its default". In practice that means Last . But that means users don't know what the default value of any config option is.
So the actual code complexifies the implementation in a few ways, to help users. Instances have a way of specifying "these are the types I look up", as long as those types have the same ConfigFor . Then looking things up from the config happens automatically; and there's a separate function to set default values to what gets looked up, which users can call manually to see what's going on. Once we have the defaults we no longer need Last , so we change to Identity at that point.
We also use a custom monad class instead of MonadReader GistContext . For now it's no more powerful, but it would be easy to add a tracing function. Then if users had trouble figuring out what was going on, they could use that to help figure it out, with no additional work from implementers.
So the actual implementation looks more like
where CanDoLookups roughly ensures that GistLookups a is a type-level list of things with a given ConfigFor . (But we can't use '[] for these type-level lists, because you can't put types of different kinds inside one of those.)
How does this fare? The big advantage over the previous solutions is the "configure every occurence of a type at once" thing. I anticipate this is usually what users want, so it's good that it's easy. Also, no nested records! And if I decide to add global config options - perhaps indent width - I just need to add them to GistContext .
I think the big downsides are that it's wildly complicated, and we've lost the ability to render anything we can't write a Gist instance for (which also means users can't override implementers' decisions). But also a bunch of other downsides. When you do want to render different occurrences of the same type differently, it's awkward. You won't get errors or warnings if your config gets out of sync with the type you're rendering. Encapsulation is tricky, internals of your types might be exposed in ways you don't want. It's not necessarily clear how you'd want newtypes to be configured, and newtype-deriving only gives you one option which might not be what you want.
I've given three different renders for all of these GameState examples. "Short form" looks like the example I gave above, except I haven't configured the floats to show as percentages. (Like I said, not yet implemented.) "Fully explicit form" is similar to the pretty-simple rendering, except with a different indent style. And "long form" is in between, with abbreviated rendering for Maybe but everything else displayed in full - there's no ambiguity here, so it seems like a good choice even if you don't want any data missing.
In this particular case, rendering GameState for the classless and one-class solutions are about as verbose as each other. I think that's kind of a coincidence based on where the type variables are and what we're doing with them. For example, GameState has no type variables, so its renderers can be passed in ConfigGameState , letting them be defaulted. Board has a type variable, but renderBoard has no other config options; so there are no cases where with one-class we can say "change this option for how we render Board , but leave the sub-renderer alone", but with classless we can only say "change this option for how we render Board , and while we're at it here's the sub-renderer to use". This kind of thing does come up once, when in the fully-explicit form we want to set showConstructors on the lastMoved renderer, and have to also repeat the renderer for the Int . But in that case the renderer is just gistShowily so it doesn't hurt much.
I expect there'd be more difference in other cases. But maybe I'm wrong? Who knows.
A thing I dislike in all of them, is how I've had to do imports to handle record field updates. As of (I think) GHC 9.2, record updates combined with DuplicateRecordFields is more awkward than it used to be, at least if you don't want to get warnings about future compatibility. So when I do the awful
that's so I can do val { Gist.ConfigMaybe.showConstructors = ... } to update the field. Another option is to use generic-lens or generic-optics to do updates, which I've also demonstrated in some cases. My guess is that would be fine in a lot of application code, but many libraries won't want to depend on them.
I could also try to choose constructor names not to conflict. But I think that basically means prefixing them all, which would also be super verbose, and it would annoy users of the generic libraries.
(Given what I've implemented so far, the name conflicts only actually exist in the one-class solution, which reuses the name gistElem . But I expect showConstructors and showFirst to also get reused, e.g. for gisting Either and Set ; and something like countRemaining could be useful for collections that get truncated, and so on. So it seemed more useful to write things this way.)
I haven't looked closely, but anonymous records might help here. They also might help with Generic -based defaulting, which is another thing I haven't looked into. But they seem like a large hammer that increases dependency footprints. And from a quick look I'm not sure they support type-changing record updates.
I'd prefer if there wasn't a single fixed indent style. But I'm not sure what to do about it. Conceivably, I could have a fixed IndentStyle type, and expect implementers to pay attention to it. (Similar to how precedence has been granted special status.) But I expect if I do that, there'll be situations where people wish the type was larger (because it doesn't support things they want), and others where they wish it was smaller (because implementing support for all the options is a pain). If I make it maximally small, we only have one of those problems. Similar thoughts on possible color support.
One reason I wrote all this is to try to gauge enthusiasm. One possible future for pretty-gist is that I use it a small amount and in personal projects and at my job, and basically no one else uses it at all. That would be fine.
Another possible future is that it becomes a package that other people do use and that I take responsibility for. But that's only going to happen if it seems like anyone cares.
So some things I'd like to know from readers:
I have some opinions on these myself, but I'd prefer to wait and see what others say before revealing. I also have another possible approach vaguely in mind; but if I waited to explore it before publishing, then this would never get finished.
The canonical public place to leave comments is the reddit thread . But I've also set up a google form you can fill in if you prefer.
