title: Bandits kill teacher, two others in Sokoto ambush
body: A newly recruited teacher in Sokoto State, Maniru Sa’adu Imam, has been killed by suspected bandits hours after reportedly attending a salary verification exercise in Sokoto metropolis. Imam, 30, and a father of one, was killed alongside two other people on Wednesday when gunmen ambushed vehicles travelling along the Gundumi-Isa road. The other victims were identified as Abdurrahman Umar, the driver of the vehicle conveying them, and his five-year-old son, Abubakar Abdurrahman. A witness, Malam Kabiru Isa, told our reporter that the victims were travelling behind a convoy of vehicles returning to Isa under heavy security escort when the incident occurred. INEC records 313,115 new voters in Zamfara RTEAN pushes for Bank of Transportation According to him, residents from Isa visit Sokoto metropolis only twice a week, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, due to the security situation in the area. He said the convoy had departed at about 4pm on Wednesday when some vehicles, including the one conveying the victims, returned to their usual meeting point after the others had left. “We wanted to wait for everyone who had travelled with us, but the security operatives insisted that we leave early, so we left them behind,” he said. Isa explained that as the convoy approached Gundumi, the security personnel escorting them spotted a group of suspected bandits and opened fire, forcing the gunmen to flee. He, however, said the assailants later laid an ambush for vehicles travelling behind the convoy and opened fire on their occupants. “They killed three people, including Imam, the driver and his son. They also injured three others, while one passenger is still missing,” he said. Isa added that the deceased were buried on Thursday morning. He said Imam was among teachers recently recruited by the Sokoto State Government and posted to Government Day Secondary School, Maitandu. According to him, the deceased had yet to receive his first salary and travelled to Sokoto on Wednesday for a verification exercise ahead of the commencement of payment. “He had not started receiving his salary. In fact, he went to Sokoto for the verification exercise ahead of their payment,” Isa said. Efforts to obtain confirmation from the Sokoto State Police Command were unsuccessful as its spokesman, DSP Ahmad Rufa’i, did not respond to calls from our reporter.

title: South Africa, India and Brazil conclude Ibsamar IX naval exercise
body:
The navies of South Africa, India and Brazil have successfully completed Exercise Ibsamar IX 2026, demonstrating their ability to conduct joint maritime operations during a week of training off Cape Town aimed at strengthening interoperability and maritime security cooperation.
The trilateral exercise, led by India, ran from 12 to 20 October and concluded at Naval Base Simon’s Town on Tuesday 20 October. This following a programme that included surface warfare, air defence, maritime interdiction, helicopter operations and live firing.
Under the theme “Stronger Together Towards a Shared Future in the Maritime Domain”, Ibsamar IX focused on improving the ability of the three forces to operate together in an increasingly complex maritime environment, while reinforcing their shared commitment to maritime security, freedom of navigation and the protection of vital international shipping routes.
Captain (IN) Rohit Mishra of the Indian Navy, Commanding Officer of INS Tarkash and Exercise Joint Task Force Commander, said the exercise had achieved its objectives.
“I am delighted to see that the exercise objectives of enhancing interoperability, promoting joint operational training, sharing best practices and strengthening maritime cooperation have been successfully met and together we are stronger,” he said in his closing address.
The exercise was divided into a harbour phase from 12 to 14 October, followed by a sea phase from 15 to 19 October.
During the harbour phase at Simon’s Town, personnel participated in joint operational planning, lectures, communications training and cross-deck familiarisation. The three navies also got to know each other via various social activities.
The sea phase put that professional engagement into practice through a range of operational serials, including maritime interdiction, surface warfare, air defence, weapon firing, anti-submarine warfare, helicopter operations and seamanship evolutions. Training also covered visit, board, search and seizure (VBSS) operations, anti-piracy drills, search and rescue, damage control and firefighting. Live firing was conducted with smaller-calibre weapons.
Mishra highlighted the successful execution of the sea-phase activities, saying the “safe and successful conduct of maritime interdiction operations, war-at-sea serials, air defence and weapon firing, helicopter flying operations and seamanship evolutions” confirmed the navies’ shared understanding and ability to operate together at sea.
Communications interoperability was further enhanced through the deployment of the Indian NISHAR system, which provided a common command-and-control communications platform. According to Mishra, the system enabled real-time, safe and reliable connectivity between participating vessels and the Joint Task Force Commander.
The participating ships were the Indian Navy’s guided-missile frigate INS Tarkash, the Brazilian Navy’s corvette BNS Barroso and the South African Navy’s frigate SAS Amatola, multi-purpose inshore patrol vessels SAS King Sekhukhune I and SAS Adam Kok III, and the submarine SAS Manthatisi.
Special forces from all three countries and embarked aviation assets added further depth to the exercise.
Cross-deck helicopter operations allowed aircrew to familiarise themselves with different aircraft, platforms and procedures. The Indian contingent included a Chetak helicopter, an Indian-built variant of the Alouette III, while BNS Barroso carried a Super Lynx. The South African Air Force contributed an Oryx helicopter and two Gripen fighters. Other South African National Defence Force elements included maritime task force personnel, military police and defence intelligence.
A major capability demonstration took place during the Distinguished Visitors’ Day on Monday 19 October, when the three navies showcased their abilities to visitors aboard SAS Amatola.
The demonstration simulated a maritime interdiction scenario involving a vessel suspected of carrying contraband, with SAS Adam Kok III serving as the target ship. The scenario was designed to demonstrate a coordinated VBSS operation, with the three navies combining their boats, helicopters and special forces capabilities.
Indian, Brazilian and South African teams approached the vessel using their respective boats and helicopters, boarded it, searched for contraband and withdrew following the simulated successful operation.
The demonstration culminated in a ceremonial sequence in which the participating surface ships steamed past SAS Amatola to salute the Chief of the South African National Defence Force, General Rudzani Maphwanya, who was embarked aboard the frigate. The submarine followed the ships, after which the three helicopters conducted a flypast, concluding with a low and fast pass by a Gripen fighter.
Ibsamar has developed considerably since its first edition, evolving beyond basic naval interaction into a complex multinational exercise involving warships, aircraft, special forces and a broad range of maritime operations. Earlier editions have included tactical manoeuvres, navigation and seamanship training, replenishment-at-sea activities, aviation operations and a variety of maritime security serials.
The latest iteration continued that progression, providing opportunities to test operational procedures and develop a better understanding of the participating navies’ respective capabilities.
Mishra said the experience gained would support future training and cooperation, contributing to improved professional competence and a greater appreciation of each navy’s procedures and operational practices.
He also stressed that the value of the exercise extended beyond completing scheduled activities.
“An exercise of this nature is successful not merely because the planned activities have been completed, but because the participating personnel return with enhanced knowledge, greater confidence and a stronger willingness to work together,” he said.
He commended the officers and sailors of the participating ships, special forces and helicopter crews, as well as the command teams, planners and coordinating personnel who supported the exercise. He also thanked the South African National Defence Force for its assistance in hosting Ibsamar IX.
DefenceWeb was invited to sail aboard INS Tarkash during the capability display, where Mishra welcomed the opportunity to provide a briefing on the ship and its activities, despite a demanding operational schedule.
The professionalism of the Indian crew and their pride in their warship were evident throughout the visit. Officers and sailors were keen to discuss the exercise, naval operations across the wider Indian Ocean region and their intended tours around Cape Town, whilst safety at sea was paramount. The Indian Navy helicopter pilots were particularly keen to discuss all things aviation.
South African and Brazilian naval personnel embarked aboard INS Tarkash were similarly impressed by the ship’s condition and the hospitality extended by its crew, as well as the experience they gained during the exercise.
Mishra concluded by wishing the participating personnel “safe operations, fair winds and following seas”, adding that he hoped the bonds developed during the exercise would continue to strengthen through future professional interactions.

title: Rosal downgraded to typhoon east of Batanes
body: MANILA, Philippines – Rosal (Champi) weakened from a super typhoon into a typhoon on Thursday afternoon, October 22, but rainfall and wind warnings have yet to be lifted for portions of Northern Luzon. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in its 5 pm bulletin on Thursday that Rosal’s maximum sustained winds are down to 165 kilometers per hour. Its gustiness has also eased to 205 km/h. At its peak, Rosal had maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h. As of 4 pm on Thursday, the typhoon was located 350 kilometers east of Itbayat, Batanes, moving northwest at only 15 km/h. It will be at its closest point to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, October 23. PAGASA said Rosal will continue to trigger heavy to intense rain in Batanes (100-200 millimeters) and moderate to heavy rain in Cagayan (50-100 mm) in the next 24 hours. On Thursday evening, the typhoon may also bring rain with gusty winds to Ilocos Norte, Apayao, and Isabela, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Ilocos Sur, La Union, and Aurora. The weather bureau added that Rosal’s trough or extension might cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in Bicol, the Zamboanga Peninsula, Western Visayas, the Negros Island Region, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, and Palawan. Meanwhile, here are the areas under tropical cyclone wind signals as of 5 pm on Thursday: Signal No. 2 Gale-force winds (62 to 88 km/h), minor to moderate threat to life and property Batanes northeastern part of Babuyan Islands (Babuyan Island) Signal No. 1 Strong winds (39 to 61 km/h), minimal to minor threat to life and property rest of Babuyan Islands mainland Cagayan northeastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, San Pablo, Palanan) Ilocos Norte Apayao Signal No. 3 could be raised in Batanes, unless Rosal’s track shifts further north northwest. The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas: Thursday, October 22 most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Northern Mindanao, Davao Region, Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani Friday, October 23 most of Luzon and Visayas, Davao Region, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Camiguin Saturday, October 24 Batanes, Babuyan Islands, Ilocos Norte, Polillo Islands, Bicol, Romblon, Capiz, Iloilo, Negros Occidental Travel remains dangerous in seaboards affected by Rosal. Up to very rough, high, or very high seas (travel is risky for all vessels) Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes – waves up to 12 meters high Seaboard of Babuyan Islands; remaining seaboard of Batanes; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan – waves up to 9 meters high Remaining seaboard of mainland Cagayan; seaboard of northern Isabela – waves up to 7 meters high Northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 6 meters high Remaining seaboards of Ilocos Norte and Isabela – waves up to 5.5 meters high Seaboards of Ilocos Sur and northern Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands and Catanduanes; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur – waves up to 4.5 meters high Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea) Seaboard of northern La Union; western seaboard of Pangasinan; northern seaboard of Northern Samar – waves up to 4 meters high Seaboard of northern Quezon; remaining seaboard of Aurora; eastern seaboards of Albay, Sorsogon, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar – waves up to 3.5 meters high Seaboard of Zambales; eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Islands – waves up to 3 meters high Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible) Western seaboards of Bataan, Lubang Islands, and Surigao del Sur; remaining seaboards of La Union, Pangasinan, and Catanduanes – waves up to 2.5 meters high Western seaboards of Batangas, Cavite, and Calamian Islands; eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining seaboard of Lubang Islands – waves up to 2 meters high ALSO ON RAPPLER DFA to China embassy: Escalatory, undiplomatic posts not helping bilateral ties [Puso at Diwa] Sara Duterte trial: Is the space for political impunity finally closing? Who is Ginbee Go, BPI’s next president and first female CEO? Rosal is still projected to leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20. After leaving PAR, Rosal is likely to be downgraded to a severe tropical storm on Saturday. Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month. The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat , which was announced last October 5. The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

title: [VIDEO] Why Vaccines Aren’t Available For Latest Ebola Outbreak — Africa CDC
body: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has explained why the continent has yet to find a vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola disease. Speaking during an interview on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday, the Director General of the Africa CDC, Dr. Jean Kaseya, said some partners consider Ebola an African issue, adding that “if this outbreak was in Western countries, vaccines would already be available”. He, however, said that the agency had initiated clinical trials of new vaccines, including a new Bundibugyo vaccine manufactured in Egypt. Watch the interview in the video below. ﻿ The post [VIDEO] Why Vaccines Aren’t Available For Latest Ebola Outbreak — Africa CDC appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Lockheed Martin says 10-year framework covers 850 U.S. F-35 fighters, upgrades and sustainment
body: The framework also includes international customer orders across production Lots 21–30. Total production would remain at 156 aircraft annually for U.S. and international customers combined. Combining aircraft production with purchases of spare and modification parts would give suppliers longer-term demand visibility. Lockheed Martin said that certainty would support investment, bulk purchasing and more efficient manufacturing. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain,” said Jim Taiclet, Lockheed Martin’s chairman, president and CEO. “That’s good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies.” Pricing and schedules remain open The framework includes initial spares associated with the aircraft and 10 years of modification kits and sustainment. If multiyear authority and appropriations are granted in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will finalize contract terms, pricing and schedules. Lockheed Martin expects long-term pricing and volume discounts to save taxpayers billions of dollars over the F-35’s lifecycle. The announcement did not disclose a contract value or provide a detailed savings estimate. Parts availability central to readiness The proposed arrangement includes investment in industrial capacity and logistics, building on Lockheed Martin’s existing contributions to the global spares pool. Integrated analytics would provide visibility into parts inventories and readiness metrics, linking spending to operational outcomes. “Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” said OJ Sanchez, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics. “This, in addition to the investments Lockheed Martin is making to the global spares pool, will directly translate into higher mission capable rates and a more resilient supply chain – critical capabilities the warfighter needs to meet today’s mission and prepare for tomorrow’s threats.” International customers would also benefit from procurement economies and improvements to the global sustainment network, according to the company. Lockheed Martin projects that the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and generate approximately $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. More than 1,375 F-35s are fielded worldwide, and the fleet has surpassed one million flight hours, according to Lockheed Martin. The aircraft operates from 42 bases, with 13 nations operating it from their own territory.

title: CJID launches Living Archives Initiative, honours veteran journalist Lade Bonuola (LIVE UPDATES)
body:
The Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) is launching its Living Archives Initiative in Lagos, alongside a digital platform aimed at preserving Africa’s media history.
The event will also feature the unveiling of ‘Ladbone: A Life in Print,’ a collection of essays honouring veteran journalist Lade Bonuola, popularly known as Ladbone, as he marks his 80th birthday.
The initiative seeks to preserve and make accessible historical newspaper records, photographs, broadcast recordings and personal accounts documenting the lives and contributions of people who have shaped journalism across Africa.
Mr Bonuola, whose journalism career spans more than five decades, began at the Daily Times before becoming the pioneer editor and managing director of The Guardian. He also co-founded The Comet newspaper in 1999 and held senior editorial positions at other media organisations.
The book features contributions from more than 80 editors, media managers, academics, political figures and industry experts, reflecting on his career and the evolution of Nigerian journalism.
CJID said the digital platform would serve journalists, researchers, students and the public, providing access to historical records that could inform discussions on press freedom, professional standards and democratic development.
The programme will feature panel discussions, a book review and the formal unveiling of the anthology.
Follow PREMIUM TIMES for live updates of the event.
Loftyhighart quartet led by violinking serenade arriving guests with calm music
At 11:32 , some guests are seated, waiting for the event to start.
At 11:40 a.m. , the celebrant, Mr Lade Banuola, arrived at the main hall for the event.
At 11: 47 a.m. , participants celebrated Mr Lade Banuola with a clap.
At 11:50 a.m. , the participants stood for the national prayer.
At 11:53 , the Publisher of PREMIUM TIMES, Dapo Olorunyomi, stated that the event was organised to celebrate an accomplished editor.
Funke Treasure comperes the event as celebrations begin.
We are grateful for his labour of love, Dapo Olorunyomi, PREMIUM TIMES publisher
At 12 p.m, Mr Olorunyomi stated that last year the Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development established the archive to document events.
Chiamaka Ozurumba of CJID, stated that the organisation had worked on this project for over a year. She noted that it has taken a lot of pain to get some of these materials out.
Ms Ozurumba stated, “Journalists have documented our political transitions, our democratic struggles, and the exercise of power and everyday experiences of our society. But journalism is not our starting point.
“Our wider ambition is to build a repository that eventually extends beyond journalism to other disciplines like medicine, like banking, like science, because all of this, all of the knowledge production over the years needs to be preserved, and we understand that importance.”
Presentation of Living Archives Initiative a digital platform aimed at preserving Africa’s media history.
Ms Ozurumba noted, “the photographs we are putting today, the articles we publish, the interviews we record, and the documents we create are the potential archive of tomorrow.”
The former Governor of Ogun State, Olusegun Osoba, stated that Mr Lade Banuola started work with Daily Times in February 1971.
Mr Osoba noted that Mr Bonuola was a professional who takes his time to look at punctuation marks in the story. He stated that Mr Banuola was a committed journalist.
Former Governor of Ogun State Olusegun Osoba recounts work experiences with Lade Bonuola
The Consul-General of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Lagos, Frank Keurhorst, stated in his remarks, “A free and independent press is essential for a functioning democracy,”
He added that preserving the stories of those who fought for and defended freedom, often under difficult circumstances, is equally important.
According to him, this is why the CJID Living Archives initiative, documenting the experiences, contributions, and lessons of journalism across generations to help ensure that this important history, “is so valuable.”
Mr Keurhorst added, “As we celebrate Mr Bonuola today, I hope we also recognise the many journalists, editors, and media professionals who continue this important work, sometimes and regrettably, under very challenging circumstances.
Mr Bonuola, congratulations on your 80th birthday today, and thank you, thank you for your contributions to Nigerian journalism and for the example you have set for generations of media professionals. Thank you.”
Panel discussion moderated by Azu Ishiekwene.
Members of a panel session titled ‘Whose Story Gets Told? The Future of Nigerian Journalism’ was announced.
Ms Ozurumba said that at CJID, most of the staff members are young people because the future belongs to them.
“There’s a new ecosystem being built. It is important for people who want to establish news organisations to embrace the future,” said Kadaria Ahmed, during panel discussion on the topic, ‘Whose story gets told? The future of Nigerian journalism’.
Ms Ozurumba said newsrooms must learn how to better present their stories. Explaining further, she noted that stories must have video explainers that capture what is in the story for young people.
Chiamaka Ozurumba of CJID said, “We must work together for the future of journalism.”
Veteran editor and author, Kunle Ajibade, reviews the book, ‘Ladbone: A Life in Print’.
Mr Ajibade reviews the book, ‘Ladbone: A Life in Print,’ a collection of essays honouring veteran journalist Lade Bonuola, popularly known as Ladbone, as he marks his 80th birthday.
Mr Ajibade said, “In honouring Lade Bonuola, they considerably honour themselves.
“In the parable of the elephant and the wise blind men, all those who touch different parts of a huge animal draw different conclusions.
“As in this book, all the different perspectives return the same verdict. Lade Banuola is a strong breed.”
He also said that The Guardian was not set up to support tyranny and murder, adding tht Lade Bonuola “did not come over to The Guardian to talk with tyrannical and murderous leaders or plans of apology.”
Chairman of the occasion, former Governor of Ogun State, Olusegun Osoba, set to unveil the book, ‘Ladbone: A Life in Print’.
Chairman of the occasion, former Ogun State Governor Olusegun Osoba, unveils the book, ‘Ladbone: A Life in Print’.
Members of Great Movement with Mr Lade Banuola
Lade Bonuola thanks Dapo Olorunyomi for organising the event in his honour.
In his remarks, Mr Bonuola said he loves Mr Olorunyomi because of his matchless application and dedication to work. He noted that he does not miss reading PREMIUM TIMES stories daily.

title: Postcards from Sant’Agata: A visit to the birthplace of Lamborghini
body: Sant’Agata Bolognese is a relatively small town between Bologna and Modena in Italy’s “Motor Valley”. Yet it is responsible for some of the world’s most ostentatious and recognisable cars ever made. This, after all, is where Ferruccio Lamborghini established his car company in 1963 and where, more than six decades later, Lamborghini continues to build its vehicles. There is something slightly incongruous about the setting. Sant’Agata still feels modest and agricultural, surrounded by the flat landscape of Emilia-Romagna. And then, amid it all, you encounter the unmistakable Lamborghini shield and a factory producing cars destined for Dubai, Miami or Tokyo. I am touring both the Museo Automobili Lamborghini and the neighbouring factory. The museum is not particularly large, something that works in its favour. Rather than trying to display everything, it tells the company’s story through a carefully curated collection before allowing visitors to see where its latest chapter is being built. From tractors to Grand Tourers The story begins, somewhat improbably, with tractors. By the 1950s, Ferruccio Lamborghini had found success manufacturing agricultural machinery, notably affordable tractors using material salvaged from the Second World War, before deciding to build grand touring cars. The 350 GTV concept appeared in 1963, followed by the production 350 GT the next year and the Jarama in 1970. Viewed today, the 350 GT seems almost conservative. Its long bonnet and curved body resemble many Italian grand tourers of the era, with little of the visual aggression that would become a Lamborghini trademark. But it marks the beginning of an ambition to challenge Italy’s established sports car manufacturers. A few steps away is the car that changed everything. I still don’t think Lamborghini has built anything more beautiful than the Miura. Sixty years after its debut, its proportions remain almost perfect. It sits incredibly low, with distinctive eyelashes surrounding the headlights and a shape that feels elegant rather than aggressive. The museum is marking the Miura’s 60th anniversary, and one highlight is the Miura Roadster, a one-off created by the automotive company Bertone in 1968. Knowing there is no copy makes standing beside it feel particularly special. Nearby is a Miura P400 S. It is less extraordinary, but perhaps better at demonstrating why the car brand has endured. You are left simply appreciating how well the aircraft-wing-inspired shape has aged. At the other extreme is the LM002 . The enormous off-roader looks almost comically out of place among Lamborghini’s sleek supercars. Developed from earlier attempts at creating a military-style vehicle, the production LM002 arrived in 1986 using the 5.2-litre V12 from the Countach Quattrovalvole. Only about 300 were built. It is not the Lamborghini most people picture when they hear the name, which makes it one of the museum’s most interesting cars. Decades before the Urus , Lamborghini was already willing to put its badge on something completely unexpected. Watching a Lamborghini come together The museum tells you what Lamborghini has built. The factory tour shows you how it happens. As I walk on to the production floor, one of the things I notice first is how human hands still play a prominent role. Partially assembled cars move between stations where small teams add components – wiring, piping and interior pieces. Timers count down roughly 24 minutes, the time each station has before the car is meant to move forward. Despite deadlines, nothing feels rushed. The operation is methodical and surprisingly calm. Watching a collection of components gradually become something recognisable is strangely satisfying. The most memorable moment comes when the powertrain and chassis finally meet, a process described during the tour as “a marriage”. It sounds overly romantic until you see it. Before that point, you have an engine and a chassis. Afterwards, you begin to have a car. There is also a special connection between the factory floor and the museum next door. Lamborghini still produces its V12 flagship in the area where the Countach assembly line was established in the 1970s. Today, that car is the Revuelto . What also becomes apparent is how much freedom customers have. Paint colours are only the beginning. Buyers can choose different leathers, stitching, trims and colour combinations. Lamborghini merges physical material selection with cutting-edge digital visualisation tools through its 'phygital' Ad Personam personalisation programme, extending those choices even further. It is one reason why seeing two Lamborghinis that have been configured exactly alike will still feel distinct. After walking through the factory, I also find that it becomes harder to view the finished cars simply as collections of performance figures. Someone fitted the pipes. Someone installed the trim. Someone checked the electronics. For all the technology involved, these still feel like machines constructed by people rather than cookie-cutter builds. The Lamborghinis we grew up with Back in the museum, the upper floor feels much more familiar. This is where the Countach, Murcielago, Gallardo, Aventador and Huracan sit alongside some of Lamborghini’s rarer creations. These are the cars that appeared on bedroom walls and in video games, and were cherished as scale models. Seeing them together – all low, wide and rarely subtle – demonstrates how consistently Lamborghini has stuck to its philosophy. The design language changes from generation to generation, but the intention remains remarkably similar: a Lamborghini should elicit excitement even before anyone turns the engine on. The special-edition cars take that idea further. In 2016, the Centenario marked 100 years since Ferruccio Lamborghini’s birth, with only 20 coupes and 20 roadsters made. The Sian combined a naturally aspirated V12 with Lamborghini’s first electrified production powertrain, with 63 coupes produced in reference to the company’s founding year. These are cars most people will only ever see in photographs, in video games or in miniatures. Finding several of them metres apart is one of the pleasures of the museum. But after moving between the historic models, the production line and the modern supercars, it is not the sense of rarity that stays with me. It is the consistency. Lamborghini has changed considerably since 1963. Ferruccio is long gone; the company passed through several owners, while Audi’s acquisition in 1998 brought greater stability, technology and production capacity. Yet the instinct behind the cars remains recognisable. The Miura was radical. The Countach looked like nothing else on the road. The LM002 was an absurd idea that somehow made it into production. Today’s cars continue to chase that sense of theatre. For all the international attention surrounding Lamborghini, it is still fascinating that these machines, some of the loudest and proudest on the road, emerge from one factory in a quiet community in northern Italy.

title: IMF forecasts sharp drop in West Asia economic output
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has forecast a sharp drop in economic output in the Middle East, North Africa, and Pakistan this year due to the US-Israel war against Iran.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has forecast a sharp drop in economic output in the Middle East, North Africa, and Pakistan this year due to the US-Israel war against Iran, followed by a rebound to 6.6 percent growth in 2027.
In a statement, the IMF said the region’s output was expected to contract by 1.3 percent as a result of the war’s impact on energy production, shipping, tourism, trade, and confidence.
The IMF said its baseline assumed that the conflict would abate in early 2027 and that trade would gradually normalise during the year, but added that the outlook remained clouded by “exceptionally high uncertainty”.
“The main risks derive from further disruption to energy production and trade routes that could drive energy prices higher,” the statement added.

title: APC Deploys Diaspora Network to Fight Anti-Tinubu Narratives
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja The All Progressives Congress (APC) has unveiled an international mobilisation and media offensive to defend President Bola Tinubu’s economic policies, counter negative narratives about his administration, and rally support for his re-election in 2027, targeting Nigerians living across major countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, the Middle East and North America. Under the plan, the party intends to activate its overseas chapters, deploy coordinated digital advocacy, establish a rapid-response mechanism to challenge misinformation, mobilise diaspora funding and encourage voter participation at home as it seeks to shape public perception of Tinubu’s first term ahead of the presidential election. The Director of the PBAT/APC 2027 Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) Directorate of Diaspora Mobilisation, Hon. Abike Dabiri-Erewa, unveiled the strategy at a press briefing in Abuja, describing Nigerians abroad as an influential constituency whose financial contributions, professional expertise and international networks could be harnessed to support the administration. The initiative signals the APC’s determination to make the diaspora an organised component of its re-election campaign, using Nigerians’ connections with relatives, communities and professional networks abroad to communicate the government’s position on its economic reforms and development agenda. Dabiri-Erewa said the directorate would not limit its mobilisation to party members, but would also reach out to Nigerians abroad who were willing to participate in the campaign. “Nigerians abroad are not outsiders. They are stakeholders. They are our doctors, nurses, engineers, students, traders, innovators and community leaders, who send over $20 billion annually back home in remittances,” she said. She identified the mobilisation of APC diaspora chapters in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, Australia, Turkey, India and Kazakhstan as a priority, alongside engagement with diaspora associations and community leaders. At the centre of the strategy is a digital advocacy campaign tagged: ‘Operation Tell Your Story’, through which supporters would receive short videos, infographics and other communication materials promoting the administration’s policies and achievements. The campaign would address the foreign exchange reforms, foreign reserves, support for small businesses, housing programmes and opportunities for students, while seeking to counter claims the directorate considers misleading. Dabiri-Erewa also announced plans for a rapid-response hub to provide data, fact-check claims and promote what she described as credible information about Nigeria’s investment climate, economic stabilisation and prospects under Tinubu. “Our directorate will serve as a rapid-response hub in case of misinformation about Nigeria and the administration. We will provide credible data, fact-check and positive narratives about Nigeria’s investment climate, stabilisation of the economy and the future under President Tinubu,” she said. The move comes amid continuing public debate over the administration’s economic reforms, particularly the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign exchange system, which have had significant implications for households and businesses. Dabiri-Erewa acknowledged the hardship associated with the subsidy removal but defended the policy as a necessary intervention to address structural weaknesses in the economy. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has decided not to manage our feelings, but to fix the system. And it takes a bold leader to do that,” she said. She argued that Nigerians living abroad could help explain the rationale behind the reforms to their families and communities, particularly because of their understanding of the challenges associated with the previous foreign exchange arrangements. However, the directorate’s strategy will face the challenge of persuading voters at home that the administration’s policies are delivering sufficient benefits to justify the economic sacrifices they have experienced. The effectiveness of the campaign will therefore depend not only on the reach of its messaging but also on the credibility of its claims and the administration’s record against measurable economic outcomes. Beyond digital advocacy, the APC plans to mobilise diaspora contributions through structured fundraising platforms to finance campaign activities, voter education materials, town hall meetings and grassroots mobilisation. Dabiri-Erewa said the proposed fundraising arrangements would emphasise transparency and accountability, but did not disclose the amount the directorate hopes to raise or provide details of the proposed platforms. The fourth strand of the strategy would focus on voter education and homecoming mobilisation, with diaspora Nigerians encouraged to remind eligible relatives and community members to register, collect their Permanent Voter Cards and participate in the election. The directorate also intends to use its overseas networks to encourage Nigerians abroad to return home, engage their communities and take part in the political process. In a related appeal, Dabiri-Erewa called on the National Assembly to consider constitutional amendments that would allow Nigerians living abroad to vote in Nigerian elections. She acknowledged that diaspora voting remained a subject of debate but expressed hope that lawmakers would address the issue, potentially expanding the formal participation of Nigerians abroad in the country’s electoral process. Dabiri-Erewa, who also heads the Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NiDCOM), said the commission had established a portal for registering Nigerians living outside the country and put the estimated diaspora population at more than 17 million. She also urged Nigerians to monitor how state and local governments utilise increased allocations following the removal of the petrol subsidy, arguing that greater public revenue should be accompanied by accountability in spending. Other members of the directorate backed the administration’s economic policies, acknowledging the hardship associated with the reforms while arguing that the intended benefits would take time to materialise. They highlighted investment, skills transfer, business partnerships and collaboration with government institutions as additional ways Diaspora Nigerians could contribute to national development. Dabiri-Erewa urged the media to support the directorate’s communication efforts, saying the campaign would focus on continuity, national development and Tinubu’s stated ambition to move Nigeria from reforms to prosperity. With the 2027 election approaching, the APC’s strategy places diaspora mobilisation, digital communication and the battle over the interpretation of the administration’s economic record at the heart of its re-election effort. Whether the initiative translates into broader electoral support will ultimately depend on how Nigerians judge the government’s performance and whether the campaign can substantiate its claims with credible evidence.

title: Zelensky names hardest day for him during war
body:
The head of state made the remarks on The Diary of a CEO podcast, hosted by British entrepreneur and investor Steven Bartlett, Ukrinform reports.
"The war started on February 24, 2022. I didn't think there would be a full-scale invasion. I was with my family and told my wife and the kids: 'The war has started. I love you. I'll call you,' and ran out," Zelensky said.
Recalling the hardest day of the war, the president spoke about visiting Bucha shortly after its liberation.
"We liberated Bucha, and I went there. Bodies of children, adults, and elderly people were lying everywhere – chopped meat, butchered them, hands tied, tortured, and then buried in pits. What if a mass grave containing 500 tortured people were found today in the United States or Britain, God forbid, how do you forgive that?" he said.
As previously reported, on the morning of February 24, 2022, Russia launched strikes against Ukraine and began its full-scale war. Russian forces carried out missile and air strikes on the airfields in Boryspil, Ozerne, Kulbakine, Chuhuiv, Kramatorsk, and Chornobaivka, as well as on military facilities of the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Russian troops, supported by Belarus, attacked Ukraine's state border along the sections bordering Russia and Belarus. Russian armored vehicles crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv, Sumy, Luhansk, and Kharkiv regions.

title: Trump blamed Russia’s failed assault on Kyiv on a ‘stupid general’ who drove his tanks into the mud. The real story is very different.
body: General Alexander Chayko at a Navy Day parade in Vladivostok, July 30, 2017 President Trump has repeatedly promised to end the Russia–Ukraine war within 24 hours, though peace talks have made little substantive progress so far. Just as often, he returns to a story about the early days of the full-scale invasion — tweaking a minor detail each time — describing Russian tanks that were advancing on Kyiv but got stuck in the mud. During a conversation with reporters at the White House on October 20, Trump repeated the story again, this time focusing on one Russian general. A stupid general for Russia, a very stupid gentleman. They had a thousand tanks riding up a concrete highway. They would have been in Ukraine in four hours, going maximum tank speed, which is 48 miles an hour, to be exact. Nothing to stop them. The war would have been over in one day. And this very stupid general — I have no idea who he is. I doubt he’s still with us. I doubt he’s still living. He decided to hang a right onto the farmland and then take a left and go up to Kyiv, rather than staying on the highway — the concrete highway, perfectly good highway — where they were doing very nicely. It would have been three and a half, four hours, and the whole war would have ended. He ended up getting stuck in the mud. BBC Russia fact-checked Trump’s claim. According to the outlet, Colonel General Alexander Chayko led Russia’s advance on Kyiv from Belarus in February 2022, and the offensive’s failure had nothing to do with any decision by him to turn off the road. Ukrainian forces stopped the advance on Kyiv. On February 26, 2022, Ukraine’s military blew up a bridge over the Irpin River on the outskirts of the capital, then destroyed the Kozarovychi dam when Russian forces tried to go around the obstruction. Ukrainian forces also destroyed a column of Russian armored vehicles in Bucha. As the Russian army’s losses mounted, its command brought in reinforcements from Belarus. After the failed advance, Russian military command removed Chayko as commander and sent him to lead the Russian contingent in Syria. He stayed there until June 2025, a tenure that spanned the coup that forced President Bashar al-Assad to flee to Moscow. None of this hurt the general’s career, BBC Russia said. He returned to Moscow, became deputy chief of the General Staff, and was later promoted to commander of Russia’s Aerospace Forces. In August 2026, General Chayko did indeed nearly die: an explosion occurred near the Balzi Rossi restaurant in Moscow, where he was celebrating his 55th birthday and his promotion to the new post. Five people were killed, including Chayko’s son-in-law, and 19 others were injured. Chayko himself was unharmed. title: Kogi Monarch Tasks FG on Technical Education to Tackle Unemployment
body: Ibrahim Oyewale in Lokoja A first-class traditional ruler and the Chairman of Lokoja Traditional Council in Kogi State, the Maigari, Alhaji Ibrahim Kabir, Maikarfi IV, has appealed to the federal government to revert to the era of technical education and Technical Colleges to tackle youth unemployment. The royal father, who made this call while speaking at the opening ceremony of the National Agency Science and Engineering Infrastructure NASENI Training and Empowerment programme in Lokoja yesterday, pointed out that in those days, the technical colleges were producing middle-level manpower as technicians, noting that the graduates were at best against the backdrop of the present-day graduates of higher institutions who solely relied on the certificate and remained unemployed for several years. The Maigari, who was represented by a high chief, the Mattawalli of Lokoja, Alhaji Adamu Mohammed, recalled that the students of Lokoja Technical College were helping to repair cars, were good at carpentry and electrical works, and other skills. He, therefore, urged the federal government to revive technical education, which he said did not require higher qualifications, to reduce the high tide of youth unemployment in the country. The traditional ruler added that it is high time the federal government and the Ministry of Education reassigned technical education in the curriculum to ignite skill acquisition. He tasked the beneficiaries to take advantage of the NASENI training and the empowerment programme to learn the skill and become self-reliant in the future. Earlier, the Executive Director/Chief Executive Officer of the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), Dr. Khalid Halilu, explained that the federal government has reinforced its commitment to eradicate youth unemployment through skill acquisition interventions to bridge the gap in the ongoing global innovations and technologies. Halilu made this known while speaking at the official flag-off of the training of 120 electricians in modern electrical installation and maintenance in Lokoja yesterday. He stated that this has become imperative with a view to ensuring that the teeming youths acquire skills which will fortify their future rather than looking for unavailable white-collar jobs, stressing that skill acquisition is the in-thing now. The Executive Director/Chief Executive Officer of NASENI, who was presented by a Research Director in the agency, Professor Abdulmaliki Ibrahim, noted that the programme is an instance of the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Tinubu, “who has magnanimously approved the training of the teeming youth in skill acquisition in various fields through NASENI to bridge the gap in global innovations and technologies.” He explained that the youths must take advantage of the presidential/NASENI training programme to acquire skills and help themselves in the near future. The executive director pointed out that the programme is simultaneously taking place across the country, noting that Kogi State is the 27th state in Nigeria, noting that the first phase is about to end and the second will start immediately across the country.

title: Ukraine receives bodies of 252 fallen – Coordination Headquarters
body:
The bodies of 252 fallen individuals, who according to the Russian side are Ukrainian service members, were returned to Ukraine as a result of repatriation efforts, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported on Thursday.
"Law enforcement investigators, together with representatives of expert institutions, will conduct all necessary measures to identify the repatriated deceased," the statement reads.
The repatriation measures were carried out following joint efforts by representatives of the Coordination Headquarters, as well as the Joint Center under the SBU, the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ombudsman's Office, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Missing Under Special Circumstances, the State Emergency Service, and other structures of Ukraine's security and defense sector.
"We express our sincere gratitude to the International Committee of the Red Cross for assistance and support in carrying out the repatriation measures," the report states.
The last time the Coordination Headquarters reported the return of bodies of the fallen was on September 17. At that time, it was also about 252 bodies, which according to the Russian side belonged to citizens of Ukraine, including service members. Prior to that, the return of 261 fallen was reported on August 13.

title: Donald Duke: Nigeria’s Vanishing Middle Class Exposes Deepening Economic Crisis
body: Ayodeji Ake The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Donald Duke, has said the disappearance of Nigeria’s middle class reflects the deepening economic crisis in the country, warning that widespread poverty, unemployment and insecurity are pushing the nation towards state failure. Duke, who spoke in an interview, said many Nigerians who previously considered themselves financially stable, were now struggling to meet their basic needs, leaving them vulnerable to economic shocks and emergencies. He argued that the country’s economic difficulties had been compounded by shrinking businesses, inadequate job opportunities and a rapidly expanding population that the economy could no longer adequately support. “The so-called middle class does not really exist anymore. Many of those we call middle class are only surviving from day-to-day. Let there be one serious emergency and they crumble,” he said. The former Cross River State governor said the widening gap between the wealthy and the poor was an indication that Nigeria’s economy was failing to provide the conditions necessary for a decent standard of living. “You have perhaps one per cent who are genuinely wealthy and then a huge number of people struggling around or below the poverty line,” he said. Duke explained that the situation had become a major motivation for his decision to contest the 2027 presidential election, arguing that Nigeria could not afford to continue on its present path for another four years. “I talk about the urgency of now because I don’t think we can go on like this for another four years,” he said. He explained that his decision to seek the presidency was driven by the need to move beyond criticism of successive governments and offer solutions to the country’s worsening economic and social challenges. “You get to a point in your life where you say, ‘Either I walk away or I do something.’ “There is no guarantee that you will win. But I don’t want to look back and say that all these things happened and I did nothing,” he said. The PRP candidate said his campaign would focus on the substantive issues affecting Nigerians, including poverty, unemployment, economic decline and insecurity, rather than political personalities. “What I want to do is focus on those who aspire to lead this nation on addressing the issues that affect us and how we can resolve them. “I talk about the options. I talk about the real issues. I don’t want to talk about personalities,” he said. Duke linked the country’s economic difficulties to the growing insecurity, including kidnapping, banditry, terrorism and other violent conflicts, arguing that the government must address the underlying causes of these problems. He described the security crisis as evidence of the state’s inability to protect citizens and create an environment in which they could live productive lives. “If we don’t address these issues squarely and fundamentally, we’re already a failed state. There’s no question about it. Look at what is happening, banditry, terrorism, kidnapping and all sorts of conflicts. These are symptoms of a state that is unable, not only to properly articulate its challenges, but to deal with them,” he said. According to him, the existence of government institutions does not necessarily mean that the state is fulfilling its responsibilities to citizens. “What is the definition of a failed state? Fundamentally, it is a state that fails to meet the aspirations of its people. “You may still have a government and institutions, but if the state cannot protect the people and provide the environment in which they can live productive lives, then it is failing them,” he said. Duke added that the experiences of victims of kidnapping illustrated the consequences of the state’s failure to guarantee security. “Talk to someone who has been kidnapped. That person does not need you to explain the definition of a failed state. His experience has already told him what failure of the state means,” he said. He maintained that poverty and unemployment were among the underlying factors contributing to banditry and kidnapping, warning that security responses would remain inadequate if the economic conditions driving criminality were ignored. “When it comes to banditry and kidnapping, poverty and unemployment are at the bottom of much of it. “We keep reacting to these crises instead of asking what is producing them. We are too reactive in our governance. Governance is not just about today; it is about laying the foundation for tomorrow,” he said. The former governor expressed concern that Nigeria was not generating businesses and employment opportunities at a rate sufficient to accommodate its growing working-age population. He said the annual influx of graduates into the labour market, coupled with the difficulties confronting existing businesses, was worsening the country’s employment challenge. “Businesses are contracting. New ones are not springing up the way they should. At the same time, we are turning out graduates every year and adding more people to the working population, but there is no work for them to do,” he said. Duke also questioned whether Nigeria’s economy had expanded sufficiently to support its population, comparing the country’s crude oil production with figures from more than four decades ago. He recalled that Nigeria produced approximately 2.5 million barrels of crude oil daily in 1980, compared with about 1.7 million barrels at the time of his remarks, despite substantial population growth. “In 1980, Nigeria was producing about 2.5 million barrels of oil a day. Forty-six years later, we are producing around 1.7 million barrels, while our population has tripled. “So you have to ask: has the economy expanded enough to carry the population? Clearly, it has not,” he said. He argued that Nigeria’s large population should serve as an economic advantage rather than a source of instability, provided the government invested adequately in education, employment and productivity. “Our numbers ought to be an asset. But a large population is an asset only when you can educate the people, employ them and make them productive,” he said. Duke warned that the failure to create sufficient opportunities would continue to encourage Nigerians with the resources to seek better prospects abroad, while those remaining in the country would face mounting economic pressure. The PRP candidate said his presidential ambition was rooted in his longstanding belief that Nigeria could become a successful nation if its resources and population were properly managed. He recalled that he had the opportunity to remain in the United States after studying and working there in his twenties but chose to return to Nigeria because he believed he had a role to play in the country’s development. “I had the opportunity in my twenties to remain in America. I went to school there and worked there for a while. “But I voluntarily decided that was not where I wanted to be. I believe the Almighty put me in Nigeria for a reason. I believe in this country’s possibilities, and this is where I believe I should contribute,” he said. He said that conviction had informed his decision to contest the Cross River governorship in 1999 and now underpinned his bid for the presidency ahead of the 2027 election. “I wanted to prove then that we were better than what we were putting forward. From experience, I know Nigeria can be a very successful nation,” Duke said.

title: Seven missing Ghanaian fishermen rescued in joint naval operation off Benin
body: Seven Ghanaian fishers who were stranded at sea for more than a week have been rescued in a coordinated operation involving the navies of Ghana, Togo and Benin. The Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture confirmed the successful rescue on Thursday, October 22, 2026, commending the three navies for their swift response and effective regional cooperation. The operation followed a distress alert issued by the Ghana Navy and the Multinational Maritime Coordination Centre (MMCC-E) on Wednesday, October 21. The Togolese Navy deployed its patrol vessel, OTI, which located the distressed fishing boat approximately three nautical miles off Grand-Popo in Beninese waters. All seven crew members were rescued and provided with assistance, while the vessel was being towed towards the Ghana-Togo maritime boundary for handover to the Ghana Navy. Scanned Document 5 Download The rescue brings relief to the crew of Second Chance, whose disappearance had prompted a multi-agency search after the canoe failed to return from a fishing expedition off Axim in the Western Region. The canoe departed Sekondi Fishing Harbour on October 9 but suffered an engine failure, leaving the crew drifting offshore. One of the fishermen, Kwame Akyim, told TV3 News that strong tides had carried the canoe more than 120 nautical miles offshore. He described the crew’s difficult conditions, saying they had limited food, relied on their catch for sustenance and resorted to boiling seawater for drinking. The canoe’s owner, Nana Kweku Atta, reported its disappearance to the Fishing Harbour Police Station in Sekondi on October 18, triggering a search involving the Marine Police, Ghana Navy, Ghana Maritime Authority, Fisheries Commission and fishing communities. Western Regional Minister Joseph Nelson subsequently disclosed that contact had been established with the crew and that their location had been identified in neighbouring waters, prompting engagement with Togolese authorities to facilitate their safe return. The Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture has reiterated the importance of safety at sea, urging fishers to check weather conditions before departure, wear life jackets, carry reliable communication equipment and strictly observe maritime safety advisories. “Safety at sea is non-negotiable,” the Ministry stressed, warning that no fishing expedition was worth a human life. It urged every fisher to take personal responsibility for safety and called for all necessary measures to ensure that those who venture out to sea return home safely.

title: Denmark puts a $112.6 million state guarantee behind the maker of Ukraine’s Flamingo missiles

The financing will run through EIFO, Denmark’s state export and investment fund. Ukraine uses its Flamingo missiles to strike defense plants deep inside Russia as Moscow continues its full-scale invasion. Fire Point broke ground in December 2025 on a plant in Vojens, southern Denmark, to make solid fuel for the missiles. The project has since grown far more expensive. title: Russia and Ukraine Exchange Bodies of Nearly 300 Soldiers
body:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged the remains of 277 soldiers killed fighting in the war, the RBC outlet reported Thursday, citing a Russian lawmaker.
Russia returned 252 bodies to Ukraine and received 25 fallen Russian soldiers in return, said Shamsail Saraliyev, a State Duma lawmaker from the ruling United Russia party and member of a parliamentary group dedicated to the conflict.
The exchange took place at the Novaya Guta border crossing in Belarus, according to Belarusian state media.
Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War later confirmed the exchange. It thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for help facilitating the repatriation.
Earlier this month, Kyrylo Budanov, the head of the Ukrainian president’s office, estimated that more than 26,000 bodies and human remains had been repatriated to Ukraine through exchange operations since the start of the war.
Russia and Ukraine previously exchanged the bodies of fallen soldiers in September and August .
Thursday’s repatriation came a day after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff concluded talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss renewing trilateral peace negotiations that have stalled since February.
