title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
body:
Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.
Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.
“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”
Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)
DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.
Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.
Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.
The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications.
Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time.
One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm.
Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says.
The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

title: Three things you should know about permafrost
body: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it. The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future. I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away. Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age. That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further. The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years. The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm. Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide. Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them. Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.) That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow. The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications. One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted. Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake? The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand. This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
body: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling. This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents. Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis. Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized. Two words for you: context matters. My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis. Welcome, Devavrat. Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here. Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises. The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision. Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come. Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there. Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one. In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom. Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization? Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better. Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision. Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer? Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate. Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that. Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it. And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it. Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two? Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that. On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go. And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time. The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner. Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well? Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one. Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this. And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed. Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about? Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one. Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak. And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly. Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com. This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thanks so much for listening. Goodbye. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: Exail wins navy contract for USV navigation systems
body:
French technology and defense company Exail has secured a contract to supply its Marins military-grade inertial navigation systems (INS) for an entire fleet of uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) operated by an undisclosed navy.
The Marins systems will provide position, heading, attitude and velocity data to support autonomous vessel operations, including in environments where global navigation satellite system (GNSS) signals are disrupted, degraded or unavailable.
According to Exail, reliable navigation is essential for USVs operating without onboard crews, particularly in contested environments where satellite navigation may be affected by jamming or spoofing.
The Marins series has previously been deployed on defense surface vessels, submarines and uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs). The new contract extends the use of the systems to the navy’s fleet of uncrewed surface platforms.
Exail said its navigation technologies are used aboard defense vessels operated by more than 50 navies worldwide. The company also supplies navigation technologies for autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), which operate in environments where GNSS signals are unavailable.
The contract comes as navies expand their use of uncrewed platforms alongside crewed vessels, creating demand for navigation systems that can maintain reliable performance without continuous human oversight.
"Navies are moving towards fleets where crewed and uncrewed vessels operate alongside one another. But deploying USVs at scale requires more than autonomous platforms: it requires trusted navigation technologies capable of meeting demanding defense requirements. Our strength lies in combining proven defense navigation technologies with first-hand experience of designing and integrating autonomous maritime systems. This dual expertise gives us a unique understanding of the navigation challenges facing uncrewed platforms, positioning Exail to meet the evolving needs of defense USV fleets," said Jean-Marc Binois , CCO at Exail.

title: Live Updates | Constitutional Court Hears Opposition Ban Case
body: Georgia’s Constitutional Court, based in the coastal city of Batumi, starts hearing the lawsuit filed by 88 MPs of the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five major opposition forces: United National Movement (UNM), Coalition for Change, Lelo/Strong Georgia, Federalists, and Gakharia’s For Georgia. The first hearings are scheduled for October 21, 22, and 23. The hearings will start at 12 pm and will be livestreamed on the court’s YouTube channel , as well as by the Georgian Public Broadcaster, which is the only media authorized to film the proceedings. Representatives of four of the five targeted parties – UNM, Coalition for Change, Lelo/Strong Georgia, and For Georgia – will be in the courtroom pleading their cases, while the Federalists said they will be “mocking” the proceedings from outside so as not to legitimize the process, even as they plan to stay in Batumi as part of the party’s campaign. The court’s seven-judge plenum, seen as dominated by the ruling party loyalists, will be hearing the case, after one judge – Manana Kobakhidze – resigned after being denied her recusal request. The proceedings have drawn widespread scrutiny and local and international criticism as an attack on democracy and political pluralism. The proceedings come as part of Georgian Dream’s broader crackdown on dissent, including funding restrictions on media and civil society, criminal proceedings against opposition leaders, and a series of laws restricting political activities for broader groups. Read more about the lawsuit in Civil.ge’s backgrounder. All times are local . October 22, 2026 15:20 – Judge Warns Lelo Representative for Using Term “Kotsi” A judge warned Lelo-Strong Georgia representative Giorgi Sioridze for using the term “Kotsi,” a colloquial term for Georgian Dream members and supporters, while addressing the Court. 13:55 – Verbal Altercation Between GD and Opposition Representatives A verbal altercation broke out during a break between Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze and Nana Malashkhia of the Coalition for Change. The confrontation began in the court corridor and de-escalated after media representatives began filming, according to IPN. 12:30 – Papuashvili Says Foreign Criticism Seeks to Pressure Constitutional Court The disputed Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili has dismissed the criticism from the foreign officials over the proceedings as “concerning” and as violating the principle of non-interference in internal affairs. “Referring the question of any political party’s constitutionality to the Constitutional Court is a right guaranteed to members of the Parliament of Georgia by the Constitution,” he wrote on Facebook. “Threatening statements by foreign governments in response to the people’s representatives exercising this right demonstrate a failure to understand democratic norms and violate the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of another country.” He continued that such statements also constitute what he called “an attempt to exert pressure on and intimidate the Constitutional Court of Georgia,” adding that “calling the legitimacy of the proceedings into question before the Constitutional Court has considered the case on its merits is a gross interference with judicial independence and a violation of the rule of law.” “Foreign officials who comment on judicial proceedings in Georgia without any real understanding of them should show basic restraint and respect for the rule of law.” 12:09 – Constitutional Court Hearing Resumes The Constitutional Court hearing has resumed, with Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia addressing the court as it continues reviewing opposition motions. October 21, 2026 22:00 – OSCE PA Vice-President: “Stop the Attempt to Ban Opposition Parties” Gudrun Kugler, Vice-President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, has called on Georgian authorities to withdraw the lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties, saying the proceedings raise serious concerns about democracy and judicial independence. “Stop the Attempt to Ban Opposition Parties and Return to the Path of Democracy,” Kugler wrote in a post on X, adding that she was “deeply concerned” over the proceedings. “Banning political parties is an exceptional measure that must meet the highest democratic and legal standards. These proceedings are particularly troubling amid serious concerns about judicial independence, including concerns raised by the European Parliament,” she said. “In my capacity as Vice-President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, I call on the Georgian authorities to withdraw this lawsuit and to end politically motivated prosecutions,” Kugler added. 21:10 – GYLA’s Chair Says Lawsuit Threatens Voters’ Choice “The line that should run between protecting democracy and protecting power has been completely erased by this lawsuit,” Tamar Oniani, the chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), wrote in a Facebook post. She added: “This process threatens not only the five parties, but also citizens’ ability to choose their preferred government. That is precisely why the damage inflicted on Georgian democracy may prove irreversible.” 18:25 – Zourabichvili: “Today Is a Shameful Day for Georgia” “Today is a shameful day for Georgia and Georgian statehood,” Georgia’s fifth President, Salome Zourabichvili, said in a video address dedicated to the lawsuit. “Today is the day Georgian Dream is trying – and will fail – to finally bury democracy, the state, and our image in the world,” she added. Zourabichvili slammed the ruling party, but also Gakharia’s For Georgia, which had asked for its case to be examined separately, accusing the latter of “somehow flirting with Georgian Dream, presenting itself as if to say, ‘I am good, I am a good slave, and I will continue to serve you.’” 15:05 – Court Rejects UNM Motion to Summon GD Founder Bidzina Ivanishvili The Constitutional Court also rejected UNM’s request to summon Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili as a witness. UNM representative Khatia Dekanoidze, who was later removed from the hearing, argued that Ivanishvili should be questioned because, according to her, he is the sole decision-maker in Georgia and is responsible for the country’s rapprochement with Russia and its distancing from Western partners. The request to summon Ivanishvili was also raised by other UNM representatives, including Ani Tsitlidze and Zaza Bibileishvili, but was denied by the court. Responding to the motions to summon party leaders as witnesses, Judge Eva Gotsiridze said the court’s task in this case is not to determine the individual responsibility of specific people. “Within the scope of this constitutional lawsuit, we do not have to decide the question of individual responsibility of specific persons,” she said. “We need to assess the activity of the political party as a whole.” 14:40 – Court Rejects UNM Motion to Summon Saakashvili and Khabeishvili as Witnesses The Constitutional Court rejected the UNM’s request to summon former jailed President Mikheil Saakashvili and imprisoned party leader Levan Khabeishvili as witnesses in the proceedings. UNM representative Ani Tsitlidze argued that the lawsuit largely concerns Saakashvili’s time in power, citing his decisions and statements, and that his testimony could provide relevant factual information to help the court reach an objective and fair decision. She added that, since the lawsuit also refers to the events of October 4, Khabeishvili should be given the opportunity to answer specific questions concerning those events. 13:50 – Constitutional Court Rejects Motions Filed by UNM, Lelo, and For Georgia Judge Nadaria, reading out the Constitutional Court plenum’s decision, announced that the court had rejected the recusal motions filed by the United National Movement (UNM) and Lelo–Strong Georgia. In addition, the court did not grant the motion announced yesterday by Gakharia’s For Georgia party, requesting that the case against it be examined separately from the broader lawsuit. 13:00 – The Court Retires to Deliberate on Recusal Motions The court has retired to deliberate on the recusal motions of UNM and Lelo. The UNM is demanding the recusal of the entire composition of the Constitutional Court plenum. The party’s representative, Ana Tsitlidze, said the Constitutional Court “is neither free nor fair and does not act in accordance with the Constitution of Georgia.” Lelo has also filed a motion to recuse three judges. According to Lelo representative Kakhi Samkharadze, one of them, Vasil Roinishvili, took part as a supervising prosecutor in the case of Sergeant Roin Shavadze , who was killed after his arrest in Batumi in 2008, and whose initial investigation the European Court of Human Rights found lacked independence and impartiality. Lelo also requested the recusal of Goga Kikilashvili and Sergo Metopishvili, two judges recently appointed by Georgian Dream, questioning their independence. 12:50 – Rally Held Outside Constitutional Court Meanwhile, in parallel with the hearing, the political party Freedom Square has organized a protest outside the Constitutional Court. “Freedom Square is not among the parties facing a ban, but that makes no difference to us. When injustice occurs, we will fight against it, regardless of whether it directly affects us or not,” party leader Levan Tsutskiridze told journalists ahead of the hearing. 12:40 – List of Political Party Representatives The following representatives of Georgia’s political parties are participating in the Constitutional Court hearing: UNM is represented by Ani Tsitlidze, Khatia Dekanoidze, Levan Bezhashvili, Zaza Bibilashvili and Irakli Pavlenishvili; Coalition for Change is represented by Nika Gvaramia, Tengo Tevzadze, Maia Kopaleishvili, Giga Lemonjava, Marika Arevadze; For Georgia is represented by Ana Buchukuri, Berdia Sitchinava, Irakli Ksovreli; Lelo/ Strong Georgia is represented by Mikheil Sharashidze, Kakhi Samkharadze, Tornike Artkmeladze, Badri Japaridze, Giorgi Soridze and Irakli Kupradze; Georgian Dream is represented by: Giorgi Kakhiani, Archil Gorduladze, Tornike Cheishvili, Tengiz Sharmanashvili. The Federalists will not participate in the hearings. 12:30 – Hearing Opens The first hearing opens in Batumi. The seven-judge plenum presiding over the case includes: Giorgi Modebadze , Judge, appointed by GD-elected President Mikheil Kavelashvili in 2025 Giorgi Tevdorashvili , Judge, appointed by President Salome Zourabichvili in 2021 Sergo Metopishvili , Judge, selected by the Supreme Court plenum in 2026 Revaz Nadaraia , Constitutional Court Chairman, selected by the Supreme Court plenum in 2025. Vasil Roinishvili , Judge, selected by the Supreme Court plenum in 2020 Eva Gotsiridze , Judge, elected by the Georgian Dream-led parliament in 2017. Goga Kikilashvili , Judge, appointed by GD-elected President Mikheil Kavelashvili in 2026 Screengrab from the hearing’s YouTube livestream 11:00 – CSOs Condemn Opposition Ban Proceedings 19 Georgian civil society organizations condemned Georgian Dream’s constitutional lawsuit in a joint statement, calling it “a direct continuation of the ruling party’s undemocratic and repressive policies” and “a new, extremely grave stage of the country’s ongoing autocratization.” The organizations described the lawsuits as “completely unfounded” and contrary to Georgia’s Constitution and European legal standards. They argued that the cases rely on a legally invalid parliamentary commission report and misrepresent legitimate democratic activities, including government criticism, parliamentary boycotts, peaceful protests and appeals to international partners, as attempts to overthrow the constitutional order. The organizations said the lawsuits come amid the “systematic persecution of political opponents, critical media and civil society.” They warned that banning opposition parties would strip hundreds of thousands of voters of political representation and “formally establish a one-party dictatorship.”

title: Ukrainian military intelligence reveals new Russian cruise missile 'Filin'
body:
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) announced details of a new Russian cruise missile called "Filin" and released a 3-D model of the missile alongside a list of components and electronics on its website on Oct. 22.
Russia began using the missile at the end of summer, HUR said , calling it a continuation of a Russian trend to build "inexpensive air attack means with jet propulsion and ground-based launch."
The missile is 3.5 meters long with a wingspan of 3 meters, ablte to carry either 50 kilogram or 100 kilogram warheads, HUR said. It can fly both at ultra-low altitudes and up to 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) high, at a top speed of 800 kilometers per hour (about 497 miles per hour), across a distance of 1,200 kilometers (about 745 miles), according to the agency.
Some parts of the missile are apparently 3-D printed, HUR said, while the electronic component base of the onboard equipment is similar to other Russian missiles, but stands out for the increased share of Chinese components. Besides Chinese components, the agency also said the "Filin" included 35 U.S.-made components.
The onboard equipment is manufactured by PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing the Harpiya drone, HUR said, while the engine is the Russian-made R500, produced by Reynolds LLC.
Russia uses cruise and ballistic missiles to strike at Ukraine, and increasingly at the country's energy infrastructure . On Oct. 22, Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," President Volodymyr Zelensky commented on the attack.
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles.

title: Ex-Deputy PM Grigorenko Nominated as Sberbank Deputy Board Chairman
body:
Russian state lender Sberbank confirmed Thursday that former Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of Government Staff Dmitry Grigorenko has been nominated to serve as deputy chairman of its board of directors.
The announcement immediately followed President Vladimir Putin’s decree officially relieving Grigorenko of his duties in the government cabinet. First Deputy Finance Minister Irina Okladnikova is set to succeed him, becoming the first woman to take on the role of chief of government staff.
At Sberbank, Grigorenko is expected to oversee strategic initiatives, including government relations and the deployment of artificial intelligence and digital services across the public sector, the lender said.
“His arrival will strengthen Sber and give impetus to the development of our systemic dialogue with the state and regions,” Sberbank CEO Herman Gref said in a statement.
Sberbank’s supervisory board is scheduled to formally vote on Grigorenko’s appointment at its next meeting on Nov. 10.
Sources close to the Kremlin and in Russia’s tech industry told the newspaper Vedomosti that Grigorenko could take charge of Sberbank’s entire digital agenda.
Russian political analysts have speculated that Grigorenko’s departure from the government will reduce Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin’s power in the cabinet given the close working relationship between the two men over the years.
Meanwhile, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, whom Putin promoted to deputy prime minister alongside his ministerial position, and other economic officials have seen their influence in government grow as balancing state finances has taken on greater importance amid surging war spending, rising inflation and high interest rates.
Grigorenko previously served as deputy head of Russia’s Federal Tax Service, which Mishustin headed for several years, before joining the prime minister’s cabinet in January 2020 as chief of government staff, where he led the digitalization of government affairs.

title: Georgia appoints new special envoy for relations with Russia: what does it mean?
body: On 21 October, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili , the first deputy foreign minister, as his special representative for relations with Russia . The post had remained vacant since December 2025. The announcement came on the same day that the Constitutional Court began hearing on the merits a lawsuit by the ruling party seeking to ban five opposition parties. Opposition figures have interpreted the timing as a signal to Moscow. Kobakhidze, for his part, insists that the appointment does not mark a new phase in relations with Russia. What Kobakhidze said The prime minister announced the appointment at a briefing in the government administration. Asked by a journalist whether this marked the beginning of a new phase in efforts to reset relations with Russia, he said it did not. Kobakhidze said the Georgian Interests Section at the Swiss embassy in Moscow had been working actively. However, the government had decided that it needed an additional channel alongside the section to “resolve the conflict peacefully, maintain humanitarian ties and develop trade and economic relations”. The prime minister also denied that the decision was linked to recent restrictions Russia had imposed on products from Georgian companies. “Of course, work on these issues is a priority overall, but this was certainly not the basis for the decision,” Kobakhidze said. New Russian trade ban on Georgian goods: why now, and what risks do Georgian experts see? Experts warn of economic pressure and see a link to the Abkhazia issue. Asked about restoring diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia, Kobakhidze said an obstacle remained: “This situation has not changed, and neither has our position.” Regarding Russia’s demand that Tbilisi provide Sukhumi and Tskhinvali (the capitals of Abkhazia and South Ossetia) with guarantees of non-use of force, the prime minister said Georgia could not sign an agreement with them because it could not recognise them as independent states in any form. Giorgi Zurabashvili Giorgi Zurabashvili will also retain his post as first deputy foreign minister, which he has held since July 2025. He previously served as Georgia’s ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Ireland from 2019 to 2024. The special envoy role Since 2012, diplomat Zurab Abashidze had served as Georgia’s special representative for relations with Russia. He held regular meetings with Grigory Karasin , a Russian deputy foreign minister. This channel of talks became known as the “Abashidze–Karasin format” . Zurab Abashidze and Grigory Karasin, 2019. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. In March 2024, Irakli Kobakhidze moved Abashidze to the post of his adviser and appointed Giorgi Kajaya as his replacement. However, the government administration told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that Kajaya left the post on 1 December 2025. The public learned that the position had remained vacant only in August 2026, when Kobakhidze answered a question from journalists. Meanwhile, on 6 October 2026, Zurab Abashidze became Georgia’s non-resident ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Albania. “A cynical signal”: opposition reaction Grigol Gegelia , one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia–Lelo opposition coalition, whose party the government is seeking to ban, believes that: “This is a direct, cynical signal that the parties are being banned at Russia’s behest, and that on the very same day, in a synchronised move, a person is appointed to pursue warmer relations with Russia.” Court begins hearing case to ban opposition parties in Georgia: first-day developments The court rejected all the opposition’s motions on the first day of hearings. According to Lasha Parulava , a member of the governing council of another opposition party, the United National Movement, the appointment serves no economic purpose and is a symbolic gesture. “Here, at the Constitutional Court, they are dismantling the pro-Western opposition while, at the same time, appointing a special representative to Russia.” The founder of the United National Movement and Georgia’s third president, Mikheil Saakashvili , wrote on social media that “the rapid restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is being prepared without de-occupation, which amounts to formally endorsing capitulation”. Moscow welcomed the appointment. Konstantin Zatulin , first deputy chairman of the Russian State Duma’s Committee on CIS Affairs, called the decision a step in the right direction. “The decision to appoint a special representative is a step in the right direction. Relations between Russia and Georgia must develop,” Zatulin said. Relations with Russia under Georgian Dream Restoring relations with Russia was one of the main campaign promises of the current ruling party, Georgian Dream. The special representative post was established shortly after it came to power, on 1 November 2012. Following the August 2008 war, Tbilisi and Moscow had communicated directly only through the Geneva International Discussions. The Abashidze–Karasin format helped restore exports of Georgian wine, mineral water, fruit and vegetables to the Russian market in 2013. The authorities also softened their rhetoric towards Russia. On 20 June 2019, mass protests broke out in Tbilisi after Russian MP Sergei Gavrilov addressed the Georgian parliament. Russia subsequently suspended direct flights to Georgia. In May 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin lifted visa requirements for Georgian citizens and restored direct flights. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgian Dream declined to join international sanctions against Russia, saying it wanted to protect Georgia’s economy. From January to August 2026, Russia accounted for around 62.5% of the value of Georgia’s wine exports . On 9 October, Russia’s food safety watchdog suspended imports of products from seven Georgian companies. On the same day, Russia’s Foreign Ministry again demanded that Tbilisi provide Sukhumi and Tskhinvali with guarantees of non-use of force and begin delimiting the so-called state borders. Georgia’s special representative for relations with Russia

title: 'Like a biblical battle': WP journalist wounded in West Bank credits Palestinian youth with rescue
body: Heidi Levine, the photojournalist for The Washington Post who was seriously wounded during an attack by extremist Israeli settlers in the West Bank over the weekend, told The Guardian on Wednesday that she had been protected by Palestinian youth."The Palestinian youth put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing," Levine said, describing the scene as being "like a biblical battle."Levine, along with a group of Palestinians, journalists, and activists, was attacked by the settlers while harvesting olives near Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah."All hell broke loose," she recounted. "Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked... all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw tear gas in the distance. I started to run."Levine said she was kicked and beaten with sticks "probably more than a hundred times," including after she tried playing dead. She also said that she feared that, if she hadn't lain down with her face to the ground, she could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye from the beating.The settlers were forced back by Palestinian youth using slingshots to hurl stones at them, allowing US journalist Jasper Nathaniel to approach and assist Levine."It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine's,” Nathaniel claimed afterward.'A teddy bear on the phone': Herzog apologizes to wounded photojournalistAfter the incident, President Isaac Herzog called Levine to apologize.“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she recalled. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they're a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”Levine was angered, however, by a claim from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office that some video footage of the "alleged attack" on her appeared to show one of the attackers knocking her down and immediately helping her back up.“That's such bulls***. They helped me up because they couldn't get my things off of me. That's why,” she said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk, and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone… That's why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”She said that she was not confident that the settlers involved would be brought to justice, arguing that "it's not just arresting these teenage thugs. It's going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they're organized.”Ten suspects arrested after attack in West BankThe IDF, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), and Israel Police arrested 10 suspects early Monday morning relating to the attack.The operation, dubbed "Operation Olive Leaf," also included the confiscation of several vehicles and the clearing of some illegal construction.Responding to the broader situation of the US and EU accusing Israel, and to some extent, specifically the IDF, of losing control of extremist settler violence in the West Bank, Defense Minister Israel Katz said he would transfer the issue to be handled by the police.Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

title: Gulf economies to contract 4.8% this year amid Iran war shock, IMF says
body: Gulf economies are set to shrink 4.8 per cent this year as the Iran war disrupts energy exports and weighs on non-oil activity, before rebounding 9.1 per cent in 2027 , the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday. The forecast marks a sharp reversal for the six-member Gulf bloc, with the IMF cutting its 2026 growth projection by 6.8 percentage points from the 2 per cent expansion it expected in April, according to its Regional Economic Outlook released in Dubai on Tuesday. The Gulf region posted growth of 4.5 per cent last year. “While some economies have remained relatively resilient, others have experienced severe disruptions, leading to a substantially weaker regional economic outlook since our April forecast,” Jihad Azour , director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia department, said at the report's launch at the Dubai International Financial Centre. “This conflict has disrupted energy production, shipping, tourism, trade, and confidence. And the burden of this disruption has fallen most heavily on oil-exporting economies, directly affected by the interruption of energy production and transport,” he said, calling the war a “severe shock” for oil importers. There is divergence between the Gulf countries, with Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar the most affected because of the drop in hydrocarbon production and exports. Their economies are projected to decline by 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, this year. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are “less affected”, with contractions of 3.9 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively, while Oman's economy is projected to grow by 4.1 per cent this year. The sultanate's geographical location, as well as focus on non-oil reforms in recent years is backing its economy, Mr Azour said. The wider Gulf's contraction for this year is similar to the level experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the bloc's GDP shrunk by 4.9 per cent. While the primarily reason for the drop in growth has been due to the oil sector, the bloc's non-oil economy is also forecast to contract by 0.8 per cent this year before returning to 4.5 per cent growth in 2027, underscoring the wider economic fallout from the conflict. Oil and gas production among Gulf exporters directly affected by the conflict plunged from 33 million barrels a day in February to about 19 million in May, with Qatar's output falling as much as 86 per cent, the fund said. Exports have since staged a partial recovery. Gulf crude shipments rose to more than 75 per cent of prewar levels in September, the International Energy Agency said. Oil prices are now projected to average close to $96 per barrel in 2026 and $87 per barrel in 2027, compared with $82.20 and $76, respectively, in April, with the forecast peaking at about $110 per barrel in late 2026 before declining steadily, the IMF said. The conflict is also eroding the Gulf's financial buffers. The IMF expects the bloc's current-account surplus to narrow to 1.3 per cent of gross domestic product this year, from 5 per cent in 2025, while its combined fiscal deficit widens to 2.3 per cent of GDP from 0.8 per cent. Inflation is projected to rise to 2.7 per cent. The diversification of trade routes and investment in resilience have significantly helped Gulf countries weather the shock from the war. While the fund anticipates a sharp rebound in Gulf economies next year, the forecast hinges on an end to hostilities and the gradual resumption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in early 2027. Saudi escalation Saudi Arabia, which has been facing an increasing number of attacks by the Yemen's Houthis, has the capacity to handle the impact of conflict, Mr Azour said. “The Saudi economy has during this war has been able to redirect flow of oil, use infrastructure that is on the Red Sea, and therefore the impact of the shock on Saudi comes … second after Oman [which has seen the least impact from the war]. This is a country that is less affected,” he said. “Of course, the recent tension we saw it's having impact on their economic activity. But overall, for a country that is still exporting five to six million barrels a day, with the depths of the market that they have and the strong internal demand, their capacity to withstand the shock is high,” he added. Looking ahead, the biggest downside risk is the “obvious one on the horizon … the risk of another escalation in fighting”, said Hasan AlHasan, senior fellow for Middle East Policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. Speaking at a panel discussion on the IMF report, he stressed that geopolitics now “occupies centre-stage in present economic performance but also in future economic planning”. Touching on the Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, he stressed that the region has the resilience to deal with the escalation, but urged for regional integration. “I think what this will depend on is the extent to which countries in the region are able to resolve their differences, and we're seeing very positive signs and encouraging signs in that direction,” he added. Also speaking at the panel, Monica Malik, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, said the Gulf economies have withstood the pressure well, and a big part of that is for energy exports to reach the market. “What is very important is that the region has entered this shock in a very strong position,” she said. “If we look at growth, really since the pandemic, you've seen multiple sectors performing well, multiple economies performing well. The resilience has not only come from looking to diversify the economy, but also from the fiscal side.” While there are uncertainties over how things get resolved and how quickly things normalise, “but given the reforms we've seen, given the balance sheets, given the focus of governments, I'm optimistic on the longer term and medium term outlook”, Ms Malik added.

title: Court Resumes Trial Of Suspects Linked To Abduction Of NYSC Members, Others In Imo
body: Court is set to resume the trial of suspects linked to the abduction of 20 members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) and others in Imo State. The suspects were apprehended in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, and Abia State during intelligence-led operations conducted between October 10 and 14 by the Department of State Services (DSS), in collaboration with the military, police, and other security operatives. Three other suspects reportedly escaped with gunshot wounds, prompting a manhunt for the fleeing members of the gang. The prospective corps members were abducted along the Owerri-Onitsha Expressway in Imo State on October 1, 2026, while they were travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to their assigned NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states. The gunmen attacked two buses conveying the prospective corps members and other passengers near Umunoha in the Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State. The victims were rescued on October 7 during a joint security operation at Amakohia-Ubi Village in Owerri West Local Government Area of the state. They were subsequently taken to the DSS hospital in Owerri for medical attention and necessary checks. During the search-and-rescue operation, the police had said their operatives located the kidnappers’ camp through drone surveillance but could not immediately advance because the location was reportedly planted with improvised explosive devices (IEDs). Security agencies later intensified efforts to reach the victims and secure their release. The post Court Resumes Trial Of Suspects Linked To Abduction Of NYSC Members, Others In Imo appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukraine to gain access to NATO procurement system for weapons, ammunition, Financial Times says
body:
Ukraine will be able to purchase weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment through NATO's centralized procurement agency, potentially giving Kyiv faster and cheaper access to defense supplies, the Financial Times reported on Oct. 22.
Ukraine is entering a partnership with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which handles procurement and logistical support for alliance members and partners, according to the Financial Times .
"It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services, and access to established industrial base," Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA's director of support to operations, told the Financial Times.
The arrangement might allow Ukraine to use NATO's existing procurement system and supplier network rather than negotiating each purchase independently.
The NSPA also held an event in Kyiv last week attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies, explaining how manufacturers could register as eligible suppliers and compete for contracts, according to the Financial Times.
The new mechanism is separate from the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List ( PURL ), under which NATO allies and partners fund purchases of U.S.-made weapons and ammunition for Ukraine. More than $6 billion in military equipment has been funded through PURL since the initiative was launched in July 2025, according to NATO.
The agreement comes as Kyiv seeks to diversify and stabilize its access to military supplies amid growing uncertainty over U.S. support.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has reported disruptions to some U.S.-provided capabilities, including intelligence sharing and the Starshield satellite system used by Ukrainian forces. President Volodymyr Zelensky said after talks in Oslo this week that efforts were underway to resolve those issues.

title: American Hubbard tortured during 4 years in Russian prison, two colonies – Book of Executioners
body:
The Ukrainian state online information project Book of Executioners of the Ukrainian People reports that 74-year-old U.S citizen Stephen Hubbard, released from Russian captivity on October 21 as part of ceasefire negotiations in Ukraine during a visit by U.S President Donald Trump's representative Steven Witkoff to Russia, was held after capture initially in a remand prison in Bryansk region of Russia, then in colonies in Vladimir region and the Republic of Mordovia in Russia, where he was subjected to torture.
"The occupiers captured him on April 2, 2022, in temporarily occupied Izium in Kharkiv region. Two and a half years later, in October 2024, Moscow City Court sentenced him to six years and 10 months in a colony under an article on 'mercenarism' (Part 3 of Article 359 of the Criminal Code of Russia). According to the occupiers, the U.S citizen, who had lived in Ukraine since 2014 and taught English, joined the territorial defense of the city of Izium in February 2022," the statement reads.
According to the project, prior to sentencing, Hubbard was held in detention center No. 2 in the city of Novozybkov, Bryansk region, and in Correctional Colony No. 7 in the village of Pakino, Vladimir region. "There, like Ukrainian prisoners, he was subjected to torture. According to his cellmate, released Ukrainian prisoner of war Ihor Shyshko, the American was beaten with sticks, batons, and kicked, shocked with stun guns, set upon by dogs, starved, forced to crawl along corridors and even simulate sexual acts. Hubbard's plight was aggravated by the fact that he is a U.S citizen and did not speak Russian, which caused staff to further abuse him," the report says.
Hubbard was held in the detention center in Novozybkov from approximately September 2022 to May 2023. "Released prisoners tell of numerous cases of torture in this institution, including beatings during 'reception,' interrogations, and inspections, dog attacks, stun gun shocks... At least three deaths of Ukrainians are known to have occurred in this detention center," the project's materials recount.
In Correctional Colony No. 7 in Vladimir region, Hubbard was held from May 2023 to the spring of 2024. "Those released from IK-7 report that colony staff beat prisoners twice a day during inspections and resorted to torture, including beatings with sticks on the soles of the feet... At least three deaths of Ukrainians are known to have occurred in this IK," the statement reads.
Russian media cite Correctional Colony No. 12 in Mordovia as Hubbard's last place of imprisonment, but project staff are currently verifying this information.
As reported, Hubbard's release became known during Witkoff's meeting with Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday. He thanked the Russian side on behalf of Trump and the American people. The day before, Trump stated that during a telephone conversation with Putin he had requested Hubbard's release. Witkoff also stated that negotiations with Ukrainian and European representatives held in Oslo were productive and the parties made progress. "I hope we have indeed established the necessary foundation to successfully reach a ceasefire," he said at the meeting with Putin.
Book of Executioners of the Ukrainian People was launched on the initiative of the President of Ukraine in 2022 to collect data for national and international judicial instances, tribunals, and accountability records. The Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense, the Security Service of Ukraine, the Office of the Prosecutor General, and other law enforcement bodies are involved in creating and verifying data. The database includes Russia military personnel and command who issued or executed criminal orders, staff of detention center and colonies involved in torturing Ukrainians, as well as judges who handed down and fabricated illegal sentences against citizens of Ukraine.

title: Podcast: The Spear – Foreign Area Officer in Iraq and Southeast Asia
body:
In this episode of The Spear , host Dr. Charlie Faint sits down with retired Lieutenant Colonel Andre Rivier, a former infantry officer and foreign area officer, to discuss a military career that took him from combat operations in Iraq to diplomatic assignments across Southeast Asia and the Pacific.
An immigrant who enlisted in the US Army at seventeen before attending West Point, Andre reflects on his early experiences leading soldiers in Kosovo during the September 11 attacks, commanding an infantry company in Iraq, and discovering the importance of understanding the cultural, political, and social dynamics of military operations. He describes his transition into the Army’s foreign area officer community, including intensive language training, attendance at the Royal Thai Army Command and General Staff College, and graduate studies at Yale University. Andre also shares insights from his assignments as a military attaché and security cooperation officer in Fiji, Laos, and other Pacific nations, emphasizing the importance of cultural awareness, language proficiency, relationship-building, and effective communication in advancing American interests abroad. Drawing on lessons from his military service and his subsequent career in international defense consulting, Andre argues that successful military leaders must be comfortable operating in ambiguity, willing to challenge their assumptions, and capable of understanding the world through perspectives other than their own.
