title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
body:
We have published the polygon triangulator of our map engine as a small library, earstrip , under the ISC license, the same one earcut uses. It is one C++ header, and a WebAssembly build on npm that takes the same arguments as earcut. In C++ it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp, in the browser 1.4 to 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js, and the comparison is near the end. This post is about how we got there.
A GPU fills triangles and nothing else. A map, on the other hand, is mostly polygons: buildings, parks, parking lots, the strip of grass between two tram tracks. Here are a few blocks of Śródmieście in Warsaw the way our renderer reads them from a map file, as outlines :
Before any of this gets a fill, every outline has to be cut into triangles . Hover over a polygon, or tap it, to see what it turns into. These blocks hold 331 polygons with 5,151 vertices, and they become 4,514 triangles.
Zoom level 13 of our offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship, the region around Warsaw, has 3,740,425 polygons. On one core of an M4 Pro, the constrained Delaunay triangulator in our engine needs 2.93 seconds to cut all of them. This October I replaced it with ear clipping. To write this post I rebuilt the ear clipper one idea at a time, one commit per idea, and timed every commit on those same 3.7 million polygons, so each section below ends with a number.
A triangulation of a set of points is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle through the three corners of any triangle. Two triangles that share an edge are enough to see how the rule works. Drag the point D:
While D stays outside the dashed circle through A, B and C, the shared edge is AC. Push D into the circle and the edge flips to BD; pull it back out and it flips back. Each flip is a local repair, and a triangulation where no edge wants to flip is Delaunay. Of all the ways to triangulate the same points, it has the largest smallest angle. The orange arc marks the smallest angle of the two triangles, and the line under the figure shows what the other diagonal would give: wherever you put D, the edge the circle rule picks wins.
"Constrained" means that the polygon's own edges must stay edges of the triangulation, even where the circle rule would flip them away. Our triangulator inserts the vertices one at a time. For each new point it walks across the triangles built so far until it finds the one the point falls into, splits it, and flips edges around the new point until the circle rule holds again. It also forces the polygon's edges in, and at the end it keeps only the triangles that lie inside the polygon and outside its holes.
Well-shaped triangles matter when you interpolate something across them or run a simulation on them. A flat fill doesn't care: a GPU fills a needle-thin triangle as correctly as a fat one. And most of the work is spent on polygons that hardly need any. Almost half of the Masovian polygons, 1.8 million, have four vertices or fewer. A triangle needs no cutting at all and a convex quad is two triangles, yet the Delaunay code spends 302 ms on them, building each triangulation from scratch.
An ear of a polygon is a corner you can cut off with one straight cut. Take three consecutive vertices a, b and c. If the corner at b is convex and no other part of the polygon reaches into the triangle abc, that triangle is an ear. Cut it off, and what remains is a polygon with one vertex fewer. In 1975 Gary Meisters proved that every simple polygon with more than three vertices has at least two ears that don't overlap. So there is always another ear to cut, and a polygon with n vertices falls apart into n − 2 triangles.
Here is one of the buildings from the blocks above. Move the slider to cut its ears one at a time, or cut them all :
The green triangle is the next ear to go. The algorithm needs one test, "is this corner an ear?", and the simplest version of it checks the corner and then every other vertex of the boundary. cross is the 2×2 determinant found in every geometry codebase; it is positive when c lies to the left of the line from a to b, so for a boundary that runs counter-clockwise a positive cross(a, b, c) means a convex corner:
A point on an edge of the triangle counts as inside: if the ear touched the rest of the boundary, cutting it off would leave a polygon that touches itself. The one exception is a point at exactly the position of a, b or c, which happens where an outline meets itself at a single vertex. Holes make that common.
Ear clipping works on one closed boundary, and 11,345 of the Masovian polygons have holes, such as courtyards and clearings in forests. The way to deal with them is to cut each hole open and stitch it to the outer ring with a bridge, an edge from a vertex of the hole to a vertex of the boundary, walked once in each direction. The boundary then runs around the outside, crosses the bridge, goes around the hole the other way and comes back. There is no area between the two copies of the bridge, so the polygon is the same, but now it is one ring.
The bridge must not cross anything. David Eberly's write-up of ear clipping has a neat way to find one. Take the rightmost vertex of the hole, m, and cast a ray to the right. The first edge the ray hits, at I, has an end P further to the right. If no boundary vertex lies inside the triangle m, I, P, the bridge m–P is safe. You can drag the hole around:
Higher up the triangle is empty and the bridge goes to P. Lower down the tip of the dent sits inside the triangle, and the bridge goes to the dent instead: of the dents in the triangle, Eberly takes the one closest in angle to the ray. Holes are bridged rightmost first, so a hole further left can bridge to one that is already part of the boundary.
Map data adds two cases of its own. Our coordinates are integers on a tile grid, so a ray along a grid line runs straight through a vertex all the time; the crossing test passes over such a vertex, and my first version got exactly this case wrong. And mappers often draw a courtyard that touches the outer wall at one point. Such a hole needs no bridge: the two rings are joined at the shared vertex.
With holes bridged, the first complete version walks around the boundary, tests corners with the isEar above, cuts every ear it finds and writes each triangle as three indices. On the Masovian polygons it takes 1.12 seconds, 2.6 times faster than Delaunay. The chart splits each time by polygon size; hover over a part of a bar to see its number, or click a row:
The naive row is shorter than Delaunay in every size class but the last. The 1,123 largest polygons, with 257 vertices or more, take 199 ms to clip and 90 ms with Delaunay. Each ear test there walks hundreds of vertices, and a polygon needs hundreds of tests, so the cost grows with the square of its size. The rest of this post is about making the ear test cheaper and needed less often.
Look at which vertices can actually stop a convex corner from being an ear. Say some vertices lie inside its triangle, and take the one closest to the corner itself. Its two edges can't cross the sides of the triangle, so both run back, away from the corner, and the polygon wraps around that vertex from the corner's side. That makes it a reflex vertex, a dent . So if anything is inside the triangle, a dent is inside it too, and the test only has to look at the dents.
The engine keeps a list of them. A dent leaves the list when cutting its neighbour makes it convex, and a convex corner never turns into a dent, so the list only shrinks. The test becomes:
The 28.1 million ear tests now look at 185 million points instead of 353 million, and the total drops to 882 ms . That is less than you might expect, because building outlines have a lot of dents. The building with the arch above has 15 of them among its 27 vertices. And the smallest polygons get slower, from 34 to 54 ms: for a triangle or a quad, sorting the corners into dents and the rest costs more than the walk it saves.
A polygon without dents is convex, and every corner of a convex polygon is an ear, so it can be cut without a single test. Checking for that needs care. "Every corner turns left" is not enough:
The star turns left at all five corners, because it goes around its centre twice. The engine adds one more condition. Walking around a convex ring, the edges go right along the bottom and left along the top, so their x direction changes exactly twice, at the leftmost and the rightmost point. The pentagon passes; the star changes direction four times, at the circled corners, and goes to the ordinary ear tests. Both counts come out of the same loop that marks the dents, so the check costs almost nothing. Triangles and quads get their own shortcut before that loop.
The shortcut removes 4.4 million of the 28.1 million ear tests, but those were the cheapest ones: a ring without dents has nothing to scan. On its own it barely moves the total, 880 ms , though the polygons with four vertices or fewer win back part of what the dents cost them, from 54 to 48 ms. It matters more in the next step, where a convex ring becomes a single strip.
So far every triangle costs three indices. A GPU can also draw a triangle strip, where each new index adds a triangle made of it and the two before. A convex ring makes one strip if you zig-zag across it:
The ear clipper can write strips too. Cutting an ear makes the corners of its two neighbours sharper, so they are good candidates for the next ear, and cutting one of them extends the strip by a single index. The engine tries them first and keeps alternating between the two ends while the ears last. In its code the neighbours of the cut vertex are a and b:
When the next corner is not an ear, the strip ends and the walk goes on from where it stopped. The 21.5 million triangles now take 35.8 million indices instead of 64.5 million. The ear tests don't get fewer: the naive walk already went on at the next corner after a cut, and now every strip also ends on a test that fails, 25.0 million instead of 23.7 million. Still, the total falls to 762 ms , and the largest polygons drop from 146 to 103 ms.
A forest or a lake can have thousands of vertices and hundreds of dents, and each ear test still reads every one of them. When a polygon has more than 32 dents, the engine sorts them into buckets along the longer side of their bounding box, about two dents per bucket. An ear test looks only at the buckets that its triangle spans. As dents turn convex and leave, the index is rebuilt once half of it is gone.
Points scanned fall from 181 million to 101 million, almost all of it on the large polygons: the polygons with 257 vertices or more go from 103 to 57 ms. Total: 697 ms .
The loop in the dent test exits at the first dent inside the triangle. Most of the time there is none: the test reads all the dents and says yes. An early exit then buys nothing, and the three comparisons per point are branches the CPU has to predict. The engine first runs a pass that only counts dents inside the triangle, with no branches at all:
The smallest of the three determinants is non-negative exactly when the point is inside the closed triangle. Only when the count is not zero does the exact loop from before run, to rule out dents that sit on a corner. The bucket version does the same with a bounding-box test, 64 points at a time into a bit mask. The total falls to 519 ms , and the middle sizes gain the most: polygons with 33 to 256 vertices go from 327 to 216 ms.
When the count is not zero, the exact loop reads all the dents again, although the first pass has already seen which ones were inside. The bucket version keeps that in its bit mask. The short list, up to 32 dents, can do the same: the first pass sets one bit per hit instead of counting, and the exact test looks only at those dents:
Points read fall from 128 million to 120 million. This is the last step, and it is the code of earstrip as published: 489 ms , 6.0 times less than Delaunay on the same polygons.
Meisters' theorem is about simple polygons. Map data is rounded to a tile grid, and rounding can break a simple polygon. Here is the outline of Warszawa Śródmieście , a railway station less than a kilometre from the blocks above, rounded to grids of different size. The orange rings mark vertices that land on the same point as their neighbour:
At 14 bits per tile side, the grid our map files use, a grid step is 18 cm. Even there 31 of the 154 vertices merge with a neighbour, because mappers often place points a few centimetres apart, and the outline survives. At 12 bits nearly half of the vertices merge, and the clipper still cuts it. At 11 bits the rounded outline touches itself in a way that leaves no ear at all, and at 10 bits it happens to work again.
When the clipper walks all the way around the boundary without finding an ear, it drops the corners that have no area and walks once more. If that fails too, it gives up, and the engine triangulates that polygon with the Delaunay code, which still exists for this. In the Masovian data 76 polygons end up there. They come from a map built before the last change on the other end: our map generator now rounds every polygon to the final grid with GEOS's snap rounding and checks that ear clipping can cut it. In a fresh build of the Masovian map that repaired 273 polygons, and ear clipping can cut every polygon in the file.
Delaunay has one more job. Every hole needs its own bridge, and finding one scans the whole boundary, so a polygon with thousands of holes pays for thousands of scans. Our world map has a polygon with 11,675 holes: ear clipping takes 606 ms on it, Delaunay 17 ms. The engine now sends every polygon with 128 holes or more to Delaunay. In the Masovian data that is two polygons.
The library keeps both of these fallbacks inside. earstrip covers a polygon with a constrained Delaunay triangulation of its ring edges when the ears run out, when the triangles they leave cover the wrong area, and when it has more than 128 rings; run() in C++ and lastStatus() in JavaScript say which way a polygon went. On the 56,472 polygons of our world map tiles, with up to 11,675 holes in one, earstrip takes 459 ms and earcut.hpp 2,892 ms. On the zoom 13 polygons that the ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles differ from an even-odd fill of the rings on 31% of the pixels on average, earstrip's on 0.15%.
Before the new clipper went into the app, I compared it with earcut , the ear clipper behind MapLibre and Mapbox GL, in its C++ version earcut.hpp 3.2.4. Natively the two are close, and that could have been the end of it. But we are working on a web renderer that runs the same C++ engine compiled to WebAssembly, so I went further and compared the browser side too: both clippers compiled to WebAssembly, and earcut.js 3.2.4, the JavaScript original that web maps run today. For that I took the clipper out of the engine into earstrip. On all 5.8 million polygons of our test sets it writes exactly the engine's strips, and its repository has these polygons and the code behind every number in this section. Its native benchmark is the one behind the chart above, and the native row below is the last step run against earcut.hpp. Every WebAssembly build gives exactly the same triangles as its native version on all 4.4 million polygons of zoom levels 13 and 9. Milliseconds for the 3.74 million polygons of zoom 13, best of 7, one thread, V8 in Node and JavaScriptCore in Bun:
Natively earcut.hpp is 14% slower than earstrip. Compiled to WebAssembly and run in V8, earstrip loses 23% and earcut.hpp loses 67%, almost all of it in its main loop that searches for ears. It isn't the allocator: builds with mimalloc and emmalloc give the same time. I haven't dug further. In V8, earcut.hpp in WebAssembly ends up only 19% faster than plain earcut.js, and 10% once each polygon is a separate call from JavaScript.
The package rows are what a web page gets, and the earcut column there is earcut.js. The call that replaces earcut takes the coordinates as JavaScript numbers and returns a new array of triangle indices every time: 1.4 times as fast as earcut.js in V8 and 1.6 times in JavaScriptCore. About half of what it loses against the loop inside the module goes into copying the coordinates in and turning the strips into a list, the rest into calling into WebAssembly once per polygon. The direct calls skip all of that: the polygons go straight into the module's memory and come back as one index buffer of strips for WebGL 2 or WebGPU, 1.7 and 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js.
Some of the ideas above are in earcut too. It also relies on the fact that only a dent can block an ear, but it checks that last, for every vertex that passes the bounding box and triangle tests, instead of keeping a list of dents. Above 80 vertices it links them in z-order and scans only the stretch of that curve the triangle's bounding box covers, which does the job of the buckets. What it doesn't have are the shortcut for convex polygons, the strips and the count without branches: it writes three indices per triangle and stops at the first point inside.
earstrip is on GitHub and npm , with the polygons from this post and the code to time it against earcut on your own machine.

title: Sweden orders four Bofors naval gun systems from BAE Systems
body:
BAE Systems has secured a contract from the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) to deliver four Bofors 57Mk3 naval gun systems and associated 57mm 3P programmable ammunition for Sweden’s naval defense requirements.
The contract covers the delivery of the gun systems and Bofors 57mm 3P ammunition, which is designed to engage different types of targets using programmable fuzing and pre-fragmented projectiles.
The Bofors 57Mk3 is a multirole naval gun designed for air defense, anti-surface warfare and naval fire support. Its capabilities allow it to engage aerial threats, including aircraft, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), as well as surface targets.
The system fires 57mm ammunition and combines a high rate of fire with the ability to switch between different types of ammunition according to the target and mission. This enables a single gun system to support several naval combat roles.
The combination of the Bofors 57Mk3 and 3P ammunition is intended to provide the Swedish Navy with a weapon system capable of responding to a range of threats without requiring a separate gun for each target category.
“This contract reinforces our long-standing role as a trusted partner to the Swedish armed forces and FMV, and our commitment to supporting the Swedish Navy with world-class capability,” said Stefan Löfström , marketing and sales director at BAE Systems Bofors.
“It demonstrates Sweden’s absolute confidence in the Bofors 57Mk3 and its advanced 3P ammunition as key capabilities for Sweden's maritime defence,” he added.
The 57Mk3 is the latest version of the system, incorporating digital fire-control capabilities and programmable ammunition to support engagements against multiple target types.
The contract adds to the Swedish Navy’s use of domestically developed Bofors naval weapon technology. The delivery schedule and the specific vessels intended to receive the four gun systems were not detailed in the contract announcement.

title: Daily Insight for CEOs: Preparing Leaders for 2027
body: By Ernest De-Graft Egyir Insight. The success of the organisation’s 2027 strategy will depend partly on whether its leaders have the skills, judgment, and capacity to execute it. CEOs must therefore assess leadership readiness before the new year begins. This means identifying capability gaps, preparing successors for critical positions, strengthening executive collaboration, and ensuring that managers can lead people through changing priorities and business demands. Key Strategies: Assess the leadership capabilities required to deliver the 2027 strategy. Identify development needs across the executive and management teams. Strengthen succession plans for critical leadership positions. Provide targeted coaching, mentoring, and practical development opportunities. Connect leadership performance expectations to strategic outcomes. CEO Leadership Actions. Review the readiness of leaders responsible for the organization’s most important strategic priorities. Identify critical roles where succession or capability gaps create significant risk. Agree on specific leadership development actions before the end of 2026. Actionable Tip. Ask each executive: “What leadership capability must you strengthen to deliver your 2027 commitments, and what will you do to develop it?” Why This Matters? Strategy depends on people who can turn plans into results. Investing in leadership readiness strengthens execution, supports continuity, and reduces the risk of entering a new year with important ambitions but insufficient leadership capacity. About the Author Ernest De-Graft Egyir, CEO advisor, Thought Leader and Founding CEO of Chief Executives Network Ghana, convenes the Ghana CEO Summit and served on Ghana’s Economic Dialogue Planning Committee.

title: Future travel starts now: 2026 JETOUR Global Technology Experience Day kicks off
body: The 2026 JETOUR Global Technology Experience Day officially opened on Tuesday, October 20 in Wuhu, Anhui Province. The group’s Global Innovation Conference, the flagship launch event, was held in the morning at the R&D Center, bringing together more than 2,000 international guests, media representatives, and users to explore key technological achievements, the product lineup, and future plans for intelligent mobility. Technology in full view: A vision of the future At the conference, Yin Tongyue, Chairman of Chery Automobile Co., Ltd. reflected on more than 30 years of innovation at the company and shared his outlook on future industry trends. “With AI, we are redefining not only the automobile, but also the enterprise and the entire industrial ecosystem. In the future, cars will become smarter companions that understand you better, providing a space for greater possibilities in intelligent mobility,” he said. Gao Xinhua, chief technology oficer, delivered a keynote speech on the group’s technological foundations for the intelligent era. “Chery’s vision for technology can be summed up in one sentence: creating greater value for human freedom,” Yin stated. The conference showcased the group’s cutting-edge technology portfolio, from the Sky Dome supercomputing center and Star Sea big data platform to V2G vehicle-to-grid technology and integrated solar-storage-charging solutions. It also highlighted advances in AI foundation models and world models, alongside the real-world application of physical AI in areas such as Robotaxi and AiMOGA Robotics. Together, these innovations contribute to an intelligent technology ecosystem spanning mobility, energy, and everyday life – powered by AI, enabled by data and coordinated across multiple domains. Meanwhile, the R&D Center hosted technology exhibitions and hands-on experience zones, with access arranged in phases for different groups, giving participants the opportunity to engage directly with cutting-edge technologies. When technology meets travel, experience comes first Within this landscape of innovation, JETOUR focuses on user needs, translating its technological foundations into tangible travel experiences. JETOUR’s two product series address diverse travel needs, balancing urban commuting and outdoor exploration. The T Series combines intelligent urban comfort with serious off-road capabilities, while the entire lineup features C-DM Super Hybrid technology, easing range anxiety on long journeys. The XWD fully automatic intelligent 4WD, with its ‘7+X’ one-touch intelligent off-road mode, makes challenging conditions such as water crossings, gravel, and steep slopes easier to tackle. Smart cockpit and intelligent driving technologies make journeys more comfortable and reassuring. The G Series is built on GAIA, a new-generation all-terrain intelligent architecture designed for premium models. It integrates a high-efficiency hybrid system with a dedicated off-road chassis. Combined with intelligent interaction and a premium cabin, it unites exceptional off-road capabilities with luxury comfort. Bringing the beach market to life: time to set off That evening, JETOUR hosted an immersive beach camping welcome dinner along the Yangtze River. The built-in high-output V2L technology in JETOUR vehicles supplied power throughout the entire market to enable outdoor cooking and entertainment, weaving technology into everyday travel experiences. JETOUR executives joined international guests to officially kick off the Experience Day’s test-drive program. Technology is meant not only for the showroom, but for the road. From technology showcases and product experiences to the camping fair and real-world test drives, the 2026 JETOUR Global Technology Experience Day connects innovation with real travel scenarios. On October 21, international guests will head deep into the rugged mountain terrain of Moganshan to test JETOUR models across varied road conditions and experience firsthand how technology unlocks new possibilities for travel of travel.

title: Why some countries rich and others poor: Books by Zitelmann and Mises presented in Ukraine
body:
On Wednesday, October 28, at 12.00, the press center of the Interfax-Ukraine news agency (8/5a Reitarska Street) will host a press conference entitled "Why some countries rich and others poor: Books by Zitelmann and Mises presented in Ukraine."

Four books by authors Rainer Zitelmann and Ludwig von Mises translated into Ukrainian will be presented; the publications are dedicated to economic freedom, causes of wealth and poverty, the impact of bureaucracy on business, and the role of market reforms in national development.

Participants include
co-founder of Nova Poshta and the International Liberty Institute (ILI) Volodymyr Popereshnyuk;
Candidate of Economic Sciences, expert of the International Liberty Institute (ILI) Dmytro Dusheyko;
Director of the International Liberty Institute Mykhailo Kamchatny.

The event will be streamed on the Interfax-Ukraine YouTube channel. Admission requires registration on the spot with press ID cards.

title: U-17 WWC: ‘We are the Brazilians of Africa’ – Ghana coach after draw with South Americans
body: Ghana coach Joe Nana Adarkwa has described his side as the “Brazilians of Africa” after coming from behind to secure a point against the South Americans at the ongoing U-17 Women’s World Cup. The Black Maidens, who suffered a 3-0 defeat to Norway in their opener, were staring defeat in the face against Brazil, which could have ended their campaign. But Priscilla Mensah struck five minutes from time to deny the South Americans victory as both sides settled for a 3-3 draw. “We all know how Brazilians play, but we are the Brazilians of Africa,” Adarkwa told FIFA after the match. “We are like them, but Brazil are up there. We are getting stronger and we will get there. I’m happy that our girls responded to our two training sessions. We did some scoring in training, and they applied that.” “We are in one of the toughest groups, but I’m proud of my girls. After equalising, we had so many chances, but they are young, they are learning, so we have a lot to do with the girls. But I’m happy for them.” Ghana sit bottom of Group C and must win their final group game, while also hoping other results go their way, to stand a chance of progressing to the next round. The Maidens face Canada on Saturday, with their opponents sitting second in the group after a 3-2 victory over Norway.

title: Court begins hearing case to ban opposition parties in Georgia: first-day developments
body: On 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court in Batumi began hearing on the merits a lawsuit brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which seeks to ban five opposition parties: the United National Movement , the Coalition for Change , Lelo – Strong Georgia , Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists . Below are the main events and statements from the first day of hearings. The court rejected all the opposition’s motions. The session ended at 19:00. The hearings continue today, 22 October, and will also take place on 23 October. The court has until 24 June 2027 to deliver its ruling. Four of the seven judges must vote in favour for the court to uphold the claim. Opening of the hearing ● The court hearing began at 12:00. Georgian Dream is represented in court by MPs Archil Gorduladze, Giorgi Kakhiani, Tengiz Sharmanashvili and Tornike Cheishvili. Georgia’s party ban: Court to begin hearing government case against opposition on 21 October Four of the five parties plan to defend themselves in court. Some opposition groups are planning protests in Batumi and Tbilisi. ● The United National Movement was represented by Ana Tsitlidze, Khatia Dekanoidze and lawyer Zaza Bibilashvili; the Coalition for Change by Nika Gvaramia; Lelo by Badri Japaridze, Giorgi Sioridze and lawyers; and Gakharia for Georgia by Berdia Sichinava. ● The Federalists did not attend the hearing, as the party believes there is no point in taking part in the proceedings. ● Two leaders of the Coalition for Change, Nika Melia and Elene Khoshtaria , are following the proceedings from prison. Melia was arrested for failing to appear before a parliamentary commission whose findings now form the main basis of the lawsuit seeking to ban the parties. ● Only journalists from Georgia’s Public Broadcaster were allowed to bring cameras into the courtroom. Other media outlets followed the hearing on the court’s YouTube channel. Until now, the Constitutional Court had been the only court exempt from the ban on filming that applies in courts of general jurisdiction. Calls for judges to recuse themselves ● The hearing began with a motion to disqualify the judges. Ana Tsitlidze, leader of the United National Movement, called for all seven members of the court’s plenary session to recuse themselves. She read out each judge’s biography and argued that the panel could not act freely and fairly. ● Tsitlidze described the proposed ban on the parties as “a decision taken by the Kremlin against Georgia’s sovereignty and freedom”. Presiding judge Revaz Nadaraya responded: “Make your political assessments elsewhere. This is a courtroom, where rules, procedures and the law apply. You are free to make assessments, but somewhere else.” ● Tsitlidze then called Nadaraya himself a member of the “judicial clan”. Nadaraya replied: “You must present your position with legal justification. When you use such insulting language, the court will not accept it. I will have to issue a warning and may have to order you to leave the courtroom.” Tsitlidze then replaced the word “clan” with other terms. ● Tsitlidze also called judge Eva Gotsiridze a “member of the clan”. Regarding judge Vasil Roinishvili, she highlighted the fact that he had served as deputy chief prosecutor in 2008–09, during the United National Movement’s time in power. ● Lelo also called for three judges to recuse themselves. The Coalition for Change joined its motion. Gakharia for Georgia did not state its position. ● The plenary session rejected all the motions for recusal. Nadaraya explained that a judge’s biography or past career, if someone dislikes it, does not constitute legal grounds for disqualification. He also recalled that the plenary session had rejected a request for judge Manana Kobakhidze to recuse herself, describing that decision as “a high-standard ruling”. On 9 October, the plenary session refused to let Kobakhidze, one of the founders of Georgian Dream, recuse herself. She subsequently left the court. “One party, one proceeding” ● The court also rejected a motion by Gakharia for Georgia to hear its case separately from those against the other four parties. The party’s representative, Berdia Sichinava, called for the principle of “one political party — one proceeding” to be upheld. The party put forward two arguments, both of which Sichinava outlined at a briefing on 20 October, the day before the hearing. First, the court must assess each party’s constitutionality individually. Sichinava called this “a minimum legal obligation and standard” that the court should meet, at least formally. Second, Gakharia for Georgia is the only opposition party that took up its seats in parliament rather than surrendering its mandates. Sichinava argued that including it in the lawsuit undermines Georgian Dream’s narrative that it seeks to ban only so-called “boycott parties” that reject the authorities’ legitimacy. He also described the ruling party’s approach as unconstitutional. Nadaraya explained that the court would base its decision on each defendant solely on the facts relating to that party. He added that the law would not allow the court to issue an adverse ruling if the evidence proved insufficient. Witnesses: from Saakashvili to Ivanishvili ● The United National Movement asked the court to summon the party’s founder, Georgia’s third president Mikheil Saakashvili , and former party chairman Levan Khabeishvili as witnesses. The court rejected the motion. ● The United National Movement also sought to summon Bidzina Ivanishvili , the founder and honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, along with current and former senior officials who had previously served under the United National Movement government. Tsitlidze argued that if the court wanted to ban the party for “systemic crime”, these people should answer questions about whether the alleged crimes were indeed systemic. Nadaraya replied: “The plenary session has not seen a specific connection to the case or the lawsuit, or any indication of what exactly these witnesses would confirm.” ● The court ordered Khatia Dekanoidze to leave the courtroom while she was arguing in favour of summoning Ivanishvili. She said Ivanishvili ran the country single-handedly and was steering Georgia closer to Russia. Nadaraya warned her several times, saying she was making political statements rather than explaining the legal grounds for calling Ivanishvili as a witness. The judge then instructed a court usher to remove Dekanoidze from the courtroom. The Tsulukiani commission’s findings: the main basis for the lawsuit ● The second half of the day focused on the findings of a parliamentary commission led by Tea Tsulukiani . Parliament established the commission on 5 February 2025 to investigate the United National Movement’s time in power from 2003 to 2012. The opposition considers the commission, like parliament itself, illegitimate. Several opposition leaders have been arrested for failing to appear before it. Georgian Dream filed its lawsuit on the basis of the commission’s findings, which also form part of the case documents. ● The Coalition for Change asked the court to exclude the commission’s findings from the evidence. Nika Gvaramia said the findings underpinned 95% of the lawsuit. He argued that the commission itself had been established in breach of the Constitution, which requires the opposition to make up half its membership. In his view, the commission could not legally operate without meeting this requirement. ● Gvaramia and Nadaraya clashed while he presented the motion. Nadaraya reprimanded Gvaramia for making political assessments. ● Georgian Dream representative Archil Gorduladze argued that the commission had been established lawfully because all parliamentary groups had the opportunity to join it. “The defendant’s problem lies with the facts cited in the findings, not with the content of the findings themselves, which cover all those facts,” he said. ● After several hours of debate, the plenary session refused to exclude Tsulukiani’s commission findings from the evidence. What happened outside the courthouse ● A protest took place outside the courthouse while the hearing was under way. Police deployed around the perimeter of the building. ● Nineteen non-governmental organisations issued a joint statement describing the hearing as a particularly grave stage in Georgia’s autocratisation. They also noted that, according to the Central Election Commission’s official results, the parties Georgian Dream wants to ban received 784,830 votes in the 2024 parliamentary election — almost 38% of the total. ● German Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Kathrin Deschauer said in Berlin: “This is another step in this trend, which is increasingly distancing Georgia from the European Union and weakening domestic democracy.” She added that Germany would convey its concerns to the Georgian side. ● The European liberal party ALDE called on the European Union to impose tougher sanctions on those responsible within Georgian Dream. ● Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili , released a video statement saying: “Today is a shameful day for Georgia and Georgian statehood.” She also criticised Gakharia for Georgia for seeking a separate hearing. According to Zourabichvili, the party was “somehow trying to ingratiate itself and present itself as saying: ‘Look, I’m good, I’m a good slave, and I’ll serve you even more.’” ● Georgian Dream MP Giga Parulava advised Zourabichvili to improve her vocabulary and “come down to earth”. Reactions after the hearing ● Georgian Dream representative Tengiz Sharmanashvili said the discussion was beginning to focus on legal issues and that he felt more optimistic. ● Archil Gorduladze said the opposition’s motions to disqualify the judges were an attempt to turn the proceedings into a political debate. “We will not allow you to politicise this case,” judges also told the opposition several times yesterday. ● Ana Tsitlidze said the first day had exposed the proceedings as a formality and that the decision had already been made. Giorgi Sioridze, representing Lelo, said the judges appeared “disorganised” and that their refusal seemed “helpless”. Nika Gvaramia said the opposition needed the allegations to be set out individually, as it could not respond to a “collective phantom”. Ban on the opposition in Georgia

title: Poland paused a military aid package over Lviv’s vote honoring WWII nationalists, Ukrainian source says. Polish ministry denies it
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Poland has paused the delivery of a large military aid package to Ukraine after a Lviv regional council honored the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a WWII nationalist force, a source in the Ukrainian government told European Pravda on 21 October. A Polish Defense Ministry spokesperson told Fakt the report was untrue, though he told WP he knew nothing about a possible delay in shipment. If confirmed, the freeze would carry a history dispute into Poland’s military aid. The row flared in May, when Kyiv named a special forces unit after the UPA, and in June Poland’s president stripped Zelenskyy of Poland’s highest honor. Even so, Ukraine’s ambassador said in August that Polish military aid was still flowing. A vote and a disputed freeze The Lviv Oblast Council voted on 20 October to name 2027 the year of the UPA, its commander Roman Shukhevych, and nationalist activist Oleh Olzhych. The UPA fought Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, but Poland holds it responsible for mass killings of Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia in 1943–1944. The resolution disappeared from the council’s website late that evening, RMF24 reported . The source blamed what it called the councilors’ irresponsible actions, saying the vote came as Poland prepared the shipment and that work through closed channels is underway. The ministry spokesperson, Janusz Sejmej, called the report untrue. Asked whether it could reflect a delay in shipment, he said he knew nothing about that. Explore further Progress on a sore point for Ukraine and Poland: remains of over 40 Ukrainians killed by Polish WWII units found in Łasków Polish officials push back On 20 October, Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote that Ukraine’s authorities must distance themselves from the council’s position. The next morning, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the vote unwise and harmful above all to Ukraine. He said he had warned Zelenskyy earlier that such gestures hinder Ukraine’s friends, though the president was not responsible for this vote. At such moments, Tusk said, Russians always rub their hands. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski then requested that councilor Sviatoslav Sheremeta, who proposed the resolution, be added to Poland’s list of unwanted persons. That afternoon, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the decision had been made. Sheremeta is barred from the Schengen zone until 2031, RMF24 reported. Poland had already barred him once, in 2017, the outlet said . Kyiv asks for restraint Earlier on 21 October, before the ban, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry called the vote counterproductive in a reply to journalists and urged Warsaw to avoid abrupt steps. Zelenskyy’s closest aides had also promised the resolution would not take effect, Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki told TVN24. title: China, Nigeria Target Billion-Dollar Opportunities As Filmmakers Push Co-production, Market Access
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja Nigeria and China are seeking to turn their growing cultural relationship into a stronger commercial partnership in film, with filmmakers from both countries exploring co-production, technology transfer and distribution opportunities that could open up two major audiences to each other’s creative industries. The push gained momentum at the Chinese Film Screening in Nigeria 2026 in Abuja, where industry stakeholders identified the combination of Nigeria’s storytelling strength and China’s cinema infrastructure, capital and distribution expertise as a potential pathway to expanding the global reach of their productions. The discussions also highlighted a major challenge facing the proposed partnership: translating cultural exchanges and diplomatic goodwill into concrete business arrangements that enable filmmakers to secure investment, distribute their works across borders and earn sustainable returns. The Director of the China Cultural Centre in Nigeria, Mr Yang Jianxing, said film remained an important bridge for strengthening understanding between the two countries, whose creative industries offered considerable scope for collaboration. “China and Nigeria share a deep-rooted traditional friendship and close people-to-people exchanges, and film serves as an important bridge for fostering mutual understanding between our peoples,” he said. Jianxing said cooperation had expanded through reciprocal film screenings, professional exchanges, festivals and the distribution of productions across national borders. The partnership involving the Chinese Embassy, the China Cultural Centre and StarTimes Nigeria has helped bring Chinese film and television productions to Nigerian audiences through initiatives including a month-long showcase, the Chinese Women’s Film Festival and screenings of works dubbed or subtitled in local languages, including Hausa. “StarTimes has successfully brought outstanding Chinese productions and knowledge series to a broader audience,” he said. He added that Nigerian films had also reached mainstream Chinese digital media platforms, exposing audiences there to Nigerian stories, characters and experiences. The commercial potential of the relationship was underscored by Fidelis Duker, founder of the Abuja International Film Festival, who said discussions with the Chinese delegation had focused on production, distribution and co-production opportunities, including engagements with Nigerian film institutions and plans to meet distributors and cinema operators in Lagos. Duker argued that the population sizes of the two countries presented an opportunity to expand the reach of their film industries, provided that investment, technology and distribution networks were developed to support the exchange of content. “What we found out today, or what we’ve known over the years, is that China has technology,” he said, adding that the Chinese delegation had told participants that China sold 1.3 billion cinema tickets in the previous year. China’s film market provides an indication of the scale of the opportunity. According to figures released by the China Film Administration, the country generated ¥51.832 billion in box-office revenue in 2025, while cinema attendance reached 1.238 billion. Domestic productions accounted for nearly 80 per cent of total box-office receipts, and the country ended the year with 93,187 cinema screens. The figures illustrate the scale of China’s production and exhibition ecosystem, offering Nigerian filmmakers potential access to a market where locally produced content commands a substantial share of cinema revenue. For Nigeria, the opportunity extends beyond exporting completed films. Collaboration could also create avenues for joint productions, technical training, improved post-production capacity and the development of distribution arrangements that give Nigerian stories a wider international audience. Duker said the combination of Nigerian creativity and Chinese industrial capacity could be particularly valuable to both sides. “When you marry Nigerian narrative vitality with China’s technical infrastructure, capital, and unparalleled distribution expertise, you can imagine the possibilities,” he said. The Chinese delegation, led by the Chairman of Huaxia Film Distribution Company Limited, Bai Yimin, also emphasised the contribution of cinema to bilateral relations. Bai said cooperation between the countries had produced results through reciprocal film festivals, professional exchanges, and the translation and broadcasting of films. “In recent years, cooperation in the film industry has become a brilliant chapter in China-Nigerian cultural and people-to-people exchanges,” he said. He added that the Chinese Embassy and the China Cultural Centre would continue to support initiatives using cinema to connect audiences and strengthen relations between the two countries. The screening coincided with the 23rd Abuja International Film Festival, which received 10 Chinese film entries this year, five of which were nominated for awards. Duker said Chinese films had featured in 22 of the festival’s 23 editions, reflecting a longstanding relationship between the event and China’s film industry. He also credited StarTimes with supporting the festival over the years, saying the relationship had contributed to its growth. Three films were screened at the event: The Shadow’s Edge, Blades of the Guardians: Wind Rises in the Desert and The Lychee Road. The screening comes against the backdrop of broader efforts to deepen Nigeria-China cooperation in the creative sector. In August 2026, the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) and China Movie Channel signed a strategic cooperation agreement aimed at promoting film co-production, technology transfer, professional training and wider distribution of creative content. The agreement, announced at the China-Nigeria Film and Literature Symposium in Abuja, signalled an interest in moving cultural relations beyond the exchange of finished productions towards more structured industry collaboration. The latest engagements at the film festival could build on that momentum by bringing filmmakers, distributors, cinema operators and production institutions into discussions about the practical requirements of cross-border business. However, access to a large audience does not automatically translate into commercial success. Nigerian and Chinese productions seeking to enter each other’s markets will need effective distribution partners, appropriate subtitling and dubbing, marketing support, clear licensing arrangements and investment structures that protect the interests of participating filmmakers. Differences in audience preferences, language, production practices and market regulations will also need to be addressed if joint projects are to attract viewers and generate revenue. For Nigeria, the immediate priority is to ensure that its creative talent benefits commercially from international partnerships rather than limiting participation to festival appearances and cultural showcases. For China, deeper engagement with Nollywood offers an avenue to broaden the international reach of its productions while building relationships with one of Africa’s most prominent film industries. The success of the partnership will ultimately depend on whether the two countries can turn screenings and professional exchanges into financed co-productions, regular content distribution and lasting commercial relationships. With both sides signalling interest in closer collaboration, the emerging challenge is to build an industry-to-industry framework capable of converting shared cultural interests and large populations into tangible opportunities for filmmakers, distributors and audiences.

title: Finnish PM Orpo arrives in Kyiv
body:
The Finnish government said this in a press release , Ukrinform reports.
In the Ukrainian capital, Orpo will meet with representatives of Ukraine's political leadership. The main purpose of the visit is to show Finland's strong support for Ukraine as the war of aggression continues and the country prepares for the winter.
"Prime Minister Orpo will also show support for the reforms needed for Ukraine's EU membership, which are important not only for Ukraine's EU integration but also for its citizens, businesses and economic recovery," the statement said.
Finland's support for Ukraine since the start of the war of aggression amounts to nearly EUR 5 billion, of which EUR 3.6 billion has been in the form of defense materiel assistance. Relative to the size of its economy, Finland is one of Ukraine's strongest supporters.
A Ukrainian-Finnish business forum will also be held in connection with the visit, with representatives of more than ten Finnish companies and other actors in attendance.
Orpo last visited Ukraine in May 2025, having previously visited in August 2023.
On October 20, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky visited Norway, where he met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere and Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
At a joint press conference with Zelensky, Stubb said that talks in Oslo between Ukraine, the United States, and European partners had made progress in the peace process on two levels: the overall vision and the short-term outlook.
Photo: Finnish government's press service

title: Europe Weighs Naming Envoy to Negotiate With Putin on Ukraine
body:
European leaders are weighing who could negotiate with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Ukraine’s future, but the Kremlin has already floated its preferred candidate: former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder, a longtime Putin ally whose ties to Moscow have made him a divisive figure in Germany.
The debate comes as US President Donald Trump pursues direct engagement with Putin, raising fears in European capitals that Washington and Moscow could shape a peace deal while leaving Ukraine’s European allies on the sidelines.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia this week to discuss a possible three-way summit involving Trump, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Putin in an effort to advance a ceasefire. The proposal has intensified pressure on Europe to establish its own channel to the Kremlin.
“President Putin disregards the European Union as an authority,” Czech President Petr Pavel said Tuesday in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters’ Network.
Pavel argued that European leaders should select “a person or a group of people who would speak for Europe,” even if they did not formally represent the EU or NATO.
The challenge is finding someone who can command enough political weight to influence negotiations without compromising Europe’s position or Ukraine’s interests.
“Much as it sticks in the craw, I do think a channel of some kind to Putin would be a good thing to have,” David Lidington, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London, told Politico .
He said such a channel might achieve little immediately but could prove useful if an opportunity for meaningful negotiations emerged.
Stubb has attracted attention because of his close relationship with Trump and Finland’s experience dealing with Russia. The two countries share a roughly 1,300-kilometer border.
“Stubb is of interest because of Finnish knowledge of and traditional dialogue with Russia,” one EU diplomat told Politico, pointing to Finland’s understanding of the security challenges involved in dealing with Moscow.
Another diplomat described Stubb as the only figure to have demonstrated high-level political leadership on the issue so far, suggesting he could represent Europe at a future peace summit.
Stubb joined Zelensky and Witkoff in Oslo on Oct. 20 for discussions ahead of the US envoy’s trip to Russia. Bjorn Seibert, a senior aide to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, also attended.
Diplomats disagree over whether Europe should appoint a single national leader or rely on its own institutions. Some argue that the EU must be represented directly, rather than leaving negotiations to a smaller group of powerful countries such as Germany, France and the United Kingdom.
“We cannot show up with two or three people all speaking on behalf of the EU,” one diplomat told Politico, arguing that the choice should be based on effectiveness rather than institutional rivalries.
Some European leaders have raised the possibility of Costa opening direct talks with Putin.
According to a diplomat cited by Politico, leaders asked Costa at a summit in Brussels last week whether he should speak to the Russian president. Costa reportedly declined for now.
The diplomat argued that refusing to establish direct communication with Moscow risked weakening Europe’s position in negotiations.
Costa has previously opened a channel to the Kremlin through his office. Von der Leyen and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are also potential representatives, although some diplomats question whether they could act as intermediaries given their strong support for Ukraine.
Former UK Cabinet Office minister David Lidington, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, said maintaining a channel to Putin could prove useful even if it produced no immediate breakthrough.
The European Commission has said the EU is already involved in preparations for potential peace talks. Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said discussions in Oslo had explored the possibility of negotiations involving Ukraine and Russia at the same table, with territory, security and Ukraine’s post-war prosperity among the issues discussed.
Putin said in May that he would “personally” prefer Schroeder, who served as German chancellor from 1998 to 2005, to help restart dialogue between Russia and Europe.
The proposal was met with skepticism in Berlin. German government sources told AFP that officials had “taken note” of Putin’s comments but viewed them as part of “a series of bogus offers” from Moscow.
Schroeder has remained close to Putin since leaving office and held senior positions linked to Russian energy interests, including roles involving the Nord Stream gas pipelines and Russian oil company Rosneft.
He gave up his Rosneft board position in 2022 but has never publicly condemned Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
His potential appointment has divided Germany’s Social Democratic Party, which Schroeder belongs to.
Michael Roth, a former SPD lawmaker who chaired the Bundestag’s foreign affairs committee, told Tagesspiegel that a mediator “cannot be Putin’s buddy.”
Any candidate must first be acceptable to Ukraine, Roth said. “Neither Moscow nor we can decide that on Kyiv’s behalf.”
Other SPD politicians have been more open to the proposal. The party’s foreign affairs spokesman in parliament, Adis Ahmetovic, told Der Spiegel that it should be “carefully considered” with European partners.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on May 11 that Russia should not influence the EU’s choice of negotiator.
“If we give the right to Russia to appoint a negotiator on our behalf, that would not be very wise,” she said .
Kallas described Schroeder as a “high-level lobbyist for Russian state-owned companies,” arguing that Putin wanted someone who would effectively be “sitting on both sides of the table.”
She also warned that Russia was seeking to expand its influence in Europe, citing Russian participation in sports organizations and at the Venice Biennale.
“Our adversaries are not sleeping,” Kallas said.
For now, Europe has no agreed negotiator and no unified position on when direct talks should begin.

title: Finland to Invest in Anti-Personnel Mines After Ottawa Convention Withdrawal
body:
In January 2026, Finland withdrew from the Ottawa Convention, the anti-personnel landmine (APL) ban it signed in 2012, alongside Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, fearful of Russia’s potential aggression.
According to Finnish outlet “Ruotuväki,” Finland is about to take the next step – to reintroduce an APL stockpile in readiness to protect its 1,300-kilometer (800-mile) border with Russia .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Colonel Riku Mikkonen, inspector of the Finnish Engineering Corps, said the Finnish Defense Forces will allocate €100 million ($112 million) for domestic production of the mines.
The outlet said Finnish companies have the production capacity and capability to meet the requirement, which is said to be around 1 million mines, about the same quantity it held before signing the convention.
Mikkonen said the aim was to begin production of the mines in 2028.
“We have a materiel project underway that is currently in the preparation and market survey phase. At the same time, we are defining the technical requirements for the mines,” he said.
It will take several years to replenish the stockpile, and production is slated to start in 2028.
The decision to purchase the mines from Finnish producers will not only support domestic industry and ensure supply security, but also serve a more prosaic purpose: Most other European countries are signatories to the APL treaty, so their industry is precluded from manufacturing mines.
According to Mikkonen, Finnish companies already have designs for the types of mines Finland wants and the raw materials, machinery, and production lines needed.
However, production will not begin until all preparations are complete.
“We want to ensure that all background work and preparations are carried out properly,” he said.
He also indicated that multiple suppliers will be necessary to manufacture mine bodies, supply fuses and explosive charges. The plan envisages two types of mines: modern pipe mines and pressure-activated APL.
Mikkonen said the country is aiming for simplicity.
“The product we are looking for at this stage is simple – easy to manufacture and easy to use,” he said.
He added that Finland is “also conducting research and development regarding more technically advanced models” that “may potentially be acquired in the next phase.”
This could include scatterable mines, directional fragmentation mines using tripwire, pressure or “proximity” initiation. A training program for the mines’ usage has already been included for the 2026 contingents of conscripts.
The article says that beyond the initial procurement, producers will be required to maintain their capabilities to address any changes in the security situation – several million mines have been laid by both sides in the war in Ukraine .
“We must ensure that companies have the capacity to rapidly produce more if the need arises,” Mikkonen said.
He also pointed out that since there is no current domestic APL industry, the program will take time to complete.
“In a sense, this has started from scratch in Finland. Everything takes time, even when we would like to get things done faster.”

title: Australia revels in big unveil of Ghost Shark payloads
body:
Australia’s Department of Defence has disclosed new details of the payloads being developed for its Anduril-built Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous underwater vehicle (XLAUV), including modules for logistics, sea mines and loitering munitions.
At the unveiling at Anduril’s production facility in Sydney on 19 October 2026, Minister of Defence Industry Pat Conroy said the Ghost Shark would be capable of carrying either twelve sea mines or Anduril Altius loitering munitions. A video released several days later showed the vehicle equipped with a dozen launch tubes designed to deploy the loitering munitions near the water’s surface.
Conroy described the Ghost Shark XLAUV programme as the fastest peacetime acquisition of a major platform for the Australian Defence Force (ADF), taking three years from concept to delivery. The first vehicle was also delivered a year ahead of schedule.
David Goodrich, Anduril Australia’s CEO, said the platform’s modular architecture would allow the Royal Australian Navy (RAN) to introduce new payloads and test missions more rapidly.
“We’re able to integrate new payloads, test missions and provide potent options to navy faster than the threats can evolve,” Goodrich said. He added that the approach would enable the RAN to deliver operational effects at scale and at a fraction of the cost of relying solely on traditional surface and subsurface assets, all without putting sailors in harm’s way.
Goodrich also said, “Ghost Shark’s large payload bays also support the deployment of heavyweight and lightweight torpedoes, including modern, unmanned, cost-effective, undersea effectors, and the vehicle will be capable of engaging threats independently.”
The announcement comes as Australia, the UK and USA advance autonomous systems and other technologies under AUKUS Pillar II. The partners have identified the development of payloads and sensors for autonomous vessels as an early flagship project, with the technologies potentially available to other partners.
Conroy indicated that the systems could be offered to existing and prospective AUKUS Pillar II partners, including Japan.
Separately, Conroy confirmed that Ocius Technology’s Bluebottle unmanned surface vessel (USV) would be equipped with a thin-line towed-array sonar for submarine detection. On 25 August 2026, Australia revealed contracts for ThayerMahan’s Outpost acoustic intelligence system and Thales Australia’s BlueSentry thin-line acoustic array.
The Australian uncrewed systems will deploy to southern California to participate in the US Navy’s (USN) Maritime Big Play Pacific exercise, which is intended to integrate mature robotic and autonomous systems into AUKUS coalition maritime operations.
According to the USN, the exercise will feature more than 40 technologies from government and industry, highlighting efforts to integrate uncrewed platforms and sensor systems into maritime operations.

Uganda Airlines to deploy Boeing 737-800 on four weekly Accra flights
body: Uganda Airlines will deploy a Boeing 737-800 on its new four-times-weekly service to Accra from October 27, expanding its West African presence and adding capacity to air links between Ghana and East Africa. The Entebbe-based carrier will operate the service through Lagos, Nigeria, using a Boeing 737-800. The four weekly frequencies will provide additional travel options for passengers moving between Accra and Uganda, including business travellers, tourists and people visiting family. The service also offers connections through Entebbe to destinations across the airline’s wider network, including Nairobi, London, Mumbai, and over 17 destinations in Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. Uganda Airlines operates a mixed fleet that includes Bombardier CRJ-900 regional jets, Boeing 737-800s, and Airbus A330-800neo wide-body aircraft. The Accra launch forms part of a wider push to strengthen connections between African markets. Ghana is a key commercial gateway in West Africa, while Entebbe can provide onward links to East Africa and beyond. More frequent connections could help businesses plan regional trips more flexibly, support tourism operators, and improve access to commercial opportunities on both sides of the continent. The route could also complement efforts to facilitate trade and investment under the African Continental Free Trade Area.

title: Rescuers extinguish all fires in Kyiv after Russian shelling, 1 killed, over 20 injured – interior minister
body:
In Kyiv, all fires caused by the massive enemy strike have been extinguished, and in the capital's Pechersky district, a part of an enemy missile stuck in the ground is being removed, reported Minister of Internal Affairs of Ukraine (MIA) Ivan Vyhivsky.
On his Telegram channel on Thursday, he informed that since night, more than 400 rescuers and police officers have been working to eliminate the consequences of the Russian shelling in Kyiv alone.
"In total, the occupiers attacked 12 regions of Ukraine and the capital. Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched on Kyiv. Unfortunately, one man was killed. Over 20 more people, including children, were injured," noted the head of the MIA.
According to him, as a result of the enemy shelling, residential buildings, an ambulance station, a hypermarket, a post office, and a monastery were damaged. "In the private sector, houses on several streets were mangled," he added.
The minister noted that rescuers and police officers worked in each district from the first minutes.
"All fires have already been extinguished, and at these minutes, cooling of structures and recording of crimes are underway. In the Pechersky district of the capital, police bomb technicians and a SES demining group are removing part of an enemy missile stuck in the ground," Vyhivsky emphasized.
The head of the MIA thanked every rescuer and police officer extinguishing fires, assisting victims, documenting the act of another Russian terror, and ensuring traffic flow.

title: Senate Rejects NMDPRA’s 2022, 2023 PMS Import Records Over Disparities With NNPC
body: The Senate has rejected records of Premium Motor Spirit importation presented by the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) for 2022 and 2023, over wide disparities between the figures and those presented by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited. The decision was taken by the Senate Committee on Public Accounts, which described the differences as unacceptable and suspicious and resolved to summon the heads of NMDPRA, NNPC and the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI). The disparities emerged during a hearing on queries raised in the NEITI Oil and Gas Industry Audit Report covering 2021 to 2023. Responding on behalf of the Authority Chief Executive of NMDPRA, Deputy Director Uzoamaka Ugwu-Ojobe insisted that the Authority’s records were credible, stating that 3.29 billion litres of PMS were imported in 2022 and 6.02 billion litres in 2023, against NNPC’s figures of 6.27 billion litres in 2022 and 3.88 billion litres in 2023. She described the gaps as slight and said reconciliation was ongoing, but the committee members faulted the claim. Senator Abdul Ningi, representing Bauchi Central, said a disparity of over 50 per cent could not be described as slight, calling it disturbing and suspicious. Senator Dayo Faduyile, Ondo South, said the figures left room to suspect foul play, while Senator Anietie Bassey, Akwa Ibom North East, insisted on a thorough investigation to prevent Nigerians from being shortchanged. Chairman of the Committee, Senator Hassan Dankwabo, Gombe North, noted that the defence was unacceptable and announced that the heads of the three agencies would be summoned for a tripartite meeting to reconcile the records or expose possible fraud. The post Senate Rejects NMDPRA’s 2022, 2023 PMS Import Records Over Disparities With NNPC appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Imam removed after campaigning for Tinubu at Bauchi mosque
body: Imam Dahiru Abubakar of a mosque in Madina quarters of Bauchi metropolis has been removed from his position for campaigning for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election. The imam was said to have been subtly campaigning for Tinubu’s reelection during preaching after every obligatory prayer. He was, however, suspended after he repeated the act following the early morning prayer (Subhi) on Sunday. “He would tell the congregation after prayer that Tinubu did not cause insecurity and he deserved to be reelected. FIBA recognises Mustapha Abdullahi as NBBF president Ex-CoS: I didn’t betray El-Rufai, he used my structure to win elections A committee was set up after he did the same thing last weekend and he was subsequently removed,” a source said. Abubakar told our correspondent that he had been telling the people in his preaching that President Tinubu was not the problem because the hardship and insecurity were caused by “end times phenomenon.” He said, “I have been preaching to the people to stop castigating President Tinubu for the insecurity and economic challenges. They prepared to vote for him and give him another mandate in 2027 to continue his mandate. “My preaching centred on telling people to embrace fear of God and stop blaming leaders for the insecurity, particularly President Tinubu, because only God’s intervention can stop the challenges with the power of prayers, and that didn’t go down well with the committee of the mosque. “My preaching priorities are fear of God and our day-to-day activities. I cited examples of what is happening, especially insecurity in African countries like Sudan, Chad, Mali and others facing crisis. I asked whether President Tinubu was responsible for their insecurity.” Confirming the incident, chairman of the mosque committee, Imam Abubakar Jibrin, said, “Our major challenge with him was not only his campaign for Tinubu but the way and manner he gathered many people in front of the mosque and sometimes entered the mosque purposely to discuss politics.” He added, “The mosque committee sat down with him and cautioned him against turning the mosque to a political platform because of the Quranic verse which says the Mosque is solemnly for worship of Allah alone. We vehemently rejected the use of the mosque for political meetings. We have warned him not once or twice but many times, but he didn’t heed our pleas. “Even though we believe that politics is the process of producing leaders in the country, there are laid down procedures, which are political parties, and the activities should take place in their political party offices and not in the mosque.” Jibrin also said that, apart from campaigning for the president, he was also insisting on changing the name of the mosque from Abdullahi Bin Zubbair mosque to Masjid Imam Bola Ahmed Tinubu mosque. “All the committee members said ‘no’ because the mosque belongs to the community. This mosque has a committee of which I am one of the members, and when he insisted, we rejected the idea and resolved that the mosque name would remain Masjid Abdullahi Bin Zubbair.” Jibrin said the committee had removed Abubakar from the position and would not reinstate him. “He should go and build his personal mosque, or politicians should go buy a mosque for him; that is not our business. Let me clarify that we, members of the committee of the mosque, are not against the candidate of any political party. Our prayer is to Allah to choose the best for the country, be it President Tinubu or any candidate among the presidential candidates that would become a blessing to the country,” Jibrin added.
