title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine works to unblock route to Oleshky
body:
Ukraine is working to unblock the route to the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region, where people, including children, have been trapped without food, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.

"In Oleshky right now, people and children are trapped without food, without anything. They are not being let through. Right now we are working to unblock this route," Zelenskyy said in an interview with Steven Bartlett.

He also noted that Kherson remains under constant threat of shelling due to the deployment of Russian forces on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River.

title: Russian strikes hit 12 Ukrainian regions overnight, killing two and injuring 34
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a Facebook post, Ukrinform reports.
“Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged: ordinary residential buildings, energy facilities, infrastructure at one of the railway stations and the metro, shopping malls, and businesses. Even a monastery is among the damaged sites. Our emergency services are working at all the affected locations,” the head of state said.
According to the President, “Twelve of our regions came under Russian attack overnight. In Kyiv and across the regions, 34 people were injured, including five children. As of now, two people have been confirmed killed.”
Zelensky stressed: “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening.”
“It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war. But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps – steps toward ending the killing. Stronger air defenses and the rapid delivery of missiles, the ability to destroy ballistic missile launchers, sanctions over the war – all of this must be in place. I am grateful to everyone who sees the situation for what it is and acknowledges the reality. The aggressor deserves to be treated accordingly. Ukraine deserves support. People's lives deserve protection. Thank you to everyone who stands with Ukraine!” Zelensky said.
As reported by Ukrinform, one person was killed and 24 injured in a Russian attack on Kyiv overnight on October 22. The injured included five minors and two young children.

title: An Investor’s Stress Test: How NHSU Rules Are Driving European Companies Away
body:
The EU designed the Ukraine Facility to make reform, EU accession, and the mobilization of private capital work as parts of a single system.
Ukraine’s healthcare sector, however, is sending the opposite signal: a European investor can commit capital, build infrastructure, and help patients, only to find itself operating under different economic conditions from those applied to state-run providers – facing rules that can change without its knowledge after an investment decision has already been made.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Synevo is part of the Swedish Medicover Group, whose shares are listed on the Stockholm Stock Exchange. So when we talk about the conditions under which Synevo operates in Ukraine, we are also talking about how the Ukrainian state treats one of its European investors.
This is where the paradox begins. Through the Ukraine Facility, the EU is providing Ukraine with up to €50 billion ($56 billion) for 2024-27. One of the instrument’s explicitly stated objectives is to mobilize investment in Ukraine’s private sector.
Its investment framework includes €9.6 billion ($11 billion) in guarantees and grants, and is designed to attract up to €40 billion ($45 billion) in public and private investment.
Now put yourself in the position of a company considering investing in Ukrainian healthcare. It sees that the legal framework for the Programme of Medical Guarantees (PMG) provides for healthcare providers to be contracted regardless of their ownership structure. The National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU) states the same principle on its contracting webpage.
Yet in practice, in 2026, private providers face downward adjustment coefficients, restrictions on increasing contract values, barriers to entry for new participants and, in our case, a failure to recognize that work has even been performed, despite the tests having already been carried out and used by doctors and patients.
(Photo courtesy of Synevo Ukraine) Advertisement
During the first nine months of 2026, approximately 700,000 tests performed by Synevo were not recognized. That represents more than 20% of the work completed.
An independent economic study presented at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry by Liliia Tymoshchyk, head of the Office of Forensic Examinations, found that the criterion of a sharp increase in laboratory records, which can trigger the application of a 0.6 coefficient, is by no means specific to private laboratories.
Depending on the growth threshold applied, ranging from 70% to 120%, between 94% and 96% of providers that exceeded those thresholds were state-owned or municipally owned.
Meanwhile, according to figures presented at a roundtable by Serhii Dzis, a partner at SDM Partners law firm, the 0.6 coefficient was applied to 58.7% of private providers, compared with just 21.1% of state and municipal providers.
In other words, a rule that is formally neutral can have an unequal economic impact. And when it comes to EU accession, the impact is what matters.
We have no intention of exaggerating the issue or resorting to legal alarmism. Equal access for private and municipal laboratories to the PMG is not explicitly listed as a separate benchmark under Chapter 28 of the EU accession negotiations, which covers Consumer and Health Protection.
But, European integration does not end with Chapter 28. There is also Chapter 8, covering Competition Policy. The Ukrainian government’s official materials describe its underlying principles clearly: an open market economy, free competition, clear and fair rules, and the prevention of state intervention that could distort competition.
It is therefore entirely legitimate to raise this issue.
In May 2026, the Association of Private Medical Institutions of Ukraine, together with Synevo, CSD LAB, and other healthcare providers, filed a complaint with the Antimonopoly Committee of Ukraine concerning Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1808. Representatives of the private sector are also challenging the resolution in administrative court proceedings. Separately, we have approached the European Commission, which has responded twice, that the matter is being considered at the European level.
The remarks made by Andreas Giallourakis of Business Sweden were particularly telling. He spoke from an investor’s perspective, emphasising transparency, predictability, long-term stability, and dialogue between regulators and the private sector before a policy comes into force. Investment decisions are not made for the short term. Any investor committing money, people, and effort to a market does so with the intention of operating there for years to come.
Private hospitals are not asking for protection or preferential treatment. They want the same requirements, the same quality standards, the same accountability, and a fair opportunity to provide care. That is the position of Oscar Gaspar, President of the European Union of Private Hospitals (UEHP), which represents more than 6,000 healthcare facilities.
UEHP has already raised the issue with Ukraine’s Deputy Prime Minister responsible for European and Euro-Atlantic integration. Next month, the association will also discuss the unequal treatment of healthcare providers separately with the European Commissioner responsible for health.
There is another stakeholder whose interest should not be overlooked – the World Bank. It is financing the THRIVE project, which is specifically designed to improve the efficiency of public healthcare spending, prioritization within the PMG and the institutional capacity of the NHSU. The program is worth $1.2 billion, of which Ukraine has already received $449 million.
In other words, the rules governing Ukraine’s public healthcare purchaser are already a matter of concern for international partners investing their own resources in the reform.
I do not want the European Commission or the World Bank to “protect Synevo.” Nor are we asking for special rules for a Swedish investor. Quite the opposite: to us, the European approach means precisely that there should be no special rules.
Ukraine is currently presenting the world with a compelling investment proposition: come now, help rebuild the country, benefit from European guarantees, and operate in a market that will one day be part of the EU. This proposition could be worth tens of billions of euros.
But that proposition is undergoing a stress test right now – and not at investment forums. The test is being faced by a company that has already invested in Ukraine and secured its first contract with the state. It comes when the company has to find out whether the rules on which it based its investment decision will remain in place, or whether they will be changed after the money has already been committed.
If these two versions of Ukraine – the one asking the world to invest and the one changing the rules after the investment has been made – look different, that is a risk not only for investors, but also for Ukraine’s European integration.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
Mykola Skavronskyi is Deputy General Director of Synevo Ukraine. He has worked at the company for 22 years, during which it has grown from a startup into a nationwide laboratory diagnostics business with billions in annual revenue.

title: U.S. strategic failure against Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – The US entered the war with Iran with the assumption that it could, by relying on military superiority, change the equations in its favor, but the reality of the confrontation.
Iran's defense power, missile and drone capability, and capacity for resistance have placed equations before Washington that cannot easily be overcome. From this perspective, America's failure must be sought in its inability to realize its strategic objectives and impose its will on Iran.
John Mearsheimer's remarks, the prominent international relations theorist, are also important from this same angle. He emphasizes that the initiative is in Iran's hands and that Israel's air defense and America's regional allies cannot completely neutralize Tehran's missile and drone capability. This assessment shows that Iran's defense capability remains a determining variable in the security calculations of Washington and Tel Aviv.
Iran: A Power That Cannot Be Removed from the Equations
One of the most important realities of the confrontation with Iran is the continuation of this country's capacity to respond. Iran's missile and drone capability, its geographical position, and its defense capacities create a set of limitations for America's military planning. For any action against Iran, Washington must calculate its potential consequences across the region, from the security of forces and military facilities to the situation of allies and the costs of continuing the confrontation.
These conditions show that Iran is not merely a military target, but an actor that has the ability to influence regional equations. Any strategy that ignores this reality will face the risk of miscalculation. America may possess extensive military resources and technology, but these capacities do not in themselves guarantee the achievement of political objectives.
One of the important factors in assessing America's confrontation with Iran is the incorrect understanding of the country's internal capacities and strategic characteristics. Calculations that assess Iran merely on the basis of military equipment or economic pressures fall short of understanding the set of factors affecting this country's power.
Iran possesses defense capacities, human resources, strategic infrastructure, and geographical position that, together, affect the calculations of the opposing side. Also, internal cohesion and social solidarity under crisis conditions can help strengthen the capacity to manage crises and sustain defense activities. Ignoring these components increases the likelihood of misjudging the costs and consequences of the confrontation.
From this perspective, the failure of America's strategy must be considered the result of its inability to convert military pressure into the desired political result. When the opposing side still maintains its capacity to respond and is not willing to accept imposed demands, the pressure strategy faces serious limitations.
Internal Unity and Defense Power: The Foundation of Iran's Authority
Iran's power is not limited to weapons capability. The ability to preserve vital infrastructure, manage crisis conditions, and coordinate among different parts of the country also plays a role in shaping national power. Under conditions of foreign confrontation, internal cohesion can become an important factor in reducing the effect of pressures and preserving the capacity for independent decision-making.
For this reason, any assessment of Iran's power must take into account a set of military, political, economic, and social factors. A country that can maintain its defense capacities, manage the costs of external pressure, and defend its independence of decision-making will have a determining place in the strategic calculations of the opposing side.
This issue also carries a clear message for America: any new military action against Iran will be accompanied by a set of risks and regional consequences. Iran's defense capability and capacity to respond make the cost of such a decision one of the main variables in Washington's calculations.
The Consequences of America's Failure for the Future of the Region
The confrontation with Iran is not merely a military issue for America; rather, it is tied to Washington's strategic credibility, the security of allies, and the future of regional arrangements. The inability to achieve the declared objectives can affect the assessment by America's allies and rivals of this country's ability to manage regional crises.
In contrast, maintaining Iran's defense capacities and the continuation of this country's role in the region's security equations consolidate Tehran's position as one of the main actors in West Asia. This situation does not mean the end of American influence, but it shows that Washington cannot establish its desired security order in the region without taking into account Iran's capability and will.
Ultimately, the message of the confrontation is clear: Iran is not a country whose political will can easily be changed through military pressure and one-sided calculations. The failure of America's strategy in achieving its objectives demonstrates the limits of Washington's power against Iran and the importance of Tehran's position in the future equations of the region. Iran's defense capability, power to respond, and national cohesion will remain among the most important deterrent factors against any new military action.

title: Ukraine on threshold of winter: Energy, defense and new diplomatic reality
Pa Fasoranti: Exit of a Titan of Awolowo’s Political Tradition
body: Fidelis David writes that the demise of the Leader of Pan Yoruba socio-political group, Afenifere, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, has marked the fading of one of the last living links to a political generation whose convictions were forged before independence and tested through the turbulence of the First Republic, Civil War, military dictatorship, the June 12, 1993 election struggle and nearly three decades of uninterrupted civil rule. When Afenifere leader, Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti died peacefully at his Akure residence on Tuesday, at the age of 100, Nigeria lost more than an elder statesman. Born on May 11, 1926, in Uso, Ondo State, Fasoranti lived through virtually every defining chapter of modern Nigerian history. Yet, while the country’s political landscape underwent repeated transformations, he remained associated with a tradition of politics rooted in the philosophy of late sage, Chief Obafemi Awolowo: disciplined leadership, social welfare, educational advancement, justice and a federal structure that accommodates the country’s diversity. His death, therefore, is not simply the loss of a centenarian. It is the departure of a custodian of Awoism whose political influence extended from Ondo State to the wider Yoruba nation and the national struggle for democratic governance. The head of the Awolowo family and Chairman of African Newspapers of Nigeria Plc, Ambassador Olatokunbo Awolowo- Dosumu, captured the historical significance of his passing when she described him as one of the last titans of the political tradition established by her father. “With his departure, we have lost, in a very real sense, the last of the titans of the Awolowo political tradition,” she said. Fasoranti’s political story did not begin in a party office or government house. It began in the classroom, where he developed the discipline and commitment to public service that would later define his political career. After his early education in Uso, he attended Ondo Boys’ High School and Yaba Higher College before proceeding to the University College, Ibadan. His academic journey later took him to the University of Hull in the United Kingdom, where he obtained a postgraduate diploma in education, and Macquarie University in Australia, where he earned a master’s degree in education administration and school management. As a teacher and principal, Fasoranti served in institutions including Ondo Boys’ High School, Oyemekun Grammar School and Iju/Itaogbolu Grammar School. He subsequently established Omolere Nursery and Primary School and Akure High School, extending his contribution to education beyond formal public service. Former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Chief Olu Falae, who described Fasoranti as an in-law and a close associate of more than 60 years, recalled his generosity towards children from disadvantaged backgrounds. As founding principal of Iju/Itaogbolu Grammar School, Falae said, Fasoranti admitted pupils whose parents could not afford their fees and allowed them to complete their education on credit, with the opportunity to repay later. That commitment offers a window into the philosophy that shaped his public life: education was not merely a personal achievement but a social instrument for expanding opportunity. Fasoranti’s political identity was inseparable from Awolowo’s progressive tradition. From the Action Group to the Unity Party of Nigeria, he remained committed to a political philosophy that placed education, healthcare and social welfare at the centre of governance. His most prominent executive assignment came between 1979 and 1983, when he served as Commissioner for Finance under the administration of the late Governor Michael Adekunle Ajasin in the old Ondo State. The period was associated with the implementation of Awolowo-inspired social programmes, particularly free education and free healthcare, which sought to make essential services accessible regardless of social status. Fasoranti’s role in the administration placed him at the intersection of ideology and public finance, where the ideals of progressive governance had to be translated into policies and expenditure decisions. His political relevance was not necessarily built on occupying the highest elective offices. Rather, it rested on his place within a network of ideological actors who helped sustain the progressive tradition across successive political generations. Former Ondo State Governor, Dr Olusegun Mimiko, described him as a man whose politics was defined by fidelity to principle rather than personal ambition. “Never for once were personal ambition or greed markers of his leadership philosophy or direction; it was all about fidelity to principle and an abiding concern for the future of the nation,” Mimiko said. That assessment captures the central paradox of Fasoranti’s political life: he exercised considerable influence without becoming a president, governor or elected legislator. Fasoranti’s place in Nigeria’s political history extended beyond the administration of public institutions. During the struggle against military rule, particularly following the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, he became associated with the pro-democracy movement and the resistance to military dictatorship. His involvement in the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) placed him within a broad coalition of political leaders and activists demanding the restoration of democratic rule. The period was dangerous for those who challenged the military establishment. Fasoranti reportedly survived an assassination attempt in 1996 during the dictatorship of General Sani Abacha. His significance in that struggle lie in the continuity he represented between Awolowo’s generation of political activism and the campaign to restore civilian government. For a man who had witnessed independence and the collapse of the First Republic, the return to democracy was not an abstract constitutional ideal. It was part of a lifelong engagement with the question of how Nigeria should be governed. Fasoranti’s influence reached another defining phase in November 2008, when he emerged as leader of Afenifere following the death of Pa Abraham Adesanya. For 18 years, he occupied the organisation’s most influential leadership position, navigating disagreements over leadership, political alliances and the direction of Yoruba politics. Under his leadership, Afenifere continued to advocate restructuring, true federalism, devolution of powers, resource control and a governance system that would give federating units greater responsibility over their affairs. Yet his tenure was not without controversy. The organisation experienced deep divisions, particularly over leadership and political alignments, culminating in rival tendencies associated with Fasoranti and Chief Ayo Adebanjo. In 2021, Fasoranti appointed Adebanjo as acting leader and Oba Oladipo Olaitan as deputy leader while retaining his position as substantive national leader. The divisions became more politically consequential during the 2023 presidential election, when Fasoranti’s endorsement of former Lagos State Governor, Asiwaju Bola Tinubu exposed differences within the Yoruba socio-political establishment over whether to support the eventual president or maintain a different political position. His relationship with Tinubu was rooted in the broader progressive political family, but the endorsement demonstrated that ideological affinity did not automatically translate into consensus within Afenifere. President Tinubu, in his condolence message, recalled visiting Fasoranti in Akure in 2022 to inform him of his presidential ambition. “Pa Fasoranti told me I would be President in his lifetime, and God answered his prayer,” Tinubu said. The president described him as one of the last great titans of Awolowo’s progressive family, praising his discipline, integrity and commitment to true federalism. The relationship reinforced Fasoranti’s standing as a political patriarch whose counsel carried weight beyond Ondo State. However, it also illustrated the delicate balance between preserving ideological traditions and navigating the practical realities of electoral politics. In July 2019, Fasoranti suffered a devastating personal tragedy when his daughter, Mrs Funke Olakunrin, was killed by gunmen along the Ondo-Ore Expressway. The killing provoked widespread outrage and renewed national debate about insecurity, particularly attacks on travellers and the vulnerability of communities across the country. For Fasoranti, the tragedy brought the national security crisis into his immediate family. It also sharpened public attention on concerns about the protection of citizens and the effectiveness of Nigeria’s security architecture. His advocacy for restructuring and a more responsive federation acquired renewed urgency amid national conversations about state policing, regional security arrangements and the distribution of constitutional powers. The incident became one of the most painful chapters in a life otherwise celebrated for longevity, discipline and public service. Fasoranti’s death now raises an uncomfortable question for Afenifere and the wider Yoruba political establishment: who now possesses the moral authority, historical experience and political reach to occupy the space he’s leaving behind? The challenge is not simply to identify a successor to an organisational title. It is to rebuild cohesion in a movement that has experienced divisions over leadership and electoral choices, while preserving its historic commitment to restructuring and social justice. His long tenure gave him a stature that cannot easily be transferred through an appointment. The next generation of leaders will have to earn legitimacy through their conduct, ideological consistency and capacity to unite competing interests. In Ondo State, his influence also formed part of the political inheritance of a state whose progressive tradition has shaped its identity for decades. His son, Dr Taiwo Fasoranti, who serves as Secretary to the State Government, represents a continuing family connection to public service, although the elder statesman’s broader legacy extends well beyond his family. Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu described the late leader as a symbol of wisdom, integrity and selfless service, noting his longstanding commitment to truth, equity, justice and good governance. Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa similarly described him as a patriarch whose contributions to the state, Yorubaland and Nigeria would remain indelible. “He lived a fulfilled life and left indelible footprints in the sands of time,” Tinubu said of the centenarian. Therefore, Fasoranti’s death closes a remarkable chapter, but whether it ends the political tradition he represented depends on what happens next. Awoism cannot survive merely as a slogan invoked during anniversaries or political campaigns. Its enduring relevance rests on whether leaders can translate its ideals into accessible education, affordable healthcare, accountable government, social justice and a federal structure that responds to the needs of Nigeria’s diverse communities. Fasoranti’s life offered an example of ideological continuity across generations, even as the political environment around him changed dramatically. His record was not without controversy, and his leadership did not resolve every division within Afenifere. Nevertheless, Pa Fasoranti’s longevity, discipline and association with the progressive tradition gave him a distinctive place in Nigeria’s political history. At 100, he had witnessed the rise and fall of political movements, the triumphs and disappointments of democratic government, and the persistent struggle to define the Nigerian federation. His departure leaves a void in Ondo State and Yorubaland, but also a test for those who inherit the institutions and ideals he defended. The ultimate measure of his legacy will not be how long his name remains attached to Afenifere, but whether the principles he spent a century representing continue to influence how Nigeria is governed. For the generation that follows him, the question is no longer what Fasoranti stood for. It is whether they possess the conviction to stand for it themselves

title: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
body:
Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.
But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.
We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.
But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .
In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .
Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.
This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.
To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.
When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.
Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters . Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough .
So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.
The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek , a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."
Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.
Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.
Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.
For more ergonomic tips, read our story .
This story includes reporting from Ruth Tam, Sylvie Douglis, Frank Festa, Andee Tagle, Manoush Zomorodi and Margaret Cirino. This story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify , and sign up for our newsletter . Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit .

title: Canada GCAP observer role to strengthen defence ties
body: Canada’s involvement as an observer in the Global Combat Air Programme will further strengthen British bilateral defence cooperation with Canada, building on decades of close collaboration as Five Eyes members and NATO allies, according to answers given in Parliament . James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what assessment the department has made of the potential merits of Canada joining the Global Combat Air Programme as a full participant, and in a second question asked what discussions the Secretary of State has had with his Canadian counterpart on the same point. Luke Pollard gave the same answer to both: “Canada’s involvement as an Observer in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) will further strengthen the UK’s bilateral defence cooperation with Canada, building on decades of close collaboration as Five Eyes members and NATO Allies.” Canada joined the programme as an observer nation this year, alongside a British commitment of £708 million into the technologies feeding the aircraft. Observer status gives Ottawa access to programme information and a seat from which to judge whether to go further, without the funding share, workshare and governance obligations that come with full membership. GCAP runs between the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan, with the industrial work carried by Edgewing, the joint venture formed by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement Company, and the aircraft is intended to enter service in 2035. Adding a fourth full partner would mean reopening the workshare and governance arrangements that took the three founding nations years to settle. Canada’s interest arrives while Ottawa is reviewing its own fast jet plans, having committed to the F-35 and then reopened the question amid the wider deterioration in its relationship with Washington. A European-led sixth generation programme offers an alternative industrial partnership for a country that builds aerostructures and avionics at scale. The post Canada GCAP observer role to strengthen defence ties first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: When Shettima Remembers: A Lesson in Unscripted Humanity
body: Rahma Abdulmajid captures the carefully managed armour of Vice President Kashim Shettima, stripping away sterile state protocol, partisan politics, and grandstand podiums to expose the raw human anatomy beneath the leader during his encounter with a longtime friend in New Delhi, India. History is obsessed with the theatre of power. It immortalizes the roaring stadiums, the blinding camera flashes, and the hollow majesty of choreographed handshakes—but real control operates in the shadows. True, transformative leadership is never born on a brightly lit stage. It is forged in the shadows, deep within the quiet, unscripted margins where teleprompters go dark and the roaring crowds fall silent. When the glittering costume of power is violently stripped away, only two things can remain: a hollow, echoing emptiness, or the raw, unvarnished force of pure humanity. New Delhi was buzzing on day two of the BRICS summit. Inside the Nigerian Embassy, the energy turned electric as Vice President Kashim Shettima arrived for a brief courtesy visit. A roaring, joyous crowd of resident Nigerians had gathered, transforming the venue into an impromptu homecoming. Excitement hung thick in the air, punctuated by rising chants and the endless, rapid-fire click of camera shutters capturing every handshake and smile. Yet beneath that surface warmth, a subtle tension shifted the room. While everyone else basked in the moment, the Vice President’s gaze fractured. His eyes darted from face to face with a sharp, urgent intensity, searching for something vital that the rest of us had completely overlooked. It was contagious. Soon, it wasn’t just his security detail on high alert. Even those of us in his inner circle found ourselves scanning the room, hunting for whatever phantom danger our principal was so desperately trying to find. Even inside the private quarters meant for his rest, there was no escape from the search. The moment the commotion outside died down, his voice sliced through the polite small talk. “Where is Mr. Prakash?” The embassy officials froze, trapped in a heavy, bewildered silence. They traded blank stares, hunting for the name in their memories. Then, understanding clicked. He spoke again, steady and firm. “Mr. Prakash,” he said. “The embassy driver. Is he still here?” Within minutes, Mr. Prakash appeared. He was an elderly, humble Indian man, his weathered face and traditional mourning haircut bearing the unmistakable scars of a life battered by time. Though he held nothing more than a modest driver’s job at an African embassy, he carried a crushing mountain of obligations alone on his narrow shoulders. He approached, his fragile gaze holding the look of someone who had just stumbled upon long-lost family. The Vice President had just sat down to his welcome meal when he spotted Prakash. In an instant, protocol and plate were forgotten. He stood straight back up, greeting Prakash with a deep reverence that hushed the entire room. “Mr. Prakash, how have you been?” he said warmly. “Thank you for everything.” Then, turning to the rest of us as if to permanently etch the man’s dignity into our minds, he explained, “He drove me around years ago during my visit to India as governor.” What followed was uniquely disarming: he began inquiring about Mr. Prakash’s family by name. He remembered vivid details from a brief encounter years ago—the kind of trivial history most leaders cast aside. When Prakash, with trembling hands, pulled out a worn-out phone, desperate for a photograph to mark the improbable reunion, my principal left his meal once more and threw an arm around him like an old, dear friend. In that moment, he posed not as a Vice President, but simply as a man with his brother. But it wasn’t the cameras that stole my breath that afternoon. It was what happened after the lenses lowered—away from the flashing lights and prying eyes. Without announcement or applause, Shettima slipped a hand into his pocket, scooped out a generous wad of cash, and tucked it quietly into Mr. Prakash’s coat. No aides were instructed. No media were invited. It was an act born purely out of kindness, deep empathy, and raw humanity. When language threatened to build a wall—because Prakash speaks little English and the Vice President speaks no Hindi—compassion found its own dialect. He switched effortlessly to Hausa, a Nigerian local language, not for Prakash to understand literally, but to universalise the moment, to say in a tongue he knows best what the heart knows in every language: “Mene ne amfanin nasarar rayuwa idan baka taimaka wa wanda yake bukatar taimakonka ba?” Translated in English, this means, “What is the benefit of success in life if you do not help those who need your help?” What I witnessed did not surprise me, but it deeply enriched my soul. You see, I too am a Prakash in the Vice President’s world. Over the past three years of working by his side, no living soul has recognised the heavy reality of my life like he has. When my husband died serving our nation, I was left to carry the immense weight of raising our children alone. Yet, His Excellency truly sees that sacrifice, honouring the burden I bear every single day. To speak the absolute truth, Kashim Shettima’s quiet, unwavering remembrance of my grief over the past three years has outshone even my closest blood relatives across the 11 long years since my husband passed away. He remembers the dates others forget. He asks the questions others avoid. He carries burdens that are not constitutionally his to bear. Seeing Vice President Shettima evokes the presence of transformative leaders. He reminds me of Uruguay’s President, José Mujica, who chose a modest farmhouse over a palace, and Nelson Mandela, whose profound friendship with Christo Brand transcended prison walls. Their stories remind us that true leadership is never about titles, offices, or protocols. It lives in an unshakeable refusal to walk past someone in need—a stubborn conviction that every human being, no matter how small their station, is worthy of being remembered. This noble, compassionate heart is precisely why President Bola Tinubu chose Kashim Shettima as his running mate—to gift Nigeria a leadership defined not by noise, but by empathy; not by showmanship, but by deep, genuine service. In a world where many leaders remember only those who can repay them, it is truly revolutionary to find one who remembers a driver. -Abdulmajid, a media assistant to the Vice President, writes from Abuja.

title: U-17 WWC: Ghana’s Jessica Appiah named Player of the Match against Brazil
body: Ghana midfielder Jessica Appiah Asamoah has been named Player of the Match after playing a pivotal role in the Black Maidens’ 3-3 draw with Brazil at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. The midfielder created four chances, won seven duels and completed three successful dribbles as Ghana fought back from behind twice to secure a point in their second group match. Brazil took the lead in the seventh minute through Nicolly, but Ghana responded in the 31st minute when Rafia Osman restored parity. The Black Maidens capitalised on their growing momentum four minutes later, with Gloria Ameaa scoring to give Ghana a 2-1 advantage. However, Kaillany Rafinah struck in the 44th minute to draw Brazil level before the break. Brazil regained the lead in the 57th minute through Indy, forcing Ghana to mount another comeback. In the 85th minute, Jessica produced a decisive piece of individual brilliance, beating two Brazilian players before threading a defence-splitting pass into the box for Priscilla Mensah to convert and secure a 3-3 draw. Ghana have one point from their opening two Group C matches and will face Canada in their final group fixture, where a victory is crucial to keeping their qualification hopes alive.

title: Yayi, 2027 and a Victory Foretold
body: Recent Developments regarding the 2027 Elections, are pointing in different directions. Remi Adefulu , posits that for Ogun All Progressives Congress Governorship Candidate, Senator Olamilekan Adeola, victory is in sight going by his overwhelming acceptance and projects delivery across the state. In the nation’s history, Ogun state has always held a pride of place in terms of human and natural endowments. Consequently, Ogun continues to earn a position of pre-eminence among its peers in all spheres of national life. For instance, it is on record that Ogun state has the highest number of universities in the country and the list keeps growing by the day. What do you expect from a state that produced the late sage, Chief Jeremiah Obafemi Awolowo, whose vision of free education became a game changer that remains unrivaled till date? When you mention Ogun state, the world remembers Africa’s first Nobel laureate, Prof Wole Soyinka, Tai Solarin, Fela Anikulapo-Kuti, Beko Ransome-Kuti, Chief Adeola Odutola, Dr Olikoye Ransome-Kuti, M.K.O Abiola, Ernest Shonekan, Anthony Joshua and many more. These and more have earned the state world acclaim, devoting their God-given endowments to the upliftment of environments they found themselves – music, sports, academia, business, medicine, et al Many are therefore worried by the state of politicking exhibited by the camp of the opposition in the state in recent times and a dent on the highly revered state is to say the least an understatement. This is largely because, over the years, Ogun politics has always been a marketplace of ideas, where opposing camps engage themselves in an intellectual contest in wooing the electorate, selling lofty programmes and ideas. Though politics is never devoid of brickbats, in Ogun, the people are always the ultimate winners as candidates try to outshine themselves in a robust battle for elective positions. However, Peoples Democratic Party in the Gateway State brought political matters to an all-time low by virtually dragging politics in the mud through their vicious propaganda machinery. The intention was to drastically reduce APC governorship candidate, Senator Adeola (Yayi) in the eyes of Ogun people, especially the electorate ahead of the 2027 general elections. In this connection, they reeled out all manner of lies, including alleging that Senator Adeola is from Ekiti, and not from Yewa in Ogun state. Rather than engaging them in propaganda, the guber hopeful has been replying them through impactful programmes across the length and breadth of Ogun state. Yayi’s “ITESIWAJU Agenda” which he recently unveiled to the people of the state as the pillars on which his administration would operate is not new after all. These are things he has used his current office to spread by way of impactful projects across the state. For the first time in the history of the Gateway state, a senator positively impacted all the 20 local governments in the state in less than four years. In an amazing fashion, Yayi has delivered schools, roads, hospitals, vocational centres, markets and empowered the youths, women, the poor and the elderly. It is one of the reasons he has run a very effective campaign where projects have been his major selling point and putting him miles ahead of his opponents. In Ogun water side alone, Yayi is already electrifying 50 communities, to boost socio-economic life of the people. A similar feat is on-going simultaneously across the length and breadth of the state with the aim of making life more abundant for its people. Ask the people of Ijebu-Igbo and Sagamu about the revolution at Molusi College and Remo Secondary School whether such has ever happened? The bitter truth: Yayi is a moving train and no one dares stop this man who is of the conviction that public office offers a rare opportunity to lift the people, especially the down trodden out of poverty. This he has done with all his energy and the results are daily manifesting for all to see across the Gateway state. Unlike the rudderless opposition which is presently fighting to have a governorship candidate in its fold, Yayi and the Ogun APC are more than ready for the coming elections. Thankfully, the people see Adeola as the beautiful bride and all segments of the state are ready to vote resoundingly for him and the APC in 2027. Hence, from teachers, transport unions, students, traders, traditional rulers, religious leaders, youths, women, artisans etc, it’s Yayi all the way. The show of support is deafening and the solidarity is more than overwhelming across all critical segments of the state. That was why the opposition suddenly went into panic mode on seeing the unprecedented show of support in cash and in kind to Yayi’s aspiration. Call it a tacit show of victory or a sign of coronation, you are surely on the right path as indications have shown that there is no stopping this uncommon public servant. Little wonder their propaganda arsenal has suddenly fired blank as the groundswell of support is getting more and more intimidating by the day. Perhaps the icing on the cake was the carnival-like event in Ilaro, to show Ogun people and the globe that Yayi is a true son of the soil and that Yewa/Awori are more than delighted with him. What a way to dismiss their tale by moonlight stories, in support of a man who has transformed Ilaro to what is now seen as “small London”. With the governorship elections still four months away, the political temperature no doubt favours the Ogun West Senator to ascend the governorship seat in 2027. As a party, Ogun APC has shown that it is miles ahead of the opposition, not minding the metrics. All may not be perfect, but it is evidently clear that the party has a brand you can take anywhere in Yayi. Unlike the opposition, the APC is well structured in Ogun and the signs are there in terms of results and acceptability by the electorate. From what is presently on ground in the Gateway state, the opposition would need more than a miracle to challenge the Yayi phenomenon. -Adefulu writes from Lagos.

title: Law Society complaint questions U of Toronto law professor’s Indigenous ancestry
body:
A complaint filed Oct. 14 with the Law Society of Ontario requests that disciplinary action be taken against a Toronto lawyer who has built a notable career as an Anishinaabe woman specializing in Indigenous law, alleging she has no evidence that she is Indigenous at all.
The complaint is against Promise Holmes Skinner, who identifies as Anishiaabe-Scandinavian.
Holmes Skinner has a private law practice and teaches Indigenous law at the prestigious University of Toronto. She served as a senior manager at Toronto’s Aboriginal Legal Services before opening her own law firm.
Her LinkedIn profile cites working ‘in Indigenous traditions’ as an “Anishinaabe-Scandinavian lawyer.”
The complaint alleges she has “no First Nations, Inuit bloodline to speak of.”
Holmes Skinner declined an interview request, but said in a statement to Global News that while she has no documentary proof of Indigenous ancestry, she has a “cherished understanding that my grandmother was Anishinaabe” from Cape Croker First Nation in Ontario. “However,” she added, “without documentary evidence to verify that, I have learned culture in other ways.”
Holmes Skinner says she has been “transparent about not being a rights-bearing individual” and that she has not taken any benefits or positions reserved for those individuals.
She says her family is from Cape Croker First Nation, but she does not claim to be from there herself.
She also said her “legal education and practice are about contributing skills, not taking space I am not invited to take.”
Her lawyer Andrea Gonsalves challenges “that Indigenous identity can validly exist only through proven blood connections to a rights-bearing community.”
Kim Tallbear, one of the world’s leading academic experts on people who questionably claim to be Indigenous, takes issue with that.
“If she can’t verify her grandmother is Anishinaabe, don’t be speaking as an Anishinaabe person,” says Tallbear, a citizen of the Sisseton–Wahpeton Oyate.
“You can be speaking as a friend or an ally to the people that you have made relationships with. We have all kinds of non-Indigenous people that do that, and they don’t claim to be us.”
The complaint was filed by Crystal Semaganis, who heads a grassroots group that tracks and exposes suspected cases of Indigenous identity fraud.
The complaint asks the Law Society of Ontario to apologize for allegedly allowing a member to take roles intended for First Nations, Inuit and Metis lawyers and to “formulate and implement a First Nations, Inuit and Metis Authentication Policy… to go beyond simple declarations of self-identification.”
It also requests disciplinary action against Holmes Skinner.
Semaganis has testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates regarding non-Indigenous people claiming to be Indigenous to access lucrative procurement contracts under Ottawa’s Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business.
Semaganis is being sued by a family of women over allegations she made that they’ve faked an Indigenous identity, a matter that remains before a Yukon court.
Many universities have implemented policies to verify indigeneity after several high-profile academics’ ancestry claims were challenged.
When asked in September how they verified Holmes Skinner’s indigeneity, the University of Toronto refused to say, citing privacy. Then it removed a page outlining its verification process from its website.
On Oct. 20, the university announced the launch of its Indigenous substantiation process . It requires genealogical evidence and membership with a rights-bearing nation.
The university tells Global News it “does not apply retroactively, it will be initiated for current faculty members who identify as Indigenous when they engage with new opportunities, such as promotions, research funding competitions and awards.”
The Law Society of Ontario spokesperson Amy Lewis says when a complaint is made, they “consider the potential risk to the public, the public’s confidence in the legal professions and the Law Society, and the administration of justice.”
They won’t comment on complaints or investigations until they’re complete.
Gonsalves says they cannot comment on the complaint itself but “anyone can put anything in a complaint” and “the fact of making the complaint doesn’t say anything about its merit.”

title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape
body:
ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.
This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.
Heavy equipment excavates an area adjacent to an Amazon data center currently under construction in Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29. Local authorities have approved dozens of data center projects for U.S. Big Tech and other companies that will transform the character of this region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.
"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."
An Amazon data center, currently under construction, is seen in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. Aragon authorities say they are betting that hosting data centers will place them at the center of a "new economy" they believe AI will bring. But many local residents and activist groups believe these projects are delivering an environmental crisis. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
An Amazon data center, currently under construction beside the quiet village of Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29. It's being built beside the village on land close to a protected wetland. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Companies building data centers in Spain's Aragon region say they will mostly rely on renewable energy. But the centers will also sometimes be powered by on-site generators. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The companies were drawn to the region with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give these data centers a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population. This order gives them the power to expropriate land, strips local mayors of veto powers, and restricts the time the public has to object to 23 working days. (For the recent Amazon Web Services development, the regional government opened the window to oppose the project over the Christmas period. Opponents of the project believe they did this to try to push it through at a time when people would be paying less attention, though the government denies this.)
The Sotonera reservoir, which serves population centers and farms in the provinces of Huesca and Zaragoza, is seen in Tormos, Spain, on Sept. 29. This is one of Spain's driest regions that, with climate change, is already suffering from repeated drought. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The rapid approval process for these large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly impact their region and lives.
Farmland that is to be developed into a data center complex is seen in Botorrita, Spain, on Sept. 28. Residents of Botorrita village say they first learned of the project when they found the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. The government of Aragon is fast-tracking planning permissions under a procedure that also significantly cuts the time the public has to object. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The first time Silvia Baselga and her family learned of the data center soon to tower over their home was when they noticed the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. "When we saw this, we went to the city hall and said, 'OK, we want information. This is really close to our house.'" But the local council told them they had no information. Only when the planning documents were later made public did they learn that the outer perimeter of the data center is to be built within 300 feet of their home in the hilltop village of Botorrita. The plans showed that the complex will be larger than the village itself.
Residents point to an area that is to be developed into a data center complex in Botorrita, Spain, on Sept. 28. Residents say the planned complex comes to within 80 meters of the garden wall of a family living at the village edge. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Baselga's parents retired here for the tranquility of a life spent in a tight-knit village community. Their home looks out over fields and gently rolling hills. To try to block the noise the data center will emit, Baselga believes the company will build a 20-foot-high wall, as happened in a nearby village. "We're going to open the window and see nothing," she said. Friends regularly visit at night to gaze at the stars in this rural setting. Baselga said the center's 24-hour security lights will block out the night sky. "It's going to be like living beside a prison."
Centers like these are set to be built across Aragon — 27 in total, according to official documents — some by Spanish and other firms, but most by American companies, taking up about 7 square miles of land. At least one is built partly on ground originally classified as protected for natural ecosystems. The companies promise employment. Amazon Web Services told NPR it will create 6,200 permanent jobs once these centers are built. But many residents fear they will also deliver an environmental crisis.
Julio Enfedaque stands at the edge of a construction site where an outflow pipe will be installed that he says will carry water from a nearby Amazon data center in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. Farmers in the region are concerned about the water these data complexes require. In this region already affected by frequent droughts, they fear they will be in competition for the resources to grow their crops. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The data centers will consume many times the current electricity needs of the region and require large amounts of water to cool their servers in one of Spain's driest regions, one that's been repeatedly blighted by drought.
Julio Enfedaque drives across the parched land his family has farmed for generations. This year it barely rained for four months, and the government cut the amount of water available for irrigation by two-thirds. "Even if they say the data centers won't take the water that we need for agriculture, I am sure it's going to become very complicated to farm like my ancestors used to." Enfedaque has advised his nephews to find different careers and leave the land.
Julio Enfedaque carries some alfalfa in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. He fears the construction of so many water-hungry data centers in this region will leave him without enough of the resource to grow his crops. His family has farmed here for generations. He believes this way of life is so under threat that he says he is advising his nephews to find other careers. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Amazon Web Services says its data centers will draw water only after temperatures hit 86 degrees Fahrenheit and that they are investing millions of dollars to help fix leaking water pipes and working with farmers to use AI technology to make their water use more efficient. "We're trying to not only use as less [sic] water as possible, but also to help those communities where we operate have the best infrastructure," David Blázquez, Amazon's head of public policy for Spain and Portugal, told NPR.
But the company remains opaque about how much water each center will use. Blázquez said it's "a company policy not to publish water usage per site." Regional figures show Amazon's three existing data centers, which are much smaller than what is planned, used 68 million liters — 48% more than the company had originally told regional officials they would need.
Swallows fly in front of wind turbines near Huesca, Spain, on Sept. 29. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Perhaps an even bigger problem is the energy these centers need to run. Unlike many data centers in the U.S., which are powered by natural gas, companies in Aragon say they will rely mainly on renewable sources (though they also have diesel generators on site). Blázquez says Amazon Web Services has secured "a hundred renewable projects in Spain," including 17 in Aragon.
While that energy is carbon-free, ecologists and biologists warn that additional wind projects could have their own devastating consequences for the environment.
The region is full of hunting grounds for vultures and other birds of prey and an important stop for migrating birds.
Ornithologist José Antonio Pinzolas looks at a dead vulture, killed by a wind turbine, in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, solar panel farms and wind turbines, which has alarmed many local residents with the high energy use, noise pollution, danger to wildlife and heat generation they are known for. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Ornithologist José Antonio Pinzolas looks for raptors and vultures, flying near dozens of windmills, in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
"The vultures look for the thermal air currents to lift them. But they run straight into the windmills — for them it's like flying through knives," explained José Antonio Pinzolas, an ornithologist.
Aragon's own environmental agency has warned that wind farms in this area pose a high risk of collision to the endangered red kite and other protected raptors, and has documented an increase in bird and bat deaths in recent years as the renewable sector expands.
"I've collected ospreys, golden eagles, kestrels by the dozen, black vultures," said Juan Ballesteros, a nature protection officer for the local government.
Juan Ballesteros, an agent with the Protección de la Naturleza (Environmental Protection), removes a dead vulture, killed by a wind turbine in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Juan Ballesteros, an agent with the Protección de la Naturleza (Environmental Protection), removes a dead vulture killed by a wind turbine in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Ballesteros used to love his job for its access to wildlife. Now, he said, he spends his days placing the corpses of birds killed by turbine blades into body bags. Ballesteros met NPR as he arrived to collect the body of a young Eurasian black vulture that lay dead on the ground, its wings splayed in the dirt at the foot of a wind turbine.
Blázquez told NPR, of the damage to this important habitat that the expansion of wind and solar farms causes, that Amazon Web Services "definitely shares those concerns." He said they work with renewable energy companies that comply with environmental legislation. But Pinzolas said the growing number of bird deaths shows the current protections in place are not working.
Environmental groups say the overall impact of wind turbines on birds isn't being properly assessed.
Several groups have crowdfunded together to mount a legal action to try to stop Amazon Web Services' expansion in Aragon. The court case challenges the Aragon government's fast-tracked approvals of the plans. "We have concerns about water consumption, about energy consumption, the impact on some other industries and on the environment," said Luis García,, an activist with Ecologistas En Accion, one of the organizations involved in the case. He said the economic benefits of data centers are not great enough to justify the "huge damage they do to the environment."
Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
One recent weekend in the region's capital, Zaragoza, an avenue filled with demonstrators protesting against a new data center to be built at the edge of a forest by the city. Residents fear the heat and noise of the complex will destroy a tranquil space that is a haven during the hot summer months.
Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
"This is a worthy fight as all the worlds invades us, to save this pine forests, to save the environment, against this voracious capitalism that thinks only of economic interests and not of people," said Marian Rams, a local resident with white hair dyed in hues of pink, green and blue. "They want to swap nature for data centers."
Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Nearby, a little girl no older than 5 chanted along with the demonstrators. Her mother, Ana Domezian, walked alongside her with her second child, a baby, nestled in a carrier against her chest. "If we don't fight now for what we have," she asked, "what are we going to leave to them in the future?"

title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
body:
Cattle feed at a ranch in Dublin, Texas, on Sept. 11, 2026. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP for Getty Images hide caption
Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.
"They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.
When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."
Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.
All of which is to say that since August, when President Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs — temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef — Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.
"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.
It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges — for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.
"The beef herd size is at an all time low — a 75-year low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."
Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound — a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically.
Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its U.S. beef purchases . In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.
And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports — specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.
That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.
"If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening — perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."
This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.
From an Economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total U.S. beef consumption .
That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.
All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.
"We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News . "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."
Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.
"She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."
In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.
Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.
"Both of them will be 2- or 3-, 4-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."
Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.
"I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, OK, didn't love the three-month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.
Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.
"As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.
He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.
"They honestly were told that tariffs were going to make markets better," he said. "They were told that we were going to enter this new golden era. I just filled up my pickup with $6.30 diesel fuel."
This is not just about Iowa. Several states with some of the tightest races this year — Texas, Nebraska, Montana and Kansas — are also major beef-producing states, meaning lots of people weighing these particular trade policies as they vote.
Back on his farm, Birker knows how he'll vote, too: "I'll vote Republican."
Birker stresses that this is purely a personal decision, and that the Iowa Cattlemen are a nonpartisan group. But for his part, he generally votes Republican, and getting to talk personally to Hinson also reinforced his choice.
As for Trump, Birker approves of how he's doing as president.
"I do, I do," he said. "I just think it's a long putt. He's a businessman, and I think we've got to stick it out with him."
Trump will have the opportunity to convince more Iowans when he travels to Sioux City this week as part of his pre-midterm push.
