title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
body:
The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., a Philadelphia suburb, closed early this year amid falling sales. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption
BENSALEM, Pa. — When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.
Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.
At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall , a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.
Trump fans Wes Alker and Joseph Flanagan pose at a going-out-of-business sale at a Trump store in suburban Philadelphia. Flanagan lives nearby and said he visited the store more than 25 times. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption
"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."
Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed — it still maintains an online presence — Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50% when he took office to 44% .
Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen 5 more points.
This Trump store in a suburban Philadelphia strip mall is one of at least four that have closed this year as the president's merchandising appeal has dimmed. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption
Hays said unpopular policies — such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts — have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.
"People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.
Trump merchandise has been big business. The MAGA Mall, a retailer and wholesaler, sells over a 1,000 MAGA, patriotic and religious products, including 400 different kinds of hats. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption
When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.
"After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."
Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.
Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman — and he tells people what they want to hear.
The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., sold a wide variety of products before it closed early this year. Items included an "Alligator Alcatraz" T-shirt, "Trump Won" caps and this patriotic Trump bear. The store continues to sell online. Frank Langfitt/NPR hide caption
Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.
In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the midterms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.
"I don't want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it," said Kligman, 69.
Given term limits and Trump's age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say "We the People."
Solomon says this is a natural progression.
Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business "will fade away."

title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
body:
For-sale signs are posted in front of condominiums for sale in July in Los Angeles. A new analysis from the Center for Responsible Lending finds that the average renter household now needs 16 years to save for a down payment and closing costs. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption
Mortgage rates topping 7% is the latest sign of how hard it has gotten to buy a first house, with aspiring owners already facing sky-high prices. A new analysis out Thursday shines a light on yet another growing obstacle: the amount needed to close a home loan.
"Over the last seven years, the time to save up that down payment and closing costs has doubled," said Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, a research nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity. The report was released by the center's Julian Bond Institute .
Since 2019, the last time the center made the same calculation, home prices have shot up, inflation spiked and has remained stubbornly high, and the rising cost of food, gas, healthcare and more has strained family budgets. Closing costs on a home loan have also ticked up, driven in part by rising homeowners insurance.
Amid all this, renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.
Today, the center calculates that for a median-income renter household, it would take a "staggering 16 years" to save up a down payment and closing costs for a starter home. That's twice as long as in 2019. And it would take even more time — 21 years — for a median-income Black renter household.
That kind of time frame upends a main reason that many look to buy in the first place. As the analysis notes, "young children at the time the family starts saving may have left the household — for higher education or the workforce — before the family will have saved enough to purchase their first home."
The report also narrows its calculations to middle-income households — making roughly $50,000 to $120,000 — whose members are more likely to be viable homeowners. For them, the savings time has also doubled, to 12 years.
For front-line workers, such as police officers, firefighters, EMTs, nurses and teachers, the researchers find that "the years to save has at least doubled and now ranges from 10 to 13 years."
As stark as those numbers are, Calhoun said they're likely an undercount.
The center's calculations are for a 3.5% down payment, since that's what the Federal Housing Administration requires for first-time buyers. The median first-time buyer actually puts down about 10% . The report also assumes families are really "stretching their savings," he said, even though many can't save at all, are forced to eat into savings or take on debt.
The Center for Responsible Lending's report highlights a sharp divide in the housing economy, exacerbated when the COVID-19 pandemic triggered a spike in inflation, mortgage rates and home prices.
"If you look at the last seven years, they have been extraordinarily good to homeowners," Calhoun said. Those who bought when prices were far lower have accumulated enormous equity as home values have shot up. Some were also able to lower their monthly payments by refinancing, as mortgage rates hit historic lows of around 2% or 3% before they spiked.
Many homeowners with low rates have decided they can't afford to move and see their mortgage payments double. That has meant fewer older adults downsizing and fewer overall putting their homes on the market, intensifying a national housing shortage.
Meanwhile, rising rents have consumed an increasing share of family incomes, according to a recent report by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. "From 2001 to 2024, renter incomes rose by 9 percent in real terms while rents rose by 30 percent," it says. This has left a quarter of renters paying more than half their income on rent and utilities.
Despite a recent softening in rental markets, a record number of renters are still considered cost burdened. Lower-income households are also hit harder by inflation, since basic goods and services make up a larger portion of their budgets.
The center calculates a starter home cost of $335,574, which is 80% of the median sales price of existing homes. And the center finds that it takes less time to save a down payment and closing costs for that in some major metropolitan areas than others — from 11 years in Houston to 24 in Los Angeles.
The report also notes that housing costs have outstripped incomes pretty much everywhere and that "the problem is even more acute in the fastest-growing rural areas than in urban areas." A recent analysis by center-left think tank Third Way found that housing construction has been unable to keep up with rural growth, creating severe pressure on affordability.
The widening housing wealth gap leaves a more privileged share of Americans who are able to buy a home. "Cash purchases are way up," Calhoun said. For younger buyers, "the overwhelming way people come up with the money is from assistance from family , the 'bank of mom and dad' and friends."
Far fewer buyers get help from down payment assistance programs, even though there are thousands of them. "The programs often run out of money," Calhoun said. "A lot of these are very small, idiosyncratic."
He'd like to see more assistance programs "to reach a broader array of people who don't have intergenerational wealth."
The center's report also calls for zoning and other reforms to boost the supply of smaller, cheaper starter homes, including duplexes, townhomes and manufactured housing. A sweeping new law passed by Congress this year aims to promote that, but the onus is on states and cities to follow up, and creating new supply will take time.
Despite all this, a related survey from the center finds that millennials and Gen Zers aspire to homeownership at the same rate as earlier generations — a "testament to the resilience of the American dream," according to Thursday's report.
It's the main way "most families generate wealth that they can pass on to the next generation," said report co-author David Silberman. "I think the case for homeownership remains really strong, despite all the trends we're pointing to in the challenges of getting there."

title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
body:
Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214 .
In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)
But it's the voters who will decide whether it works.
Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.
Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.
Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.
In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states — only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities .
In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s , when courts set the current rules.
Here's where states redistricted — or didn't.

title: A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?
body:
Rep. David Valadao, R-Calif., leaves the stage after speaking at a campaign event in Bakersfield, Calif. on Sept. 30, 2026. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
Ulises Hernandez, of Bakersfield, Calif., has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember.
But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.
This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News .
Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao's Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what's ahead.
"I couldn't eat, I couldn't drink, I couldn't do anything, and I was in pain," said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. "I'm livid."
Hernandez, 41, said Valadao "should be ashamed of himself" for voting for the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.
Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.
A pumpjack stands idle on Oct. 19 in an agricultural field in Kern County, part of California's 22nd Congressional District. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for " Medicare for All " and called out Valadao for a vote "that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families," since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.
Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said "there are no actual cuts" to Medicaid.
A protest outside U.S. Rep. David Valadao's district office in Bakersfield, California focused on healthcare costs and the congressman's vote last year to cut Medicaid. Bakersfield resident Ulises Hernandez uses a wheelchair and fears the cuts will lead to even longer wait times for care. Jackie Fortiér/KFF Health News hide caption
An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.
Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.
Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River's bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields.
Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.
Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao's district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections.
A sign from a long-shuttered restaurant in the city of Wasco, part of California's 22nd Congressional District. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
Valadao has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last remaining Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.
"This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters," Cummins said.
But California's congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao's Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.
"Valadao knows that he's on notice," Cummins said.
Stacey Augustson holds up a homemade sign during the protest outside U.S. Rep. David Valadao's district office in Bakersfield. Jackie Fortiér/KFF Health News hide caption
Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll . Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump.
On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.
"The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes," Villegas said during the debate.
On Sept. 30, Valadao held a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser. It was hosted by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber.
Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-LA) speaks to the media at a campaign event for U.S. Rep. David Valadao (R-CA), on September 30, 2026 in Bakersfield, California. Democratic nominee Randy Villegas, a college professor and former school board member, is challenging Republican incumbent David Valadao in California's 22nd Congressional District, a Central Valley swing district. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience.
After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News' questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents' Medicaid coverage, saying, "I think you are distorting the truth."
Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao's district.
They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao's votes closely. She called him "a hero for the Central Valley," citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the "breadbasket of the world."
Gas prices displayed in California's 22nd Congressional District on Oct. 17, near Fresno, California. Democrat Randy Villegas is challenging Republican incumbent David Valadao in the redrawn 22nd Congressional District, amid local concerns about federal cuts to Medicaid and food assistance, as well as intensified Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong's district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.
A few days later during the televised debate, Valadao said he was among the negotiators who secured community engagement provisions in the law, which will require certain adults on Medicaid to prove they're working or completing other activities such as job training or volunteering.
"It's not an actual cut," Valadao said. "We need people to actually put in and make a fair effort to try to cover their expenses and be a part of their community. This is not an unreasonable ask."
In a sign of how vital this district is, Republicans and Democrats have each booked more than $16 million in ads here through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact.
"When you start getting over $10 million of spending total in the district, I would say that that's pretty high," Cummins said.
Some of the ads are reaching voters in unexpected ways.
Outside a local library, Seslie Maese, a stay-at-home mom from Bakersfield, said her 7-year-old, who often watches Lego videos on YouTube, runs to her whenever a certain ad plays.
"David Valadago is going on vacation again , Mom," he'll tell her, mispronouncing the congressman's name. Her son doesn't realize the ad, paid for by a Democratic political action committee, means that as a criticism.
Maese is undecided. Even though she's a registered Republican, she said what she has heard about Valadao doesn't sound positive, such as that he went back on his pledge not to cut Medicaid for vulnerable populations by voting for the federal tax-and-spending law.
For Maese, a politician who says one thing and does another is a deal-breaker.
"He just hasn't come through with anything he said," she said, "especially since he cut off a lot of Medicaid."
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KFF Health News , a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Beskrestnov: Russians attack central Kyiv with Iskander carrying cluster warhead
body:
Russian occupiers used Iskander ballistic missile with a cluster warhead to strike the center of Kyiv on Thursday night, reported Serhiy Flash Beskrestnov, Advisor to the President of Ukraine on Defense Technologies, expressing conviction that this was done not for a military purpose, but to injure as many civilians as possible.
"Tonight, Russia attacked the historic center of Kyiv with Iskander ballistic missile carrying a K5 cluster warhead. This warhead explodes above ground and is used specifically for maximum destruction of personnel and equipment over an area of 400 by 400 meters. 58 bomblets explode in the air. This strike was not carried out for military purposes. The goal was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible," Beskrestnov wrote on Facebook on Thursday morning.
As reported, as a result of the massive Russian strike on Kyiv on Thursday night, October 22, consequences were recorded in six of the capital's ten administrative districts. One death and 24 injuries were reported, with 16 of them hospitalized.
According to the Air Force, the Russian occupiers launched a massive combined strike on Ukraine overnight using Iskander-M/S-400/Zircon/Onyx missiles and 210 attack UAVs and decoy drones. The main direction of the strike was Kyiv. As of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down and suppressed 181 enemy UAVs (including 87 jet-powered ones), but hits were recorded at 32 locations, along with falling debris at eight locations.

title: Civil Society Urges INEC To Clarify Voting Arrangements For IDPs In Zamfara
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has been urged to make adequate provisions to ensure that internally displaced persons (IDPs) are not disenfranchised in the 2027 general elections. The call was made during a stakeholders’ meeting organised by INEC in Zamfara State, held at the commission’s office in Gusau. The meeting, which brought together political party representatives, civil society organisations, the media and groups representing persons with disabilities, aimed to provide updates on INEC’s preparations for the 2027 general elections. Speaking at the meeting, the Zamfara State Resident Electoral Commissioner disclosed that the state recorded 313,115 registrations under the Continuous Voter Registration exercise as of August 2026. He said the figure represented approximately 16.04 per cent of the 1,952,060 registered voters recorded in the state during the 2023 general elections. On the collection of Permanent Voter Cards, Dr. Isah said the exercise would continue at INEC offices across the 14 local government areas following the conclusion of ward-level collection on October 15, 2026. Meanwhile, a member of the Zamfara State Civil Society Organisations, Ibrahim Tudu, called on INEC to clarify how internally displaced persons living in host communities would participate in the forthcoming elections. He noted that some displaced persons were residing in Gusau, while others were scattered across different communities, stressing the need for clear guidelines on how they could vote using their existing Permanent Voter Cards. Similarly, the Chairman of the Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities in Zamfara State, Bilyaminu Umar, appealed to INEC to ensure fair representation of persons with disabilities in the recruitment of ad hoc election personnel. The association said inclusive recruitment would provide opportunities for persons with disabilities to participate actively in the electoral process. The meeting also featured questions and contributions from participants, with INEC officials providing responses and clarifications on issues raised concerning preparations for the 2027 general elections. The post Civil Society Urges INEC To Clarify Voting Arrangements For IDPs In Zamfara appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukraine to be able to buy military supplies via NATO agency: report
body: NATO will allow Ukraine to buy weapons, ammunition and military equipment via its centralized procurement agency, potentially allowing Kyiv to obtain defense supplies faster and more cheaply, the Financial Times reported on Thursday. “It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services and access to established industrial base,” the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) director of support to operations, Jacqueline Borsboom, told the FT. The deal comes amid worsening U.S.-Ukraine relations since U.S. President Donald Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia this month to lower U.S. fuel prices. Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and its use of the Starshield satellite system, though Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said a meeting in Oslo on Tuesday had agreed to resolve those issues.

title: How is the Swedish drone industry doing?
body:
Industry Survey of Drone Operators 2026 – Transportföretagen and Svenska Drönarnätverket (the Swedish Drone Network)
The Swedish drone industry is maturing. Profitability has improved significantly in the professional drone sector, regulatory compliance has increased markedly, and views on the industry’s development are more positive than last year. The industry still consists largely of small operators: most have fewer than ten employees and a similarly small number of drone pilots, but both profitability and confidence in the future are clearly improving.
However, the positive development is unevenly distributed. Advanced drone operations—those in the Specific and Certified categories—are experiencing worsening conditions across several of the most important barriers, while the rest of the industry is experiencing some relief.
Waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency are seen as an increasingly serious obstacle by this group, during the same period in which they are becoming a less significant obstacle for the Open category. Advanced operators now rate waiting times as almost twice as serious a barrier as Open-category operators do.
The proportion of operators in the advanced category has not grown either. Official permit statistics show that Sweden is well behind Denmark, Norway and Finland in the number of operational authorisations per registered operator, despite otherwise normal interest in drones. The bottleneck is therefore not a lack of demand, but the step from the Open category to advanced operations.
Permits for disseminating aerial images and video remain the industry’s single largest obstacle. This particularly affects the media, photography and film sector, one of the largest in terms of number of practitioners, but also the most pessimistic about the future.
The remaining obstacles fall into two clear patterns. Permits for disseminating images and video weigh most heavily on image- and media-producing businesses, while waiting times and the design of regulations weigh most heavily on more technical and institutional sectors and on advanced drone operations.
A shortage of skills is not a major problem for the industry as a whole. Where shortages exist, they primarily concern pilots rather than advanced technical expertise. Customers’ knowledge of both drone services and the applicable rules remains low among a significant proportion of customers, an area where the industry itself has good opportunities to make a difference.
The purpose of the survey is to provide a recurring picture of how Sweden’s drone industry is developing and to serve as a basis for decision-makers in government, public authorities, the public sector and the industry itself. The report is based on the annual industry survey conducted by Transportföretagen and Svenska Drönarnätverket, sent to all registered drone operators that are organisations, using the Swedish Transport Agency’s register. The 2026 survey was conducted from 25 June to 3 August, following up on the 2025 survey (3 June–2 July). The analysis of the survey responses and preparation of this report were carried out with the help of AI. Survey details:  Organisations invited: 3,560 in 2025; 3,834 in 2026.
 Responses: 265 in 2025; 378 in 2026.  Response rate: 7.4% in 2025; 9.9% in 2026.
The register grew by 7.7% between the two years, independently of survey responses, and the same sampling frame was used in both years. The 2026 survey is substantially more extensive than the 2025 survey, with a revised industry classification (a harmonisation key makes comparison possible) and several new sets of questions, including respondents’ roles in the drone ecosystem, BVLOS status and skills needs by role.
Revenue per flight hour and electronic visibility were included in 2025 but not in 2026.
Several questions were answered by only a subset of respondents, as determined by the survey’s routing logic; the base is stated separately for each question.
The margin of error is approximately eight percentage points when comparing the full samples, and considerably larger for year-on-year comparisons in the Specific/Certified category. Results for that segment should therefore be read as indicative of direction.
The report is descriptive throughout, without formal significance testing, and is based on respondents’ own estimates rather than verified figures. This applies particularly to regulatory compliance. In the industry section, “Other industry” responses were reclassified based on a pattern in free-text responses relating to media, photography and film. This is an analytical interpretation rather than an original response category. “Open category” refers to flight categories A1 to A3. “Specific/Certified category”, referred to in this report as “advanced drone operations”, covers an operator declaration, an operational authorisation (SORA), a LUC or the Certified category. This is the strategically most important but smallest segment in the report (18 respondents in 2025 and 21 in 2026). Private companies in which drones account for at least 10% of activity are referred to as the “professional drone industry” (91 organisations).
EXAMPLES OF DRONE TECHNOLOGY IN USE Example A — Delivery of a defibrillator Drones are now often used in emergency services and, in several places in Sweden, to rapidly deliver a defibrillator when someone suffers a cardiac arrest. Example B — Railway inspection Work that previously took two people two weeks on the tracks can now be completed in a day and a half by one person and one drone, with better data. Example C — Precision spraying of crops Agriculture and forestry are moving from data-driven drone analysis to precision spraying and fertilisation of each individual plant. Example D — Infrastructure inspection One of Sweden’s most successful companies automatically inspects power lines across Europe and North America using drones. Example E — Drone detection Interest in and demand for detecting and identifying drones is growing rapidly. Example F — Wind turbine inspection and repair An innovative solution to the challenge of maintaining wind turbine rotor blades is to use a drone to lift a robot into place and attach it. Example G — Building façade inspection Different types of sensors can be used to detect defects in a structure.
Example H — Firefighting at height Large quadcopters capable of carrying more than 500 kg are being built in Sweden and could, for example, be used for firefighting. Example I — Traffic monitoring In addition to inspecting wear on bridges and road surfaces, traffic engineers can analyse traffic flows and intersections using drones. Example J — Returning ash to forests Forestry uses drones in several ways to improve sustainability, including returning ash to forest land. Example K — Film and photography Photography and filming are among the most common uses of drones, capturing everything from weddings and homes for sale to events from an aerial perspective.
Four out of five respondents primarily fly in the Open category (A1–A3), while 5.6% fly in the Specific or Certified category—the advanced drone operations described in this report. The remaining just under 13.5% report a national permit or are unsure which category they fly in.
The distribution of drone classes follows the same pattern. Lighter, CE-marked drones in the lower weight classes dominate in the Open category, while heavier and more advanced equipment is more common in advanced operations. This is discussed further in a later chapter.
Recruitment difficulties are relatively uncommon in the industry as a whole. Among organisations with at least one drone pilot, 9.1% report difficulty recruiting people with the right drone skills, while 90.9% do not experience such difficulties. The question was shown only to organisations with at least one pilot. A total of 5.8% of all respondents have no pilot and are therefore not included in that figure. Expectations for staffing over the next three months are mostly stable. Eight in ten expect staffing levels to remain unchanged, while just over one in ten expect an increase. Only a few expect their workforce to shrink. Pilots are the most sought-after skill Among organisations that do experience recruitment difficulties—a smaller group of 21 organisations—the picture is clearer. The main shortage is pilots: two thirds are looking for Open-category pilots and one third for pilots in the Specific/Certified category. Next come a person responsible for authorisations or regulatory affairs, a role sought by about one in five, probably linked to the administrative burden described in the chapter on barriers and regulation. AI development, SORA risk analysis and instructors received no responses in this year’s survey, while technical specialist roles such as software development, GIS and LiDAR were each sought by individual organisations. Skills missing or needing recruitment:  Open-category pilots: 66.7%.  Specific/Certified-category pilots: 33.3%.  Authorisation/regulatory specialist: 19.0%.  Drone technician: 14.3%.  Sales/business development: 14.3%.  Software developer: 9.5%.  Electronics/hardware engineer: 9.5%.  GIS specialist: 9.5%.  Image analyst: 9.5%.  Telecoms: 9.5%.  LiDAR specialist: 9.5%.  Security/counter-drone personnel: 9.5%.  Project manager: 9.5%.  Legal expertise: 9.5%.  UTM/air traffic management: 4.8%. Expected demand for advanced pilot skills It is reasonable to expect demand for pilots in the Specific and Certified categories to increase as the Swedish Transport Agency’s processing times shorten and more operators move into advanced drone operations. Already, one third of organisations with recruitment difficulties are seeking such pilots, and waiting times are a barrier that has grown particularly in this segment (Chapter 6). This is an assumption, not a measured result. The evidence base is small and should be treated as indicative rather than statistically conclusive. Even so, the gap between demand for pilots and demand for other roles is so large that the conclusion is likely to hold. The skill most in demand in today’s drone industry is basic flying ability, not advanced technical specialist knowledge.
followed by the design of unmanned aviation regulations (2.67) and waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency (2.25). Access to airspace, a new question this year, also scores relatively highly (2.22). At the lower end of the scale are shortages of skills and access to training, both below 1.8. Eight of the ten barriers can be compared with last year. The overall picture is that most are seen as less significant now than in 2025. The score for image/video dissemination permits fell from 3.73 to 3.32; regulatory design fell from 3.00 to 2.67; and waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency fell from 2.51 to 2.25. The same pattern applies to GDPR, the Camera Surveillance Act and illegal competition. Shortages of capital and skills were rated almost the same in both years. The fact that barriers are perceived as less significant across the industry is positive, but the picture is not uniform. Some parts of the industry, primarily advanced drone operations, see the same issues as greater obstacles over the same period. This is covered in more detail in the chapter on the Specific and Certified categories. Barriers to operations, average scores (2026; 2025 where available):  Waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency: 2.25; 2.51.  Regulatory design: 2.67; 3.00.  Image/video dissemination permits: 3.32; 3.73.  GDPR: 2.11; 2.39.  Camera Surveillance Act: 1.88; 2.22.  Shortage of capital: 1.80; 1.84.  Shortage of skills: 1.72; 1.82.  Illegal competition: 1.82; 2.10.  Access to airspace: 2.22 in 2026.  Access to training: below 1.8. Free-text responses are consistent with the scores on image/video dissemination permits and waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency. Several respondents describe processing times of several weeks, sometimes more than a month, and say that assignments have been lost or delayed because of waiting. Several also mention that being billed per hour of processing makes the cost difficult to predict.
Five per cent of all organisations have been inspected by a supervisory authority in relation to their drone authorisations, down from 12.5% in 2025. A new answer option, “don’t know or not applicable”, was not available last year and was selected by 6.6%, so the figures are not fully comparable between years. Customers’ knowledge remains a weakness The question was asked only of private companies, excluding organisations whose main role is in-house operations, research or exercising public authority, giving 289 respondents. Half believe customers’ general knowledge of drone services is low or very low, and almost six in ten say customers’ understanding of what is legal and illegal is low or very low.
operators are inspected by supervisory authorities almost four times as often: 19% compared with 5%, which is to be expected given that their operations are more complex and therefore attract more attention. Which industries? Agriculture and forestry, and real estate, are over-represented compared with the Open category; each accounts for six of the 21 respondents, with construction close behind. This is plausible because large-scale flying over sparsely populated areas, common in agriculture and forestry, fits the profile of the advanced category. The figures should nevertheless be treated as indicative rather than conclusive. Summary Despite limited growth in its share of the industry and significantly greater barriers on several fronts, advanced drone operations show stronger profitability trends and a more positive outlook than the rest of the industry, as reported in Chapters 2 and 8. This suggests that underlying demand is strong, but administrative obstacles—primarily waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency and the design of regulations—risk slowing the part of the industry with the greatest growth potential. The next chapter compares Sweden with other countries.
 VisionAir Production AB, with the broadest privileges of the three, including BVLOS flights over populated areas.  Fem D Konsulterna AB, whose authorisation is limited to flights within visual line of sight. Norway has twice as many certificate holders despite having a substantially smaller registered operator base. Overall, the international comparison independently supports the conclusion of the previous chapter: advanced drone operations in Sweden are limited, not because interest is lacking, but because fewer operators make it through the authorisation process to the more demanding privileges.
The overall picture is positive. Profitability has improved significantly in the professional drone industry, regulatory compliance has increased markedly, and views on the industry’s development are more positive than last year. It is reasonable to believe that these three trends are connected. A maturing, more profitable industry also invests more in regulatory compliance, reinforced by the fact that regulatory breaches became punishable during the survey period. However, this picture does not apply equally across the whole industry. Advanced drone operations—the Specific and Certified categories—are experiencing the opposite trend in several of the most important barriers, while the rest of the industry is seeing some relief. The media, photography and film sector is similarly an outlier in its outlook for the future: it is the most pessimistic sector even though it is one of the largest in terms of practitioners. On average, the industry is doing better, but the improvement is uneven. It is absent precisely in the part of the industry with the greatest growth potential. The regulatory burden is specific, not general A recurring pattern is that different parts of the industry face different kinds of obstacles. Image/video dissemination permits are the dominant barrier for image- and media-producing businesses, construction, real estate, consulting, IT and, especially, media, photography and film. Waiting times at the Swedish Transport Agency are particularly significant for advanced drone operations, where they are the single largest barrier. The design of unmanned aviation regulations is instead the most important barrier for more technical and institutional sectors such as agriculture, defence and energy. This suggests that general rhetoric about “reducing the regulatory burden” is less effective than targeted action addressing the specific bottlenecks affecting different parts of the industry. Sweden is losing ground where it matters most The international comparison independently supports this picture. Sweden has a normal proportion of registered drone operators compared with its neighbours, but substantially fewer operational authorisations in the Specific category per operator. What separates Sweden from Denmark, Norway and Finland is therefore not declining interest in drones, but the ability to move from the Open category to advanced operations. This coincides with the finding in Chapter 3 that the skills needed by the relatively small group of organisations experiencing recruitment difficulties are primarily pilots, including pilots in the Specific and Certified categories. Shorter processing times and more operators in the advanced category would likely reinforce one another: more authorisations create more assignments, increasing demand for pilots in that category.
Public authorities The Swedish Transport Agency should immediately make its processing more efficient and clear the current backlog, which the agency itself says stands at eight months. Applications for operational authorisations should be digitised and automated to enable faster processing and improve competitiveness. The agency should actively drive progress, learn from other countries and work to ensure that regulatory development at European and global level better reflects Swedish conditions: a large, sparsely populated country whose circumstances differ from those of many other EU states. Cooperation with corresponding authorities in the Nordic neighbouring countries should also increase, creating more consistent conditions regardless of which Nordic country drone operations take place in. Greater cooperation with the industry, both on working methods and regulatory development, is another way to strengthen the process. The authority should also investigate why so many operators stop at the simplest route into the advanced category—the STS declaration—instead of proceeding to more comprehensive operational authorisations, despite Sweden already lagging behind the rest of the Nordic region. Industry The industry should work to strengthen the supply of pilots qualified for the Specific category. It should also continue collecting concrete data on cases, waiting times and volumes to support continued engagement with public authorities and policy-makers. The industry should help improve customers’ knowledge of both what drone services can be used for and what is permitted under the regulations. The survey shows that half of customers have low or very low knowledge of drone services, and nearly six in ten have low or very low understanding of what is legal and illegal.

title: NPC Seeks Unified System For Marriage, Divorce Registration As N’ east Zonal Consultation Opens In Adamawa
body: Daji Sani in Yola The National Population Commission (NPC) has commenced moves to harmonize marriage and divorce registration in Nigeria with the opening of the North-East Zonal Consultation on the Draft Harmonized Protocol for Marriage and Divorce Registration. The consultation, held at the City Green Hotel in Yola, Adamawa State, brought together stakeholders from the six states of the North-east geopolitical zone for a two-day review of the draft framework aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system. Declaring the consultation open on Wednesday, the Commissioner Overseeing the Chairman’s Office of the NPC and Hon. Federal Commissioner for Plateau State, Hon. (Mrs.) Mary Ishaya Afan, who was represented by Mr. Teniola Caxton, said the exercise marks an important stage in developing a unified and functional civil registration system in the country. Mrs. Afan said marriage and divorce are more than social or cultural events, describing them as significant legal acts that create rights and obligations with far-reaching implications for individuals, families and communities. According to her, proper notification, registration and certification provide a basis for protecting rights relating to spousal support, child custody, inheritance, property and other legal entitlements, while also generating vital statistics for planning, social protection and service delivery. She noted that such statistics are required for evidence-based planning, prevention of child marriage, promotion of gender equality and effective delivery of public services across the country. The commissioner lamented that despite their importance, marriage and divorce registration in Nigeria have remained fragmented, with different institutions operating different procedures, forms and record-keeping arrangements. She listed the institutions to include the NPC, the judiciary, Ministries of Interior and Justice, local governments, faith-based organizations and traditional institutions, adding that processes remain largely paper-based with limited coordination and data integration. Afan explained that it was against this background that the commission, in collaboration with relevant stakeholders and development partners, developed the Draft Harmonized Protocol at a national workshop held in July 2025 at the United Nations House in Abuja. She said the Draft Protocol seeks to establish common procedures, clarify institutional mandates and responsibilities, strengthen data management within the electronic CRVS system including the VITALREG platform, and recognize Nigeria’s statutory, customary, Islamic and Christian marriage systems, while also providing for digitization, decentralization and data protection. Also speaking at the stakeholders’ event, the Deputy Director of Civil Registration of the NPC, Mrs. Obodo Adaku, recalled that the NPC is statutorily mandated to register births, deaths, stillbirths, marriages and divorces across the country. Mrs. Adaku said many Nigerians who are married or divorced do not have their unions officially registered, a gap the commission is determined to close through the harmonized framework. She said the NPC is aimed at strengthening the registration of all categories of marriages and divorces to ensure every union has legal backing and can be defended where necessary. She added that proper registration will give married couples and divorced persons the legal rights to seek redress, claim entitlements and protect the interests of children and families in accordance with the law.

title: ‘We Outplayed Them’: Ukraine Claims First Underground Counteroffensive
body:
With no GPS, no daylight, and Russian positions overhead, Ukrainian troops pushed through more than 15 kilometers (9 miles) of underground infrastructure before emerging behind enemy lines near Kupiansk.
The operation, code-named Veles, used concealed underground routes to bypass Russian positions in northeastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, according to a press release from the National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps, which commanded the operation.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The operation’s name, Veles, refers to a Slavic deity associated with the underworld – a reference to the concealed route Ukrainian troops used to reach Russian positions.
The corps said the maneuver helped prevent Russian troops from moving into the rear of Ukrainian positions around Kupiansk. More than 30 Russian personnel were captured, while Russian losses exceeded 100.
The distance of more than 15 kilometers (9 miles) refers to the troops’ underground movement, rather than a confirmed advance of the front line by that distance.
“Russians believed underground infrastructure was their exclusive tool for bypassing our defenses,” Brig. Gen. Ihor Oboliensky, commander of the Khartiia Corps, said in the statement. “We studied their experience, outplayed them on their own ground, and turned that threat into an advantage for our counteroffensive.”
The operation required soldiers to navigate confined spaces without GPS, daylight, or reliable conventional radio communications. Emerging above ground meant entering combat under difficult conditions.
Engineers, combat engineers, and support personnel prepared the underground route. Troops underwent physical and psychological preparation for operating in enclosed spaces, while the corps employed its own systems for navigation, communications, and sustaining personnel underground.
Above ground, other Ukrainian units advanced in coordination with the underground force. Drone operations, including strikes by the 429th Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade, were coordinated through a joint center, according to the corps.
The intended effect was to confront Russian troops with simultaneous threats from different directions: Ukrainian forces approaching on the surface while another contingent emerged behind their positions.
“Veles proves that there is no positional deadlock for those who possess initiative and technology,” Obolienskyi said. “Our troops traveled 15 kilometers [9 miles] underground, where no army in the world has yet advanced, and we will continue driving the enemy from our land.”
Khartiia described Veles as the world’s first full-scale underground counteroffensive maneuver.
The operation involved a grouping under the headquarters of the 2nd Khartiia Corps.
Participating forces included the National Guard’s 13th Khartiia Brigade, the 23rd R.U.G. Assault Regiment, the 21st Lava Unmanned Systems Regiment, and the Achilles drone brigade, according to the statement.
Units of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) also participated, including the Freedom of Russia Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps. The release listed additional Ukrainian defense units without identifying them.
Khartiia said the operation formed another stage of its campaign to reclaim occupied parts of the Kharkiv region and disrupted a Russian effort to reach the rear of Kupiansk.
The formation began as a volunteer territorial defense unit in 2022, became a National Guard brigade in 2023, and later formed the basis of the 2nd Khartiia Corps, established in April 2025.
Kateryna investigates today's most important topics, from geopolitical challenges and defense strategies to stories that change the course of events. She explores the secrets of Ukraine's intelligence services and shows the hidden side of global events. Her passion is uncovering secrets that change history. Born and lives in Kyiv.

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
body: Ukraine’s capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was “ready in principle” to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said. The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday – a day after meeting Ukraine’s leader. Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles. Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: “The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we’re getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we’ve been.” The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this. Trump’s special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday. It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that “strong” security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed. Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very “useful”. Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war. Russia blamed last month’s “massive” Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption. Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. Speaking to reporters after Wednesday’s talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. He stressed that the talks must focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict.” Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a “strategic initiative”. Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin’s claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front. On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line. “We call it ‘ceasefire’ or ‘stop killings’ like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today,” he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this. Witkoff described the latest talks as “constructive”, while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: “There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come.” The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US. Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently “for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine”. He has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia – allowing it to release tonnes of diesel “to the American and global marketplace”. That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier. Zelensky – and Ukraine’s European allies – criticised Trump’s move. Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as “scandalous”, and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing “works now”. Ukraine’s military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia. US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation. Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine. Trump said the former teacher was “on his way back home” and “there was no ‘swap’ necessary”, while Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian” for agreeing the release. When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: “I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. “Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family.”

title: Air Ghana Foundation commissions 14-seater toilet facility at Attakrom Amanfro
body: Air Ghana Limited, through the Air Ghana Foundation, has commissioned and handed over a 14-seater community toilet facility to residents of Attakrom Amanfro in the Eastern Region. The facility, constructed as part of the company’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programme, is expected to improve sanitation and public health in the predominantly pineapple-farming community. The commissioning ceremony was attended by the chief and people of Attakrom Amanfro, local authorities, the wife of Air Ghana’s late founder, Mrs Karen Traboulsi, and staff of the company. Speaking at the ceremony, Chief Executive Officer of Air Ghana, Karim Michael Traboulsi, said the project was undertaken in memory of his late father, Marwan Traboulsi, who founded Air Ghana about 33 years ago. He said the late founder began his working life as a farmer at Insakyi, a farming community near the project area, before moving into the air cargo business. According to Mr Traboulsi, his father subsequently helped transport fruits, including pineapples, from Ghana to European markets. He said the sanitation project therefore held special significance because of its connection to his father’s background in agriculture and Air Ghana’s role in facilitating the export of Ghanaian produce. Community identified need Chief Operating Officer of Air Ghana, Hans Asiedu Ansah, said the project followed consultations with the chiefs, elders, assembly member and residents of Attakrom Amanfro. He said the consultations were aimed at identifying the community’s most pressing needs, with residents identifying the need for a modern toilet facility. The Foundation subsequently committed to the project, with the sod-cutting ceremony held on May 27, 2026. Mr Ansah said the facility was completed in just over four months and handed over to the community. He said the project reflected Air Ghana Foundation’s motto, “A Shared Sky, a Shared Responsibility”, and its commitment to responding to needs identified by communities. The facility has 14 seats and includes water closets designated for older persons and persons with disabilities, while squat pans are available for other users. The company said the facility was designed to be accessible to all members of the community and would support improved sanitation practices and a cleaner environment. Community pledges maintenance The chief of Attakrom Amanfro, Nana Obirikorang Yeboah III expressed appreciation to Air Ghana for the project and pledged that the community would ensure the facility remained clean, functional and beneficial to residents. He said the community would take responsibility for maintaining the facility and protecting the investment. The ceremony was also attended by Air Ghana staff and other stakeholders, including Municipal Chief Executive Paul Osae Offei and Assembly Member Prince Apietu Appiah. Air Ghana acknowledged the contribution of Alister Djimatey, whose guidance and consultation supported the CSR team during the project. The company also expressed appreciation to the Municipal Chief Executive and his team for assistance with the necessary permits and support throughout the project. Air Ghana said the project formed part of its broader commitment to community development and responsible corporate citizenship.

title: Russian forces spreading false claims of capturing settlements in Zaporizhzhia region – military
body:
Meanwhile, Vozdvyzhivka, Mala Tokmachka and Omelnyk remain under the control of the Ukrainian Defense Forces. Russian positions are about 23 kilometers from Zaporizhzhia, not five kilometers as claimed by the Russian military command.
Anastasiia Shevchenko, Deputy Spokesperson for the Operation Task Force South, said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Russian claims of significant advances in the Zaporizhzhia region have practically become a meme. The enemy regularly reports to their senior military command that they have supposedly captured settlements and achieved battlefield successes, but the actual situation is entirely different,” she said.
According to Shevchenko, late last week, Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov told the Russian leadership that Russian troops were allegedly just five kilometers from Zaporizhzhia and were already striking Ukrainian Defense Forces positions within the city itself. These claims, however, are false: according to the Ukrainian side, Russian forces remain 23 kilometers from the regional capital.
“Similarly, the Russians regularly claim to have captured Vozdvyzhivka and Mala Tokmachka. But Vozdvyzhivka remains under the control of the Ukrainian Defense Forces, including units of the Operation Task Force South. Mala Tokmachka is also still held by our defenders,” the Deputy Spokesperson emphasized.
She described the situation in Vozdvyzhivka as particularly telling, noting that Russian forces have been trying to capture the settlement for more than six months. According to available information, during that time, command of Russian assault units has changed, as have the units directly conducting assault operations in this sector. Despite these changes, the enemy has still failed to achieve their objective.
“So, their only way out is to submit false reports,” Shevchenko explained.
She also said that on October 20, Russian propaganda media reported the alleged capture of Omelnyk in the Orikhiv sector. According to the Ukrainian side, a two-person Russian infiltration group did enter the settlement and staged a conspicuous flag display.
“Our unmanned systems successfully eliminated the enemy along with their tricolor flag. Therefore, reports that Omelnyk has been captured are also false. The Ukrainian Defense Forces have full control of the settlement,” she stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, claims that Russian troops could directly enter Zaporizhzhia in the winter of 2026 are unfounded.
Photo: Anastasiia Shevchenko, Deputy Spokesperson for the Operation Task Force South

title: Russian attacks damage Epicentr hypermarket, Retail Park Pochaina in Kyiv
body:
A Russian attack on the capital overnight into Thursday damaged an Epicentr hypermarket and the Retail Park Pochaina shopping complex.

According to photographs published in the media, the most extensive damage was sustained by the premises of JYSK, Puma, Colin's and Nova Poshta (NP) stores, as well as the office of Nhood Ukraine, the management company of the retail park.

Nhood Ukraine declined to comment to Interfax-Ukraine on the losses for the time being.

The press service of Auchan told the agency that the facade and entrance area of the Auchan Pochaina store had sustained minor damage and that the store was operating as usual.
