title: Advans Ghana, Group leadership visit BoG Governor
body: Advans Group and Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Ltd., have reaffirmed their commitment to responsible finance and financial inclusion following a courtesy call on the Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr. Johnson P. Asiama during Advans Group Board Week 2026 from 6 th October to 14 th October 2026. The meeting brought together senior executives and board members of Advans Group and Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Ltd. to discuss developments in the financial services industry, regulatory priorities and the role of savings and loans institutions in expanding access to finance. The delegation commended the Bank of Ghana for its leadership and the introduction of regulatory reforms aimed at strengthening the country’s financial sector. The Governor and his team, in turn, acknowledged Advans Ghana’s contribution to the industry, recognising it as one of the leading and best-performing savings and loans companies in the country. Discussions also covered the Bank of Ghana’s liquidity framework and its implications for regulated financial institutions, highlighting the importance of constructive engagement between regulators and industry players. Dr. Asiama said effective collaboration between the regulator and financial institutions was important in maintaining financial stability while broadening access to financial services. Steven Duchatelle, Chief Executive Officer of Advans International, said the visit reinforced the Group’s commitment to maintaining strong relationships with regulators in its markets. “Our engagement with the Bank of Ghana reflects our commitment to responsible finance, sound governance and sustainable growth. We value the opportunity to exchange perspectives on developments in the financial sector and reaffirm our support for expanding access to appropriate financial services,” he said. Advans Group operates across multiple markets, providing financial services to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, entrepreneurs and individuals who face barriers to accessing conventional banking services. Guillaume Valence, Managing Director of Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Ltd., said the institution would continue to work within the country’s regulatory framework while supporting customers with financial services tailored to their needs. “A strong relationship with the regulator is essential to sustainable growth. We remain committed to responsible lending, sound risk management and expanding access to finance for individuals and businesses, while contributing to the stability and development of Ghana’s financial sector,” he said. BoG Governor, Dr. Johnson Asiama in discussion with Advans leadership The courtesy call formed part of Advans Group Board Week 2026, which brought together Group leadership, board and Management members from all the subsidiaries and group office for strategic engagement and review of its operations. There were members from Advans subsidiaries in Cameroon, Cote D’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Nigeria, and Tunisia. The delegation comprised of Cyrille Arnould, Chairman of Advans Group Board, Advans SA; Claude Falgon, Founder and Board Member, Advans SA; Steven Duchatelle, Chief Executive Officer, Advans International; Brieuc Cardon, Business Development Director, Advans International; Eli Hini, Chairman of the Board, Advans Ghana; Guillaume Valence, Chief Executive Officer, Advans Ghana; Kwame Owusu-Boateng, Deputy Chief Executive Officer, Advans Ghana; and Rufina Acquah, Chief Legal Officer and Board Secretary, Advans Ghana. About Advans Ghana Advans Ghana Savings and Loans Limited is a financial institution focused on providing accessible and tailored financial solutions to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) and individuals in Ghana. Incorporated in 2007 and commencing operations in 2008, the company is licensed by the Bank of Ghana and is a subsidiary of the Advans Group, headquartered in Europe. Advans Ghana offers a range of financial services, including loans, savings and investment products, current accounts and digital banking solutions, designed to support business growth, financial inclusion and the evolving needs of its customers. The institution also provides non-financial services in the form of business advisory services and financial literacy for its clients. The company currently operates 21 branches across nine regions of Ghana and serves almost 160,000 clients. Advans Ghana is committed to responsible and client-focused financial and non-financial services, with a particular focus on supporting the sustainable growth of MSMEs and expanding access to finance for underserved segments of the market.

title: Achieving AI-style reasoning without an LLM
body:
In the last post we introduced Minotaur, an AI that reasons with no language model and no GPU. This post looks at why language models think the way people do, at what was tried before them and where each attempt stopped, and at how Minotaur’s brain does the same kinds of reasoning differently: not by imitating how people write their thinking down, but by working on the structure of the system it’s reasoning about.
In the last post we introduced Minotaur , an AI architecture built on ELC that works out its answers by measuring rather than predicting. We showed it checking real regulations against records of how they were applied: finding which organisation broke a rule, by how much and where, and telling a broken rule from a badly recorded measurement.
Checking rules against records is one kind of thinking. Today’s language models are admired for something broader: they can deduce, explain, diagnose, weigh a hypothesis, imagine what would have happened if things had been different, and change their minds when told something new. Can a machine with no language model, and no GPU, do all of that?
A large language model is trained to predict the next word of a piece of text. It learns this from an enormous amount of writing, from books, papers, textbooks, forums and code, by doing it trillions of times on thousands of GPUs.
To predict the next word of a proof, you have to follow the proof. To predict the next line of a doctor’s notes, you have to follow the diagnosis. Much of the writing in the world is people thinking on paper, so a model that gets very good at continuing it ends up very good at imitating the thinking. That’s why simply asking a model to “think step by step” makes its answers better.
So a language model mirrors the way people think. It inherits our strengths: explaining, drawing analogies, using common sense, taking a question in ordinary words. Researchers have also found that it inherits our weaknesses. Like people, language models find a logical argument easier to accept when its conclusion sounds believable, and harder when it doesn’t. Their answers can shift with how a question is framed or the order things are put in. And like ours, its explanations are often written after the fact, not a record of how the answer was reached.
The model never sees the world, only our words about it.
It does mean that if you want reasoning that can be checked, replayed and certified, imitating the way people write their thinking down may not be the best place to start. Exact, checkable reasoning was what most approaches to AI before language models were trying for.
People tried to build machines that reason for some sixty years before language models. Each attempt worked up to a point and then stopped, and where they stopped explains why we ended up with language models.
In 1956 Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon built the Logic Theorist , a program that proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell’s Principia Mathematica . Their next program, the General Problem Solver , tried to do the same for any problem that could be written as a starting point, a goal and a set of moves. The idea was that reasoning is search: try the possible steps until you reach the goal.
It worked on puzzles. On real problems the number of possible steps grows so fast that no computer could search them. In 1973 the Lighthill report to the British government named this the combinatorial explosion , and funding in Britain was cut sharply.
The answer in the 1970s was the expert system , which gave the machine knowledge instead of search: hundreds or thousands of hand-written rules of the form if this, then that , collected from human experts. MYCIN , built at Stanford, recommended antibiotics for serious infections, and in a 1979 evaluation its advice compared well with that of specialists. XCON , at Digital Equipment Corporation, configured computer orders and saved the company a great deal of money.
They stopped for two reasons. Every rule had to be got out of an expert’s head and written down by hand, which came to be called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck . And they were brittle: just outside what the rules covered, the system had nothing sensible to say. By the end of the 1980s the market for them had collapsed.
Logic programming aimed to have the machine reason exactly, in a proper logic. That was the bet behind Prolog , created in Marseille in 1972, and behind Japan’s Fifth Generation Computer Systems project, which ran from 1982 to 1992 and was built around logic programming.
Logic gives exact answers, and its descendants, the solvers that check whether a set of conditions can all be true at once, are now used every day to verify computer chips. But logic only reasons about what someone has written down as logic. The world doesn’t arrive in that form, and the Fifth Generation project ended without the thinking machines it had promised.
In 1984 Douglas Lenat started Cyc , an attempt to write down, by hand, the common sense that expert systems lacked: that water runs downhill, that people have mothers, that a thing can’t be in two places at once. Over the following decades its team entered millions of such facts.
It showed how large the common sense people take for granted is, and that writing it down by hand never comes to an end.
From the late 1980s, led above all by Judea Pearl , reasoning under uncertainty got a proper mathematical footing. A Bayesian network says which things affect which and how strongly, and lets a machine work out what an observation implies. Pearl went on to make precise the difference between seeing something and doing it : seeing a wet pavement suggests it rained, but hosing the pavement yourself tells you nothing about the weather. In the same years, Raymond Reiter, Johan de Kleer and Brian Williams turned diagnosis into a precise method for finding which component of a system has failed.
These are some of the best ideas in the field, and Minotaur reproduces them. But someone has to hand them the model first: the causal graph , or a description of every component. Given only a column of numbers, they can’t begin.
From 2012, neural networks trained on large amounts of data, known as deep learning , began to beat everything else at recognising images and speech. They need nothing handed to them except examples.
What they learn is a pattern, with no structure to reason on. A network that has learned how a production line behaves can predict its output. It can’t tell you that one of its inputs is a safety cut-off, or answer the question “what if that cut-off were stuck open?”, because there’s no cut-off anywhere inside it to be stuck.
Language models, built on the transformer design published in 2017, reached the public in 2022, and from 2024 began to be trained to reason step by step before answering. Language models won because they’re the one approach that needs nothing handed to it. You don’t write a model of your problem for it; you describe the problem in plain words, and it reads them.
The price is the one we discussed in the last post. The reasoning runs through hundreds of billions of weights on data-centre GPUs, and the answer comes with no certificate of how it was reached.
Each way of getting a machine to reason has had a price:
Minotaur sits in the middle. It can be given a description or learn one from data, puts it into typed roles it can reason on, and reasons exactly enough to certify each answer, on one ordinary processor core.
The ideas behind ELC are set out on the MINOS page , and the last post gave the short version. Every system, whatever it’s about, is read in three roles:
E and C never connect directly. A drive doesn’t say what is allowed, and a limit doesn’t say which drive it answers. The relation between them always has to be supplied, and supplying it is what the system’s logic is.
Each element of a system is read as a share. Of what arrives at it, some passes and some is held back, and the two always add up to the whole. At one end everything passes, at the other everything is held, and in between there is a balance point.
This is a minimal representation of a system; MINOS stands for the minimal ordinal representation of systems. A whole boiler can be read as a single element: something drives it, something constrains it, and its logic relates the two. When more detail is needed, the same reading is applied to its parts. The boiler becomes a pump, a fan, a burner and a gas valve, each an ELC element with its own drive, constraint and logic, connected so that what one element passes on becomes the next one’s drive. The description gets finer, but it never leaves the ELC format: it’s the same three roles at every scale, just more finely divided and more interconnected.
On this representation we built Minotaur’s brain.
A brain that reasons in general turned out to need two kinds of faculty, best kept apart, a little like the two hemispheres of a human brain.
The ELC side holds the system being reasoned about, as a network of ELC elements. It has exactly one operation, settling , described below. It can also learn a system it has never been told about, from records of what that system did. By design, it contains no counting, no exact arithmetic and no matching of text. Its results are measured : the network came to rest, or it didn’t, to within a stated tolerance.
The exact side is a calculator. It reads a description of a system, lists every case when every case has to be checked, does exact arithmetic and checks results. Its results are exact : true in every case, or here is a case where it isn’t.
Nothing passes between the two sides except through a named, one-way crossing :
Every crossing is recorded, along with the certificate it carries. When an answer rests on several steps, it carries the weakest certificate among them.
That record is also the brain’s chain of thought. When a language model shows its reasoning, it writes a new piece of text. When Minotaur shows its reasoning, it shows the crossings it actually made, in order.
Picture the network as a set of nodes, each holding a share between “all passed” and “all held”, joined along the lines ELC allows: drives into logic, constraints into logic, logic on to logic and to constraints. Never drives straight to constraints, or back.
To ask a question, you say what each node is doing:
The rest follow their laws. Then the network settles, a little like water finding its level:
If the stress falls to almost nothing and every fact reads back as it was held, the world closes : there’s a way for things to be that fits everything given. If no setting of the holes will close it, the stress says where the contradiction sits.
Every kind of reasoning is the same settle, asked differently. What changes is only which nodes are held, which are cut and which are left free.
The ELC side has no special code for any of these kinds of reasoning. Where an answer needs every case checked, as deduction does, the exact side lists the cases and the ELC side settles each one. So deduction gets an exact certificate, because no case is left out.
All of the systems below were written in a simple format that lists a system’s drives, constraints and laws. The first two were written by us for development. The others were written by people who never saw Minotaur’s code, and we come to how they were tested afterwards.
Start with a house’s lighting. The supply comes in through a main breaker and splits into a hall circuit and a kitchen circuit, each with its own fuse, switch and bulb, and the kitchen circuit also feeds a socket and a kettle. All the switches are on. The kitchen lamp is lit and the hall lamp is dark. What has failed?
The exact side supposes, one at a time, that each part has failed, starting with the smallest possibilities. For each supposition, the ELC side settles the network and reports whether the world closes. Supposing nothing has failed, it doesn’t close, and the stress is at the hall lamp. Supposing the hall bulb has failed, it closes. The kitchen bulb doesn’t close. The hall fuse closes. Larger combinations that already contain one of those answers are skipped, because a smaller explanation is always better. None of the rest closes.
The answer is either the hall bulb or the hall fuse , which is what a good electrician would say. Asked for an experiment to tell the two apart, Minotaur says that no setting of the switches can: both faults leave the hall dark whatever you do. That is also correct.
The same lighting circuit answered 29 questions of every kind, and all 29 matched the answers of an independent checker. On 40 planted faults it found the exact set of possible explanations 40 times out of 40, with no false ones. The whole question file took about a second and a half.
The second system is a greenhouse watering controller, with a hidden cause in it. When it rains, the beds get wet, and the rain gauge also reads wet. When the gauge reads wet, the controller stops the pump.
Ask: if we see the gauge reading wet, are the beds wet? Minotaur holds the gauge as an observed fact, with its law intact. The misfit is carried back through the gauge to its cause, rain, and the answer is yes : the gauge says it rained, so the beds are wet.
Now ask: if we force the gauge to read wet, are the beds wet? This time the gauge is held and its own law is cut , because forcing it says nothing about what caused it. Nothing is carried back through it. The pump stops, rain stays unknown, and the answer is undetermined .
This is Pearl’s distinction between seeing and doing. In Minotaur it comes from the difference between holding a node and cutting it, not from a special rule.
The third system was written by someone outside the project, from the format alone: a home combination boiler with 30 parts, including a timer, a pump, a fan, an igniter, a flame sensor, a gas valve, and a mains supply that feeds both the fan and the pump. Here are some of the 36 questions it was asked, with Minotaur’s answers. Each one matched the independent answer key.
Saying no test exists , as in the second-to-last row, is a valid answer, and a reasoner that always proposes a test will sooner or later propose a useless one. In the last row, Minotaur doesn’t invent a single threshold; it reports the exact range the cases seen allow, and where to look next to narrow it.
Ordinary logic assumes that facts don’t change when you look at them, but a witness’s memory can. Ask a witness a leading question , “did he have a beard?” , and you can plant the beard you asked about.
The fourth system, again written by someone outside the project, was a police interview. It has a robbery, a witness, a line-up , a detective who may or may not ask leading questions, a lawyer who may or may not be present, and a video recorder. And it has a list of what each question does to the witness’s memory: a leading question about a beard plants one, a leading question about a jacket can wipe the jacket out, and picking someone in a line-up makes the witness more confident.
Minotaur handles this by reasoning over a chain of worlds . The first world is things as they happened. Each question produces the next world: the answer is read in the world before, and then whatever the question changes is reset. The whole chain is turned into one network and answered by the same settle.
In the diagram, the witness was asked twice, with leading questions, whether the robber had a beard, and answered no and then yes . Did the robber have a beard? Minotaur answers no . The first answer was the true memory, and the first question planted the beard behind the second.
Reasoning over fixed facts can’t do this. To it, “no” and then “yes” about the same fact is a contradiction, so it calls the story impossible. On the 15 questions whose answers depend on the order of asking, fixed-fact reasoning got 0 of 15 . Minotaur got 15 of 15 , and all 30 questions in all, including one in which leading questions led to a wrongful charge. The whole set took seven and a half seconds.
Everything so far started from a description of the system. The harder test is a system nobody has described.
So we gave Minotaur 400 rows of what a production line did. Each row had four readings, demand, feed, pressure and the ambient temperature, plus the line’s output. It got no laws, no diagram and no labels saying which column did what. Behind the scenes the line was driven by demand and feed, shut off by a safety cut-off when the pressure rose too high, and unaffected by the temperature. Then we broke the line, without saying how, and gave Minotaur 80 rows of what it did afterwards.
First Minotaur learned the line, into ELC’s typed roles. It found that demand and feed were drives, that pressure was a constraint that shut the line off above a certain level, and that the temperature was inert. When the network learns, the drive part and the constraint part can come out the wrong way round, each fitting the data equally well. ELC’s own algebra says how to put them back the right way round without changing anything the network does.
Then it supposed , one at a time, each kind of fault a system with those roles can have: the cut-off has moved, the cut-off is stuck open, it’s stuck shut, a drive has stopped counting. It fitted each supposition to the 80 new rows. One fitted far better than the rest: the pressure cut-off has moved to 0.557. We had planted it at 0.55.
Finally it went back out. The altered network predicted what the broken line would now do under new conditions, with an average error of 0.023, against 0.080 for the network before the fault was found.
On ten fresh lines, each with its own planted fault, Minotaur named the fault ten times out of ten and predicted the broken line’s behaviour every time, with errors between 0.002 and 0.023. Each line took about 10 to 15 seconds on one processor core, learning included.
The faults it could suppose, the cut-off has moved or a drive has gone dead , are faults of typed roles. A generic learner can fit the same 400 rows just as well, but it has no cut-off inside it to move and no drive to lose, so “what if the cut-off were stuck open?” isn’t a question it can be asked. The ELC neural network that does this learning is patent pending.
Our production line feeds a packing station, and the packing station keeps its own books, in kilograms a minute rather than shares. It was learned separately, from its own records alone.
MINOS holds that two systems framed independently can only be joined through a supplied relation between their frames, which we call a transport . So the exact side fitted one from 30 rows logged on both systems: how the line’s output shows up at the station, in the station’s units. Then Minotaur ran its conclusion about the broken line forward, through the transport, into the station: what will the station pack now?
On ten fresh pairs it predicted the station’s output ten times out of ten, with errors between 0.010 and 0.034. Leaving the transport out, and pretending the two systems speak the same units, made the predictions 2.6 to 12 times worse , every time. Asked to find a single fault that could be anywhere in either system, it found the right system and the right fault eight times out of ten.
Any new way of reasoning should first give back the old logic that we know is right. Physicists call this the correspondence principle : a new theory has to agree with the old one where the old one is secure.
So we read Aristotle’s four classical statements in ELC’s own terms. “S is P” becomes the share of S that passes into P, which MINOS writes as an angle. Every S is P is the end where everything passes. No S is P is the end where everything is held. Some S is P and some S is not P are everything short of one end or the other. Checked on every small case, 1,302 pairs of terms, every one came out right.
Then the syllogism , Aristotle’s two-premise argument such as every M is P, every S is M, so every S is P . We gave Minotaur none of the classical rules. It had only the angle, the fact that what passes and what is held always add up to the whole, and the MINOS rule for chaining two elements one after another. Out of the 256 possible forms it proved exactly the 24 that are valid, proved nothing false, and refused the other 232, each with a reason. It even said, for each argument that needs it, which term has to be non-empty for the argument to hold, which matches the classical account term by term.
One of the oldest mistakes in logic, the undistributed middle (every S is M, every P is M, so every S is P), is, in this reading, an attempt to chain two elements without a transport between their frames. It’s the same mistake, at the scale of a sentence, as leaving the transport out between the production line and the packing station.
Every result in this post was produced under the same rules:
On the police interview and the two learned systems, Minotaur matched the language model, on one ordinary processor core and with every answer certified. Where there was nothing described to start from, reasoning over fixed facts couldn’t begin.
Each of the older methods does one kind of reasoning well, in its own specialty, once it’s handed a description. Minotaur does every kind with one operation, typed and certified, on one processor.
And where the system isn’t described, ELC can’t be replaced. For every other approach, the question is what it would have to be handed to do what Minotaur did.
ELC supplies, from its form alone, what the others have to be handed: the roles of drive, constraint and logic, the places where a fault can be, and the frames and transports between systems. In the learned tests, ELC’s own algebra decided which learned part was the drive and which the constraint. Every diagnosis was a fault of a typed role. And leaving the transport out made the predictions up to twelve times worse.
A language model reasons the way people do because it learned from people writing. That has made it the best general reasoner we have, and also a reasoner that inherits our habits: confident when it shouldn’t be, swayed by framing, and unable to show what its answers rest on. The alternatives of the previous seventy years either had to be handed the model or had nothing to reason on.
Minotaur’s brain reasons in a different way. It doesn’t imitate how people write about a system; it holds the system itself in ELC’s typed roles, whether described or learned from data, and answers every kind of question with one operation: hold some things, cut some, leave some free, and settle. Every answer comes with the chain of steps it actually took and a certificate of what kind of answer it is, and gives the same result every time it’s run. Head to head on blind tests, it reached the level of a current language model, on one ordinary processor.
One network, one operation, every kind of reasoning: and the working is always shown.
The ideas behind Minotaur, from the three roles of Energy, Logic and Control to the mathematics of MINOS, are set out on the MINOS page . The mathematics itself is in the paper An Operational Representation of Systems: A Worked Construction in Lattice Gauge Theory ( doi:10.5281/zenodo.23491024 ). The first post, Introducing Minotaur: A GPU’less AI Architecture , describes the ELC adapter and its tests on real regulations. The ELC adapter and the ELC neural network are patent pending.

title: NIGGSA 2026: Daniel, Others Seek Stronger Community Policing, LG Autonomy
body: Funmi Ogundare Former Ogun State Governor and senator representing Ogun East Senatorial District, Otunba Gbenga Daniel, has called on governments at all levels to strengthen accountability, transparency and grassroots participation to rebuild public trust in government. Daniel, who made the call Wednesday while delivering the keynote address at the third edition of Nigeria Grassroots Governance Summit and Awards (NIGGSA) 2026, in Lagos, said public confidence could only be sustained through responsible leadership, effective service delivery and measurable improvements in citizens’ welfare. He spoke on the theme, ‘Focusing on Community Policing, Building Trust at the Grassroots.’ Daniel, who was represented by a former Commissioner for Special Duty in Ogun State, Akogun Kolapo Onadipe, explained that democracy goes beyond the conduct of periodic elections. He stated that while elections conferred legitimacy on government, performance was essential to sustaining it. “My central message today is simple: Trust is the foundation of good governance, accountability is its currency, and service to the people is its ultimate test,” he said. He noted that citizens expected governments to provide security, create economic opportunities, improve infrastructure, strengthen education and healthcare, and ensure that public resources were deployed for the common good. He warned that repeated unfulfilled promises could erode public confidence, discourage investment, weaken civic participation and widen the gap between government institutions and the people they were established to serve. According to him, rebuilding public trust should not be treated as a public relations exercise but as a deliberate commitment to transparency, responsible leadership and measurable results. “The people must not merely hear their government; they must experience its impact in their daily lives,” he stated. The former governor identified grassroots governance as a critical starting point for building public confidence, noting that citizens often assessed government performance through their everyday experiences with public services and infrastructure. Daniel called for the strengthening of local governments through adequate empowerment, professional management and accountability, urging authorities to ensure that development initiatives reflected the needs and priorities of the communities they served. He added that community engagement should extend beyond ceremonial consultations to provide citizens with meaningful opportunities to identify their needs, contribute to development priorities and monitor the implementation of public projects. “Policies are more effective when they respond to actual needs rather than assumptions made from a distance,” he said. On transparency and accountability, the former governor urged governments to make openness a fundamental principle of public administration, noting that citizens had the right to know how public resources were generated, allocated and utilised. Earlier in her remarks, the Convener, Oluwatomisin Adebukola, called for stronger community policing and greater local government autonomy, saying poor governance and inadequate security at the grassroots are undermining public trust and democratic accountability. She said the summit would develop a policy paper and proposed bill for presentation to the National Assembly to address security challenges, strengthen community participation in governance and bridge the gap between local governments and traditional institutions. According to her, the initiative is aimed at addressing democratic attrition, the gradual erosion of accountability, transparency and public participation in governance, particularly at the local government level. Badewole, who is also the Executive Director of Hope for the Masses Foundation, said many communities across Nigeria remained neglected despite the constitutional responsibilities of local governments in primary education, healthcare, community security, environmental management and rural development. She attributed the situation not only to inadequate administrative capacity but also to a lack of political will among those responsible for delivering governance at the grassroots. The convener stated: “The summit’s first edition in 2024 assessed local government service delivery against parameters aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with only seven of Lagos State’s 57 local governments and local council development areas scoring above average and receiving awards. “In 2025, the summit focused on building the capacity of aspiring local government officeholders, particularly councillors and chairmanship candidates, to improve their understanding of legislative responsibilities and effective governance.” She explained that the two editions had laid the foundation for a proposed grassroots governance accountability model, a framework designed to enable communities, youth groups, journalists, civil society organisations and local leaders to monitor governance and hold public officials accountable. “This year’s focus is community policing, building trust at the grassroots, and ensuring we bridge the gap between local governments and traditional institutions,” she said. Badewole identified financial autonomy as a critical factor in effective local government administration, arguing that local government chairmen could not fulfil their constitutional responsibilities if funds meant for their councils failed to reach them. Also speaking, the former Deputy Inspector-General of Police (rtd), Adeleye Olusola Oyebade, emphasised the need for a shift from reactive security operations to community-based policing, urging traditional rulers, local government authorities, youth and women groups, and security agencies to strengthen collaboration, intelligence sharing and public trust to tackle insecurity in Nigeria. He stated that the country’s security framework must prioritise crime prevention, early identification of threats and the resolution of local grievances rather than relying predominantly on arrests, investigations and the deployment of security personnel after criminal incidents had occurred. According to him, community policing goes beyond establishing vigilante groups or deploying additional patrol teams, as it requires trust, partnership and shared responsibility between citizens and professional security agencies. He said: “Security is not merely the absence of threats; it is the presence of trust, cooperation and collective responsibility.” The former police chief noted that families, farmers, traders and schoolchildren deserved to live, work and pursue their activities without fear, stressing that achieving this required a coordinated approach involving all stakeholders.

title: US Coast Guard awards $300M in infrastructure contracts
body:
The US Coast Guard has awarded two contracts working with the US Navy totaling more than $300 million towards infrastructure improvements supporting cutter operations.
The US Navy awarded a $271 million contract to Skanska USA Civil Northeast Waltham, Massachusetts, on September 22 to build new homeport facilities for Coast Guard major cutters at Naval Station Newport in Newport, Rhode Island.
On September 28, it awarded a $31.5 million contract to Orion Government Services of Houston, Texas, to repair hurricane damage to Coast Guard major cutter piers at Naval Air Station Pensacola in Pensacola, Florida.
Both projects use Coast Guard funding and leverage the navy’s site expertise and existing design contracts to reduce costs and minimize technical and schedule risks.
The Newport project includes a new pier to provide berthing for four major Coast Guard cutters, a new bulkhead, stormwater management modifications and full utility installations.
This collaboration with the navy advances critical Coast Guard missions, providing access to strategic operating areas in the Western Hemisphere and the Arctic.
The work in Pensacola, funded by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, provides for repairs to Wharf Bravo, including structural and utility improvements to the north berth, and underwater structural repairs for both the north and south berths.
The Naval Station Newport contract is funded through fiscal year 2022 major acquisitions infrastructure funding and funding allocated to the Coast Guard under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
The act provides nearly $25 billion for the Coast Guard, of which the service has ordered approximately $20 billion in assets, capabilities, and infrastructure to date.
“These investments will provide vital infrastructure to support the modernizing Coast Guard fleet,” said Admiral Kevin Lunday , Commandant of the Coast Guard.
“These major investments in shore infrastructure for our cutters will ensure the Coast Guard’s ability to secure America’s borders and maritime approaches far at sea.”

title: Why Europe observation is now Europe’s biggest satellite market [OPINION]
body: Some say that the war in Ukraine is reaching its ‘endgame’ ; others, that Russia believes it can finally crush Ukraine this winter. Certainly, the recent changes in the Ukrainian forces’ access to Starlink, SpaceX’s internet network, has led many to wonder if something significant has changed. But we’ve heard speculation of this kind many times before since the start of the conflict, and it would be unwise to try to predict the future. What we can say with more certainty is that it put defence, and particularly, European defence, in the spotlight. And this has changed the market for satellites. In ways that were unthinkable a relatively short time ago, today’s governments want to know with increasing accuracy what is happening along their borders, at sea and in other places where military activity could threaten their security. More and more, they are turning to Earth observation satellites to provide a key layer situational intelligence. And the effect on the European space industry has been considerable. According to Eurospace, sales of Earth observation systems exceeded those of telecommunications systems by 24 per cent in 2025. Telecommunications had long been the industry’s leading satellite manufacturing market; now Earth observation has overtaken it, largely because of growing military demand. The change is particularly evident in Spain, France, Germany, Poland and Finland, which Eurospace identifies as Europe’s strongest markets for Earth observation systems. All five countries have good reasons to improve their ability to observe events beyond their borders. Satellites allow them to examine large areas without sending aircraft or people into potentially dangerous places. They can monitor ports, follow ships, identify changes at military installations, and keep watch over important infrastructure. The same satellite can return to an area repeatedly, allowing analysts to compare what they see today with what they saw yesterday, last week or last month. The war in Ukraine has helped governments appreciate just how valuable this can be. Satellite images have provided information about troop movements, damaged infrastructure and the condition of transport routes. They have also demonstrated the importance of being able to observe the same location regularly. A single image might reveal vehicles gathered beside a road. A later image might show that they have moved, or that more have arrived. Such information does not remove the need for drones, aircraft or intelligence gathered on the ground. It does, however, give commanders a better understanding of events over a much wider area. This growing military interest has important consequences for satellite manufacturers. Defence customers want systems capable of producing useful information often enough, and quickly enough, to support decisions on the ground. This places considerable importance on the satellite’s imaging equipment. The spacecraft itself supplies the power, communications and control systems, but it is the optical payload itself that determines the detail and extent of what can be photographed. A camera intended to examine individual buildings, for example, must meet different requirements from one designed to survey hundreds of square kilometres. There are also choices to be made about the kind of information a camera should collect. Conventional optical imagery allows analysts to recognise familiar objects such as roads, vehicles, buildings and ships. Multispectral and hyperspectral instruments, meanwhile, can reveal differences in materials and surfaces that may not be visible in an ordinary photograph. None of these systems can do absolutely everything. Optical cameras must contend with cloud cover and, depending on their design, limited light. Radar satellites can help overcome some of these restrictions. Defence customers therefore have good reasons to use several kinds of imaging system together, rather than depend entirely on one. Image quality is only part of the problem, however. Consider a satellite that photographs a ship approaching a sensitive area. The picture may contain precisely the information an analyst needs, but its value will diminish if it takes several hours to reach the people responsible for responding. Processing some of the information aboard the satellite can help by reducing the volume of data that needs to be transmitted. A constellation of satellites can also revisit the same places more often, giving customers a more regular, richer picture of developments on the ground. This helps explain the rising interest in smaller spacecraft and optical payloads. Traditionally, many of these payloads have been designed for a particular mission, with components and engineering work tailored to the customer’s requirements. Where customers need dozens of similar cameras, manufacturers have a stronger incentive to use established designs and common components. Repeated production can lower costs and make delivery times more predictable. Greater military demand would give European manufacturers a larger home market and more reason to invest in production. It could also reduce Europe’s reliance on foreign suppliers for equipment vital to its security. And the benefits would extend beyond defence. The same cameras could help farmers monitor crops and governments assess flood or fire damage. In short, Europe has an opportunity not just to buy more satellites, but to strengthen its ability to see the world for itself – if you like, through its own eyes.

title: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear through gas pipelines near Kupiansk, Khartiia says
body:
Ukrainian troops infiltrated the rear of Russian forces near Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast after moving about 15 kilometers (9 miles) through underground gas pipelines, Ukraine's National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps said on Oct. 22.
The operation, code-named "Veles," was carried out by the 2nd Khartiia Corps together with other Ukrainian units, according to the corps.
Khartiia commander Brig. Gen. Ihor Obolienskyi said Ukrainian forces had studied how Russian troops were using underground routes and anticipated that they would try to exploit major gas pipelines running through Kharkiv Oblast.
"The Russians intended to use the gas routes to penetrate the rear of our forces. So we went underground ourselves," Obolienskyi said.
According to Khartiia, Ukrainian troops moved through the pipelines before combining the underground advance with operations above ground, including drone strikes.
The corps said more than 30 Russian soldiers were captured during the operation and that Russian forces suffered more than 100 casualties. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify those figures.
Obolienskyi said the aim was both to stop Russian troops underground and to undermine tactics they had been using on the ground and from the air.
"We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground," he said.
Russian forces have used gas pipelines on several occasions to move troops covertly around the Kupiansk sector. In January, Ukrainian troops said they had stopped a Russian assault involving about 50 soldiers attempting to advance through the Soyuz gas pipeline.
More recently, Khartiia said, Russian troops retreating near Kupiansk used civilians as human shields , leading a group that included children and elderly people to the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk pipeline and forcing them inside the pipe toward Russian-held territory. Ukrainian troops said they did not open fire, because civilians were present
"When the battlefield became transparent, the war went underground," the corps said when it first announced the operation on Oct. 21.

title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
body: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning. As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind. Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip. And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade. A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more. “You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention. Matching storage to the AI data life cycle Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer. This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage What this means for how AI gets budgeted For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators. Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished. A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand. Building for economically scalable capacity Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it. What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives. Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales. There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget: What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it? Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing? If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse? Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after. This content was produced by WD. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

title: Asaval-Dasavali Journalist Dito Chubinidze Arrested on Treason Charges
body: Dito Chubinidze, a journalist from the Asaval-Dasavali weekly newspaper, has been arrested and will be charged with treason as the Prosecutor’s Office of Georgia accuses him of deliberately spreading false reports about Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze handing parts of the historic Davit Gareji complex to Azerbaijan. The prosecution follows a controversy surrounding a series of allegations made by jailed former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili, who, among others, raised questions about the alleged suicide of Lazare Jorbenadze, a commentator who, in months preceding his death, made similar accusations against Kobakhidze in interviews with Chubinidze for Asaval-Dasavali, a conservative publication known for conspiratorial reporting. Chubinidze will be charged “with high treason, particularly sabotage” and face up to four years in prison, the Prosecutor’s Office said on October 22. Since February 2026, Chubinidze “has systematically disseminated false and disinformative reports through various media outlets and social media platforms and has claimed, based on fabricated facts, that the Prime Minister of Georgia, under a secret agreement concluded with a neighboring state, transferred part of the Davit Gareji Monastery Complex to the Republic of Azerbaijan,” the Prosecutor’s Office said. According to the agency, the investigation “conclusively established” that the state border “is determined by an international treaty or agreement concluded with the neighboring state, which subsequently requires ratification by the Parliament of Georgia, while the authority to conduct negotiations and make decisions on matters concerning the delimitation and demarcation of the border is vested exclusively in the Government Commission on the Delimitation and Demarcation of the State Border of Georgia.” Prosecutors say that no such agreement regarding the delimitation or demarcation along the Davit Gareji section has been reached within the Commission’s mandate, adding that the statutory procedure “rules out, even theoretically” that Kobakhidze may have singlehandedly handed the territory to another state. The agency further said that Chubinidze, to create a “real perception” of a fabricated story in the public, has “repeatedly linked” the death of his respondent, Lazare Jorbenadze, to “revenge killing” prompted by Jorbenadze’s disclosure of incriminating information about Kobakhidze. By that, Chubinidze “deliberately carried out sabotage to the detriment of the lawful interests of the Georgian state, thereby obstructing the normal functioning of a state agency and the Government Commission on the Delimitation and Demarcation of the State Border of Georgia,” the agency concluded. Garibashvili and Asaval-Dasavali Controversy Chubinidze came to the public spotlight through a series of allegations made by former PM Garibashvili about being pressured by former colleagues to take blame in a corruption case in order to stay away from politics for good. The journalist’s name was mentioned in the alleged letter of pressure that Garibashvili claimed was sent to him by Mamuka Mdinaradze, a now-resigned Georgian Dream figure. The alleged letter, published on Garibashvili’s social media page, warned about anticipated corruption charges that purportedly followed the actions of Georgian conservative figures such as Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze and campaigns “organized” on social media. “‘Supporters like Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze and the campaigns organized on social media have sown serious suspicions and greatly damaged us,” the alleged letter read. The controversy escalated after Garibashvili was indeed charged with bribery , and he made subsequent allegations that the pressure on him increased in February, when a copy of an Asaval-Dasavali was sent to him in jail “on the instruction of” Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Garibashvili said he was told about “suspicions” that he was behind an interview by Chubinidze with “former rights defender” Lazare Jorbenadze, which was “mainly devoted to criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.” Garibashvili then pointed to “unanswered questions” over the suicides of “multiple” people during the “Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze rule,” including Jorbenadze, who died by alleged suicide in April. In months preceding his death, Jorbenadze had accused Kobakhidze of handing lands to Azerbaijan, including in a series of comments given to Asaval-Dasavali. The ensuing debate led the authorities to summon Garibashvili, opposition members, and conservative figures for questioning over Jorbenadze’s death, even if the prosecutors argued the investigation had “conclusively established” that he had died by suicide. In 2020, Georgian Dream has escalated rhetoric, led by Garibashvili, indirectly accusing the former United National Movement government of handing historic lands to Azerbaijan, including through the controversial Cartographer’s Case that led to the arrest of two state experts at the time. title: CSG unveils Meander, a 33-tonne amphibious vehicle for crossing rivers and wetlands
body: Meander was developed by Excalibur Army, part of CSG, together with New Space Technologies (NST), a member of the Krill Business Partners (KBP) group. CSG believes the vehicle has strong commercial potential, as there are very few versatile amphibious vehicles on the market. Excalibur Army says armed forces have little to choose from in this category, and that equipment decades old is still in service. Meander is meant to let troops cross watercourses and marshy ground without having to build pontoon or engineer bridges first. “In many situations, armed forces need vehicles that can carry troops, materiel or smaller vehicles across watercourses or marshy terrain without having to build pontoon or engineer bridges. That is why we designed Meander from the outset around the real requirements of military users,” said Adam Liška, CEO of Excalibur Army. “For CSG, Meander is a significant expansion of our land military equipment offering in a segment where choice is very limited and where equipment that is decades old is still in service. Meander’s design also allows us to offer specialised versions or variants capable of carrying weapon systems,” Liška added. The vehicle shown in Prague was the basic transport version, built to carry materiel, vehicles, ground equipment or personnel. CSG says the design can be adapted for other roles, including specialised and combat versions armed with weapon systems. The company calls Meander one of the most modern and capable vehicles in its class. It is designed to work on land and water alike, including in swamps, rivers and wetlands. Meander is more than eleven metres long and weighs up to 33 tonnes fully loaded, of which 13 tonnes is payload. A twelve-cylinder, air-cooled Tatra engine producing 440 kW gives it a top speed of 48 kilometres per hour on the road and around 12 kilometres per hour in the water. The flat cargo deck has room for up to 70 standing troops, 12 stretchers, a medium-sized military truck or a standard twenty-foot container. An electrically operated rear ramp, which can also bear 13 tonnes, makes loading easier. On land the vehicle runs on tracks, while in the water it is driven by propellers. It needs a crew of two, a driver and an operator, with a third crew member added when required. Perhaps its most unusual feature is that the driver steers with a wheel and pedals, like an ordinary car, whether on land or in the water. CSG says the electronic steer-by-wire system makes it very precise and comfortable to handle, and the crew also gets a touchscreen showing vehicle data and a camera system with a very good view all around. Meander is based on KALAN, a vehicle NST unveiled earlier and which Czech firefighters are now testing. Excalibur Army and NST put their partnership on paper with a memorandum signed at Eurosatory 2026, and the first prototype was ready just a few months later. Excalibur Army is in charge of the military, operational and user requirements. NST is responsible for the technical, design and production work, including the first prototype. “In designing Meander, we drew on our experience from developing the KALAN vehicle, which Czech firefighters are now trialling. As a result, Meander has a different propulsion system for movement on water, among other improvements suited to military use,” said Václav Zajíc, executive director of NST. “Combining our design capabilities with Excalibur Army’s experience shows that Czech industry can offer a vehicle with world-class performance for demanding military operations. Moreover, it has virtually no competition in its category,” Zajíc said.

title: Anthropic takes on Grok Bot, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's Dots with its always-on agent "Claude Duet"
body:
Anthropic has answered Grok Bot, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's Dots with a research preview of Claude Duet. The standalone app runs Claude as a proactive agent that keeps working on tasks while the user is away and asks for approval before taking sensitive steps.
Anthropic is pitching Claude Duet to professionals and small business owners who have "more on their plates than they can track." The app runs on iOS, Android, and the web at claude.ai and is built on Claude Opus 5.5. Pro and Max subscribers in the US can get access through a waitlist. Team and Enterprise plans aren't included yet.
Anthropic says the big difference from the regular Claude app is which way things flow. In the Claude app, users open a chat. Duet comes to them instead. Every morning, the agent sends a short summary of the most important items from connected apps. After that, it only reaches out when something needs attention. It pulls memory, skills, and app connections from the user's existing Claude account. Ad
Users assign tasks by text or voice message in a single ongoing thread. According to Anthropic, that covers everything from scheduling to dashboards and financial forecasts to prototypes and web apps. The agent works on a virtual machine, its own cloud computer with a browser, so the user's laptop or phone doesn't need to stay on. Ad
Duet connects to services like Gmail, Slack, Stripe, Docusign, and Shopify through more than 6,000 connectors and plugins from the Claude Marketplace . That lets it track down unpaid invoices and draft payment reminders, or get payroll ready. For purchases, it uses Stripe Link with a virtual card, so the user's real card number never gets shared.
Several competitors have launched similar products in recent months. SpaceXAI opened the Grok Bot beta in August. In September, Meta followed with Muse and OpenAI with its Dots . All of them are betting on personal agents that handle tasks independently and act on their own initiative. Ad
Anthropic says Duet can only read, draft, and prepare on its own. Before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows exactly what it plans to do and waits for the user's approval. Trading securities and moving money between accounts are off the table, even with approval.
Technical safeguards add another layer. The company says the agent never sees passwords or login tokens directly, because credential handling follows the design of Claude Managed Agents . To fend off hidden instructions, known as prompt injections, Anthropic uses defenses from its research on browser use . Red teams and an outside firm also ran attack tests to probe Duet for weak spots. Ad
Anthropic also built a new classifier for Duet. This screening system works with special safety instructions in the system prompt to check every message for leaking sensitive data. Together, they're meant to refuse requests to share credit card numbers or ID details. Health or personal finance information only gets through when the user explicitly says so. Ad
Anthropic concedes that the early version can misread a message thread, misjudge urgency, and miss things that arrive between two checks. It's also weaker at personal errands like booking tickets, since its core features are built for work.
Duet only checks connected accounts every few hours, and Anthropic says that comes down to usage. Constant checking would burn through subscription limits much faster. Duet shares those limits with other Claude products, and the background checks count against them too.
Anthropic plans to use tester feedback to tune when the agent should reach out. How Duet fits with the Claude app is still an open question. For now, it runs separately, and early users' experience will shape how the two work together.

title: Ukrainian forces advance 15 km behind Russian lines through underground routes on Kupiansk front
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, the Khartiia Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine published on Facebook details of the Veles underground counteroffensive operation conducted in the Kharkiv region.
“The grouping under the command of the 2nd Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine’s Khartiia Corps combined an underground offensive with operations on the surface and drone strikes. This deprived the invaders of the opportunity to get into the rear of Kupiansk,” the Khartiia Corps said.
As the military reported, more than 30 invaders were taken prisoner as a result of the operation. The enemy suffered more than 100 casualties.
“We observed how the enemy operated underground. And we studied how they did it. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to infiltrate the rear of our forces. So, we went underground ourselves. We anticipated the enemy’s actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground,” Khartiia Corps Commander Brigadier General Ihor Obolenskyi explained.
According to him, troops were trained to operate in confined spaces for the operation, an underground route was prepared, and in-house technological solutions were used for communications, navigation and life support. Underground and surface operations were coordinated with drone strikes, including through a joint coordination center with the Achilles Brigade.
The operation involved the 13th National Guard Brigade Khartiia, the 23rd Separate Assault Regiment R.U.G. of the 2nd Corps of the National Guard’s Khartiia Corps, the Lava Unmanned Systems Regiment of the 2nd Corps of the National Guard’s Khartiia Corps, units of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, including the Freedom of Russia Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade, and other Defense Forces units.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 27, Russian troops were evacuating civilians from the Kupiansk community in the Kharkiv region through a gas pipeline, apparently using children and elderly people as cover for the withdrawal of their forces.

title: Nordic force should turn north, committee suggests
body: The government should consider whether the Joint Expeditionary Force concentrates its finite resources on the High North instead of operating as often in the Baltic, and may need to build the British Army force in Estonia up to brigade strength to offset the change, according to a report by the Defence Committee. The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets out that Britain permanently leads the ten-nation force, which brings together the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and the three Baltic and five Nordic countries, and that Britain has taken over command of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk. Dhesi said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.” The report recommends: “The government should consider whether the JEF focuses on the High North, concentrating finite resources on maximising its ability to operate more frequently in the harsh climate there while undertaking the demanding anti-submarine mission, rather than operating as often in the Baltic as previously.” On Estonia it states: “To offset this greater focus on the High North the UK may need to reassure Baltic members of the JEF by reinforcing its commitment there in other ways; for example, by building up the current British Army force in Estonia to brigade-size, to match what Germany is already doing in Lithuania.” A separate recommendation asks the government, within a year of assuming leadership of Joint Force Command Norfolk, to reassess the added value the force brings to European security, stating that either it provides distinct value alongside NATO and should be strengthened and aligned more closely with it, or it does not and Britain should focus its finite resources on NATO. The committee sets out that the force was established in 2014 for rapid, scalable operations with northern European allies, and that its principal value lies below the Article 5 threshold where it can respond to hybrid threats, protect undersea infrastructure and act more quickly than NATO’s full consensus-based machinery. During an overseas committee visit, one commentator referred to the force as “a jack of all trades and therefore master of no military tasks.” The report records that the force overlaps with NATO tasks and has not always proved faster than NATO in practice, that it lacks some major NATO powers including Canada, and that it neither specialises in the shallow waters of the Baltic nor in anti-submarine operations in the harshness of the High North. Canada applied to join the force in September 2026, and the committee notes that it could add valuable experience and capabilities given its long experience of operating in harsh regional conditions and its membership of the Five Eyes intelligence group, but that adding the North American Arctic to the European High North would significantly increase the force’s area of responsibility. With Sweden and Finland having joined NATO, the committee observes that eight of the nine countries around the Baltic Sea are now members of the alliance and offer significant capabilities of their own in that region. The Ministry of Defence told the committee that “[o]nce we transition into crisis, the chances are that the JEF will, in some way, fold into the regional plan north-west anyway. There is not a competition between the two; they are entirely complementary and one supports the other.” The post Nordic force should turn north, committee suggests first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Ghana’s U-15 Boys depart Accra for Azerbaijan ahead of FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival
body: The Ghana U-15 Boys team departed Accra for Azerbaijan on Wednesday to participate in the FIFA U-15 Boys World Cup and Festival. The contingent, made up of players and technical staff, will represent Ghana at the global youth festival which brings together talented U-15 sides from around the world for both competitive matches and developmental programs. The FIFA U-15 Festival is part of FIFA’s Talent Development Scheme aimed at giving young players early international exposure. Ghana will be hoping to make a strong impression in Azerbaijan after months of screening and preparations. Ghana have been drawn in Group W alongside Uzbekistan, Myanmar, Guam, Bahamas, and Kazakhstan. The team will open their campaign against Uzbekistan on Saturday, October 24, before playing two matches on Sunday against Myanmar and Guam. They will round off the group phase with fixtures against the Bahamas and Kazakhstan on Monday, October 26, 2026. The format will see Ghana play five group games in three days as FIFA looks to give maximum game time and exposure to all participating talents.

title: Ukraine and Russia Trade Deadly Strikes After U.S. Tries to Reboot Peace Talks
body:
Ukraine and Russia exchanged a flurry of drone and missile attacks overnight, leaving at least seven dead across Ukraine and one person killed in southwestern Russia, officials in the two warring countries said Thursday morning.
Authorities in the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine said a man was killed when a Ukrainian drone crashed into the truck he was driving. In a separate strike in the region, a man riding a motorcycle was wounded.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 630 Ukrainian drones had been tracked in the skies above the wider Moscow region overnight, with air defense systems intercepting 163 of the unmanned aircraft that were on a direct approach to the city. Two people were wounded in the Voronovo district, located to the southwest of central Moscow.
There were also reports of an explosion and fire south of the capital. The exiled news outlet Astra, using eyewitness footage of the fire, identified the targeted facility as a storage and logistics facility belonging to the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate, located in Serpukhov.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify those reports.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 808 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
Russian officials reported injuries in the border regions of Kursk amid the overnight air barrage. Residential buildings in the Lipetsk region were also damaged. Power lines were knocked down in the Voronezh and Kaluga regions.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, Russian attacks killed at least seven people across the country, including three in Zaporizhzhia, two in Donetsk, one in Sumy and a woman in the Kharkiv region.
The exchange of attacks came just hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff concluded talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss renewing trilateral peace negotiations that have stalled since February.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that Kyiv supported a U.S. proposal for three-way talks with Moscow and Washington. The Kremlin said Putin had agreed to resume the U.S.-mediated talks as early as next month.
