title: Pink dolphin in Oman sparks curiosity as experts question second video
body: Muscat: The pink dolphin swimming in the waters of Oman has been generating curiosity. This is the first time a pink dolphin has been spotted in the waters of Oman. Experts clarified to the Observer that while the first video of the pink dolphin in Qantab is valid, the second video of the pink humpback dolphin is questionable and is being rejected as fake. Aida al Jabri, Marine Environment Specialist at the Environment Authority, explained the first identified pink dolphin in the video is a Risso's dolphin."The species is known to become lighter with age as scars accumulate on their bodies. The video of the humpback dolphin claimed to have been spotted in Muscat has raised doubts because they are never found in the waters near Muscat. "Humpback dolphins are found in Musandam, Masirah, Al Wusta, and Dhofar. They are always in shallow waters, which is why it is difficult to believe they were in waters off Muscat," Al Jabry pointed out. According to scientific explanations, dolphins turn pink primarily due to increased blood flow near the surface of their skin (vasodilation) to release body heat, as well as age-related color changes and scar tissue.Dolphins also have incidents like humans when it comes to skin pigmentation. "In September a fisherman spotted a dolphin that was completely white in Masirah," she noted. Risso’s dolphins are dark gray or brown when they are born, but their skin is known to be extremely sensitive and scratches easily. Adding to the pink effect is the bright sunlight and reflection from water. They are known to wrestle, and the white scar tissue is also known to contribute to the change in color. In addition, their blood vessels dilate to regulate body temperature. But for now the sighting of the pink dolphin continues to attract attention, and maybe there could be more beach goers heading out to the sea in boats.

title: Dayne Viernes out to cement status as Power Slap greatest in Abu Dhabi
body: Dayne “Da Hawaiian Hitman” Viernes is looking to cement his status as the greatest super heavyweight of Power Slap when he defends his title against Vasilii “Dumpling” Kamotskii in Abu Dhabi next month. Viernes made his second title defence against the man he dethroned in June 2025, taking a majority decision over Kamotskii in five rounds at Power Slap 13. Power Slap 25 takes place at Abu Dhabi’s Space42 Arena on October 23, a day before UFC 333, and Viernes said he is “locked in” ahead of his rematch. “Physically and mentally, I’m ready to make a statement. Right now I’m just perfecting my slap and ready to win the title. Training daily and excited to showcase my skills,” Viernes told The National . After beating Kamotskii, Viernes successfully defended his belt against top-ranked super heavyweight Makini “Big Mak” Manu, taking a split decision over the American. This will be his first time competing in Abu Dhabi, and Viernes is determined to put on a show. “Yes, first time in Abu Dhabi. I’m excited to put on a show for the fans at the Space42 Arena and around the world to get the win, be known as the greatest super heavyweight of Power Slap of all time and hopefully getting some knockout reactions.” The rivalry between Kamotskii and the Viernes family goes back even further and has strong ties to Abu Dhabi. “Dumpling” first faced Dayne’s older brother, Layne Viernes, in the UAE capital in October 2024, with the contest ending in a majority draw. The pair later met again, with the Russian defeating Layne to claim the super heavyweight title. The return to Abu Dhabi brings that family history back to where it began. While October 23 will mark Dayne’s first appearance in the UAE capital, it will be the third year straight Kamotskii has competed in Abu Dhabi. For Viernes, the mission is clear: “I’m expecting his best and nothing less and I’m looking for a KO win.” For former champion Kamotskii, owner of multiple high-profile first-round KOs, a return to Abu Dhabi offers a shot at redemption. “The audience and atmosphere in Abu Dhabi are really great. I love performing in Abu Dhabi. I haven't been able to win in Abu Dhabi before, but this time it'll be different,” he said. “We need to knock out Dayne to reclaim my title and for me to be the best superheavyweight of all time in Power Slap.” For Power Slap chief executive Frank Lamicella, being part of Abu Dhabi Showdown Week helps elevate Power Slap on the global stage. “In Power Slap, we always want to put the best against the best. Abu Dhabi is the world’s fight capital,” he told The National . “There is no bigger stage to hold two super heavyweights – weighing in at nearly 800 pounds together – vying to be named the best in the world in the super heavyweight division.”

title: From “bad-guy fleet” to “good-guy fleet”: US will let investors buy sanctioned tankers and return them to legal trade
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Investors who buy idle sanctioned tankers and refit them could put the ships back into legal oil trade, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on 19 October, Bloomberg reported . He laid out the plan five days after a US official described it to Reuters. That official said the aim was to cut record tanker freight rates. The Energy Department added that any relief would not help Russia move its oil. The plan comes weeks before the 3 November midterms, with voters worried about fuel costs after gasoline and diesel prices surged in the Mideast conflict. Yet the shadow fleet is also how Russia sells oil past sanctions, and those sales fund its war against Ukraine. In December 2025, Ukraine’s foreign intelligence counted more than 1,100 tankers serving Russia alone, 226 of them under US sanctions. An approval process Wright didn’t detail Many sanctioned tankers sit idle, Wright told Bloomberg’s Annmarie Hordern, and buyers keep approaching the administration offering to fix them up and carry only legal oil. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’” he said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore.” The ships must go through an approval process, Wright said, but he gave no criteria. He insisted “there is no removing of sanctions.” He put the global dark fleet at about 1,600 ships, a count covering vessels that hauled Venezuelan, Iranian, and Russian oil. Dozens or even hundreds could turn legitimate, he said. The ships are no longer needed for Venezuelan oil, Wright said, and no Iranian oil is moving. Russian oil exports, he added, “are certainly not growing.” Diesel, a waiver, and the tankers Earlier, on 9 October, the Treasury issued General License 135, allowing some deals in Russian diesel until 7 April 2027. On 16 October, US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act, leaving earlier sanctions intact. That law had directed him to review and sanction shadow-fleet vessels. Trump defended the waiver as a way to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News host Larry Kudlow on 18 October that he had asked the White House team to “carefully consider the unintended consequences,” The Hill reported . He added that he thought “the right decision will be made” in the end. title: US diplomats, families leave Saudi Arabia missions as regional conflict with Houthis escalates
body: The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to leave its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from several other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.The order came as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oil field.State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a post on X/Twitter that the department ordered the departure of "non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only" amid attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen on civilian targets in the country.Washington had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February."Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said.Four US officials told Reuters that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave. Pigott did not address changes to other missions outside Saudi Arabia.Yemen escalation opens new front in regional conflictThe latest withdrawals follow an escalation of the fighting in Yemen, opening another front ​in the regional conflict triggered by the US-Israeli ⁠war on Iran. The wider conflict has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies.After the departure order, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority reported an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam that killed one person and injured eight others. Earlier in the day, two people were killed after Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oilfield, the energy ministry said.The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, after recent deadly strikes, including on Riyadh's airport.The embassy and a CIA station hosted there came under attack by drones in early March, as Iran began launching attacks across the region.

title: Banks and Businesses Face Major Anti-Money Laundering Changes
body: Banks, financial institutions and businesses across Europe must prepare for sweeping changes to financial crime prevention as the European Union’s new anti-money laundering framework takes effect on 10 July 2027, placing greater emphasis on effective controls, reliable data and artificial intelligence. The new requirements aim to strengthen efforts to prevent money laundering and detect suspicious transactions. Organisations must review their governance, policies, procedures, systems and staffing to ensure they meet the new standards. The European Union’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (AMLR) will introduce the main changes from July 2027. In 2028, the European Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) is expected to begin directly supervising selected high-risk financial institutions, while national supervisory authorities will retain a central role. The changes, market challenges and technological opportunities formed the focus of Deloitte’s third Financial Crime Symposium, held at the Athens Conservatoire and attended by representatives of supervisory authorities, financial institutions and businesses. Preparing for the New Rules Discussions highlighted the need for organisations to prepare early and coordinate changes across their operations. Participants stressed the importance of assessing gaps against the new requirements and developing flexible implementation plans that account for evolving technical standards and supervisory guidance. Organisations must also demonstrate that their financial crime prevention systems work effectively in practice, detect suspicious activity and support timely, well-founded decisions. Risk assessments should guide both daily operations and strategic decisions, with controls proportionate to each organisation’s actual exposure. Senior management involvement, clear responsibilities, adequate resources and effective reporting to boards will also play a crucial role. Data and Artificial Intelligence in Financial Crime Prevention Reliable, up-to-date data with a verifiable source will be essential for effective customer due diligence, transaction monitoring and regulatory reporting. Regularly reassessing customer risk profiles as their circumstances or transaction patterns change can help organisations identify emerging threats more quickly. Targeted checks and redesigned procedures can also reduce unnecessary delays and improve the customer experience. Artificial intelligence can support investigations, document processing and transaction monitoring. However, organisations must move beyond pilot projects and establish clear objectives, defined accountability, measurable success criteria and reliable data before integrating AI into everyday operations. Human oversight and the ability to explain and trace decisions will remain essential. Organisations will retain responsibility for the technologies they deploy. Industry-Specific Risks and Greater Cooperation The symposium’s sector-specific discussions highlighted the need to tailor prevention measures to different business models. Sectors facing distinct challenges include payments, credit management, insurance, real estate, gambling, and the art and antiquities markets. Effective prevention requires specialised knowledge and controls suited to the risks in each sector. Participants also stressed the importance of cooperation between operational teams, compliance professionals, technology departments and relevant authorities. Information sharing, subject to legal safeguards and personal data protection requirements, can improve the detection of suspicious activity and strengthen overall prevention efforts. The discussions presented financial crime prevention as a strategic responsibility that strengthens organisational resilience, market integrity and public trust. Deloitte Highlights Need for Early Action Alexis Chatzipavlou, Partner and Risk, Regulatory & Forensic Leader at Deloitte Greece, said organisations needed clear priorities, reliable data and controls that worked effectively in practice to prepare for the new European framework. He described the changes as an opportunity for organisations to strengthen their resilience and build trust among customers and business partners. Chatzipavlou also stressed that the evolving nature of financial crime requires continuous learning, the exchange of experience and closer cooperation. Through the Financial Crime Symposium, Deloitte aims to strengthen dialogue between businesses and supervisory authorities, improve understanding of shared challenges and identify practical solutions that help organisations respond more effectively and prepare for upcoming regulatory changes. title: Elbit Systems buys Canadian autonomous underwater systems company
body:
Israel-based international military technology company Elbit Systems has completed the acquisition of International Submarine Engineering (ISE), a Canada-based company specializing in advanced autonomous underwater and remotely operated systems for the maritime domain.
Headquartered in the Vancouver area, ISE is a high-technology company engaged in the development and manufacture of undersea vehicles, including autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), as well as computer control systems and robotics.
With more than 50 years of experience in subsea robotics, ISE has delivered over 250 underwater vehicles to customers in more than 20 countries worldwide.
Elbit Systems’ naval portfolio includes unmanned surface vessels, underwater systems, integrated command-and-control (C2) suites, electro-optical and sonar systems, communications and electronic warfare technologies.
Through its subsidiaries and global centers of excellence, Elbit Systems delivers proven naval capabilities supporting missions ranging from coastal security to blue-water operations.
The addition of ISE’s underwater autonomous technologies is intended to expand Elbit Systems' capabilities in underwater Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), mine countermeasures (MCM) and anti-submarine warfare (ASW), further strengthening the Company's end-to-end maritime offering.
"This acquisition marks another milestone in Elbit Systems’ strategy to expand its offerings in the naval domain. Combined with our existing capabilities in naval electronic warfare, autonomous systems, naval precision munitions and maritime mission systems, ISE’s underwater technologies will further strengthen our position as a global provider of comprehensive, integrated maritime solutions," Bezhalel (Butzi) Machlis , President and CEO of Elbit Systems, said.

title: PASOK Demands EU Sanctions Over Turkish-Libyan Memorandum
body: Greece’s opposition PASOK party will bring the Turkish-Libyan maritime memorandum before the European Parliament in November, demanding its unequivocal condemnation and concrete EU sanctions while accusing the Greek government of failing to protect the country’s sovereign rights. The party’s four MEPs — Giannis Maniatis, Nikos Papandreou, Sakis Arnaoutoglou and Nikolas Farantouris — have launched a joint initiative with the full backing of the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) political group. The upcoming parliamentary debate will focus on what PASOK describes as violations of Greece’s and Cyprus’s sovereign rights, as well as the rejection of the Turkish-Libyan agreement, which the party considers illegal and invalid. PASOK’s delegation will also press the European Union to adopt specific political, institutional and economic measures, arguing that verbal declarations of support no longer suffice. In a joint statement, the four MEPs launched a strong attack on the New Democracy government, arguing that recent developments in Libya have undermined its assurances of diplomatic progress. They pointed to the Libyan House of Representatives’ approval of the memorandum, saying the decision exposed the shortcomings of the government’s diplomatic handling of the issue and its failure to present a clear plan to safeguard Greece’s national interests. “The developments in Libya disprove the government’s assurances of diplomatic progress. The New Democracy government owes explanations for its failed handling of the issue and must present a concrete plan to protect Greece’s sovereign rights,” the MEPs said. “Defending national interests requires results. The government’s assurances, designed for public consumption, have already been disproved,” they added. PASOK insists that the European Union must move beyond formal resolutions and expressions of solidarity and introduce tangible sanctions against all parties involved in the agreement. The party argues that the memorandum undermines stability in the Eastern Mediterranean and violates international law. “Through our initiative, we are calling for the European Parliament to unequivocally condemn the illegal and invalid Turkish-Libyan memorandum and for the EU to provide tangible support to our country at every level,” the four MEPs said. “Declarations of support alone are not enough. We must finally move towards concrete sanctions against all parties to this illegal agreement, which runs entirely counter to international law of the sea,” they added. title: PM Petteri Orpo in Ukraine to show Finland's 'strong support'
body:
Orpo is meeting with Ukraine's political leadership in Kyiv.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) is visiting the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Thursday.
Orpo is due to meet Ukraine's political leadership in Kyiv. The main purpose of the trip is to demonstrate Finland's strong support for Ukraine and for the reforms required for its EU membership.
Since Russia's war of aggression began, Finland has provided Ukraine with nearly five billion euros in support, including 3.6 billion euros in defence materiel assistance. Relative to the size of its economy, Finland ranks among Ukraine's strongest backers, according to the Finnish government.
In connection with the visit, a Ukrainian-Finnish business forum will also take place, bringing together representatives from more than ten Finnish companies and other organisations.
Orpo visited Ukraine in May last year, and before that in August 2023.
Efforts to secure peace in Ukraine have intensified this week.
A meeting was held in Oslo on Tuesday , with attendees including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , Finnish President Alexander Stubb and United States special envoy Steve Witkoff .
Witkoff then discussed the meeting's proposals with Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, but the Russian president said the talks had not produced significant results.

title: Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow and surrounding region leave two injured
body: Ukrainian forces attacked several Russian regions with drones overnight on October 22, including Moscow and the surrounding Moscow region. In Voronovo, part of the New Moscow area, two people were injured in the strike. In Serpukhov, outside Moscow, a strike hit the Defense Ministry’s “75 Arsenal” plant, which produces weapons and ammunition, according to the independent Telegram channel Astra. The Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ said the strike on the Moscow region involved not only drones but also missiles. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 163 drones were shot down as they approached the city since the evening of October 21. In total, he said, 630 Ukrainian drones were headed toward Moscow and the Moscow region, and most of them were destroyed at “distant frontiers.” Ukrainian drones also struck Lipetsk. Lipetsk Governor Igor Artamonov said the attack damaged windows and facades of private homes and apartment buildings, as well as a clinic, in the regional capital. A man born in 2001 was injured and hospitalized. Astra reported that the strike sparked a fire on the upper floors of a building in the “Atmosfera” residential complex. Voronezh Governor Alexander Gusev said 44 drones were shot down overnight over the city of Voronezh and the Voronezh region. Local authorities in the Tula region said 70 Ukrainian drones were destroyed overnight. In Voronezh, the attack damaged the roofs and facades of private homes, apartment buildings, and a public facility. In Tula and the Zaoksky district, private homes sustained damage. title: Romania shot down two drones it believes were Russia’s new Geran-4s. Europe isn’t ready for swarms of them, analyst warns
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); In a direct confrontation with Russia, European NATO states would likely be even more vulnerable than Ukraine to swarms of Russia’s new jet-powered strike weapons, Fabian Hoffmann of the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies (NIDS) argued in a 20 October op-ed for the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA). He calls them low-cost cruise missiles. Just three days earlier, Romania met what it believes were two of them over the Black Sea. Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two jet-powered Geran-family drones over Romania’s territorial waters on 17 October, the Defense Ministry said . Interim Defense Minister Radu Miruță said they flew at about 450 km/h and were likely Geran-4s, the first of that type Romania had downed. Faster drones for a faster war Russia began using the Geran-4 in May in response to effective Ukrainian interceptor drones, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said , adding that it reaches up to 500 km/h. By June, those interceptors were downing about half of slower Shahed-type drones, defense adviser Serhii Beskrestnov estimated. Hoffmann traces the shift to the Geran-3, a model Ukraine recovered intact in 2025. In his account, a Chinese JT80 turbojet roughly doubled its speed, from 185 to 350 km/h. However, he puts newer models, including the Geran-4, at 600 km/h or more, above HUR’s figure for that model. By his estimate, each costs $150,000–$250,000, against about $50,000 for a long-range drone. Still, from Russia’s perspective, he wrote, that buys a significantly higher chance of getting through. Explore further Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans Engines are the bottleneck Hoffmann argues defenses must match the threat’s speed, for example with jet-powered interceptor drones. Ukraine already fields some. On 4 October, President Zelenskyy said its Bars interceptors had shown the highest percentage among Ukrainian interceptors, about 30% of targets, according to Militarnyi. One unit destroyed five aerial targets with five Bars interceptors, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara later told journalists. He also called aviation one of the most effective tools against jet drones. Hoffmann’s concern is scale. Jet engines are in short supply, he wrote, because too few European and US suppliers can meet demand. Ukraine’s Defense Industry Council flagged a shortage of such engines for its drones in April. In his view, gun systems and higher-end missile defenses are too scarce or too costly to fill the gap. Read also Russia’s jet drones fly near 600 km/h now. title: Ukraine’s air defenses down over 180 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, the press service of the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram .
“According to preliminary data, as of 9:00, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 181 enemy UAVs, including 87 jet-powered Shahed drones, as well as Gerbera and other types of drones. Ten attack UAVs remain in the air, combat operations are ongoing,” the statement said.
According to the report, impacts by enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at eight locations.
The press service noted that during the attack, the enemy used Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon and Oniks missiles, launched from areas in Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk and Rostov regions, as well as 210 attack UAVs, including Shahed drones (110 of them jet-powered), Gerbera and Italmas drones, and Parodiya decoy drones. The UAVs were launched from Millerovo, Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and Shatalovo in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea.
As reported by Ukrinform, one person was killed and 22 injured, including four children, in the Russian ballistic attack on Kyiv. Fires and damage were reported in six districts of the capital.

title: Klinton Cod, Joins José Mourinho on Global Football TV Network
body: Nigerian content creator Klinton Cod is among more than 150 presenters, journalists, pundits and digital creators recruited for Football.com TV, a new 24-hour global football talk network launched by Sporty Group. The network, which went live on YouTube on October 19, features Portuguese football manager José Mourinho as its global ambassador. It will focus on football news, analysis, debates and fan reactions, bringing voices from five continents together on a single digital platform. Klinton Cod, who has close to one million followers across his social media platforms, joins a line-up of Nigerian football commentators and creators that includes Shina Oludare, Olawale Ayeni, Solace Chukwu, Ayotunde Onabolu, Michael Adegbile, Adaeze Michael and Femi Farawe. Ghanaian journalist Nathan Quao also represents West Africa on the network. According to Sporty Group, the platform aims to give African football voices greater visibility in global conversations about the game, while allowing fans to engage directly with presenters and pundits across different time zones. Mourinho, one of football’s most recognisable managers, will serve as the network’s global ambassador, helping to promote a platform built around strong opinions, football knowledge and audience participation. Unlike conventional sports television channels, Football.com TV will not broadcast live matches. Instead, it will offer continuous coverage of conversations around the game, including pre-match analysis, watchalongs, interviews, breaking stories, and post-match debates. Its programming will feature rotating groups of presenters and pundits, with viewers able to contribute through live chats, comments and polls. Fans may also be invited to join programmes and debate directly with the hosts. Elías Gallego, Vice President of Media, Marketing and Business Development at Sporty Group, said Nigerian supporters had a strong culture of football debate and that the platform would give them an opportunity to engage with audiences around the world. “Nigerian fans have never needed permission to have an opinion about football. They watch everything, they know everything, and they will tell you exactly where you went wrong,” Gallego said. “Football.com TV gives those voices a seat at the biggest table in the game, alongside the best of the rest of the world.” The launch expands Sporty Group’s investment in digital sports media. Football.com TV is the television arm of Football.com, which has a community of more than 500,000 followers across its social media platforms. The company recently introduced a live-score application for Android users, combining real-time match updates with features for football fans.

title: EDGE supports UAE Navy trial of autonomous systems
body:
UAE-based defense group EDGE has led the integration of sovereign autonomous systems for a UAE Navy demonstration of national and allied unmanned maritime capabilities, conducted with the participation of the US Navy.
As informed, the company contributed planning expertise, host facilities and operational assets, with EDGE specialists working alongside both navies on the design and execution.
The demonstration presented the latest advances in maritime autonomy through a series of practical operational scenarios, in which unmanned surface vessels (USVs) carried out reconnaissance and protection missions supported by artificial intelligence, advanced sensors and sophisticated command-and-control (C2) systems. It also promoted expertise exchange among participants and offered insight into emerging innovations.
“Building smarter machines is no longer enough to stay ahead. What matters is how well those machines are commanded and controlled, and the greater their autonomy, the more important orchestration becomes. Our focus is on connecting every system through a single command layer, with people defining the mission and AI managing how it is carried out," Hamad Al Marar , Managing Director and CEO, EDGE, said.
"Through that layer, our sovereign capabilities and those of our allies shared a unified common operating picture, turning collaboration between partners, industries and technologies into coordinated action in the air and at sea.”
Technologies integrated by EDGE included TACTICA AI’s Naval Warfare C2 Centre for Autonomous Systems and HADAF, the targeting system grounded in doctrine, knowledge of military operations and rules of engagement, as well as the maritime autonomy kit developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII).
The assets deployed also included the 170 M-DETECTOR, a 17-meter vessel with advanced autonomous control systems, the VORTEX-E counter-drone interceptor and the SKYSHIELD-N naval counter-unmanned aerial system. GPS-PROTECT anti-jamming technology safeguarded satellite navigation, while the MIRSAD-X multi-spectral electro-optical imager and radars supported detection and tracking, EDGE said.

title: Greece Challenges Turkish Survey Claims in Maritime Showdown
body: Greece has issued a counter-NAVTEX rejecting Turkey’s authority to announce geophysical surveys by the research vessel KOBI RUEGG in the Eastern Mediterranean, stating that most of the designated coordinates fall within the Greek continental shelf. The Hellenic Navy’s Hydrographic Service issued the notice through the Heraklion Hydrographic Station on Tuesday evening, 20 October 2026, in response to Turkish NAVTEX FA41-1032/26, which the Antalya station had issued earlier that day. The Greek notice describes the Turkish station as unauthorised and states that most of the coordinates specified for the planned surveys lie within the Greek continental shelf, as defined by international law and Greek Law 4001/2011. The latest exchange comes amid renewed tensions over maritime jurisdiction in the Eastern Mediterranean, just hours after the House of Representatives in eastern Libya approved the Turkish-Libyan maritime memorandum. Turkey Announces Geophysical Surveys Turkey’s Antalya station issued the original NAVTEX on Tuesday, announcing geophysical surveys in maritime areas south of Rhodes, east of Crete and west of Cyprus. According to the Turkish notice, the research vessel KOBI RUEGG was due to begin operations on Wednesday, 21 October. The notice instructed passing vessels to maintain a safety distance of five nautical miles from the research ship. Ankara maintains that the activities have the approval and coordination of the relevant Turkish authorities, asserting its authority to issue navigational notices for the designated maritime areas. Greece disputes that authority, arguing that most of the coordinates in the Turkish notice fall within its continental shelf under international law and Greek legislation. Turkish-Libyan Memorandum Adds to Tensions The latest maritime dispute coincides with the approval of the Turkish-Libyan maritime memorandum by the House of Representatives in eastern Libya, a development that has drawn strong reactions from Athens and the European Union. Greece considers the agreement contrary to international law. The memorandum seeks to establish a maritime boundary between Turkey and Libya while disregarding the maritime entitlements of Greek islands. The European Union has described the memorandum as invalid and without legal effect, while reiterating its support for the sovereign rights of Greece and Cyprus. Greek assessments link Turkey’s recent activity to Ankara’s broader efforts to strengthen its presence in the Eastern Mediterranean, as regional countries advance major energy projects and exploration plans. These include the Great Sea Interconnector, the planned electricity link between Greece and Cyprus, and proposed hydrocarbon exploration south of Crete involving US energy company Chevron. Libya has already expressed objections to the planned exploration, adding another complication to efforts to delimit maritime zones in the region. title: UAE leads $39 billion global digital fraud crackdown with more than 900 arrests
body: The UAE has led an international digital fraud crackdown in which hundreds of arrests were made and more than $39 billion in illicit funds and assets uncovered. Operation Confrontation Ghost – overseen by the Ministry of Interior – thwarted more than 123.7 million online fraud attempts worldwide, blocked 4,126 bank accounts, shut down 570 social media accounts and involved 29 raids on locations linked to fraud. The major crime-fighting campaign brought together law enforcement agencies from 30 countries, Interpol, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance and 13 private-sector partners specialising in technology, digital platforms and financial services. The three-month drive – conducted from July 1 to September 30 – focused on three major forms of digital crime: AI-enabled fraud, digital financial fraud and online "sextortion", state news agency Wam reported. The cross-border collaboration resulted in the arrest of more than 960 people, the identification of a further 3,500 suspects and 15,500 victims of crime and the exchange of more than 9,000 pieces of intelligence. The operation helped to secure more than four billion financial transactions made each month through tokenisation technology, bolstering user data protection and curbing fraud threats. The UAE's partners in the organised crime clampdown included the UK, Japan, Korea, Canada, Italy, France, the Netherlands, Brazil, Ecuador, Jordan and Bahrain. Private sector support in tackling wide-ranging fraudulent activity was provided by the likes of the UAE's Bayut and Dubizzle, as well as social media giants Meta and TikTok. Fighting financial crime Col Dana Al Marzouqi, director-general of the International Affairs Bureau at the Ministry of Interior, said the operation demonstrated the importance of international partnerships in addressing fraud networks that seek to exploit online platforms, financial services and emerging technologies to conduct cross-border criminal activities. She said the Ministry of Interior continued to strengthen co-operation with countries, international organisations, and technology and financial services companies to combat transnational digital fraud and protect both the public and organisations. Dr Monica Juma, executive director of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, described Operation Confrontation Ghost as a model of international co-operation in addressing emerging forms of crime. She stressed that the growing use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in fraud, alongside the exploitation of digital platforms, bank accounts and cryptocurrencies to transfer funds and conceal their origins, highlighted the need to continue to bolster counter-measures and strengthen global collaboration.

title: 'I have lived that hell': Former Iran detainee calls for release of British couple in Evin Prison
body: More than four years after his release from an Iranian jail, Anoosheh Ashoori still wakes up with nightmares from the “dark, dark moments” he experienced there. Mr Ashoori, 72, was speaking on a dreary wet day outside the UK Parliament. The former inmate of Tehran's most notorious prison was out on the street to call on the UK government to do more to release another detained British couple, Lindsay and Craig Foreman . The British-Iranian survived more than five years in Evin Prison until the British government secured his release in a high-profile deal in 2022. “I still have my nightmares. I still have my moments of remembering all the hard times that I went through,” he told The National . “I do dream about my former inmate and friends, in different scenarios – but horrible ones. Then I wake up in the middle of the night and I have to deal with that feeling until I can manage to go back to sleep again." Mr Ashoori’s experience with Iran's hostage-taking and hopes that it can be stopped for good is what compelled him to campaign outside Parliament on Wednesday for the Foremans. "I have lived in that hell. And I know that Lindsay and Craig are going through the same thing I did, even perhaps worse. So I felt that I must participate in this campaign." The couple were arrested while on a motorcycle tour of Iran in January 2025, and have since been sentenced to 10 years in prison for espionage. Their family have repeatedly raised concerns about their health and welfare in prison. Since their arrest, a war with the US and a popular uprising against the regime have rocked Iran – leading to greater paranoia and oppression from security officials. Mr Ashoori fears the couple may be going through an incarceration that is worse than his own. “I have met a few of my former inmates who were released and it is far worse than what it was when I was there,” he said. “Diseases have intensified, food quality has diminished. The tyranny itself has intensified. My condition there is nothing compared with what we are what is happening now." Arbitrary detention Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in Parliament on Wednesday that the Foremans' sentence was “appalling and unjustifiable”. “We will continue to pursue the case relentlessly until Lindsay and Craig are safely returned home to the UK and reunited with their family,” he said. Tension between the UK and Iran is at an all-time high after a suspected terror attack at a British airbase used by US bombers this month. This followed attacks on Jewish businesses and Iranian dissidents in the UK , which police suspect were ordered by Iranian officials. But the couple’s family are calling for stronger action from the UK government to secure their release. Lindsay’s son Joe Bennett and other members of the family delivered a petition to the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office, signed by about 110,000 people, calling on the UK government to call the Foremans' imprisonment “arbitrary” and “unlawful”. Richard Ratcliffe, husband of former Evin detainee Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe who was released in the same deal as Mr Ashoori in 2022, also joined the family, alongside MPs and supporters. Mr Ashoori's release in 2022 was secured by a payment of £400 million ($535 million) made by the UK government to Iran – which Tehran had claimed was debts owed over a historic arms deal. “The options are limited because we don’t understand what Iran wants. They seem to be holding them as hostages pending any demands that they may have,” Tony Vaughan, the couple’s MP, told The National . “The government has to call a spade a spade and call it unlawful and arbitrary detention. " The family will be meeting Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband next week. “We’re very thankful that he’s given us his time. But we need to make sure this isn’t another sort of meet and greet,” Mr Bennett said. “What we have to get next week is concrete answers as to [why] you’re not calling it arbitrary detention." He hopes that a declaration of arbitrary detention by the UK government would enable diplomatic protection for the couple. The family was also considering an application to the International Court of Justice in the Hague. “From there, this is a bit further down the line, we'd be looking to apply for International Court of Justice. this all takes a lot of political will and the right person to get behind it,” Mr Bennett said. Wider impact UN experts have described the couple’s detention as a “state hostage-taking for political leverage”, citing “irregularities” in their trial last year. Mr Ashoori warned that the detainees' families were also victims of trauma, just as his were. "This is what I call shrapnel, because it is not only the victim who has been tyrannised, it is the family members who are hit. Shrapnel is exactly what hits the family members, and they go through the same trauma, but in a different way," he said.

title: Meganisi Council Unanimously Rejects Floating Moorings
body: Meganisi’s municipal council has unanimously rejected a private company’s request to install and commercially operate floating moorings in four bays around the Ionian island, citing environmental, social and economic concerns. The proposal covers the coastal areas of Atherinos, Ampelaki, Limni and Elias/Petalou. Mayor Gerasimos Katopodis told the council that the company had advanced its plans without first informing or consulting the municipal authority or local community. He also criticised the procedure, saying the Port Authority had asked the municipality to express an opinion on the request rather than seek a substantiated recommendation or formal council decision. The council argued that the proposed moorings could alter the natural landscape and turn the bays into commercial anchorages, reducing the available sea space for independent fishers and visitors. It also raised concerns about navigational safety in enclosed bays and the potential impact of increased boat concentrations on the marine environment. The council highlighted the inclusion of Meganisi’s marine and coastal areas in the Natura 2000 network, warning that the project could threaten sensitive ecosystems, including Posidonia seagrass meadows and local biodiversity. The municipality called for an immediate halt to any licensing process that could lead to the privatisation or degradation of the island’s coastline and waters. It authorised the mayor to forward the decision to the relevant ministries and authorities and urged local associations and organisations to state their positions. The council also warned that it would take legal action if authorities proceeded with licensing or implemented the project despite its opposition. title: Buyer and Supplier: How China Sustains Russia’s War
body:
Chinese buyers are locking up Russian oil for October and November, and Indian refiners are paying the price.
According to Reuters, Chinese buyers are booking Russian cargoes in advance and offering firmer prices. That leaves Indian refiners with tighter Russian supplies for October-November. Russian crude arrivals in India were expected to fall to around 1.75 million barrels per day in September, down from roughly 2.1 million in August. Refiners squeezed out of those cargoes are being pushed toward more expensive supplies from the Middle East and North Africa.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The episode shows how far the balance has shifted since 2022. Sanctions, export controls and the loss of European markets cut off many of Russia’s traditional sources of revenue, technology and industrial inputs. They did not end Russia’s economic ties. They pushed Moscow to redirect its trade toward a smaller group of Asian partners, and China has become the most important of them.
China matters the most to the Russian war economy for two reasons. It buys large amounts of Russian energy, and it supplies the machinery, components and materials Russia needs to sustain military production. The two countries now depend on each other, but the balance increasingly favors Beijing.
Russia has vast energy and industrial resources. Turning them into revenue and weapons, however, relies more and more on Chinese markets, supply chains and manufactured goods. China has more room to maneuver. It can diversify its energy suppliers and has a wider range of international economic partners. Russia’s dependence on China therefore has two connected sides: China as a major market for Russian energy, and China as an enabler of Russia’s military-industrial complex. Together, they show that the post-2022 economic order has not simply weakened Russia. It has also pushed Moscow into a deeper and more lopsided relationship with Beijing.
Russia’s pivot away from European energy markets has made China central to its wartime economy. The link is strongest in crude oil. According to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) , China took around 50% of Russia’s crude oil exports between December 2022 and August 2026, making it by far the largest single buyer. It also absorbed roughly 37% of Russia’s coal exports over the same period. By August 2026, China accounted for approximately 51% of Russia’s fossil-fuel export revenues from its five largest importing countries, worth around $8.4 billion.
China is no longer just an important customer. It has become one of the main external markets that lets Moscow turn hydrocarbons into cash and support its wartime economy. This gives China growing influence over the price, volume and terms on which Russia can sell its energy.
That influence became visible in September 2026, when Chinese demand for Russian crude rose amid disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies. Chinese buyers were not just absorbing extra Russian production. They were competing directly with other major Asian buyers and shaping the prices Russia receives.
China has also helped solve one of Russia’s central economic problems after losing much of its European market in 2022: finding buyers large enough to replace it.
Russia remains a major energy producer, but that output is only useful to the Kremlin if it can be shipped, sold and converted into hard currency or other resources. China offers an outlet at a scale few other countries can match. In August, crude oil made up roughly 70% of China’s purchases of Russian fossil fuels. Pipeline gas, liquified natural gas (LNG), coal and oil products accounted for the rest. China’s role therefore spans across several major parts of Russia’s energy-export system, not just one commodity.
This creates a clear imbalance. Russia has the resources, but China has the depth of demand needed to absorb them. If Chinese demand weakens, Moscow has few comparable markets to turn to. China, by contrast, can draw on other suppliers and adjust its purchases to prices and geopolitical conditions. Reuters’ September reporting offers a concrete example. When Chinese buyers began booking Russian cargoes earlier and paying firmer prices, Indian refiners were pushed toward more expensive supplies from the Middle East and North Africa.
The newly enacted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 allows President Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, which could include both China and India. On paper, the law puts the two countries under the same pressure. In practice, there is reason to think Washington may apply it more forcefully against India than against China.
India is deeply tied to the US market and relies heavily on American demand for its exports. China is the main US strategic rival and has far greater economic and geopolitical capacity to hit back. Washington may have more leverage over India precisely because India has more to lose if its access to the American market deteriorates.
Whether the United States will treat China differently remains uncertain.
Suppose India is pressed to cut its Russian crude purchases while China keeps absorbing a large share of the oil Europe no longer buys. Moscow would then rely even more on Chinese demand.
US pressure meant to reduce Russia’s energy revenues could have an unintended effect: it could concentrate Russia’s remaining energy trade around China and strengthen Beijing’s hand in setting the terms on which Russia sells its resources.
China’s dominance should not be overstated, though. CREA’s data show that the European Union still took a substantial share of Russian LNG exports through August 2026. Turkey also remained an important destination for Russian oil products and pipeline gas. China’s position is strongest in specific segments, above all crude oil and coal, and not across every category of Russian energy exports.
China’s importance to Russia’s war effort shows up less in finished weapons than in the machinery, materials and components that make weapons production possible. Across Russia’s military-industrial complex, Chinese inputs are filling gaps created by Western sanctions and export controls. The supply relationship reaches deep into the foundations of Russia’s defense industry.
The scale is striking. China supplied around 62% of the computer numerical control (CNC) machines, components and consumables Russia imported between January 2023 and July 2024. These are not peripheral products. CNC machines are essential for the precision manufacturing of missiles, drones, artillery and other weapons. China also accounted for around 70% of Russia’s machine-tool imports in late 2023. US assessments cited by Newsweek found that roughly 90% of Russia’s microelectronics imports in 2023 came from China.
The pattern extends to aviation. In 2024, China supplied about 85% of Russia’s imported aircraft tires, worth roughly $10.3 million. A component that seems mundane can matter strategically when it keeps combat aircraft flying. The Economic Security Council of Ukraine notes that Russian military aviation operates at such a high tempo that tires on aircraft like the Su-34 and Su-35S may need frequent replacement. China also supplies other industrial inputs, including aramid fibers and rubber.
Russia’s drone production offers perhaps the clearest example. Shipping documents reported by Politico indicate that a Chinese state-owned company supplied 46 tons of PAN precursor, a material used to make high-strength carbon fiber, to Alabuga-Volokno. This Russian producer is linked to the manufacture of Geran drones. According to weapons expert David Albright, the shipment could supply enough material for up to 1,300 drones. The documents reportedly classified the material as a civilian synthetic fiber, not a dual-use product. That raises concerns about how such trade can slip past existing export controls.
Together, these cases point to a broader shift in Russia’s wartime supply chain. China is not just a source of consumer goods or a trading partner that props up Russia’s wider economy. Chinese companies supply parts of the industrial base Russia needs to make, maintain and replenish its weapons. That includes machine tools, microelectronics, raw materials and other dual-use goods. These goods may have civilian uses, but they become strategically important once they enter military production.
This also exposes a central weakness in the sanctions regime. Restricting direct Western exports to Russia works less well when the same technology or material can reach Russian firms through third countries or Chinese intermediaries.
China’s part in sustaining Russia’s wartime economy goes well beyond that of a major trading partner. In energy, Chinese demand gives Russia a critical outlet for crude oil and other fossil fuels it can no longer sell to Europe at the same scale. At the same time, Chinese machinery, microelectronics, industrial materials and other dual-use goods help Russia sustain its military-industrial complex. China has become critical to the flow of revenues that finance Russia’s war and to the industrial capabilities that let it keep fighting.
The dependence is also lopsided. Russia needs Chinese markets and supply chains to offset Western sanctions. China has more access to alternative energy suppliers and can adjust its engagement to its own economic and strategic interests. The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission’s 2025 report puts the asymmetry even more starkly: Russia depends on China for about 34% of its external trade, compared with only 4% for China.
If Western pressure leads other major buyers, particularly India, to cut their purchases of Russian energy while Chinese demand holds up, Russia’s reliance on China could deepen, further undermining the very essence of the existing sanctions regime.
Andrew Thompson is an Irish journalist based in Asia, covering regional developments for the Kyiv Post . A long-time supporter of Ukraine’s independence, he previously worked on democratic development projects with international organizations in Kyiv.

title: IBM AI Releases Granite Speech 5.0 2B for Multilingual Transcription and Translation
body: IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B , a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models : the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, dense. LLM backbone uses YaRN extension to 16k positions. IBM recommends audio segments of up to about 2 minutes. Runs on: GPU via Transformers or vLLM, Apple Silicon via mlx-audio, local CPU/Mac via llama.cpp GGUF (Q8_0 recommended). Performance: #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, 5.68% average English WER. Best: 0.99% WER on LibriSpeech Clean. Worst: 13.79% WER on the leaderboard’s private conversational set. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B work? The model has 3 parts, per the model card . A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks. A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz. The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base . IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters. Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs. What is new versus Granite Speech 4.1 2B? Language ID prompting: name the input language in the prompt to steer transcription. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: bias output toward product names, people and acronyms. Punctuation and capitalization on request: capitalization F1 runs from 90.16 to 99.51 across test sets. Robustness: better handling of noise, reverberation and distant microphones. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B perform on benchmarks? On the Open ASR Leaderboard , IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%. Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only. Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set. On the noisy FFASR leaderboard , it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there. Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%. For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated. Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8. window.addEventListener("message",function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.gs5h){var f=document.getElementById("gs5frame");if(f)f.style.height=e.data.gs5h+"px";}}); How does it compare with other open ASR models? Feature Granite Speech 5.0 2B Qwen3-ASR-1.7B Cohere Transcribe 03-2026 Canary-Qwen-2.5B Size 2B 2.35B (Hub count) 2.07B (Hub count) 2.5B License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 (gated) CC-BY-4.0 ASR languages 6 30 + 22 Chinese dialects 14 English only Speech translation Yes Not disclosed Not disclosed No Open ASR avg WER (Oct 21, 2026)* 5.68% 5.40% 5.77% 5.94% FFASR avg WER (Oct 18, 2026)* 14.80% 13.41% 15.03% Not disclosed Keyword biasing Up to 2,000 terms Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Long audio ~2 min segments Long audio supported Not disclosed 40 s max in training *Leaderboard averages as charted in IBM’s model card from the Open ASR and FFASR leaderboards. What changed in Turbo CTC and 4.1 2B Plus? Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC keeps its 470M footprint. It now transcribes 7 languages with native punctuation and capitalization. IBM compiled one Conformer block and reused its graph across the stack. That lifted throughput to 19,870 RTFx, up from about 12,600 at launch. The updated Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus is a drop-in weight update. Average timestamp shift falls from 210.86 to 98.54. Long-form WER drops from 13.53 to 10.22. Biased-keyword WER falls from 11.79 to 6.48. How can developers deploy it? Granite Speech 5.0 2B runs in Transformers , vLLM, llama.cpp and mlx-audio. For GGUF, IBM recommends Q8_0. Lower-bit quantizations lose accuracy on audio longer than about 1 minute. Key Takeaways #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard at 5.68% WER. 2B parameters, Apache 2.0, runs on GPU, Mac and local CPU. 2,000-term keyword biasing across all supported languages. Turbo CTC reaches 19,870 RTFx and now covers 7 languages. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B still leads on accuracy and noisy audio. Check out the model card , IBM blog and Granite Speech paper . title: Iran demands UN condemnation of illegal US naval blockade
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations called the US naval blockade of Iran a flagrant violation of international law and the UN Charter and demanded the Security Council condemn it.
Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, called the US naval blockade of Iran a flagrant violation of international law and the UN Charter in a letter to the UN secretary-general and the Security Council president.
In the letter to Antonio Guterres and Aglaia Balta, the Security Council's current president, Darzi asked them to reject and strongly condemn the continuation of US aggressive actions against Iran through the naval blockade, calling it a clear violation of the UN Charter and international law, including the prohibition on the use of force and respect for Iran's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The full text of his letter is as follows:
Upon instructions from my Government, and pursuant to our previous letters on the acts of aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Islamic Republic of Iran, I wish to inform Your Excellency and the members of the Security Council of the continuing grave consequences of the persistent acts of aggression being committed by the United States of America against the Islamic Republic of Iran, which began on 28 February 2026, as well as of the subsequent imposition and continuation of an illegal blockade against Iran. These acts of aggression, compounded by the repeated and continuing threats by the President of the United States to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, constitute a grave threat to international peace and security and a flagrant violation of the Charter of the United Nations, particularly Article 2(4), as well as the peremptory norm of general international law (jus cogens) prohibiting aggression. Such threats and actions further endanger the civilian population and violate the fundamental obligations under international humanitarian law to protect civilians and civilian objects irrespective of the unlawful nature of the war of aggression imposed against the Iranian nation.
The United States has further continued and escalated its hostile acts by a campaign of economic coercion through the so-called “Operation Economic Outcast” and sweeping unlawful sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector and other vital sectors of its economy. These cumulative measures, in tandem with an aggressive maritime blockade, have compounded the grave consequences of the aggression and inflicted further harm on the civilian population amounting to collective punishment prohibited under international humanitarian law and international human rights law.
First, the continuation of the maritime blockade is neither an isolated measure nor a merely economic one. It forms part of the broader context of the original acts of aggression, the continuing use of military force, and the resulting violations of Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. While the blockade has been accompanied by broader unlawful coercive measures, the legal implications of these actions are particularly serious and must be assessed in light of Article 2, paragraph 4, of the Charter of the United Nations, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any State. Article 3 (c) of the “Definition of Aggression” annexed to General Assembly resolution 3314 (XXIX) of 14 December 1974 expressly qualifies “the blockade of the ports or coasts of a State by the armed forces of another State” as an act of aggression. Such acts therefore give rise to Iran’s inherent right to self-defense under international law, which continues as long as the blockade is in force against Iranian territory.
Second, the United States cannot evade its international responsibility by replacing or supplementing direct military attacks with a sustained campaign of military interdiction and economic coercion. The law of State responsibility requires that the United States cease its internationally wrongful acts and make full reparation for the injury caused thereby, including all moral and material damage inflicted upon the Iranian nation as a result of the U.S. acts of aggression, as well as the direct targeting of civilians, including women and children, homes, schools, hospitals, other civilian objects and infrastructure. Where internationally wrongful conduct continues, the obligation to cease that conduct persists. The United States therefore bears international responsibility both for its initial acts of aggression and for its subsequent military actions, including the enforcement of the maritime blockade.
Third, the blockade and the associated restrictions have grave humanitarian implications extending far beyond military considerations. By impeding maritime commerce, restricting the movement of commercial vessels and disrupting access to essential supplies, these measures threaten the availability and affordability of food, medicines, medical equipment, fuel, agricultural inputs and other goods indispensable to civilian life. International humanitarian law imposes specific obligations concerning the protection of civilians, the prohibition of starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, and the facilitation of humanitarian relief subject to the applicable legal conditions. A military blockade cannot be used to impose collective punishment upon a civilian population or to deprive civilians of objects indispensable to their survival. In light of these obligations, the continued enforcement of the blockade constitutes a separate and distinct violation of international humanitarian law, compounding the unlawfulness of the original acts of aggression.
Fourth, the imposition of economic pressure through unlawful measures targeting Iran’s civil aviation sector and broader commercial and financial networks compounds these humanitarian and economic risks. Restrictions on airlines impede access to aircrafts, spare parts, equipment, maintenance, repair, inspection, and technical services indispensable to the safe operation of civil aircrafts, thereby exposing passengers and aviation personnel to risks and restricting the movement of millions of civilians. These measures also constitute a stark disregard for the binding Order of the International Court of Justice of 3 October 2018. The Court expressly recognized the potential impact of U.S. measures on civil aviation safety and the lives of its users, and ordered the United States to remove impediments to the free exportation to Iran of goods and services necessary for the safety of civil aviation. The systematic use of economic and financial measures to deliberately inflict severe and widespread hardship upon Iran’s civilian population for political coercion constitutes collective punishment and amounts to a crime against humanity, in flagrant violation of the Charter of the United Nations and fundamental rules of international law, including international human rights law.
The Islamic Republic of Iran emphasizes that respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force, and the peaceful settlement of international disputes are foundational principles of the international legal order upon which the United Nations was built. No State, irrespective of its military power or permanent membership in the Security Council, is entitled to disregard these obligations or to impose its will on another sovereign State through military coercion.
The continued enforcement of the maritime blockade, in the context of the war of aggression launched on 28 February 2026, risks perpetuating the unlawful use of force and normalizing violations of international law. It further undermines confidence in the authority of the Charter and in the capacity of the United Nations to uphold international law without selectivity or double standards. In this context, the Islamic Republic of Iran calls upon you, in the discharge of your responsibilities under the Charter, to:
Categorically reject and strongly condemn the continued acts of aggression by the United States against the Islamic Republic of Iran through maritime blockade as a flagrant violation of the Charter of the United Nations and international law, including the prohibition of the use of force, and the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Islamic Republic of Iran;
Urge the United States to immediately cease its military aggression against Iran and lift the maritime blockade, respect Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and to comply fully with its obligations under the UN Charter and international law;
Recognize that the United States remains internationally responsible for its internationally wrongful acts, including its military aggression and any continuing violations of international law, and that the obligations to cease wrongful conduct and to make full reparation remain applicable in accordance with the law of State responsibility; and
Urge all Member States to refrain from recognizing, supporting, facilitating or implementing unilateral coercive measures by the United States which violate international law and the Charter of the United Nations, particularly measures that cause, or are foreseeably capable of causing, widespread humanitarian harm to civilian populations.
Accountability for aggression and other internationally wrongful acts is indispensable to the maintenance of international peace and security. The Islamic Republic of Iran will pursue all available legal avenues to ensure accountability, reparation and redress, and to hold those responsible to account for the consequences of these unlawful acts. The internationally wrongful acts of the United States entail its responsibility, including the obligation to make full reparation for the injury caused, encompassing restitution, compensation, and satisfaction in accordance with international law. This is without prejudice to any applicable individual criminal responsibility arising from the conduct of persons who have ordered, directed, facilitated or otherwise knowingly abetted the commission of war crimes against the Iranian nation during the recent wars of aggression imposed against Iran.
Iran will continue to exercise its inherent right of self-defence, consistent with Article 51 of the Charter, in response to any acts of aggression.
I should be grateful if you would have the present letter circulated as an official document of the Security Council.
Please accept, Excellencies, the assurances of my highest consideration.

title: AI power demand underestimated, say 81% of energy executives
body: More than eight in 10 energy industry decision-makers expect artificial intelligence to drive electricity demand beyond current forecasts, raising concerns about whether there is enough global infrastructure to power the rapid expansion of data centres. A global survey commissioned by Adipec , Abu Dhabi's annual energy conference, found that 81 per cent of energy industry insiders believe AI-driven electricity consumption will exceed existing projections, with 32 per cent expecting demand to be significantly higher. Only 3 per cent expect demand to fall below current forecasts, according to Adipec's Global Energy Report 2026, released on Thursday. Those surveyed included executives from energy companies, technology providers, investors and industry suppliers. The findings come as technology companies accelerate investment in energy-intensive data centres, creating opportunities for power producers while putting additional pressure on electricity networks. The International Energy Agency expects data centres to consume about 950 terawatt-hours of electricity by 2030, roughly double the 2025 level, according to figures cited in the report. The growth in data centre power demand has become an increasingly important consideration for energy producers and governments. At Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week in January, Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc , said global electricity requirements from data centres could increase fivefold by 2040. The report's findings build on the “power is knowledge” message that was the theme of discussions at Adipec last year, as The National reported. The relationship between AI and electricity remains a central focus of this year's event, which will take place at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi from November 2 to November 5. Technology companies reign The expansion of AI is also expected to change the balance of influence within the energy industry. About 43 per cent of respondents believe technology and AI companies will gain the most influence over the sector, compared with 15 per cent who selected governments and regulators. Financial institutions were also selected by 15 per cent, followed by international oil companies at 14 per cent and national oil companies at 9 per cent. The findings reflect the increasingly close relationship between AI and energy , as technology companies become major drivers of investment in electricity generation and infrastructure. For oil and gas companies, the shift is creating new commercial opportunities. While gas and liquefied natural gas growth currently ranks as the biggest commercial opportunity for oil and gas insiders, AI-driven efficiency is expected to take the top position over the next decade. About 27 per cent identify AI-driven efficiency as a leading opportunity in 10 years, while 25 per cent cite supplying power for AI and data centres. The report also found that 81 per cent of oil and gas insiders believe adopting AI will become essential to remain profitable over the next decade. The findings are particularly relevant to the UAE, where Abu Dhabi is developing a 5-gigawatt AI campus that will house the Stargate UAE computing cluster, expected to cost more than $30 billion . However, a quarter of energy insiders believe the industry is unprepared for AI-driven electricity demand, with grid delays among the biggest obstacles. At Adipec last year, Dr Al Jaber called for “massive” energy investment to meet growing requirements. The Adipec report, conducted by global strategic communications consultancy Kekst CNC between August and October 2026, surveyed 1,832 energy industry decision-makers across 78 countries and included 17 executive interviews. Its findings reflect industry expectations rather than independently verified demand forecasts.

title: AI, cloud services help lift Nokia profits in Q3
body:
"Nokia’s strengths are uniquely suited to meet growing demands for AI infrastructure that is larger, more distributed and hyperconnected," the company's CEO said.
Networking technology company Nokia on Thursday reported stronger-than-expected growth in its third quarter earnings report.
The company said its net sales rose by 9 percent in Q3 (to €5.2bn), compared with the same period last year. Comparable operating profit for July to September climbed 35 percent year-on-year to 605 million euros.
Nokia said its revenue and profitability had developed positively, driven in particular by rising demand from AI and cloud service customers. Sales to AI and cloud service customers more than doubled, up 123 percent, while orders from the sector grew by 118 percent compared with last year. Orders totalled 1.5 billion euros.
Nokia said its strengths put it in an excellent position to meet the growing demands of an increasingly large, distributed and networked AI infrastructure. It pointed to its partnership with Google as an example.
"Nokia’s strengths are uniquely suited to meet growing demands for AI infrastructure that is larger, more distributed and hyperconnected. We are investing where we can differentiate and co-innovate with hyperscalers," Nokia President and CEO Justin Hotard said in the firm's Q3 earnings release.
"Our partnership with Google in support of their 13 billion euros investment in Finland is an example of how our optical and IP networks provide the critical connectivity AI infrastructure requires," he continued.
"Overall, growth is accelerating, operating leverage is becoming more visible and I’m confident in the long-term shareholder value Team Nokia is creating."
