title: Eisenkot leads Netanyahu as Winter, Hendel-Zelekha may not cross electoral threshold - poll
body: An N12 News poll published Wednesday evening ranked Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party first with 23 seats, down one seat from the previous poll. A Channel 13 poll published at the same time also put Yashar in first place; however they only received 20 seats.In both polls, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party came in second, trailing Yashar and falling to 19 seats.Neither poll found that either of the political blocs would win a clear majority; however, the opposition bloc continued to lead Netanyahu's.N12 projected that the opposition bloc would win 55 seats and Netanyahu's bloc 51. By comparison, the Channel 13 poll showed Eisenkot's bloc gaining one seat to 52, while Netanyahu's bloc lost one seat to 49.Whether Ofer Winter's People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha's Reservists-Economic Party cross the 3.25% electoral threshold could affect the balance between the political blocs in the upcoming elections.Other party numbers remained similar to previous pollsFormer prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party remained unchanged at 14 seats, while the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, gained one seat to reach 10, Channel 13 found. In N12, the Democrats remained at nine seats, while B'Yachad gained one seat to reach 15, its highest showing in a month and a half.In both polls, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu polled at eight seats, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit received seven.Shas, led by Arye Deri, received eight seats in the N12 poll but seven on Channel 13, while United Torah Judaism, led by Yakov Asher, received seven in the N12 poll but eight on Channel 13.The Religious Zionist Party (RZP) and Zehut, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, received six seats in the N12 poll, which rose to eight in the Channel 13 poll.The Joint List, comprising Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad and led by Yousef Jabareen, received nine seats in both polls; however, N12 found that Mansour Abbas's Ra'am was polling at five, while Channel 13 placed Ra'am at 6. In both polls, the Arab parties remained stable, earning the same number of seats as in the previous poll.People of Israel, Reservists-Economic parties teeter on the electoral thresholdIn the N12 poll, the People of Israel party won four seats, crossing the electoral threshold after falling below it in the previous two polls. However, the Reservists-Economic Party remained below the electoral threshold with 2.8% of the vote.In contrast, the Channel 13 poll reversed the two. The Reservists-Economic Party kept its four seats and remained above the electoral threshold. Meanwhile, the People of Israel party fell below the electoral threshold after receiving four seats in the previous poll.A pollster for The Madad and Channel 13 News spoke with 103FM about the latest Channel 13 poll, explaining how the results of the two parties could affect the distribution of Knesset seats between the blocs.Which party will fail to cross the electoral threshold could be significantAddressing a scenario in which one or both parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, he explained which bloc could benefit from the redistribution of seats."In terms of the balance between the blocs, if neither crosses the threshold, eight seats can be redistributed among other parties. However, one scenario is that one fails to cross the threshold and the other does, leaving four seats to be redistributed. Which party fails to cross the threshold could be significant. The side that would benefit more would be what we call the 'change bloc,' rather than the coalition bloc," he said, adding, "That is the conclusion we reached."He also addressed where the two parties draw their support from and the differences between voters backing Winter and those supporting Hendel and Zelekha."People of Israel and the Reservists receive votes from both sides in almost equal measure. The question is when we start counting, whether we use the 2022 election as our starting point and ask where those votes were in the previous election," he explained."It is true that Hendel and Zelekha's votes come more evenly from both sides, while most of Winter's votes come from the coalition side. Nevertheless, Winter also took roughly one seat, out of the nearly four he has, from the opposition side, mainly from Liberman's party," he added.

title: Over 100 SPLM-IO members defect to SPLM Party in E. Equatoria
body: More than 100 members of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO) in Eastern Equatoria State have announced their defection to rejoin the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) Party ahead of South Sudan’s anticipated December elections. The group, led by former Eastern Equatoria Deputy Governor Karlo Andrew Akwo, announced its decision during a welcoming ceremony at the SPLM Party State Secretariat in Torit on Wednesday. Reading a declaration addressed to SPLM-IO interim chairman Stephen Par Kuol, Akwo said the members requested that their names and membership records be removed from the party’s registers and structures. The group also communicated its decision to rejoin the SPLM Party under the leadership of President Salva Kiir Mayardit through Eastern Equatoria SPLM Chairperson General Louis Lobong Lojore. Akwo said the decision was guided by the spirit of the Arusha Agreement on the reunification of the SPLM. He said more than 100 members were joining the ruling party, although some could not attend the ceremony because of logistical challenges. Akileo Mboya Peter Anyanga, the SPLM Party State Secretary, welcomed the returning members, describing their decision as an opportunity to promote reconciliation, forgiveness and renewed cooperation. “You are our brothers and sisters. Your return reminds us that no matter the differences we may have experienced, the bonds that bind us are stronger than those that divide us,” he said. “Your decision to rejoin the SPLM (Party) demonstrates that our shared aspirations for peace, stability, and development are stronger than our political differences.” He urged party members to put past disagreements behind them and strengthen grassroots mobilization, membership registration, and participation in party activities. Meanwhile, Dr. Margaret Itto Leonardo, the SPLM Party Deputy Chairperson in the state, called on political leaders across South Sudan to abandon hatred and conflict and work towards peaceful coexistence. “Today is great because we are receiving our brothers and sisters who have joined us. I was happy to hear that there are more with you,” she said. “If we go back to our history when we stood together in the liberation [struggle] as Southern Sudanese, we won because of being together.” She said Eastern Equatoria had room for political leaders willing to contribute to public service and development, urging members to work together in preparation for the elections. Relatedly, Mussa Albino Karmato, a former chief whip of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA) in the Eastern Equatoria State Transitional Parliament, also announced his return to the SPLM. Karmato called on political leaders and party members to embrace unity, warning that internal divisions could undermine their ability to serve communities. For his part, Mathew Ugwak, a former member of the State Peace Commission nominated by the SPLM-IO, said he left the SPLM Party in 2015 following disagreements linked to divisions within his community in Lafon County. He said he had to work outside the party to help reunite his community and was now returning with a renewed commitment to unity. He warned that political disagreements among leaders could spill over into communities and undermine social cohesion. Ruth Marious Bugga, the SPLM Party deputy secretary for research in Eastern Equatoria State, described the return of former members as a significant political development and urged members to embrace forgiveness and work towards a common goal. The announcements come as South Sudan prepares for general elections scheduled for December 22, 2026. The extent to which the return of former opposition members will affect the SPLM Party’s membership and electoral support in Eastern Equatoria remains to be seen. The post Over 100 SPLM-IO members defect to SPLM Party in E. Equatoria appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Talks resume in Geneva as Sudan war deepens humanitarian crisis
body: Talks aimed at halting the fighting in Sudan and easing the humanitarian crisis resumed in Geneva on Wednesday, with representatives of 21 countries and five international institutions discussing possible ceasefires, security arrangements and political solutions to the conflict. The two-day meeting brought together international and regional partners to coordinate peace initiatives and explore a path towards a ceasefire and a peaceful political transition that reflects the aspirations of all Sudanese people. “Our first session, devoted to de-escalation, will offer an opportunity to explore practical ways forward,” said Pekka Haavisto, the United Nations secretary-general’s personal envoy for Sudan, urging delegates to identify practical measures and use their “respective channels of engagement to build confidence and help create conditions conducive to a comprehensive ceasefire”. The conflict, now in its fourth year, began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), former allies who jointly seized power in a 2021 coup. Deadly drone attacks targeting civilians and public infrastructure have become a feature of the war and have been repeatedly condemned by humanitarian and human rights officials. “The war in Sudan has become a drone war; it kills mostly civilians,” said Alexandre Fasel, Switzerland’s state secretary, whose country is co-hosting the meeting with the United Nations. “Famine-like conditions persist in Darfur, the Kordofan state and elsewhere in the country; it is the war that drives this hunger,” Fasel said. Highlighting the protections afforded to civilians under international law, Fasel said the Geneva Conventions “are very clear: the protection of civilians and humanitarian access must not wait for a ceasefire and a political solution. Civilians are suffering and dying today.” Working Together in #Geneva 21 States & 5 international organizations agreed at the 6th Consultative Meeting on #Sudan to strengthen coordination of #Peace efforts. The population needs a ceasefire. The risk of widespread famine is stronger than ever. pic.twitter.com/5rgjEChc4X — SwitzerlandUN (@swiss_un) October 21, 2026 Millions in need Nearly 34 million people across Sudan need humanitarian assistance, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Fasel said. He also cited warnings from the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) that eight million Sudanese children are out of school. “This is not only a violation to the right of education but an immense risk factor for a future stable Sudan. Conflict-related sexual violence has re-emerged as a tactic to terrorise and humiliate the civilian population, often targeted along ethnicity or perceived affiliations,” he said. Alongside efforts to secure a ceasefire, delegates are expected to discuss a Sudanese-led transitional political phase that reflects the aspirations of the country’s people through an inclusive and credible dialogue, Haavisto said. “Our role is to support the Sudanese in shaping their country’s shared future, with due regard for the diversity of their voices and experiences,” he said. Coordinating peace efforts The talks, officially known as the Consultative Meetings on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts in Sudan, are intended to help mediators coordinate their approaches to ending the conflict. Previous meetings have been held in Cairo in June 2024 and January 2026, Djibouti in July 2024, Nouakchott in December 2024 and Brussels in June 2025. Neither the Sudanese government nor the RSF is represented at the Geneva meeting, as the mechanism was established to coordinate the efforts of mediators and international partners. On the sidelines of Wednesday’s meeting, Haavisto was also expected to engage with key regional and international partners from the so-called Quad mechanism, comprising the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt, and the Quintet, which includes the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the United Nations, the European Union and the League of Arab States. In #Geneva today, the Special Representative of the Chairperson of the Commission ( #SRCC ), Amb. Mohamed Belaiche led the #Quintet at the Sixth Consultative Meeting on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts for #Sudan . Building on convergence with the Quad, the… pic.twitter.com/Xv7yuo6lKX — African Union Political Affairs Peace and Security (@AUC_PAPS) October 21, 2026 The Geneva talks followed a day of humanitarian-focused discussions involving delegations, senior United Nations officials and international non-governmental organisations operating in Sudan, including the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the Sudan INGO Forum. Haavisto highlighted intensified coordination between the Quad and the Quintet, describing the increased cooperation as “maybe the most important fact”. He said the discussions aimed to link security negotiations with political planning for the period following a possible ceasefire. Swiss Ambassador Tim Enderlin, head of the Swiss Foreign Ministry’s peace and human rights division, also stressed the need for coordinated international efforts and an inclusive, Sudanese-led peace process. “We tried these two days to come up with coordinated efforts that will help to establish a peace process that can be inclusive, that involves the people of Sudan, where their voices are heard,” Enderlin said. He said the aim was to establish a process that “in the end, is Sudan-owned and Sudan-led”. Enderlin warned that the consequences of the conflict extended beyond Sudan to neighbouring countries. The post Talks resume in Geneva as Sudan war deepens humanitarian crisis appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,572,790 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,572,790 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 22.
The number includes 2,250 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,439 tanks, 25,594 armored combat vehicles, 165,641 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,447 artillery systems, 2,229 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,719 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,997 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Women leaders push Kiir to fast-track gender bills
body: Women leaders in South Sudan have urged President Salva Kiir Mayardit to prioritise legislation addressing gender-based violence, women’s empowerment, enterprise funding and family law, warning that women’s rights and political participation require stronger protection. The call was made in a communiqué issued in Juba on Wednesday at the end of a two-day consultative workshop organised by the Centre for Inclusive Governance, Peace and Justice (CIGPJ), with support from Norwegian People’s Aid (NPA) and the Swiss Mission in Juba. The communiqué urges Kiir to issue a provisional order to pass four bills: the anti-gender-based violence bill, women’s empowerment bill, women enterprise fund bill and family law bill. Participants said protecting women’s rights and strengthening their participation in political and public life are essential as South Sudan prepares for elections scheduled for December 22, 2026. Jackline Nasiwa, Executive Director of CIGPJ, said women’s political participation is a human rights issue requiring practical support from the government and development partners. “Women’s political participation is a human rights issue,” Nasiwa said, urging partners to invest in efforts to ensure women could participate effectively in the electoral process. She said some women could not afford registration fees or the cost of travelling to their constituencies, while insecurity posed additional barriers. Nasiwa also urged the government to honour its affirmative action commitments, warning against further declines in women’s representation in political institutions. The communiqué calls on the Political Parties Council (PPC) to develop gender policies for all political parties and urges the appointment of gender advisers in the Office of the President, caretaker state governments and administrative areas. It also recommends that the National Elections Commission (NEC) establish a situation room on Women, Peace and Security to monitor and address issues affecting women during the elections. Dr. Angelina Mathijo Bazugba, a Women, Peace and Security analyst and assistant professor at the University of Juba, read the communiqué on behalf of the participants. The statement cited the 2018 Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan, which provides for a minimum 35% quota for women’s representation in transitional governance structures. According to the communiqué, women’s representation in senior leadership has fallen from 26% to 15% nationally and from 31% to 22% at state level under the current caretaker government. Participants attributed women’s underrepresentation to structural barriers, stereotypes, cultural norms, insecurity and shrinking civic space. Prof. Pauline Elaine Riak, a national peacebuilding expert and deputy vice-chancellor of Rumbek University of Science and Technology, urged women leaders to strengthen cooperation across political and ethnic divides to increase their participation in national affairs. Riak recalled women’s involvement in previous peace negotiations in South Sudan, saying collective action had helped them secure a place in important political discussions. She urged women to look beyond local and political affiliations and work together to promote inclusive participation and national unity. Nunu Diana Alison, Director General of the Directorate of Gender, Child and Social Welfare in Central Equatoria State, called for stronger safeguards for women in politics, including protection against intimidation and gender-based violence. She also proposed a women’s political convention to help leaders agree on strategies to secure representation in the upcoming elections. Alison said women need to coordinate their efforts to compete for positions beyond seats reserved for women while safeguarding the 35% affirmative action commitment. Michael Gorgin Kuol, women and youth coordinator at Norwegian People’s Aid, urged women leaders to move beyond issuing statements and communiqués and engage political leaders directly to secure commitments on representation. He encouraged them to lobby collectively across political parties and engage the National Elections Commission and Political Parties Council to advance their demands before the elections. The workshop brought together more than 50 participants, including women political leaders, current and former public officials, political party representatives, civil society organisations, academics, youth groups, faith-based organisations and development partners. The participants concluded by condemning what they described as a regression in women’s participation in nation-building and called for sustained efforts to protect women’s political gains. The post Women leaders push Kiir to fast-track gender bills appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: 630 Drones Toward Moscow, Russian Military Repair Plant Reportedly Hit
body:
Ukrainian drones reportedly launched a large-scale overnight attack across several Russian regions, with footage suggesting a strike on a military repair plant near Moscow that services Russian air defense systems.
Russian officials reported damage to residential buildings and infrastructure in multiple regions, while Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that 630 drones had been heading toward the capital since the evening of Oct. 21.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Sobyanin said 163 drones had been shot down as they approached Moscow. Two people were injured near the village of Voronovo, and were receiving medical assistance, he added.
Footage analyzed by the Russian outlet Astra suggests that one of the targets was the 75th Arsenal military plant in Serpukhov, near Moscow. Videos shared by eyewitnesses reportedly show an explosion followed by a fire at the facility.
Residents also reported in local chat groups that at least three missiles had struck the area. These accounts have not been independently verified.
The 75th Arsenal falls under Russia’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate (GRAU) and is involved in manufacturing and storing weapons and ammunition, as well as repairing military equipment, including artillery systems and air defense complexes.
According to Russian state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec, the facility has repaired equipment for the Buk-M1, Buk-M2 and S-300V air defense systems.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the plant had previously attracted attention from the open-source intelligence (OSINT) community. In a March 29, 2024 post, an OSINT researcher identified as Jompy described the 75th Arsenal as the only storage base for Russian anti-aircraft systems he had managed to locate.
The reported strike on the facility has not been independently confirmed.
Overnight attacks were also reported in Lipetsk, Tula and Voronezh regions.
Lipetsk Region Governor Igor Artamonov said a man born in 2001 was injured in the attack. Several private homes and apartment buildings sustained damage to their windows and facades, while Polyclinic No. 7 was also struck, with no injuries reported at the medical facility.
According to Astra, which analyzed eyewitness footage, a drone struck the Atmosfera residential complex in Lipetsk, sparking a fire on its upper floors. Local media reported that the injured man was near the building when he was hit by falling drone debris.
In Tula region, regional head Dmitry Milyaev said 70 drones had been destroyed. No casualties were reported, but private homes in Zaoksky District and buildings in Tula sustained damage, he said.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev reported that 44 drones had been destroyed overnight. He said there were no casualties, although private homes and an apartment building were damaged in one municipality, while power infrastructure was affected in another.
As of publication, Russia’s Defense Ministry had not released an official total for the number of drones downed during the attacks. Ukraine has not confirmed its involvement.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Closed joint stock companies must meet governance requirements
body:
MUSCAT: Closed joint stock companies in Oman must comply with the Corporate Governance Principles before the end of their financial year, according to guidance issued by the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Investment Promotion. The guidance, which refers to Ministerial Decision No. 5/2025, outlines requirements for electing independent board members and nominating candidates for vacant board seats. Independent directors must be elected under the board election agenda item. Seats will be allocated to candidates receiving the highest number of votes, subject to the company’s circumstances and the provisions of Article 6/3. The ministry clarified that independent directors may serve on both the board and its committees, with the same obligations applying to them as to other board members. All candidates, including those seeking independent seats, must contest under the same board election agenda item. Candidates cannot stand for election in more than one capacity to fill vacant board seats. The guidance sets out the steps boards must follow when implementing the governance principles and bringing their companies into compliance within the stipulated timeframe.

title: SalamAir launches lights to Erbil, Damascus
body:
SalamAir, Oman’s low-cost airline, held a joint ceremony at Muscat International Airport to celebrate its services to Erbil and Damascus, highlighting the airline’s continued expansion and commitment to making travel more accessible. The ceremony was held under the patronage of Eng. Khamis bin Mohammed Al Shamakhi, Undersecretary of the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology and Chairman of SalamAir, and attended by Dr. Razzaq Salman Mashkoor Minister Plenipotentiary and Deputy Head of the Iraqi Diplomatic Mission, and Khalid Al Ayoubi, Chargé d’Affaires at the Embassy of the Syrian Arab Republic in the Sultanate of Oman. The Muscat–Erbil service will commence on October 25, 2026 with two weekly flights, introducing SalamAir’s second destination in Iraq and complementing its existing Baghdad operations. Known for its historic citadel and vibrant markets, Erbil brings another distinctive destination to the airline’s growing network. SalamAir will commence direct flights between Muscat and Damascus on October 28, 2026, becoming the first Omani airline to operate this route. The service will strengthen connectivity between Oman and Syria, providing a convenient travel option for passengers travelling for tourism and business. The route will also offer travellers opportunities to discover the Syrian capital’s rich cultural heritage, historic landmarks and traditional markets. Eng. Yaqoob bin Saif bin Hamoud Al Kiyumi, Chief Executive Officer of SalamAir, said: “Each destination creates new opportunities for people to connect, whether they are travelling for business, exploring somewhere new or returning home to their families. title: UTME: 108 underage candidates meet FG’s admission criteria
body: The Federal Government said only 108 out of approximately 39,000 underage candidates who sat the 2026 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) have met the requirements for possible admission into tertiary institutions. The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, disclosed this on Wednesday in Abuja while receiving the two highest-scoring UTME candidates and six outstanding underage candidates presented by the Registrar of the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB), Prof. Segun Aina. Alausa said 2,244,149 candidates registered for the 2026 UTME, while 2,174,396 sat the examination. Approximately 39,000 of those who took the examination were below the minimum admission age of 16. He explained that underage candidates seeking exemption from the age requirement had to meet stringent academic and maturity criteria, including scoring at least 320 out of 400 in the UTME and a minimum of 80 per cent in their post-UTME examinations. JAMB had also stipulated that candidates must attain at least 80 per cent in their O’Level results, equivalent to 24 points out of 30, in a single sitting. Combining WAEC and NECO results is not permitted, while candidates must meet the subject requirements for their intended courses. Those who satisfy the initial benchmarks undergo further assessment by the National Committee on Underage Admission, which evaluates their psychological, emotional and intellectual readiness for university education outside the standard Central Admissions Processing System (CAPS). According to Alausa, only 391 underage candidates scored at least 320 in the UTME, with further assessments narrowing the number that met the requirements to 108. He described the successful candidates as exceptionally gifted, representing approximately 0.005 per cent of those who sat the examination. “You are the geniuses in our society,” the minister told the students, urging them to use their abilities to develop innovations and solutions to Nigeria’s challenges. Alausa said the minimum admission age policy was not intended to deny gifted children educational opportunities but to ensure that younger candidates possessed the maturity required for higher education. He added that officials were impressed by the candidates’ confidence, intellectual ability and responses during the screening exercise. The minister urged the successful candidates to see their education as an opportunity to contribute to national development and congratulated them on behalf of President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Ministry of Education. Among those recognised were Owoeye Daniella Jesudunsin, who scored 372, and Enwere Kingsley Ikenna, who scored 370. All eight candidates received plaques and certificates from the minister.

title: 4 vessels hit by IRGC, 3 others hit mine in Strait of Hormuz
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 22 (MNA) – The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy said four violating vessels transferring oil cargo ship-to-ship in the northern Persian Gulf were hit simultaneously and are burning, while three others struck mines overnight.
Four violating vessels transferring oil cargo ship-to-ship in the northern Persian Gulf were hit simultaneously and are burning, the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy said, adding that three other violating vessels struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz overnight and were stopped after sustaining damage and fire.
In a statement, the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy praised the Iranian people's steadfastness, saying it gives strength to the country's military forces and has brought humiliation and despair to Iran's enemies. It said its naval forces continue to manage and control the Strait of Hormuz with this broad national backing.
Following earlier warnings to violating shipping companies that it said were deceived by the aggressor US army and crossed illegal routes, Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy forces tracked and pursued four violating vessels that had previously crossed the illegal route. They discovered the vessels conducting ship-to-ship transfers of oil cargo in the northern middle of the Persian Gulf, and all four were hit simultaneously and are burning, the statement said.
It said three other violating vessels struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz overnight, were damaged, caught fire and were stopped.
The statement said the arrogant US regime's insistence on inciting vessels to cross the mined illegal route has increased maritime incidents day by day. It warned that the aggressor US army should know that continuing this scope of confrontation will draw it to its aggressor bases in the region, describing this as a serious warning.

title: Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, top stories this morning
body:
News in Georgia , Armenia , and Azerbaijan . Key headlines and top stories covered by local media, from 12-16 October, 2026
● The Constitutional Court continues hearing a lawsuit filed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia – Lelo, the Federalist Party and Gakharia for Georgia. At the second hearing on 22 October, the seven-member plenary court rejected all motions, including requests for an advisory opinion from the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg and for experts from the Venice Commission to be invited. The hearing continues today, 23 October, and, according to court president Revaz Nadaraia, proceedings will be intensive over the coming days.
● OSCE Parliamentary Assembly Vice-President Gudrun Kugler urged Georgia’s authorities to withdraw the lawsuit seeking to ban opposition parties and “stop politically motivated persecution”. Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili described “threatening” statements by foreign governments as an attempt to pressure the Constitutional Court. He said MPs had a constitutionally guaranteed right to file the lawsuit.
● Dito Chubinidze, a journalist with the Asaval-Dasavali newspaper, has been arrested on charges of treason and sabotage. According to the indictment, since February 2026 he has spread false information by accusing the prime minister of secretly handing over part of the ancient David Gareji monastery complex to Azerbaijan. Located directly on the border between the two countries, the complex is disputed, leaving this section of the border undelimited. Chubinidze also claimed that the prime minister’s alleged actions had obstructed the work of the government commission on border delimitation and demarcation. The charges carry a prison sentence of up to four years. His lawyer says Chubinidze rejects the accusations. The Georgian Charter of Journalistic Ethics has called on the prosecutor’s office to make its evidence and arguments public.
● Foreign ministers from Georgia and four Central Asian countries – Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan – will meet in Batumi today, 23 October. Bilateral talks between Georgia’s foreign minister and his counterparts are also expected. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze met the ministers on the eve of the meeting, saying that expanding cooperation with Central Asian countries across various sectors was a priority for Georgia.
● According to Freedom House’s annual Freedom on the Net 2026 report, Georgia has lost its “free” status and is now classified as “partly free”. The country scored 68 out of 100, down from 70 last year. Georgia had been rated “free” since 2012. The report says the government restricts online activism and criticism of the ruling party, while critical social media users and online journalists face fines, searches and investigations.
● High fuel prices will continue to contribute to inflation until the second quarter of 2027, according to the National Bank’s monetary policy report. Annual inflation reached 5.6% in September, with energy prices directly accounting for around two percentage points. The report says long-term loans in lari, mainly mortgages, have become cheaper, while lending conditions in foreign currencies are expected to tighten.
● The Georgian Diplomatic Society has described the extension of the mandate of the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia as a “dangerous move”. First Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili was appointed to the role, with “peaceful resolution of the conflict with the Russian Federation” added to his mandate. The society’s members argue that appointing a serving diplomat to the position could be seen as a step towards restoring diplomatic relations, while the new wording “threatens the international Geneva talks format” on the conflict stemming from Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories.
● Russia has announced that two Georgian dairy-processing companies will be allowed to enter its market from November. The decision followed a meeting in Tbilisi between representatives of Russia’s food safety watchdog and Georgia’s National Food Agency. Russia had previously imposed a ban on imports of a range of Georgian products. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the restrictions introduced on 9 October were not politically motivated.
● Georgia’s Public Defender’s Office has called on the prosecutor’s office to investigate the alleged abuse of David Peikrishvili, a jailed crime boss, including possible involvement by prison staff. According to the office, Peikrishvili provided detailed information through his representatives at Vivamedi clinic, where he was hospitalised. He alleges that he was severely beaten at Gldani Prison No. 8. The Special Penitentiary Service denies that physical abuse took place. The case is currently being investigated by the Justice Ministry’s General Inspection. More on the case here.
● A court has found Levan Zardiashvili and Saba Mindashvili guilty of obstructing journalists’ professional activities and fined them 3,000 and 4,000 lari, respectively (approximately $1,100 and $1,500). The incident took place on 8 September 2025, during a protest against Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze amid his election campaign. Reports at the time said Publika journalists Aleksandre Keshelashvili and Keto Mikadze were beaten and had their phones taken away.
PHOTO: Well-known animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who had been arrested, has signed a plea deal and was released from the courtroom. He was accused of threatening an opponent with death and physical violence during a dispute in Tbilisi on 30 August. He later published a letter on social media admitting guilt. Photo: Vano Gorgishvili / Interpressnews.
● Azerbaijan’s Media and Broadcasting Council has dismissed reports in Turkish media and on social media alleging mass arrests in Azerbaijan for wearing hijab and claiming that people are leaving the country as a result, calling them disinformation. The statement also strongly condemned Turkish politicians and public figures who spread such claims in offensive terms. The Council urged media outlets and public figures to act responsibly when publishing information and to verify it through reliable sources.
Context. Experts point to two reasons for the ongoing deterioration in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey. One is Azerbaijan’s partnership with Israel, while Turkey’s relations with Israel have sharply worsened. The other is the strong backlash in Turkey against Azerbaijan’s de facto ban on wearing hijab in schools. Critics include an adviser to the Turkish president, ruling party representatives, prominent public figures and journalists. Azerbaijan’s ruling party issued a strongly worded response, describing the statements made in Turkey as interference in the country’s internal affairs. Read more here.
● Eight imprisoned religious activists have appealed to foreign embassies in Azerbaijan, asking them to grant asylum to their families or at least arrange for their children to attend schools run by the embassies. The signatories say their children face rough treatment and psychological pressure at school because they wear hijab. The activists have also asked for help ensuring their safety in prison. The Interior Ministry reported that 37 people had been detained amid protests against new secular school uniform rules that exclude hijab. Religious activists claim that around 400 people have been detained across the country.
● Defence cooperation between Turkey, Azerbaijan and the United States has considerable potential, Mert Yunsal, head of the defence, aerospace and space industries committee at the Turkish-American Business Association (TABA-AmCham), said at an investment summit in Baku. According to Yunsal, the current volume of defence-related transactions between Turkey and Azerbaijan stands at $160–197 million, while trade between Turkey and the US in this sector is worth $1.2–1.4 billion. Figures for US-Azerbaijan defence trade are not available. Yunsal said the three countries share numerous interests and could benefit from cooperation in producing missile systems, aircraft and drones. However, he noted that entering the US market involves complex licensing procedures for Azerbaijani companies, requiring considerable time and financial resources. TABA-AmCham plans to help companies from all three countries find partners and establish joint ventures in the defence industry.
● Azerbaijan’s Supreme Court has upheld a prison sentence of seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki, a social affairs expert and head of the Ubuntu association, who is one of the defendants in the criminal case against NGOs. Like other civil society representatives charged in the case, Zaki was accused of money laundering, abuse of office and official forgery over the handling of a grant worth 50,000 manats (approximately $29,000). Zaki denies the charges. His lawyer said the allegations had not been proven and that receiving a grant should not, in any case, carry criminal liability.
Around 50 people are involved in the broader NGO case; some have already been sentenced, while others are awaiting verdicts. They include staff from international organisations that provided grants in Azerbaijan. None of the defendants admit guilt, and they describe the prosecution as politically motivated.
● Following a meeting in Rome between Italy’s Minister of Enterprises and Made in Italy Adolfo Urso and Azerbaijan’s Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov, the two sides agreed to expand investment, technological cooperation and trade ties, with the aim of increasing bilateral trade from €8 billion in 2025 to more than €10 billion. They also discussed joint projects involving critical raw materials, innovation and strategic supply chains. During the visit, the Azerbaijani delegation met representatives of Italian companies including Eni, Snam, Saipem, Ansaldo Energia, Danieli, Aruba and TIM. Italy is the largest market for Azerbaijani exports and ranks seventh among suppliers of goods to Azerbaijan.
● Azerbaijan has approved a national strategy to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 40% by 2035 compared with 1990 levels and achieve net-zero emissions by 2060. The plan includes expanding solar and wind power, developing clean transport, reducing methane leaks, improving waste recycling and restoring forests. “Green energy zones” are planned for Karabakh, East Zangezur and Nakhchivan. To implement the strategy, Azerbaijan is seeking international funding, investment and the transfer of modern technologies.
● Azerbaijan has protested against a report by the UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief, accusing the rapporteur of ignoring damage to religious heritage during more than 30 years of Armenian occupation of Azerbaijani territories. The report focused on religious rights and, among other issues, referred to the destruction of Christian gravestones and cemeteries in Nakhchivan, an Azerbaijani autonomous republic. “Why did the rapporteur fail to mention that at least 65 mosques were completely destroyed in Azerbaijani territories during the Armenian occupation, while cemeteries were extensively desecrated and looted?” asked Shahriyar Hajiyev, Azerbaijan’s representative to the UN. He said the report contained unverified information and questioned the rapporteur’s impartiality. Hajiyev said Azerbaijan has 994 officially registered religious communities, 2,387 mosques, 16 churches and seven synagogues.
● Azerbaijani media are quoting Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan as saying: “I said that a peace agreement with Azerbaijan could be signed before 2031. To be precise, I believe we should sign the agreement in 2027–2028. We must work with Azerbaijan.”
● Azerbaijani media are also quoting Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan, who told a government meeting that signing a peace agreement with Azerbaijan as soon as possible is a political commitment of Armenia’s government.
● Javid Aghamaliyev, chairman of the board of the state-owned Nakhchivan Agroservice company, has been arrested in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic on suspicion of embezzling state funds. A criminal case has been opened.
● The 2026 FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival will take place in Baku from 24 to 30 October. FIFA is organising the tournament and festival for the first time. A total of 189 countries are expected to participate, with around 1,000 matches planned. Azerbaijan’s team will play its first match against Timor-Leste on 24 October, followed by two matches on 25 October against Andorra and Australia. On 26 October, the Azerbaijani team will face Israel and Haiti.
● Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan commented at a briefing on warnings from the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) that Armenia’s membership could be suspended because of its deepening ties with the EU. The EAEU statement forecast substantial economic losses for Armenia in such a scenario. “For the first time in our history, the ‘metropole’ is not drawing us towards itself but, on the contrary, is effectively saying: ‘We will push you away’,” Pashinyan said. He stressed that Russia’s restrictions on imports of virtually all Armenian goods “did not produce the results that certain circles, both inside Armenia and beyond its borders, had expected”. “This step did not work either economically or politically,” the prime minister said. Full details here
● EU Ambassador to Armenia Vassilis Maragos declined to comment on warnings issued by the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) to Armenia. “This is a matter for the Armenian authorities. But, of course, the EU is monitoring developments. We are here to support the Armenian people,” Maragos said.
● A peace treaty with Azerbaijan could be signed in 2027–2028, the prime minister told journalists. He was commenting on statements by Azerbaijani leaders that a condition for signing the treaty is the removal from Armenia’s Constitution of a provision that Baku regards as a territorial claim against Azerbaijan. Nikol Pashinyan said he had personally told Azerbaijan’s leadership that raising this issue in Baku was unacceptable to him. According to Pashinyan, he was told in response that Azerbaijan had no intention of interfering and was merely stating its political position. Pashinyan stressed that Armenia intends to amend its Constitution regardless. He did not rule out holding snap elections if the opposition opposes the changes.
● An Azerbaijani shepherd who illegally crossed the Armenian border has been handed over to Azerbaijan, the prime minister said. Armenia’s National Security Service had earlier reported that the man had got lost. “The man was walking along the road. What, were we supposed to start shooting at him and kill him? He was detained and handed over to Armenia’s National Security Service,” Nikol Pashinyan said. He added that there was no border in the world that a person could not somehow cross.
● Vazgen Galstanyan (Archbishop Bagrat), who previously led a movement demanding Nikol Pashinyan’s resignation, says the border has been left unguarded. “This is already the second such incident referring to the 1 October incident, when an Azerbaijani serviceman illegally crossed the border and wounded a local woman – JAMnews]. They talked a lot about how well protected we were, and now two people have crossed the border. Imagine if they had been armed groups, even just three people, or even two. What would we have done then?” he said.
Galstanyan is under house arrest. He was detained in June 2025 on charges of plotting terrorist attacks and attempting to seize power in the country.
● A working group led by Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan has travelled to Syunik Province, on the border with Azerbaijan, to begin practical work on the transit project known as the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP). “We are talking about railways, roads and energy infrastructure,” Grigoryan said.
● Security Council Secretary Alen Simonyan met in Yerevan with Cosmin Dinescu, head of the European Union Mission in Armenia. Simonyan stressed the importance of EU support in strengthening Armenia’s state institutions. They discussed prospects for further developing cooperation.
● Armenia’s Prosecutor General Anna Vardapetyan is on a working visit to Tbilisi at the invitation of Georgia’s Prosecutor General Giorgi Gvarakidze. She also met Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Both sides stressed the importance of strengthening the partnership between the two countries in the legal sphere and joint efforts to combat crime.
● The conditions in which former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan is being held in a detention facility do not meet standards, MP Agnesa Khamoyan, an ally of Kocharyan, told journalists. She said she was speaking from personal observation, having seen the cell where he is being held. However, she believes Kocharyan himself will not complain about the conditions. Public criminal proceedings were launched in August this year against Kocharyan and nine other people. According to the charges, while president, Kocharyan abused his office to carry out transactions through which he obtained valuable state property for himself and transferred it to his son and people and companies linked to him at prices significantly below market value. The prosecution says the deals were often conducted without tenders and according to prearranged schemes.
● The state budget has allocated 148.5 million drams (approximately $412,000) to purchase two manuscripts for the Matenadaran’s historical archive.
● Armenia’s National Security Service has confirmed that an Azerbaijani citizen illegally crossed the Armenian border on 19 October. Yashar Gasimov, son of Ali, born in 1968, reportedly lost his way. “Appropriate measures are being taken to return the Azerbaijani citizen,” the NSS said. Armenian media were the first to report that an Azerbaijani shepherd had illegally crossed into Armenia. Some reports said he was carrying a white flag.
● Armenia is discussing a report by the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), led by Russia, which warns of serious economic consequences if the country leaves the bloc. Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan believes the report greatly exaggerates the potential impact. According to Papoyan, leaving the EAEU would have a limited effect on Armenia’s economy, estimated at -0.61%. Responding to the report’s claim that gas prices in Armenia would rise by 69% if the country left the bloc, Papoyan argued that changes in gas prices could affect the economy by around 5–7%. “There will be no situation from which we cannot find a way out. We have already paid, or are still paying, the difference in the price of supplied gas one way or another. An increase in gas prices is undesirable, but I believe that, over time, buying gas at market prices should become a logical decision. Through adaptation, we should reach that point,” Papoyan said.
● Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan commented on a statement by the secretary general of the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO), a military alliance led by Russia, suggesting that Armenia could resume active participation in the organisation “in view of the changing international situation”. “I cannot imagine how Armenia would return to the CSTO,” the minister told reporters.
Armenia froze its participation in the CSTO two years ago and has since neither taken part in its activities nor paid membership fees. Yerevan’s decision was a response to what it saw as the allies’ failure to help when Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory. Several such incidents occurred in 2021–2022. The CSTO justified its failure to intervene by saying that the border with Azerbaijan had not been delimited.
● Ararat Mirzoyan said Armenia should wait for the results of a joint Armenian-Russian commission before deciding the future of the country’s railways, which are currently under Russian concession management. The minister said Armenia has Western partners interested in using the railway but unable to do so because it falls under sanctions due to its management by Russia. The Armenian-Russian commission has three months to find solutions. Mirzoyan stressed that Armenia has a historic opportunity to become an important hub on the Middle Corridor and should not let it slip away.
● Law enforcement officers carried out large-scale searches in the city of Stepanavan from early morning. Around 15 people have been detained on suspicion of distributing electoral bribes, including Arsen Gevorgyan, a candidate for head of the local community representing the pro-Russian opposition party Strong Armenia. Elections are scheduled for this weekend. Courts are currently considering pre-trial measures for more than ten detainees.
● The Strong Armenia party has accused the authorities of political persecution. “The detention of our candidate only shows that the authorities are afraid that, after losing in Stepanavan, they will lose elsewhere as well,” said Tigran Abrahamyan, secretary of the party’s parliamentary faction. He vowed that “the struggle in Stepanavan will continue”.
● Armenia and Azerbaijan have reached an understanding that the TRIPP transit route — connecting Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory — will not be used to transport weapons, ammunition or hazardous chemical cargo, Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan told MPs. He added that carriers would have to obtain prior authorisation for certain categories of goods.
● The parliamentary Committee on Foreign Relations has issued a positive opinion on a bill to ratify the agreement on strategic partnership between Armenia and the United States concerning the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP). The bill will be discussed during the National Assembly’s next four-day session.
● Armenia’s exports to the EU have increased by 51%, from $475 million in 2025 to $717 million currently, Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan wrote on Facebook.
● The Anti-Corruption Committee has brought a new charge against Gyumri Mayor Vardan Ghukasyan, accusing him of abuse of office. He is already under house arrest on corruption charges. According to Radio Liberty’s Armenian service, one of the new charges concerns the October cinema, while another relates to an alleged violation of Article 60 of the Land Code. Ghukasyan’s lawyer said the statute of limitations had expired in either case.
● Employees of the Hrazdan Cement plant held a protest demanding clarity about the future of around 450 workers, as the factory has been inactive for years and its status remains uncertain. Local media reported that businessman Narek Nalbandian intended to acquire Hrazdan Cement, secure loans and restart production. However, financing problems subsequently emerged, and the acquisition may not go ahead. One factor was a statement by Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan: “If we obtain evidence that any businessman, including Narek Nalbandian, is trying to create the impression that he has some connection with the prime minister’s family, I assure you the response will be very harsh.” Protesters said restarting the plant would benefit both the workers and the country. “We can produce cement locally, but instead we are helping develop production in Georgia and Iran by buying cement from them,” they said.
● The health minister has warned that someone has created a fake Telegram account using her name and photograph and is sending messages to doctors.
● Pro-government media in Azerbaijan are publishing comments criticising the “belated and insufficiently open and clear assessment by Turkish officials” of the current deterioration in relations between the two countries. At the same time, the reports stress that a significant part of Turkish society supports respect for Azerbaijan and opposes interference in its internal affairs. Media outlets have highlighted the fact that on 21 October, the Turkish president called his Azerbaijani counterpart and invited him to the upcoming summit of the Organisation of Turkic States in Ankara. The conversation, they write, “demonstrated mutual political will to develop cooperation and fraternal ties”.
Context. Experts cite two reasons for the deterioration in relations. One is Azerbaijan’s partnership with Israel, while Turkey’s relations with Israel have sharply worsened. The other is the strong negative reaction in Turkey to Azerbaijan’s de facto ban on wearing the hijab in schools. The Turkish president’s adviser and representatives of the ruling party have criticised the move, while social media in Turkey has been flooded with comments condemning Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan’s ruling party responded sharply, describing the statements made in Turkey as interference in the country’s internal affairs. More here.
● Azerbaijan has added 31 Turkish citizens to its list of undesirable persons and banned them from entering the country. According to the Foreign Ministry, the decision was prompted by statements these individuals had posted on social media and other online platforms against Azerbaijan’s sovereignty, national security, constitutional order, people and leadership. Their posts also allegedly called for the violent overthrow of the government and incited religious hatred on extremist grounds. The list includes numerous journalists, as well as religious figures and members of parliament. The Foreign Ministry said that “measures in response to calls directed against Azerbaijan and activities that encourage hostility will continue”.
● Armenia’s National Security Service has confirmed that an Azerbaijani citizen illegally crossed the Armenian border on 19 October. Yashar Gasimov, son of Ali, born in 1968, reportedly lost his way. “Appropriate measures are being taken to return the Azerbaijani citizen,” the Armenia’s NSS said.
● Senior-level talks between Italy and Azerbaijan took place at the headquarters of the Confederation of Italian Industry (Confindustria) in Rome. The discussions focused on strengthening economic and industrial cooperation and preparing for a major bilateral business forum to be held in Baku shortly. Participants included Italy’s foreign minister and minister for enterprise, Azerbaijan’s economy minister, and representatives of leading Azerbaijani state-owned and private companies. They included the state oil company SOCAR, the Azerbaijan Investment Holding, AzerGold, Azeraluminium, Baku Steel Company, PASHA Holding, the Centre for Analysis and Coordination of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4SIM), and the Azerbaijan Business Development Fund.
● Italy and Azerbaijan signed a joint declaration on cooperation in critical raw materials following the meeting in Rome. Italy’s Minister for Enterprise and Made in Italy, Adolfo Urso, said on X that the two countries aimed to attract Azerbaijani investment into Italian industry and expand cooperation in innovative sectors, including artificial intelligence and robotics. Urso said the goal was to combine Azerbaijan’s resources with Italy’s expertise across all stages of the production chain. “Azerbaijan could also become an important partner in the strategic critical raw materials storage facility that Italy has proposed establishing in Porto Marghera. This would be Europe’s first pilot facility of its kind, designed to protect Italian and European industry from supply disruptions and strengthen strategic autonomy,” the minister wrote.
● The EU–Azerbaijan business forum was held in Baku. It was stated that European companies view Azerbaijan as a reliable alternative to transit routes through Russia, despite the fact that the Middle Corridor is not yet operating at full capacity and cargo deliveries take longer than planned. Key obstacles include a shortage of funding, uneven infrastructure development and delays in digitalisation along the Georgian section of the corridor. European businesses, however, continue to expand their presence in Azerbaijan.
● The speed of freight transport along the Middle Corridor depends on three main factors: the capacity of the Caspian Sea, congestion at border crossings and transit hubs, and effective integration between countries. Elmir Poladov, deputy chair of the Azerbaijan Freight Forwarders Association, made the statement at the EU–Azerbaijan business forum in Baku. As an example, he cited weather conditions and a shortage of ferries, which meant that Kazakhstan’s Port of Aktau operated for only 10 days out of 60 in December and January. Further delays are caused by cargo transfers due to different railway gauges on the route to Turkey, as well as an imbalance in freight flows: containers mainly travel from east to west, while returning them in the opposite direction incurs additional costs. The lack of a unified cargo-tracking system also creates major difficulties. Poladov cited the construction of new vessels, the expansion of the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway’s capacity to 5 million tonnes, the expansion of Azerbaijan’s Port of Alat and the introduction of a national “single window” system as improvements.
● The EU and European Commission are working to attract private European investment into Azerbaijan’s strategic sectors, EU Ambassador to Azerbaijan Mariana Kujundžić said at the business forum. She stressed that the EU remains Azerbaijan’s largest trading partner and that Azerbaijan is an important energy supplier to the EU, particularly through the Southern Gas Corridor. Kujundžić also noted that negotiations have resumed on a new comprehensive EU–Azerbaijan agreement to replace the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement in force since 1999. Two rounds of talks have already taken place, in Brussels and Baku.
● Azerbaijan’s state-owned AzerGold is entering gold exploration at the Akba deposit in Uzbekistan. The company has registered its first foreign subsidiary, AzerGold Uzbekistan. Once a licence is obtained, an 18-month exploration programme will assess the gold resources and the deposit’s potential for development in the Kashkadarya region. AzerGold also plans joint geological surveys with Uzbek partners at other prospective sites in the country.
● Azerbaijan’s Press Council has warned of scams involving fake WhatsApp accounts impersonating well-known journalists. Law enforcement agencies say organised cybercrime networks based abroad are behind the schemes and use artificial intelligence to deceive people. The council urged the public to verify senders, avoid responding to suspicious messages, and report incidents to the police or the national cybersecurity agency.
● Representatives of the Azerbaijani public association Families of Missing Persons in Karabakh, who are holding a peaceful protest in Brussels, met with Ocke Bouwman, an adviser to the EU Special Representative for the South Caucasus, and Marco Cardinali, the EU’s coordinator for relations with Azerbaijan. During the meeting, which lasted about an hour, the families of Azerbaijanis who went missing during the First Karabakh War said Armenia bore direct responsibility for the fate of their relatives and was obliged to provide information about the locations of mass graves, but had failed to do so even after the conflict. They said that 32 mass graves had already been discovered in Azerbaijani territories retaken from Armenian occupation during the 2020 Second Karabakh War, illustrating the scale of the humanitarian tragedy. The families said they would continue protesting outside EU buildings in Brussels until they learned what had happened to their loved ones.
● Fixed broadband speeds in Azerbaijan have increased by 10.6% over the past year, reaching an average of 98.92 Mbps. Azerbaijan has retained 47th place among 100 countries in this ranking.
● The Constitutional Court has begun hearing a lawsuit filed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia – Lelo, the Federalists and For Georgia. The seven-member plenary court rejected all opposition motions, including requests to recuse judges; summon Georgian Dream founder and honorary chairman, billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, and jailed former president Mikheil Saakashvili as witnesses; and exclude evidence from a parliamentary investigative commission that spent several months examining the authorities’ actions during Saakashvili’s presidency. During the hearing, National Movement representative Khatia Dekanoidze was removed from the courtroom at the court president’s request. The hearing will continue today, 22 October. A ban requires the support of four of the seven judges.
● Germany’s Foreign Ministry described the planned ban on opposition parties in Georgia as a cause for concern. Ministry spokesperson Kathrin Deschauer said such a decision would distance the country from the European Union and weaken domestic democracy. The Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe (ALDE) said Georgian Dream was intensifying authoritarian repression and called on the EU to impose tougher sanctions on those responsible.
● Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has appointed First Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili as special representative for relations with Russia. Zurabashvili will retain his position as deputy minister. Kobakhidze said the appointment did not mark the beginning of a new stage in relations with Russia, adding that the obstacles to restoring diplomatic ties remained unchanged. He also stressed that the appointment was unrelated to Russia’s recently introduced ban on imports of a range of Georgian products, including several wine brands, alcoholic beverages and mineral water.
● The General Inspection of the Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into injuries sustained by prisoner David Peikrishvili under the article concerning violence. According to his lawyer, Peikrishvili, a criminal underworld figure, suffered broken ribs and facial bones. He accuses fellow inmates and other underworld figures, Vato Kipiani and Avtandil Bilanishvili, of the attack. Kipiani’s lawyer previously denied the allegations, while the Special Penitentiary Service said Peikrishvili’s fellow inmates had not assaulted him. The prime minister said the investigation would also establish whether prison officials had played a role. Read more about the case here.
● A working group of the State Committee for the Prevention of Corruption has concluded that the major power outages on 24–25 July, which left the entire country without electricity, could have been avoided. According to the group’s findings, violations were identified at electricity transmission and generation facilities, including Enguri HPP. The Energy Commission will consider imposing the maximum fine of 75,000 lari (around $29,000) on energy companies for each violation and will make a decision within two weeks.
● The Government Administration has published details of the expenses incurred for the funeral of Catholicos-Patriarch Ilia II. The Ministry of Culture spent 722,645 lari (around $280,000) and signed 26 contracts. Of the 3 million lari (around $1.1 million) allocated from the government’s reserve fund, 2,277,355 lari was returned to the budget. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the figures did not warrant an investigation.
● A court has sentenced Giorgi Papashvili to life imprisonment for the murder of 22-year-old Tamaz Mtivlishvili. According to investigators, Papashvili tortured the victim for six hours. The defence said it would appeal the verdict.
● The Roads Department has announced an international tender for construction of an approximately 31-kilometre, four-lane section of a new highway in the Kakheti region, running from Badiauri to Bakurtsikhe. The estimated cost of the two sections is $183 million. The project will be funded by the Georgian government, the World Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Bids will be accepted until 21 December.
● The Government Administration has published data on applications for foreign grants. Between 1 October 2025 and 16 October 2026, 215 of the 330 applications received were approved, 13 were rejected and 88 remain under review.
● The Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission has said natural gas and water tariffs will be reviewed at the end of the year, as the current rates expire in late December.
● For three days, from 21 to 23 October, the Constitutional Court’s plenary session will hear on the merits a lawsuit filed by 88 MPs from the ruling majority seeking to declare five opposition parties unconstitutional and ban them. The parties named in the lawsuit are Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia – Lelo, the Federalists and For Georgia. The court approved a request from Georgia’s Public Broadcaster to allow the hearings to be streamed live. A final ruling must be issued by 24 June 2027. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said of the parties targeted by the lawsuit: “Their days are numbered.” Georgia’s opposition party ban: detailed analysis here
● The opposition has announced a protest rally outside the Constitutional Court building in Batumi, starting at 11:00 on 21 October.
● Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset has urged Georgia’s ruling majority to “protect political pluralism and preserve space for political opposition”. He said that, under the European Court of Human Rights’ case law, banning a political party requires compelling justification and strict scrutiny of whether the measure is necessary and proportionate. Berset said the Council of Europe would “follow developments closely”.
● The Foreign Ministry expressed concern over recent statements by EU representatives regarding the case. “This is an attempt to exert excessive pressure on a constitutional institution and interfere in Georgia’s internal affairs,” the ministry said, urging European officials to refrain from making statements until Georgia’s Constitutional Court has delivered its ruling.
● Representatives of opposition parties met with the ambassadors of the United Kingdom, Germany and France at the British Embassy. The meeting was attended by representatives of the Federalists, the United National Movement, Lelo, For Georgia and the Coalition for Change. According to Badri Japaridze of Lelo, the discussion focused on “how to protect the interests of our state”. Tengiz Sharmanashvili, an MP from the ruling Georgian Dream party, claimed that the politicians had been given “their final briefing” ahead of the Constitutional Court hearings.
● Lawyers have reported a suspected violent confrontation between criminal figures in prison. According to reports, David Peikrishvili, described as a criminal underworld authority, suffered four broken ribs and fractures to his skull and facial bones. His lawyer said Peikrishvili claimed that the injuries had been inflicted by criminal figures Vato Kipiani, Avtandil Bilanishvili, known as “Katsro”, and others. The Special Penitentiary Service denied that Peikrishvili had been assaulted by fellow inmates, saying he had smashed a corridor window and threatened to harm himself. A lawyer for Kipiani ruled out any physical confrontation. Peikrishvili was taken to Vivamed clinic in the evening, where fresh injuries to his upper limbs were diagnosed.
Context: The Peikrishvili brothers were arrested on 22 September on charges of violence and extortion, while Kipiani and Bilanishvili were arrested on 15 October on suspicion of group violence. Bilanishvili is frequently described in the media as a friend of Bera Ivanishvili, the son of billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, widely regarded as the country’s shadow ruler. The alleged links between the individuals involved and elite circles have long been discussed in Georgian media and on social networks, and their arrests have attracted considerable public attention.
● Rikard Jozwiak, editor of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Europe bureau, has offered his prediction of what the European Commission’s annual enlargement report, due to be published on 4 November, will say about Georgia. He expects the report to reaffirm the assessment that Georgia is a candidate country “in name only”. In his view, new sanctions are unlikely because EU member states lack consensus on the issue.
● The government has established the Georgian Economic Development Corporation on the basis of the Enterprise Georgia agency. The new corporation will also take over the functions of the Energy Development Fund and the Georgian Development Fund, formerly known as the Partnership Fund. According to the prime minister, the corporation will co-finance energy projects and major strategic infrastructure. The initial draft budget for 2027 allocates 200 million lari (around $77 million) to the corporation.
● The National Agency of State Property has announced electronic auctions for the privatisation of 10 former sanatoriums in the resort town of Tskaltubo, with bidding scheduled to close on 15 November. The properties have a combined starting price of 49.2 million lari (around $20 million). The winning bidders will be required to invest at least 314 million lari (around $120 million) in total over five years. According to the prime minister, developing Tskaltubo resort is one of the government’s priorities.
● The Roads Department has signed an agreement with China Railway Tunnel Group to build a 7.3-kilometre section of the Tbilisi bypass road between Tsitsamuri and Avchala. The section will include a four-lane road and two parallel tunnels with a combined length of 3.4 kilometres. According to the prime minister, a continuous four-lane motorway will also be built by 2030 from Sarpi on the Black Sea coast to Sadakhlo in the Kvemo Kartli region, spanning the country from west to east. Construction of all motorways is scheduled to be completed by 2031.
● Police in Marneuli municipality have arrested three people who, according to the Interior Ministry, forced their children, including minors, to marry men from their villages against their will. The charges concern two separate cases and include forced marriage and domestic violence. The relevant articles of the Criminal Code carry prison sentences of up to four years.
Photo: The opposition alliance has announced a protest against the Constitutional Court hearing on the lawsuit seeking to ban political parties.
● The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), led by Russia, has warned Armenia of serious consequences if its membership in the bloc is suspended. Representatives of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have prepared a report predicting a 69% increase in the price of Russian gas for Armenia, a 30–50% drop in Armenian exports and a decline of more than 90% in re-exports. The report also forecasts the reintroduction of customs controls and tighter labour migration rules. Yerevan has repeatedly said it has no plans to leave the EAEU, while EU membership remains an aspiration. However, the report suggests the EAEU could suspend Armenia’s participation until the country holds a referendum on whether to choose the EAEU or the EU.
● A decision to suspend Armenia’s EAEU membership could be taken at the next meeting of the bloc’s heads of state in December, Nikolai Silaev of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Institute of International Studies told Armenian media. The EAEU treaty contains no provision setting out a procedure for suspending membership, but it refers to the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, which would provide the legal basis for such a decision, Silaev said. “The convention says that all parties to an international treaty must comply with its terms. Armenia is not complying, and this has been demonstrated in the report. Thus, a legal mechanism for suspending Armenia’s participation has been found. At the same time, nobody wants this decision to have to be taken,” he said.
● Pro-Russian opposition forces have warned that Armenia’s departure from the EAEU would be a disastrous decision. Arthur Khachatryan, secretary of the parliamentary faction of the Armenia party, said: “If even half of the report’s forecasts are realistic, the consequences for Armenia will be apocalyptic.”
● Bloomberg has published an interview with Konstantin Sokolov, an American businessman who heads the US-based TRIPP+ fund, also known as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund. The fund, with a budget of $201 million, was established to support the implementation of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit route linking Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory. International media have reported that Sokolov has ties to Donald Trump’s administration. He told Bloomberg he plans to expand his investments in Armenia’s copper industry. In September, he acquired the country’s second-largest copper mining company. “The peace agreement initialled by the leaders of Armenia and Azerbaijan is an unprecedented development that could fundamentally transform the region. It has opened the way for greater US involvement in the South Caucasus. I am extremely interested in expanding my activities across the region, as I firmly believe in its combined potential,” Sokolov said. More on Sokolov and the fund here.
● An employee of the Hrazdan municipal administration has been charged with offering an electoral bribe and official forgery. According to the Investigative Committee, he issued forged certificates, some of which enabled recipients to qualify for reduced electricity bills. In another case, a forged certificate helped a citizen obtain an agricultural loan with an interest-rate subsidy from the Economy Ministry. The official thereby facilitated the fraudulent embezzlement of state funds, the committee said.
● The Corruption Prevention Commission could be granted direct access to the electronic border management system to verify officials’ asset declarations. This would allow it to check whether officials have declared their trips abroad and establish when officials or family members were outside the country. The commission currently has to submit written requests to government agencies to obtain such information, adding administrative work and slowing investigations.
● An Armenian delegation led by Defence Minister Suren Papikyan has left for an official visit to the Czech Republic.
● Armenia has exported 908.6 tonnes of flowers to 30 countries since the beginning of the year, the Economy Ministry said. Destinations include neighbouring Turkey, Iran and Georgia; 14 European countries; the United Arab Emirates and Oman; Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan; and the United States. The ministry said the export geography had expanded significantly compared with the same period last year, with 23 new markets added. On 10 October, an EU decision allowing more than 80% of Armenian products to enter the bloc duty-free came into force.
● Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has urged citizens to organise protests if anyone obstructs their voting rights or subjects them to unlawful pressure. He previously invited candidates and voters who claim to have faced illegal pressure to contact him directly by email. Pashinyan has said any official found responsible for such actions will be publicly reprimanded.
● A manager at the Gustav restaurant in Yerevan has been placed on a wanted list after allegedly secretly filming inside the women’s toilet. A criminal case has been opened on suspicion of violating privacy. A female customer accidentally discovered a phone recording under a sink.
