title: Pioneers Across Europe Deploy NVIDIA Earth-2 Open Models to Power Real-World Weather and Climate Prediction
body: Weather forecasts shape more than daily plans; timely weather information is crucial for energy producers, insurers and transport operators to plan around changing conditions. A global forecast can show a storm taking shape, but decisions about solar farms, shipping routes or insured property depend on what happens locally. NVIDIA Earth-2 gives developers and researchers a family of open AI models and tools they can customize with their own data. Running on NVIDIA computing, these technologies support global weather prediction, detailed regional forecasts and environmental research. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements StormScope EU is the latest model to join Earth-2 — a regional version of the StormScope model for short-term forecasting, trained over Europe weather and climate data. It uses EUMETSAT satellite observations to predict evolving cloud conditions across 16 Meteosat channels at 10-minute intervals. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing a live StormScope EU pipeline in an interactive weather demo built in partnership with Earthmover . The demo uses Earth2Studio to run forecasts and Earthmover’s data platform to manage and serve the real-time results, which are updated as soon as new satellite observations come in, every 10 minutes. Earthmover serves these results as map tiles, letting visitors explore predictions across Europe without downloading entire datasets. Developers can combine Earth-2 models in workflows tailored to regional needs, using StormScope for short-term forecasting and CorrDiff to add local detail to coarser weather data. Developers can also pick up these model architectures and train them for new environmental applications such as air-quality modeling. The open source NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework provides training and customization tools so teams can build applications that incorporate proprietary data and domain expertise to meet regional needs. Organizations building on Earth-2 capabilities include: AXA is using NVIDIA Earth-2’s FourCastNet 3 to study regional cyclone risk beyond the historical record across more than 1,000 simulated seasons, generating insights that can inform risk assessments and help customers target prevention efforts. Vaisala Xweather is combining Earth-2 with its proprietary observations , lightning data and forecasting expertise to enhance its weather intelligence platforms for government, energy, maritime, transportation and insurance customers. Its work includes adapting StormScope with lightning data to advance short-term forecasting lead time and make these warnings accessible through Vaisala Xweather’s software-as-a-service offerings and AI-assistant integrations. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Vaisala-Xweather-Nvidia-StormScope.mp4 Video courtesy of Vaisala Xweather. University of Manchester researchers adapted the Earth-2 CorrDiff model for U.K. air-quality modeling. It trained the model on the NVIDIA-powered Isambard-AI supercomputer and ran it locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark systems, bringing environmental modeling from a national supercomputer to the desktop. TotalEnergies is exploring NVIDIA Earth-2 for solar-energy forecasting, evaluating StormScope-based solar-radiation nowcasts at two photovoltaic sites and developing models to provide weather information at subhourly intervals. The work explores how more detailed forecasts could help anticipate changes in solar-power generation. Space42 developed SARDiff4Height using CorrDiff and NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. The research estimates surface heights from a single radar image and produces uncertainty maps, helping analysts understand where estimates need closer scrutiny. Explore NVIDIA Earth-2 open models and tools , and explore with Earth2Studio’s forecasting examples . Read AXA’s hurricane-risk case study and Manchester’s air-quality story to learn how teams are adapting weather AI to specialized challenges. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open to celebrate fifth anniversary as 2027 tournament is announced
body: Preparations are in full swing for the fifth edition of the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open at Zayed Sports City. The tournament will run from January 30 to February 6, 2027, at the International Tennis Centre. Last season, the WTA 500 tournament welcomed more than 60,000 supporters, further cementing its status as an elite event on the international tennis calendar. The 2027 tournament will once again feature 28 singles players and 16 doubles teams competing across eight days, with a $1.2 million prize fund and WTA ranking points on offer. Aref Hamad Al Awani, Secretary General of Abu Dhabi Sports Council, said: “The fifth edition of the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open is another important milestone for Abu Dhabi’s sporting journey. The tournament has grown significantly in just a few years, while its impact reaches beyond the court through its engagement with young players, schools and the wider community. Through these initiatives, we aim to support the development of tennis, strengthen sporting culture and encourage people to make sport a way of life." Homaid Al Shimmari, deputy group CEO, Mubadala Investment Company, said: “The Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open reflects our long-standing commitment to tennis and to creating a positive impact in our community. Beyond bringing the world’s best players to Abu Dhabi , the tournament serves as a platform to inspire young people, encourage greater participation in sport, and bring families and communities together.” 2026 Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open final – in pictures Nigel Gupta, tournament director at MARI, the tournament’s organiser, said: “The fifth edition is a significant milestone for the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open, but what is most exciting is how much the tournament has grown in such a short space of time. Seeing over 60,000 in attendance in 2026 was remarkable and a real testament to the appetite for world-class tennis in Abu Dhabi and the kind of fan experience we have tried to build.” Earlier this year, Czech qualifier Sara Bejlek won her first ever WTA Tour title by defeating Ekaterina Alexandrova in the 2026 Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open final. For the 2027 edition, the tournament will introduce a new Village pass, giving fans of all ages access to the 15,000-sqm Mubadala Village. A programme of live entertainment, tennis clinics, player Q&As, food and beverage, sponsor activations, children's activities and merchandise will be on offer for both Village pass and Stadium ticket holders. On January 30-31, the Village pass will also include access to all qualifying matches taking place across both days. Adult Village passes will be available for Dh10 per day, while children under the age of 12 can attend free of charge throughout the opening weekend. The event has also made its mark on the wider sporting landscape, becoming the first WTA-only event to stage a wheelchair tennis tournament and reinforcing its commitment to inclusion and growing opportunities to engage with the sport. Attendees will require a valid ticket for entry and/or participation in the Mubadala Village activities. For ticket information, visit www.mubadalaabudhabiopen.com.

title: NVIDIA Open Models Power a New Wave of European Public Sector Projects
body: Governments need modern solutions to serve the public while keeping sensitive information under their control. Open models provide a path forward, letting governments evaluate them, adapt them to local languages and public services, run them on infrastructure they control, apply their own safeguards and keep sensitive data within controlled environments. Some open models go further, with the datasets they were trained on published so governments can verify if training data was licensed, biased or compliant. NVIDIA partners and European governments are teaming to bring advanced models to boost the efficiency of public administration while retaining control of data and infrastructure. Several are also building editions of the NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas collection , the partner-grounded datasets behind NeMo User Sim , NVIDIA’s open source library for population-scale user simulation that dynamically evaluates and trains models and agents in local languages. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements European Commission: Scaling Governed AI Applications Berlin-based software company deepset is expanding its Haystack Enterprise Platform , the foundation of AI@EC, the European Commission’s shared platform for building and running AI applications on commission-managed infrastructure. The update connects agent development, execution, optimization and governance for all customers, adding capabilities to compare operating costs, evaluate answer quality and trace problems. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server supports the shared services used to find and rank relevant information. The expansion builds on operating requirements demonstrated by deployments such as AI@EC, where reusable components, role-based access, audit trails and guardrails support applications including document summarization, knowledge management and multilingual policy analysis. Poland: Advanced Computing for Healthcare and Employment Deloitte is helping Poland build agentic systems for healthcare and employment services using open models. Poland’s eHealth Centre is building its Intelligent Services Platform for medical imaging with NVIDIA DGX BasePOD and the MONAI framework. The tool will help physicians analyze X-rays, CT scans and MRI images, detect abnormalities and prioritize urgent cases, reducing the time patients wait for results. With Deloitte’s support, Poland’s Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy is developing an agentic factory on NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure. Designed to support more than 400 labor offices, it will run models including PLLuM, GPT OSS and Inkling for document search, summarization and digital assistants, helping staff more efficiently assist job seekers. NVIDIA is also working with SpeakLeash in Poland and the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia on country-specific additions to its synthetic personas program, with localized datasets planned to follow. UK: Data for Locally Relevant Advanced Modeling London-based Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK , a dataset of 1 million synthetic personas reflecting the U.K.’s demographic and geographic diversity while reducing privacy risk. Potential uses include healthcare evaluation and bias testing across age groups, education levels and rural and urban populations. For developers building public-service models, it offers a way to test whether models work consistently across different communities. Germany: Digital Assistants and AI for Classified Work In Germany, Materna is introducing Sinfonie, an on-premises platform combining generative AI, voice interaction and 3D avatars, with NVIDIA Audio2Face available for animation. Built on a project for a German state administration, it helps employees access institutional knowledge through spoken questions while keeping data on their organization’s infrastructure. For organizations handling classified information, secunet, NVIDIA, Red Hat and deepset are going a step further. The four companies are developing a sovereign cloud offering built on secunet’s proven SINA Cloud foundation, which includes security components that have been authorized for use with classified information. The planned offering combines four components: NVIDIA accelerated computing and NVIDIA Nemotron open models; Red Hat OpenShift AI for deploying and managing AI workloads; deepset’s Haystack AI agent orchestration; and infrastructure operated by secunet in German data centers. To support local development, the Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models research initiative (Soofi) is developing a family of AI models for German industry and the public sector. That includes Nemotron-Personas-Germany, an open dataset of 1 million records, each with six synthetic personas, grounded in the 2022 census across all 16 federal states and 400 districts. Created with NVIDIA NeMo Data Designer without real people’s private data, the dataset helps developers test whether public-service models work consistently across regions, age groups and communities. Like the U.K. edition, it can be used with NeMo User Sim so developers can evaluate and train models against simulated users based on synthetic German personas. France: Advanced Open Models in the Public Sector Workspace CANUT, France’s public purchasing body for digital services, selected LINAGORA and Docaposte to provide a sovereign collaborative workspace built on Twake.ai. More than 2,500 eligible organizations, including municipalities, schools and healthcare institutions, can access the framework without running their own tender. The workspace offers public employees email, document sharing and collaboration tools, with NVIDIA technology supporting speech transcription and infrastructure hosted in France. Région Occitanie is the preferred partner for scaling deployment. Greece: A Local Agentic Ecosystem Greek AI and energy company KIEFER is developing an agentic factory built on NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD with DGX GB200 alongside Sophea open weight models and Greek-language tools for knowledge retrieval, speech and digital assistants. These capabilities stand to make institutional information easier to find and use for Greek-speaking public sector teams, while giving organizations control over where agents run and how data is handled. Codefest: Building the Next Applications In an effort to support public sector organizations in integrating agentic AI in Europe and beyond, NVIDIA Open Models Codefest brings together startups, software providers and labs across the region to turn open models into locally controlled solutions for public sector challenges, including medical reasoning, AI tutoring and model governance. The top five teams are Pleias , Zehnlab.ai , Disseqt , Algoritmica GmbH and ABA Technology . Deutsche Telekom and T-Systems have provided the compute infrastructure for teams to train and deploy large language models. title: Perplexity and NVIDIA Researchers Introduce JOLT: a Joint Teacher-Student Reinforcement Learning Method
body: Perplexity , along with NVIDIA team, has introduced JOLT, a new post-training method for language models. JOLT stands for Joint On-policy Learning and Teaching . It trains a single model in 2 roles. The teacher sees privileged information; the student does not. The key change is that the teacher is trained too, so its feedback stays usable. On MATH, JOLT matched GRPO’s accuracy with 6.5x fewer processed training tokens. For teams running RL post-training, that is a direct compute question. TL;DR What it is: a post-training method. Size: tested on Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Runs on: 1 shared model plays both roles, so no separate teacher model. Training hardware: Not disclosed. Performance: JOLT+ posts the highest mean score in every setting tested against GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill. Best: AppWorld state-test pass rate of 72.09% with JOLT+, vs 62.20% for GRPO (+9.9 points). Worst: JOLT without student reward scores 51.92% on AppWorld, below GRPO. What is Perplexity JOLT? JOLT is a self-distillation method from Perplexity and NVIDIA that trains one model as teacher and student. It builds on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) . Why does RL post-training need a better teacher? Outcome-reward RL, such as GRPO , gives one reward per attempt. That signal is sparse. It does not say which tokens helped. On long agentic tasks, successes are rare, so learning is slow. On-Policy Distillation fixes sparsity by having a stronger teacher score each student token. OPSD removes the separate teacher. The same model becomes the teacher when given privileged context, such as a verified solution. The research team argues this is not enough. A teacher holding the answer can take shortcuts the student cannot follow. Its guidance may sit beyond the student’s reach. In the paper, OPSD’s teacher-student disagreement grows during MATH training. How does JOLT work? JOLT trains both roles of one shared model at the same time: Teacher: gets privileged information. It learns from outcome rewards, plus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the student. Student: sees only the task. It learns from the teacher’s token-level distillation signal on its own attempts. On-policy: each role learns from trajectories generated under its own context. JOLT+: adds the student’s own outcome reward to the student update. The research stands in the center on a ‘reward-consistent’ teacher. Its distillation update should point the same way as the student’s reward gradient. The ideal teacher favors high-advantage actions while staying near the student’s policy. The research team tested 5 settings, each with a different base model and type of privileged information: GSM8K: DeepSeek-V2-Lite; teacher gets the verified answer. MATH: Qwen3-0.6B; teacher gets worked reference solutions. LiveCodeBench v6: Qwen3-8B on 131 problems; teacher gets a passing sibling solution or execution feedback. AppWorld: Qwen3-4B-Instruct; teacher gets summaries of past attempts. Terminal-Bench 2.1: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct trained on TMax ; teacher gets private verifier files. JOLT+ had the highest mean score in every setting. Against GRPO, the strongest baseline, it gained 1.5 points on GSM8K. It also gained 4.2 on MATH, 3.0 on LCBv6 and 9.9 on AppWorld. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 , JOLT+ reached 10.96% pass@1 and 34.83% pass@32. GRPO scored 8.25% and 30.34%. Even plain JOLT, with no student reward, beat GRPO on MATH: 72.14% versus 68.36%. How much training compute does JOLT save? On MATH, the research team fit accuracy curves against training-token budgets. At 63.44% accuracy, GRPO’s checkpoint used 8.40M processed training tokens. JOLT’s fitted curve needed 1.30M, a 6.5x reduction. Counting completion tokens only, the gap widens to about 13x. Across 55% to 65% accuracy targets, savings range from 4.3x to 7.4x on processed tokens. JOLT also levels off higher. It plateaus near 72%, against about 70% for GRPO and 62% for OPSD. How does JOLT compare with GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill? All scores below come from Perplexity’s own runs in the JOLT paper , with hyperparameters tuned per method. title: Airbnb Restricts Checkout Chores After Years of Guest Complaints
body: Airbnb is changing its rules for hosts, restricting the cleaning tasks they can require guests to complete before checking out after years of complaints about excessive demands. The new guidelines will apply to all bookings made from November 20, 2026, according to the company’s announcement. The changes aim to make checkout expectations clearer and prevent guests from being asked to carry out time-consuming cleaning duties, particularly when they have already paid a separate cleaning fee. Airbnb Limits Checkout Cleaning Demands Under the updated policy, hosts will be able to establish seven basic house rules and make additional requests, provided those requests are considered reasonable. However, hosts will generally be unable to require guests to complete chores that involve significant time or effort, or tasks that would normally be handled by a professional cleaner. These include: Removing bed sheets before departure. Taking rubbish out of the property. Washing dishes and putting them away. The changes address a long-running source of frustration for travellers who say they are sometimes expected to clean accommodation extensively despite paying cleaning fees as part of their booking. Airbnb told the BBC that house rules should help guests understand what hosts expect, but acknowledged feedback that some requirements have become confusing, excessive and difficult to manage. Exceptions Remain Under the New Policy Airbnb will still allow certain additional requests in specific circumstances. For example, hosts in areas experiencing drought or water restrictions may ask guests to limit their shower time. The platform will also make property rules more prominent during the booking process and include them in reservation reminders, giving guests a clearer understanding of their obligations before arrival. Additional contractual requirements will be permitted only in limited circumstances, such as when they are required by law or by a homeowners association. Hosts will also be prohibited from imposing fines for breaches of house rules under the updated policy. They will retain control over their property’s rules and requests, but requirements that do not comply with Airbnb’s policy may be flagged, with hosts given an opportunity to appeal. Viral Videos Fuel Debate Over Airbnb Rules The policy change follows years of complaints from guests about strict checkout instructions, particularly when cleaning fees are charged separately. The debate has also gained attention on social media, where videos from American hosts Cassie and Jon, who operate properties in Georgia, have attracted widespread discussion. In one video, the couple criticised guests for allegedly failing to follow house rules, including leaving a television remote in a different location. Their detailed inspections and strict expectations prompted a backlash, while the couple argued that viewers had misinterpreted their content. Other creators subsequently produced satirical videos highlighting what they viewed as unreasonable demands placed on short-term rental guests. What the Changes Mean for Travellers The revised rules are intended to establish clearer boundaries between reasonable checkout expectations and cleaning work that should be handled by hosts or professional cleaners. For guests, the changes could mean fewer departure chores and greater clarity about what is expected before they leave. For hosts, the policy means reviewing existing house rules to ensure their requirements comply with Airbnb’s updated standards. The central issue is the balance between asking guests to leave accommodation in an appropriate condition and expecting them to undertake substantial cleaning work before departure. With the new rules applying to bookings made from November 20, travellers and hosts will need to pay closer attention to the platform’s updated requirements. title: Nearly half of youths in Finland use AI every day, survey finds
body:
More than half said they trusted the information given by AI, with boys reporting slightly higher levels of trust than girls.
A new survey has found that nearly half of children and young people aged 11 to 17 use artificial intelligence every day.
The survey was commissioned by two organisations working to protect children, Digirauha and the Itla Children's Foundation.
Nearly 80 percent of the pre-teen and teenage survey respondents said they used AI in some form. The most common uses were looking up information and getting help with schoolwork.
Nearly 40 percent of primary and secondary school-aged children said they could not tell the difference between AI-generated images and real photos and videos.
More than half of the respondents said they trusted the information given by AI, with boys reporting slightly higher levels of trust than girls.
Digirauha is a nonprofit aiming to protect children and young people from harms linked to commercial digital platforms. The Itla Children's Foundation aims to promote and support the wellbeing, equality, and position of children and families.
Polling firm E2 Research carried out the online panel-based survey in September. More than 1,000 individuals aged 11 to 17 took part.

title: Oil tops $110 as Houthi drone strike near Saudi Shaybah field rattles markets
body: Oil extended gains above $110 a barrel on Thursday after a Houthi drone attack near Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oilfield heightened concerns over supply disruptions as Yemen's rebels stepped up strikes on the kingdom's energy infrastructure. Brent crude rose 1.7 per cent, or $1.81, to $110.63 a barrel as of 7.36am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate gained 1.4 per cent, or $1.37, to $98.52. Two people were killed and two injured on Wednesday when debris from a drone intercepted by Saudi air defences fell near a processing plant at Shaybah, one of the kingdom's largest oilfields. The drone targeted the plant, but its debris struck a contractor's vehicle outside and caused a fire, the Saudi Energy Ministry said. Operations were unaffected. Shaybah, deep in the Empty Quarter near the UAE border, produces about one million barrels of crude a day. The strike came hours before another attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one person and injured eight, according to Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority. The Houthis have not commented on the airport attack. The latest strikes follow an attack on Riyadh's main international airport earlier this month, the deadliest on the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline , a critical alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, has also come under attack. Crude flows were reportedly halted on October 5 after a Houthi strike damaged a pumping station east of Riyadh. The pipeline, which has a capacity of about seven million barrels a day, carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields to Red Sea export terminals, allowing shipments to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Washington has ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. The widening campaign is adding to the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices as attacks threaten Saudi production facilities and alternative export routes already strained by the Iran war.

title: Greece Signals Response After Libya Approves Turkey Maritime Pact
body: Greece is preparing further diplomatic and political moves after Libya’s eastern-based parliament approved the controversial 2019 maritime agreement with Turkey, as Athens seeks to prevent the deal from being implemented and protect its maritime claims in the eastern Mediterranean. The development has renewed tensions over competing maritime boundaries and raised questions about the future of Greek-Libyan negotiations, with Athens warning that the agreement cannot override international law or the rights of third countries. The Greek government maintains that the Turkey-Libya memorandum is legally invalid and contrary to international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). However, Athens is concerned that Ankara and its Libyan partners could use the parliamentary approval to reinforce their positions on the ground, regardless of Greece’s objections. Athens signals diplomatic and political countermeasures Greece has intensified its diplomatic efforts following the vote, seeking support from European institutions and international organisations against the maritime agreement. The European Union has criticised the memorandum, arguing that it infringes on the sovereign rights of third countries and does not comply with the law of the sea. Athens is also signalling that its response will extend beyond diplomatic statements. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis said Greece had the means to prevent the agreement from being implemented in practice. He pointed to Greece’s role in regional diplomatic processes and European decision-making, including matters involving Libya’s financial arrangements, peacekeeping operations and Turkey’s ambitions to deepen its relationship with the European Union. The remarks underline Athens’ intention to use its diplomatic position and influence within European institutions to challenge Ankara’s regional strategy. Turkey’s EU ambitions could become a point of leverage The European Union’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence programme has emerged as another potential point of pressure. Turkey has sought access to the EU’s defence cooperation framework, while Greece has argued that Ankara’s participation should be conditional on changes to its longstanding casus belli declaration against Greece. The declaration refers to Turkey’s 1995 parliamentary decision to regard a Greek extension of its territorial waters in the Aegean Sea to 12 nautical miles as a potential cause for war. Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis had already made clear that the casus belli issue must be addressed in discussions concerning third-country participation in SAFE. Marinakis indicated that Athens would take the latest developments into account when determining its position towards Turkey. The approach reflects Greece’s broader effort to link Ankara’s ambitions for closer European defence cooperation with outstanding disputes between the two NATO members. Libya’s maritime claims raise concerns for Greece The 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime memorandum remains a major source of tension between Athens and Ankara. The agreement established a claimed maritime boundary between Turkey and Libya, crossing an area where Greece asserts maritime rights based on its islands, including Crete. Greece argues that the arrangement disregards the maritime entitlements of Greek islands and cannot lawfully deprive them of their rights under international law. Turkey maintains that the agreement is valid and supports its claims in the eastern Mediterranean. Libya’s eastern-based parliament has now approved the memorandum, although the implications for its legal status and implementation remain contested. Athens is particularly concerned that the agreement could complicate negotiations with Libya over the delimitation of maritime zones. Greece and Libya have competing positions on the boundaries of their respective maritime claims, making any future settlement diplomatically sensitive. The parliamentary move could strengthen Ankara’s political argument that the agreement has backing from both sides, even as Greece continues to reject its validity. Egypt’s reaction adds another regional dime Greece is also monitoring how the development could affect relations among other eastern Mediterranean powers, particularly Egypt. Cairo, which has maintained close ties with the eastern Libyan authorities, has strongly opposed the ratification of the Turkey-Libya memorandum. Egypt has its own maritime interests in the region and has previously disagreed with Turkey over competing claims and regional influence. At the same time, Ankara and Cairo have pursued a rapprochement in recent years, creating uncertainty over how their improving relations could affect the wider dispute. Athens will be watching closely to determine whether Egypt’s opposition to the memorandum translates into further diplomatic coordination or whether its broader relationship with Turkey limits the scope for joint action. A wider contest over influence in the eastern Mediterranean The dispute extends beyond the maritime agreement itself, touching on energy exploration, regional security, European defence cooperation and the balance of power across the eastern Mediterranean. For Greece, the immediate objective is to prevent the Turkey-Libya memorandum from being used to establish maritime claims that Athens considers incompatible with international law. The government is pursuing diplomatic support while signalling that Turkey’s relations with the European Union could become part of its response. Much will depend on how the Libyan authorities proceed, whether the agreement is acted upon in practice and how other regional powers respond. For now, Athens is seeking to contain the consequences of the parliamentary approval while protecting its position in a dispute that continues to shape relations between Greece, Turkey and Libya. title: Ballon d'Or 2026 predictions: Who will be crowned the world's best footballer?
body: All eyes will turn to London on Monday evening when the 2026 Ballon d'Or winner will be announced. Paris Saint-Germain attacker Ousmanne Dembele took the honours last year with the Frenchman finishing ahead of Barcelona's Lamine Yamal, who was second, and third-placed Vitinha, also of Uefa Champions League winners PSG. The women's prize was claimed by Barcelona's Aitana Bonmati for the third year running, with other award winners including Yamal in the men's under-21 section and England's Sarina Wiegman as best women's coach. Below, we give our predictions about who will be walking away from the 2026 ceremony at the London Palladium with a prize. Ballon d’Or (Best men's player) 1) Harry Kane (Bayern Munich and England): The stage is surely set for the Three Lions captain to lift the prize on home turf. And what better timing for Kane to become the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001. He smashed a remarkable 61 goals in 51 games last season as the 33-year-old striker spearheaded Bayern Munich to the domestic double, while also scoring six times at the Fifa World Cup, helping England finish in third place. 2) Lamine Yamal (Barcelona and Spain): Could be runner-up for the second year running is only a matter of timer of time before Yamal takes first prize. The 19-year-old provided 24 goals and 18 assists in 45 Barca matches as the Catalan side retained the La Liga title . Helped Spain become world champions but a pre-tournament injury seemed to hinder his impact as he registered only one goal and one assist in North America. 3) Kylian Mbappe (Real Madrid and France): For Los Blancos, the 27-year-old striker ended last season with 42 goals in 44 appearances, securing the Spanish Golden Boot award for a second consecutive campaign. For Les Bleus, Mbappe also won the World Cup Golden Boot award with 10 goals and became the all-time tournament top-scorer with 22 goals, overtaking Lionel Messi. But neither Real nor France won a trophy, most likely scuppering his Ballon d'Or chances. Ballon d’Or Feminin (Best women’s player) 1) Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses and Spain): In what was her final season in Spain before moving to London, two-time Ballon d’Or winner Putellas helped Barcelona power to a stunning quadruple with 26 goals and 15 assists. Spain also retained the Uefa Nations League title last October, while the 32-year-old also scored twice as La Roja hammered England 4-0 to seal World Cup qualification. Ballon d’Or hat-trick should be safely in the bag. 2) Ewa Pajor (Barcelona and Poland): Pajor should seal a Barca one-two after scoring 33 goals and assisting a further seven to her club's quadruple cause. The 29-year-old top-scored in the Champions League with 11, while her 16 Liga F goals was only bettered by teammate Claudia Pina's 21. Pajor also ended her miserable run of five Champions League final defeats in a row as she scored twice in the 4-0 final win over OL Lyonnes. 3) Khadija Shaw (Manchester City and Jamaica): A stunning season in front of goal for City as her 21 goals in 22 games helped her club secure the league and FA Cup double. The 29-year-old dominated the individual awards, winning a third consecutive Women’s Super League Golden Boot as well as the PFA and FWA Player of the Year awards. Shaw also scored nine goals in this year’s Concacaf Women’s Championship qualification, helping her country reach the finals. Kopa Trophy (Best men's under-21) 1) Lamine Yamal (Barcelona and Spain): For second year running, winger Yamal might have to make do with the consolation of winning the best young player prize. 2) Pau Cubarsi (Barcelona and Spain): A rock at centre-back for club and country. The 19-year-old played 48 games across all competitions as Barca claimed another La Liga title, then played every minute of every match as Spain lifted the World Cup, earning the tournament's best young player award. 3) Warren Zaire-Emery (PSG and France): The 20-year-old midfielder played a key role in PSG retaining their Champions League crown, while making 54 appearances across all competitions as the French side secured four trophies. Only a World Cup spent warming the bench and playing just 109 minutes can take a little shine off an impressive campaign. Kopa Trophy (Best women's under-21) 1) Vicky Lopez (Barcelona and Spain): The winner of last year's inaugural award for women is favourite to triumph again this time round. The 20-year-old attacker contributed 17 goals and 15 assists in 53 matches as Barca lifted four trophies. She earned her first senior title when Spain won the Nations League. 2) Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes and United States): An excellent first season in France, after moving from Dutch side Ajax, saw the 19-year-old contribute six goals and 10 assists in 48 appearances playing in midfield as OL Lyonnes won the treble and reached the Champions League final. 3) Clara Serrajordi (Barcelona and Spain): Has established herself in the Barca midfield at the age of just 18, making 48 appearances in the quadruple-winning campaign, and already has four senior Spanish caps. Yashin Trophy (Best men's goalkeeper) 1) David Raya (Arsenal and Spain): A magnificent season for Arsenal which saw him win a third consecutive Golden Glove for keeping 19 clean sheets in 37 Premier League games, helping the Gunners end their title drought . Also produced nine clean sheets in 14 Champions League games as Arsenal finished runners-up to PSG. The 31-year-old just beats Spanish teammate Simon for the top prize. 2) Unai Simon (Athletic Club and Spain): Preferred between the sticks by Spain manager Luis de la Fuente ahead of Raya, Simon proved it was a good call by winning the World Cup Golden Glove award after keeping seven clean sheets and conceding just one goal in eight matches, as La Roja beat Argentina in the final. The 29-year-old also started 37 out of 38 La Liga games for his club, keeping six clean sheets. 3) Joan Garcia (Barcelona and Spain): Completes a Spanish clean sweep of the top three after a stellar season for Barca, where he kept 15 clean sheets in 30 La Liga appearances, conceding only 21. The 25-year-old earned the Zamora Trophy for having the lowest goals-to-games ratio in the Spanish top-flight in what was his first season at the club following his move from Espanyol. Best women's goalkeeper 1) Cata Coll (Barcelona and Spain) Barcelona and Spain's domination of the women's awards goes on. Coll kept 23 clean sheets in 39 matches for club and country, with the 25-year-old conceding just 18 goals. 2) Ayaka Yamashita (Manchester City and Japan): Earned the domestic double with City, keeping eight clean sheets across 20 matches. The 31-year-old was also named best goalkeeperthe Asian Cup, which Japan won after beating Australia in the finalinal. 3) Lorena (Kansas City Current and Brazil): Enjoyed a remarkable debut season in the NWSL which saw her set a league record for not conceding a goal in 900 minutes. The 29-year-old set another league record by keeping 14 clean sheets in 24 games, helping Kansas win the NWSL Shield. Luis Enrique ❤️💙 #UCLfinal pic.twitter.com/Z6I3zg2UzJ — UEFA Champions League (@ChampionsLeague) May 30, 2026 Best men's coach 1) Luis Enrique (Paris Saint-Germain): The Spaniard has guided PSG to a second consecutive Champions League crown and five trophies in all and will retain his coach of the year crown. PSG look on course to become only the fourth club to win three or more consecutive European Cups. 2) Luis de la Fuente (Spain): Spain produced a devastating performance on the way to lifting the World Cup for a second time, with De la Fuente's side winning seven out of eight matches, drawing the other. Spain are now a record 42 games unbeaten and are the reigning European and world champions. 3) Vincent Kompany (Bayern Munich): Belgian led Bayern to a domestic double and the Champions League semi-finals. Followed that up by winning the German Super Cup in August. Best women's coach 1) Pere Romeu (Barcelona): The 32-year-old Spaniard masterminded Barca's domination of the women's game in Europe. Lost just once across all competitions last season. 2) Jonatan Giraldez (OL Lyonnes): Another Spaniard who achieved great things, leading Lyon to the Premiere Ligue title without losing a single game. But were swept aside in the Champions League final by Barca. 3) Andree Jeglertz (Manchester City): Swede's first season in charge saw City win their first WSL title in a decade while also thrashing Brighton in the FA Cup final.

title: Kherson region to install 227 mobile shelters along school routes
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Kherson Regional Military Administration reported this on Telegram .
“As part of a pilot initiative in the Kherson region, 227 mobile shelters are planned to be installed along school routes,” the statement reads.
It is noted that they will provide protection from Russian attacks for nearly 1,450 children on routes to ten educational institutions in nine communities across the region.
Contracts have already been signed for the installation of 110 shelters. The first ten mobile shelters were set up in the Kherson district.
As Vitalii Bezgin, Minister for Communities, Territories, and Internally Displaced Persons, reported on Facebook, six frontline regions were selected as pilot areas: Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Chernihiv.
A total of 840 shelters need to be installed along school routes. This will require approximately 1.4 billion hryvnias.
Communities in the donor regions have already provided over 800 million hryvnias in co-financing.
It is noted that the next step on the ground is to manufacture and install the shelters. More than 350 shelters have been contracted so far. Work is already underway. The Shelter Coalition is also actively involved. Thanks to the support of international partners, an additional 90 shelters will be funded.
As reported by Ukrinform, during a meeting of the Shelter Coalition, the European Union announced the allocation of 10 million euros to Ukraine for the installation of mobile shelters throughout the country. Meeting participants were shown a project to set up 840 mobile shelters along school routes in six frontline regions : Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Kharkiv, Kherson, and Chernihiv.

title: Sheikh Khaled and Greek Prime Minister set out plan to expand $4bn investment strategy in Athens talks
body: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis on Thursday set out plans to expand a $4 billion joint investment initiative in place between the countries during high-level talks in Athens. The two men said the decision – announced as part of Sheikh Khaled's working visit to Greece – underlined their shared commitment to advance robust economic ties. Discussions between Sheikh Khaled and Mr Mitsotakis at the Prime Minister's Office also centred on efforts to bolster collaboration across a range of key sectors, including energy, infrastructure, health care, advanced technology and health care. Sheikh Khaled emphasised the UAE's desire to strengthen long-standing relations with Greece to support the aspirations of both nations. He highlighted the successes of the investment initiative, which has provided a framework for the completion of a number of key projects. He said it had demonstrated the ability of the allies to translate investment opportunities into transformative projects with tangible economic impact, Abu Dhabi Media Office reported. The two sides reviewed ways to boost co-operation in key and future-focused sectors and encourage partnerships between Emirati and Greek institutions and companies. During the talks, Sheikh Khaled and Mr Mitsotakis also reflected on regional and international developments, stressing the importance of reinforcing security, peace and stability. Sheikh Khaled was greeted on arrival at Athens International Airport by George Gerapetritis, the Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs, state news agency Wam reported early on Thursday. The visit holds particular significance as the two allies mark 50 years since diplomatic ties were formally established. UAE-Greece relations have expanded greatly in the decades since, underpinned by a comprehensive strategic partnership encompassing vital sectors such as the economy, investment, energy and technology. President Sheikh Mohamed has held a series of phone calls with Mr Mitsotakis this year in a further demonstration of the flourishing friendship between the countries. In May, Sheikh Mohamed hosted Mr Mitsotakis for high-level talks in Abu Dhabi, centred on co-operation across the economic, investment, technology, artificial intelligence, renewable energy, sustainability, infrastructure and cultural sectors. Sheikh Khaled is accompanied by a high-level delegation, which includes Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc, Reem Al Hashimy, Minister of State for International Co-operation, Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade, and Mohamed Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment.

title: Using a lookup-table to correct an approximation
body:
I often find myself writing (by which I mean generating) functions to convert enums to strings. A naÃ¯ve implementation of such a function might look like:
Compiling the above with a modern gcc at -O0 or -O1 gives some fairly horrible assembly code. Thankfully, at -O2 and above, a modern gcc can rewrite it to something more along the lines of:
The assembly code for this is much nicer, although the table of pointers still takes up more space than I'd like (and that's before you account for each table entry needing a relocation entry...). It can be made smaller by concatenating all the strings together into a single contiguous piece of memory and then using a table of offsets into that memory, taking advantage of the fact that a relative offset can be much smaller than a pointer:
This is pretty good, but the offsets table can be made even smaller. Consider the function x â¦ offsets[x] : it maps 0 to 0 and 22 to 382 , so one possible linear approximation of this could be x â¦ x * int(round(382.0 / 22.0)) , also known as x â¦ x * 17 . It is rarely the case that x * 17 exactly equals offsets[x] , but the difference between x * 17 and offsets[x] happens to always end up being in the range [-9, +10] . As such, the offsets table can be replaced with x * 17 and a table of corrections, where the corrections table occupies less space than the original offsets table:
There's a general pattern here: an exact function can be computed via a fast but incorrect approximation followed by a table of corrections, and doing so can be profitable if this allows a smaller table than other approaches would require. This is not a novel idea, but it still needs repeating from time to time, even if only to remind compiler developers that there are still optimisations they're missing.

title: A Coding Guide to Cactus Whistle: Does a 16.9 MB Speech Model Hold Up Against Whisper Base? Word Error Rate, Speed, Streaming, Timestamps, Keywords, and Speech-to-Tool Calls on a CPU
body:
In this tutorial, we use Whistle , Cactus Compute’s speech-to-text model, a 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU, transcribes seven languages, and returns word timestamps and probabilities. The model card claims it beats Whisper base on LibriSpeech; we test it on seeded test-clean and test-other samples, comparing Whistle with Whisper tiny and base on identical clips, judged by paired speaker-cluster intervals with Holm correction. We find a lead over greedy Whisper base on test-other, no significant gap against beam search, and a speed advantage that narrows as clips grow. Beyond the headline, we probe a 30-second window where the pinned engine silently drops the middle of longer audio, plus streaming latency, timestamps, keyword biasing, other languages, noise, embeddings, and speech-to-tool calls. Our figures are one-run samples from an Apple M4, and published full-split numbers are quoted, not measured. Pinning the Hub revision of each, and printing the hashes, # is what makes this run reproducible. The engine version is read from the package, not typed in. WHISTLE_REV = "ca5287601bef25af26dcf2e1b2bdc0843a7c19e5" # Cactus-Compute/whistle, 2026-10-10 NEEDLE3_REV = "93e88ede867e4311c39151285e74df513e4b835b" # Cactus-Compute/needle3 (engine + Needle 3 weights), 2026-10-10 from needle.agent import fetch as needle_fetch TAG = needle_fetch._platform_tag() ENGINE_VERSION = needle_fetch.engine_version(3) weights = hf_hub_download("Cactus-Compute/whistle", "whistle.cact", revision=WHISTLE_REV) wheel = hf_hub_download("Cactus-Compute/needle3", needle_fetch.engine_wheel(ENGINE_VERSION, TAG, 3), revision=NEEDLE3_REV) with zipfile.ZipFile(wheel) as z: member = next(n for n in z.namelist() if n.startswith("needle/libneedle")) os.makedirs("engine", exist_ok=True) engine = os.path.abspath(os.path.join("engine", os.path.basename(member))) open(engine, "wb").write(z.read(member)) needle3_weights = hf_hub_download("Cactus-Compute/needle3", "needle3.cact", revision=NEEDLE3_REV) os.makedirs(needle_fetch.cache_dir(3), exist_ok=True) # Needle(tools=...) reads its weights from this cache path shutil.copyfile(needle3_weights, os.path.join(needle_fetch.cache_dir(3), needle_fetch.base_weights(3))) os.environ["NEEDLE_WHISTLE_WEIGHTS"] = weights # both variables are honoured by the package os.environ["NEEDLE3_LIB_PATH"] = engine import needle import importlib.metadata as md sha = lambda p: hashlib.sha256(open(p, "rb").read()).hexdigest()[:12] CPU = platform.processor() or platform.machine() if sys.platform == "linux" and os.path.exists("/proc/cpuinfo"): CPU = next((l.split(":", 1)[1].strip() for l in open("/proc/cpuinfo") if l.startswith("model name")), CPU) elif sys.platform == "darwin": CPU = subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip() or CPU print(f"cactus-needle {needle.__version__} (engine {ENGINE_VERSION}, wheel tag {TAG}) python {platform.python_version()} " f"soundfile {md.version('soundfile')} soxr {md.version('soxr')} numpy {np.__version__}") print(f"hardware: {CPU}, {os.cpu_count()} cpus visible") print(f"whistle.cact {os.path.getsize(weights)/1e6:.1f} MB sha256 {sha(weights)} @ {WHISTLE_REV[:12]}") print(f"engine {os.path.getsize(engine)/1e6:.1f} MB sha256 {sha(engine)} @ {NEEDLE3_REV[:12]}") print(f"needle3.cact {os.path.getsize(needle3_weights)/1e6:.1f} MB sha256 {sha(needle3_weights)} @ {NEEDLE3_REV[:12]}") SR = 16000 W = needle.Whistle() # one model per process, not thread-safe; every later step reuses this object def fetch(url, tries=7): """GET with retries. The datasets-server rate-limits anonymous callers (HTTP 429): honour Retry-After when it is sent, otherwise back off 5, 10, 20, 40 ... seconds, and never give up on the first refusal.""" for k in range(tries): try: with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60) as r: return r.read() except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: if k == tries - 1: raise wait = int(e.headers.get("Retry-After", 0) or 0) if e.code == 429 else 0 time.sleep(max(wait, 5 * 2 ** k) if e.code in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) else 2) except Exception: if k == tries - 1: raise time.sleep(3 * (k + 1)) def page(dataset, config, split, offset, length=100): """One page of a Hub dataset through the datasets-server rows API: metadata plus signed audio URLs.""" url = (f"https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/rows?dataset={dataset}&config={config}" f"&split={split}&offset={offset}&length={length}") time.sleep(0.25) # stay under the anonymous rate limit when paging a whole split return json.loads(fetch(url)) def load_audio(row): """Download one row's clip; return 16 kHz mono float32 samples and the sha256 of the original file.""" data = fetch(row["audio"][0]["src"]) audio, sr = sf.read(io.BytesIO(data), dtype="float32") if audio.ndim > 1: audio = audio.mean(axis=1) if sr != SR: audio = soxr.resample(audio, sr, SR, quality="HQ") return audio, hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()[:12] first = page("openslr/librispeech_asr", "clean", "test", 0, 1)["rows"][0]["row"] clip, _ = load_audio(first) t0 = time.perf_counter() out = W.transcribe(clip, word_timestamps=True) wall = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 print(f"
clip {first['id']} {len(clip)/SR:.1f} s reference: {first['text']}") print(f"-> {out['text']!r}") print(f" language {out['language']} engine time to first token {out['ttft_ms']:.1f} ms decode {out['decode_tps']:.0f} tok/s" f" wall {wall:.0f} ms") print(" first words:", [(w["word"], w["start"], w["end"], w["probability"]) for w in out["words"][:3]]) RESULTS["1. Install Whistle, pin its weights and engine by Hub revision, transcribe one clip"] = \ f"{os.path.getsize(weights)/1e6:.1f} MB weights, {len(clip)/SR:.1f} s clip in {wall:.0f} ms" We install cactus-needle 3.2.0 with its dependencies pinned and turn off its anonymous telemetry. The package downloads Whistle’s weights, its engine and Needle 3’s weights from Hugging Face repositories whose files are replaced in place, so we pin both repositories to fixed revisions and print SHA-256 hashes. The page() helper reads the datasets-server rows API with rate-limit backoff, and load_audio() resamples clips to 16 kHz. The first test-clean clip, 3.5 s of speech, transcribes in 33 ms of wall time, each word carrying its start, end and probability. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import jiwer import whisper import torch from whisper.normalizers import EnglishTextNormalizer, BasicTextNormalizer NORM_EN = EnglishTextNormalizer() # the normalisers Whistle's own benchmarks use; applied to both sides, always NORM_BASIC = BasicTextNormalizer() SEED = 2026 N_WHISTLE = 300 # clips per LibriSpeech split that Whistle transcribes (it is cheap) N_PAIRED = {"other": 100, "clean": 60} # the first N of them also go through Whisper (it is not); test-other is primary MAX_CLIP_S = 30.0 # Whistle's single-pass window; longer clips are declared out of scope here WHISPER_SECONDS = collections.Counter() def all_rows(dataset, config, split): out, offset = [], 0 while True: rows = page(dataset, config, split, offset)["rows"] out += [r["row"] for r in rows] offset += 100 if len(rows) < 100: return out def dataset_sha(dataset): return json.loads(fetch(f"https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/{dataset}"))["sha"][:12] def wer_counts(ref, hyp): """Errors (S+D+I) and reference words for one normalised pair; an empty hypothesis is all deletions.""" n = len(ref.split()) if not hyp.strip(): return n, n o = jiwer.process_words(ref, hyp) return o.substitutions + o.deletions + o.insertions, n def sdi(ref, hyp): if not hyp.strip(): return 0, len(ref.split()), 0 o = jiwer.process_words(ref, hyp) return o.substitutions, o.deletions, o.insertions def corpus_wer(errs, words): return 100.0 * sum(errs) / max(sum(words), 1) def _by_cluster(clusters, *arrays): tot = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0.0] * len(arrays)) for i, c in enumerate(clusters): for j, a in enumerate(arrays): tot[c][j] += a[i] return tot def wer_ci(clusters, errs, words, B=2000, seed=0): """95% percentile interval of a corpus WER, resampling clusters (speakers) with replacement.""" tot = _by_cluster(clusters, errs, words) keys, rng = sorted(tot), random.Random(seed) boots = [] for _ in range(B): d = rng.choices(keys, k=len(keys)) boots.append(100 * sum(tot[c][0] for c in d) / max(sum(tot[c][1] for c in d), 1)) return np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5]) def paired_contrast(clusters, errs_a, words, errs_b, label_a, label_b, B=2000, seed=0): """WER(a) - WER(b) with a paired speaker-cluster bootstrap: the same resampled speakers for both systems.""" tot = _by_cluster(clusters, errs_a, errs_b, words) keys, rng = sorted(tot), random.Random(seed) boots = [] for _ in range(B): d = rng.choices(keys, k=len(keys)) w = max(sum(tot[c][2] for c in d), 1) boots.append(100 * (sum(tot[c][0] for c in d) - sum(tot[c][1] for c in d)) / w) boots = np.array(boots) lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5]) p = 2 * min((boots <= 0).mean(), (boots >= 0).mean()) return {"a": label_a, "b": label_b, "diff": corpus_wer(errs_a, words) - corpus_wer(errs_b, words), "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "p": max(p, 1 / B), "clusters": len(keys)} def holm(ps, alpha=0.05): order, keep = np.argsort(ps), [False] * len(ps) for rank, i in enumerate(order): if ps[i] <= alpha / (len(ps) - rank): keep[i] = True else: break return keep def verdict(c, significant): """Verdict rule: diff = WER(other system) - WER(Whistle). CI entirely > 0 and Holm-significant -> Whistle ahead; entirely < 0 and significant -> Whistle behind; otherwise no significant difference at this sample size.""" if c["lo"] > 0 and significant: return "Whistle ahead" if c["hi"] < 0 and significant: return "Whistle behind" return "no significant difference at this n" def fmt_contrast(c): return f"{c['diff']:+.2f} pts (95% CI {c['lo']:+.2f}..{c['hi']:+.2f}, {c['clusters']} speakers)" @section("2. Fixed, seeded samples of LibriSpeech test-clean and test-other, and the rules for the verdicts") def sample_english(): global EN print("Rules for the verdicts below, written into this notebook before its final run (exploratory probes on the") print("same splits came first; the prose says which):") print(f" * simple random sample of {N_WHISTLE} rows per split (seed {SEED}); the first {N_PAIRED['other']} (test-other) and " f"{N_PAIRED['clean']} (test-clean) are the paired Whisper subsets") print(f" * clips longer than {MAX_CLIP_S:.0f} s are excluded and counted (Whistle's single-pass window), as are empty references") print(" * the same normaliser on both sides of each comparison (Whisper's EnglishTextNormalizer for LibriSpeech, its") print(" BasicTextNormalizer for MLS); corpus WER = summed errors / summed reference words") print(" * interval: 95% speaker-cluster paired bootstrap, 2,000 draws, the same resampled speakers for every system") print(" * verdict per contrast: unadjusted CI of WER(other) - WER(Whistle) entirely > 0 and Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 ->") print(" Whistle ahead; entirely < 0 and significant -> behind; otherwise no significant difference at this n") print(" family A (published claims): test-other and test-clean vs base greedy and vs base beam 5, MLS pooled vs base greedy;") print(" family B: the keyword contrasts. Holm at alpha = 0.05 within each family. Whisper tiny rows are descriptive.
") global MANIFEST EN, manifest = {}, {"dataset_sha": dataset_sha("openslr/librispeech_asr"), "seed": SEED, "splits": {}} MANIFEST = manifest for split in ("other", "clean"): t0 = time.time() rows = all_rows("openslr/librispeech_asr", split, "test") idx = random.Random(SEED).sample(range(len(rows)), N_WHISTLE) kept, too_long, empty = [], 0, 0 for i in idx: r = rows[i] audio, h = load_audio(r) ref = NORM_EN(r["text"]) if len(audio) / SR > MAX_CLIP_S: too_long += 1 continue if not ref: empty += 1 continue kept.append({"id": r["id"], "spk": str(r["speaker_id"]), "text": r["text"], "ref": ref, "audio": audio, "dur": len(audio) / SR, "sha": h}) EN[split] = kept manifest["splits"][split] = {"rows": len(rows), "sampled": N_WHISTLE, "too_long": too_long, "empty_ref": empty, "ids": [c["id"] for c in kept], "sha": [c["sha"] for c in kept]} durs = [c["dur"] for c in kept] pk = kept[:N_PAIRED[split]] print(f"test-{split}: {len(rows)} rows -> {len(kept)} clips kept ({too_long} over {MAX_CLIP_S:.0f} s, {empty} empty), " f"{len(set(c['spk'] for c in kept))} speakers, {sum(durs)/60:.1f} min, clip {np.mean(durs):.1f} s mean / {max(durs):.1f} s max" f" [{time.time()-t0:.0f} s]") print(f" paired subset: {len(pk)} clips, {len(set(c['spk'] for c in pk))} speakers, {sum(c['dur'] for c in pk):.0f} s of audio, " f"{sum(len(c['ref'].split()) for c in pk)} reference words") json.dump(manifest, open("manifest.json", "w")) print(f"
manifest.json: LibriSpeech revision {manifest['dataset_sha']}, clip ids and file hashes (the MLS and MInDS-14 clips are added to it in") print("steps 9 and 12), so a rerun can prove it used the same audio") return f"{len(EN['other'])} + {len(EN['clean'])} clips, manifest written" sample_english() A verdict means little if its rule is set after the final numbers arrive, so we wrote ours into the notebook before the final run, after exploratory probes that touched some of the same clips. We draw a seeded sample of 300 rows per split and drop clips longer than Whistle’s single-pass window, leaving 299 clips in each. The paired subsets, the first 100 test-other and 60 test-clean clips, go through Whisper, and few speakers make their intervals approximate. A difference counts only when its 95% paired speaker-cluster bootstrap interval excludes zero and its Holm-adjusted p is below 0.05. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser WHISPER = {} def whisper_model(size): if size not in WHISPER: WHISPER[size] = whisper.load_model(size, device="cpu") return WHISPER[size] def run_whisper(size, audio, language="en", **kw): """openai-whisper with its defaults (greedy with temperature fallback) unless kw says otherwise. Seeded per call, because the fallback samples. Returns text, whether any segment needed the fallback, and the wall time.""" torch.manual_seed(0) WHISPER_SECONDS[size] += len(audio) / SR t0 = time.perf_counter() r = whisper_model(size).transcribe(audio, language=language, fp16=False, **kw) fell_back = any(s.get("temperature", 0) > 0 for s in r["segments"]) return r["text"], fell_back, time.perf_counter() - t0 SYSTEMS = {"other": [("whisper tiny, greedy", "tiny", {}), ("whisper base, greedy", "base", {}), ("whisper base, beam 5", "base", {"beam_size": 5})], "clean": [("whisper tiny, greedy", "tiny", {}), ("whisper base, greedy", "base", {}), ("whisper base, beam 5", "base", {"beam_size": 5})]} FAMILY_A = {"test-clean: Whistle vs whisper base, greedy", "test-clean: Whistle vs whisper base, beam 5", "test-other: Whistle vs whisper base, greedy", "test-other: Whistle vs whisper base, beam 5", "MLS pooled: Whistle vs whisper base, greedy"} PUBLISHED = {"other": "Whistle 10.49 / Whisper base 11.0 (paper table 9, beam) / 12.4 (table 8, greedy)", "clean": "Whistle 4.31 / Whisper base 4.9 (paper table 9, beam) / 5.0 (table 8, greedy)"} CONTRASTS = [] @section("3. Word error rate against Whisper tiny and base, paired by clip, with a verdict per contrast") def english_wer(): global HYP HYP = {} for split in ("other", "clean"): clips = EN[split] t0 = time.perf_counter() hw = [W.transcribe(c["audio"], language="en")["text"] for c in clips] tw = time.perf_counter() - t0 HYP[(split, "Whistle")] = hw e_w, n_w = zip(*[wer_counts(c["ref"], NORM_EN(h)) for c, h in zip(clips, hw)]) lo, hi = wer_ci([c["spk"] for c in clips], e_w, n_w) print(f"test-{split}: Whistle on all {len(clips)} clips: WER {corpus_wer(e_w, n_w):.2f}% (95% speaker-cluster CI {lo:.2f}..{hi:.2f}) " f"in {tw:.1f} s ({1000*tw/len(clips):.0f} ms per clip)") print(f" published full-split figures, different sample: {PUBLISHED[split]}") pk = clips[:N_PAIRED[split]] spk = [c["spk"] for c in pk] e_wp, n_p = list(e_w[:len(pk)]), list(n_w[:len(pk)]) s = np.sum([sdi(c["ref"], NORM_EN(h)) for c, h in zip(pk, hw[:len(pk)])], axis=0) print(f" paired subset, {len(pk)} clips / {len(set(spk))} speakers / {sum(n_p)} words:") print(f" {'Whistle, 5-beam':22s} {corpus_wer(e_wp, n_p):6.2f}% S/D/I {s[0]:3d}/{s[1]:3d}/{s[2]:3d}") for label, size, kw in SYSTEMS[split]: res = [run_whisper(size, c["audio"], **kw) for c in pk] hyps = [r[0] for r in res] HYP[(split, label)] = hyps e_o = [wer_counts(c["ref"], NORM_EN(h))[0] for c, h in zip(pk, hyps)] s = np.sum([sdi(c["ref"], NORM_EN(h)) for c, h in zip(pk, hyps)], axis=0) con = paired_contrast(spk, e_o, n_p, e_wp, label, "Whistle") con["name"] = f"test-{split}: Whistle vs {label}" CONTRASTS.append(con) better, worse = sum(a < b for a, b in zip(e_wp, e_o)), sum(a > b for a, b in zip(e_wp, e_o)) print(f" {label:22s} {corpus_wer(e_o, n_p):6.2f}% S/D/I {s[0]:3d}/{s[1]:3d}/{s[2]:3d} fallback on {sum(r[1] for r in res):2d} clips " f"{np.median([r[2] for r in res])*1000:5.0f} ms/clip | {fmt_contrast(con)} clips Whistle better/worse {better}/{worse}") fam = [c for c in CONTRASTS if c["name"] in FAMILY_A] print(f"
Contrasts so far (family A: {len(fam)} of 5; the Holm correction and the verdicts come once the MLS contrast is in):") for c in CONTRASTS: tag = "family A" if c["name"] in FAMILY_A else "descriptive" print(f" {c['name']:48s} {fmt_contrast(c)} p~{c['p']:.3f} [{tag}]") print("
 Whistle decodes with a 5-beam length-normalised search. openai-whisper's default is greedy with temperature") print(" fallback; the Whisper paper's LibriSpeech numbers come from beam search, so the beam-5 rows are the like-for-like ones.") print(" Every gap here is a system gap (model plus decoder), not a model-only one.") return " | ".join(f"test-{s}: Whistle {corpus_wer(*zip(*[wer_counts(c['ref'], NORM_EN(h)) for c, h in zip(EN[s][:N_PAIRED[s]], HYP[(s, 'Whistle')][:N_PAIRED[s]])])):.2f}% " f"vs base greedy {corpus_wer(*zip(*[wer_counts(c['ref'], NORM_EN(h)) for c, h in zip(EN[s][:N_PAIRED[s]], HYP[(s, 'whisper base, greedy')])])):.2f}%" for s in ("other", "clean")) english_wer() Whisper’s default decoder is greedy with temperature fallback. At the same time, the paper’s LibriSpeech numbers come from beam search, and Whistle decodes with a five-beam search, so every comparison must name its baseline. Scored with one normaliser, Whistle’s WER is 10.47% on the test-other sample, near the published full-split 10.49, which we quote rather than measure. On the paired subset it scores 10.27%, against 12.46% for greedy Whisper base and 10.83% for beam search. The 2.19-point lead over greedy survives the Holm correction, but the beam gap does not, so the baseline wins. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def audio_seconds(clips, seconds): """Exactly `seconds` of speech: clips concatenated in sample order, then trimmed.""" out, total = [], 0 for c in clips: out.append(c["audio"]) total += c["dur"] if total >= seconds: break return np.concatenate(out)[:int(seconds * SR)] PROBE_SCRIPT = r""" import sys, json, time, resource, numpy as np kind, paths = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2:] scale = 1 << 20 if sys.platform == "darwin" else 1 << 10 # ru_maxrss is bytes on macOS, kilobytes on Linux rss = lambda: resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / scale out = {"kind": kind} if kind.startswith("whistle"): import needle out["after_import"] = rss() W = needle.Whistle() run = lambda a: W.transcribe(a, language="en") else: import whisper, torch out["after_import"] = rss() size, kw = kind.split("-")[1], ({"beam_size": 5} if kind.endswith("beam5") else {}) m = whisper.load_model(size, device="cpu") def run(a): torch.manual_seed(0) return m.transcribe(a, language="en", fp16=False, **kw) clips = {p: np.load(p) for p in paths} run(clips[paths[0]]) # warm-up reps = 5 if kind.startswith("whistle") else 3 for p, a in clips.items(): ts = [] for _ in range(reps): t0 = time.perf_counter(); r = run(a); ts.append(time.perf_counter() - t0) out[p] = {"wall_ms": 1000 * float(np.median(ts)), "spread_ms": 1000 * float(np.ptp(ts))} if kind.startswith("whistle"): out[p].update(ttft_ms=r["ttft_ms"], tps=r["decode_tps"]) out["peak"] = rss() print(json.dumps(out)) """ @section("4. Speed and footprint: identical arrays, one fresh process per engine, total wall time and peak memory") def speed(): pool = EN["other"] print(f"hardware: {CPU}, {os.cpu_count()} cpus visible. Each engine runs in its own fresh process so torch's threads cannot slow") print("Whistle down (or the reverse); Whistle's engine picks its own thread count. Primary measure: total wall time on the same") print("float32 array, median of 5 (Whistle) or 3 (Whisper) after a warm-up. ttft_ms is the engine's own clock, for reference.

title: ‘Our hearts beat together’: Wainwright gathers for prayer vigil
body:
About 150 people gathered at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene Wednesday night for a prayer vigil as the community continued to grieve.
The gathering came days after a deadly training exercise at nearby CFB Wainwright . Four Canadian Armed Forces members were killed and dozens of others were injured when soldiers were caught in a fast-moving grass fire on Saturday. The soldiers killed were Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.
Wednesday night’s vigil brought the focus back to a community coping with that loss.
Residents filled the church for an evening of prayer, songs and reflection. Ministers representing seven area churches led those gathered in prayer. They asked for blessings for the soldiers who died, those who were injured, their families, first responders and the wider community.
Pastor Ryan Wood said there are no adequate answers for the suffering and loss the community has endured.
Residents bowed their heads during a moment of silence while prayers also recognized those who stepped forward to help.
Bruce Pugh, Wainwright’s mayor, described the gathering as an opportunity for residents to come together and let their “hearts beat together.”
Wood said people in Wainwright have been looking for ways to demonstrate their support. “We just want to let everyone know that’s been affected by this that they’re loved and cared for – and give people an opportunity to express their own sense of grief and mourning as well,” he said.
For many people in Wainwright, the connection to the military is personal, almost every church in the community has a parishioner who is a soldier at the nearby base.
Wainwright resident Elaine Smith said attending the vigil was a way to pay respect to the military and show support. “We’ve taken it just as hard as anybody would, because we’re a small community and we really are close,” she said.
As time passes and residents learn more about the victims, those at the vigil said emotions surrounding the loss continue to surface.
Pugh said feelings that may initially have been pushed aside are now beginning to emerge.
The evening included hugs and other gestures of support as residents continued to mourn together.

title: Russian attack targets transport facility in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district
body:
According to Ukrinform, Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced this on Telegram .
“A strike on a transportation infrastructure facility in the Darnytskyi district. Emergency services are heading to the scene,” the message reads.
The Kyiv City State Administration added that damage caused by an enemy strike has been reported in the non-residential sector of the Darnytskyi district.
As reported by Ukrinform, explosions were heard in Kyiv on the evening of October 21; a warning about ballistic strikes had been issued beforehand.

title: Give people who stutter the time to be heard
body: When I was in Grade 7, I raised my hand and volunteered to read aloud in class. After a few words, I began to stutter. My teacher stopped me and told me to raise my hand again when I could “speak properly”. I still remember those words. I had done what children are encouraged to do: participate. I knew how to read. I knew the words. But in a few seconds, I learnt something about participation: I could speak up, but only if my words came out the “right way”. For a child who stutters, experiences like these can influence whether they raise their hand the next time, volunteer to speak, ask a question, or decide that staying quiet feels safer. Although the classroom may change, the assumption can remain. About one in 100 adults stutter, across languages and dialects. Up to one in 10 children experience stuttering at some point during childhood. Fluency is often mistaken for confidence. A quick answer can seem more prepared. A smooth presentation can appear more persuasive. A block, that is when a word gets stuck and no sound comes out, can be mistaken for nervousness. However, stuttering is not caused by anxiety. Research points to differences in how the brain produces speech , and it often runs in families. A pause does not mean someone does not know the answer. A repetition does not mean they are unprepared. Taking longer to say something does not make the thought behind it any less valuable. Yet many people who stutter learn to manage other people’s reactions to their speech. That can mean changing a word before anyone notices it is difficult to say, avoiding a phone call, rehearsing an introduction repeatedly, or staying quiet in a meeting because finding the right moment to enter the conversation feels harder than letting the idea go. These behaviors are often invisible. The listener may never know how much planning went into a sentence before it was spoken, or how many sentences were never spoken at all. This is where it becomes important to separate fluency from competence. Nowhere is that distinction more consequential than in the places where participation shapes opportunity: schools, recruitment and the workplace. Consider a typical job interview. An interviewer may unconsciously interpret hesitation as a lack of preparation or favour the candidate who responds quickly and smoothly. But what is the interview actually trying to measure? Is it the candidate’s knowledge, judgment, experience and ability to do the job? Or is it how fluently they can deliver an answer under pressure? Sometimes the changes needed are remarkably small. Give someone time to finish. Do not complete their sentence unless they ask you to. When someone takes longer to speak, resist filling the pause simply because the silence feels uncomfortable. At home, the same patience matters: listen to what a child says, not how smoothly they say it. But individual behaviour is only part of the answer. Inclusion should not depend on whether a child happens to have an understanding teacher or an employee happens to have an considerate manager. We can build better defaults into the places where people speak. In Abu Dhabi, Department of Education and Knowledge policies already provide a framework for supporting students with additional learning needs and providing assessment accommodations. The next step is for schools to make sure stuttering is understood within that framework, including when children are reading aloud, giving presentations or participating in class. Teachers should give advance notice before oral work, ask what helps and provide appropriate flexibility. The goal should not be to remove speaking opportunities, but to make sure participation does not become a test of fluency. A moment costs the listener nothing. For someone who stutters, it can be the difference between speaking and staying silent Recruitment processes deserve the same scrutiny. Employers should build flexibility into recruitment from the start. Interview invitations should make clear what options are available, such as sufficient time to answer, the opportunity to supplement an answer in writing, or alternatives to phone-only screening where spontaneous speech is not essential to the role. Crucially, the process should build in basic flexibility rather than making it available only after someone discloses a stutter. Job descriptions also matter. Employers should define communication according to what a role genuinely requires, rather than using terms such as “articulate” as shorthand for ability. In addition, inclusion should continue once someone is hired. Meetings should not reward the fastest speaker only. Sharing agendas in advance, limiting interruptions, providing more than one way to contribute and helping managers understand that a block is not a sign of nervousness are simple changes that can benefit far more people than those who stutter. None of this lowers standards – it makes them clearer. Assess knowledge when knowledge is what matters. Assess ideas when ideas are what matter. Assess fluency only when fluency is genuinely relevant. This is not special treatment, it is better design. For more than a decade, The Stutter Community has created spaces where people with speech impediments can connect and speak without first proving they can articulate fluently. Yet most of life happens outside those spaces, in classrooms, interviews and offices. That is why our work also extends into schools and workplaces, helping those environments become more inclusive. When I think back to that classroom, what I needed was simple: I needed time to finish. In that spirit, inclusion begins not by asking people who stutter to sound more like everyone else, but by creating classrooms, recruitment processes and workplaces where different ways of speaking have the same opportunity to be heard. A moment costs the listener nothing. For someone who stutters, it can be the difference between speaking and staying silent. Give us one.

title: NVIDIA Nsight Python Tutorial: How to Profile GPU Kernels
body:
In this tutorial, we implement on Nsight Python , NVIDIA’s open-source Python interface to its kernel profilers. Instead of running a script under the Nsight Compute command line and digging through a report afterward, we mark the code we care about with nsight.annotate, decorate a benchmark function with nsight.analyze.kernel, and get back a pandas DataFrame of hardware metrics per annotated region, per configuration, and per run. Since version 1.0, the library attaches Nsight Compute to the running Python process, making it usable in Jupyter and Colab, and the upcoming 1.1 release adds an experimental CUPTI backend, explicit tool management, and custom information collectors. We run everything on a free Colab T4: we install a current Nsight Compute next to the one Colab ships, profile a first kernel, decide how many runs a measurement needs, measure what cache and clock control do to the same kernel, sweep matrix sizes in fp32 and fp16 with a derived TFLOP/s metric, use hardware counters to tell compute-bound from memory-bound work, measure kernel fusion in bytes moved, record clocks and temperature per run, compare the CUPTI backend with Nsight Compute, and keep the raw report for deeper analysis. The [cupti] extra is used in step 9.  Order matters: `import nsight` loads Nsight Compute into this Python process, and it can only") print(" attach to CUDA work started after that. Every profiled function below runs in this same") print(" process; nsight-python starts `ncu --mode attach` on its own PID for each one.") We start by checking the GPU and the profiler. Nsight Python requires the Nsight Compute command-line tool, ncu, at version 2026.2.1 or later, and finds it by looking it up on the PATH. Colab’s GPU image ships an older Nsight Compute. Still, it already has NVIDIA’s CUDA package repository configured, so we install Nsight Compute 2026.3.1 with apt-get, ask dpkg where the ncu launcher landed, and put that directory first on the PATH. We then install Nsight Python, pinned to the commit of the 1.1.0 pre-release this notebook was written against, and the cupti-python package into a separate directory, because it needs a newer CUPTI library than the one Colab’s PyTorch is pinned to. The import order matters: import nsight loads Nsight Compute’s injection library into the Python process, and it can only attach to CUDA work started after that, so nsight must be imported before torch touches the GPU.
