title: From borrower to lender: How Louvre Abu Dhabi is sharing its masterpieces with the world
body: More than five centuries ago, the workshops of Mamluk Cairo produced an elaborate wool carpet decorated with three medallions. Prized across the Mediterranean, such carpets were coveted by Europe's wealthy and powerful, commissioned by popes and exchanged as diplomatic gifts. The rare carpet, now part of Louvre Abu Dhabi 's permanent collection, returned to Europe last year to be displayed at the Louvre in Paris in a major exhibition examining the Mamluk dynasty and its artistic legacy. The loan may seem like a routine exchange between museums , but it reflects how far Louvre Abu Dhabi has come since opening in 2017, when many of the artworks in its galleries were borrowed from international institutions and collectors. “We were originally a borrowing institution, but we are moving towards a lending institution as well,” Guilhem Andre tells The National . “Since the opening, we've lent many of our masterpieces abroad.” Andre, who joined Louvre Abu Dhabi project in 2012 and helped to build its collection and Asian art programme, is now the museum's director of scientific, curatorial and collections management. As editor of Birth of a Collection , an elegant coffee table book documenting much of the work he has witnessed and helped to oversee, Andre brings together contributions from 42 scholars, curators and historians who examine 240 objects, from ancient artefacts to modern and contemporary artworks. The book is available online and select bookstores in English, Arabic and French. But the artworks seen at Louvre Abu Dhabi tell only part of the story. Andre recalls how the museum began lending works even before the building opened in 2017, with that activity expanding considerably in recent years. Since opening, it has lent 42 works to exhibitions in the UAE, the Gulf and internationally, including at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, Musee d'Orsay in Paris and the Galleria Borghese in Rome. Outgoing loans have more than tripled since 2021, he adds. Meanwhile, visitors to Louvre Abu Dhabi are also seeing more works that belong to the museum itself. Andre says that when it opened, approximately 30 per cent of the artworks in its permanent galleries came from its own collection. By 2021, owned works outnumbered loans for the first time, with their share reaching 56.8 per cent in 2025. The collection has expanded from around 600 works at opening to more than 6,000 today, including those held in storage or conservation rather than displayed. The growth is documented in Birth of a Collection , a successor to Birth of a Museum , published in 2013 to introduce the founding collection and plans for a universal museum in the Arab world. The new book arrives nine years after Louvre Abu Dhabi opened, with a much larger collection to examine and a decade of curatorial work to draw upon. “The more you move forward, the more you notice that you have gaps, in fact. So that's an unending process, collecting,” Andre says. “Private collector know this as well. But as a museum, of course, we are acting at a very high level, and it's slightly different because we focus on masterpieces at Louvre Abu Dhabi. That's why the book is so important, because it shows the process of collecting.” Some of those gaps have been addressed through acquisitions of Asian, African and Oceanian art , which Andre says were underrepresented in the museum's earlier holdings. He stresses, however, that the museum's ambitions go beyond expanding its holdings. “We are not there to unfold in our galleries endless lists and piles of artworks. We are there to feature the cross-cultural relations, to show the artistic production across time during more than 10,000 years of history .” Among the acquisitions noted in the book is an ornate ivory casket made around 1543 in the Kingdom of Kotte, in what is now Sri Lanka. Decorated with gold, rubies and sapphires, it belongs to a small group of objects sent by the rulers of Kotte to the Portuguese royal court as diplomatic gifts. Acquired by Louvre Abu Dhabi in 2024, the casket is an example of the interesting stories Andre wants the museum's collection to tell, with galleries bringing together artworks from different civilisations to examine artistic and cultural connections that might otherwise be overlooked. “Of course, you could think about collecting everything when you see the word universal museum. In fact, it's very different because we have a specific mandate of featuring the diversity, the cross-cultural relationships across time, the encounters,” he says. “We not only focus on the artworks themselves, but on the relationship between them, because we put them in dialogue. So this is also the immaterial relationship between them.” Looking ahead, Andre is already imagining what a follow-up to Birth of a Collection might reveal in another decade. “We have to dream that one day we can present our permanent galleries entirely through our own collection, allowing the museum to achieve full autonomy,” he adds. “And not only that, but also to lend more of our masterpieces to museums internationally and share our story with audiences abroad.”

title: Abu Dhabi Finance Week to make half of 2026 sessions private to drive deals
body: Abu Dhabi Finance Week will hold about half of its sessions behind closed doors this year, as organisers seek to encourage more candid discussions among global financial leaders and generate tangible business outcomes. The event to be held from December 7 to 10 is expected to draw more than 40,000 attendees, including 8,000 senior executives, with financial leaders representing about $70 trillion in assets under management. Chris Hughes, editor-in-chief of ADFW, said private meetings enable senior executives to exchange information more openly than on public stages, potentially influencing investment decisions and corporate strategies. "I find that when they are in the private rooms there's a little bit more openness, a little bit more dialogue," he told ADGM's Global Media Forum on Tuesday. "It's not just monologue, it's dialogue," he added, which is physically represented by attendees and speakers alike being seated face-to-face rather than shoulder-to-shoulder. The shift towards invitation-only discussions, he said, reflects growing demand among executives for meetings that deliver practical outcomes rather than simply provide networking opportunities or public exposure. ADFW recorded 82 memorandums of understanding and partnerships in 2025, according to the organiser, Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM, which was almost double the 44 agreements and announcements in 2024. The agreements involved major financial institutions and businesses including BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, Mubadala, Mastercard and Swiss Re. While the figures demonstrate the event's growing role as a platform for forging partnerships, ADGM has not disclosed how many resulted directly from private meetings or their combined monetary value. From dialogue to deals Private meetings could allow investors, regulators and executives to discuss commercially sensitive issues, identify investment opportunities and advance potential transactions without the scrutiny of a public audience. Mr Hughes referred to a closed-door leadership meeting involving the International Monetary Fund during last year's ADFW, attended by chief executives of major financial institutions. He recalled watching senior executives take handwritten notes throughout the discussions, which suggested that information exchanged in such settings could influence decisions within large organisations that aren't directly seen, but have major implications. "That extra grain of information they didn't usually have, that can change the economy of... a city or town, or company, or country, just by a tiny little 0.1 degree." The growing emphasis on private engagement comes as Abu Dhabi attracts more international financial institutions. Fourteen global financial firms managing more than $5 trillion announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM during the first half of this year, according to figures disclosed by ADGM chairman Ahmed Al Zaabi this week. ADFW is also expected to host more than 80 events and 400 content sessions this year, compared with more than 70 events and 350 sessions in 2025, according to organisers' projections. The preparations come amid regional uncertainty as the Iran war continues to disrupt business activity, energy markets and travel across the Middle East. Saudi Arabia this week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26 to 29 in Riyadh, until 2027, after a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The attacks, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, have raised security concerns among international executives and investors. Asked about contingency plans for ADFW amid the regional tension, Mr Hughes expressed confidence in Abu Dhabi's security and preparations to welcome international delegates in December.

title: Judge curbs DHS efforts to conduct sweeps for possible noncitizen voters
body: A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters. In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens."Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal.  Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts."Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."Martinez-Olguin also pointed to the "high likelihood of error" in the government's process for assembling a list of potential targets, which includes data from government agencies and commercially available data.Homeland Security said in a statement on Thursday that the department is "laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens." The department added that they have "no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."Protect Democracy, one of the groups that sued over the policy, celebrated the ruling."It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, said in a statement to CBS News. "Today's ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise."CBS News has reached out to DHS for comment.President Trump has prioritized cracking down on voter fraud during his second term, although there has been little evidence to back up his claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Justice Department. The Justice Department reported earlier this week that it arrested several dozen green card holders in California on allegations they illegally registered to vote in U.S. federal elections.

title: Bruno Fernandes turns on Michael Carrick as Manchester United crisis deepens
body: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes publicly criticised head coach Michael Carrick's tactics after their 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como. The humiliating defeat has left Carrick fighting for his future after a run of seven games without a win in all competitions. He apologised to the 700 travelling fans and ignored his beaten players after the final whistle in scenes reminiscent of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in 2021, which preceded his dismissal 24 hours later. Fernandes, who has made a poor start to the season and performed badly in Italy, took aim at Carrick's setup after Wednesday's game. “It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence,” he said. Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: “That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.” Carrick offered a rebuke when told of the comment, as he said: “There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win.” Fernandes's comments come just weeks after defender Lisandro Martinez laid into the club's board over a lack of investment in the squad. Kane put the hosts ahead from the penalty spot in the 61st minute after his shot struck Jurrien Timber's raised hand, blasting his 58th ​Champions League ⁠goal into the roof of the net. title: Witkoff Reveals US Treasury Working With Putin’s Envoy on Economic Ties
body:
US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff publicly confirmed Wednesday, Oct. 21, that Washington and Moscow are discussing future trade and economic cooperation alongside negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, revealing that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
The disclosure came during Witkoff’s meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, where discussions extended well beyond peace proposals to include Russian diesel shipments to the US, financial arrangements and potential fertilizer exports.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Our Treasury Department is working with you now independently,” Witkoff told Dmitriev during the meeting.
He said the contacts were helping both governments assess possibilities for renewed economic relations, which Washington was also discussing with Ukrainian officials.
The remarks provide explicit confirmation that the Trump administration has been pursuing economic engagement with Moscow, even as the US maintains extensive sanctions imposed over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
They are particularly significant because Washington largely suspended official bilateral trade and investment engagement with Moscow following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, although limited commercial trade continued.
Dmitriev, the chief executive of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and Putin’s special representative for international economic cooperation, has played a central role in Moscow’s contacts with the Trump administration.
Addressing Dmitriev directly, Witkoff praised his contribution to discussions between the two governments.
“You’ve been outstanding, Kirill,” he said.
Witkoff described the economic discussions as an indication of the opportunities that might become available if relations between Washington and Moscow improve.
He also revealed that the US was speaking openly with Ukraine about potential economic developments following the war.
“We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is ended,” Witkoff said.
His comments did not establish whether the Treasury Department’s contacts concerned sanctions relief, investment, banking arrangements or specific commercial agreements.
Nor did he identify the Treasury officials involved or explain what commitments, if any, Washington had made.
The contacts are notable because the US Treasury Department sanctioned Dmitriev and RDIF in February 2022 , identifying the fund as part of the financial network supporting Putin’s government.
Treasury also administers and enforces major US financial sanctions on Russia through its Office of Foreign Assets Control.
Witkoff’s comments therefore raise questions about how discussions with Dmitriev fit into Washington’s broader sanctions policy and whether the administration is exploring ways to restore economic relations with Moscow.
The acknowledgment represents a departure from the sharply restricted economic relationship that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In 2022, Washington imposed sweeping financial and trade restrictions on Moscow, including measures affecting Russian banks, energy imports, technology exports and investment.
The US also withdrew Russia’s normal trade relations status, exposing Russian imports to higher tariffs.
Formal bilateral engagement on trade and investment issues was largely halted, although commerce between the two countries did not end entirely.
According to the US Trade Representative , American goods trade with Russia totaled approximately $4.4 billion in 2025, compared with about $36 billion in 2021.
Against this backdrop, Witkoff’s confirmation that Treasury officials are working with Dmitriev indicates that the administration is considering future economic opportunities beyond the narrow trade that has continued under existing restrictions.
The remarks do not establish that Washington has lifted its broader Russia sanctions or agreed to restore normal trade relations.
The economic discussions were not limited to prospective cooperation after the war.
Witkoff thanked Putin for removing Russian diesel export restrictions, saying the decision would benefit American consumers and help ease pressure on global fuel markets.
He said Trump was deeply grateful, particularly because farmers and truck drivers had been affected by higher diesel costs.
Putin responded by claiming that global diesel prices had fallen between 5% and 6% following the announcement of Russian supplies to the US.
He said Moscow was preparing several tankers to begin deliveries, with the first carrying 40,000 metric tons of diesel and scheduled to depart within two or three days.
Additional shipments would follow, Putin said, adding that financial arrangements needed to be finalized to ensure the transactions could proceed.
The Russian leader also offered to supply large quantities of fertilizer to the American market, referring to Trump’s concerns about US farmers.
The discussion revealed that the two governments were addressing not only the political implications of closer economic cooperation but also practical questions about deliveries, payments and trade.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov later confirmed through Interfax that the diesel arrangement was discussed during the meeting and that practical implementation had begun following Washington’s decision to ease certain restrictions.
The diesel deal comes amid criticism in Washington that increased Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue while its military continues attacking Ukraine.
Despite the emphasis on trade, Witkoff said ending Russia’s war against Ukraine remained a central objective of his visit.
He proposed resuming trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, suggesting that technical teams begin examining the next steps toward a settlement.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
body:
Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.
But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.
AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.
“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.
Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, tells WIRED that the organization was unaware of AWS's research prior to publication and did not immediately have a comment on the findings. She added, “Although we agree that upgrading is absolutely imperative, to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution.”
Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.
“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”
Updated 10/22/2026 at 10:10 am ET to include comment from the PHP Foundation.

title: Como v Manchester United player ratings: Who got a three on disastrous night for Michael Carrick?
body: Serie A side Como secured the biggest result in their history when they thrashed Manchester United 4-1 in the Uefa Champions League on Wednesday night. Cesc Fabregas's side , who are playing in the tournament for the first time, produced a sensational performance, dominating the three-time European champions from start to finish. Argentine attacker Nico Paz scored two and assisted another in a man-of-the-match performance, with the other goals coming from Tasos Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon. Substitute Joshua Zirkzee grabbed United's late consolation. It was a dismal night for United manager Michael Carrick who is now under intense pressure after going seven matches without victory – their worst run since 2015 – as his side became the first English team to concede in the first two minutes of consecutive major European games. Como are now on six points, having won two and lost one of their opening three Champions League matches. United are on three points and have not tasted victory in any competition since beating Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on September 10. "I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/8bzmLGkRAX — Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) October 21, 2026 What they said : Como boss Cesc Fabregas: “It's a special night, but we are still at the beginning for everything we have in our minds. The team played well this evening, but we need to keep our feet on the ground and remember there is another match coming up on Saturday.” Man United captain Bruno Fernandes: “It's not the first time, we started on the wrong foot, and they scored very early. Not much pressure on the ball, not many good movements with the ball, not many things going our way. “Conceding early makes us go into game with a mood of defeat, it's difficult to get out of that, trying to be brave, to have the ball and make something happen. If we are not able to do that, it is going to be very difficult to get out of this situation. “It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.” Como ratings : Jean Butez – 7/10: Not much to do in first half as United failed to register shot on target. First save came in 65th minute when he tipped Diallo shot over bar. Missed out on clean sheet when Zirkzee beat offside trap to score late on. Yan Couto – 8/10: Brazilian full-back was full of energy up and down right after being rested for weekend win at Fiorentina. Lovely pass through to set-up first-half chance for Douvikas. Marc-Oliver Kempf – 8/10: Como's defence was so cool in and out of possession at the back with the German a key part of that. Late booking for foul on edge of box on Diallo. Jacobo Ramon – 8/10: Spanish under-21 defender headed home Como's fourth goal. Fantastic in defence as Como kept United's attack very quiet. Alex Valle – 8/10: Like Yan Couto on other flank, left back Valle was excellent defensively and always looked to push forward and help Como attack. Luis Milla – 8/10: United had no answer to Como's midfield dominance with the 32-year-old Spaniard superb at Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia. Fabregas has his team so well drilled from front to back. Maximo Perrone – 8/10: Helped home side dominate possession in middle of park alongside Milla with slick, intricate passing. A masterclass performance from the boys in blue, albeit against woefully passive opponent. 3 - Nico Paz is the youngest 🇦🇷 Argentinian player (22 years, 43 days) to be involved in three goals (2 goals, 1 assist) in a UEFA Champions League game since 21-year-old Lionel Messi in April 2009 against Bayern Munich. Game-changer. pic.twitter.com/3iZH5xQj08 — OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) October 21, 2026 Lucas Da Cunha – 8/10: The captain earned an assist for first goal after cutting inside from right and playing ball into Paz's feet. Involved in build-up for second goal. Almost made it 3-0 but sent shot wide. Nico Paz – 9/10: Young Argentine curled home his first Champions League goal from Como's first attack in some style. Supplied perfectly weighted pass to set up second goal. Took advantage of Baleba error and open defence to finish superbly and make it 3-0. Came close to a hat-trick on several occasions. Martin Baturina – 8/10: One lovely flash of skill early on when he flicked the ball through legs of Dalot on the turn. Croatian midfielder hit shot straight at keeper just before break. Another who was involved in slick move ahead of Douvikas goal. Tasos Douvikas – 8/10: Saw his first effort, a low shot in the 35th minute, saved at near post. Should have scored a few minutes later but sliced wild effort over bar. Did score straight after break with clinical finish following slick Como move Substitutes: Maxence Caqueret (on for Baturina, 64') – 7/10: First touch in penalty area let him down or Como might have been on for another goal. Kaiki Bruno (on for Da Cunha, 69') – 7/10: Supplied perfect cross for Como's fourth goal from Ramon. Samuele Ricci (on for Paz, 80') – N/A . Ivan Smolcic (on for Yan Couto, 80') – N/A . Man United ratings : Senne Lammens – 5/10: Just three minutes before Como went ahead through Paz’s excellent finish, Lammens stretched but couldn’t reach the ball. He saved from Douvikas on 35 minutes and Baturina on 42 minutes, although the latter was offside. Three minutes into the second half, he conceded a second to Douvikas, followed by Paz’s second on 56 minutes. Como scored a fourth, but Lammens was not at fault for any of the goals. Diogo Dalot – 4/10: Back at right back and fired wide in the first minute. Switched to left back for the second half for no discernible reason. Poor, like the rest of them. Matthijs De Ligt – 5/10: First start since last November – and how he was needed with all the other injuries. Extended a leg to turn away an 11 th minute attack. A fragment of positivity on a wretched night that he’s back, but he couldn’t have expected to be up to speed. And he wasn’t. Harry Maguire – 4/10: Couldn’t close down Paz for the first. Headed wide on 18, then made a diving challenge at the other end which saw some appeals for a penalty. It wasn’t. Noussair Mazraoui – 3/10: Left back at the start and stretched by a team who kept the ball well and passed patiently left to right. It was the worst combination for United, who couldn’t contain their extreme possession and diagonal balls. The Moroccan was too slow on the ball. Andrey Santos – 3/10: Booked on 22 after catching Paz, who’d easily bested him on a night where United found little peace. Off at half-time. Poor performance from the Brazilian. 7 - Manchester United are winless in seven consecutive games in all competitions for the first time since a run of eight matches between November and December 2015. Problems. pic.twitter.com/2CCZsu6kLX — OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) October 21, 2026 Mason Mount – 4/10: Left side of United’s attack and picked up ball in tight areas. Dropped back more in second half, shot well over on 50. It’s hard to come into a game like this against such a good team and playing for a team with so many injuries and have a positive outcome. Youri Tielemans – 4/10: Played behind Fernandes in the middle, but United have struggled to press all season and struggled in Como. Linked with Mbeumo a couple of times on a desperate night for United. Bruno Fernandes – 3/10: Tried to thread tricky balls to Mbeumo, whom he alternated with. Shot miles over, like every other United effort on goal. Smart ball towards Amad on 65. Subbed off early. Said after it was the decision of the staff not to press man to man and leave space behind, which Como exploited. Dire season for United’s best player. Matheus Cunha – 4/10: Started where he prefers on the left. Good early header from a Lammens ball, but nobody around him to get it. Turned and shot well over on 44. Off at half-time. Bryan Mbeumo – 4/10: Drove down the right, shot well over on 78 – as was the norm from his teammates. Not a good night. He had a couple of half chances, but it was an awful night for United. Substitutes: Carlos Baleba (on for Santos, 46') – 4/10: I mmediately into the fray, but lost the ball to Paz who ran forward and scored the third. Amad Diallo (on for Cunha, 46') – 5/10: Made a lovely run into the box on 63 and shot pushed over two minutes later, but it was all too late. United were 3-0 down. His free-kick on target on 86 and crossed for Zirkzee to score a consolation on 90. Joshua Zirkzee (on for Fernandes, 66') – 5/10: A bit of pace, a bit of energy, but the damage was done. Still, he scored after bringing the ball down beautifully, which is something United had failed to do. Harry Amas (on for De Ligt, 79') – N/A: Another youngster who should be enjoying Champions League minutes. Shea Lacey (on for Mbeumo, 85') – N/A: Deserves minutes, it’s such a shame he had to be introduced in these circumstances.

title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
body:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.
The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.
When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.
Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.
A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.
What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.
The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videos
Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.
I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.
Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.
The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.
This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)
After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.
The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:
In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.
Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.
I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.
Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.
When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.
Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.
A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.
The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.
Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.
That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.
I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.
Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own.
The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one.
The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.
I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.
I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage.
I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.
Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves.
In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.
To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations. 2
The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.
There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.
For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.
Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.
About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.
Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.
In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.
I use three tests. ShellBench has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. PresetBench has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.
The memory test has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training. 3
The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.
It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after echo green >> colors , running cat colors often doesn't show the appended line.
For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.
But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen ( vim test.txt , man , clear ) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.
What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.
That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.
The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.
This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.
This might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to vim opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.
Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.
Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.
The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft.
In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like man test takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification. 5
I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens, 6 so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB).
I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB.
The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab.
Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output.
My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens.
That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory.
This was the part I was most interested in. Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged.
The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with cat , I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive!
It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux.
In vim, it handles the mode switch on esc and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode.
What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model.
It even manages environment variables and variable expansion.
Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: pythoon launches Python, but ython doesn't.
I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring. Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations.
Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path. There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency.
In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause.
As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it.
Back in 2022, people were already prompting ChatGPT to act as a Linux terminal . More recently, GameNGen simulated Doom using diffusion, and NeuralOS tackled a desktop GUI.
WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux.
I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected.
What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath.
It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding.
One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues.
Try it here . It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find.
I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here.
It's monochrome: only characters, no colours or text styles. Unicode characters, including tmux's box-drawing borders, are mapped to ASCII before encoding, so those borders don't need multibyte character tokens. ↩
Not too dissimilar to the scheduled sampling in my midi post . ↩
These are short-gap tests, with 0–1 intervening commands. ShellBench also tests persistence across 18 commands. ↩
Both prompted models got three worked examples each. They predict whole command outputs rather than individual screen updates, so it's not quite the same task. ↩
Speculative decoding gives a much bigger speedup on a 4090 than on my M4. My suspicion is that the bottleneck shifts between compute and memory bandwidth, but I haven't investigated this properly. ↩
Simon Edwardsson is co-founder of V7 , where he leads engineering and product. We're hiring.
Then I write up what worked, what failed, and what I learned. Get the next experiment by email, a few posts a year.

title: Oman earns international recognition for patient experience project
body:
Muscat: Oman’s Ministry of Health (MoH) received an honourable mention in the 2026 International Hospital Federation (IHF) Awards for its Patient Experience Project, recognising efforts to improve the quality of healthcare and make services more responsive to patients’ needs. The recognition came under the Excellence in Leadership and Management category during the 49th World Hospital Congress in Seoul, South Korea. Dr Abeer bint Abdullah Al Maamari, head of the Patient Experience Project team, received the certificate on behalf of the ministry. The awards attracted more than 750 entries from 38 countries across eight categories this year. A panel of 62 international experts assessed the submissions. Dr Al Maamari said the project is founded on the principle that patients and their families should be active partners in planning, developing and evaluating healthcare services. This approach aims to ensure that care is designed around their needs and expectations.

title: LLM agents play Pokemon showdown
body:
https://github.com/OliverGrabner/multi-agent-poke-showdown
The future is in LLM collaborations, and it is important to be able to understand how good agents are at working together, communicating and negotiating actions. Most multi-agent research is about workflows, where agents pass tasks down a pipeline ( Hong et al., 2024 ; Qian et al., 2024 ). To test this, I built a multi-agent environment on Pokémon Showdown's 2v2 format to evaluate these abilities.
"Both opps are Water types … so my Fire moves are resisted on both. … I plan to Wisp Dondozo … can you open with Fake Out to flinch one of them this turn?"
"Good call on Wisp-ing Dondozo. Quick correction though - Fighting isn't actually resisted by Water or Ground, so my Close Combat is neutral (1x) on both. … Locking in Fake Out → Whiscash."
Pokémon doubles is a game-theory environment without full information. The opponents' sets are hidden and damage is random, so winning takes real strategy: reading the other team, splitting targets and planning around your partner. Recent work like the PokéAgent Challenge ( Karten et al., 2026 ) benchmarks Pokémon battling, but each side is played by a single agent, and specialist RL agents still outplay general LLMs there. It doesn't test teammates who have to coordinate.
The goal is a controlled environment where I can measure how LLM agents coordinate, and that can later be used to train them with RL to encourage these collaborative behaviors.
The official Pokémon Showdown simulator, wrapped as a Gym-style environment. Four players each control one Pokémon from a team of three, two per side.
Each turn, an agent reads a plain-English summary of the battle and a numbered list of its legal moves. It can say a private message to its partner or choose a move, and once it chooses, its partner is told what it picked.
Free talk (keep talking until both have chosen), one message each, no talk, and one model controlling both Pokémon.
Qwen3.8-27B plays both teammates against a scripted max-damage bot. Battles are seeded and every team draw is played from both sides, so each talk mode faces exactly the same battles.
Talking helps. Teammates who could talk freely won 64% of their battles against the max-damage bot, while teammates who couldn't talk at all won 42%. Even a single message each (52%) beat no talk. One model controlling both Pokémon (54%) did better than no talk but worse than two agents talking freely, so I think the gain comes from the conversation itself, not just from one mind planning both moves.
Talking also costs. Free talk used 978k prompt tokens per battle, 3.8x the 259k of no talk, since every message means another model call that re-reads the battle and the conversation so far.
I also checked that the environment can tell models apart. A Qwen3.8-27B team won 96% of its battles against a team of 2B models and 74% against a team of 9B models, compared with 64% against the max-damage bot. The stronger the opponent, the closer the games, which is what makes the environment usable as a benchmark for comparing models.
I'm separating the effect of talking from the effect of seeing your partner's move. I'm also looking into turning the environment into a benchmark with a leaderboard across models, and using it for RL training to encourage collaborative behaviors.
Through this project I wanted to learn more about agent collaboration and RL environments, and thought I'd share the results! I ran these experiments on Texas A&M's Grace cluster. Thank you to Maria Teleki and to my advisor, Prof. James Caverlee , for the guidance and feedback along the way.

title: His Majesty stresses investment opportunities in UK-Oman ties
body:
His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik stressed the importance of strengthening British-Omani relations through political engagement and private sector cooperation, who highlighted the role of stability, transparent legislation and clear investment plans in supporting trade and economic growth. "We can see that bilateral investment and trade are moving in a positive direction, with concrete efforts being made to encourage investment and build stronger partnerships in sectors such as sustainability, financial services, and technology. Markets can prosper only in a stable environment; businesses can grow only when supported by transparent and flexible legislation; and investment opportunities can flourish only when underpinned by clear, well-defined and promising plans and projects", His Majesty said. The remarks were delivered during a banquet hosted at the Guildhall of the Lord Mayor of the City of London on the occasion of the state visit undertaken by His Majesty the Sultan to the United Kingdom (UK).

title: Two UAE scientists recognised in programme to support female researchers
body: A programme to support women scientists in the Arab world has selected two female researchers in the UAE for grants. The L’Oreal-Unesco For Women in Science Middle East Programme has awarded Dr Marieh Al Handawi, of New York University Abu Dhabi , and Jawaher Al Hammadi, of Khalifa University, for its 2026 iteration. They are among half a dozen female researchers in the Arab world, working in fields including pandemic preparedness, water security and personalised medicine, recognised in this round of the scheme. Ms Al Hammadi, an Emirati PhD student from Sharjah who grew up in Abu Dhabi, works on lab-based models of cell membranes. She told The National that recognition from the programme provided “a valuable opportunity to increase the visibility of my research”, forge connections with researchers internationally and potentially create collaborations. “I think these opportunities are incredibly important especially for young researchers, because science thrives when we exchange knowledge and learn from one another,” she said. Her research focuses on developing customisable cell membrane models that could lead to ways to test personalised treatments for patients. “The cell membrane surrounds every cell in our body and plays an essential role in how cells communicate, recognise signals, and respond to their surroundings,” she said. “By recreating these membranes in the laboratory, we can study these interactions in a more controlled environment.” Complex achievements Conventional cell membrane models are often made from synthetic materials, which, Ms Al Hammadi said, meant that they could not fully replicate the complexity of real cell membranes. “To address this, I combine synthetic components with tiny particles derived from cells, known as extracellular vesicles, which carry characteristics of the cells they originate from,” she said. “I then integrate these membranes with electronic sensors that allow us to detect and monitor changes in the membrane through electrical signals. “Ultimately, my goal is to develop a technology that can help researchers better understand diseases and evaluate how cells respond to different treatments.” She said that, with her method, it may be possible to recreate cell membranes that represent specific cell types, diseases or even particular patients. It is, Ms Al Hammadi said, “a very exciting time” to be a woman working in her field in the UAE, adding that the country “places great importance on science, innovation and empowering women”. “Over the years we have seen more women entering Stem [Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics] fields, taking on leadership positions, and making important contributions to scientific research, and that is something I am very proud to witness,” she said. Growing in numbers In total, 69 female scientists, including 25 in the UAE, have been supported by the L’Oreal-Unesco For Women in Science Middle East Programme, which was launched in 2014. In total the programme has In total, the programme has awarded Dh4 million to support research in the region. Six women in the Arabian Peninsula have been recognised in the programme’s latest edition. According to Unesco, 41 per cent of scientists in the Arab world are female, behind only Central Asia, where the figure is 50 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean, where it is 44 per cent. In East Asia and the Pacific, for example, only 27 per cent of scientists are female, while in sub-Saharan Africa the figure is 32 per cent and in western Europe, 34 per cent. Dr Al Handawi, a Syrian born and raised in the UAE, has been working at NYU Abu Dhabi after completing master’s and doctoral degrees at NYU in New York. She looks at how plants adapt to salty and dry conditions, in the hope this may highlight ways in which people can extract water from their environment. Among the plants she has analysed is the native tree Tamarix aphylla , which lives in salty sabkha habitats. The plant excretes a salt solution that evaporates, forming salt crystals. “These crystals act as magnets, capturing moisture directly from the air, even at relatively low humidity and condensing it on the plant,” she said. “This showed me that desert plants can provide us with natural solutions to the same problems we are trying to solve: how to access and manage water under extremely dry and challenging conditions. “My research explores whether we can use the significant amount of water already present in the UAE’s atmosphere as humidity and extract it with much lower energy requirements.” She said there were many more plants in the region waiting to be studied that “may offer completely different strategies for water harvesting”. Ultimately she would like to establish an independent research programme focused on “bioinspiration” and learning from natural systems, especially those adapted to the Middle East’s harsh environments, and on translating those mechanisms into practical solutions. “I want my research to go beyond discovery and ultimately lead to materials and technologies that can be tested and used to support communities,” she said. Women in science Sarah Al Amiri, Minister of Education, said in a statement that in the UAE women were “playing an increasingly prominent role in research” and in fields including advanced technology, health care, sustainability and aerospace. “Our focus is on strengthening the journey from education to research, and from research to real-world impact, so that young people have the skills, confidence, mentorship and opportunities to shape the future,” she said. “The L’Oreal-Unesco For Women in Science Middle East Programme advances this ambition by recognising women researchers, supporting their careers and giving the next generation visible examples of what scientific leadership can achieve.” Other programme recipients are Alaa Al Mushaikeh, a Saudi physicist at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (Kaust), and Qatar University’s Hadeel Zedan, who researches antiviral medications against, for example, coronaviruses. Also awarded were Dr Aljawharah Al Rubayyi, a Syrian scientist at Kaust who works on vaccines and immunotherapies, and Dr Sara Al Araimi, who researches ways to turn waste into water and useful materials at Oman’s University of Technology and Applied Sciences. Laurent Duffier, managing director of L’Oreal Middle East, said the scientific talent emerging across the region was “remarkable”. “Women are increasingly at the heart of that progress,” he said. “Our responsibility is not only to recognise that talent, but to help create the visibility, networks and opportunities that allow it to thrive."

title: A 4,700-year-old shipwreck and the stories it brings to life
body: This week on Culture Bites , Enas Refaei and Farah Andrews ponder the connections that civilisations built through travel almost 5,000 years ago. They share the story of a shipwreck that was discovered off Turkey's Mediterranean coast, believed to date back to the early Bronze Age . Archaeologists were able to unlock some of the vessel’s history based on pottery that they found at the underwater site. The ship was likely travelling from east to west, possibly trading goods between the Levant, Egypt and Anatolia. Enas and Farah talk about how discoveries like this can reveal the similarities in crafts and architecture between different civilisations, and how much more connected they were than we expect. The hosts also discuss the revival of HBO’s TV series, Girls . Five new episodes are expected to begin production in 2027, a decade after the original show ended. Farah and Enas discuss what a reboot of a show about women in their 20s could look like now that they are entering their 40s.

title: Two killed, eight injured in attack on Saudi Arabia's King Fahd Airport, Saudi Civil Aviation says
body: Two people were killed, and eight others were injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, on Wednesday, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said.The statement said officials were assessing the extent of the damage.The aviation authority noted on Thursday morning that flight operations resumed at the airport.The Indian Embassy in Riyadh identified at least one of the killed victims and two of the injured victims as Indian nationals in a Thursday statement.Additionally, in a separate incident, two people were also killed after Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oilfield on Wednesday, the energy ministry said.The incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on the kingdom.The incident caused a vehicle fire outside the facility's perimeter but did not affect operations at the field, the ministry said, citing an official source."The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two residents, one Filipino and one Nepali, and injuries to two residents, one Pakistani and one Indian, due to falling debris following the interception," the ministry said.Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.US orders diplomats to leave Saudi ArabiaThe US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to leave its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from several other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.The order came as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oil field.State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a post on X that the department ordered the departure of "non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only" amid attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen on civilian targets in the country.

title: What a Russian Satellite Stalking a Commercial Spacecraft Means for the Space Force
body: Over a two-week period beginning in late September and culminating in mid-October, a Russian satellite maneuvered dangerously close to a commercial Finnish satellite currently providing intelligence to the Ukrainian military. The apparent provocation has experts wondering why Russia made the move—testing new capabilities, collecting intelligence, or trying to intimidate the Finnish company—and what, if anything, the U.S. Space Force could or should do about these types of events in the future. While the incident did not involve a U.S. asset, the Russian action highlights the growing importance of commercial space assets to military operations and how those relatively defenseless assets could be vulnerable in or before a conflict. Between Oct. 15-19, a Russian satellite dubbed COSMOS 2612 performed deliberate, fuel-intensive maneuvers to close in on the Finnish ICEYE-X36 satellite, according to a report by LeoLabs, which the company shared with Air & Space Forces Magazine. Instead of a somewhat standard flyby, COSMOS matched, shadowed, and orbited around the ICEYE satellite, coming as close as 500 meters to it, according to the report. The Russian satellite spent months adjusting its orbit, then rapidly closed the distance with the ICEYE satellite, continuously maneuvering around it before COSMOS abruptly ended its movements and distanced itself Oct. 18-19. The LeoLabs report characterizes the event as a “red” on “blue” engagement in orbit and calls it a planned, highly coordinated rendezvous and proximity operation, which required precise navigation and onboard sensing. An ICEYE spokesperson declined to provide a detailed response to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine about the incident. “We are aware of the situation and tracking it closely. Our constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” the spokesperson said in an email. The Center for Strategic and International Studies held an online event Oct. 21 to discuss the incident and its implications for the U.S.. Neither of the two experts at the CSIS event claimed to understand Russia’s goals with the stunt, but Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Integrity ISR, called it unusual and said it indicated Russia’s intent to send a message to the Finnish company. “I still scratch my head about what the Russian endgame is with this,” Gillinger said. Clayton Swope, deputy director of the CSIS Aerospace Security Project, said the event certainly was not “benign.” “I don’t think we have enough information right now to know whether or not Russia achieved the objectives it wanted to achieve here,” Swope said. The COSMOS/ICEYE incident comes about a month after Space Force leadership publicly announced that the force has on-orbit offensive space weapons at its disposal and under Guardians’ control. “Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said during the opening keynote at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14. “This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.” The timing of the satellite maneuvers, following Meink’s comments, could be a Russian signal, threat, or influence campaign meant to deter outside, commercial support for Ukraine—or even a bluff, retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves , the senior resident fellow for Space Studies at the Mitchell Institute, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. ICEYE Satellite (ICEYE) What USSF Can Do In 2025, USSF’s Rapid Capabilities Office kicked off a project to field threat-awareness sensors that communicate close hazards to space asset operators. Such sensors would presumably alert operators if a Russian satellite came as close as it did to the ICEYE bird. Beyond sensing and communicating, though, an April report from the Secure World Foundation noted that more nations are starting to fund “bodyguard” capabilities for their space assets, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported at the time. Germany, India, France, and Japan are all either building or planning to acquire such space-based bodyguards, which could protect and counterattack any space-based incursions. Swope, speaking on the COSMOS/ICEYE incident, said spacefaring nations need clearer expectations for behavior in space, and predicted events like the recent incident would likely happen again. “I just feel like it’s not a question of if; it is a question of when we see these satellites do something that we’re going to say is hostile again,” Swope said. He also said any use of bodyguard satellites needed to include a clearer explanation of what they will accomplish in orbit. Reeves likewise said the Space Force needs to be prepared to both understand and respond to future incidents like this one. While the service has been building its space domain awareness capabilities in recent years, that’s only one piece of the larger puzzle, she said. “There’s a big difference between knowing where something is and understanding what it’s doing,” she said. The force has made “tremendous progress” in tracking orbits and objects with a sophisticated sensor network and other tools, she said. But the Pentagon must put more “rigor” into protecting both military and commercial assets in space, Reeves said. “The Space Force needs to be running through these scenarios on the regular, and hopefully they are,” Reeves said. “I’m going to trust that they are in their wargames and exercises.” Those exercises need to include both allies and commercial partners, Reeves added. “We’ve got to determine how quickly we can determine what happened,” she said. “Can we distinguish an accident from something deliberate? How confident are we in attribution?” Both Reeves and Swope separately noted that any counterattacks or deterrence to space-based provocations don’t have to involve space-based retaliation or actions. Reeves pointed to the U.S. ability to strike ground-based facilities to sever links to satellites. Swope noted increased pressure on Russia’s oil “ shadow fleet, ” a network of an estimated hundreds of old tankers used to export oil while evading sanctions, could be a lever to nudge Russia away from space tomfoolery. Necessary Guidance Ultimately, while the Space Force will be the entity dealing with satellite harassment or attacks, the force’s role needs clearer definitions on what constitutes aggression and merits a response, especially given the long-term consequences of space debris and other factors involved in kinetic actions in orbit, Reeves said. “I don’t think it’s necessarily the Space Force itself that should be determining that,” Reeves said. “I think it should be our national leadership that’s coming up with that. … Because at this point in time, we don’t have that coming from the national-level leadership.” That lack of guidance has placed the burden on military leadership to decide what the U.S. believes hostile actions in space look like and how the military should respond. “We don’t want to be doing this thought work when we’re living it in real time,” Reeves said. “There are dire consequences in space if the wrong action is taken or a hostile action is taken.” The post What a Russian Satellite Stalking a Commercial Spacecraft Means for the Space Force appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
