title: Hezbollah rebuilding military capabilities in Beirut as IDF prepares for possible renewed fighting
body: Hezbollah is rebuilding its military capabilities in Beirut, while the IDF is preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting with the terrorist organization if it attacks the Israeli home front during an escalation involving Iran, a security official told Walla on Wednesday.According to the official, Israel is dissatisfied with the Lebanese Armed Forces' (LAF) enforcement of existing understandings intended to curb Hezbollah's military activities.Several days ago, the Lebanese military uncovered a tunnel linked to Hezbollah in the Roueissat el-Jadida area of eastern Beirut.The security official said the discovery was intended to demonstrate that the Lebanese military was taking action in the heart of Beirut, where Hezbollah has relocated some of its military capabilities from southern Lebanon.In some cases, the organization has restored military assets that were damaged or destroyed in IDF strikes."We are not satisfied with the Lebanese mechanism, and the issue of Hezbollah's tunnels comes as no surprise to us," the official said."We assess that this report stems from Israel's discussions with Lebanon in Rome. Ultimately, the understandings are not being enforced as we would expect. There is terrorist infrastructure and a presence of terrorist operatives in southern Lebanon," the security official stated.Hezbollah rebuilding military infrastructure in Beirut, TyreAddressing Hezbollah's military infrastructure in the Beirut area, the official said the terrorist organization was continuing efforts to restore and expand its capabilities beyond southern Lebanon."We know there is significant terrorist infrastructure there, alongside Hezbollah's efforts to bolster its capabilities. They are working on rehabilitation and military buildup, not only in southern Lebanon, but also in Beirut and Tyre, where the largest concentrations of the Shiite population are located."Regarding the operational readiness of Hezbollah's military wing, the official remarked, "They are making a major effort to regain operational experience and return to peak combat readiness."One of the scenarios presented to IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir envisions Hezbollah joining a broader regional conflict, including by launching strikes against the Israeli home front, should the US or Israel attack Iran.Hezbollah can sustain several months of fightingWalla learned that Hezbollah retains a diverse range of combat capabilities sufficient to sustain several months of fighting.These include rockets, missiles of various ranges, fiber-optic and SIM-controlled drones, which pose a significant operational challenge to the IDF. The organization also maintains tactical drones and suicide drones, also known as loitering munitions.Meanwhile, Hezbollah is working around the clock to train anti-tank and observation squads as part of its preparations for a future round of fighting against IDF troops in southern Lebanon and along the Israeli-Lebanese border.

title: Stealthy F-117 Nighthawk Goes on Display at Smithsonian
body: A historic Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk is now on permanent display at the National Air and Space Museum’s Stephen F. Udvar-Hazy Center. The exhibit debuted Oct. 21, showcasing the first operational stealth aircraft at one of the most visited aircraft museums in the world. The F-117 joining the collection at Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Va., is unique: Dubbed “Overachiever,” tail number 85-0818 is the only F-117 to have flown combat missions in all four of the major conflicts from when the F-117 was active: 1989’s Operation Just Cause in Panama; 1991’s Operation Desert Storm in Iraq; 1999’s Operation Allied Force in Kosovo; and 2003’s Operation Iraqi Freedom in Iraq.. The F-117 Nighthawk was the first operational aircraft designed to evade radar with its unique shape and materials and was a triumph of technical ingenuity and skill at a time before computer-aided design. The aircraft proved how reducing an aircraft’s radar cross-section could provide a decisive advantage in combat. Michael Hankins, the museum’s curator of modern military aviation, said today’s F-35 stealth fighter builds on the foundation set by the F-117. Beyond the “jaw drop moment” he expects visitors to experience when they see its sharp, angular features, he hopes the display teaches them to appreciate the visionary designers and groundbreaking pilots and maintainers who took the F-117 into battle and kept the jets running. Jeff Corbets, a program manager at Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works, oversaw the Overachiever’s restoration, which included removing parts of the plane that remain classified secrets to this day. He said he hopes the jet will connect future generations to the story of stealth. “This was the aircraft that ushered in the era of [stealth],” he said, noting that the F-22, F-35, B-2, and B-21 followed. “All of them now are kind of based on the legacy of this airplane.” Skunk Works engineers developed the sharply faceted jets’ shape to minimize its appearance on radar screens. Subsequent stealth aircraft have used curves to achieve the same effect, but in the 1970s when the F-117 was developed, the computer power to calculate those curves was not yet available. Air Force tests calculated the radar signature as being on par with a marble. A 37th Tactical Fighter Wing F-117 Stealth Fighter aircraft lands during Operation Desert Storm. National Archives photo by Tech. Sgt. Rose Reynolds The Nighthawk went into service in the early 1980s and wasn’t officially acknowledged until 1988. Although it debuted operationally in Panama in 1989, that operation was not deemed a success. Rather, it was the role the Nighthawk played in 1991’s Operation Desert Storm that demonstrated its value: an ability to fly undetected, without jammers or other escorts, into contested enemy territory and deliver ordnance at will. “The F-117 was the centerpiece of the success that we experienced during the Desert Storm air campaign,” said Lt. Gen. David A. Deptula, USAF (Ret.), dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies and principal attack planner for the campaign. “It was the linchpin of our success.” Deptula said the combination of stealth jets and precision munitions enabled planners to strike more targets in the first 24 hours than would have been possible with standard force packages of conventional aircraft. “We’re pretty sure that this one [the Overachiever], on the first night of Desert Storm, took out a main communication center in Baghdad,” Hankins said. He cautioned that details are hard to come by because much of the jet’s history remains classified. It will likely take years for information to be cleared for public release. F-117s remain in rare but limited use in training and other activities. The Overachiever is among several F-117s to become museum pieces, but the first to join the Smithsonian collection. The Air Force, working with Lockheed and Smithsonian officials, spent years orchestrating the transfer, which was officially announced at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference in September. Lockheed donated the hours to restore and demilitarize classified elements of the aircraft, including removing its original stealth coatings. The work was completed over about eight months, after which the jet’s wings were removed so that it could be loaded onto a C-5M Super Galaxy cargo aircraft for the flight to Washington. Now, hundreds of thousands of people will get to see the “Overachiever” and learn about the origins of stealth. The Udvar-Hazy Center is open every day except Christmas from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Admission is free, but parking costs $15. The aircraft that changed airpower is now on display for the public to see. The F-117 Nighthawk laid the foundation for every stealth platform that followed and proved its revolutionary capabilities in conflicts from Panama to Operation Iraqi Freedom. After lots of preparation… pic.twitter.com/4SzcwLrdVi — Air & Space Forces Association (@AFA_Air_Space) October 21, 2026 The post Stealthy F-117 Nighthawk Goes on Display at Smithsonian appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Amy Acton campaign slams Ramaswamy over controversial ad featuring estranged mother
body:
The GOP candidate told reporters Tuesday that the ad was from his campaign.
Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's campaign slammed her GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy Tuesday, alleging his campaign used her estranged mother, whom she has accused of abusing her and standing by the man who sexually abused her, to urge voters not to support her in the toss-up race.
A video that appears to be a campaign ad circulated on social media late Monday showing Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, saying that she loves her daughter, but adds, "Amy has a serious problem" and has lied about her past.
ABC News has not been able to verify the content or authenticity of the video, which has been shared by many users online, including Donald Trump Jr.
Ramaswamy told reporters on Tuesday that the ad did come from his campaign and that he viewed it as "legitimate." He said that Acton's mother was not compensated.
"It is an ad from our campaign, and the thing that I want to say is that I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans, and unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues. She won't debate me," he said.
In the campaign ad, Arthur describes her daughter as a "liar," saying, "She lies about her past."
"My daughter needs help, and she can't help you if she needs help herself," Arthur says in the video.
Arthur couldn't immediately be reached for comment.
Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, criticized Ramaswamy over the "disgusting attack."
"It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point," Stearns said in a statement.
"After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," he added.
This is not the first time Arthur has publicly accused her daughter of lying.
In an interview with an anti-abortion access group in 2020, Arthur accused Acton's father of convincing their daughter to lie.
When asked earlier Tuesday if the ad was made with the campaign's knowledge or consent, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy, released a lengthy statement Tuesday, but did not deny making the ad or denounce it.
"We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor," Luck said in a statement.
Luck's statement went on to accuse Acton of "lying about Vivek and his family, lying about her own record, and then hiding from debates," and questioning her actions during the pandemic when she was the director of the Ohio Department of Health.
"If Amy disagrees with these criticisms, she should stand before the people of Ohio, answer the questions, and let voters decide for themselves. The fact that she won't, and Vivek will, should tell you everything about who's really lying," Luck ended her statement.
Acton pushed back in an interview with Spectrum News Tuesday.
"I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is something I'm just complaining about. Who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect and sexual abuse; my brother and I were removed," she said.
The campaign released a video ad later Tuesday where Stearns echoed his criticism over Ramaswamy
"Shame on Vivek,” he says, adding, "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio. He's not fit to lead."
Acton has been public about her experience with abuse and seeking therapy for it, She has also openly spoken about her tumultuous relationship with her mother.
In an interview with the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019, when she was first appointed director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton described a childhood that was "out of control", shuffling between houses with her mother and brother and the "cast of characters" her mother dated.
She alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him.
A newspaper article from August 1978 corroborates Acton's account.
The article in the Youngstown Vindicator describes that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was "bound over to the Mahoning County grand jury in connection with the rape of a 12-year-old girl." Acton was born in 1966, making her 12 at the time.
The article says he was "arrested at his home on August 4 th following an investigation initiated by the girl's father."
Cledith Arthur died in 2004. He and Acton's mother remained married after the allegations.
"In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her," Acton said in the 2019 interview about her mother. "I was lucky that it got bad enough, because it got me out of there."
Acton's father received custody, which she credited for turning her life around. She then graduated top of her class in high school, was homecoming queen, and became a doctor.
Ramaswamy has also been criticized for making comments seen as dismissive of his opponents' experiences, saying that Acton "only ever talks about something that happened to her" rather than having a positive message.

title: Vance praises Ramaswamy for having 'audacity' to run controversial Acton ad
body:
Acton called the ad "a horrible and hideous thing to do."
Vice President JD Vance, during a rally in Cincinnati on Wednesday, praised Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy for having the "audacity" to cut a controversial ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother calling her daughter a "liar" -- a move that has sparked bipartisan backlash.
"Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said.
The ad, which circulated on social media late Monday, shows Acton's long-estranged mother, Donna Arthur, saying that she loves her daughter but that "Amy has a serious problem" and has lied about her past and her struggles growing up. The ad came nearly two weeks out from the high-stakes midterm elections where Ohio is home to not only a gubernatorial race, but also key Senate and House races that could determine the balance of power in Congress.
At a campaign event in Wyandot County on Wednesday, Acton called the ad "horrible and hideous."
“I think it was a horrible and hideous thing to do, a sad thing, and I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do," she said. "I think it's despicable, but it's exactly like he has been this entire campaign."
Ramaswamy, on Tuesday, confirmed his campaign had made the ad and said he wanted the race to be about "substantive issues," but that Acton had ducked accountability, debates and what he claimed were her own lies about him. Acton and other Democrats, as well as some Republicans, have excoriated Ramaswamy for the ad and for bringing up his opponent's childhood trauma.
Acton has been public about her experience with abuse and openly spoken about her tumultuous relationship with her mother, whom she says she has not spoken to since she was 12 years old. Acton alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him.
Acton's campaign responded to the ad with one of its own in which her brother, Philip Stearns, criticized Ramaswamy for the ad and noted she had been the victim of abuse.
"Shame on Vivek,” Stearns said in the ad, adding, "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio. He's not fit to lead."
Acton's campaign released a statement on Tuesday from Stearns as well saying Ramaswamy "has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."
ABC News White House Correspondent Karen Travers asked President Donald Trump about the ad on Wednesday. The president said he knew "nothing about it," later adding that "it's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much, but I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek."
The vice president said he "wasn't even supposed to talk about" the ad -- which he called the "biggest controversy" -- but couldn't "help myself."
Vance said Wednesday that voters should "focus on the substance" rather than the controversy, turning to attack Acton over her role as Ohio’s health director during COVID.
"And my message, ladies and gentlemen, is very simple: Whether -- whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts. And the fact is that Amy Acton was the woman who tried to mask your children."
Vance later said Acton "could never" be governor because she is "worried about whether somebody says something mean about" her.
"I think that a person who is more worried about whether somebody says something mean about them, that person -- that person could never serve in the governor's mansion of the great state of Ohio," Vance said.
ABC News has reached out to Acton's campaign for comment on Vance's comments.
Speaking ahead of Vance on Wednesday, Ramaswamy made no reference to the controversial ad. During his remarks, Ramaswamy did not mention Acton's name or even reference his opponent at all -- a contrast from how he often mentions her on the trail.
Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a toss-up race for reelection in the state, told the Associated Press after Wednesday's rally, " I would not have run that ad."

title: Israel cannot secure lasting peace while Gaza remains in crisis
body: News this week that a lack of funding could result in the UN's World Food Programme cutting aid to roughly half a million people in Gaza is a sobering reminder that a ceasefire is not the same as peace. Although Israel ’s assault on the territory may have slowed somewhat since last year’s truce, the dire conditions that have made life unbearable for so many civilians remain largely intact. The WFP has made clear that the cuts do not reflect declining need. About 1.4 million people in Gaza face acute food insecurity, and hundreds of thousands depend on assistance for even the most basic needs. For families who have lost their homes and any realistic prospect of earning an income, a food parcel or cash payment is an essential lifeline. Beyond the sheer moral urgency of rectifying the situation, however, lie broader consequences. The international community should be under no illusion about what allowing this aid lifeline to fray could mean. As Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative of Gaza's Board of Peace, n in The National earlier this month, leaving the territory in a state of permanent uncertainty is no alternative to a political settlement. His warning that despair is an excellent recruiting tool for extremism should be taken seriously by all those who claim to seek lasting regional security. This is a warning that some Israeli voters will be considering ahead of next week’s general election. Polls suggest a closely contested race, with no clear path to a parliamentary majority. For Palestinians in Gaza, the result carries enormous significance, even though they have no say in determining it. Some have postponed marriages, rebuilding homes or restarting businesses while waiting to see whether a change of Israeli government might offer a different future. Their hopes may prove misplaced. A new Israeli leadership would not automatically bring a significant change in policy, and the security concerns that shape Israeli politics will not disappear overnight. On the other hand, Israeli security cannot be achieved through indefinite military pressure while Gaza’s population remains trapped in poverty . To make matters worse, most Palestinian officials have largely failed their people. The elections that were due to take place next November have been postponed by at least a year, eliminating any hope for renewal at the leadership level. In the short term, donors must urgently close the funding gap In the short term, donors must urgently close the funding gap, while those controlling access to Gaza must ensure that essential supplies can get in. Humanitarian aid is not the same as political progress, but without it, the prospects for progress will deteriorate further. Those responsible should be aware that allowing hunger and despair to deepen may defer the next crisis, but it will not prevent it. Israel’s next government, Palestinian political leaders, international donors and regional partners should recognise that the price of neglecting a two-state solution that is fair to both Palestinians and Israelis will be paid long after the immediate headlines have faded.

title: Canada expands military space launch access and funds Arctic satellite communications
body: The C$20 million NordSpace agreement covers launches and research at the Atlantic Spaceport Complex in Newfoundland and Labrador. It complements a separate 10-year agreement with Maritime Launch Services announced in March 2026. The government said independent launch access would help Canada maintain critical satellite services during geopolitical tensions or disruptions to foreign launch markets. Budget 2025 allocated C$182.6 million over three years to establish a sovereign launch programme. “A sovereign spacefaring Canada needs the ability to launch a payload into orbit on its own schedule, from its own soil, on its own rocket when national security demands it,” said Rahul Goel, founder and CEO of NordSpace. “That capability is only possible if a Canadian company vertically integrates the full stack from launch vehicle to launch pad, as we are at NordSpace.” Laser links for Arctic communications Kepler’s C$4.7 million, two-year contract will fund the development and testing of laser links that let satellites exchange data directly. The aim is to make space-based communications faster and more resilient, particularly in the Arctic and other remote regions. The project will also support Arctic surveillance and threat-detection objectives under the Northern Wide-Area Tracking and Continuous Horizon programme. It forms part of the C$17.9 million Gateway to the Stars challenge within Canada’s Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security programme. “Canada’s North is strategically vital, yet remains underserved by traditional connectivity infrastructure,” said Mina Mitry, Kepler’s CEO and co-founder. “Kepler’s optical data relay network is designed to move mission data quickly and reliably, providing the Canadian Armed Forces with more persistent access to timely intelligence and shortening decision timelines.” Canada joins NATO launch initiative Canada has become a full member of NATO’s STARLIFT initiative. The project aims to create a more resilient, responsive and cost-effective launch network, allowing allies to send assets into space at short notice. The Canadian Armed Forces is also establishing a Space Mission Operator occupation. The new career path is intended to help the Royal Canadian Air Force attract, train and retain specialist personnel. A further C$1.2 million over two years will support workforce development through Launch Canada and a space rocketry initiative. The funding covers student projects, competitions, hands-on training and early-stage research. The latest announcements bring the value of space-related contracts, grants and contributions announced this year to more than C$3 billion, according to the government. It expects recent space investments to support approximately 3,000 jobs annually. Source: Government of Canada (press release) .

title: U.S. Air Force Undecided on New F-16 Procurements as F-35 Continues to Fall Short
body: The U.S. Air Force does not expect to decide whether to purchase newly built F-16 fighters for at least another year, despite concerns over an ageing fleet and the need to expand its combat aircraft inventory. Lieutenant General David Tabor, the service’s deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, said on October 20 that acquiring new F-16s was not an urgent priority, although the service recognised the need to prepare for the retirement of older aircraft during the 2030s. The deliberations come as the Air Force seeks to increase its combat-coded fighter inventory to 1,509 aircraft by 2035, up from 1,168 at the beginning of fiscal year 2026. The F-16 is by far the lightest and least costly fighter type in production in the United States, and is currently being built exclusively for export. Tabor said the service was examining a range of options for replacing older F-16s, rather than committing to a single aircraft or procurement strategy. He described the purchase of new-build F-16s as potentially the easier option, but stressed that the service had time to evaluate alternatives. He warned that although the decision did not need to be made immediately, the Air Force wanted to avoid reaching a point at which replacement became urgent before a suitable solution had been selected. The proposal has gained attention following reports that Lockheed Martin had offered the Air Force an enhanced version of its latest F-16 Block 70, provisionally designated the F-16G. The proposed aircraft could incorporate conformal fuel tanks, additional external fuel capacity, an infrared search-and-track system, advanced targeting equipment and other improvements intended to extend its operational relevance. The primary factor leading the Air Force to consider resuming procurements of F-16s is that the F-35A fifth generation fighter failed to provide a direct replacement. Despite the aircraft being decades newer, their availably rates remain tens of percentage points lower, while operational costs and maintenance needs are considered excessively high. This has prevented the aircraft from serving as a one-for-one replacement for the F-16 as it was intended to, and resulted in serious cuts to pilot training levels. Despite close to 500 F-35s being in service in the Air Force, the F-16 has been relied on much more heavily for combat operations against Iran, as the newer fighters have suffered continued delays to planned updates, including lacking any air-to-ground missile capabilities which limits their viability for critical air defence suppression operations. A newly manufactured F-16 would offer a substantially longer remaining structural life than many aircraft currently in U.S. service. The F-16 Block 70/72 production standard is designed around an airframe service life of up to 12,000 flight hours, potentially allowing new aircraft to remain in service for decades without the extensive structural work required by older fighters. Purchasing additional F-16s could therefore provide a way to sustain fighter numbers. Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) could also influence the eventual decision, as the Air Force aims to acquire at least 500 such uncrewed aircraft by 2032, including the General Atomics YFQ-42A and Anduril YFQ-44A, which are intended to operate alongside crewed fighters. General Tabor stated future CCA developments could reduce the number of crewed fighters required, although the current generation has not yet changed the assumptions underpinning the service’s fighter force structure calculations.

title: Understanding Nix flakes
body:
Subscriptions are the lifeblood of LWN.net. If you appreciate this content and would like to see more of it, your subscription will help to ensure that LWN continues to thrive. Please visit this page to join up and keep LWN on the net.
This article was contributed by Tyler Langlois
Nix flakes are an experimental feature of the Nix package-management tool designed to build projects in a more self-contained and reproducible way. Despite the feature's experimental status, it has become increasingly popular for open-source projects to publish flake.nix files that offer predefined development environments and build automation even when those repositories may not offer an upstream package or module for the NixOS Linux distribution . Although Nix flakes have a complicated history, and the path for stabilization is uncertain, flakes can provide useful capabilities for projects that choose to include them.
The promise of flakes is to provide reliable and reproducible methods for acquiring and building software. Let's say that an open-source project is trying to provide Linux users with an easy way to set up a development environment for its software. Distributions tend to have different versions of programming languages, libraries, etc. which means that a user on Debian 13 is going to have slightly different versions of software than a user on Fedora 45. Some dependencies may not be packaged for the distributions at all. This is a headache for everyone involved.
Projects can avoid the headache by shipping a Nix flake that pins the versions of its dependencies and lets each user install the same software regardless of which distribution they are running. End users can reliably install dependencies, build projects, and run tests often just with a local (and properly configured) Nix installation and few (if any) other toolchain requirements.
Flakes are written in the Nix language and are primarily used by the Nix package manager. While NixOS can use flakes via utilities like nixos-rebuild , flakes function independently from NixOS. flake.nix files are at the core of how flakes work: these files contain inputs that are defined as URL-like remote resources (typically software repositories) and outputs that flake consumers can use, like packages or tests for those packages.
A simple flake might look like the following snippet of Nix code:
The legacyPackages name is a bit deceptive because its Nix packages are not literally legacy packages: the name is a compatibility shim to avoid a situation in which a command such as nix flake show might list more than 100,000 packages in the terminal. When legacyPackages is used, instead of packages , the nix command will avoid listing all packages when printing its values, as documented upstream .
Upon adding the input called nixpkgs to the flake.nix file, nix flake lock will create a flake.lock file that pins the nixpkgs input against the NixOS/nixpkgs repository at the commit referenced by the nixpkgs-unstable branch. Like a Cargo.lock file in a Rust project or a Gemfile.lock file in a Ruby project, the flake.lock JSON file anchors each input to a concrete upstream revision. Doing so permits the flake to consistently refer to its dependencies and reliably build its outputs with a known-compatible set of inputs.
Locking a flake's inputs against the latest commit for a branch is one way to express an upstream reference, but the flake reference format permits a few additional strategies including a specific tag or other forms like absolute paths. A locked revision remains part of the repository and can be updated later with the nix flake update command (if the reference refers to a non-specific target like a branch name rather than a Git hash).
The outputs attribute of a flake is written as a Nix function. When Nix processes a flake.nix file, the inputs are fetched and passed to the outputs function where it can actually use the concrete values from inputs like nixpkgs . In this case, the flake will simply provide the hello package drawn from the nixpkgs-unstable branch.
By default, Nix assumes that each reference under inputs itself contains its own flake.nix and, therefore, its own set of outputs . These are the values that are used as each input is referenced in the outputs function (like nixpkgs.legacyPackages in the example code).
This example illustrates bundling a package into a Nix flake, but there are more top-level attributes that offer other uses when present in a flake's outputs . For example, devShells provides development environments pre-populated with libraries and environment variables, while nixosModules may be imported into a NixOS configuration for use in one's NixOS configuration. The nix command-line tool recognizes many attributes as part of a flake's schema, although the structure of a flake's outputs outside these conventional names is arbitrary.
Locked inputs are one important trait of flakes, but another behavior that is arguably just as important is that flakes are evaluated in pure evaluation mode , which means that external factors that may change the values that Nix computes are forbidden by default. For example, environment variables may not be read and network access is gated by checking downloaded artifacts with checksums. Although this behavior can be relaxed with the --impure flag, enforcing it adds to the reproducible quality of a flake.
It should be noted that some features of Nix flakes are also addressed by other libraries or tooling. For example, locked dependencies (akin to a Nix flake input ) can be achieved without the use of flakes with niv , a project that provides capabilities similar to a flake.lock file. Development shells are supported by existing, non-experimental commands with shell.nix files . For many users, Nix flakes serve as a more general, unifying umbrella for useful concepts like inputs, lock files, and Nix commands.
How does one use flake.nix when encountering these files in a source code repository? First, the nix utility must be installed and Nix flakes enabled before use: each nix command must include the --experimental-features 'nix-command flakes' command-line option or the stanza experimental-features = nix-command flakes must be set in $HOME/.config/nix/nix.conf or /etc/nix/nix.conf per the Nix flakes setup documentation .
Most nix operations that interact with flakes can do so via either a local checkout of a repository or with a flake reference (which can be any of the URL-like formats accepted under a flake's inputs attribute). The following command, for example, displays all the outputs available from the Ghostty repository for the Ghostty terminal emulator:
In this example, the github:ghostty-org/ghostty flake reference is internally expanded into an upstream GitHub URL that fetches tarballs rather than cloning entire repositories. The following output from the nix flake show command has been trimmed down for readability:
In addition to the ghostty package for the x86_64-linux architecture, there are other outputs like checks that define tests that may be run directly against the flake with commands like nix flake check .
The devShells output is particularly useful. As a Zig-based project, Ghostty requires a compatible language toolchain for contributors to build and test the project. Manually installing zig is one option, but using the Nix flake development shell can make the process easier. Entering the development shell is done with the develop subcommand:
After nix starts a shell with the environment populated from the flake.nix file, the zig command is available:
This installation of zig is scoped only to Ghostty's development shell and is not installed system-wide ( zig and its supporting libraries are installed into the Nix store ). In addition to zig , all of the other dependencies relevant for development are added to the $PATH and necessary libraries are included as well. When part of a repository, flake.lock files ensure that downstream users of nix develop will end up with the same versions of all utilities and libraries as the original Nix flake author. Because the development shell is constructed from separate and distinct paths in the Nix store, multiple versions of the same toolchain can coexist on the same host without executables or shared libraries colliding.
The same principles apply for any repository that provides a flake.nix , whether the project relies on C++, Rust, or any other language. The --command flag lets a command run within an indicated development shell non-interactively. Niri and pandoc are just a few of the many projects that provide flake.nix files and development shells that bundle each of their respective build environments:
In each of these cases, none of the cited toolchains were present beforehand on the host system. Each command and its associated libraries necessary for project compilation are provided entirely through the Nix flake development shell.
Shipping around locked dependencies and development shells are useful capabilities, so why do flakes remain an experimental feature gated behind additional configuration steps?
Flakes were first introduced in July 2019 in NixOS RFC 49 by Eelco Dolstra, the original author of Nix. Throughout the year-long RFC process, development of the underlying plumbing for what would ultimately become Nix flakes continued in the Nix GitHub repository . After a period of extended discussion, the proposal PR was closed and the RFC withdrawn in July 2020 because of a failure to reach consensus for adoption. Concerns about scope, design, and other considerations remain visible in the (large) discussion thread attached to RFC 49 that eventually led to its closure.
Since RFC 49 failed to pass, flakes were included in the Nix 2.4 release in 2021 as an experimental feature. Nix flakes remained accessible only when explicitly enabled, and that requirement remains in place for the upstream Nix project. As we'll see later, this is one aspect of flake usage that has splintered across different implementations.
In the years following the initial release, Nix flakes have been widely adopted. In the 2025 NixOS Community Survey , which drew input from nearly 3,400 Nix users, 78.9% of respondents reported using flakes . A smaller random sampling of 300 repositories , conducted by Nix maintainer Jörg Thalheim, across GitHub repositories with shell.nix or flake.nix files present found significant adoption over the traditional development shell method using shell.nix files.
Community growth around Nix flakes without a formal plan laid out by an RFC has become somewhat of a sore spot in the Nix community. Contributors eager for the features within Nix flakes are frustrated at the ongoing experimental label, while some involved in the original RFC process remain dissatisfied with the expansive scope and design of Nix flakes that has arguably escaped the limited scope intended by attaching the experimental label.
Contributor Graham Christensen wrote in 2021: " I believe Flakes are astonishingly important and will be very powerful, but the RFC experience has turned so many people against it on principle. " Jade, a contributor to the Lix alternative to Nix reflected on flakes with a more hesitant tone: " Even assuming that flakes are good at macro-level composition, they often are accompanied by poor use of micro-level composition, which still is best done by using the old primitives. ". Former contributor Samuel Dionne-Riel opined that Nix flakes was an experiment that did too much at once, " and it sucks because so much of it is good, or are good [but] undercooked ideas ".
Despite these and other concerns, the use of flakes is widespread at this point; many third-party utilities work as expected with flakes regardless. In practice, the ways to use flakes via Nix have remained consistent in terms of their commands and configuration settings although there are no guarantees without the removal of the experimental label by maintainers.
The rift within the Nix community on the subject of flakes has become so wide that alternative implementations have cited their stance on flakes as a distinguishing characteristic. The Nix package manager (usually referred to as CppNix in reflection of its C++ code base) still marks the feature as experimental, but Lix has designated flakes as a frozen feature slated for future extraction into a plugin , while Determinate Nix (a downstream distribution of CppNix) expressly supports flakes and has marked them as a stable feature enabled by default.
As for Nix itself, RFC 136 ("A plan to stabilize the new CLI and Flakes incrementally") lays out a path forward for Nix flakes to become a stable feature. It was proposed in October 2022, and ultimately accepted in August 2023. There is a flakes stabilization milestone to track the work needed to remove the "experimental" label from flakes. Some work heralds potential breaking changes for flakes (such as changing lock attributes ), while other plans offer less-visible but significant performance improvements such as " lazy trees " (to avoid spurious file copies to the Nix store). In addition to work on the flakes feature, the design of the newer command-line interface for nix will have to be stabilized before moving on to complete the implementation of flakes and mark them as a stable feature. There will need to be an additional RFC for the final design of flakes once that happens. The need to address command-line design stems from the fact that flake-related commands are often conflated with other Nix commands. For example, the experimental feature that provides alternative commands like nix env shell in contrast to nix-shell that often rely on flake-like semantics. As noted in the text of the RFC: There are many criticisms about Flakes. But one of them especially relevant to stabilizing is a perception that Flakes have encroached on other new features, in the sense that it ought to be possible to use those other features without Flakes but isn't in practice. For example, there is no reason in theory that pure evaluation of Nix expressions requires Flakes. Despite its criticisms, the RFC expresses optimism about the future of flakes: We could, of course, just "rip off the band-aid" and stabilize everything at once. The argument for that would be that enough time has passed and the concerns of (less numerous) long-time users are not important. But we think the plan here has little downsides; we can instead make everyone happy with only some delay. If that is true, why not do that instead! Flakes remain an experimental feature of the nix command-line utility but development continues. There is no concrete target completion date for the stabilization effort, so when (or if) flakes will finally graduate into stable status remains unclear, but with a plan in place and their adoption still growing, Nix flakes are likely to appear more often across the software landscape. Posted Oct 21, 2026 15:18 UTC (Wed) by Athas (subscriber, #104895) [ Link ] (2 responses) I have used NixOS for a while, and for most of that period, flakes have been available. For years I disliked them, for various reasons: I am opposed to experimental features on principle, in particular because I like to distribute my software to other people, and I could not expect that they would have flakes enabled. Further, the error message emitted was confusing, as --experimental-features 'nix-command flakes' somehow feels against Unix convention (a space in an option!). I didn't get the point, as it was always trivial to fix Nixpkgs to ensure reproducibility, and tools like niv make it easy to do so systematically. I don't mind having multiple shell.nix files for different environments, and in fact I like having the different options visible as distinct files, rather than the often extremely complicated and unreadable flake.nix files. Flakes have weird interactions with version control that I don't fully understand, such as refusing to work if flake.nix is not under control of Git. This goes against my intuition of how software ought to work. Nevertheless, I finally switched to using flakes for most of my own projects earlier this year, despite none of the above concerns actually changing. One reason is that the flake commands are aesthetically nicer to use (mostly because the legacy nix commands are truly awful, and seemingly inspired by rpm conventions). But the real reason is that I finally had a reason to use the ability to easily compose multiple flakes into larger environments and projects. This was useful in putting together a project that involved various exotic dependencies, each of which are developed independently but come with flake.nix definitions. The result is not beautiful by any means, since it is an overly complicated mess, but it is solid. Overall, I am a little surprised that I somewhat like Nix by now, since it is fundamentally an ugly tool meant to solve ugly problems and I prefer avoiding such things in the first place, but when you have to solve ugly and overly complicated build problems, I think Nix is the most principled tool available. One reason is that the flake commands are aesthetically nicer to use (mostly because the legacy nix commands are truly awful, and seemingly inspired by rpm conventions).
