Drawing on experience across diverse AI/ML use cases and production deployments, he works closely with customers to solve their AI/ML challenges. He also shares AI/ML knowledge with data scientists, developers, and analysts, aiming to contribute to positive change in Korea and around the world. Chloe Kwak Chloe is a Senior Solutions Architect on the Korea Retail team at Amazon Web Services. She helps retail and e-commerce customers in Korea design scalable, cost-effective cloud architectures and adopt AI/ML services to accelerate their business outcomes.

title: ‘Capitulating to a Dictator Shows Weakness’ – Republican Senator Slams Trump’s Russia Policy
body:
Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah sharply criticized President Donald Trump’s recent decisions on Russia, warning that easing sanctions, importing Russian diesel and restricting military support for Ukraine were strengthening Vladimir Putin’s war machine while undermining American leadership.
In an opinion article titled “When Freedom Comes Knocking at Our Door,” published Tuesday, Oct. 20, Curtis, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the administration of taking steps that benefit Moscow as Russian forces continue their attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“These actions embolden and materially support a regime that is currently waging a war of conquest against a sovereign nation,” Curtis wrote.
He warned that Washington’s decisions were damaging international security and undermining confidence among allies in America’s commitment to shared Western values.
“Capitulating to an authoritarian dictator shows weakness and sets back the cause of freedom,” the senator declared.
Curtis singled out Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order suspending additional sanctions and tariffs authorized under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
The legislation had received broad bipartisan support in Congress and was intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow and countries purchasing Russian energy.
Curtis said the administration’s decision to freeze those measures, combined with an agreement to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, would provide additional revenue to Russia while its military continues fighting in Ukraine.
During an October Senate discussion , Curtis emphasized that restricting Russia’s energy revenues was necessary to weaken its ability to sustain the invasion.
His latest intervention places him among Republicans publicly challenging the administration’s recent Russia policy, despite their party’s control of the White House.
Curtis also questioned recent restrictions affecting Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications system, which Ukrainian forces use in battlefield operations.
He said the restrictions had disrupted Ukrainian drone operations and raised questions about who authorized the changes.
Citing Elon Musk’s statements that the US government controls the restrictions, Curtis demanded greater clarity over the decisions affecting Ukraine’s military capabilities.
He also criticized Washington’s demands that Kyiv halt attacks on Russian petroleum facilities without securing an equivalent commitment from Moscow to stop striking Ukrainian infrastructure.
The senator further raised concerns about an interruption in US intelligence sharing that provides Ukraine with warnings of incoming long-range ballistic missile attacks.
These concerns have become especially urgent as Russia intensifies strikes against Ukrainian energy facilities and residential areas ahead of winter.
Curtis based part of his argument on his recent congressional visit to Ukraine, where he traveled to Kyiv and Kharkiv with Republican Senators Thom Tillis and Alan Armstrong.
The delegation examined Ukrainian battlefield innovations, including unmanned aerial systems and counter-drone technologies, and met Ukrainian officials and military personnel.
Curtis said the experience demonstrated that Ukraine was contributing directly to American national security through technological innovation and battlefield intelligence.
“Ukraine is no longer a dependent friend,” he wrote, describing the country as an increasingly important strategic partner.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Opinion| The unfinished transition and why dissolving government cannot replace implementing the R-ARCSS: A response to Mogga Loyo
body: South Sudan’s political crisis cannot be resolved by dissolving the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity (R-TGoNU), establishing a caretaker administration, or changing the electoral legal framework while leaving the substantive obligations of the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS) unfulfilled. Such measures may change the appearance of government without addressing the political, constitutional, security and economic structures responsible for the country’s persistent instability. In responding to four reasons put forward by Mr. Mogga in his arguments for dissolving the transitional government, which include, first, to bring the existing transitional government to an institutional end; second, to start a new journey through a caretaker administration; third, to pave the way for elections by changing the legal framework; and fourth, to end the concentration of executive authority amid financial uncertainty, I would like to say that these are not the reasons. Rather, they are effects of a prolonged transitional period without accountability. I think Mr. Mogga, in writing the article, did not pay attention to the fundamental distinction between ending the transition administratively and completing it constitutionally, institutionally, and democratically. What he was supposed to look into critically is the way the R-ARCSS was designed. It was designed to guide South Sudan from armed conflict and concentrated executive authority towards inclusive governance, a unified professional security sector, an accountable public finance sector, transitional justice, a permanent constitution, and credible elections. Therefore, ending the transition without these issues in place is a mere wild goose chase. In other words, dissolution alone cannot deliver these outcomes, and without these issues in place, the future of South Sudan is in limbo. Dissolution and a caretaker government are not substitutes for reform Mr. Mogga’s concerns about ineffective governance, delayed elections, concentrated executive authority, and financial uncertainty that make him support the dissolution reflect genuine challenges facing South Sudan. However, dissolving the R-TGoNU, destroying the R-ARCSS, and going for premature elections without implementing the R-ARCSS in letter and spirit is putting the cart before the horse. The issues the R-ARCSS was designed to address cannot be addressed through elections. A caretaker administration may maintain essential public services, but it cannot substitute for implementing the political and institutional reforms prescribed by the R-ARCSS. Without clear constitutional authority, effective oversight and enforceable accountability, a new administration could reproduce the same concentration of power under a different name. The relevant question is therefore not simply whether the existing government should continue, but whether the country has fulfilled the substantive obligations necessary to move beyond the transitional order. Replacing the government without completing those obligations risks perpetuating the crisis rather than resolving it. Elections must follow credible preparations, not replace them It is important to remind Mr. Mogga that elections are an essential outcome of the transition, not an alternative to implementing the peace agreement. Credible elections require an independent electoral administration, reliable voter registration, adequate funding, political freedoms, security guarantees, a functioning judiciary, and meaningful participation by eligible citizens, including refugees and internally displaced persons. They also require an agreed and legitimate constitutional framework and public confidence in the electoral process. Merely changing electoral laws, shortening preparations or announcing a polling date cannot compensate for deficiencies in these essential conditions. An election conducted without adequate safeguards risks turning unresolved political and security disputes into a contest for control of an unreformed state. The objective must therefore be elections that are peaceful, inclusive, free, fair and credible, not elections conducted simply to declare the transition complete. Five structural reforms that made the SPLM-IG carry out a bureaucratic coup It is important to draw to the attention of Mr. Mogga that the dissolution was not legal, but it was a bureaucratic coup. This is a type of coup that occurs when non-elected civil servants or administrative officials quietly seize, retain, or override power through rules, executive manoeuvring, or withholding institutional support rather than military force. The SPLM-IG dissolved the R-TGoNU because the implementation of the R-ARCSS has consequences for the distribution and exercise of political power. Therefore, the following five reasons can explain the occurrence of the said coup: First, power-sharing and executive accountability. Chapter I establishes an inclusive governance framework intended to constrain unilateral decision-making. Genuine implementation requires consultation, negotiated governance, and respect for the participation of the agreement’s signatories. This forced President Kiir to dissolve the R-TGoNU because it is weakening his grip on power. Second, security-sector unification. Chapter II provides for transitional security arrangements aimed at establishing a unified, professional, and accountable national security sector. This process requires moving away from fragmented military structures and armed political leverage towards institutions governed by law. President Kiir and the SPLM-IG fear security arrangements because they do not want to lose political leverage that is achieved through control over the fragmented security sector. Third, inclusive electoral participation. Reliable population data, credible voter registration, and appropriate arrangements for refugees and internally displaced persons are essential to electoral legitimacy. Uncertainty surrounding these processes can create opportunities for manipulation where independent oversight is weak. This is what President Kiir wants so that he can hold elections that he can manipulate and rig. Fourth, transparency in public finances and oil revenues. Chapter IV addresses resource, economic, and financial management. Effective implementation would have strengthened public accountability, transparent resource allocation, and independent oversight. This was what the SPLM-IG and President Kiir feared, as implementing the R-ARCSS had implications of losing control over public finances. Fifth, transitional justice and constitutional reform. Chapter V provides for transitional justice mechanisms, including the Commission for Truth, Reconciliation and Healing, the Hybrid Court for South Sudan and the Compensation and Reparation Authority. Their effective operation is essential to accountability, reconciliation and redress. Chapter VI and the wider constitutional process are equally important for establishing permanent constitutional safeguards, protecting fundamental rights and ensuring that public authority is exercised within the law. These reforms may challenge entrenched interests, but their purpose is not to punish a political party. It is to establish institutions capable of serving citizens, holding leaders accountable, and outlasting individual administrations. These are issues that the SPLM-IG and President Kiir fear the most, and this is one of the reasons that made President Kiir and the SPLM-IG dissolve the R-TGoNU. The Tumaini Initiative must complement, not undermine, the peace framework I have seen in several comments from some writers trying to invoke the Tumaini Peace Initiative as the replacement of R-ARCSS, which Mogga emphasised in his article. I would like to caution him and the rest that the relationship between the Tumaini Peace Initiative and the R-ARCSS raises important questions about legal continuity, political inclusion and the authority of the existing peace agreement. A supplementary initiative may help engage holdout groups and resolve outstanding issues, but its legitimacy depends on its consistency with the established framework and the applicable procedures for changing agreed arrangements. Parallel processes that bypass relevant parties, create competing institutions, or weaken existing commitments risk producing legal uncertainty rather than lasting peace. Dialogue must not become a substitute for implementing obligations already agreed upon. The proper test is whether any new initiative strengthens the R-ARCSS, broadens meaningful participation, and advances enforceable reforms. Changing the name of a peace process or creating another administrative structure cannot, by itself, resolve the underlying causes of conflict. The destination must be a permanent constitutional state South Sudan needs an inclusive constitutional settlement that ends the cycle of provisional political arrangements. A permanent constitution should define the distribution of public powers, protect fundamental rights, establish effective checks and balances, and provide independent judicial and constitutional oversight. The process should consider an appropriate federal system based on territorial arrangements and fiscal accountability, alongside professional security institutions, credible elections, transparent public finance, and accessible justice mechanisms. Transitional justice must address past violations through lawful and independent processes, while reconciliation and reparation should contribute to rebuilding public trust. These are not optional additions to the transition. They are essential foundations of sustainable peace and democratic government. Conclusion Mr. Mogga’s concerns about governance, elections, executive power, and financial uncertainty deserve examination. However, dissolving the transitional government cannot, by itself, correct the institutional weaknesses that have prolonged South Sudan’s transition. A caretaker administration without enforceable safeguards may simply inherit the same problems, while elections without adequate constitutional, security, and institutional preparations may deepen political disputes. The priority must be to implement the R-ARCSS in letter and spirit, establish accountable institutions, unify the security sector, strengthen public financial management, advance transitional justice, and complete an inclusive constitutional process. South Sudan does not need merely to end the transition administratively; it needs to complete it constitutionally, institutionally and democratically. Ending a government on paper while leaving the causes of the crisis intact is not a solution; it is the risk of beginning another cycle of political uncertainty under a different name. The writer is a South Sudanese constitutional lawyer, academic, and political figure. He studied law at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda. He is an independent legal researcher and constitutional expert and serves as a lecturer and Deputy Dean of the College of Law at Starford International University in Juba. He is also a member of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition (SPLM-IO). He can be reached via nhomngekjuol@gmail.com . The views expressed in ‘opinion’ articles published by Radio Tamazuj are solely those of the writer. The veracity of any claims made is the responsibility of the author, not Radio Tamazuj. The post Opinion| The unfinished transition and why dissolving government cannot replace implementing the R-ARCSS: A response to Mogga Loyo appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: How The U.S. Army’s ‘Navy’ Aims To Go More Autonomous With Its Vessels In The Pacific
body: The U.S. Army wants to infuse new autonomous capabilities into its current and future fleets of amphibious landing ships and other watercraft. The service is also aiming to acquire up to 100 new purpose-built uncrewed surface vessels (USV). The maritime assets the service has now , often referred to as ‘the Army’s Navy,’ are obscure and generally underappreciated . However, the small force offers an important additional set of naval logistics capabilities, especially for any future fight in the Pacific, which could be further bolstered with optionally-crewed or entirely uncrewed platforms. Army Maj. Gen. Frederick Crist, head of 8th Theater Sustainment Command (TSC), issued plans for future autonomous watercraft capabilities during a talk last week during a talk at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual symposium . 8th TSC, which has its main headquarters at Fort Shafter in Hawaii, is one of the top formations tasked with managing U.S. military logistics across the Pacific. An uncrewed surface vessel (USV) passes by the US Army’s General Frank S. Besson class Logistics Support Vessel USAV General Brehon B. Somervell . US Army “In order to be able to increase theater distribution, we have the two composite watercraft companies, at end state there, west of the IDL [International Date Line],” Crist explained, referring to the Army’s future planned maritime force posture in the Pacific. “We continue partnering with industry to be able to move into autonomous watercraft systems to be able to conduct other means of maritime distribution.” To take a step back quickly, as part of its broader regional role, 8th TSC also has forward-deployed elements in Japan. This includes the 5th Transportation Company, which is currently organized as what the Army calls a composite watercraft company. As of 2024, the unit had a pair of General Frank S. Besson class Logistics Support Vessels (LSV), as well as 10 smaller Landing Craft Utility (LCU) type vessels and four small tugs, according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO). The Army has eight LSVs, in total, and these are by far its largest and most capable ships. The two youngest LSVs, which were acquired in the mid-2000s, also form a distinct subclass, and their design is optimized for long-distance open-ocean operations, as you can read more about here . It’s not immediately clear which LSVs are currently assigned to the 5th Transportation Company. The unit is also set to receive new Maneuver Support Vessel (Light) landing craft . Examples of the original LSV design, at left, and the open-ocean-optimized design, at right. An LCU-type landing craft is also seen at far right. US Army Until very recently, the 10th Support Group (Regional), headquartered in Okinawa, was more directly responsible for overseeing forward-deployed Army logistics units in Japan. Earlier this month, the Army performed a so-called ‘reflagging’ of that formation, a largely administrative process that transformed it into the 45th Sustainment Brigade . As part of the reflagging of the 10th Support Group into the 45th Sustainment Brigade, the Army has also been pushing ahead with plans for “the standup of a second composite watercraft company in Yokohama North Dock,” in the port city of the same name on the Japanese home island of Honshu, Maj. Gen. Crist explained last week. “That end state will have two composite water[craft] companies west of the IDL [International Date Line] under the command and control of the 45th Sustainment Brigade.” A US Army LSV at the pier in Japan. US Army When it comes to the watercraft assigned to these units, “we’re also moving into the autonomous lane,” Crist added. “Just in August, USARPAC [U.S. Army Pacific] had an opportunity to conduct an experiment by retrofitting an existing commercial vessel, the HOS Resolute [sic; HOS Resolution ], with a kit to provide autonomous navigation.” Maritime autonomy firm Sea Machines was able to integrate its SM300 software package on the HOS Resolution in just nine days for this demonstration. The ship is a 257-foot-long offshore support vessel more typically used to support oil and gas rigs. However, it features a stern ramp and four jack-up legs that also make it well suited to loading and unloading cargo at remote beaches. A US Army truck drives off the HOS Resolution during the experimenting in August where the ship was fitted with the Sea Machines autonomy package. US Army For years now, the U.S. Marine Corps has also been experimenting with the HOS Resolution and other similar ships more generally. That service has been using the vessels to help refine its new expeditionary and distributed concepts of operations , which are themselves heavily centered on future conflict scenarios in the Pacific . The Marines have brought those capabilities to Army demonstration exercises in the past, as well. Another look at the HOS Resolution , in 2023, while operating under contract to the US Marine Corps. USMC The Army sees the August experiment as a potential stepping stone to integrating increasing degrees into its existing watercraft fleets. “You could increase the fleet of autonomous vessels by tapping into the existing manned fleet,” Maj. Gen. Crist said. “Put on retrofitting kits to be able to conduct navigation, and then eventually propulsion and engine room activities, and eventually get to a fully autonomous system.” Even just adding in autonomous navigation capabilities could help reduce the workload for the human crews on Army vessels and provide added margins of safety. Blending autonomy with “propulsion and engine room activities” could improve reliability and reduce maintenance demands. Being able to operate those ships in a fully uncrewed mode, if desired, would open up additional operational possibilities, including just for repositioning ships across the broad expanses of the Pacific. Army Maj. Gen. Frederick Crist, head of 8th Theater Sustainment Command (TSC), speaks at AUSA last week. US Army Reduced manning requirements could be especially attractive for the Army’s ‘Navy,’ which is already a very small part of the service’s overall force structure. Last week, Maj. Gen. Crist also talked about further leveraging traditional crewed vessels owned and/or operated by contractors. “It’s going to be a broad portfolio of systems of systems,” he said of the overall watercraft vision for the Pacific. “Army watercraft with Army Mariners will be, of course, one aspect of it. We also look for the opportunity to be able to leverage USTRANSCOM’s (U.S. Transportation Command) contracting capability to leverage operational support vessels that are commercially owned and commercially operated. We’re considering ways of being able to have commercial vessels that become manned by Army mariners.” It is also interesting to note here how extremely similar this all sounds to the modifications the U.S. Navy made to the Spearhead class Expeditionary Fast Transport USNS Apalachicola ahead of its commissioning in 2023. However, despite tens of millions of dollars spent and successful demonstration of autonomous capabilities, the Navy curiously decided to put the Apalachicola into service without any plan to make use of these features operationally. There does not appear to have been any effort to integrate these capabilities more broadly within the Spearhead class since then, either. The Spearhead class Expeditionary Fast Transport USNS Apalachicola . Austal USA USNS Apalachicola . Austal USA Last year, the Navy struck the four oldest Spearhead class ships from its rolls entirely and has put several others on reduced operating status, ostensibly as a cost-saving measure . The service is still acquiring new Expeditionary Fast Transports, including members of the Expeditionary Medical Ship subclass that feature expanded medical facilities. The Spearhead class was born out of a program specifically to meet Army and Marine Corps requirements, and the ships are regularly used to support those services in the Pacific and elsewhere globally. The Army also wants to expand its fleets of purpose-built uncrewed surface vessels (USV) for use in the Pacific, as well as elsewhere globally. Just earlier this year, Army Maj. Gen. Gavin Gardner, who preceded Maj. Gen. Crist as head of the 8th Theater Sustainment Command, said he wanted to rapidly acquire as many as 100 drone boats. His vision included larger USVs capable of carrying eight to 10 standardized shipping containers. “I could see those operating in the U.S. PACOM area of responsibility,” Gardner told reporters at a roundtable in June, according to Military Times . “I think that gives you a ton of operations, inventory in motion, easy to respond. And then because they’re autonomous, and we can work with our partner nations forward, you have those berthed up everywhere from Korea to Japan, the Philippines, Australia, Singapore, Thailand, etc.” “Clearly, [the autonomous vessels] would be forward in the theater, kind of moving supplies, because we have a constant demand for Army watercraft time now, to deliver equipment and supplies forward in the theater,” Gardner added at that time. One of the inherent benefits of the Army watercraft fleets, and its LSVs in particular, is their ability to help alleviate the need for the U.S. Navy to meet more localized littoral logistics needs, if they are even available to help in the first place. Navy amphibious and military sealift ships would already be heavily strained by high demand during any major conflict in the Pacific or elsewhere globally. This could easily be further exacerbated by threats to those supply lines . All of this has already been underscored this year by pressure on maritime logistics chains in the context of the war with Iran. The Army’s ‘Navy’ also offers valuable additional capabilities and capacity in non-combat contingencies, such as responding to natural disasters . Marine vehicles drive off an Army LCU landing craft during an exercise. USMC/Cpl. Ernesto Lagunes More generally, the Army has been working to expand its use of smaller USVs, including speedboat-like designs, in various roles. The service has clearly been paying close attention to Ukraine’s very successful use of drone boats in one-way kamikaze attacks , as well as ones armed with guns and rockets and examples configured as launch platforms for surface-to-air missiles and weaponized uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) . The 7th Infantry Division, one of the Army’s main maneuver combat formations in the Pacific, just recently experimented with a Ukrainian-developed Magura-series USV during an exercise in Michigan . That particular USV was configured to launch a quadcopter-type drone. Another member of the Magura family was observed being used in a one-way-attack configuration by U.S. Army Green Berets from the 1st Special Forces Group during the annual Balikatan exercise in the Philippines earlier this year. A Magura-series USV seen in use at the annual Balikatan exercise this year. US Army Another Magura-series USV in use during Exercise Bayonet Quest 2026 in Michigan. US Army The Magura USV launches a quadcopter-type drone during Exercise Bayonet Quest 2026. US Army The Army has also been experimenting with American-designed USVs. The aforementioned recent exercise in Michigan also featured a Saronic Corsair , the same type of USV that the Navy used to rescue the crew of an Army AH-64 Apache attack helicopter that went down in the Gulf of Oman in June. Explosive-laden Corsairs were also used to carry out the first known U.S. kamikaze USV attack , which was launched against a coastal target in Iran in July. A stock picture of a Saronic Corsair. Saronic During another separate exercise in the Philippines this year, Salaknib 2026, Army forces used unarmed Rampage USVs from U.S. firm Havoc , as seen below. As part of that exercise, the USVs escorted a crewed General Frank S. Besson class LSV to its destination, heading out in front to help spot potential hazards. US Army “There’s all the work that the Department’s already doing with autonomy and autonomous systems that we look to take advantage of in the [Pacific] theater, as well,” Maj. Gen. Crist said at AUSA. The Navy and the Marine Corps have both been working to grow their operational fleets of smaller USVs , as well as larger ones, in recent years. At the same time, the Navy has suffered years of setbacks and shakeups in its efforts to operationalize bigger and more capable designs. The service awarded contracts for a total of 30 new medium-sized USVs last month in its latest attempt to reverse that trend. In September, Secretary Pete Hegseth also announced several new initiatives aimed at further expanding use of uncrewed platforms and advanced autonomous capabilities across the U.S. military and all domains. The Pentagon is presently laying the groundwork for the establishment of an all-new top-level Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM), which it hopes to see come to fruition next year. What is clear now is that the Army’s vision for future watercraft operations, especially in the Pacific, is increasingly autonomous. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post How The U.S. Army’s ‘Navy’ Aims To Go More Autonomous With Its Vessels In The Pacific appeared first on TWZ .

title: Upper Nile election committee starts recruiting for various positions
body: The High Election Committee in Upper Nile State has commenced recruiting staff for various positions as part of the ongoing preparations for the general elections scheduled for 22 December. On 19 October, the committee announced its intention to recruit an Election Administration Officer for the state, 12 election administration staff for the various geographical constituencies, and a number of voter registration personnel to be deployed across the state’s constituencies. Key requirements include holding an academic qualification—specifically a bachelor’s degree or a diploma—and proficiency in written English, among other criteria. The Commission also encouraged women to apply. The deadline for the submission of applications is at 5 p.m. on24 October 2026. Peter Mayom, the head of the High Election Committee for Upper Nile State, told Radio Tamazuj that even though they are moving ahead with recruitment, they face several challenges, primarily the insufficient time allotted for the volume of work that must be completed within a short period. “Additionally, there are transportation difficulties for the commission’s staff, as Upper Nile State is vast and requires reliable means of travel to reach its various parts,” Mayom said. He further highlighted a shortage of personnel within the High Election Committee and requested that the National Election Commission provide additional staff in accordance with the commission’s organizational structure. Meanwhile, John Chol, who said he is applying for the position of Elections Voter Center, told this publication that the recruitment process is straightforward but that the short notice poses challenges for applicants from far-flung areas. “I encourage young people, especially women, to submit their applications so they may participate in the electoral process,” he said. “I urge the committee to uphold integrity and transparency in its operations to ensure the success of the elections.” For his part, Yin Chan, an applicant, stated that the requirements are reasonable and that information has been effectively communicated to the public via radio broadcasts and the commission’s notice boards. “The only challenge is the time constraint,” he said. “I encourage individuals with disabilities to join the commission’s workforce to enable them to participate in the electoral process.” The post Upper Nile election committee starts recruiting for various positions appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: UNISFA condemns Abyei drone attacks
body: The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) on Wednesday reiterated the strong condemnation by UN Secretary-General António Guterres of the drone attacks that occurred near Amiet Market and Todach, some 15 Kilometers from Abyei town, on 19 October 2026. In a statement extended to Radio Tamazuj, UNISFA said it is deeply concerned by the attack, which represents a serious threat to peace and security in Abyei. “Dozens of people were killed and injured, with the toll expected to rise as the assessment and evacuation of casualties continue. Many people are still reported missing,” the statement reads in part. “UNISFA reiterates its concern over the targeting of civilians and extends its deepest condolences to the families of those who lost their lives and wishes a swift recovery to the injured.” UNISFA said it is taking all measures to strengthen security in the area and has intensified day and night patrols to protect civilians. “Our peacekeepers are continuing to provide emergency medical assistance, support the evacuation of casualties, and have extinguished most of the huge fires in the area,” the statement said. “UNISFA commends the collaboration of the relevant authorities and communities and continues to closely monitor the situation.” “We urge all parties to refrain from any retaliatory actions that could further endanger civilian lives and undermine peace and security. UNISFA remains committed to implementing its mandate to promote peace and stability in Abyei,” the statement concluded. The post UNISFA condemns Abyei drone attacks appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Trump Envoy Grilled for Calling Putin a ‘Humanitarian’
body:
US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff sparked outrage among Republican lawmakers Wednesday, Oct. 21, after praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” during talks in St. Petersburg, despite Moscow’s continuing deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
The remarks came as Putin released Stephen Hubbard, an American citizen imprisoned in Russia for more than four years, while Washington sought to revive negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian – you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin during the televised meeting.
“I commend you, and I thank you again,” he added.
The praise drew immediate condemnation from Republican lawmakers, who pointed to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, attacks on civilians and the deportation of Ukrainian children.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina condemned Witkoff’s praise of Putin as Russian forces continued to bombard Ukrainian cities.
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis wrote on X .
“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” he added, urging Witkoff to speak with Ukrainian families whose children have been killed or taken to Russia.
Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas also rejected the envoy’s characterization.
“No. Putin is a stone cold killer,” Cornyn wrote on X.
Republican Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, another outspoken critic of Washington’s approach to Moscow, described the episode as “another embarrassment.”
Trump played down the controversy when questioned about Witkoff’s remarks, suggesting that the description could be understood in the narrow context of Hubbard’s release.
“Well, I guess you could say (it) for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out,” Trump said.
“But you know, I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other.”
Vice President JD Vance offered a more direct defense, arguing that Witkoff’s comments were part of the diplomacy required to secure an American citizen’s freedom.
“I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage,” Vance said during an event in Ohio.
“Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done.”
The administration has presented Hubbard’s release as a diplomatic success. Trump said Washington had not been required to release another prisoner in exchange.
Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher and US Air Force veteran, had been held by Russia since 2022 after Russian troops detained him in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum, when the Russians occupied it in April of that year.
Russian authorities accused him of fighting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces, allegations his family and legal representatives denied.
He was subsequently sentenced to nearly seven years in prison. The US government designated him as wrongfully detained.
According to the Associated Press , Hubbard’s family described harsh conditions during his detention, including beatings and deprivation of food.
His sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, expressed relief at his release following years of uncertainty over his fate.
The Kremlin presented the decision as a goodwill gesture toward Trump, saying Hubbard had been pardoned following requests from Washington.
Witkoff’s meeting with Putin came one day after discussions with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners in Oslo.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Code word Gospel: How UK secret service caught soldier selling plans to ‘save Lebanon’
body: At lunchtime on March 16, 1965, Chief Inspector Jock Wilson of London’s Special Branch followed his suspect through the streets surrounding London’s Charing Cross Underground station. Under the railway arches nearby, he witnessed Peter Sydney Allen exchange envelopes with another man. It was time to move in. He arrested Allen, a soldier and desk sergeant working at the Ministry of Defence who had been under surveillance for a month. His companion, Maj Abdul Hafidh Khazal Al Abbassi, an assistant military attaché of the Iraqi embassy, was also detained. Maj Al Abbassi was taken to Canon Row Police Station, where he claimed diplomatic immunity. When his official car arrived a little over an hour later, he was allowed to leave. Allen, however, was taken to New Scotland Yard and charged with selling state secrets to agents from Egypt and Iraq. Among the documents he handed over during a dozen meetings over the course of a month were Top Secret UK and US plans to help Lebanon in the event of an attack on the government. There were also files marked “Assistance for Kuwait”, “Family of Weapons” and an alphabetical list of file names Allen would be able to get his hands on from the cabinets he could access at the War Office. He was later sentenced to 10 years in prison. The operation to arrest Allen, which was given the code word Gospel, has been revealed through the release of a trove of documents from the UK’s National Archives relating to the 1960s. Many cover the Cold War, including a succession of officers working for Russia, plus members of society with Communist affiliations. Labour politician and founder of the National Health Service, Aneurin Bevan, came to the notice of MI5 due to his association with the Communist Party in Russia and the UK and his unspoken criticism of the War Cabinet. Mayfair surveillance Mark Dunton, principal records specialist at the National Archives, told The National the Allen file revealed a remarkably casual attitude to security at the MoD, particularly given the fall-out from spy scandals within its ranks during that era. They appeared to rely on trust and vetting to ensure staff did not betray secrets, but were clearly not always successful. The Allen file appears to suggest that the security services were monitoring the Egyptian embassy in South Street, Mayfair, when they became aware its diplomats were clandestinely meeting a British official – described as 5ft 10in with brown hair and blue eyes, often wearing a brown suit and sheepskin coat – and set about trailing him. Allen had only just begun selling secrets. Astonishingly, his trail of deception had begun when he used a payphone in a corridor of the War Office to ring the Iraqi embassy to ask if they would be interested in meeting him. His reason for selling secrets was simple: he needed money. His wife had been in hospital for a cancer operation, his four children had returned from his mother-in-law’s in Wales, and his bills had mounted up. In his statement he gave when he was questioned, he said: “I was desperate for money and the only way I could see of obtaining any was by use of the top secret documents. “I thought about it for about a fortnight and then telephoned the Iraqi embassy. I used the public call box in the corridor at the War Office and got the military adviser's phone number from the directory. I didn't at that time know who I spoke to but I have since found out that he is Maj Abassi, the assistant military attaché. I told him I was in possession of something which I thought he would be interested in seeing.” His first drop-off, for which he received £20, was made at the embassy in Queen’s Gate, South Kensington, and involved papers regarding Kuwait. Payment for secrets A scrap of paper from that first meeting, on which he had scribbled the name and phone number of a colonel who would decide how much he should be paid depending on the usefulness of the secret papers, was found on him when he was arrested. He told police that the colonel asked him if he could get more papers regarding Middle Eastern countries. “A few days later I found a top secret paper, in one of the combination lockers, on the Lebanon, which I thought might be of interest to him,” he said. His agreed drop-off was not at the embassy, but near Charing Cross. This time he was not paid, as he was told they were “of no value to them”. He was also told he should instead try agents at the embassy of Egypt, then known as the United Arab Republic. “I kicked up a bit of a fuss about this so he said if I could bring them something of value, especially on Israel, then they would pay me,” he said. Action plan The top secret Lebanon papers are contained in the file, and cover the US and UK’s “joint theatre” plan for action if the Lebanese government requested military assistance to “meet aggression” and “maintain order”. The plan says that Syria and Israel would constitute “a potential external threat” but that it was considered “most unlikely” that either neighbour would carry out any “aggressive acts”. Instead, Syria and Egypt were thought likely to aggravate any internal disorder with the use of propaganda and agents with the aim of aligning the Muslim population with Syria. “The greatest and most likely threat to Lebanese stability lies in the recurrence of internal religious strife,” it said. The action plan involves air and naval surveillance before committing forces “by amphibious assault if necessary”. The 29-page plan says ships of the Mediterranean Fleet and RAF planes should be at seven days' notice, and an army company on 24 hours' notice. Forces would move from a base in Cyprus directly into Lebanon. “Although it is visualised as a limited operation in support of a friendly government, organised military opposition may be encountered and forces should be constituted and prepared for entry against a measure of organised resistance,” it states. Securing the airfield, port and city of Beirut would be the priority. Financial straits Allen, who had served in Egypt in the 1950s, admitted he had a dozen meetings in total, several of them witnessed by MI5, at which he often received £15. He would meet his contact near Park Lane and they would walk around Curzon St in the heart of Mayfair, or near Charing Cross. He said he did not believe he was offering “anything of consequence”. He was in charge of 11 clerks, but was the person responsible for custody and processing of all top secret documents which came into the office. The papers were kept in two cabinets, and he was the only person who knew the combination. “I would never have handed any information to any Soviet bloc countries and I only did what I did because I was in serious financial trouble,” he said. “Any money I got I passed over to my wife for housekeeping. I have kept nothing for myself. At no stage have I told any of these people who I really am, where I worked or how they could contact me.” Clobbered The files also contain accounts of discussions by British authorities about what should be done with the agents Allen was meeting. It was decided it was not necessary to demand their removal, but in any case, they were spotted flying out of the UK from London after they had “become compromised”. The Home Secretary, Frank Soskice, was said to be “impressed” when given an account of the case. Chief Inspector Wilson was sent a letter thanking him for his work by Courtenay Young, a senior MI5 officer who was head of the security service’s Soviet counter-espionage section during the Cold War. “Thanks to efficient co-operation and mutual goodwill we managed to clobber Gospel from the start to finish within a month and a day,” he wrote. Lax attitude Mr Dunton has written a book, The MI5 Archive: Official Secrets, with his colleague Stephen Twigge, studying thousands of secret papers released decades after they were filed away. There remains a “massive interest in espionage and spycraft”, he said, with the files rich in detail about surveillance reports, transcripts of telephone calls, listening devices and intercepted letters. Although MI5 does not fall under the usual rules for government records to be released after 30 years, it had chosen to release a plethora of files 50 years or more after the fact. He said the Allen case had echoes of the Portland Spy Ring in its simplicity. Unlikely spies Harry Houghton and Ethel Gee, who worked at the Admiralty Underwater Weapons Establishment, stole classified documents and passed them to a KGB handler before returning them. Mr Dunton said that despite posters with the message “Keep Secrets Secret” being displayed around its offices, the MoD had relied on staff's civil service values to keep them honest. Only when they slipped up, and colleagues became suspicious, would they be caught.

title: Why Kazakhstan Joined Both the American and Chinese AI Initiatives
body:
Looking ahead: Kazakhstanâs President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev chairs the presidential council on AI development, established in May 2025. Image: Imago/Adobe
Kazakhstan did not choose between Washingtonâs Pax Silica and Beijingâs WAICO: it joined both. It needs technology from both superpowers, and a say in the rules.
âNo country should remain only a consumer of artificial intelligence,â Kazakhstanâs President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told the opening ceremony of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on 17 July. Every state, he said, should have the opportunity to build its own digital infrastructure and institutional capacity.
He stood at Xi Jinpingâs right for the group photograph , sat beside him through the session and spoke second , ahead of two prime ministers and the UN Secretary-General. He opened in Mandarin . Such arrangements are settled in advance.
The day before, 29 governments had signed the founding agreement of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), to be headquartered in Shanghai. Kazakhstan was among them.
Three weeks earlier, the countryâs AI minister, Zhaslan Madiyev, had been in Washington signing the Pax Silica declaration , the State Departmentâs initiative on AI and supply chain security. Of the 25 signatories, Kazakhstan is so far the only one that also belongs to WAICO.
Kazakhstan does not produce the core technology it is trying to acquire for its AI agenda. What a country in that position can build, and what it has to trade to do it, is a question most of the world will face. Yet the reporting concentrates on the AI race between Washington and Beijing, and much less on what everyone else is doing.
Since mid-2025, AI has become a central focus of the state. A presidential council on AI development, chaired by Tokayev, was established in May 2025 . His annual address to the nation that September was devoted to the subject, and ten days later the country had a ministry for it headed by a deputy prime minister. This year was declared the year of digitalisation and artificial intelligence , and on 18 January an AI law came into force. In June, the government adopted Digital Qazaqstan , a national strategy for digital transformation and AI development running to 2029. The Digital Code took effect on 12 July, five days before Tokayev spoke in Shanghai.
The drive has two sources. The first is systemic. Competition between the frontier laboratories has produced rapid and visible gains in what the leading models can do, and with them a widening expectation that this technology will transform economies and societies faster than earlier industrial transitions did. Most states are moving because they do not want to arrive late.
The second is country-level. Kazakhstanâs economy depends on natural resources, above all oil, which is about half of what it sells abroad . Diversifying away from that has been declared policy for decades. Broadly, AI is being asked to do two jobs: improve how the state and the wider economy run, and become an export industry in its own right.
Meeting any of those targets requires technology and infrastructure Kazakhstan cannot supply on its own. Several suppliers provide it.
The US supplies the chips, the model foundations and, in time, the cloud. The chips matter most. Both national supercomputers run on Nvidia H200s, and the first was delayed while Kazakhstan waited for an American export licence . In June 2026, the AI ministry and Kazakhtelecom signed framework agreements with Firebird â an American data centre developer partnered with Nvidia â for the Data Center Valley at Ekibastuz, a coal-mining and power-generating city. The minister says it will run 100,000 GPUs (graphics processing units), including Nvidiaâs GB300 and Vera Rubin, on a planned $10 billion investment. The site is under construction . On 2 October, Kazakhtelecom, KT-Telecom and Firebird AI KZ signed an initial agreement to build a data centre, and the minister plans to commission 186 megawatts of capacity in 2027. KazLLM and Sherkala , the two flagship Kazakh-language models, are built on weights published by Meta. Google Cloud has agreed to run a node in Astana.
China supplies pieces of several layers, and the full extent is harder to establish. AlemLLM , the largest Kazakh model, was developed with technical support from 01.AI. At Ekibastuz, where Firebird is installing the compute, Kazakhtelecom has agreed guiding principles with Hengtong, one of Chinaâs largest optical fibre manufacturers, for the same project. Huawei signed agreements with both the AI ministry and the sovereign wealth fund. Chinese firms have taken connectivity and cloud roles at the Akashi data centre in Astana, which is also under construction. Several of these were signed during Tokayevâs July visit to Shanghai, among more than 70 agreements worth over $15 billion whose full list has yet to be published.
Get a weekly round-up of the latest commentary and research straight into your inbox.
Russia supplies the routes for Kazakhstanâs international internet traffic. It is by far the countryâs main source of bandwidth to the outside world, and most local providers send their traffic through Russian networks, over an estimated 17 cross-border fibre connections. A new cable across the Caspian, launched on 15 October, opens a route to Europe through Azerbaijan and Georgia that could reduce overreliance on Russia, but its effects have yet to show. Electricity is another critical layer. In September, Russiaâs state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, signed a contract to build Kazakhstanâs first nuclear plant. The countryâs Atomic Energy Agency says demand for reliable power will keep rising with digitalisation and AI, and that nuclear energy will provide stable baseload generation for decades. The Rosatom contract, however, still needs government approval, and no completion date has been announced.
The UAE is the recurring partner. In 2024, Presight, part of G42, signed an agreement with Kazakhstanâs digital ministry and the sovereign wealth fund to develop a national AI supercomputer, the first project of its joint venture with the fund. Sherkala was co-developed by G42âs Inception and Abu Dhabiâs AI university and trained on Condor Galaxy , the G42âCerebras supercomputer. On 1 October, Tokayev discussed G42âs possible participation in the Data Center Valley .
The legal architecture borrows from Europe, selectively. The AI law that came into force this January takes five of the eight practices the EU AI Act prohibits , leaving out the three that restrict policing and surveillance. It takes its rule on training data from the EUâs copyright opt-out rather than from American fair use.
Kazakhstanâs moves in AI, whether procuring hardware and models or joining institutional arrangements, broadly rest on two grounds. The first is pragmatism, exercised within external constraints and on the strength of what the country holds. Bloc-building is not pragmatic. The US and China hold the leading positions in the technology, so going to both is going where the capability is.
What Kazakhstan holds sits on the other side of that exchange. It is the worldâs largest producer of uranium, at a time when AI is driving demand for nuclear power. It is, the UK government says , âa globally significant producer of 18 mineralsâ on Britainâs priority list. That is why minerals have moved to the centre of its external engagement, and why it is increasingly described as an alternative to Chinese supply. Yet selling to a country seeking to reduce its dependence on China is not, from Astanaâs perspective, taking a side.
Tungsten shows it plainly. Boguty in the Almaty region, developed by a subsidiary of Hong Kong-listed Jiaxin International Resources, reached commercial production in April 2025 and made Kazakhstan the worldâs third-largest producer that year. The countryâs first exports of the metal went entirely to China. While that mine was coming onstream, Samruk-Kazyna, the sovereign wealth fund, was taking bids for the larger Karaganda deposits. Bloomberg reported in October 2025 that the American firm Cove Capital faced competition from at least one state-backed Chinese firm prepared to pay above market price, and that it needed US government backing to raise the financing at all. Kazakhstan signed in November with Cove , which holds 70% of the venture and markets all of the output.
The second ground is a view of international politics. Kazakhstan, just like most states, prefers a world that is predictable because it runs on clear rules. It also works to build the institutions that make them. The memberships deliver practical benefits as well as a seat at the table where rules are written.
On that reading it is unsurprising that Kazakhstan joined both Pax Silica and WAICO, and others are likely to follow. Since its launch, WAICO has enlarged once, adding eight members , taking it to 37. Uzbekistan, also a WAICO founder, has asked to join Pax Silica and Indonesia, another founder, sees room for both . Washington, however, may press for a choice: in August, Reuters reported on an undated draft State Department letter to the 35 signatories of a US AI statement, which warns that âto be part of everything is to be part of nothingâ. It is unclear whether the letter has been sent. In Samarkand on 19 October, though, Marco Rubio said that US engagement in Central Asia was not about telling countries to stop working with others, but he was speaking of economic ties generally. For now, the mixed signals leave room for Kazakhstan to keep both memberships.
Yet what neither initiative supplies is what Tokayev himself named in Shanghai: AI capabilities âare advancing faster than our collective ability to understand, evaluate and govern themâ. That ability sits almost entirely inside the companies building the systems, and the weeks after Shanghai showed its limits there. OpenAI , Anthropic and Meta each disclosed that their models had reached outside their test environments. OpenAI established that its models were behind an intrusion Hugging Face had detected. Anthropic found its own cases only after OpenAIâs disclosure prompted it to check its test records, and Meta attributed its case to a misconfiguration by the outside firm it uses to run tests.
Kazakhstan runs models built on weights it did not produce, on chips it cannot make, and has no means of inspecting either. Nor does almost any state outside the frontier. Tokayevâs two proposals â common standards for testing and certifying AI systems and a permanent expert platform on regulation and ethics â describe a capability that exists nowhere.
This is a technology without precedent and it is moving quickly, so the machinery for governing it is needed now. That falls at a moment when existing rules are being disregarded, including by the power that wrote most of them. Whatever WAICO and Pax Silica are eventually asked to do matters more to Kazakhstan than to the US or China, because rules, however imperfectly, constrain the strong in a way that bilateral bargains do not.
