title: War and peace: Trump team now says Putin is a 'humanitarian'
body: Washington has called Russian President Vladimir Putin many things since his 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Joe Biden branded him “a butcher”, a “murderous dictator” and a “pure thug”. Four years later, the White House has a new adjective for the man wanted by the International Criminal Court: humanitarian. President Donald Trump ’s peace envoy Steve Witkoff used the descriptor yesterday as he met Mr Putin in the grand Constantine Palace ​in St Petersburg, after the Russian leader freed Stephen Hubbard, ⁠a 74-year-old American citizen who had been held in custody since 2022. “You talk so much about my President, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Mr Witkoff said. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.” Mr Witkoff’s comment stunned US politicians from both sides of the aisle. “No. Putin is a stone-cold killer,” Republican Senator John Cornyn wrote on X as he shared footage of the envoy's remarks. “What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” said another Republican senator, Thom Tillis. No. Putin is stone cold killer. https://t.co/wZwl2Ak7WB — Senator John Cornyn (@JohnCornyn) October 21, 2026 Mr Witkoff’s praise was jarring, but it was hardly surprising given recent events. On October 9, Mr Trump announced a deal to bring Russian diesel into US and global markets as he tries to ease energy costs before the November 3 midterm elections. On October 16, he went further, waiving parts of a Russia sanctions bill he’d signed less than a month earlier. It's a significant reversal from years of US-Russia policy, and makes a mockery of Washington's sanctions, which were designed to punish Moscow for invading its smaller neighbour. Estimates vary, but Moscow is expected to garner an additional $300 million to $700 million in revenue from the waivers, much of which will be funnelled into Russia’s war machine against Ukraine. Mr Trump has been dogged by accusations that he has a soft spot for Russia ever since he emerged as a presidential candidate in 2016. Hillary Clinton famously called him a “puppet” for Moscow, a claim he angrily rejected. On Monday, he offered a fresh illustration of his appreciation for Moscow. "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," he said, on the same day a Russian drone strike killed six people, including two children, according to Ukrainian authorities. Mr Trump's now open embrace of Mr Putin comes even as Russia has been accused of helping Iran to pinpoint US forces in the Middle East. But Mr Trump is prepared to give Moscow the benefit of the doubt on that. If Russia and China are helping Iran, "it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all", he said on October 12. Underscoring the deepening ties between the Trump White House and the Kremlin, Mr Trump has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying it is time for him to step down and reacting furiously at his unwillingness to capitulate. Ukraine’s struggle for survival appears to be secondary to the President’s desire for a deal to end the war, which is killing tens of thousands of Russian and Ukrainian troops each month. “It's time to make a deal,” Mr Trump said on Tuesday. “Remember this: Though we've given a lot to Ukraine, we've gotten absolutely nothing back.” The cost of the Ukraine war to American taxpayers is a legitimate concern. But the claim that the US has got nothing back from Kyiv reminds me of Monty Python’s “What have the Romans ever done for us?” scene in the Life of Brian. Nothing really, except aqueducts, sanitation, roads and so on. Ukraine has inflicted enormous losses on what until recently was a major US adversary without American troops getting involved. Its battlefield experience has provided the Pentagon with an up-close view of Russian military capabilities and the realities of modern warfare, exposing weaknesses in equipment and assumptions about how a future conflict might play out. The conflict has also given the US lessons in drone warfare, electronic jamming, missile defence and the performance of US weapons against a "near-peer" competitor. Meanwhile, much of the money Mr Trump says went to Ukraine actually supported domestic defence manufacturers, propped up US jobs and expanded America's missile and ammunition production capacities. Perhaps the Trump-Putin bromance will result in a peace deal that Ukraine can stomach, thereby saving countless lives. But given Mr Putin's track record, this seems more like wishful thinking by Mr Trump, who nonetheless appears eager to take Russia at its word. None of it helps the US President or his Republican Party make a coherent closing argument to voters in the final stretch before the midterms.

title: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
body:
Russian forces launched successive waves of ballistic missiles and attack drones against Kyiv overnight into Thursday, Oct. 22, killing one and injuring at least 24 people, including four children, and damaging a metro bridge, an ambulance station, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure across the Ukrainian capital.
Initially, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported in a Telegram update Thursday morning that the number of injured had risen from six to 15, including two 15-year-old children.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported at 7:55 a.m. that one person had been killed and 22 others injured, including four children, in Russian attacks on the capital.
In a statement issued at 9:21 a.m., the Kyiv City Military Administration said that 24 people had been injured, 16 of whom had been hospitalized.
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on six districts of Kyiv starting on the evening of Oct. 21, causing fires and damage, the DSNS said:
Dniprovskyi district: One person was killed, and a child was hospitalized. Homes and vehicles were damaged, while residential and non-residential buildings caught fire. Five other people were injured.
Darnytskyi district: Transport infrastructure was damaged. No injuries were reported.
Sviatoshynskyi district: A non-residential building and a restaurant complex caught fire. The blaze, which covered 1,100 square meters, has been extinguished.
Obolonskyi district: Non-residential buildings were damaged, and fires broke out. Two people were injured. The fires have been extinguished.
Pecherskyi district: Buildings, ambulances and a monastery were damaged. Eight people were injured, including three children.
Holosiivskyi district: Six people were injured when a non-residential building was struck.
The overnight bombardment also damaged metro infrastructure on Kyiv’s South (Pivdennyi) Bridge, prompting traffic restrictions on a key crossing over the Dnipro River.
In the central Pecherskyi district, Russian strikes damaged an ambulance station and six emergency medical vehicles, according to the mayor.
The latest attack marks another assault on essential civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, with Russian missiles hitting residential neighborhoods, transport facilities and emergency medical services.
The Russian bombardment also struck part of the capital’s metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, a major crossing connecting Kyiv’s two banks.
“As a result of the shelling, part of the metro infrastructure on the South Bridge was damaged,” Klitschko reported on Telegram .
The Kyiv City Military Administration announced traffic restrictions on the bridge in the direction from the right bank to the left bank because of the attack.
The bridge carries both road traffic and a section of Kyiv’s green metro line across the Dnipro.
Damage to the crossing adds pressure to Kyiv’s transport network as the capital faces repeated Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Russian strikes also damaged an emergency medical facility in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district.
Klitschko confirmed that the damaged building was an ambulance station and that six ambulances had also sustained damage.
No medical personnel were injured, the mayor said.
The damage to emergency medical services came as ambulances and rescue crews were responding to casualties elsewhere in the capital.
The overnight strikes also sparked a fire at a restaurant building in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported that the fire broke out following the Russian attack, adding another civilian site to the growing list of damaged properties.
Earlier Wednesday evening, Russian missiles struck residential buildings and businesses in Dniprovskyi district.
Klitschko reported direct hits on a vehicle repair workshop and a private residential building, while debris damaged another house.
Emergency crews were dispatched amid concerns that people could be trapped beneath the rubble.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell near a gas station, causing additional damage.
In Darnytskyi district, a Russian strike hit the grounds of a transport infrastructure facility, according to the mayor.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued repeated warnings as Russian ballistic missiles approached the capital late Wednesday and after midnight Thursday.
The warnings began during Wednesday evening’s assault, when explosions were reported across Kyiv.
Further ballistic missile threats followed after midnight, including warnings shortly after 12 a.m. and another at approximately 12:31 a.m.
The Air Force also tracked Russian attack drones approaching the Kyiv region and subsequently warned of a drone over the capital.
The successive threats forced residents to remain in shelters as emergency crews responded to damage across multiple districts.
Russian forces launched a massive combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine beginning at 6 p.m. on Oct. 21, targeting Kyiv as the primary strike location, the Ukrainian Air Force reported.
The attack involved Iskander-M and S-400 missiles, Zircon and Oniks missiles, and 210 strike drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera and Italmas drones, and Parodiya (Parody) decoy drones.
“The primary target of the strike was Kyiv,” the report said.
The attack was countered by Ukrainian Air Force aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare (EW) and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
As of 9 a.m. on Thursday, preliminary data showed that Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 181 Russian drones, including 87 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones and other types.
“Ten strike drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing! Do not ignore air raid alerts!” the Air Force warned at 9.01 a.m.
Russian weapons struck 32 locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at eight other locations.
The latest strikes came amid renewed US-led diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
On Wednesday, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg after holding discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European officials earlier in the week.
The Kremlin subsequently signaled willingness to resume trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
However, Moscow has not abandoned its territorial claims or its opposition to Ukraine joining NATO.
Meanwhile, Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure as winter approaches.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly stressed that any negotiated settlement must include reliable security guarantees to prevent renewed Russian aggression.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1701: Kyiv finds remains of 40 Ukrainians killed by Polish WWII units
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusives Ukraine’s best answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds is its own jet Shahed, turned around to hunt them . It’s called Bars, and Zelensky says it has the best hit rate of any Ukrainian interceptor against the jet drones, about 30%, but the small jet engines it needs may be in short supply. Progress on a sore point for Ukraine and Poland: remains of over 40 Ukrainians killed by Polish WWII units found in Łasków . The find is the first in years from Ukraine’s searches in Poland, coming as Warsaw keeps pressing Kyiv over how it remembers the UPA. Military Ukraine’s interceptor crews destroyed thousands of Russian aerial targets during Vivaldi. Jet-powered Shaheds remain a challenge . The battalion’s commander said its work prevented Russian forces from tracking Ukrainian troop movements and striking advancing soldiers. Two nights, two occupied capitals, two telecom operators running on seized Ukrainian assets: drones go after Russia’s communications in Donbas . The strikes on Donetsk and Luhansk hit the companies the occupation built on Ukrainian telecom property it seized. Intelligence and technology Some of Ukraine’s artillery soldiers were TikTokers yesterday, ComBat Vision says. Their new plugin teaches them to aim . Ukraine needs gunners fast but gets less-prepared recruits. Ukraine’s top war charity names only way to save $25,000 to $4 million each time cheap Russian jet-powered drone is shot down . Russia’s jet drones now behave like small cruise missiles, the foundation of volunteer Serhii Sternenko, believes. Starlink slowdown makes Ukraine’s Shahed-hunting drone maker rethink air-launched interceptors . Its spokesman says other companies that lean harder on Starlink have voiced concerns, and points to interest in Europe’s Eutelsat. Who capped Ukraine’s Starlink? “Ultimately POTUS,” Musk said. Ultimately Musk, reports now say . The Pentagon says it gave no order, and Ukraine’s drones were still losing their link above 160 km/h as of 20 October. Nuclear safety risk grows: Russian-occupied nuclear plant’s cooling pond keeps sinking, Russia runs short of diesel and staff, Ukraine says . The occupied plant depends on a single external line, its fuel reserve has not been resupplied for months, and its cooling pond keeps dropping, according to Ukraine’s intelligence and the IAEA. International In Oslo, US pushes Zelenskyy toward deal with Russia again. Day later, in same city, Norway discusses arming Ukraine with more NASAMS missiles . As Washington eases pressure on Russia and leans on Kyiv, Ukraine’s European partners are moving the other way. European Parliament vice president launches hunger strike demanding a truce and evacuation for Russian-occupied Oleshky . Pina Picierno is calling on associations, citizens, and national and local institutions to join her campaign for the Russian-held town in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast. Humanitarian and social impact Russian strikes close plant of Ukraine’s biggest aid backer. Its 3,600 workers and millions in taxes now hang in balance . Russia is now hitting the German investment that helps keep Ukraine’s economy running. Not just the grid: Russia struck a 24-story block, a university, and warehouses overnight, and four people are dead . Kyiv and Kharkiv Oblast counted the dead by morning, while hypermarkets burned and a hotel was damaged in other regions. Political and legal developments Her own city is under Russian fire, yet Kyiv woman urges killing Ukrainians among nearly 100,000 pro-Kremlin posts in two years. She faces up to 12 years . She is one of six pro-Kremlin agitators the Security Service has charged, accused of spreading hatred on the internet. Norway bars deals with 33 more Russian financial institutions—and 22 more from India to Nigeria . The new rules also bar deals with Moscow’s Sheremetyevo airport and curb exports to 51 entities, some in China and Türkiye. Russia resumes diesel exports to Türkiye, Brazil, after Trump lifts sanctions on fuel supplies, boosting Moscow’s war revenue – Reuters . Moscow has lifted its export ban, with US sanctions relief opening the way for renewed sales even as Russia continues to face domestic fuel supply pressures. Read our earlier daily review here .

title: F-35s to Make Up 40 Percent of the U.S. Air Force Fighter Fleet By 2035: Are Force Composition Goals Viable?
body: The U.S. Air Force plans to expand its combat-coded fighter fleet to 1,509 aircraft by 2035, with the F-35A scheduled to account for approximately 40 percent of the force, according to a new force structure report submitted to Congress on October 16. The F-22 fifth generation fighter and its planned successor, the sixth-generation F-47, will together account for another 20 percent, while the remaining 40 percent will be divided approximately equally between F-15 and F-16 fourth generation fighters. This would mark a substantial change from the current composition, in which F-16s account for approximately 45 percent of the fleet, F-35s 30 percent, F-15s 15 percent and F-22s 10 percent. With the F-22 having seen production ended in 2011, while F-16 procurements ended in 2005, the F-15 and F-35 are the only fighter types that have been procured for the last 15 years. The F-16 currently forms the backbone of the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet, with the planned composition of the fleet in 2035 indicating that mass retirements of these older aircraft are intended. The Air Force has nevertheless considered resuming F-16 procurements over 20 years after they concluded, largely as a result of shortcomings with the F-35 in terms of affordability, maintainability, and availability rates. Resumed procurements would likely alter the composition of the planned 2035 fighter fleet considerably. The Air Force previously ended all F-15 procurements in 2001, only to resume them in the early 2020s due to major shortcomings with the F-22 program, which could set a precedent for issues with the F-35 similarly leading to a revival of F-16 procurements. The rate of fifth generation fighter procurements in the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force has far exceeded that of the U.S. Air Force, which combined with the much more advanced stages which its sixth generation fighter programs have reached, indicates that a far greater proportion of the Chinese fleet will be comprised of fifth and sixth generation fighter types. The U.S. Air Force plans to replace its 186 operational F-22s with a roughly equivalent number of F-47s, although the transition will take place over an extended period as the new aircraft enters service. It is highly possible that the planned force composition for 2035 will be influenced by expected delays to the F-47’s development, with the aircraft having yet to make its first flight, which makes service entry before the late 2030s appear unlikely. While the F-35 is expected to become the backbone of the future fleet, funding for the proposed F-35 purchases remains a particular concern. The Air Force’s fiscal year 2027 budget plan relies on $2.34 billion in additional funding through budget reconciliation to finance 14 of the 38 F-35s requested. If that funding is not approved, the service could attempt to redirect money from other programmes or postpone the purchases until 2028, either of which would complicate efforts to modernise the fleet. Tabor warned that diverting funds would mean sacrificing other planned capabilities to pay for the additional fighters. F-35 procurements were initially planned at 110 per year, before major cost overruns, budget shortages, and dissatisfaction with the performances of pre-Block 4 configurations of the aircraft, resulted in this gradually falling to around 24 per year.

title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
body:
During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.
Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.
His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.
Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.
All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”
Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.
But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

title: Recursive Releases Flint, an Open-Weight 40B MoE Local Coding Model for Agents with 2.5B Active Params
body: Recursive Superintelligence has released Flint , its first model. The Recursive Flint local coding model is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 40B total and 2.5B active parameters. Recursive team states that its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. The weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. TL;DR Size: 39.8B total, about 2.5B active per token. Context: 262,144 tokens documented on the model card; the blog cites up to 512k. Runs on: 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs (M4 Pro, M5 Pro, M5 Max) or 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs. 4-bit weights take about 23 GB. Performance: Tops Recursive’s chart among MoE models under 50B on agentic coding. Trails the strongest dense models. Best: IFEval 95.1%. SWE-bench Verified 74.2%. Worst: Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 54.9%, versus 73.0% for dense Qwen 3.8. What is Recursive Flint? Flint is a decoder-only MoE Transformer for coding agents. The model investigates codebases, fixes bugs, implements features and writes tests. It is text-only and supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Introducing Flint, @Recursive_SI ’s first model: a fast local coding model built with our automated research system, the Eureka Machine. • Best-in-class fast local coding • Up to 2x faster than comparable models: 125+ tokens/sec on a MacBook Pro, 150+ on RTX Spark • Built from… pic.twitter.com/ufg2xScSGw — Richard Socher (@RichardSocher) October 21, 2026 How does Flint’s architecture work? Flint has 49 layers: 2 dense layers, then 47 MoE layers. Each MoE layer has 256 routed experts. A router selects 6 per token, plus 1 always-active shared expert. Attention mixes 2 types. 35 layers use a 513-token sliding window. 14 layers use full attention with no positional encoding. There are 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 2.5B active figure includes the output head. The active body alone is about 2.2B parameters. How did the Eureka Machine build Flint? The Eureka Machine proposes ideas, implements them, tests them and picks what to try next. Recursive highlights 3 contributions: Architecture: It started from a 35B-total, 3B-active baseline. It searched expert configurations and widths, landing on 40B total and 2.5B active. Quantization: It quantized the output layer (lm_head) to 4 bits, against common practice. An offline distillation stage, with the 16-bit model as teacher, recovered accuracy. This nearly halved training steps versus a quantization-aware training baseline. The NVFP4 model scores within 0.7 points of the 16-bit model. Kernels: It wrote specialized kernels for low-bit projections, MoE operations, attention and prompt processing. On M4 and M5 chips, a Metal megakernel fuses the entire decode forward pass. How does Flint perform on coding benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported by Recursive. Sampling used temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20. Benchmark Flint BF16 Flint NVFP4 Terminal-Bench 2.1 54.9% 53.7% SWE-bench Pro v2 89.7% 88.5% SWE-bench Verified 74.2% 74.1% LiveCodeBench v6 80.3% 80.8% IFBench 89.2% 88.1% IFEval 95.1% 94.6% Terminal-Bench used the Terminus 2 harness. Solutions found through web retrieval counted as failures. SWE-bench runs used mini-swe-agent with no internet access. Agentic scores average pass@1 over at least 5 attempts. In Recursive’s chart, Qwen3.6 scores 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified. Dense Qwen 3.8 scores 73.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, well above Flint. Recursive’s own comparison chart (scores in %, † measured by Recursive, others developer-reported): Model Terminal-Bench 2.1 SWE-bench Pro v2† SWE-bench Verified LiveCodeBench v6 IFBench IFEval Flint BF16 54.9 89.7 74.2 80.3 89.2 95.1 Flint NVFP4 53.7 88.5 74.1 80.8 88.1 94.6 Qwen 3.5 (MoE) 38.7 68.6 69.2 74.6 70.2 91.9 Qwen 3.6 (MoE) 44.9 73.8 73.4 80.4 67.9 89.6 Laguna XS 2.1 (MoE) 24.7† 38.6 70.9 49.5† 34.4† 73.7† Qwen 3.8 (dense) 73.0 94.9 75.6† 90.3 79.5 94.6† Muse Glimmer (dense) 51.7 86.0 76.0 63.5† 77.0 94.7† Gemma 4 (dense) 43.4 61.7 66.6 80.0 76.0 94.6 window.addEventListener("message",function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.mtpFlintH){var f=document.getElementById("mtp-flint-frame");if(f&&e.source===f.contentWindow){f.style.height=e.data.mtpFlintH+"px";}}}); How does Flint compare with Qwen3.6, Laguna XS 2.1 and Gemma 4? Competitor figures below come from each developer’s own model card, not Recursive’s chart. Feature Recursive Flint Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Laguna XS 2.1 Gemma 4 31B Developer Recursive Qwen (Alibaba) Poolside Google DeepMind Total params 39.8B 35B 33B 30.7B Active params ~2.5B 3B 3B 30.7B (dense) Context 262,144 (blog: up to 512k) 262,144 native, up to 1,010,000 262,144 256K Modality Text Text + image Text Text + image License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 OpenMDW-1.1 Apache 2.0 Local hardware 48 GB Mac or GPU Not disclosed Mac with 36 GB RAM Consumer GPUs, workstations SWE-bench Verified 74.2% 73.4% 70.9% Not disclosed Terminal-Bench 54.9% (v2.1) 51.5% (v2.0) 37.5% (v2.0) Not disclosed LiveCodeBench v6 80.3% 80.4% Not disclosed 80.0% SWE-bench Pro 89.7% (v2) 49.5% (public) 47.6% (public) Not disclosed How fast is Flint, and what hardware does it need? Recursive reports more than 125 tokens per second on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro. It reports more than 150 tokens per second on a 64 GB NVIDIA RTX Spark. Both are short-context figures, up to 2x faster than comparable models. It also claims Flint runs more than 5x faster than dense 25-40B models with similar coding scores. There are 3 local options: Apple Silicon: Flint INT4 MLX weights take about 22.6 GB. The rec engine needs an M4 Pro, M5 Pro or M5 Max with 48 GB memory. It reports 1.4 to 2.6x the throughput of llama.cpp on an M4 Pro. NVIDIA: The NVFP4 GGUF file is 22.9 GB. Recursive recommends at least 48 GB of GPU memory. Server: The 80 GB BF16 checkpoint needs 1 B300 or H200 GPU per replica. Flint also works with llama.cpp, Ollama, Unsloth, LM Studio, vLLM and SGLang. Key Takeaways Flint is a 40B MoE coding model with only 2.5B active parameters. It scores 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. 4-bit weights run in about 23 GB on a 48 GB Mac or GPU. Recursive’s Eureka Machine helped design the architecture, quantization and kernels. SWE-bench Pro v2 scores are Recursive-measured and not comparable to public SWE-Bench Pro. Check out the technical details , model weights and rec engine on GitHub . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: Florida mayor arrested on grand theft and fraud charges over COVID relief funds: AG
body:
Jackie Espinosa pleaded not guilty Thursday.
A Florida mayor was arrested Wednesday on theft and fraud charges alleging that she illegally enriched herself and family members through a COVID-19 small business relief program launched under her administration, according to the state's attorney general.
Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa is being charged with grand theft, a second-degree felony, and organized scheme to defraud, a first-degree felony, according to Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier.
Espinosa is accused of improperly appropriating $50,000 in funds through the city's Business Boost 2.0 program, according to the arrest warrant.
"This is the local government equivalent of insider congressional stock trading," Florida's chief financial officer, Blaise Ingoglia, said during a press briefing on Wednesday.
Espinosa, 58, was booked Wednesday morning into the Osceola County Jail under her full name, Eva Jacqulyn Espinosa, online jail records show. During her initial court appearance on Thursday, a not guilty plea was entered on her behalf and her bond was set at $70,000.
An audit of COVID-19-related grant programs by Ingoglia's office found that three businesses owned or controlled by Espinosa or members of her immediate family allegedly received $50,000 total in grant funds through Kissimmee's Business Boost 2.0 program, according to the warrant. The businesses include a dance production studio, a diner and a real estate company, according to the warrant. She and her family members allegedly applied for the grants on the day applications opened in September 2025, according to the state attorney general's office.
"The evidence makes very clear that there was intent to engage in this conflict of interest that ultimately abused her office to enrich herself," Uthmeier said. "Mayor Espinosa demonstrated an intent to create, streamline and simplify, reduce oversight of and more easily enable a process whereby herself and immediate family could apply for and receive city funds to which she was not entitled."
Espinosa's attorney said the mayor "maintains her innocence" and that they plan to challenge the allegations "vigorously in court."
"This case involves a publicly approved grant program administered by City staff, not a secret scheme to steal taxpayer money," her attorney, Migdalia Perez, said in a statement to ABC News.
"The prosecution must establish that the mayor acted with criminal intent. We firmly maintain that she did not," Perez said. "There is a fundamental difference between an alleged ethics violation and a criminal offense. The State cannot transform one into the other without proving every element of a crime beyond a reasonable doubt."
Espinosa faces up to 30 years in prison if convicted as charged, officials said.
She has served as the mayor of Kissimmee since November 2024. Her term ends in 2028.
According to the city, an arrested mayor "remains in their seat until a qualifying act, such as suspension, removal, or resignation takes place." Vice Mayor Angela Eady will perform mayoral duties at City Commission meetings and ceremonial events in Espinosa's absence, the city said.
Following Espinosa's arrest, city manager Mike Steigerwald authorized an internal investigation of the Business Boost 2.0 Program, the city said.
"The investigation will establish how the Business Boost 2.0 Program was designed, administered, and overseen, and whether the City’s policies and procedures regarding the awarding of grants were followed and whether those policies and procedures are adequate," the city said in a statement.

title: War-hit Kyiv puts 85 European-funded buses on its streets. Here’s what riders find inside
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Kyiv has put 85 new buses into service. They have been bought under a financing agreement with the European Investment Bank, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said , after meeting EIB Group Vice-President Karl Nehammer to mark the project’s completion. The buses were purchased under the “Ukraine Urban Public Transport” project, backed by an EIB loan of 18.5 million euros, and arrived in several batches. All 85 will carry passengers on the capital’s routes, part of a push to modernize the fleet of the municipal operator Kyivpastrans even as the war grinds on. “The purchase made it possible to increase the accessibility of public transportation in the capital and improve passenger travel conditions,” Klitschko said, thanking the EIB for its help. What riders get on the new buses The vehicles are built for accessibility. The 12-meter low-floor buses carry ramps for people with disabilities and limited mobility, information displays, air conditioning and heating, video surveillance cameras, stop announcements, energy-saving LED lighting, and tinted glass. Each bus seats 27 passengers and holds another 80 standing. The vehicles are Turkish-built low-floor models that entered Kyiv service in batches between 2025 and 2026, aimed at riders whom older high-floor buses left behind, from wheelchair users to parents with strollers. A European bank rebuilding the way Kyiv moves The buses are one piece of a longer partnership. Since Russia’s war began, the EIB has provided more than 2 billion euros for emergency repairs to Ukraine’s infrastructure, the bank reported . Its urban-transport work for Kyiv has already delivered 20 new low-floor trams, and the bank signed a separate 50-million-euro loan, the first tranche of a 200-million-euro package, to help the Kyiv metro replace coaches that were 80% Russian-made before the war and end its dependence on Russian spare parts, the EIB said. A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.
New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.
Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”
In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.
That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.
NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.
Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

title: U.S. moves to establish Autonomous Warfare Command to accelerate battlefield adoption of drones and robotics
body: Project leaders Owen West and Senior Chief Max Strasiser outlined the plan in an October 21 open letter. Competitions, exercises and combat performance will determine which systems receive wider adoption and which are dropped. “The goal is not a particular drone. It is a system built to adapt at scale,” they wrote. Agincourt has two assignments: establish the Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, and continue the work of the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems. The second task includes developing an acquisition model that connects suppliers directly with operational forces. The project will work with the Joint Staff, military services and operational units to test that approach. Its leaders said spending should produce measurable reductions in the cost of engaging targets or the risk to forces. “The power of the purse demands strict stewardship. To flip the cost exchange, every auditable dollar we spend should reduce cost-per-kill or risk-to-force,” the letter states. West and Strasiser argue that low-cost drones have changed the speed and economics of warfare, disrupting an approach built around small numbers of sophisticated, expensive weapons. They want the United States to respond by developing and adapting systems faster at the operational level. The roadmap would allow each theater to develop its own combination of capabilities, rather than use a uniform portfolio. It specifically notes that the systems suited to the Pacific will differ from those needed in Europe. “We have set a hard test for ourselves. These new systems will not be declared ready on paper,” the leaders wrote. Combatant commanders must be able to use the equipment in combat, while the new model must also strengthen the military services. One measure of progress will be how quickly an operational problem receives a fielded solution evaluated for wider use. The letter calls for removing barriers to service members’ initiative by bringing operations and development together. AUTOWARCOM is intended to make that process a permanent part of how the military develops and employs new capabilities.

title: Army Special Forces leaders see promise, high demand for new robotics technician integrator job
body: After Army Special Forces graduated the first batch of robotics-focused warrant officers earlier this month, hopes — and demand — for the new job are high. Ten warrant officers became Robotics Technician Integrators on Oct. 2, heralding a new class of experts charged with galvanizing the Army’s technological crusade by embedding with units and guiding commanders on how to effectively employ an ever-evolving stable of systems. Nearly two weeks later, top Army leaders called for an expansion of the role and tasked the new robotics technicians with helping drive the service’s autonomy push. At the same time, Special Forces leaders told DefenseScoop they believed the technicians will bring foundational change, but recognized high demand for the new role as the service charts the program’s path. “The demand just inside of our formation is huge,” Brig. Gen. Joseph Wortham, the head of 1st Special Forces Command, said in an interview at the annual AUSA conference in Washington last week. The leaders called the Army-wide adoption of the role a boon for the force, while acknowledging that the nascent program was akin to “building a plane in flight.” The Army’s top two acting leaders, Adam Telle and Gen. Christopher LaNeve, offered some details at AUSA about the service’s new Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM). Part of that effort will see robotics integrators, also known by their military occupational specialty code 390A, going to experimental units focused on autonomy efforts. While course throughput is managed by the Special Operations Center of Excellence, Wortham said the center was working to meet the increasing need for integrators and that it was “doing that math right now.” “It’s an example of something, a capability or a requirement being identified, an initial idea to meet that requirement, and now it’s being adapted by the entire Army,” said 1st Special Forces Command Chief Warrant Officer 5 Jerimiah Brown. “That’s a win for all of us. How we get there, the throughput, how do we produce the numbers that are required? To the [commanding general’s] point, we’ll figure that part out, but the fact that this will be integrated throughout the Army, it’s a great news story.” Underpinning the initiative was a recognition that Army units needed to better understand how to integrate unmanned platforms into their operations, a realization informed by technological developments in the Ukraine-Russia war. A technician whose full-time job was robotics integration — who could also keep up with technological advancements — was the answer. Throughout the 19-week course, held between facilities in North Carolina and Alabama, prospective 390A troops learn the ins-and-outs of various uncrewed systems that have wrought deadly change on modern battlefields. Not only do the candidates learn how to operate and program the systems, which include aerial drones, unmanned ground vehicles and sensors, but where they fit into mission planning, so they can advise commanders on operational use cases upon graduation. The Special Forces leaders said that the pilot course is already changing, with the second cohort building off of the “growing pains” of the first and completing tasks quicker than before, according to Brown, the command chief warrant officer. “This started on a napkin to where we are right now with the first class that just graduated,” said Command Sgt. Maj. Joshua King, the senior enlisted advisor for the command. “I think it’s going to grow, but it’s always going to evolve. It’s almost evolving as fast as tech.” The Special Forces leaders said the integrators also play a crucial role in reducing work load for operators who are now being handed a bevy of new, technical kit, the adoption of which DefenseScoop previously reported was stretching thin certain specialty jobs. “When you look at our detachments and our units of action, they’re already pretty task saturated with all the things they have to do in a modern environment,” Wormath said. But the integrators are meant to alleviate some of that pressure. The general likened the new integrator job to existing Special Forces technicians who know how to maintain, update, fix and employ dive equipment, freeing up combat divers to focus on their missions. “That resident knowledge sits so that the tasks aren’t kept at the lower level,” he said. “We took that same model that we do for our combat divers, we applied it to robotics.” In various exercises and events over the last few years, Army leaders have recognized an overreliance on civilian-contracted field service representatives employed by the companies selling products to the service. They want an “open architecture” approach to tech. The integrators, according to Wormath, will give Army leaders an organic technician for fixes without relying on FSRs “that we can’t take into modern combat.” A fundamental part of the course is teaching integrators the basics of coding and constructions so that when they get a new system from the defense industry, they know how to build it. “One of the things that we’re asking industry for is that open architecture,” he said. “It’s truly system dependent and company dependent on what they give us access to, and not.” King added: “It’s almost like a pre-req that we have the ability to adjust the software or at least [have] access to it immediately because the enemy is doing the same thing. So if we can’t overmatch them, then we’re missing out.” The post Army Special Forces leaders see promise, high demand for new robotics technician integrator job appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Deadly Russian missile strike on Kyiv used cluster warheads, hours after Putin-Witkoff meeting
body:
The scene after a Russian ballistic missile struck Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 22, 2026. (Chris Occhicone / The Kyiv Independent)
Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, according to Ukrainian officials, only hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported these numbers in the morning, saying Russia had struck across Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Svyatoshynskyi and Dnipro dsitricts in Ukraine's capital.
Among the injured are four children, one of whom has been hospitalized, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said .
"Last night, the Russians used, among others, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. The peculiarity of these missiles is that they explode in the air, hitting the target, and hit everything around within a diameter of 400 meters," President Volodymyr Zelensky said .
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," Zelensky commented on the attack earlier.
During a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff lauded Putin — wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine — as a "humanitarian."
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered ones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the Iskander missiles carried a K5 cluster munitions warhead.
"This warhead explodes above the ground and is specifically designed to cause maximum damage to people and equipment in an area of ​​400 by 400 meters," Beskrestnov said.
"This strike was not carried out with a military purpose. The goal was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible," he added.
Zelensky said one of the missiles struck Pechersk, in Kyiv's historic center, in an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Sviato-Vvedensky Monastery. Buildings belonging to the monastery, residential buildings, shops, cafes and other civilian infrastructure were damaged, he said.
"There was not even theoretically any military facility nearby," Zelensky said. "It was a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of the area of use, a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties and as much damage on civilians as possible."
Zelensky reported two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast as a result of the attacks.
A source in Ukraine's energy sector speaking on condition of anonymity told the Kyiv Independent that Russia targeted energy infrastructure in the capital, particularly substations.
Zelensky said Russia had carried out more than 170 strikes on important Ukrainian energy facilities since Oct. 11, despite Ukrainian forces intercepting many of the drones and some of the missiles used in the attacks.
The capital is particularly vulnerable as it is reliant on thermal and cogeneration plants that are exposed to enemy strikes, while substations that connect it to generation sources, including nuclear plants in western Ukraine, are protected against drones but not against ballistic missiles.
DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, announced around midday that emergency power outages were in place on the Holosiivskyi District.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground first reported power and Wi-Fi outages in parts of the city after a wave of ballistic missile strikes at around 3:34 a.m.
In the Dniprovskyi District, a car service station and a house were damaged late on Oct. 21 after the two sites were struck, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko .
"In the same district, debris also hit another house," he said . "There may be people trapped under the rubble."
At around 2 a.m. local time on Oct. 22, Russian attacks on Kyiv continued, filling the sky with the sounds of explosions.
In the Darnitsky District, also on the left bank of the Dnipro River that cuts through the city of 3 million, missiles hit near a transportation infrastructure facility. "I was at home, in my private house," said Vladyslav, a resident of Kyiv living near one of the strikes. "When the explosion happened, our windows were blown out. Then we saw a terrifying glow outside; we ran out and saw a house on fire, and heard people screaming.
"Fortunately, we managed to rescue a man and his wife who were inside the burning house. It's a stroke of luck that neighbors were nearby to help save these people."
Ballistic missiles again targeted Kyiv at around 3:00 a.m. local time, with at least 13 explosions rocking the city in less than eight minutes, the Kyiv Independent's Chris York said.
Following a series of explosions, the Kyiv City Military Administration said that a building housing a medical facility was damaged in the city's Pecherskyi District.
"All I see is broken windows on the floor, my neighbors are screaming, going out of their houses, and all they can do is just pray," Heorhii Rezhenko, a 26-year-old resident of Pecherskyi District, told the Kyiv Independent.
"In Europe, in the democratic world, everybody knows what happened here. The people know what happened, ... but they, for now, I think, can do nothing to stop it. Maybe all that I can say is please do something to stop it," Heorhii said.
"I am just very tired, because it was a very difficult day. But we will have more of these days."
Klitschko later confirmed that a paramedic station in the district was damaged, where six ambulances were also wrecked. Videos posted to social media suggest an Epicenter home improvement store in the Obolon District was destroyed.
The Museum of Ukrainian Diaspora, a branch of the Museum of Kyiv History, was also damaged in the attack, the museum said . Windows were blown out and the building's facade and roof were damaged. No one was injured, but the museum said it would remain closed for several days while repairs were carried out.
"In the Sviatoshynskyi District, a fire broke out inside a restaurant as a result of the enemy attack," the Kyiv City Military Administration added.
A further ballistic missile warning was issued in Kyiv around 12:30 p.m.
The latest attack comes as Russian forces continue to intensify missile and drone campaigns against Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin.
On the city's crucial Southern Bridge, transit infrastructure for the Kyiv Metro was damaged as a result of Russian strikes, Klitschko said.
The Military Administration also said that traffic in the direction from the right bank to the left bank has been restricted on the bridge.
The DSNS later reported that a monastery in the Pecherskyi District was damaged in the Russian attack as well.
The strikes on Kyiv on the night of Oct. 21 came after shows of support for trilateral peace negotiations by both President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We hope that Russia—which has stated many times that it is ready for a meeting in one format or another—will follow through," Zelensky said.
As Kyiv was under red alert from the incoming ballistic missiles late on Oct. 21, around the world in Washington, D.C., U.S. President Donald Trump said that a deal to "settle the war" is "maybe now the closest we've been," in a roundtable conference.
Earlier on Oct. 21, a Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least two people and injured two others in the morning.
On Oct. 20, Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv, damaging a hospital in Solomianskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, injuring 12 people, according to local authorities. That morning, three people were killed , and four people were injured after a Russian drone struck early-morning commuter traffic.
The U.N. Human Rights Office reported in early October that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025.

title: Former U.S. officials urge D.C. Circuit to reconsider decision in Anthropic-Pentagon fight
body: A bipartisan group of 17 former senior national security officials, diplomats and intelligence professionals filed a legal brief on Tuesday urging the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to rehear Anthropic’s challenge to the Pentagon’s designation of the company as a supply-chain risk. “Left undisturbed that ruling will threaten all defense contractors,” they argue in the 26-page submission. This brief marks the latest move in the messy saga between the Defense Department and Anthropic. The two remain at an impasse over safety guardrails and unrestricted military use of the company’s frontier AI models. Anthropic was positioned as a premier AI partner for the U.S. government between 2024 and mid-2025. Through collaboration with Palantir and Amazon Web Services, Anthropic’s Claude was the first frontier AI model to deploy inside highly restricted, classified government networks. But DOD’s alignment with Anthropic shattered in early 2026. The company’s leadership refused to accede to new demands from Pentagon leadership that would permit the military to deploy commercial AI models for “all lawful use cases” — without limitation. In particular, Anthropic took issue with the government potentially using its models to surveil Americans en masse, and for applications of autonomous weapon systems that can attack targets without human intervention. Following a series of failed negotiations, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in February officially designated Anthropic as a “supply-chain risk to national security.” That severe regulatory label is typically reserved for foreign, adversarial entities and functionally bars defense contractors and components from doing commercial business with Anthropic. The firm subsequently sued the federal government. This summer a federal judge in San Francisco ruled in favor of the Claude maker, deeming the Pentagon’s actions against Anthropic to be troubling and retaliatory. However, last month, the federal circuit court in D.C. ruled 2-to-1 in favor of the Pentagon in a simultaneous challenge. In the new legal brief, the 17 former officials noted that — because Congress vested that specific court with exclusive jurisdiction over supply-chain risk designations — the panel’s decision is the governing law nationwide. “No other court can revisit it,” they wrote. “If it stands, it will establish how DOD may deal with every defense contractor from here on out. Few questions could be of more exceptional importance for this Court to rehear en banc.” The crew of subject matter experts behind this brief said they share “decades of combined experience” in federal procurement, supply-chain security, and protecting America’s technological edge in matters of national defense. The brief states that many held senior roles “in both Republican and Democratic administrations, at the White House, National Security Council, Departments of State, Defense, Justice, and Homeland Security, Office of Management and Budget, and other national security and intelligence institutions, where they implemented or advised on the statutory and constitutional authorities at issue here.” Some of the more prominent members of the group include former Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines, former National Security Advisor Susan Rice and former National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan, among others. The officials warned that the court’s decision “would set a dangerously erroneous standard” for supply chain risk designations moving forward, if a rehearing is not set. Their key arguments include that the Pentagon’s national security risk label “was pretextual.” The brief points out that DOD announced the penalty and public denunciations on social media, before generating any administrative steps or formal justifications. The experts also contend that the designation was made in retaliation against Anthropic for its leaders’ public comments, policy stances, and refusal to meet certain government demands — essentially serving as what they see as an unconstitutional warning to other military contractors and frontier AI makers. “Further, had DOD engaged in a lawful process, it would have considered the specific risks posed by the two capabilities Anthropic refused to provide: mass domestic surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons. DOD has not explained why DOD should have the first, much less how it could exercise it lawfully. Nor has DOD reconciled the second with the United States’ commitment that [its military use of AI be in compliance with applicable international laws],” the brief stated. Ultimately, the former officials argued that if “the panel decision stands, this Court will validate a sham process that not only weakens national security but gives this and future administrations authorization to punish any company that falls out of favor.” Pentagon spokespersons did not immediately provide comments on the matter before publication. FedScoop Senior Reporter Madison Alder contributed reporting. The post Former U.S. officials urge D.C. Circuit to reconsider decision in Anthropic-Pentagon fight appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Vercel Open-Sources durable-harness for Crash-Proof Coding Agents
body:
Vercel has released durable-harness , an open-source package that keeps coding agent sessions alive through crashes and timeouts. Vercel durable-harness wraps existing harnesses, including Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code and Codex, without changing them . Each session lives in a durable log. A dead function no longer means lost work. For teams moving agents off laptops and into the cloud, that closes a real gap. TL;DR Size: npm package, version 0.0.x, Apache-2.0. Adapters cover 5 harnesses: Pi, OpenCode, fx, Claude Code, Codex. Runs on: Vercel Functions plus Vercel Queues, Node.js 22+ with Postgres, or laptop files. Claude Code and Codex need a Vercel Sandbox. Performance: No latency or throughput benchmarks published. All recovery claims are self-reported by Vercel. Best: Finished model and tool calls are read back from the log, never re-run or billed twice. Worst: Experimental 0.0.x API. Claude Code and Codex run only in a Vercel Sandbox, even self-hosted. What is durable-harness? durable-harness is a set of adapters from Vercel that store a harness session in a Workflow SDK World . A World bundles storage, a queue and a stream behind one interface. The package uses the same machinery that powers Vercel’s Workflow SDK . Why do coding agents lose work in the cloud? Harnesses like Pi and Claude Code were designed as long-lived local processes. They keep the session in memory. Locally, the workspace and history sit on the same disk, so resuming takes 1 prompt. In the cloud, a VM with persistent storage does not track which calls completed. Vercel team notes a failed turn or network error then means lost work. How does durable-harness work? It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model or tool call runs, it records an intent. When the call finishes, it records the outcome. Each turn is backed by a message on Vercel Queues . If the function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function. That function reads the log and continues. After a crash, the log shows what finished, what was running and what never started: Completed calls are read from the log, so finished model tokens are not billed again. replay: 'safe' tools , such as lookups, can run again. replay: 'never' tools , such as refunds, never run twice. The model is told the call may have happened. Harness session files are mirrored into the log as well. That covers Claude Code’s transcript, Codex’s rollout and OpenCode’s event store. Where do files and shell commands run? Model-chosen commands never run on the function’s own disk. The tools docs list 3 workspace options: virtual() keeps files in the session log, with a bash-compatible shell and no network. It holds about 500 files. virtual({ durable: false }) keeps scratch files in memory and clears them every turn. sandbox() gives each session a Vercel Sandbox , with /workspace on a Drive. Typed JSON documents , such as a to-do list, also live in the log. Each holds at most 64 KB. Run turn

title: Hegseth Directs Air Force to Establish New Guard Special Tactics Squadron
body: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has directed the Air Force to establish a new Special Tactics Squadron under the Florida Air National Guard, growing a small but elite group of special operators. The Pentagon announced Hegseth’s order Oct. 21, releasing a brief Sept. 23 memo from Hegseth to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, directing him to create the new squadron at Hurlburt Field “with an associated new organization at MacDill Air Force Base,” both in Florida. Pentagon and Air Force spokespersons offered no further details. The Air National Guard did not immediately respond to a query. Hurlburt is the headquarters of Air Force Special Operations Command, and MacDill is home to U.S. Special Operations Command. Connecting the new unit to both “creates an unparalleled ecosystem of combat-ready training and mission execution,” the Pentagon’s announcement states. “This move maximizes joint-force synergy, ensures seamless operational readiness, and provides the President with highly responsive, lethal options to counter pacing threats.” Special tactics squadrons are some of the Air Force’s premier ground forces , consisting of combat controllers, pararescuemen, special reconnaissance, and Tactical Air Control Party specialists. They conduct a wide range of missions in covert, remote, or hostile areas, including combat search and rescue, airfield seizure, emergency air traffic controller, and coordination of close air support. There are just a handful of special tactics squadrons across the Air Force, and only two in the Guard—the 123rd Special Tactics Squadron in Kentucky and the 125th Special Tactics Squadron in Oregon. The Florida Air National Guard has one special ops unit, the 249th Special Operations Squadron, which flies the CV-22 Osprey. It is unclear how quickly the new unit will be established and be fully manned. Hegseth’s memo states that “any further resourcing for this direction, to include military construction, equipment, and manpower authorizations will be developed in the President’s Budget 2028 budget cycle.” The memo also directs the National Guard Bureau and the Air Force to follow Air Force policy for establishing the new unit, “consistent with applicable DAF Strategic Basing process and environmental legal requirements.” It is highly unusual—if not unprecedented—for the Secretary of Defense to direct the establishment of a squadron-level unit in any component. Hegseth, a former Army officer, has praised special operations forces , seeing them as a model for innovation and acquisition reform, and they have played key roles in operations during his tenure, including Operation Absolute Resolve to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, Operation Rough Rider in Yemen in 2025 , and the ongoing strikes against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. The post Hegseth Directs Air Force to Establish New Guard Special Tactics Squadron appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Ukraine’s Navy killed Russian Shahed: one drone boat launched another drone, which shot down third, all unmanned, all at sea
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); One drone launched another drone, which then shot down a third. All three were unmanned, and all at sea off Ukraine. Ukraine’s Navy has destroyed a Russian Shahed attack drone with a Sting interceptor launched from the Sargan 3000 unmanned surface vessel, the Navy said , showing sailors adapting to new aerial threats with sea-launched interceptors. Russian Shaheds threaten Ukraine’s ports, coastline and the ships that approach them, so meeting those drones out at sea, before they reach land, matters for the whole southern defense. A Ukrainian Navy sea drone, the Sargan 3000, destroyed a Russian Shahed kamikaze drone with a Sting interceptor drone Ukrainian troops continue to adapt to new threats to protect civilians and infrastructure Ukrainian Navy pic.twitter.com/kXvnqaebAw — Euromaidan Press (@EuromaidanPress) October 21, 2026 The Sting is built to destroy Russian kamikaze drones such as the Shahed, Geran and Lancet, as well as reconnaissance drones, with quick deployment, a short training course and a top speed of 280 km/h, its producer, Wild Hornets, says. The interceptor that has become Ukraine’s Shahed-killer The Sting has earned its place at the front. The Ukrainian FPV interceptor has proven highly effective in combat, with a typical hit rate of 80 to 90% depending on the unit, and on some days reaching 100 percent, one launch for one kill. It is currently Ukraine’s most productive Shahed interceptor, according to the Wild Hornets, having destroyed more than 3,000 drones in its first seven months of use. Mounting it on a sea platform extends that record from land into the Black Sea. A drone boat that keeps finding new ways to kill The Sargan 3000 has become a multi-purpose hunter. In July, Ukrainian naval personnel used a Sargan 3000 to sink a Russian second-rank border patrol ship. In October, the same drone boat shot down a Russian Shahed with a turret-mounted machine gun over the Black Sea. Ukraine’s Navy took the Sargan 3000 into service in April 2026, and the drone boat has a combat radius of up to 1,600 kilometers, letting it clear the sky far from shore without putting a sailor in range. title: Security Disclosure
body:
Earlier this morning, Railway detected anomalous activity involving systems that store customer environment variables. After further investigation, our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.
We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers. We have notified these upstream providers to revoke all keys proactively, as we take these kinds of events extremely seriously.
While our initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, we are nevertheless recommending that all users take the actions described below as a precaution to protect your systems while we complete our review.
What you should do: As such, we strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity.
All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume.
As we confirm which accounts were affected, we will contact those customers directly by email with additional details.
We will provide new updates on this announcement, and on status.railway.com as we narrow the scope of impact.

title: Dozens of IAF jets, refueling aircraft flew 'as far as Iran border' in practice sortie - report
body: Dozens of Israel Air Force fighter jets flew "as far as the Iranian border" before turning around and returning to Israel in a practice sortie on Monday, according to an Axios report on Wednesday citing US and Israeli officials.The fighter jets and accompanying refueling aircraft allegedly passed through Syrian and Iraqi airspace, following a flight path consistent with that taken during strikes on Iran.While some sources told Axios that the sortie was not unusual and was intended to deter Iran, US officials said that Israel knew Iran's air defense systems would detect the jets.Israel reportedly notified the US of the operation in advance, describing the training exercise as a “power projection” aimed at deterring Iran from attacking Israel ahead of the October 27 Knesset elections.On Tuesday, Fox News' Trey Yingst also reported that Israeli fighter jets had conducted drills during which they flew over Syria and Iraq.Report: Iran operating on assumption that US-Israeli attack is foregone conclusionLater on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)-run Fars News Agency reported that the regime is operating on the assumption that a US-Israeli attack is a "certainty."The report, which cited a senior Iranian security official, added that Iran will consider US politicians legitimate targets if such an attack involves the assasination of Iranian officials.

title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
body: Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “ The Software Tax .” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide , conducted the survey. Read full article Comments

title: Ukraine sends ground robot to string wire obstacles in open, taking its sappers out of kill zone
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Stringing wire in the open is one of the deadliest jobs at the front, and Ukraine is handing it to a robot. Ukraine’s Ground Forces have shown a ground robotic vehicle from the 16th Separate Support Brigade laying wire obstacles in open terrain, letting combat engineers do the dangerous work remotely. Laying obstacles in the open exposes sappers to Russian drones and artillery, so moving the task to a machine takes a soldier out of the kill zone. The vehicle carries a sloped frame holding a heavy coil of wire and unrolls the barrier on its own while the operator drives it from a safe distance. Ukraine’s Ground Forces have shown a ground robotic vehicle laying wire obstacles in open terrain. Source: The 16th Separate Support Brigade “Laying obstacles in open terrain always means risks for combat engineers. But today this hard work is done by ground drones,” the Ground Forces said. Ukraine’s Ground Forces have shown a ground robotic vehicle laying wire obstacles in open terrain. Source: The 16th Separate Support Brigade From supply runs to combat engineering, one machine at a time The wire-laying robot is one of many jobs in a fast-growing fleet. Ukraine’s ground robots ran more than 100,000 missions in the first eight months of 2026, with monthly runs logged in the Delta system climbing from 7,511 in January to nearly 20,000 in July. Kyiv has contracted over 22,000 of the machines since January, nearly double the total for all of 2025. The number of units operating them grew from 117 at the end of 2025 to 230 by mid-2026, and those machines already haul supplies, evacuate wounded and carry out strikes. From laying wire to leading the assault Robots are increasingly going where the fighting is hardest. For the first time in the war, Ukraine air- dropped kamikaze ground robots more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines from heavy drones during Operation Vivaldi near Lyman, a counteroffensive in which the 3rd Army Corps retook more than 125 square kilometers of Donetsk Oblast. “In assault operations, drones and ground robots always go ahead of the infantry,” corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said. In another Vivaldi tactic, ground robots each fitted with two Bullspike grenade launchers attacked Russian positions and then detonated inside their shelters. This year, Ukraine’s Defense Procurement Agency began tendering logistics and strike ground robots against Defense Ministry specifications, with no manufacturer allowed more than half the order. title: Sweden orders four Bofors 57Mk3 naval guns and programmable ammunition from BAE Systems
body: The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration, FMV, said the guns would replace systems installed on some existing navy vessels. Separately, Sweden’s new Luleå-class frigates are set to carry the same gun type, although the latest order has not been confirmed as supplying those ships. The 57Mk3 is designed for air defence, anti-surface warfare and naval fire support. Its pre-fragmented, programmable, proximity-fused ammunition enables engagement of drones, aircraft, missiles and surface targets, according to BAE Systems. “This contract reinforces our long-standing role as a trusted partner to the Swedish armed forces and FMV, and our commitment to supporting the Swedish Navy with world-class capability,” said Stefan Löfström, Marketing & Sales director at BAE Systems Bofors. “It demonstrates Sweden’s absolute confidence in the Bofors 57Mk3 and its advanced 3P ammunition as key capabilities for Sweden’s maritime defence.” Image: BAE Systems. Sweden already operates the guns aboard five Visby-class corvettes, two Gävle-class corvettes and two Stockholm-class patrol vessels. The Visby installations have stealth turrets that conceal the barrel when stowed. Naval Group began cutting steel for the first Swedish FDI frigate at its Lorient shipyard on 1 October, a month after signing the four-ship contract. HMS Luleå is due for delivery by the end of 2030, followed by HMS Norrköping in 2032, HMS Trelleborg in 2033 and HMS Halmstad in 2034. The schedule relies on an established production line that also builds FDI frigates for France and Greece. The Lorient line has a stated capacity of two ships a year. Sweden announced its selection of the French design in May. It chose the FDI over Navantia’s Alfa 4000 and Babcock’s Arrowhead 120, which was offered with Saab. The Luleå class will combine French construction with Swedish weapons, including Saab RBS15 Mk3 surface-to-surface missiles, 400mm Tp47 lightweight torpedoes and TrackFire weapon stations. Bofors 57Mk3 and 40Mk4 guns are also part of the planned armament. The frigates will use MBDA Aster 30 and CAMM-ER missiles for air defence. Their planned weapons fit will extend the 57Mk3’s presence in the Swedish fleet beyond the classes already operating it.
