title: Space Force Needs Third Launch Range by 2030, Acquisition Leader Says
body: The head of the Space Force’s largest acquisition organization said the service needs a third spaceport to support medium and heavy launch by 2030—a goal he called “aspirational” even as he stressed the importance of building out the U.S. military’s launch infrastructure. “We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” Space Systems Command boss Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant said Oct. 21. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities … There are a lot of considerations.” The Space Force operates ranges at Cape Canaveral Space Force Base, Fla., and Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., but those expect to run out of space in the coming years as demand for government and commercial launch surges. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed in May that the service expects to need a third site . “We probably need another site that’s capable of heavy and super-heavy launch capability, both from a resiliency perspective and just, even at the Cape, limitations on how much space we’ve got,” Meink said at the time. The White House signed out an update to its National Space Transportation Policy in August, predicting the U.S. could see its annual launch cadence grow to 1,000 launches by 2030 —a fivefold increase over 2025. The document calls on the Defense Department to work with the Department of Homeland Security and NASA to explore options to build additional spaceport infrastructure on federal property. Garrant, who spoke to reporters during AFCEA’s annual Space Industry Days event, said the Space Force recently formed an operational planning team to “take a hard look” at what building a third spaceport would require. “That work is pretty nascent, but we’re going to take some ideas to leadership at NASA, the National Reconnaissance Office, and the Space Force, and get some suggestions on how we might actually pursue a third spaceport,” he said. “That’s a recognition that the demand is there, and that we want to make sure that we meet those needs and support our launch service providers.” The team right now is looking at a range of options for buying or leasing land for the third site, Garrant said—from a public-private partnership to using commercial land to building a new federal installation. “All have pros and cons,” he said. “We haven’t made that decision yet, but we’re not discounting any of those.” In the meantime, the Space Force is deepening its partnerships with commercial spaceports like the Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport on Wallops Island, Va., and the Pacific Spaceport Complex in Alaska . The service is also investing heavily in its existing coastal spaceports and has plans to expand capacity at both ranges over the next five to 10 years. Congress allocated $1.3 billion in 2024 for “Spaceport of the Future” upgrades through 2028, and the Space Force plans to request more funding in the fiscal 2028 budget request to add more pads and launch support facilities, improve roads and bridges, and give launch companies better access to commodities like propellant and water. Both ranges are also looking to expand their harbors to support more providers. The post Space Force Needs Third Launch Range by 2030, Acquisition Leader Says appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Automattic begins layoffs following board upheaval and executive departures
body:
Automattic, the parent company to WordPress.com , WooCommerce, Tumblr, and others, has begun layoffs, and insiders tell us they are bracing for more cuts to come.
Over at least the past week, the cuts have impacted its communications team, social team, WordPress.com, and its VIP enterprise business.
The departures represent more turmoil at Automattic, whose team is still reeling from the board’s failed attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg in September, resulting in a complete board turnover and other exec departures, including its CFO, interim CFO , and chief legal officer.
Automattic’s director of communications, Megan Fox, posted about her departure last week on LinkedIn, saying the move was an “unexpected end” and that her role had been “eliminated.”
Meanwhile, after TechCrunch reported that Automattic’s interim CFO Jeremy Klaperman left earlier this month , only weeks after the board shake-up, Mullenweg posted on X suggesting Klaperman may have been “offended” by the company’s decision to seek external candidates to fill the role. (Internally, however, Mullenweg had asked Klaperman to reconsider leaving, we had heard.)
At one point, Mullenweg also shared personal information about one of the recently departed execs in the company’s internal Slack, according to screenshots viewed by TechCrunch. The post was related to a health matter impacting the person’s spouse and claimed that the company was not providing this person with much-needed COBRA insurance. Mullenweg said the exec was threatening to sue over this. Mullenweg also shared that his own fiancée had been impacted by the same health condition. Some employees told us they were shocked that the CEO would share something so private and personal in such a forum.
Throughout this month, TechCrunch has heard from different sources that members of Automattic’s team have also been let go, including those in marketing and product at WordPress.com.
Reached for comment about the layoffs last week, Mullenweg said the terminations were not above its normal numbers. Asked on Wednesday about the growing total, Mullenweg said that today he was “mostly focused on PHP.” (He posted on X about the PHP security issue hitting the internet, which is taking priority.)
The company’s About page lists the total number of staff at 1,397, but insiders tell us that the plan is likely to spread out the layoffs over the months ahead, in the hopes of improving Automattic’s Q4 revenue figures ahead of a debt renegotiation that’s coming up in June.
In a statement shared with TechCrunch, Automattic spokesperson Chenda Ngak said, “We’re staggering our organizational changes to be more generous with severance and allow more time with each Automattician.”
Updated after publication with Automattic’s statement.

title: Meduza surveyed more than 4,000 readers. Most respondents still in Russia want to emigrate, but half of those hoping to leave rate their chances of doing so within a year at two out of 10 or lower.
body: Cars line up at the Russian border in the Kaliningrad region, waiting to enter Lithuania. October 28, 2022 In July 2026, a group of independent sociologists led by Anna Kuleshova asked Meduza readers how they were feeling in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. More than 4,000 people took part in the study: 2,922 live in Russia and have never emigrated, 359 left but returned, and 857 live abroad. The sociologists asked respondents about their anxieties, self-censorship, experiences of emigration and return, life abroad, future plans, and views. At Meduza’s request, Kuleshova discusses the findings. The sample is representative of neither Russia’s population nor its emigrants. Participants were our readers who chose to complete the questionnaire. Many have a college education and are critical of the authorities; nearly half of the respondents in Russia live in Moscow or St. Petersburg. The figures therefore describe Meduza’s audience specifically, rather than all Russians or everyone who has left. Despite these limitations, the data allow us to draw reliable conclusions about differences between the groups. Those living in Russia, those who left, and those who returned read the same publication and are similar in age and education, so the differences between them are primarily associated with their experiences of emigration. This audience matters in its own right: Educated urban residents critical of the authorities accounted for a substantial share of the 2022 emigration wave. The same milieu also produced those who stayed but had once intended to emigrate or simply disagree with the regime. Obtaining such data through a representative survey is now virtually impossible. There is no sampling frame from which to draw a random sample of emigrants, and conducting a survey like this in Russia today poses too many practical difficulties. The analysis also draws on material from the study “Novye rossiyskie diaspory v Armenii, Izraile, Kazakhstane, Serbii i Turtsii” (“New Russian Diasporas in Armenia, Israel, Kazakhstan, Serbia, and Turkey”), conducted at the initiative of the Boris Nemtsov Foundation. What can we say about Russia’s 2022 emigration wave almost five years later? It will soon be five years since the war began. Much has changed in people’s lives over that time, and plenty of myths, prejudices, and stereotypes have emerged. Let’s start with a theme Russian propaganda likes to promote: the claim that those who stayed hate those who left, and a broader split in values and views. Every forecast seemed to say that the two Russias — the one that “left” and the one that “stayed” — would stop understanding each other and learn to hate each other. But among Meduza’s audience, about 5% of those living in Russia, including those who left and returned, have negative feelings toward people who left after 2022. By contrast, 87% have positive feelings. Those who left believe their compatriots in Russia view them more negatively than the figures suggest. It would be more accurate to say that Russian society already had various divisions over values — the war simply made many of them more visible. As one respondent put it: “Everyone already knew what they could say and who they could say it around. Not much has changed in that respect.” About half of those who left (48–55%) and 39% of those living in Russia believe Russian society views emigrants with suspicion or disapproval. Those who returned see their compatriots’ attitudes toward people like themselves as less hostile than those of other groups: 22% report suspicion or disapproval. Among respondents living in Russia, 89% have not heard of discrimination against people who left and then returned — in hiring, for example. Only about 1% know of such cases among acquaintances or from personal experience. A good future for Russia is possible, according to 56% of those living in Russia and 48% of those who left. Yet just 0.2% (!) of all respondents are satisfied with the current state of affairs in Russia. Among those living in Russia, 83% cannot picture their lives in concrete terms more than a year ahead, and 39% cannot see beyond three months. Those living abroad can plan further ahead. But even among those who left in 2022 or later, 63% cannot picture their lives more than a year ahead. What is life like for different groups of Meduza readers? Four years after the war and large-scale emigration began in 2022, the Russian diaspora has not become a unified community. The lives of those who left were shaped less by their political and moral convictions than by their financial, intellectual, psychological, social, educational, and other resources, as well as their points of entry into host communities. People who left during this period are often mistakenly called “relokanty,” a Russian term that implies relocating with a job and an employment contract already in place. As a rule, only people working in IT had these, and even in IT, many did not. We are therefore talking more about evacuees : people forced to emigrate who might have qualified for refugee status but whose circumstances denied them that opportunity. For the overwhelming majority, leaving in 2022 was their first experience of living abroad. Most became emigrants in an emergency, usually with no preparation at all. Of those who left between February and August 2022, 18% returned; among those who left between September and December that year, during mobilization, 38% returned. Of those who returned, 77% would have stayed abroad if they had been able to obtain legal status and find work without major obstacles. And 65% want to leave again. A line at the Russian-Georgian border during Russia’s “partial” mobilization. September 28, 2022 Meanwhile, 10% of those who left in 2022 or later and still live abroad want to return to Russia. This desire is more common among people with a strong Russian identity, high anxiety, and financial difficulties. The perception that Western countries are pushing Russians out, as well as a lack of legal status, is also associated with thoughts of returning, though the connection is weaker. By contrast, knowing the language of one’s country of residence and working in its local labor market are not associated with a desire to return home. The view that Western countries have a policy of pushing Russians out is shared by 32% of those living in post-Soviet countries and 11% of those living in Western Europe. Fewer than half of respondents living in Russia (45%) believe most people around them share their views. Among Russians surveyed abroad, 82–84% are confident that they are surrounded by like-minded people. Why haven’t those who left become a fully formed diaspora? Those who left after 2022 have indeed not formed a single Russian diaspora. Instead, several parallel communities have emerged, divided by profession, political views, ethnicity, or religion; some overlap. Sociologist Rogers Brubaker identified three defining features of a diaspora: dispersal, maintenance of group boundaries, and a sustained orientation toward the homeland. The new emigrants meet the first criterion, but the boundaries are drawn within the emigrant population rather than between Russians and locals — for example, between “newcomers” and those who left before the war. Or those who left define themselves in opposition to those who stayed. Leaving is described as a break with Russia rather than a continuation of “Russianness,” whether understood in ethnic or national terms. People who emigrated in 2022 were condemned by those who had left earlier, for example, immediately after the annexation of Crimea; those fleeing mobilization were condemned by those who left Russia as soon as the full-scale war began; the 2024–2025 wave was condemned by people who had been abroad since 2022, and so on. Other sources of solidarity took the place of national belonging: profession, a shared fate, and religion. Profession is the main organizing principle, especially in IT, design, media, and the creative industries. This is reinforced by the narrative that “the best people left” and by comparisons with the Philosophers’ Ship of 1922. Professional communities often bring together Russian-speaking professionals of all nationalities rather than Russian citizens specifically. What connects them is their profession and the Russian language, rather than Russian citizenship or their country of origin. As sociologists Peter Baehr and Viktor Vakhshtein use the term, a community of shared fate is a group united by a common threat. “We’re in the same boat,” but we’re not victims — we’re people who take an active role in shaping our lives. Some even romanticize this turn in their lives. But there is a downside: alienation from those who stayed, who, in respondents’ words, “live in a different information bubble.” Some who left rediscovered their identities as Tatars, Bashkirs, or Jews, setting aside Russian citizenship as a defining feature. These identities provide the most support where they fit with the host country’s culture: in Israel for Jews, and in Turkey for Turkic peoples. For example, Bashkir communities in Turkey and Kazakhstan help with housing, work, and joint business ventures. These bonds of solidarity function as economic infrastructure. Professional networks give rise to migrant economies, coffee shops, coworking spaces, salons, IT hubs, and cross-border partnerships between Russians who have moved to different countries. They help those still in Russia find clients, handle paperwork, and deal with other work-related matters. But the same selectivity that makes these networks effective shuts out outsiders. A journalist in Kazakhstan would like to change careers but doesn’t know how to afford six months of retraining. A waitress in Astana, listening to IT workers at a party discuss investments and moving to Italy, realizes that such prospects are out of her reach. In Serbia, “Russian establishments” charge “Moscow prices” that many of their compatriots cannot afford. Emigration reproduces, and sometimes deepens, the inequalities of prewar Moscow and St. Petersburg. Access to work, housing, and advice depends not only on a person’s human capital and the host country’s laws but also on their place within these overlapping yet partly disconnected networks of solidarity. Hi, I’m N. I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously. Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about. What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work. What do the different survey groups have in common, and how do they differ? We compared those living in Russia, those who left, and those who left and returned across several measures. Judging by anxiety levels, life inside Russia appears more stressful , despite all the problems Russians face abroad. Average overall anxiety among those living in Russia is 7.7 out of 10 , compared with 6.0–6.4 among those living abroad. Those living abroad are significantly less anxious about their personal safety: 3.0 compared with 7.2 in Russia. Yet their anxiety about Russia’s political situation remains high: 7.3 abroad compared with 8.9 in Russia. Among respondents living in Russia, 95% reported at least one form of self-censorship. Between 66% and 72% do not discuss politics with colleagues or people they do not know well, and this proportion is the same among people with different views. Those who returned differ little from those who never left in either anxiety levels or self-censorship. They are more afraid of losing the ability to leave the country than those who have never left. National Guard officers patrol Red Square ahead of the Victory Day military parade. May 6, 2026 Abroad, rates of self-censorship are one-half to one-quarter of those in Russia. For example, 40% avoid discussing politics with colleagues, compared with 69% in Russia; 12% are cautious about using their phones in public, compared with 43% in Russia. After 2022, respondents living in Russia all but stopped expressing their views publicly; no more than 3% take part in protests. Meanwhile, 18% began reading independent media only after 2022. On either side of the border, people avoid contentious subjects with loved ones at almost the same rate : 33% versus 35%. Silence helps preserve family relationships, and emigration does not eliminate the need for it. Do many readers living in Russia want to emigrate in 2026? Yes. More than half of respondents living in Russia want to leave , but half of that group rate their chances of leaving in the next 12 months at 0–2 out of 10. Their political views differ little from those of others who want to leave, but they are older and have fewer resources to make the move, less savings, and weaker English. Respondents who do not want to leave Russia are by no means always loyal to the authorities. Only 4% agree that Russia’s leadership protects the country’s interests, and just 1% say they are satisfied with the current state of affairs in Russia. What distinguishes them from those who want to leave is their connection to the country, rather than their attitude toward the authorities. Of this group, 65% see Russia as the community they identify with most, compared with 42% of those who want to leave; 71% believe Russia can have a good future, compared with 45% of those who want to leave. Where did those who left Russia after 2022 move? People in the 2022 wave went where they could enter immediately, rather than where life would be better. Their first destinations were Georgia (13.7%), Turkey (11.2%), Kazakhstan (11.1%), Armenia (10.1%), and Serbia (7.1%). All five could be entered without a visa or much preparation. Only about one in four went to Europe, including Eastern Europe and the Baltic states — those who had a visa, a residence permit, or other grounds for entry. Using Everett Lee’s classic “push-pull” framework, we can see that people in the 2022 wave cite push factors more often than prewar emigrants do. Shock at the outbreak of war was cited by 65.3% of those who left, and the threat of mobilization by 61%. Yet this wave is not uniform. It contains two large subwaves that can be described as distinct phenomena. The February subwave , from February to August 2022, accounted for about a third of the wave. These emigrants left of their own conviction, “voting with their feet,” and were more often prepared for the move. Women make up 43% of this group. Compared with the mobilization subwave, a larger share speak English at the B2–C1 level (73% versus 58%), and a larger share have enough savings for six months (44%). Almost one in four left because their employer moved its operations abroad. In spring 2022, a substantial share of departures were organized through relocation programs, primarily in IT. Of respondents in this subwave, 27% went directly to Europe. Those in the mobilization subwave , from September to December 2022, fled the threat of mobilization. It was cited as the decisive reason for leaving by 80%, compared with 46% in the “February wave.” This subwave has the highest proportion of men — women make up 29% — and fewer resources: Only 36% had enough savings for six months. More than half chose post-Soviet countries as their first destination, while 13% went directly to the EU. Both groups cited political reasons: opposition to the country’s direction (83%), inability to speak freely (81%), and unwillingness to live in a country at war (79%). The subwaves differed in the circumstances of their departure rather than their views. Some left “with a job lined up”; others fled through the nearest open border within a matter of days. These subwaves still differ in legal status, country of residence, and the proportion who returned, though not in optimism or anxiety levels. It’s also important to remember that both subwaves included people who left to preserve their businesses, set up parallel imports, or study, as well as people driven by a wide range of personal motives and circumstances. Where have Meduza readers who left settled? Over the past four years, Russians who left after February 2022 have gradually moved toward Europe. But the widely circulated image of an emigrant who moved straight to the EU and obtained a residence permit there applies to only a fifth of this wave. Most either still live outside Europe (39%) or have already returned to Russia (28%). Meanwhile, one in five of those still abroad lacks legal status. About half of those who left have lived in more than one country; one in five has lived in three or more. This mobility conceals deep social inequality. Of those who went straight to Western Europe, 96% stayed there. Of those who started in visa-free countries, only a quarter made it to Europe. In economic sociology, this is called path dependence : An early choice narrows all subsequent ones. For many, their first destination became less a springboard than a rut. A “temporary” stay in Georgia or Armenia eventually became permanent residence. Much of this depended on host countries’ policies. Armenia and Serbia, for example, took a relatively lenient approach. They sought both to make newcomers comfortable and to benefit from their arrival, without making it drastically harder to stay. Kazakhstan, however, ended border runs in January 2023 in an effort to stop being a transit country. And starting in early 2023, Turkey began denying Russians residence permits en masse without explanation. Israel initially offered a quick route to legal status under the Law of Return , but ended its emergency repatriation program for Russian and Belarusian citizens in April 2023. The outcome was predictable. Where governments treated newcomers leniently, stable communities and migrant businesses emerged, although some people still live in the gray area of tourist status. Where conditions for staying grew stricter, planning horizons shrank, and people either moved on to other countries or returned to Russia. Decisions by foreign governments, not only by Russia’s, shaped the lives of Russians who left. If we consider their first destination, their current country, and whether they returned, this wave divides into four groups: Those who went straight to Europe, usually through a relocation program for skilled workers Those who reached Europe through transit countries Those who settled outside the EU Those who were forced to return to Russia How are Meduza readers feeling abroad? Those who have stayed abroad have integrated into their host communities to a degree. Of these respondents, 80% have legal status — a temporary or permanent residence permit, or citizenship — while 36% speak the country’s language at B1 level or above, and 33% work in the local labor market. Another 31% work exclusively in the international market, for employers or clients in other countries. Another 17% work for Russia-based employers or clients despite living abroad. About a third of those still abroad (34%) look to the future with hope and optimism, while 27% experience high anxiety. An intense fear of being forced to return, rated 8–10 out of 10, is reported by 46%. It is more common among those without legal status (56% versus 42%) and those in worse financial circumstances (53% versus 42%). What troubles emigrants most is precarity: the feeling that everything they have built could be lost at any moment. Their fear comes down to this: “What if I have to go back?” For example, their residence permit might not be renewed, a relative in Russia might become seriously ill, or they might lose the job that enables them to maintain legal status abroad, among other possibilities. Russians vote in the presidential election on the grounds of the Russian Embassy in Warsaw. March 17, 2024 Conditions are worst in post-Soviet countries. There, roughly a third have legal status (39%, compared with 96% in Western Europe); in some countries, rates of refusal to open bank accounts or continue providing banking services can reach 74%. Fear of being forced to return compounds these difficulties. People also often face suspicion and prejudice in their host countries. All this feels like a double blow to those who sold their only home in Russia, leaving themselves without a home, yet gained neither a sense of belonging nor social protection in their host country. Moving on becomes increasingly difficult for them, while returning home usually entails real risks and losses: Many have already publicly expressed their views on social media and taken part in antiwar protests. Sociologist Abdelmalek Sayad described the migrant’s condition as a “double absence”: A person no longer belongs to the place they left and does not yet belong to the place they have arrived in. This is precisely the position of the 2022 emigrants. Among those who emigrated in 2022, 30% are ready to say of Russia, “This is no longer part of my life,” compared with 39% of longer-established emigrants. But this distancing happens gradually, rather than immediately upon crossing the border. There is also a sizable group for whom emigration has been a gift: the start of a new life. Their prevailing mood is a general sense of upheaval mixed with hope, rather than despair. What about those who left Russia after 2022 but eventually returned? More than a quarter of the 2022 wave returned to Russia (28%): one in six of the “February” emigrants (18%) and more than a third of those who left during mobilization (38%). Those who returned have the fewest resources of any part of the wave. Their English is weakest, their savings are smallest, and they were more likely than others to start in transit countries. They cite the following reasons for returning: Financial difficulties: 43% Missing loved ones: 36% Inability to find work: 31% Liking life in Russia: 29% Inability to obtain legal status: 25% Having planned a temporary stay from the outset: 24% The central question is whether they would have stayed abroad if they had been able to resolve their financial and legal-status problems. Two-thirds of those who returned (65%) would like to leave again. There are two competing interpretations in return migration theory. In one, returning means achieving a goal: You earned money, learned something, and came back. In the other, it means failure — an inability to establish yourself. Sociologist Jean-Pierre Cassarino linked the outcome to a migrant’s “preparedness”: their resources and the degree to which they left voluntarily. The returnees among our respondents fall into the second category. As a rule, they returned because they could not overcome barriers created by host countries, rather than because they preferred Russia. Meanwhile, among those who have not returned but are considering it, the desire to return is also associated with Russian identity: a sense that Russia is “where I belong.” Among those with a strong sense of belonging to Russia, 17% want to return, compared with 4% of those with a weak sense of belonging. Actually returning, however, is associated with practical difficulties: a lack of work, problems obtaining legal status, or a shortage of money. Those who returned resemble people who want to leave but cannot yet do so, rather than people who never wanted to leave. Most were unable to establish themselves abroad; they did not change their minds about Russia and the current regime. Some simply ran out of money. Others were given an ultimatum by their Russian employer — “Come back or we’ll fire you” — and never found a job in their host country. Others found themselves unable to access medical care. With a couple of exceptions, no one in our sample described returning as a reconciliation with their homeland. Since returning, they have shown anxiety levels indistinguishable from those of people who never left, and they practice slightly more self-censorship to protect themselves. But there is one difference: They are more afraid of losing the ability to leave (75% versus 65%). So what does our survey tell us about the “wartime” emigration wave? The wave of emigration after 2022 was driven by push factors. Where people end up is determined by host countries’ policies and visa rules, rather than by their life plans or ideas about an ideal place to live. People went wherever they were allowed in, and the greater the urgency, the narrower their choices. An emigrant’s well-being depends above all on how secure their status is. Their greatest anxiety stems from the uncertainty surrounding their lives and their inability to make long-term plans. We might say that moving does not restore a sense that the world is a secure place. What a person wants — to leave, return, or stay — is most often determined by their sense of belonging to Russia. But what actually happens to them is determined by money, immigration status, professional skills, and foreign-language proficiency. The new emigrants do not unite around a national identity; they connect mainly through Telegram chats. People come together around their professions and a sense of shared fate, rather than Russian citizenship or Russia as their country of origin. Each network provides “insiders” with jobs, clients, and protection while shutting out “outsiders.” Instead of leveling the playing field, solidarity reinforces inequalities by creating another layer of unequal access to resources. Russian emigration Russians are leaving the country again amid fears of another mobilization. In Georgia, Serbia, and Armenia, the housing rush has already begun. Russians are leaving again, amid repression, economic strain, Ukrainian drone attacks, and rumors of another wave of mobilization. This time, earlier émigrés have left them a roadmap. Russians who fled after the 2022 mobilization tell Meduza how they rebuilt their lives abroad — and what they’ve lost along the way At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter . Anna Kuleshova

title: Two killed after drone interception in Saudi Arabia
body: Two people were killed and two injured in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after falling debris from a drone intercepted by Saudi air defences struck near a processing plant at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield in the Eastern Province. The two killed were Filipino and Nepali citizens, while the injured were Pakistani and Indian. In a statement on X, the Ministry of Energy said the drone had been aimed at the plant and that falling debris caused a fire in a contractor’s vehicle outside its perimeter. The ministry said the incident had no impact on operations at the oilfield. Meanwhile, the US State Department has ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, due to increased Houthi attacks on the kingdom, spokesman Tommy Pigott said. This is inaccurate. The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only. Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on… https://t.co/yNrCwDcfIg — Tommy Pigott (@statedeptspox) October 21, 2026 The order applies only to non-emergency US government personnel and their families. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have increased hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure, resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions, Mr Pigott said.

title: UAE's Lana Nusseibeh enters race to be next UN secretary general
body: UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh has entered the race to become the next UN secretary general. State media agency Wam reported on Wednesday that Ms Nusseibeh would be joining the list of candidates for the role leading the world body. Ms Nusseibeh previously served as the country's representative to the UN, and led its delegation during its recent two-year membership on the Security Council. Wam said that in a letter submitted to the UN Security Council from President Sheikh Mohamed, Ms Nusseibeh’s “deep experience of the United Nations, her judgment in addressing the ongoing international challenges, and her record of constructive work” were highlighted. “I have spent much of my professional life working in and around the United Nations, and I have seen first-hand what determined diplomacy can achieve – countries with profound differences finding common ground, and agreement where people said agreement was impossible," Ms Nusseibeh said after her candidacy was announced. "But I have also seen the cost when diplomacy falls short. When the distance between what we promise and what we deliver grows, trust erodes, and so does our ability to act. "I am standing to be Secretary General because I believe this is a moment to act with greater urgency: to act earlier, bring people together across difference, and drive the work forward until it produces concrete results. That is how we rebuild trust in the United Nations and ensure it delivers meaningful change for the people it exists to serve.” Secretary General Antonio Guterres's second and final term will finish at the end of the year. Ms Nusseibeh joins a crowded list of candidates to become UN secretary general. #الإمارات ترشح رسمياً معالي لانا نسيبة لمنصب الأمين العام للأمم المتحدة #وام https://t.co/FTL9qrdI1o pic.twitter.com/5OrWJQJpJP — وكالة أنباء الإمارات (@wamnews) October 21, 2026 Eight people have been put forward for the role: Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Argentina’s Rafael Grossi ; Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan; Senegal's Macky Sall; Ecuador's Ivonne Baki ; Chile's Michelle Bachelet; Ecuador's Maria Fernanda Espinosa; and Uganda's Olara Otunnu. But none of the candidates has been able to get enough support among the members of the UN Security Council's members. Deliberations continue at the Security Council, with straw polls indicating that Ms Grynspan is the front-runner. With the current deadlock, it was expected that new candidates would enter the race. If selected, Ms Nusseibeh would be the first woman to hold the position of Secretary General of the UN and only the second Arab, after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali. She would also be the first Gulf Arab to assume the role. Ms Nusseibeh was appointed the UAE's ambassador to the UN in 2013. Before that, she served in a number of positions in the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, launching its Policy Planning Department and serving as its first director for three years. She also served as the head of the International Renewable Energy Agency (Irena) campaign task force at the ministry, and as director of research and communications for the Ministry of State for Federal National Council Affairs. She stepped down from her role as UN ambassador in mid-2024 to take up her role as UAE Minister of State. Former US official Brett McGurk described Ms Nusseibeh as a diplomat “who knows everyone and works with them” to get things done. “She would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said in a post on X. Priorities Ms Nusseibeh spoke to The National last month at the General Assembly in New York about the UAE's key messages at the UN and its commitment to multilateralism. “Although it seems that this is a really uncertain time ... a challenging time, it is not a time to give up hope. It is not a time to give up optimism about the future. It is not a time to give up diplomacy and a recommitment to multilateralism,” she said. In announcing her candidacy, Ms Nusseibeh said she wished to "offer myself to this office as I would serve it: speaking frankly with every government and answering to none". According to Wam, if elected, Ms Nusseibeh would prioritise ensuring peace and security worldwide. She called for clearer priorities, leadership and resources closer to the problems the UN exists to solve, stronger accountability for results, less duplication and empowering people to deliver on the field. The UN development system must also respond to a changing world in which progress on the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals remains deeply uneven. As secretary general, she said she would help to forge trustworthy commitments that governments can explain to their citizens. In addition, Ms Nusseibeh would focus on ensuring the equal application of international law, without double standards, which was necessary for the UN to maintain credibility.

title: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan
body: Using torchtitan on AWS Trainium means using it the way you always have. TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, which lets torchtitan use it through standard PyTorch interfaces. You can use these configurations to pre-train from random initialization or fine-tune published weights. You can also customize the model implementation and kernels for your workload. In this post, you train Qwen3 three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge . The first method uses Transformers v5 as a modeling backend in torchtitan. It runs Hub models through AutoModelForCausalLM and reads and writes published safetensors directly. The second method switches to torchtitan’s native Qwen3 by changing config.model_spec . The third adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernels from the torchtitan-neuron recipes and then uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach your own kernel. All three configurations use the same torchrun launch pattern and config structure. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container. Both environments provide the Neuron driver, runtime, and compiler required to train on Trainium. Before you install torchtitan-neuron , check whether your environment already includes it. The following command prints the installed version and package path: python3 -c "import torchtitan, torchtitan_neuron; print(torchtitan.__version__, torchtitan_neuron.__file__)" This walkthrough uses the versions in the following table. To reproduce the examples, pin these versions. The Transformers v5 integration and Trainium-specific override modules can change between torchtitan releases. Component Version Instance trn2.48xlarge, 16 Trainium2 accelerators, 128 physical NeuronCores Logical NeuronCores 64 at LNC=2 torch, torch_neuronx 2.14.0, 2.14.3 transformers 5.16.0 torchtitan-neuron release-2.33 (0.2.2+neuron.1) When torch_neuronx is installed, TorchNeuron registers Trainium as the neuron device and torchtitan detects it at startup. In eager mode, Neuron compiles operations as they execute. With torch.compile , Neuron compiles the captured graph. This same launch pattern works across all three configurations. For the versions used in this walkthrough, install torchtitan-neuron and torchtitan’s remaining dependencies with --no-deps to preserve the Neuron build of torch: git clone https://github.com/aws-neuron/torchtitan-neuron cd torchtitan-neuron pip install -r requirements.txt Before you start training, get the Qwen3 model artifacts from Hugging Face Hub. Store them in a local directory that you can pass to the training config: hf download Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 \ --local-dir "$PWD/assets/hf/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" Each training configuration is a Python config function. The three examples start from a base config that you update for each step. Train with Hugging Face Transformers v5 In the first configuration, Transformers v5 builds Qwen3 through AutoModelForCausalLM . The Hub model definition supplies the implementation used for the forward and backward passes. You select the model by setting its Hub ID in the config. Start with transformers_modeling_backend_full() . It leaves the fields that map to Hugging Face configuration keys unset, so AutoConfig.from_pretrained() loads the model architecture from the Hub. Create neuron_qwen3.py in the torchtitan-neuron repository root, where you run the training command. Add the imports, model artifact path, and base config: import os from torchtitan.experiments.transformers_modeling_backend.config_registry import ( transformers_modeling_backend_full, ) from torchtitan.experiments.transformers_modeling_backend.configs import ( TransformersBackendConfig, ) ASSETS = os.path.abspath("./assets/hf/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507") def v5_qwen3_4b() -> TransformersBackendConfig: config = transformers_modeling_backend_full() config.hf_model = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" config.hf_assets_path = ASSETS config.dataloader.dataset = "c4_test" config.training.steps = 10 config.training.local_batch_size = 1 config.parallelism.data_parallel_shard_degree = -1 return config torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config v5_qwen3_4b This command launches 64 training processes, one for each logical NeuronCore. --module neuron_qwen3 imports the local config module. --config v5_qwen3_4b selects the configuration function. The data parallel setting shards the model across all 64 ranks. Load and save Hugging Face checkpoints To fine-tune from published weights, enable checkpoint loading and point initial_load_path to ASSETS . The state-dictionary adapter adjusts the leading model. prefix and handles tied embeddings. It saves the final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors. def v5_qwen3_4b_finetune() -> TransformersBackendConfig: config = v5_qwen3_4b() config.checkpoint.enable = True config.checkpoint.folder = "checkpoint_qwen3_4b_ft" config.checkpoint.initial_load_path = ASSETS # absolute path required config.checkpoint.initial_load_in_hf = True config.checkpoint.initial_load_model_only = True config.checkpoint.last_save_in_hf = True config.checkpoint.last_save_model_only = True return config Use the first training-step loss as a quick check that torchtitan loaded the published weights. For Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 , the verified run produced a step 1 loss of 6.54 from published weights and 12.43 from random initialization. After training, load the exported checkpoint with AutoModelForCausalLM and load_state_dict . A successful round trip reports no missing or unexpected keys other than lm_head.weight , which Qwen3-4B ties to the token embeddings. This confirms that the files remain a standard Hugging Face checkpoint. Figure 1: The published checkpoint starts with a loss of 6.54, and the exported weights load without missing or unexpected keys Train with torchtitan’s native models In the second configuration, torchtitan builds its native Qwen3Model . Add the native Qwen3 imports and config function to neuron_qwen3.py : This example starts from qwen3_32b() because the tested torchtitan build does not provide a generic qwen3_4b() config builder. The next line replaces the 32B model specification with the 4B specification. The remaining fields reproduce the tested run. from torchtitan.models.qwen3 import model_registry from torchtitan.models.qwen3.config_registry import qwen3_32b from torchtitan.trainer import Trainer def native_qwen3_4b() -> Trainer.Config: config = qwen3_32b() config.model_spec = model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") config.hf_assets_path = ASSETS config.dataloader.dataset = "c4_test" config.training.steps = 10 config.training.local_batch_size = 1 config.training.global_batch_size = 64 config.parallelism.data_parallel_shard_degree = -1 return config torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config native_qwen3_4b config.model_spec selects the model class and defines how torchtitan shards the model and maps its checkpoint keys. Here, model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") selects torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation with scaled dot product attention (SDPA). Add NKI kernels for mixture of experts In the third configuration, torchtitan runs mixture-of-experts layers with kernels written in NKI, the Neuron kernel language. Add the required imports and Qwen3 MoE config function to neuron_qwen3.py : from torchtitan.config import CompileConfig from torchtitan_neuron.models.qwen3.config_registry import qwen3_nki_moe_config def nki_qwen3_30b_a3b() -> Trainer.Config: config = qwen3_nki_moe_config( "30B-A3B", compile_config=CompileConfig(enable=False, backend="neuron"), n_layers=4, num_experts=64, top_k=4, ) config.hf_assets_path = ASSETS return config torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config nki_qwen3_30b_a3b This configuration uses data parallel sharding across 64 ranks with a tensor parallel degree of 1. It does not use expert parallelism. num_experts=64 sets the number of experts in the model, not the expert parallel degree. Setting CompileConfig(enable=False) runs this example in eager mode. TorchNeuron supports registered NKI operators in both eager execution and torch.compile . In the torchtitan build used for this walkthrough, qwen3_nki_moe_config() replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped-experts implementation. It also selects SDPA and the gather-free rotary embedding. When you enable torch.compile , add "grad_clip" to CompileConfig.components to compile gradient-norm clipping. NKI kernels enter training as PyTorch operators. wrap_nki makes an NKI kernel callable from PyTorch, and nki_op registers the operator. register_autograd attaches its backward pass using routing metadata saved during the forward pass. The example reduces Qwen3-30B-A3B to 4 layers and 64 experts so it fits on one trn2.48xlarge . It routes each token to 4 experts with top_k=4 . Attach your own NKI kernel In some cases, you might want to optimize an operation for the tensor shapes in your model. A specialized kernel can tailor its tiling and data movement to those shapes. It can also replace a performance-critical sequence of PyTorch operations with one optimized operator. You can write the kernel yourself or start with one from nkilib . This example uses rope_hf from nkilib.core.embeddings , which expects the Hugging Face tensor layout and supports its own backward mode. This example demonstrates kernel registration and autograd integration, not a performance improvement. Create my_neuron_kernels.py in the repository root, where you launch training. torchtitan stores query and key as [batch, seq, heads, head_dim] , whereas rope_hf expects [batch, heads, seq, head_dim] . Convert the layout inside the operator and allocate the output tensors with torch.empty_like() : import torch from nkilib.core.embeddings.rope_hf import rope_hf from torch_neuronx import nki_op from torch_neuronx.nki_hop import wrap_nki from torch_neuronx.utils import get_logical_neuron_cores LNC = (int(get_logical_neuron_cores()),) wrapped_rope = wrap_nki(rope_hf) @nki_op("my_kernels::rope_fwd") def rope_fwd(query, key, rope_cache): q = query.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() k = key.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() cache = rope_cache.reshape(-1, rope_cache.shape[-1]) q_out, k_out = wrapped_rope[LNC]( q, k, torch.empty_like(q), torch.empty_like(k), rope_cache=cache, ) return ( q_out.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), k_out.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), ) rope_hf computes gradients when you call it with backward=True . Register a second operator for that mode. Save the rotary cache during the forward pass so the backward pass can reuse it. Return None for the cache gradient because the cache is not differentiable. @nki_op("my_kernels::rope_bwd") def rope_bwd(grad_query, grad_key, rope_cache): gq = grad_query.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() gk = grad_key.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() cache = rope_cache.reshape(-1, rope_cache.shape[-1]) out_q, out_k = wrapped_rope[LNC]( gq, gk, torch.empty_like(gq), torch.empty_like(gk), rope_cache=cache, backward=True, ) return ( out_q.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), out_k.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), ) def _setup_context(ctx, inputs, output): ctx.save_for_backward(inputs[2]) def _backward(ctx, grad_query, grad_key): (rope_cache,) = ctx.saved_tensors grad_q, grad_k = rope_bwd(grad_query, grad_key, rope_cache) return grad_q, grad_k, None rope_fwd.register_autograd(_backward, setup_context=_setup_context) Because rope_hf requires a supported sequence length, validate that constraint before calling the kernel. Subclass CosSinRoPE and call rope_fwd from apply_rotary_emb : from dataclasses import dataclass from torchtitan.config import derive, override from torchtitan.models.common.rope import CosSinRoPE class NKIRoPE(CosSinRoPE): @dataclass(kw_only=True, slots=True) class Config(CosSinRoPE.Config): pass @staticmethod def apply_rotary_emb(query, key, rope_cache): stride = 128 * LNC[0] if query.shape[1] % stride: raise ValueError( f"rope_hf requires a sequence length that is a multiple of " f"128 * LNC={stride}, got {query.shape[1]}" ) q_out, k_out = rope_fwd(query, key, rope_cache) return q_out.type_as(query), k_out.type_as(key) Register NKIRoPE as the replacement for CosSinRoPE . derive() copies the shared configuration fields into the replacement config: @override( "nki_rope", target=CosSinRoPE.Config, exact=True, description="nkilib rope_hf kernel in place of the PyTorch rotation", ) def _nki_rope(cfg: CosSinRoPE.Config) -> NKIRoPE.Config: return derive(cfg, NKIRoPE.Config) To load the custom override, pass its module name to --override.imports . torchtitan imports the registry entry before it builds the model: torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config native_qwen3_4b \ --override.imports my_neuron_kernels Before training starts, torchtitan logs each config node that the override replaces. Confirm that the output contains one nki_rope entry for each Qwen3 layer: [Override] nki_rope: model_spec.model.layers.0.attention.rope CosSinRoPEConfig -> NKIRoPE.Config [Override] nki_rope: model_spec.model.layers.1.attention.rope CosSinRoPEConfig -> NKIRoPE.Config Set the sequence length to a multiple of 128 * LNC , which is 256 when LNC is 2. Reshape the rotary cache to [seq, head_dim * 2] , with cosine values in the first half and sine values in the second. The kernel validates these constraints before training begins. For a complete torchtitan example, see torchtitan_neuron/models/gpt_oss/nki_attention.py . It connects nkilib flash-attention kernels through the same operator and override mechanisms. It also handles DTensor inputs for tensor parallelism. Before you train with a custom kernel, compare its outputs with the implementation it replaces. In the numerical test with float32 inputs, rope_hf and torchtitan’s PyTorch rotary embedding produced a maximum absolute difference of 0.0 for both query and key. When you register multiple overrides, limit each one to the intended module instances with fqns . For example, fqns=["layers.1[0-9].attention.rope"] targets the rotary embedding in layers 10 through 19. torchtitan stops when two overrides claim the same node and warns when an override matches no nodes. Review the training output At startup, confirm that torchtitan reports 64 ranks and the expected model. The first step includes compilation and takes longer than later steps. Each training step reports the loss, gradient norm, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) usage, throughput, and model FLOPs utilization (MFU). For the checkpoint run, confirm that the first-step loss is near 6.54. For the custom kernel run, confirm that the nki_rope override appears once for each Qwen3 layer. Scale across the instance The same parallelism settings apply to the Transformers and native model configurations. A trn2.48xlarge exposes 64 logical NeuronCores at LNC=2. Set data_parallel_shard_degree = -1 to shard the model parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across every rank that torchrun starts. Set config.parallelism.tensor_parallel_degree to shard each layer’s weights across a group of ranks. Each rank computes a slice of every matrix multiplication. With sequence parallelism enabled by default, normalization layers run on activations sharded along the sequence dimension. torchtitan combines tensor parallelism with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) on a multidimensional DeviceMesh . Watch per-rank HBM as you increase the model size, sequence length, or local batch size. These values determine how much memory each rank requires. Clean up If you want to keep your checkpoints, copy them to persistent storage before you clean up. If you plan to reuse the instance, stop it . When you no longer need the instance, terminate it . Conclusion AWS Trainium works as a supported torchtitan device across all three configurations in this walkthrough. You can train Qwen3 through Hugging Face Transformers v5 and load or save published safetensors directly. You can also train with torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation by setting config.model_spec . For mixture-of-experts models, use the torchtitan-neuron NKI recipes. For custom kernels, use the override registry to attach NKI operators through the same launch flow. For setup guidance, see the AWS Neuron documentation . For current source and training recipes, see the torchtitan repository. About the authors Josh Longenecker Josh is a Solutions Architect on the Annapurna Labs ML accelerator team at AWS. He helps customers design, optimize, and deploy distributed AI training and inference workloads on AWS Trainium. His technical interests include distributed PyTorch, large language model training and inference, and NKI kernels. Alex Hoffman Alex is a Software Engineer working on distributed training at AWS Annapurna Labs. He enables end-to-end training experiences for AWS Trainium customers on TorchNeuron with torchtitan-neuron.

title: Vance defends Trump envoy’s ‘humanitarian’ praise for Putin
body: U.S. Vice President JD Vance backed President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, who called Vladimir Putin a “humanist.” After meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff thanked the Russian president for releasing U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was convicted in Russia of serving as a mercenary. Witkoff said: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you, and I thank you again.” American journalists later asked Vance whether he agreed with Witkoff’s remarks. Q: Witkoff called Putin 'a humanitarian' for agreeing to release Stephen Hubbard. Do you agree with that? JD VANCE: I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. pic.twitter.com/BV7MnDxApp — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 21, 2026 I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family. Vance said Americans “should all be celebrating” Hubbard’s return, “not be complaining about what [he] said in order to get it done.” Witkoff and Putin met the day after Witkoff held talks with Volodymyr Zelensky and representatives of European countries in Oslo. Witkoff brought new Ukrainian and European proposals for ending the war to the meeting in Russia. After the meeting, the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks with the United States and Ukraine between November 10 and 19 (after the U.S. midterm elections). However, Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said the EU’s and Kyiv’s “new approaches” contained “not all that much that was useful for a settlement in Ukraine.” Read more Who is Stephen Hubbard, the American Putin just freed? Anthropic just announced an AI agent competitor to Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots: Claude Duet. The new agent, designed for professionals and small business owners, is launching as a “research preview,” according to Anthropic , and it’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android and through Claude on the web.
The AI agent is built around Claude Opus 5.5. Here’s Anthropic’s description of what it can do:
Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.
Claude Duet pulls in memory, skills, and connected apps from Claude, and it has a virtual machine with a browser that it can use for completing work. Before any big step, like sending a payment or deleting something, Claude Duet messages you for approval. Given that Duet may be taking action on sensitive information, it has a new “new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt” that are “designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information,” such as credit card numbers.
Anthropic says Claude Duet is currently an “early version” and that it “still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent.” It’s also not “as strong” at personal errands like booking tickets.
If you want to try Claude Duet, you can get on the waitlist , though you’ll need to be a Pro or Max subscriber in the US to use it.

title: Russian FPV Drone Destroys Swiss-Donated Evacuation Vehicle in Donetsk Region
body:
A Russian first-person-view (FPV) drone struck an armored evacuation vehicle of the Proliska Humanitarian Mission near Kramatorsk, Donetsk region on Wednesday, Oct. 21, in what marked its 120th attack on the group since the beginning of Russia’s war in 2022.
The drone, armed with a shaped-charge anti-tanked munition, hit the vehicle at 2:50 p.m. local time, as the crew was heading back to Kramatorsk on a mission to evacuate people with limited mobility. According to the head of the organization, Yevhenii Kaplin, the charge burned through the vehicle’s armored capsule and set it on fire.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“All crew members ran from the vehicle a second before it was hit,” Kaplin said in a statement on social media, confirming that there were no casualties.
Proliska humanitarian crews had reportedly spent the day evacuating immobile, seriously ill and wounded residents from Sloviansk and Kramatorsk to an intermediate point, after which they were handed over to other crews for further transport in specialized medical vehicles.
According to Kaplin, the organization had rescued 18 people by midday.
While driving along the Oleksandrivka-Kramatorsk highway through the village of Ocheretyne, local residents began running away and signaling to the crew that a drone was approaching.
The warning prompted the team leader to order everyone out of the vehicle before it was hit.
“This armored vehicle had been handed over to us just two months ago by the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation on behalf of the Swiss government,” Kaplan said, adding that the evacuations “were carried out with financial support from the Ukraine Humanitarian Fund.”
Since receiving the vehicle, the Proliska humanitarian organization evacuated more than 500 residents of the Donetsk region and helped deliver humanitarian convoys to isolated frontline settlements.
According to Kaplan, Wednesday’s strike marked the 120th attack on Proliska’s staff, volunteers, vehicles or warehouses since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
On the same day, Russian forces repeatedly struck nearby Sloviansk, injuring at least eight people, including two boys aged 7 and 12.
Donetsk Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin reported that the city was attacked with guided aerial bombs (KABs) and an FPV drone, damaging six apartment buildings, a hotel, a shop and three cars. Five other vehicles were destroyed as well, he said, without providing further details.
“Children should not pay with their health and lives for adults’ decisions to stay under constant shelling,” Filashkin said, urging residents to evacuate to safer region of Ukraine.
“There are no safer places in the Donetsk region,” he continued. “No home and no circumstances are worth a child’s life.”
On Monday, Oct. 19, Russian forces struck a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv region with a drone, killing six people, including two children.
The youngest victim was a little girl just over a year old, who was killed sitting in her stroller. Her mother, Inna, later died in hospital.
Such attacks reflect a pattern that has defined the war, now in its fifth year. Although international humanitarian law prohibits deliberate strikes on civilians, Russian strikes on private homes, parks, and public transport have continued almost daily across Ukraine.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini 4 Argon found critical PHP flaw affecting millions of websites
body:
AI models from OpenAI and Google found a critical PHP vulnerability that could affect millions of websites worldwide.
GPT-5.6 Sol tracked down the flaw as part of the Patch-the-Planet initiative , which OpenAI calls one of the "most impactful security issues in recent memory." The model spotted the vulnerabilities before attackers did, giving developers and security vendors a window to respond. A tool on GitHub now lets server operators check whether their PHP version is affected.
Security firm Wiz found the same flaws independently, using its own Wiz Atlas platform alongside Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. Gemini 4 Argon proved especially useful for finding the vulnerability, developing exploits, building attack detection, and validating the patch, according to Wiz. Ad
An exploit that worked against one specific PHP installation used to require significant effort to adapt to other versions and configurations, Wiz explains. Large language models remove that barrier because they can automatically adjust exploits across different PHP versions, configurations, and memory layouts. "This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments," the firm writes, adding that "vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets." Ad
The fix was coordinated over two months across five phases, involving PHP developers, Wiz, Cloudflare, and US agencies including CISA and the White House. OpenAI is proposing this process as a repeatable framework for future AI-driven security discoveries.
The company expects findings on the scale of the PHP2Shell flaw to "increase sharply in the coming months," but warns that the same AI capabilities that find vulnerabilities can help attackers too. The discovery feeds into a months-long debate over AI models' offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities. Ad

title: US urged by Lebanese diaspora to pressure Lebanon to repeal law criminalizing ties with Israel
body: Washington must urge Beirut to repeal Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which criminalizes social and business ties with Israel, and ensure that Hezbollah does not regain the explosives seized from the group several weeks ago, the American Mideast Coalition for Democracy said in an open letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday.Lebanese Americans Tom Harb and John Hajjar, AMCD co-chairs, argued that the 1955 law was being overextended beyond its original intentions and is now being used to criminalize basic conversations with Israelis and prevent religious pilgrimages to the Land of Israel, which holds religious sites for Abrahamic faiths.AMCD calls for dialogue between Lebanon and Israel's militaries“The law is not only impractical; it has become a tool for politicized prosecutions of those who advocate peace,” the letter stated.“One of AMCD's own co-chairs, Tom Harb, an American citizen born in Lebanon, was summoned to appear before the Lebanese military court, as have so many others. Americans should not face criminal charges abroad for speech that is protected at home,” it noted.Beyond calling for contact between Israeli and Lebanese citizens to be legalized, particularly ahead of the Christmas season, the signatories said channels of communication should be established between the two countries' militaries to prevent the loss of innocent lives due to miscalculations during military operations. They also called for diplomatic channels to be opened to advance peace.To advance this goal, AMCD said that the US should condition financial and military assistance to Lebanon on the repeal of the 1955 law and on Beirut implementing concrete steps to facilitate military, diplomatic, and civilian communication with Israel, and impose sanctions against any Lebanese government body, institution, or individual that prosecutes or penalizes people for peaceful contact with Israelis or for visiting the holy sites.“American taxpayers should not underwrite a government that criminalizes the pursuit of peace,” the letter said. “We respectfully urge you to continue pressing [Lebanese] President Aoun on these issues and to support these measures in Congress.”

title: LLM-D 1.0 Takes Open-Source Kubernetes AI Inference into Production
body:
The Kubernetes-native project adds traffic priorities, upgrade controls and stable APIs to improve performance and reduce AI inference costs.
SAN JOSE — At the PyTorch Conference , lead developers of llm-d , the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) open-source, Kubernetes-native framework for running large language model (LLM) inference across a cluster, rolled out llm-d 1.0 .
Keeping a fleet of models serving thousands of competing AI agents, without wasting accelerator capacity or taking the service down for maintenance, is a major pain. That’s where llm-d, which Red Hat helped launch in 2025 , comes in.
Stephen Watt, a Red Hat Distinguished Engineer, explained during the launch presentation that they created it to bridge the gap between running inference on one machine and operating it as a shared service.
With the release of version 1.0, this Kubernetes-native distributed inference stack adds multi-tenant traffic controls, high-availability routing, and a stable configuration API to its existing performance-oriented serving capabilities. The project brings together model-serving engines such as vLLM and SGLang with Kubernetes used to operate distributed services.
This, in other words, is an infrastructure project for running LLMs, not an AI project per se. Its existing capabilities include prefix-cache-aware and load-aware routing, key-value cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, and wide expert parallelism for distributing mixture-of-experts models across nodes.
The challenge was not simply fitting model weights into accelerator memory. It was supporting development and production workloads, different model sizes, and operational requirements while getting more useful work from existing infrastructure. As Watt put it, the stack needed to meet “the day-to-day operational expectations of the IT and SRE teams for running production services.”
Version 1.0 focuses on keeping those capabilities useful after the initial deployment, when traffic patterns change, users compete for capacity, and operators need to upgrade software. As Carlos Costa, an IBM Distinguished Engineer, explained during the presentation: “When your traffic is competing for priority, you have to do those rollouts for updates and maintenance. All of these without your service going down.”
To accomplish this, llm-d has added four new features. These are:
The upgrade controls are especially important for disaggregated serving, which separates processing an incoming prompt, or prefill, from generating output tokens, or decoding. Its DisaggregatedSet component manages these pools as one unit for coordinated updates while allowing each phase to scale independently.
That all sounds good, but does it work? Abdullah Gharaibeh, a Google Cloud Senior Staff Software Engineer, showed it with a live demo featuring 1,000 sandboxed agents sending requests to a shared inference service. The demonstration compared a baseline Kubernetes setup with the llm-d router and then with llm-d flow control enabled. It used vLLM and SGLang across a mixed fleet of Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs.
According to Gharaibeh, in the baseline setup, the fleet produced roughly 900 to 930 tokens per second, with a cache hit rate of about 30%. However, after switching llm-d routing on, we saw a much more impressive cache hit rate of 75%. Throughput roughly doubled, while latency fell by half. That was enough to make the audience sit up and take notice.
The point was that routing, not additional hardware, drove the performance improvement. “This is the same hardware,” Gharaibeh said. “Same model server, same traffic,” but drastically better performance. I was impressed, and I’m not easily impressed.
It does this by context reuse. Multi-step agents repeatedly submit requests containing shared conversation history, instructions, or other prompt prefixes. Sending a request to a server that already holds the corresponding cached state avoids recomputing that work. llm-d’s router considers cached context as well as load and predicted latency when choosing a model-server replica.
That makes routing more than a matter of distributing an equal number of requests to each server. The useful destination depends partly on what each server already remembers.
The demo also showed why higher aggregate throughput does not, by itself, solve the production problem. It needed more, and enabling flow control provided it. Without flow control, requests from different user tiers waited in a shared queue. That meant, Gharaibeh noted, that paid-tier users could wait as long as free-tier users. That doesn’t make for happy customers. But after enabling flow control, the demo showed much shorter waits for the highest-priority users while lower-priority requests still received service. Or, as he said, “The pro members waiting the least, the free members waiting the most, but they’re all still getting served.”
That matters a lot for providers supporting interactive customers alongside background agents or other bursty workloads. A system can be busy and efficient overall while still failing to meet response-time commitments to its highest-priority customers. llm-d 1.0’s flow-control features let operators enforce those priorities while using remaining capacity for other work.
Mistral ’s inference engineers explained in a Google press release that llm-d’s prefix-cache-aware routing, flow control and disaggregated serving allow the company to enforce priority bands across its commercial tiers. When capacity is saturated, the system can hold or shed lower-priority requests to protect latency objectives for paying customers.
llm-d 1.0 is already in production. DigitalOcean uses llm-d to underpin its Serverless Inference and Managed Agents services, which serve trillions of tokens. JetBrains says the software runs in production behind its Junie Lite coding-agent plan and handles a significant share of that traffic.
Looking ahead, Google is integrating the llm-d stack with Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) . This deployment will include a managed routing path via the GKE Inference Gateway and support for TPU and GPU pools behind a common endpoint.
The companies behind llm-d also claim substantial performance and cost improvements. They state it can deliver estimated per-token costs five to 10 times lower than equivalent commercial API pricing. Of course, you might not get the same results, but if llm-d can deliver even half of what it promises, it will be a success.
As Mark Collier, the PyTorch Foundation’s executive director, recounted at the demo’s end, the team’s aim was straightforward: “We want to be able to take it into these production environments, cloud native environments, and have people really be able to trust it.” I’m pretty sure after what I saw they’ll see that happen.

Walmart will soon let AI agents shop on its website for you. Next month, the retail giant will allow you to use an AI agent on the site, with systems in place to let you approve and review purchases and set spending limits.
The embrace of AI agents stands in stark contrast to Amazon, which blocked Perplexity’s shopping agent and Meta’s Muse AI assistant . But Walmart is opening its doors to AI shoppers — as long as they follow the retailer’s rules. It has outlined a set of terms for agents, saying that “agents must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends” and cannot change a customer’s payment method. Agents also can only access information needed to complete their task. Walmart says it will block agents that don’t follow these terms.
Agents will connect to new “Agent Profiles” within Walmart. By default, Walmart will require approval for all AI agent purchases, but you can also let it shop within a certain budget, such as up to $100. You’ll also be able to review your agent’s purchases separately from your own in Agent Profiles, as well as turn off the agent at any time.
The retailer has built an “Agent Gateway,” currently available in beta , that connects AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that allows AI agents to plug into different services on the web. Walmart says this not only enables AI agents to shop without running into hiccups that they might encounter when navigating a browser, but also prevents them from accessing your shopping history and personal information.
“For example, if a customer tends to buy sourdough bread or a particular brand of milk, Walmart will help the agent find those usual items for the customer without sharing the customer’s broader shopping history with the agent,” Walmart says. The company will let users shop with AI agents on Sam’s Club as well.
