title: Italy Investigates Russia’s Possible Role in Violent Protests
body:
Italian authorities are investigating whether Russia or other foreign actors had a role in the violent cost-of-living protests that swept Milan and other European cities over the weekend, as concerns rise across the EU over Moscow’s escalating hybrid warfare.
Italy’s government, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, has reportedly requested a briefing over what role – if any – foreign provocateurs may have played, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Oct. 21, citing people familiar with the matter.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The scale of the violence and the apparent coordination of some attacks led officials to question whether the unrest was entirely spontaneous.
“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other periods,” Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said in Rome on Tuesday.
“They are the product of what I call ‘hybrid warfare,’ which someone is bringing into our countries with unconventional tools that are called TikTok, social media and YouTube, without the West realizing or reacting,” he continued, according to Bloomberg.
Meloni’s spokesperson had declined the request to comment.
According to a report from The New York Times (NYT) on Monday, Oct. 19, thousands of people were brought to the streets by rising food and fuel prices, combined with low wages, high taxes and public spending cuts.
Milan reportedly saw the largest turnout, with about 2,000 demonstrators according to the city’s police, while protests also took place in Bologna, Turin, Brescia and Bergamo.
The initial call to protest came from an anonymous social media account created earlier in October, which urged nationwide anti-government demonstrations to “bring the birth of a new Italy and a new Europe.”
While most participants in Milan marched peacefully, masked groups looted shops, set fires and threw objects at police, who responded with water cannons and tear gas.
War just meters from the Milan cathedral, Duomo. The symbol of Christianity in Italy and Europe, surrounded by smoke bombs, firecrackers and police vans under attack. This is not a protest. This is urban guerrilla warfare in the heart of our history and faith. And many of those… pic.twitter.com/vqD4612ReR
The NYT reported that police arrested 32 people, most of them minors, and reported 14 officers injured. A local business association put the damage at more than €1 million (roughly $1.1 million).
“Demonstrating is a right, devastating our cities is not,” Meloni said in a statement on X.
The unrest mirrored similar movements elsewhere in Europe, including student-led riots in France, the country’s worst in decades.
In southern Italy, farmers and truckers have blockaded ports and highways over soaring fuel prices linked to the war in Iran.
Crosetto also said that children as young as 11 or 12 who took part appeared to have undergone a form of “counter-education.” He, however, offered no further details on what that would entail.
With more demonstrations expected this weekend, the government announced the deployment of 500 military personnel in Milan until the end of the year.
According to Bloomberg, opposition critics accused Meloni’s conservative coalition of exploiting the unrest ahead of the next year’s elections while neglecting grievances behind it.
Italy’s scrutiny of the protests comes as Meloni has positioned her government among Kyiv’s prominent backers in Europe, which could – in Kremlin’s view – make it a legitimate target for a hybrid operation.
“If Ukraine stopped defending itself tomorrow, as many wish and openly call for, we would not achieve peace,” Meloni said on Oct. 14, speaking ahead of the EU summit in Brussels.
“Instead, we would be discussing the occupation of a European country and the return of Soviet-style imperialism, which Europe endured for half a century,” she continued.
Her support for Kyiv, she said, alongside pressure on Moscow, remained the pillars of Italy’s foreign policy; even at the cost of voter support.
Italy’s foreign actors probe comes as EU governments report a sharp rise in Russian hybrid operations, ranging from drone incursions into NATO airspace to sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament on Sept. 17 that intelligence assessments showed Moscow planned “hybrid” drone and missile strikes on countries supporting Ukraine , which it could later portray as accidents.
Around the same time, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia could attack another European country directly as Moscow seeks to fracture Western unity and weaken support for Ukraine.
On Oct. 17, Tusk reiterated his earlier warning that Russia may escalate its hybrid warfare before Christmas , pointing to possible attacks on railway lines and energy transit conduits supplying Ukraine.
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) said on Oct. 7 that Russia had begun carrying out sabotage against Danish defense firms supplying Ukraine , often through untrained proxies recruited via Telegram.
Days later, the Financial Times reported that European intelligence agencies had warned arms executives of Russian assassination plots , with Germany’s domestic intelligence agency (BfV) advising them to hire private bodyguards.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in hybrid operations or sabotage in Europe.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Flow Typing, A New Lens on Linearity
body:
In my various efforts to develop new programming languages, I’ve occasionally looked sidelong at linear types, as something that looks like it could be really useful if it wasn’t so incredibly cumbersome.
And now some folks have come up with a way to make them much easier to use [1] ! Or at least that’s the hope. This past week I’ve been trying to implement their execution model into a new programming language , to get a feel for what it’s like to actually use. Check out my field notes , if you’re already familiar with the paper.
I’m going to quote the abstract in full, as it does a great job of introducing the paper:
Linear type systems often suffer from a threading problem: if a value is used more than once, then it must be explicitly threaded through each usage. Existing solutions introduce extra language features to mitigate this, but at the cost of complicating the core language and its semantics. This article introduces flow typing, a new solution to the threading problem that avoids the need to extend the core language. Flow typing is based on the theory of lenses, a functional presentation of mutable references, in which lens terms mutate parts of a stateful typing context in a controlled way. Because this approach is purely functional, it can be implemented in a standard linear lambda calculus, providing flow typing with a simple and direct semantics.
Ok I’ll admit that there are a number of terms in there that likely aren’t totally familiar to the average programmer, and I also want to convince myself that I know what they mean, so let’s break things down a bit.
A type system is “linear” if all values must be used exactly once . You might be thinking (a) that sounds incredibly restrictive, I quite like using values multiple times, and (b) why would you even want that. I’ll speak to the second one first.
Some reasons a linear type system might be attractive:
Have you ever forgotten to close a file, and had a dangling file descriptor? Have you ever forgotten to free a pointer? To put it in web dev terms, what about failing to close a database connection, or to unsubscribe a listener?
If a value (say a DBConnection ) must be used exactly once , and the library offers you (a) functions that take the connection as an argument and then give it back to you in the return value, and (b) a close ( ) function as the only way to “get rid of it”, then you suddently have a statically enforcable mechanism for ensuring you never forget to close a db connection.
If the final sqlite . close ( db2 ) line were missing (in a fictional javascript with a linear type system), you’d get a type error db2 must be used exactly once , but was used 0 times . (the save function is a stand-in for “doing something with the records we got from the db”)
In such a system, you’re also statically disallowed from ignoring (or forgetting about) a return value.
Pure functional languages tend to achieve purity via immutability, to the extent that you’d be forgiven for thinking that it was a necessary component of having a pure language. “Pure” here meaning that “if you give a function the same input, it is always guaranteed to return the same output” [2] . A simple example of an impure function in javascript would be:
This is a rather tame example of action at a distance , an ill that pure functional programming saves you from.
In Haskell or Elm, the above code is impossible to represent because you can’t “mutate the value that lie represents” after initializing the variable. All variables are immutable, giving you purity by construction.
In a linear type system, by contrast, purity is achieved by preventing any variable from having multiple observers . Essentially, “if mutation happens but no-one else can observe it, does it make a sound?” [3] The above code would be disallowed because line 7 is a “second reference to the variable lie ”, and therefore a type error.
Rust is famous for its linear-inspired setup for mutable variables; if a variable is marked as mutable, there can only be one “accessor” (reader or writer) at a time. This allows them to have some pretty strong guarantees about safety, especially in the context of concurrency. However, they also want to be able to provide access-by-reference for mutable variables (as it would be terribly inconvenient to have to pass-by-value anything that’s mutable), which is accomplished via the infamous “borrow checker”. The linear-style requirements are represented by a system of “borrowing”, where the compiler needs to track which variables are “live” at any given point in the code, and ensure there’s only one live reference to a given value at a time. This is famously confusing and hard for people to learn. In spite of this, Rust is a wildly successful language.
Let’s accept for the moment that a linear type system is desirable (or at least interesting), and circle back to the “terribly inconvenient to have to pass-by-value anything that’s mutable” issue. This is what Wilshaw & Hutton call the “threading problem”. I’ll demonstrate with some simple typescript code:
We create an object, we mutate it with a couple of functions, and we display it.
In typescript, we’re passing by reference, which is how setName etc. are able to affect our object. Passing by reference isn’t allowed in a linear type system (only one accessor is allowed per variable); so here’s what our code would look like with pass-by-value [4] :
And setName would have to change, from e.g. ( person , name ) => { person . name = name } to ( person , name ) => ( { ... person , name } ) .
This is almost linear-valid, but on line 4 we’re using person3 twice, which is illegal. We’d have to change it to this:
Extremely cumbersome: we’re having to “thread” the person object into and out of every function that touches it.
My understanding of lenses is that they are a way to operate on (often in a functional/immutable way) a potentially deeply-nested subset of a given piece of data. Lodash’s set and update are related to this, and ramda has explicit support for lenses.
The innovation of this paper is using some clever syntax sugar to give you the convenience of mutable references (potentially many layers deep into an object, that’s the lens part) while retaining the simplicity and purity of a traditional linear type system. This essentially gives you something akin to a borrow-checker, but with dramatically simpler semantics and implementation, enabling things like a formal proof that it works ;).
The big question for me, though, is what does this feel like to use? How hard is it to actually implement in a language, and is the resulting code easy to write, read, and understand?
And so I’ve started writing a language that attempts to implement their system of “flow typing”. Here are my field notes .
I got turned onto this paper by this tweet from Alexis King asking for people’s favorite PL papers this year. ↩︎
Paraphrased from wikipedia . This is of course only true within certain assumptions about the reliability of the underlying system; other actors on the same machine could corrupt your heap, or a cosmic ray could flip a bit, etc. ↩︎
Clojure takes this approach with their transients, though of course there are not any kind of static guarantees that they are correctly used. ↩︎
In truth, typescript is still doing pass-by-reference, but we’re treating the values /as if/ they were pass-by-value, by doing immutable updates. ↩︎

title: BBC Russian reveals that journalist Darya Shipacheva raised 1.5 million rubles for Ukraine’s military before receiving a 12-year treason sentence
body: Darya Shipacheva during her sentencing at Moscow City Court, July 29, 2026 The case of medical journalist Darya Shipacheva, sentenced to 12 years in a penal colony for treason in July 2026, drew widespread attention. A photograph of her in handcuffs in the courtroom spread across social media. Her trial was held behind closed doors, and almost nothing was known about the substance of the charges. BBC Russian has learned exactly what led to her conviction. Meduza summarizes its findings. Shipacheva raised money for Ukraine’s armed forces on behalf of Ukrainian blogger Vasilisa Levchenko, BBC Russian reported. According to investigators, Shipacheva transferred more than 1.5 million rubles to Levchenko. Darya Shipacheva is 35. Before her arrest, she wrote about medicine, health, and feminism for RBC, Takie Dela , Wonderzine, and Forbes Woman . She also published a book about medicine and health, “Bez paniki” (“Don’t Panic”). As an activist, she organized demonstrations in support of the Khachaturyan sisters and feminist activist Yulia Tsvetkova . She also volunteered at a residential school for children with autism spectrum disorder. After the war began, Shipacheva chose to stay in Russia. She called Moscow her home and wasn’t considering emigrating. Still, a friend said, she had noticed the security services taking an interest in her. When she traveled abroad, border guards asked why she had been born in Ukraine. Shortly before her arrest, a stranger warned her that people would “soon come” for her. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Vasilisa Levchenko ran a Russian-language psychology blog and had about 60,000 Instagram followers, including some in Russia. After the invasion, she began collecting donations for Ukraine’s armed forces through her Sberbank account. According to the BBC, Russian followers who “felt ashamed” sent her more than a million rubles in the first few days. In May 2022, Russian propagandists took notice of the fundraising. Sberbank later blocked Levchenko’s card, and Rosfinmonitoring, Russia’s financial monitoring agency, subsequently added her to its list of terrorists and extremists. Shipacheva, who did not know Levchenko personally, then offered to collect donations through her own bank account. According to investigators, Shipacheva raised 1.558 million rubles and transferred the money to Levchenko in cryptocurrency. In letters to BBC journalists, Shipacheva wrote that concern for her family had driven her decision. She was born in Kharkiv but spent most of her life in Russia. She still has relatives in Ukraine, and her cousin serves in the Ukrainian military. “I faced an unbearable choice: Supporting one homeland meant betraying the other. I chose to support those who, in my view, are the injured party,” Shipacheva wrote. She emphasized that she had raised money for first-aid kits, jackets, and sleeping bags. Shipacheva said she realized she would end up in prison as soon as she was detained. There was no point denying it, she said — the officers “had all the evidence.” She pleaded guilty “out of fear and weakness” and signed a pretrial cooperation agreement after being threatened with 18 years in prison. A transfer “to a Sberbank card belonging to a Ukrainian blogger” may also have been the basis for another criminal prosecution. IT consultant Nina Slobodchikova was sentenced to 12 years for treason over a transfer of 5,000 rubles. Although Slobodchikova declined to tell journalists whom she had sent the money to, her account matches the circumstances of Levchenko’s fundraising, the BBC reported. Shipacheva hopes to be included in a prisoner exchange and is counting on Levchenko’s help. In letters to her friends, she asks them to let Levchenko know that she has been sentenced to 12 years. “Remind Vasilisa — maybe she’ll put in a word for her somewhere. It would be good if Vasilisa remembered her,” acquaintances of Shipacheva told the BBC. BBC journalists reached out to Levchenko. She confirmed that Shipacheva had followed her blog but said she had not known her personally. Levchenko declined to answer any other questions. “I don’t see any point in this. I don’t do volunteer work anymore,” she wrote, before blocking the BBC correspondent. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. title: Russian-led EAEU bloc warns Armenia of possible ‘serious blows’ to its economy
body: Report on suspension of Armenia’s membership of EAEU Four countries in the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) may discuss suspending Armenia’s membership of the bloc. A report prepared by experts from the intergovernmental council of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan says so. The report’s main argument is that Armenia would face serious economic difficulties if it left the Eurasian Economic Union. These would include a 15.6% contraction in GDP. “All the figures in this report are exaggerated by around 50%,” Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said in response. He assured journalists that the impact on the country’s economy would be negligible, at around -0.61%. Papoyan cited figures from a study conducted in Armenia. The country set up a working group to assess the potential consequences of leaving the EAEU. It included representatives of the Central Bank and two ministries: the economy and finance ministries. Unlike members of the ruling party, the parliamentary opposition considers the figures in the report alarming. Arthur Khachatryan, an MP from the Armenia bloc, said that even if the forecast proved only half accurate, the consequences would be “apocalyptic”. Moscow has yet to comment on the document. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration had not yet reviewed the report. Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev’s statement about ‘Ukrainisation’ of Armenia How Armenia is reacting to export restrictions on Russia: farmers’ views and official statistics Pashinyan: ‘Eurasian Economic Union must make clear whether it still exists’ Context At a meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council in Astana on 29 May 2026, the presidents of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement . They expressed concern about Armenia’s moves to strengthen ties with the European Union . In their view, European integration by an EAEU member could pose risks to the economic security of the bloc’s other countries. They urged the Armenian authorities to hold a nationwide referendum as soon as possible on whether to choose the EAEU or the EU. “We are working within the Eurasian Economic Union and will continue to do so until a choice between the European Union and the EAEU becomes unavoidable,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan replied at the time. He stressed that the people would make the decision in a referendum. However, he said he currently saw no grounds for a nationwide vote on the issue. He explained that Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make such a choice: “Until Armenia officially applies for EU membership or comes close to obtaining candidate status, holding any referendum would make no sense.” The heads of state also instructed their representatives to prepare a report by December 2026 on “the possible consequences of suspending the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union in respect of the Republic of Armenia”. A closer look at the report According to the report, Armenia’s actions contradict an obligation set out in Article 3 of the EAEU Treaty. The article requires member states to help create favourable conditions for the union to fulfil its functions and to refrain from actions that threaten its objectives. The authors apparently mean a law adopted by Armenia’s parliament to launch the process of joining the EU. The EAEU may also have taken note of Armenia’s more active political dialogue and growing economic ties with the European Union. The report again calls for a referendum in Armenia on “the EAEU or the EU”. The authors note that if the decision to suspend Armenia’s EAEU membership goes ahead, the suspension could remain in force until the referendum takes place. However, the authors themselves acknowledge that the EAEU Treaty contains no explicit mechanism allowing member states to unilaterally suspend another country’s membership. Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan nevertheless invoke the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. The report says the four countries could consider adopting a joint decision to suspend Armenia’s membership under the convention’s provisions. The document specifically warns that suspending Armenia’s membership would reduce the total volume of trade with other EAEU member states by 55.6%. The EAEU report also warns of the following consequences: the reintroduction of customs controls and duties, comprehensive sanitary inspections and taxation of goods; a 30–50% decline in exports of Armenian-made goods and a reduction of more than 90% in the re-export of goods; a 15.6% contraction in the country’s GDP, a 14.9 percentage-point rise in inflation and a 14.6% fall in consumption; an increase in the price of gas for Armenia from $177.50 to $300 per 1,000 cubic metres, a rise of 69%; tighter restrictions on labour migration for Armenian citizens. ‘No grounds for referendum yet’: Yerevan responds to calls to choose between EU and EAEU Four members of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union have urged Armenia to hold a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU. Here is how the prime minister and economy minister responded. How Yerevan has responded to the report “Armenia has always honoured its obligations to the EAEU in good faith” Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said Armenia had always honoured its obligations to the EAEU in good faith. “There are no obligations that we have failed to fulfil. We see this as an economic dispute, one that also concerns economic restrictions.” Papoyan said Yerevan had lodged a complaint with the Eurasian Economic Commission and was awaiting a meeting on the issue, scheduled for 3 November. “What do the EAEU rules say? They say that if you believe you have been treated unfairly — for example, if someone has imposed unjustified restrictions on you — you have the right to file a complaint.” The dispute concerns economic restrictions that Russia imposed on imports of Armenian products. They have been in force since May and remain in place. Other EAEU member states have also backed them. Although Armenia has already filed a complaint, the minister doubts it will secure a favourable ruling. He noted that the commission requires consensus, meaning all member states — including Russia — must agree. As for the threat of higher gas prices, Papoyan expects a negative impact. “A change in gas prices can have varying effects: one scenario could see a 5% impact, another 7% or more. Even a 1% increase in the price would be highly undesirable.” However, the minister said that even a rise in gas prices would not have consequences so severe that Armenia’s economy could not cope with them. “In principle, I find this acceptable, even normal. Everything should be paid for at market prices. If we do not pay the market price for something, we ultimately pay for it in some other way.” Amid debate over a possible increase in the price of Russian gas, some Armenian experts and residents say that “Armenia has spent decades paying for cheap gas with its sovereignty”. “They cannot expel Armenia from the EAEU” Hasmik Hakobyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, is not worried about Armenia being expelled from the EAEU because no such procedure exists. “They cannot expel Armenia from the EAEU, even if every other member state wants to.” She stressed that Armenia is not leaving the union and has expressed no intention of doing so. Under EAEU rules, the only way to end membership is for the country itself to decide to withdraw. “We want to continue cooperating in the same spirit and, where possible, discuss all issues and challenges at the negotiating table,” she said. Armenia begins shift from Russia towards EU – but finish line remains distant JAMnews reviewed the latest developments and spoke to analysts with opposing views. Residents of Armenia also shared their opinions on how they believe the country should shape its future. Commentary According to analyst Vahe Davtyan , the most interesting part of the document concerns the potential losses for other EAEU member states. It says that suspending Armenia’s membership would not cause them serious economic problems. In Russia’s case, for example, the projected decline in the total volume of imports and exports of goods and services would not exceed 1%. “The report’s political message is crystal clear. Economic pressure on Armenia could prove virtually painless for the other EAEU countries, while dealing a heavy blow to Armenia itself,” he argues . He warns that if Armenia leaves the EAEU, the sectors hardest hit would include agriculture, food processing, alcoholic beverage production and light industry. “These are industries for which the Russian market has been one of the main destinations for sales for many years.” On the possibility of higher prices for Russian gas, the analyst notes: “Suspending membership of the EAEU does not automatically mean that gas prices will be revised. The inclusion of this scenario in the document can therefore be seen as a political signal.” In Davtyan’s view, the report’s authors have overlooked an important detail: bilateral agreements between Armenia and Russia also govern gas supplies. Nevertheless, he stresses that any change in gas prices would inevitably affect electricity generation costs and the competitiveness of Armenian industry. title: Japan Sends Senior Diplomat to Russia to Seek Release of Arrested Journalist
body:
Japan sent a senior diplomat to Moscow this week to discuss the release of a journalist arrested in Russia on spying accusations, Tokyo said Wednesday.
Russia’s FSB security service said last week that a Japanese national had been arrested on the Far Eastern island of Sakhalin.
The individual was later identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, who faces accusations of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory."
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has denied that Japan conducts spying activities in Russia, while the Hokkaido Shimbun has stressed its independence from the government.
On Tuesday, Kimitake Nakamura, Japan's top diplomat for Europe, met Lyudmila Vorobyova, the head of the department at the Russian Foreign Ministry dealing with much of East Asia, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry.
"We lodged a request... that calls for the earliest possible realization of consular access to the Japanese national detained in Russia, as well as the individual's immediate release," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Wednesday.
Japan also summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a formal protest over the arrest, while its foreign ministry has urged Moscow to provide him "fair and impartial treatment."
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls "unfriendly" countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.
Kihara said the meeting on Tuesday was also held to discuss tense bilateral relations.
"Japan-Russia relations are in a difficult state," he said. "Precisely for that reason, it is necessary for the diplomatic authorities to engage in exchanges on the various issues."
For decades, Russia and Japan have been locked in a territorial dispute over the southern Kuril islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan — which are located northeast of Japan’s Hokkaido prefecture and southwest of Far East Russia’s Sakhalin. The Soviet Union seized control of the islands at the end of World War II.
Japan has also sanctioned Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
body:
Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security ( via ) If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.
This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:
On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]
As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.
This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:

title: Fighter Jet Crashes in Kaliningrad Region During Training Flight
body:
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed in the western Kaliningrad region during a routine training flight, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Wednesday.
The two-member crew successfully ejected from the aircraft and was later found by a search and rescue team, the ministry said, adding that “there is no threat to the lives of the pilots.”
It added that the fighter jet crashed in an unpopulated area and was not carrying any weapons on board.
The cause of the incident was not immediately clear.
Some Russian news outlets reported that the Su-30 went down in an area surrounding the Chernyakhovsk naval airbase, a hub for the Russian Navy’s Baltic Sea Fleet.
An eyewitness video circulating on social media showed a fireball and a thick column of smoke rising in the air following the crash.
In the video, a group of men in military uniforms are seen standing at a cemetery, which is located east of the airbase, looking toward the site of the incident.
A similar military air crash took place in the Far Eastern Amur region late last month when six crew members on board a Russian bomber plane were killed.

title: Russian-born Kazakhstani billionaire Timur Turlov is the new president of world chess. His election has divided Ukrainian officials, and Russia has abruptly dropped its case against him.
body: The election of a new head of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) has sparked a political scandal in Ukraine. Ukraine’s national chess federation criticized the choice of Timur Turlov, a Kazakhstani businessman who lived and did business in Russia for many years. But Turlov received unexpected support from Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the head of President Zelensky’s office. A week later, Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office withdrew its lawsuit seeking to seize Turlov’s income for the Russian state. Writing for Meduza, Ukrainian journalist Konstantin Skorkin explains everything that is known about FIDE’s leadership changes and the events that followed. How the FIDE presidential election unfolded Many international sports federations readily recruit influential businesspeople and politicians to lead them, using their connections to secure support and funding for their sports. For example, Sebastian Coe, a former member of Britain’s House of Lords, heads the International Association of Athletics Federations; Swedish billionaire Johan Eliasch leads the International Ski and Snowboard Federation; and French politician David Lappartient heads the International Cycling Union. For the past two decades, FIDE has been led by Russians. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russians’ presence in international sports has often been seen as legitimizing the aggressor state. Some members of Russia’s elite have left international sports federations because of sanctions. Billionaire Vladimir Lisin, for example, no longer heads the International Shooting Sport Federation. Others have held on to their positions. Alisher Usmanov, who had headed the International Fencing Federation since 2008, temporarily stepped aside in 2022 to keep the personal sanctions imposed on him from affecting the federation’s work. Just two years later, however, Usmanov won reelection . The chess world has been home to a particularly large number of influential Russians. From 1995 to 2018, FIDE was headed by Kirsan Ilyumzhinov , who was president of the republic of Kalmykia when he was elected. Ilyumzhinov sought to make Elista, which hosted international chess tournaments, a global center for chess. In the late 1990s, a complex called City Chess was even built near the city. In 2018, FIDE’s leadership called on Ilyumzhinov to resign: He had been placed under U.S. sanctions, which were hurting the federation’s work. Ilyumzhinov refused to leave voluntarily, however, and FIDE’s ethics commission had to remove him . His successor was another Russian politician, former Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich, who had served in the leadership of the Russian Chess Federation. By the time he was elected head of FIDE, he was already chairman of the supervisory board of the Russian Agricultural Bank. Dvorkovich is the son of the well-known chess coach Vladimir Dvorkovich, who was part of the coaching team that trained world chess champions Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov. The younger Dvorkovich led the world chess federation until July, when, like his predecessor, he was placed on a sanctions list — in his case, the EU’s, for “publicly supporting the actions of the Russian Federation” — and was forced to step away from FIDE’s leadership . Earlier that year, in February, Ukraine had sanctioned the former deputy prime minister for supporting “Russian aggression,” along with nine Russian athletes. FIDE World Rapid Chess Championship in Doha, Qatar. December 28, 2025 The Ukrainian president’s website says the sanctions list was drawn up in response to a petition by Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych. During the 2026 Winter Olympics, Heraskevych was disqualified for wearing a helmet bearing portraits of Ukrainian athletes killed during the war. Dvorkovich’s name, however, did not appear in Heraskevych’s petition, which was published on the Ukrainian government’s website. The former FIDE head currently holds no government or political posts. Since leaving the chess federation, he has been working as a professor at the New Economic School in Russia. It recently emerged that Dvorkovich plans to challenge the European sanctions in an EU court. Russia’s FIDE membership was suspended in June because the Chess Federation of Russia had established branches in occupied Ukrainian territory: the Donbas and the annexed parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. The election for a new FIDE president took place in September in Samarkand. Ilyumzhinov tried to run again but did not even make the official list of candidates . Three candidates made the list: Vadim Rosenstein: A German businessman and founder of the WR Chess team , born in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, who holds Russian and German citizenship Jan Henric Buettner: A German businessman who invests heavily in chess championships Timur Turlov: A Kazakhstani businessman of Russian origin who has headed Kazakhstan’s chess federation since 2023 Delegates from FIDE’s national member federations elect its president. Delegates from 196 of the 202 countries eligible to vote officially registered for the election in Samarkand and received ballots. Turlov and Rosenstein received the most votes in the first round. In the second round, Turlov won 110 votes to Rosenstein’s 85, with one FIDE delegate abstaining. Who is Timur Turlov? After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Timur Turlov was among the Russian businesspeople who tried to distance themselves from Russia. Born in Moscow, he graduated from the Tsiolkovsky Russian State Technological University (MATI) and began his business career as a trader for Moscow companies operating on the U.S. stock market. In 2008, Turlov founded Freedom Finance , which gave clients access to U.S. stock market infrastructure, including initial public offerings. In 2012, he opened a subsidiary in Kazakhstan and began doing business there. In 2015, he established Freedom Holding Corp. , registered in Nevada. It brought together the Russian and Kazakhstani Freedom Finance companies, the Freedom24 app, and Freedom Finance Bank. Turlov became the main shareholder. Freedom Finance Kazakhstan Bank joined the holding company in 2020, followed in 2021 by Freedom Finance Insurance, a group of Kazakhstani insurance companies . In October 2019, Turlov listed Freedom Holding Corp. on Nasdaq. It became the first financial institution from the Commonwealth of Independent States to be listed on the exchange. In January 2021, Turlov’s holding company acquired Prime Executions Inc. , a U.S. broker-dealer registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. This gave the holding company’s clients direct access to the U.S. market. That same year, Turlov entered the Forbes global billionaires list in 1,517th place, with a fortune of $2.1 billion. In June 2022, Turlov obtained Kazakhstani citizenship . To do so, he had to give up his Russian passport and the “offshore” passport he had previously obtained from St. Kitts and Nevis. At the same time, he announced that he was ending his business ties with Russia. By October 2022, the company’s Russian operations had been transferred to co-founder and Deputy CEO Maxim Povalishin. The deal was worth $140 million; the company soon rebranded as Tsifra . Timur Turlov According to Forbes Kazakhstan, Turlov ranks second among the country’s richest people and sixth among its most influential. In December 2025, he expanded his influence by acquiring the Kazakhstani telecommunications operator Transtelecom. Around the same time, his holding company began publishing a local edition of the glossy magazine Tatler. After 2022, Turlov became involved in charitable projects in Kazakhstan. In spring 2023, he founded Kazakhstan’s QJ League for youth soccer and became chairman of its board of trustees . Late that year, Turlov launched Qalam, an online publication “devoted to the history and culture of the world as seen from Kazakhstan and Central Asia.” His company spent a total of $66 million on charity in 2023, its representatives said. Severing his business ties with Russia, however, did not help Turlov avoid sanctions. In October 2022, Ukraine placed him and his holding company’s Ukrainian subsidiary on its sanctions list alongside other figures in Russian or Russia-linked businesses. More than 2,500 individuals and 1,300 companies were sanctioned at the time . Others listed alongside Turlov included businessmen Mikhail Fridman, Oleg Deripaska, and Alexey Mordashov; pro-Russian Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk; and members of Alexander Lukashenko’s circle. Turlov called his inclusion on the sanctions list “a clerical error.” The company promised to challenge it, though it took no concrete steps to do so. In 2023, Hindenburg Research investigated Freedom Holding Corp. and accused it of evading sanctions . The holding company’s shares fell 8% as a result. The investigation also drew the attention of the SEC, which launched its own inquiry . In January 2024, Freedom Holding Corp. commissioned an independent review that refuted Hindenburg’s findings . Turlov has been involved in chess since January 2023, when he became head of Kazakhstan’s federation. He told journalists that he regularly plays as an amateur on Chess.com. “I try to enjoy the game itself,” Turlov said. “I’m not out to prove anything to anyone in chess.” Why Ukraine’s federation opposed Turlov’s election as FIDE president — and where Mykhailo Podolyak comes in The news outlet Agentstvo, citing an acquaintance of Turlov’s, reported that he has close ties to Kazakhstani President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and “does nothing without his approval.” In July, the outlet reported, Kazakhstan’s president met with Vladimir Putin and asked him to help Turlov win the FIDE election. Another source told Agentstvo that Putin agreed. After Turlov won the FIDE presidential election, Tokayev personally congratulated him . Turlov’s victory sparked another scandal. The Ukrainian Chess Federation issued a statement saying it did not support his candidacy. It had initially nominated its own candidate, federation head Oleksandr Kamyshin, an outside adviser to Ukraine’s president and a former minister for strategic industries. Kamyshin, however, declined to run , saying his “priority during the war is developing chess in Ukraine.” The FIDE presidential election uses a secret ballot, and it is not known whom the Ukrainian delegate voted for. Champion, Ukrainska Pravda’s sports website, reported that Ukraine’s federation most likely supported Buettner, who failed to reach the second round, because Ukrainian media also suspected Turlov’s main rival, Rosenstein, of doing business with Russia. According to the news outlet UNIAN, revenue at 2R Integra, a company linked to Rosenstein’s family, grew roughly 40-fold after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and its website advertised services for supplying industrial equipment and electronics to Russia in circumvention of sanctions. After Turlov’s victory, he received unexpected support from Mykhailo Podolyak, an adviser to the head of the Ukrainian president’s office. At the new FIDE president’s invitation , Podolyak became a vice president . Indian grandmaster and former world champion Viswanathan Anand became first vice president. Mykhailo Podolyak The alliance between Turlov and Podolyak came as a surprise for several reasons. First, there had been no previous public reports of contact between the Kazakhstani businessman and the Ukrainian adviser. They also had no business ties or known history of political cooperation. Second, Podolyak had no connection to the chess world and had never expressed an interest in the game. Discussing his new post in interviews, he gave an exclusively political rationale : He wanted to use the vice presidency to reduce Russian influence in the chess world while leaving sporting matters to the Ukrainian Chess Federation. Yet it was with the Ukrainian Chess Federation that his relationship soured. Turlov arranged the appointment without involving the national federation, which sharply condemned Podolyak’s decision. The federation said it had received no offer to nominate a Ukrainian representative to the new FIDE head’s team, and its regional organizations sent a letter of protest to President Zelensky. The letter said: By working with sanctioned individuals [Turlov — Meduza], Mykhailo Podolyak is legitimizing Russians’ presence in FIDE’s leadership and helping Russia maintain its influence over international chess. This undoes the efforts of Ukrainian chess players who have spent years fighting that influence. Podolyak, in turn, criticized the Ukrainian Chess Federation for its “passive stance.” In his view, its officials had not done enough to counter Russian influence within FIDE. “They weren’t involved at all in getting rid of Dvorkovich’s team. They did absolutely nothing. Not publicly, not behind the scenes,” Podolyak said. Ukrainian Chess Federation Vice President Volodymyr Kovalchuk maintains that Turlov is part of Dvorkovich’s team and simply “swapped in” for the sanctioned Russian. In Kovalchuk’s view, Podolyak helped legitimize this “castling” maneuver. Kovalchuk believes that “nothing will change” under Turlov: Only the name has changed — Turlov will replace Dvorkovich. But I’m sure Dvorkovich will keep handling all of FIDE’s affairs. The entire Russian team is still there, and Dvorkovich will be the one actually running things, while Turlov will keep running his business. After all, he’s a Russian oligarch who made his money in Russia and is now investing it in Kazakhstan. One detail supporting Kovalchuk’s prediction is the appointment of former Russian Sports Minister Alexander Kolobov as second vice president. Podolyak continued to defend Turlov, calling Ukraine’s sanctions against the businessman “strange.” “When the full-scale invasion began, he became a Kazakhstani citizen and left Russia — which, unfortunately, still exists — behind for good. He also invested in humanitarian programs in Ukraine for a long time,” Podolyak said on Instagram . Citing sources, Kommersant reported that Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office moved in early October to have Turlov declared an “extremist” and his Russian assets confiscated over that humanitarian support. Law enforcement officials cited Freedom Holding’s transfer of 2 million euros for humanitarian aid to Ukraine. The money was intended to buy ambulances. A representative for Turlov said the businessman no longer had any assets in Russia. In mid-October, it emerged that the Prosecutor General’s Office had withdrawn its lawsuit and the court had dismissed the case against Turlov. A representative of the prosecutor’s office did not give a reason for the decision. In Ukraine, sanctions against Turlov’s company have begun to ease. In January 2025, Zelensky issued a decree allowing Ukrainian clients of Turlov’s brokerage to recover their assets . Their accounts had been frozen when sanctions were imposed three years earlier on the company, through which Ukrainians invested in government bonds and other securities. For now, however, lifting the sanctions entirely is not on the table. Although the restrictions against Turlov were imposed for five years and expire in late 2027, his holding company acknowledges in its annual report that there is no guarantee he will be removed from the sanctions list. title: Armenia Appeals to Eurasian Economic Union for Removal of Russian Trade Restrictions
body:
Armenia has asked the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) to designate Russia’s growing trade restrictions on Armenian goods as illegal market barriers, the newspaper Kommersant reported Wednesday, citing the South Caucasus country’s economic minister.
Russia has issued sweeping bans on a range of Armenian products this year as Yerevan, Moscow’s historical ally, began the process of joining the European Union. Amid the mounting restrictions, the EU relaxed tariffs on around 80% of Armenian exports for the next two years.
“We consider the [Russian] restrictions against us to be unlawful,” Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan told reporters, according to the Kommersant.
“If these restrictions are recognized as a barrier, then Russia is obliged to remove them within 30 days per EAEU procedures,” Papoyan was quoted as saying.
He added that Armenia has already submitted individual appeals to each trade restriction introduced in recent months, and in one case, it allegedly secured the support of three other members of the economic union. However, Russia has used its veto power to block those appeals, Papoyan said.
A translation of Papoyan’s comments cited by Kommersant states that the EAEU will consider Armenia’s latest, more sweeping appeal on Nov. 3. “We’ll see if there will be a tangible result,” he was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, a joint report released Tuesday by the remaining EAEU members Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan warned that Armenia’s exit from the economic union or alignment with the EU would hit Yerevan’s trade, labor and energy markets.
Relations between Russia and Armenia have soured in recent years after neighboring Azerbaijan took control of the disputed Nagorno-Karabakh region in September 2023. Officials in Yerevan accused Russian peacekeepers of failing to protect the region and its Armenian population from advancing Azerbaijani forces during a shock offensive.

title: In Honour of His Majesty, Banquet hosted at Guildhall of Lord Mayor of London
body:
London: In honour of His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, banquet was hosted at the Guildhall of the Lord Mayor of the City of London on Thursday, within the framework of the state visit undertaken by His Majesty the Sultan to the United Kingdom (UK). Upon the arrival of the Royal motorcade of His Majesty the Sultan, he was received by Susan Langley, Lady Mayor of the City of London; Gary Langley, husband of the Lady Mayor; His Royal Highness Prince Richard, Duke of Gloucester and officials, who welcomed His Majesty the Sultan, expressing their profound delight and great honour at this visit.
London: In honour of His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, banquet was hosted at the Guildhall of the Lord Mayor of the City of London on Thursday, within the framework of the state visit undertaken by His Majesty the Sultan to the United Kingdom (UK).
Upon the arrival of the Royal motorcade of His Majesty the Sultan, he was received by Susan Langley, Lady Mayor of the City of London; Gary Langley, husband of the Lady Mayor; His Royal Highness Prince Richard, Duke of Gloucester and officials, who welcomed His Majesty the Sultan, expressing their profound delight and great honour at this visit.
The Lady Mayor then presented a number of senior officials of the City of London to His Majesty the Sultan, after which His Majesty ascended the dais of honour, where the Guard of Honour rendered the royal salute and the Royal Anthem of Oman was played. His Majesty then graciously inspected the Guard of Honour, drawn up in salute to His Majesty, and a commemorative photograph was taken on the dais to mark the occasion. His Majesty the Sultan then proceeded to the Art Gallery Hall, accompanied by the Lady Mayor, members of the British Royal Family and the official delegation accompanying His Majesty, where a reception was held to mark the occasion, and the High Commissioners and Ambassadors resident in London came forward to shake hands with His Majesty the Sultan. His Majesty the Sultan also graciously signed the visitors' book. At the outset of the dinner, the Recorder of the City of London delivered a welcoming address on the occasion of the gracious visit of His Majesty the Sultan, in which he expressed his pride in the occasion.

His Majesty the Sultan also graciously signed the visitors' book.
At the outset of the dinner, the Recorder of the City of London delivered a welcoming address on the occasion of the gracious visit of His Majesty the Sultan, in which he expressed his pride in the occasion.
Following the conclusion of the banquet, the Lady Mayor of the City of London delivered an address in which she renewed her welcome to His Majesty the Sultan. The text of the address reads as follows: "Your Majesty, Your Royal Highnesses, Your Excellencies, My Lords, Aldermen, Sheriffs, Chief Commoner, Honoured Guests… Your Majesty, On behalf of the entire City of London Corporation, it is my enormous pleasure to welcome you, and members of the Omani Royal Family and other distinguished delegates to the City of London tonight. We are so delighted to present you with an Address of Welcome, contained here in this case, which I hope you will accept as a sincere expression of the deep and enduring friendship between our nations. This magnificent Guildhall, where we sit tonight, has been at the very heart of the City for more than 600 years. Within these ancient stone walls, history has been made, friendships forged, and momentous occasions celebrated. Including, of course, the banquet held here in honour of His late Majesty Sultan Qaboos. And so it is a very special privilege to add another chapter to that remarkable history tonight. At first glance, the United Kingdom and Oman might seem worlds apart. One, a land of green meadows, ancient forests, and mist-covered mountains. The other, a land of sweeping golden deserts, dramatic cliffs, and breathtaking coastlines. And yet, look beyond the geography, and something extraordinary emerges. Two nations, yes, separated by distance, but united by history and by a friendship that has endured for centuries. We are both outward-looking. We understand that the freedom of the seas, the security of trade routes, and global stability are the very foundations upon which prosperity and peace are built. But our connections extend well beyond this - through education, culture, science, and the countless friendships formed between us, we have built something far more powerful than any agreement. Trust. For ultimately, it is not treaties alone that sustain great friendships. It is people. Shared experiences. And the understanding that we have more that unites us than divides us. Our diplomatic relationship stretches back to 1646. Lord Nelson himself travelled to Muscat as a young midshipman. And the name of his ship, HMS Seahorse, was visible on the cliffs around Muscat Harbour for many years. It’s fitting, then, that we should sit here tonight, on Trafalgar Day, in the shadow of a monument to Nelson. A wonderful reminder that the threads connecting our people run deep. But the threads of our shared history must also weave the future we build together. Because nations, like cities, never thrive by standing still. They thrive by adapting, innovating, and having the courage to look forward. And this is reflected in this year’s landmark free trade agreement between the UK and the Gulf, opening doors to new markets and partnerships. The remarkable number of British and Omani businesses represented here tonight is itself a testament to the strength of our economic ties. The United Kingdom accounts for more than half of foreign direct investment into Oman. And the opportunities ahead are greater still. The UK-Oman Sovereign Investment Partnership is helping channel investment in both directions. And I am particularly delighted that the Oman Investment Authority has recognised the extraordinary potential of British innovation, investing in university spinouts at the frontiers of artificial intelligence and robotics through Cambridge Innovation Capital and Oxford Science Enterprises - both here tonight. It’s turning ideas into industries. Research into discovery. And the ambitions of one generation into opportunities for the next. So here in the City of London, Your Majesty, we stand ready to play our part. To bring together expertise and investment, connect innovators with opportunity, and ensure that the prosperity we create is shared by both our nations…more important now than ever. Not simply a place to do business, but a partner you can depend on. A friendship sustained not only by governments and institutions, but by the thousands of Omanis who live, work, and study here. People who enrich our communities, strengthen our institutions, and whom we are so proud to call part of our City of London family. Your Majesty, more than two centuries ago a treaty between our nations expressed the extraordinary hope that: “The friendship of our two States may remain till the sun and moon have finished their revolving career.” Remarkable words. Written in another century, by people who could scarcely have imagined the changes that lay ahead. And tonight, within the walls of this ancient hall, we celebrate not simply what has been, but what is still to come. Because the greatest friendships are not those that never face adversity. They are those that hold true through it, grow stronger because of it, and step forward ready to face the future hand-in-hand."

The Royal Anthem of Oman was then played, after which His Majesty the Sultan graciously delivered an address on this occasion, the text of which follows: “Lady Mayor, Excellencies, dear friends, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the Lady Mayor for this gracious invitation, which reflects the esteem in which my country is held, and the openness of the City of London to the wider world, and its commitment to strengthening the bridges of communication and trust among nations of the world. Each time I visit London, I am reminded of why it attracts bright minds and innovators. As one famous predecessor of the Lady Mayor put it, it really does feel that the streets are paved with gold. London is not merely a political capital, nor is it simply a global financial centre. It is a vibrant hub where ideas are exchanged and innovation flourishes across many fields of human achievements, above all, trade and investment, where expertise, cultures and human aspirations come together. A city's true value lies in the ideas it inspires, the strategies it shapes, and the relationships it fosters, all of which can leave a lasting mark on the world. Our gathering today has provided us with a new opportunity to develop further, our shared vision for British Omani friendship, both in terms of political engagement and private sector cooperation. We can see that bilateral investment and trade are moving in a positive direction, with concrete efforts being made to encourage investment and build stronger partnerships in sectors such as sustainability, financial services, and technology. Markets can prosper only in a stable environment; businesses can grow only when supported by transparent and flexible legislation; and investment opportunities can flourish only when underpinned by clear, well-defined and promising plans and projects. In light of these important considerations, Oman stands ready to welcome all those who wish to join us on this journey. Looking back, much attention is rightly paid to the historic treaties of 1798 and 1800, which marked an important stage in government to government relations between Oman and Britain. But the roots of this relationship stretch back even further, to an agreement concluded as early as 1647, long before formal agreements were signed between the two governments. This early agreement was not with the British government but with the merchants of this City of London, namely the British East India Company. It granted the British East India Company a favourable trading privileges and access to Omani governed ports. Not for the last time, the private sector got there first. These historic agreements reflect a much deeper connection rooted in the shared heritage as seafarers and traders, a legacy that has brought lasting benefits to the peoples of Oman and Britain and continues to do so today, as thriving trade ties and the strength of private enterprise testify to the enduring value of this relationship. Building on this longstanding relationship, the UK GCC Free Trade Agreement will unlock new opportunities for trade and investment, as the exchange of goods is expected to increase, creating further opportunities for economic growth in the years ahead.
The text of the address was then presented to His Majesty the Sultan within an ornate casket, offered as a commemorative gift in accordance with the traditions of the City of London.
The Royal Anthem of Oman was then played, after which His Majesty the Sultan graciously delivered an address on this occasion, the text of which follows:
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the Lady Mayor for this gracious invitation, which reflects the esteem in which my country is held, and the openness of the City of London to the wider world, and its commitment to strengthening the bridges of communication and trust among nations of the world.
Each time I visit London, I am reminded of why it attracts bright minds and innovators. As one famous predecessor of the Lady Mayor put it, it really does feel that the streets are paved with gold.
London is not merely a political capital, nor is it simply a global financial centre. It is a vibrant hub where ideas are exchanged and innovation flourishes across many fields of human achievements, above all, trade and investment, where expertise, cultures and human aspirations come together. A city's true value lies in the ideas it inspires, the strategies it shapes, and the relationships it fosters, all of which can leave a lasting mark on the world.
Our gathering today has provided us with a new opportunity to develop further, our shared vision for British Omani friendship, both in terms of political engagement and private sector cooperation.
We can see that bilateral investment and trade are moving in a positive direction, with concrete efforts being made to encourage investment and build stronger partnerships in sectors such as sustainability, financial services, and technology.
Markets can prosper only in a stable environment; businesses can grow only when supported by transparent and flexible legislation; and investment opportunities can flourish only when underpinned by clear, well-defined and promising plans and projects. In light of these important considerations, Oman stands ready to welcome all those who wish to join us on this journey.
Looking back, much attention is rightly paid to the historic treaties of 1798 and 1800, which marked an important stage in government to government relations between Oman and Britain. But the roots of this relationship stretch back even further, to an agreement concluded as early as 1647, long before formal agreements were signed between the two governments. This early agreement was not with the British government but with the merchants of this City of London, namely the British East India Company. It granted the British East India Company a favourable trading privileges and access to Omani governed ports. Not for the last time, the private sector got there first.
These historic agreements reflect a much deeper connection rooted in the shared heritage as seafarers and traders, a legacy that has brought lasting benefits to the peoples of Oman and Britain and continues to do so today, as thriving trade ties and the strength of private enterprise testify to the enduring value of this relationship.
Building on this longstanding relationship, the UK GCC Free Trade Agreement will unlock new opportunities for trade and investment, as the exchange of goods is expected to increase, creating further opportunities for economic growth in the years ahead.
Lady Mayor, From the East India Company’s first treaty, to Oman investments in London real estate, to British consultancy in smart cities and economic zones, our ancestors have long collaborated to bring together enterprise, expertise, and ambition. And, as I join you here today, I have no doubt that our collaboration will continue to blossom for many more generations to come. Lady Mayor, dear friends, thank you for your hospitality.” The ceremonies of the dinner concluded with an address of thanks delivered by the Lady Mayor of the City of London, in which she expressed her profound gratitude for the honour of His Majesty's visit to the City of London. title: Iran ready to give diplomacy another chance if US is honest
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 21 (MNA) – Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says that Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if Iranians see US honesty.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," wrote Araghchi in a post on his X account on Wednesday evening Tehran local time.
"But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure," the top Iranian diplomat added.

title: USS Abraham Lincoln to shift home port to Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton
body: The USS Abraham Lincoln is shifting its home port from San Diego to Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton, Washington, according to a recent service announcement. The relocation is expected to be completed later this year and executed as a permanent change of station for the aircraft carrier’s crew and family members. The move, while long planned, had left many family members in limbo after the USS Abraham Lincoln’s routine six-month deployment was extended twice after the U.S. jointly launched Operation Epic Fury with Israel on Feb. 28. The ship, which returned to San Diego, California, on Oct. 8, spent 322 days at sea — and 265 consecutive days without a port call. At an August town hall meeting in San Diego, family members spoke with Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and other senior officials, expressing frustration with Navy officials over reported food shortages, concerns about self-harm and confusion over the timeline regarding the impending move to Washington . According to the release, the home port shift is part of the Navy’s “strategic dispersal of ships,” while noting that “Regularly scheduled depot-level maintenance maximizes the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keeps our fleets lethal, modern, and ready to defend the nation. The work conducted during the maintenance period will maximize the lifespan of Abraham Lincoln and re-establish the carrier at the highest state of material and combat readiness.” The Navy did not provide a start date for the maintenance period. Naval Base Kitsap is the Navy’s third-largest Fleet Concentration Area and its most complex multi-mission installation, according to its website. The Lincoln will join its fellow Nimitz-class carrier, USS Ronald Reagan, in Kitsap. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Oct. 7 that the carrier strike group had been awarded the Presidential Unit Citation, the military’s highest unit-level valor award. Hegseth, who visited the carrier one day prior to the ship reaching shore, announced the award to the 5,000 sailors aboard the Lincoln, citing the “historic mission” that included completing “3,693 combat flights, sinking 64 Iranian warships, launching 450 Tomahawk land attack cruise missiles and shooting down 77 one-way aerial attack drones.”

title: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security, report says
body: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security through greater co-operation and surveillance technology, a new analysis says. The report from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington said that although offshore wind infrastructure has become more prevalent in recent decades, too little progress has been made in looking at how it could benefit national security. “By planning for dual-use capability from the outset, the United States can turn energy infrastructure into a force multiplier for national security, one that strengthens surveillance and warning in an increasingly contested maritime environment,” the CSIS report said. The analysis pointed out that in recent years, maritime and subsea infrastructure have become increasingly important – and also vulnerable to attack. “Subsea cables, which carry roughly 95 per cent of the world’s internet traffic, are particularly vulnerable to disruption,” the report said. In May, undersea internet and data cables were damaged in the Red Sea, causing connectivity problems for users in the Middle East, India and Pakistan. The cables were eventually repaired and most experts said that they had probably been severed by accident, but the incident still put subsea cable vulnerability in the spotlight. CSIS's report indicated that the proliferation of aerial drones, autonomous naval tools and unmanned underwater vehicles were also putting maritime security and subsea infrastructure in a more vulnerable position. It added that, concerningly, drone threats no longer come from state actors, but also from gangs and drug traffickers. The report concluded that if private offshore wind farm developers and governments could reach a consensus on how to best equip turbines with surveillance, sensors and data tracking tools, the end result could be “enhanced maritime domain awareness”. It highlighted the addition of surveillance systems to wind farms in and around Norway, Belgium, Poland and the UK. During a round-table discussion on Wednesday, Allegra Dawes, an energy security fellow at CSIS, said greater co-operation in enhancing offshore wind farms for maritime security could create a “force multiplier” effect, particularly for the US. “I think it gives guidance on the technologies that can actually create a stronger national security environment and also a stronger infrastructure backbone for energy,” she explained. Doug Wolfe, chief technology officer for Mighty Waves Energy, added that artificial intelligence could also be used along with the surveillance-enhanced wind turbines to bolster security on several levels. AI, he said, could help automate a lot of different maritime security workflows, while also helping to better understand what's happening under the sea. “It could very quickly characterise and detect whales, different types of whales and frequencies and all of those kinds of things,” he said.

title: Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds: a jet drone named Bars, built to strike Russia and now turned around to hunt them
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); One of Ukraine's best and fastest interceptor drones is an air-to-air version of the Bars one-way attack drone Bars are some of the best defenses against Russia's fastest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones But there may be too few small jet engines to rapidly scale up Bars production Russia's latest jet-propelled Geran-4 and Geran-5 one-way attack drones fly at 500 km/h or more , nearly three times as fast as an older, propeller-driven Geran-2. That's too fast for many of Ukraine's air defenses. In particular, the inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukrainian forces deploy by the thousand. Russia launched more than 2,700 jet Gerans at Ukraine in September, and Ukraine is shooting down only about 55% of them, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The speed disparity is a big part of the problem. Ukrainian forces are scrambling for new defenses against the speedy Gerans. Among the best is actually a Ukrainian take on the Geran-4 and Geran-5: a fast, jet-propelled one-way attack drone that the Ukrainians have modified for air-to-air use. Against jet drones, the air-to-air Bars have a hit rate of around 30%, Zelensky said during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on 4 October. "The Bars have shown positive results," Zelensky said. "They currently have the highest percentage. Others are also catching up." Explore further Did Ukraine just unleash its first Bars cruise missiles? A 500 km strike deep inside Russia suggests it In July, Ukraine and Germany agreed to jointly produce Bars, with Germany financing the first phase. Ukraine has reportedly been launching Bars at targets on the ground since at least the summer of 2025. But it was only recently that clear photos and videos of the drones have circulated. Over the weekend, Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade released footage of one jet drone hunting another. Observers identified the interceptor as a Bars and its target as a Geran-5. After launching from an elevated ramp with help from a rocket booster, the drone's operator—seeing what the drone saw through a front-facing infrared camera—steered the drone toward the Russian drone, possibly destroying it. Exactly how the operator controlled the Bars—whether by satellite or mesh radio or some other command and control system—is unclear. Equally unclear: what kind of warhead a Bars would employ in the air-to-air role. Many smaller interceptor drones lack warheads. Instead, they simply slam directly into their targets, wrecking them in the collision. Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade has released the first footage of the Ukrainian Bars jet-powered drone in its interceptor configuration engaging a Russian Geran-5 drone. https://t.co/FRBKZQR9lF pic.twitter.com/njPJWXsDwo — Special Kherson Cat (@bayraktar_1love) October 17, 2026 Mystery drone Bars isn't small. It likely packs an explosive warhead. Potentially one that the operator can remotely trigger when the interceptor passes near its target. Bars is adaptable. Its maker has reworked it from a 22-kg warhead and a 700-km range to a 60-kg warhead and a stated range of more than 1,000 km, and a heavier variant can carry a 105-kg warhead. In the air-to-air interceptor role, long range is terribly important but speed is everything. There's an obvious way for the Ukrainians to boost the Bars' speed from its reported 700 km/h top speed to potentially even faster. They could shrink the drone's warhead and its fuel load, making it lighter in order to make it faster. That may explain how a Bars can chase down a Geran-5 even as the Russians, by one Ukrainian analyst's estimate , try to push the Geran-5 toward 700 km/h or more. Explore further Turkey’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through Cost is important, too. Russia churns out Gerans for an estimated $100,000 or so per drone. The cheaper the drone, the more copies the Russians can fling at Ukrainian cities. If it takes three or more interceptor drones to take down each of those 2,700 jet Gerans, Ukraine may need to deploy 8,000 to 10,000 interceptors a month. Ukraine already builds more than 2,000 Bars a month, its maker says, but mostly in strike versions. How many go to air defense, and how much each costs, isn't public. The supply of small jet engines could be a constraint. “Engines are a key element; we really import them in large quantities,” Zelensky said in an interview with Financial Times . "There are also domestically produced engines, but there are not enough of them.” A Ukrainian-made engine for Bars passed final tests in September.

title: Russian strikes close plant of Ukraine’s biggest aid backer. Its 3,600 workers and millions in taxes now hang in balance
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia is now hitting the German investment that helps keep Ukraine’s economy running. Russian strikes have forced one of the Zhytomyr Oblast's largest employers, the German-invested Kromberg & Schubert plant, to shut down completely, putting 3,600 jobs at risk, the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration said . Germany is Ukraine’s single biggest partner by volume of security aid, providing about a third of all support the country receives, according to Ukraine. Russia’s destruction of a German-owned factory strikes at the economic ties Kyiv most depends on. The plant produced electrical onboard cable systems for world-class cars. Its closure will cost the region millions of hryvnias in tax revenue. Some of its workers may leave the country, while others move to company sites in other cities. Regional Administration Head Vitalii Bunechko said the plant’s management and owners are working out options for the workers’ future. The authorities also promise maximum support if a decision is made to restart operations. A war that now reaches every corner of the economy The factory is one loss in a campaign that has widened far beyond the front. Russia has escalated its drone and missile attacks through 2026, striking first at power plants and residential blocks, then trains, factories, retailer warehouses and medicine depots across Ukraine. Ukraine’s Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year, the same report noted. By late August, officials said Russia had destroyed about 90% of retail chains’ food logistics, a measure of how deep into civilian commerce the attacks now cut. The slow bleed on businesses that survive Even companies left standing lose working days to the strikes. Russia’s air war cost the average Ukrainian shopping mall 166.8 working days between 2022 and mid-2026, more than eight months of closed floors. For Zhytomyr, the Kromberg & Schubert shutdown turns that slow erosion into an outright closure, removing a budget-forming employer at a stroke.
