title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
body: Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found. The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters. "What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote. As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections. "HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities. "In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident or initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering. Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS." One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand. The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment. Hours after this article was published, Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee, wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand the that DHS immediately cease "law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway." He said the DHS operations "reflect an anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department, and serve only President Trump's voter suppression agenda, not a legitimate enforcement objective."For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters."It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University."And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that —  because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens. … Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear.""Target List"In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS. In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters. "Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally,"  said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law .""There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden. She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

title: Passkeys Attestation Trap
body:
Like the Trojan Horse, passkeys are legitimately elegant on the surface, but there is something troubling inside.
What’s important to know is that unlike with any other kind of login credential, you do not have ultimate control over your passkeys . With passwords, you can choose where to write them down; with authenticator apps, you can decide for yourself which ones to use (they’re pretty interchangeable); and with physical security keys you can hand them to your colleague if you really trust them. But with passkeys come a hidden dial that lets the websites you use them on gradually remove your ability to do as you please with them.
This is the feature that means you no longer get to make the calls about your passkeys. Fortunately, attested passkeys are not yet required on most websites. But the FIDO Alliance standard makes attestation a part of the passkey ecosystem, whether you want it or not. And even if the website doesn’t require attestation now, simply by using passkeys you indicate to the website that your setup supports the FIDO Alliance’s passkey standard and that you as a user are capable of using passkeys. This means that once Twitter (formally X) is satisfied that the overwhelming majority of its users would be unaffected, they can flip the switch – perhaps not all at once, perhaps just for ten thousand users at a time so as not to cause a fuss – and start rejecting non-attested passkeys.
My expectation is that the industry will start off with very few constraints on your passkeys, and gradually add more and more, not all at the same time, but staggered on different sites, and then in a few years people will forget that they were ever offered a choice in which security measures they want to enable on their passkeys (if they even knew there were different kinds of passkeys at all).
Remote attestation can allow them to verify that your device is not capable of, say, sending and receiving encrypted messages, or running a competitor’s app, or using social media without verifying your ID.
Apple’s passkey implementation currently does not support attestation , but it sounds like this is only until they can work out how to do syncing:
Attestation was designed to attest to a specific device, exclusively at the point of creation, with a specific set of security properties. It doesn’t make sense for synced credentials for a number of reasons, including syncing to devices with different security properties, changes in security properties that happen after key creation, security properties of the sync fabric, sharing the passkey, or exporting to other passkey providers. We’re working hard with W3C and FIDO to solve these problems.
The post is predicated on the idea that a feature of WebAuthn called “attestation”, which is only used in high-assurance and usually corporate scenarios, and usually with physical hardware security keys, will be leveraged to hurt people, somehow.
The post posits that a website like X will bait and switch users: first, you get a passkey. Then, later, scary “attested” passkeys! This simply isn’t possible to do because attestation isn’t supported on the web for mass market, consumer authentication.
Attestation for passkeys (software-based, syncable credentials) is antithetical to their mass market goals, and would freeze out independent, non-corporate-backed credential managers. It’s an explicit non-goal of the designers of passkeys, who work together in a forum anyone can join.
And trust me, websites and apps like banks repeatedly asked for attestation at the beginning of the industry’s passkey journey. The platforms, browsers, and credential management apps have held firm that the goal of passkeys is reducing phishing and not some kind of trusted computing scheme. (And I will note: over my dead body!)
I believe this is not the goal of Mondello and some of the others working on this, but so far I’ve not been convinced that they will be able to control it. It sounds like Apple is working on it, and once the technology is out there, what’s to prevent key sites from forcing it on users? It seems like all this would take is the cooperation of a few big credential managers. This would be to their benefit in the sense that it would make their products required. Smaller credential managers who resisted would be frozen out.
The fact that websites and apps have been asking for attestation just reinforces the main point of the passkeys post! Sure, browsers aren’t supporting it yet, but that’s the sort of thing that can change, and the sort of thing that has changed in the past. See the footnote on Widevine and Firefox. (“Currently not supported” is also very subject to change.)
And we already have sites and apps allowlisting passkey vendors. That’s no theoretical, slippery slope fear -- it’s a real restriction on user freedoms that’s already happening right now.
I don’t think that a couple of bad points (e.g. the TOTP thing) invalidate the main point of the post, because the post wasn’t an argument from authority. The author makes some good points that stand on their own.
To be clear, the websites have stopped asking for attestation. Or at least, they’ve stopped asking me. Why? Because they know there’s no use in asking — that the OS vendors, browsers, and passkey managers are unified on this front. And now they’ve seen firsthand that passkeys without attestation are awesome and a big step forward.
This is antithetical to users, as the types of authenticators that can pull this off are difficult to use (security keys). Companies with IT departments who can do account recovery for the user can handle this, an average user cannot. Synced passkeys are the answer to this for consumers and therefore attestation does not belong in the consumer space. Which is why password managers are in the spec groups pushing back against this every time it comes up.
If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that?
If you’re worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that’s worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn’t happened, the biggest providers don’t support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won’t protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.
It seems like rejecting passkeys is the only way the average user has to push back. The main thing protecting us is that sites don’t want to lock out their users who rely on passwords and 2FA. Once most people have adopted passkeys, if Apple and Google sell us out, I don’t think it matters much what the rest of the alliance thinks. Sites would be able to require attestation with the assurance that users could easily comply. Safari would probably opt everyone into attested passkeys, as it currently opts you into passkeys in general (unless you uncheck “Allow Automatic Passkey Upgrades”).
iOS iOS 27 Mac macOS 27 Golden Gate Passkeys Security Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
For all of the protestations to the contrary, about how passkeys are so great for preventing phishing and increasing password security they do seem to be a real trap that gives more power to corporations we have no control over and whose goals have been clearly shown not to align with users. Google is already using attestation to attack third party app stores and non-Google Android, I have zero confidence they would not do the same for passkeys.
Generally I think the passkey supporters are well meaning but naive when it comes to their belief that corporations wont try and use them as another means of exerting control over their customers. Just look at App Store and CTF/CTC in the EU, I strongly doubt Apple will remain on the side of the angels forever.
It’s kind of astounding that anyone who has paid even the slightest bit of attention over the past few decades (centuries? millennia?) would think that powerful institutions won’t take advantage of the ability to control and extract power from others when given even half a chance. If it is possible for them to gradually tighten the screws and extract more power and money, they will.
I don't use passkeys for this exact reason. Every single time there's a way to increase lock-in or interfere with open standards, these companies do it. It's not an *if* they do this, it's a *when* they do this. But only if we let passkeys get too popular
I guess I'm a useful idiot in that I take advantage of passkeys when available, but I store them in a KeePass database and KeePass is clearly on the side of the user. Of course I'll be against the wall when attestation means I can't do that anymore, at which point I (and BitWarden users too, presumably) will suddenly wake up and notice I've been boiled.
Ricky Mondello writing their own reputational epitaph there.
"Ricky, thanks for joining us. We've decided to make Passkeys into handcuffs" "Passkeys will become handcuffs over my dead body!" *bang* "ok, so next on the agenda"
As for why vendors have stopped asking Ricky to make passkeys into handcuffs... the obvious explanation is they're speaking to someone higher in the org.
I'm sorry, but all the anti passkey backlash is just conspiracy theories for technical people. Of course there are many things that *could* happen. A service could simply stop providing a website and require all access via apps, where they could do anything attestation does and more. But that doesn't mean it's going to happen.
We have seen over and over again how giving big companies the power to control something almost always leads them to trying to do so. For a long time Google androids attestation was also just a conspiracy and yet today Google is doing more and more to control android and prevent apps from working without Google’s approval. Any system where the specification allows for centralization of power is at risk and given the way the big companies who are pushing this have behaved in the last ten years it is quite clear they would like nothing better than yet another method to control us. Apple hasn’t released a new open platform since Mac OS X cheetah back in 2000… that’s 26 years of closing down competition and locking things down.
@Alex R Follow up. The conspiracy could have been avoided if they had made the spec explicit about interoperability, standardization, and exclusion of centralized attestation. They didn’t do any of that.
"Of course there are many things that *could* happen."
Experience shows that if companies *can* do something to lock people into their ecosystems and extract more money, they *will*. The only variable is how long it takes.
That's not a conspiracy theory. That's observable reality.
Over started experimenting with account free apps, and I find it surprising how nice it feels when things like "your two lists of books, plus your favorite podcasts and all the settings you've done in the app" are expected and imported via a rather tiny file.
And it saves me all the hassle of managing a user database.
Depressing prospect. The only way out is user-friendly regulation. Let's hope our elected representatives don't screw us over.
Another way out is to not support this. To build apps that aren't in the hands of a handful of SV companies run by craven old men. Up your things and leave. Make Enhsittification Resistant Software
Some people are seriously addicted to these platforms. For example, Gruber has now written multiple posts justifying his Twitter use, which clearly goes against his very public political opinions.
Just telling people to leave these platforms doesn't work. The underlying problem is a lack of antitrust regulation, which lets a small number of tech companies dictate these decisions to everyone else.
Plume: Gruber also recently wrote about how Apple contributed $25 million to the Trump ballroom and won't vote for any democratic candidate who won't promise to bulldoze it, but still buys all his computers from that same company that presented Trump with a gold trophy in the Oval Office.
We are all a mess of contradictions. Every tech product is one point in the infinitely-dimensioned potential product space. Every large organization is a complex mess of decisions and ideologies and relationships. Adam Smith and James Madison are long dead, and it's no longer possible to use our dollar or our vote to express precisely what we want.
> Just telling people to leave these platforms doesn't work. The underlying problem is a lack of antitrust regulation, which lets a small number of tech companies dictate these decisions to everyone else.
I 100% agree. But we as developers can start looking for alternate ways of doing things. Just as people are putting free time towards becoming Microsoft MVP they can experiment with foss solutions, interoperability etc.
We can chip in. We're not helpless. But absolutely stronger consumer protections and antitrust laws. Those are the ones that really will create change.
You guys are right, can’t help but agree. It’s a slippery slope.
>Safari would probably opt everyone into attested passkeys, as it currently opts you into passkeys in general (unless you uncheck “Allow Automatic Passkey Upgrades”).
Good reminder, thanks. Seems I have to opt out on each device, which may explain why some site (Google?) had decided "for me" (how nice) that I "want" to use a passkey.
I get the benefits of passkeys (including, for example, making phishing much harder), but they feel like a loss of user control+autonomy to me. I can scribble a password on a piece of paper. I _shouldn't_, but I can. I cannot meaningfully look at a passkey much less transport it without some intransparent API. It feels like a bridge too far.
We are not a "mess of contradictions." We are a "mess of monopolies" and a "mess of unenforced laws." Another way of saying this is just "corrupt."
I'm heartened to see that at least a large portion of the commenters here have their eyes open to the past 25 years of evidence: that if there's an opportunity to take more power and control, big tech always eventually does.
I find it truly disheartening, on the other hand, to see how naive these engineers seemingly are to the realities of the systems they work in and the downstream effects of the tools they're building..

title: Solzhenitsyn Statue Temporarily Returned to Original Vladivostok Site After Relocation Mishap
body:
Authorities in the Far Eastern port city of Vladivostok have temporarily returned a controversial monument to Nobel Prize-winning Soviet dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn to its original location after a failed attempt to relocate it.
The statue was dismantled from the waterfront promenade in central Vladivostok on Tuesday, with plans to place it in a nearby, smaller square.
However, on Wednesday, the Vladivostok city hall’s press service told Interfax that workers realized the statue was too large for the smaller square when attempting to install it there.
“The monument visually overloads the small recreational zone,” a press spokesperson was quoted as saying.
Officials confirmed that the Solzhenitsyn monument will remain at the original Ship Embankment until architects finish modifying the Faith and Hope Square, where it was intended to be moved. They did not provide a timeframe.
Solzhenitsyn, the Soviet Union’s most famous literary dissident who spent years in prison camps before being exiled to the United States, passed through Vladivostok when he returned back to Russia by plane in May 1994.
Some local activists have criticized the statue, which was installed in 2015, for depicting Solzhenitsyn stepping off a ship gangway.
Vladivostok’s city hall had agreed in March to move the Solzhenitsyn monument following complaints from the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet, which argued that a statue dedicated to a Soviet dissident was out of place on a waterfront reserved for World War II memorials and warships.

title: Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet Spotted Carrying New AIM-174B And AIM-260 Long-Range Missiles Together
body: A U.S. Navy F/A-18F Super Hornet assigned to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 31 (VX-31) has been spotted carrying both the AIM-174B and AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM) during a flight over Ridgecrest, California. This represents the first known publicly documented instance of these two advanced air-to-air weapons appearing on the same aircraft. The aircraft was photographed on October 14 by aviation photographer @photosxlyss2 , who shared the result with TWZ . The same Super Hornet was also carrying an IRST21 infrared search-and-track pod on its centerline station. A close-up of the AIM-174B, AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, and IRST21 infrared search-and-track pod under an F/A-18F Super Hornet assigned to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 31 (VX-31) during a flight over Ridgecrest, California. @photosxlyss2_ RY Two critical elements of the modernization of the U.S. military’s air-to-air missile arsenal, the AIM-174B and AIM-260 provide complementary capabilities, addressing different aspects of the Navy’s evolving air-combat requirements. Based on the SM-6 missile family, the AIM-174B provides the Navy with an extended-range air-to-air weapon. Its size and reach make it particularly relevant to engagements against high-value airborne assets, including aerial refueling tankers and airborne early warning and control aircraft . A U.S. Navy F/A-18F Super Hornet test jet with four AIM-174B missiles under its wings. point_mugu_skies Threatening these support platforms at extended distances complicates an adversary’s ability to sustain fighter operations, maintain airborne surveillance, and coordinate engagements across domains. Such targets are especially important in the Indo-Pacific, where distances are vast and combat aircraft may depend heavily on tanker support to reach and remain on station over contested areas. The range of this missile is classified but should be far in excess of that of the AIM-120D AMRAAM, probably in the hundreds of miles, as discussed in the video below. The AIM-174B has already appeared in several major exercises , including RIMPAC 2024 and Northern Edge 2025. Following developmental trials at RIMPAC, the weapon entered Live Fire Test and Evaluation in 2025. Some examples of the missile have since reached forward-deployed Navy squadrons in Japan. The AIM-260, meanwhile, is being developed to provide a next-generation beyond-visual-range air-to-air capability. It is intended to address increasingly sophisticated aerial threats and improve upon the capabilities of the very widely used AIM-120 Advanced Medium Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM) family. It was another F/A-18F from VX-31 on which the AIM-260 was first publicly seen when departing Eglin Air Force Base in Florida in May of this year. The same type of weapon has since also appeared on a Royal Australian Air Force F/A-18F, as you can read about here . An F/A-18F from VX-31 carrying the AIM-260. Jonathan Tweedy/ @flightline_visuals The AIM-260’s precise specifications remain classified, but it is designed to deliver significantly greater range than the AIM-120 AMRAAM while maintaining a broadly similar form factor. Its compact design is important, as the missile is intended for both external carriage and internal carriage aboard aircraft such as the F-22 Raptor and F-35 . A rendering depicting an F-22 Raptor firing an AIM-260 JATM. U.S. Air Force The AIM-260 is being developed to counter the growing long-range air-to-air threat posed by China’s PL-15 and other advanced missiles . Although no official range figures have been disclosed, previous reporting has indicated a target range of at least 120 miles, with the potential to reach considerably farther. Inert PL-15s in the weapons bay of a Chinese J-20 fighter. via Chinese internet It is unclear when the first operational AIM-260s may begin entering the U.S. inventory. Together, however, the two weapons give the Super Hornet access to a broader range of engagement options, depending not only on the range of the target, but also on the nature of the engagement and overall tactical situation. The presence of an IRST21 pod is also noteworthy. The infrared search-and-track system passively detects and tracks airborne targets rather than relying exclusively on radar emissions. Passive sensing is especially valuable in environments where electromagnetic emissions must be managed carefully. Although an IRST system does not automatically provide all the information needed to support a long-range missile engagement, it can contribute to a broader sensor picture and potentially help crews detect targets without immediately revealing their own position through radar emissions. After a long and troubled development , a full-rate production contract for Block II IRST21 sensors to go into pods for U.S. Navy and U.S. Air National Guard fighters was awarded this time last year, as you can read about here . An IRST21 built into the centerline tank on a Super Hornet during early tests. U.S. Navy The appearance of both missiles on a VX-31 Super Hornet is a notable development in the Navy’s ongoing testing of advanced air-combat capabilities. VX-31, based at the sprawling Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake in California, conducts test and evaluation activities involving naval aviation weapons and systems. On this occasion, the jet is carrying inert missiles (denoted by their blue bands) in a captive-carry configuration. The flight may have been part of ongoing weapons-integration testing, handling and compatibility evaluations, or another test activity. At the very least, the configuration offers an intriguing glimpse into how a Navy Super Hornet might go into battle in a future high-end air combat scenario. Pairing the extended-range AIM-174B with the next-generation AIM-260 would provide a powerful combination. Added to those two will be the AIM-424 Malice , an all-new, very long-range air-to-air missile, the existence of which was only disclosed in August of this year. This is reportedly a two-stage design, which should result in extreme range — said to be in excess of 250 nautical miles — and very high speed. It isn’t known where Malice slots in next to the AIM-174B, although the newer missile is purpose-designed for air launch, unlike the Standard-derived weapon. Four AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missiles (LRAAM) are loaded on an F/A-18E Super Hornet for a test event. U.S. Navy U.S. Navy As the service prepares for increasingly demanding scenarios in the Indo-Pacific, the new photo underscores the fact that the ability to threaten a wider range of targets at greater distances is one of the key considerations in the evolution of the Navy’s carrier-based fighter force. With thanks to @photosxlyss2_ ; check out more of her work via PhotosxLyss on Facebook . Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet Spotted Carrying New AIM-174B And AIM-260 Long-Range Missiles Together appeared first on TWZ .

title: US imposes new sanctions on Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 21 (MNA) – The U.S. Department of the Treasury has imposed new sanctions on Iran as part of its continued hostile measures against the country.
In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the Treasury Department announced that the new Iran-related sanctions target five individuals, four companies, and nine vessels.
According to reports, the U.S. Treasury Department also extended its general license for the sale of Russian oil giant Lukoil’s foreign assets until November 21.

title: Navy offers explosive ordnance disposal warfare officers up to $100,000 in bonuses
body: The U.S. Navy announced Tuesday that it is offering sizable financial incentives to service members who neutralize explosive devices in a bid to retain their services. Explosive ordnance disposal warfare lieutenants with six years of commissioned service and lieutenant commanders with 10 years of commissioned service are eligible for bonuses of up to $100,000. Both ranks can commit to a 2-year or 4-year contract with different payment plans. Lieutenants who sign up for the 4-year contract bonus receive a $100,000 retention bonus and must complete the EOD Department Head Qualified training by 8 years of commissioned service. Lieutenants can also opt for a 2-year contract bonus, netting $12,500 annually, with the possibility of another two-year bonus worth the same amount at eight years of commissioned service. This track would ensure $50,000 in bonuses. The Navy is offering lieutenant commanders $100,000 in retention bonuses if they sign a 4-year contract after notching 10 years of commissioned service. They can also instead sign up for a 2-year contract after those 10 years, with a $15,000 annual payment. If they re-up the 2-year contract at 12 years, they are eligible for the same yearly payment until they reach 14 years of commissioned service. Eligible officers can submit an application through their commanding officer for the retention bonus within one year of being eligible. The officer must submit a copy of their original signed contract and commanding officer approval to the Bureau of Naval Personnel for consideration. The Navy has recently devoted its explosive ordnance resources to Arctic training, as the U.S. and allied nations focus on defending the frozen terrain from Chinese and Russian infiltration. U.S. sailors worked alongside Swedish and Norwegian troops during February’s Arctic Specialist 26 exercise to destroy explosives underwater and on land.

title: Any Decision To Buy New-Build F-16s Not An “Urgent” Priority: USAF
body: The U.S. Air Force says any decision on whether or not to acquire new production F-16 Viper fighters is likely a year or more away. The service’s top officer in charge of force structure planning has also now raised the prospect of using a “spectrum of capability” to eventually supplant aging older-model F-16s. All of this comes as the Air Force has laid out a new vision to have 1,509 combat-coded fighters in inventory, hundreds more than it has now, by 2035, amid questions about whether industry and budgets can keep up. Inside Defense and Air & Space Forces Magazine were among the first to report on the Air Force’s latest long-term fighter force structure plan late yesterday. This followed a roundtable with Lt. Gen. David Tabor, the service’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Plans and Programs. At the time of writing, an unclassified copy of the report, which was submitted to Congress last week, has not been released publicly. TWZ has reached out for more information. Air Force Lt. Gen. David Tabor, seen here testifying before the Senate Armed Services Committee in 2024. USAF Tabor said yesterday that the target fleet of 1,509 combat-coded fighters by 2035 would be approximately 40 percent F-35s , 40 percent F-15s (inclusive of F-15E Strike Eagles and F-15EX Eagle IIs ) and F-16s, and 20 percent F-22 Raptors and F-47s , according to Air & Space Forces Magazine . As an aside, the final expected F-47 fleet size remains unclear, though the Air Force continues to say it plans to acquire at least enough of those jets to replace its 185 F-22s on a one-for-one basis. The current breakdown of the service’s fighter force structure is 45 percent F-16s, 30 percent F-35s, 15 percent F-15s, and 10 percent F-22s. Last year’s long-term fighter force structure report said the service was aiming for an eventual inventory of 1,558 combat-coded fighters and hoped to hit a milestone of 1,369 aircraft by Fiscal Year 2030. As of the start of Fiscal Year 2026, the Air Force had 1,168 combat-coded fighters, not including 103 A-10 Warthog ground attack jets , which have been part of this force structure planning in the past. The plan now is for the last of the A-10s to be retired by 2030 . The new 2035 figure also does not include the hundreds of Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drones the service wants to have acquired by that time, something we will come back to later on. The US Air Force included these graphs showing projected fluctuations in fighter inventories in its annual force structure report last year. Not that the combat-coded tally for Fiscal Year 2030 shown here is lower (1,304) than the one the service said it was aiming for (1,369) at the time. The reason for that discrepancy is unclear. USAF Currently, the Air Force expects fighter fleet expansion to be driven by the acquisition of new F-35As, F-15EXs, and F-47s. This was also the case when last year’s fighter force structure report was released. The possibility of the Air Force also acquiring new-production F-16s has come up several times in recent years. Most recently, there were several reports last month that prime contractor Lockheed Martin had made a new pitch to the service for a version of the latest Block 70 version of the fighter, tentatively dubbed the F-16G . New Block 70 and Block 72 F-16s , which differ in what engine they use, are being actively produced at Lockheed Martin’s plant in Greenville, South Carolina . At that time, TWZ did a deep dive into the benefits that this could offer the Air Force. The new-production F-16D seen here, destined for Morocco, became the first Block 72 version to fly just earlier this month. Lockheed Martin “There is a spectrum of capability that we might want to replace the F-16s with,” Lt. Gen. Tabor said amid a discussion about the prospect of acquiring new Vipers at the roundtable yesterday, per Air & Space Forces Magazine . “It’s not urgent, frankly. What we don’t want to get to is a point where it is urgent, and we haven’t done the homework and decided ‘hey, this is really the right place to be.’ We do have time to churn through that and make sure that we have a good option going forward.” “We’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately,” Tabor added, while acknowledging that “we are very conscious” that older-model F-16s are set to begin reaching the end of their lifespans in the 2030s. He also said any such planning was unlikely to be part of the process of developing the service’s Fiscal Year 2028 budget proposal, which will be released sometime early next year. The Air Force is “in the initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program ,” a spokesperson for the service had told us last month without specifically mentioning any particular type of aircraft. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.” When it comes to the current F-16 fleet, the Air Force had 774 Vipers in inventory at the start of Fiscal Year 2026 and expected that number to drop to 768, according to past budget documents. This includes a mixture of subvariants, and not all of them are assigned combat-coded units. The Air Force has been substantially upgrading at least a portion of its existing F-16s, including with the addition of new active electronically scanned array (AESA) radars and electronic warfare suites , to ensure their operational relevance for years to come. A new AN/APG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar (SABR), an active electronically scanned array type, seen being integrated onto a US Air Force F-16. USAF The Air Force has also already been taking newer F-16s from squadrons transitioning to the F-35 and using them to replace older Vipers in other units. Last year’s fighter force structure report explicitly highlighted plans to supplant Block 30 F-16s in five Air National Guard formations – three combat-coded squadrons and two training units – with Block 40 and 50 types in this way. As we’ve previously written : “A new F-16 offers a fresh and highly mature airframe — one with a full service-life ahead of it, on the order of 12,000 flight hours without the need for structural upgrades — double that of the original F-16. This is compared to existing F-16s in the inventory with the decades of wear and fatigue already accumulated on them, with structural upgrades keeping them in the air. That difference in remaining structural life is arguably the single biggest advantage a new-build aircraft has compared with extending an existing one.” “Dumping more money into existing F-16s is becoming questionable. Service life extensions and technical upgrades can only go so far and supporting these jets is becoming harder as parts dry up and suppliers who made them are long gone. A new airframe would give the Guard many decades of highly efficient service and the piece of mind for future force planning that goes with it.” … “The new [F-16G] proposal would let some Guard and Reserve units swap their F-16s for vastly improved F-16s — the same logic that drove the F-15EX buy — while also keeping the Greenville line hot, which is a significant benefit in its own right. And it accomplishes both in the most efficient way possible: not just in acquisition cost, but in sustainment cost, which is really the more problematic burden of the two. In the end, this points to another glaring reality check for the all-stealth-force concept, a vision the Air Force has effectively already abandoned.” A row of Texas Air National Guard F-16s. USAF “The Air Force has spent years describing the F-35 as the replacement for its F-16 fleet, yet it now has to contend with aging F-16s, delayed or constrained fighter production, a larger stated requirement for total fighter capacity, and the lengthy transition toward the F-47 and uncrewed combat aircraft. In that environment, a new-build F-16 provides an option that sits between extending legacy aircraft and buying the most sophisticated — and expensive — fighters available.” You can read our full prior deep analysis on this topic here . Lt. Gen. Tabor acknowledged many of these exact same points at the roundtable yesterday. He notably described acquiring new F-16s as “maybe the lazy” option, but also one that would benefit from “practically a ready-made aircraft” that is in production now, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine . “The question is, can industry produce at those levels?” he also said, speaking more generally. “They’ve assured us that they can, and we believe them, but we also actually need to see it manifest.” In the context of acquiring new F-16s, especially, it is important to note here that Lockheed Martin order books are very full already as a result of demand for these fighters from U.S. allies and partners. The company’s capacity, at least at present, to add a substantial new Air Force acquisition program on top of that is a real question. This, in some ways, mirrors questions that surround Boeing efforts to meet surging Air Force demand for F-15EXs . A new F-16 being built at Lockheed Martin’s Greenville plant. Lockheed Martin On top of all this, the Air Force’s still-evolving CCA plans remain something of a wildcard in these discussions. The Air Force has ordered General Atomics FQ-42 Vengeance and Anduril’s FQ-44 Fury CCAs into production , and is now aiming to have a combined fleet of at least 500 of these drones in inventory by 2032. The service is also still expecting to acquire additional CCAs, which could be of entirely different types, through a second iterative development cycle, or Increment 2, under this program. This is influencing the service’s crewed fighter force structure plans, but the full scale and scope of those impacts remain to be seen. An F-35A flies in formation with a pre-production YFQ-42A CCA drone. USAF “CCA is very much a reality,” Tabor said yesterday, per Air & Space Forces Magazine . “It is going to be a part of our future, and there is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters. That’s not the CCA that we have right now, but it is advancing very, very rapidly. We’re confident that it will play a major role in future versions of the fighter force structure report.” The Air Force’s F-22s are currently set to be its first ‘aerial quarterbacks’ for CCAs , with F-35s and F-47s expected to follow. At the same time, TWZ has highlighted previously how CCA could offer particular value when paired with fourth-generation fighters like the F-16. This, in turn, could actually bolster the case for new Viper acquisitions as a more affordable force multiplier. A pre-production YFQ-44A Fury drone flies in formation with an F-35. USAF The Air Force’s ability to secure necessary funding and other factors will play in all this, too. 2035 is a long way off from a budgetary perspective. It also stretches across multiple election cycles, including the one that will decide the next presidential administration, all of which could lead to major changes in defense spending priorities. Congress can and routinely does demand that the U.S. military alter major procurement plans. Just in the past two years or so, legislators have intervened to force the Air Force to move ahead with the acquisition of new E-7A Wedgetail airborne early warning and control planes and to save the U.S. Navy F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter program . In the meantime, the Air Force clearly faces many continued questions about how to balance the need to modernize its fighter fleets while ensuring it retains enough tactical airpower to meet current and future operational demands. Even so, the service says it sees no need to rush to make a decision about whether to choose the “lazy” route of just buying new F-16s. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post Any Decision To Buy New-Build F-16s Not An “Urgent” Priority: USAF appeared first on TWZ .

Inside the same city, a single account spent two years pumping out nearly 100,000 posts in Russia’s favor. Ukraine’s Security Service has served notices of suspicion on six more pro-Kremlin agitators across the country, among them the Kyiv woman behind those posts, which included calls to kill Ukrainians, the agency said . Social media has become a channel for spreading hatred during the war, and the scale is striking. Except for Russian narratives, the Kyiv suspect also incited violence against a national minority and called for destroying the churches of religious communities, the agency said. Six accounts, one message from the Kremlin The others span the country. The sweep continues a long campaign against homegrown pro-Russian propagandists. title: Sudan Founding Alliance ‘Tasees’ claims 21 civilians killed in West Kordofan airstrikes
body: The RSF-alligned Sudan Founding Alliance (Tasees) has accused the Sudanese Armed Forces of carrying out strikes that killed 16 people in El Odaiya and five more in Abu Zabad, West Kordofan. According to Tasees, 16 civilians, including two women, were killed in a drone strike on El Odaiya on Tuesday evening. The alliance identifies the aircraft as a Turkish-made Baykar Bayraktar Akıncı drone (see photo) operated by the SAF and says several other people were wounded. Turkish-made Baykar Bayraktar Akıncı drone (File photo: Azerbajani Air Force / CC BY 4.0) In a separate statement seen by Radio Dabanga, Tasees’s official spokesperson attributes a second airstrike, on Abu Zabad, to the SAF and says it killed five people, including a child. The alliance condemns the attacks, describing them as a disregard for local and international appeals to halt strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure. It says the attacks are worsening the suffering of Sudanese people and increasing the humanitarian cost of the war. Tasees calls for investigation Tasees calls on the United Nations, relevant international and regional organisations, and human rights mechanisms to launch an urgent, independent, and transparent investigation into the reported attacks, particularly the latest strike on El Odaiya. The alliance urges investigators to establish the circumstances of the attacks, verify the casualty figures, and identify those responsible. It also calls for effective measures to protect civilians in West Kordofan, and other areas affected by the war, and to halt airstrikes that threaten their lives and safety. Tasees says evidence should be collected and preserved, the names of those killed documented, and survivors’ testimonies recorded to prevent the facts from being obscured or victims being denied their rights. The alliance calls for anyone found responsible for violations to face legal accountability, stressing that impunity must not be allowed. It warns that continued attacks amid international silence, or a response limited to expressions of concern and condemnation, would entrench impunity and encourage further violations. Radio Dabanga has approached the SAF for comment. title: Russia’s Supreme Court allows father to keep daughter taken to Russia without permission, citing France’s ‘unfriendly’ status and NATO membership
body: Russia’s Supreme Court has ruled that a Russian man does not have to return his daughter to her mother in France, even though he took the child to Russia without permission, Kommersant reported. The case concerns Veronika Tishkova, a Ukrainian citizen who married Russian citizen Alexey Yermakov in 2018. They lived in Kyiv, where their daughter was born. The couple divorced in 2021, and the child stayed with her mother. Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, Tishkova moved to France with her 3-year-old daughter, while Yermakov remained in Ukraine. In June 2023, he asked a Kyiv court to order his former wife to bring their daughter to Ukraine every six weeks. The court denied his request. Yermakov also took legal action against his former wife in France. In April 2024, he consented to the child’s living permanently in France. The following March, he asked for permission to take his daughter on vacation to Turkey and Slovakia, promising the court he would return her in two weeks. He did not. It soon emerged that he had taken the child to Russia. In July 2025, Tishkova asked a court in Novosibirsk to order her daughter’s return. During the proceedings, the girl was granted Russian citizenship at her father’s request. The court nevertheless sided with Tishkova and ordered Yermakov to return the child to France under the Hague Convention. Higher courts rejected Yermakov’s appeals. He then appealed to Russia’s Supreme Court, which ruled in his favor in July 2026. The court found that the girl had adjusted to life in Russia and that moving to France could therefore adversely affect her. It cited an article of the Hague Convention that allows courts to refuse to return a child “if there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm.” The court also said the girl has Russian citizenship and that France is an “unfriendly” country and a member of NATO and the European Union. Tishkova challenged the ruling, which is now under review by the Supreme Court’s Presidium. Her lawyer, Dmitry Litvinsky, said the Supreme Court had “put its own political interpretation of the situation above the applicable law.” Andrey Targashov, Yermakov’s lawyer, said the court’s position was “in line with international practice.” At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. title: Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña”
body: Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña” Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña” or “JL,” was the charismatic leader of the Choneros , which, for years, was Ecuador’s most enterprising and powerful criminal group. Rasquiña oversaw the group’s transformation from a localized criminal group into a nationwide prison-based criminal federation with links to transnational drug-trafficking organizations. He was assassinated in 2020. What’s in this profile: What Is Rasquiña’s Story? What Were Rasquiña’s Main Criminal Activities? Where Did Rasquiña Operate? Who Were Rasquiña’s Allies and Enemies? What Is Rasquiña’s Legacy? What Is Rasquiña’s Story? Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña” or “JL,” was born in Manta , in Ecuador’s Manabí province around 1981 . Little is known about his early criminal career, but in the early 2000s , he became associated with Jorge Bismarck Véliz España , alias “Teniente España” or “El Chonero.” España’s gang, the Choneros , whose name was a nod to its leader’s hometown in Chone, initially operated in and around Manta, where they were involved in small-time criminal activities like robberies and drug peddling. After Teniente España was killed in 2007, several potential leaders were on deck to replace him, among them Rasquiña, But police operations took out many of the other contenders, leaving Rasquiña as the group’s top leader, with his friend and criminal ally José Adolfo Macías Villamar, alias “Fito” by his side. After the two were arrested and charged with murder in 2011, they were sent to La Roca maximum security prison. In 2013, Rasquiña engineered a Hollywood-style escape with Fito and 16 other inmates. Rasquiña remained on the run for nine months but was eventually recaptured in Bogotá, Colombia . After he was returned to prison in Ecuador, Rasquiña began to co-opt smaller gangs of bank robbers, extortionists, and microtraffickers whose leaders were in the prisons, bringing them under the umbrella of the Choneros. It was a revolutionary strategy. Through these strategic alliances, Rasquiña gradually transformed the Choneros into a federation. With time, the network took over most of the prison system,then began expanding into important territories outside prison walls. It soon became the main drug transport group for transnational criminal organizations looking to use Ecuador as a springboard to reach the United States and the burgeoning European market. But the Choneros had competition both inside and outside the prisons, most notably the Lagartos. Rasquiña launched a war in 2019 against the rival group, murdering the Lagartos’ leaders and members over the course of more than a year. In June 2020, Rasquiña was released from prison following an allegedly corrupt court ruling. In December, while shopping with his wife and daughter in a Manta shopping center, he was gunned down. His death sparked an explosion of violence as the Choneros’ criminal federation atomized, propelling Ecuador into a wave of unprecedented violence. What Were Rasquiña’s Main Criminal Activities? The Choneros, under Rasquiña’s command, became the key service providers for transnational drug traffickers in Ecuador. The Choneros were also involved in a range of criminal activities, including extortion, robbery, kidnapping, murder-for-hire, and money laundering. Under Rasquiña’s command, the Choneros also leveraged their control over prisons into a lucrative criminal business, charging prisoners for access to basic services, including food, and overseeing the sale of contraband liquor, cigarettes, and other vital goods. Where Did Rasquiña Operate? While the Choneros’ traditional stronghold is in the coastal province of Manabí, under Rasquiña’s leadership the group expanded its influence across Ecuador. Rasquiña coordinated the expansion of the Choneros in the prison system, where they took control of most of the wings in the country’s main penitentiaries. Law enforcement repeatedly attempted to break up prison gangs by relocating gang leaders and dangerous inmates to other penitentiaries, but ultimately this led to gangs like the Choneros extending their presence to more prisons. Using the other gangs he had allied with, Rasquiña successfully expanded the group’s control into the streets. In the first phase of expansion, the Choneros prioritized two strategic provinces that served as primary dispatch corridors for transnational drug trafficking: Esmeraldas in the north and Guayaquil in the south. Who Were Rasquiña’s Allies and Enemies? Rasquiña’s closest ally was José Adolfo Macías Villamar, alias “Fito,” who acted as his principal lieutenant and later became the Choneros’ leader after Rasquiña’s death. Rasquiña also cultivated relationships with other gang bosses who would go on to become key figures in the Ecuadorian underworld. Among them were Wilmer Chavarría Barré, alias “Pipo,” top leader of the Lobos; William Joffre Alcívar Bautista, alias “Negro Willy,” who founded the Tiguerones ; Junior Roldán, alias “JR,” who established a group called the Águilas; and Terry Israel Camacho, alias “Trompudo,” who formed the Chone Killers . Rasquiña also fostered connections with Mexico’s Sinaloa Cartel . His enemies’ list was just as long. Early in Rasquiña’s criminal career, the Choneros principal enemies were the Queseros, a rival gang from Manta that was allegedly responsible for the murder of Teniente España in 2007. During the Choneros’ expansion, the group famously feuded with rival gang leader William Poveda Salazar, alias “El Cubano,” who first led his own gang known as Los Cubanos that eventually merged into the Lagartos . El Cubano was murdered in prison by the Choneros, but the Lagartos remains one of the Choneros main rivals. Rasquiña’s rivals also included many of his one-time allies. Among the list of suspects for Rasquiña’s murder, which remains unsolved, are Lobos leader Pipo and Rasquiña’s own top lieutenant, Fito , who is purported to have staged a mutiny before taking over the Choneros after Rasquiña was murdered. What Is Rasquiña’s Legacy? Rasquiña’s most important legacy is his federated organized crime model. Under this model, different criminal groups retained their organization’s names, and leaders maintained their operational autonomy, even while they recognized the authority of the Choneros leadership. Rasquiña could therefore assemble a large criminal force without having to directly administer every affiliated group. Rasquiña also helped pioneer the use of the prisons as criminal centers of operations. He achieved this by transforming the prisons into hugely lucrative criminal economies in and of themselves. That buildup of criminal forces unleashed an unprecedented wave of violence in Ecuador. And while Rasquiña was known for his ability to manage a complex coalition, ultimately his legacy may be more closely associated with the brutal gang wars that followed his murder. The post Jorge Luis Zambrano, alias “Rasquiña” appeared first on InSight Crime .

title: Meta ordered to pay $25B penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
body:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

title: Google Cloud now offers OpenAI models alongside Gemini and Claude, becoming the only major provider with all three
body:
Google Cloud is now the only major cloud provider offering Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI models on one platform. Three OpenAI models are available starting today : GPT-6 Astra for demanding tasks like coding and research, GPT-6.1 Sol as a cheaper alternative with similar performance, and GPT-6 Luna as a fast, cost-efficient option for everyday use.
The models launch as a private preview for select enterprise customers, with sign-ups open now . They'll also appear in Gemini for Business and Google Antigravity. All charges run through a single Google Cloud bill and count toward existing contracts. Google says customer data won't be used for training.
The move highlights a recurring tension at Google: compute capacity spent serving cloud customers strengthens the biggest rivals of its own Gemini team. This resource conflict reportedly even pushed two-billion-dollar researcher Noam Shazeer back to OpenAI. Ad Ad

title: Ukraine Counts on Beijing’s ‘Constructive Role’ as Sybiha Meets Chinese Ambassador
body:
As the Kremlin claimed China is already preparing a trilateral summit with Russia and the US, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met Beijing’s ambassador in Kyiv to discuss further steps Beijing could take toward a just peace.
The meeting focused largely on reviving bilateral dialogue ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Political contacts and visits, as well as additional coordination in international organizations, growing trade and wider access to the Chinese market for Ukrainian goods were also on the agenda.
“The Ukrainian side is counting on Beijing to play a constructive role,” the ministry said, adding that Sybiha thanked the ambassador and his staff for continuing work in Kyiv despite daily large-scale Russian attacks.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov claimed that China was already preparing a meeting among the Russian, US and Chinese leaders. The idea was reportedly brought up during talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and senior US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on the same day. None of the three capitals had rejected it.
“The hosts of the APEC summit will take charge – or rather, are already taking charge – of the preparations,” Ushakov said according to Interfax-Russia on Wednesday.
“And, should circumstances prove favorable, they – our Chinese friends – will certainly incorporate this meeting into the program of events in Shenzhen,” he continued.
Neither Washington nor Beijing has publicly confirmed this account, and Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning previously said on Oct. 19 that China has no information on the rumored trilateral meeting .
Meanwhile, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned against excluding Ukraine on Tuesday, Oct. 20, insisting Kyiv must participate in any talks concerning its sovereignty and the war’s outcome.
According to the Wall Street Journal on Oct. 19, Putin first proposed the format during an Oct. 9 telephone call with US President Donald Trump, hoping to settle the war with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on terms favorable to Moscow.
During that same telephone discussion, Trump struck a controversial diesel deal with Russia that led to a week of escalated tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit will be held in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19, Bloomberg reported, noting that the Russian president rarely travels abroad because of security concerns – primarily Western sanctions and a 2023 International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant.
However, he plans to attend the summit in person for the first time since 2017.
Ushakov also said, according to Russian state-owned media TASS , that Putin told Witkoff Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US in November.
Moscow wants the talks to focus on postwar security arrangements for Russia and Ukraine, he said.
Witkoff had arrived with documents outlining approaches to ending the war, developed during his talks with Zelensky, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb in Oslo, Norway on Oct. 20. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin would review the proposals, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov ruled out political concessions.
Although China presented itself as neutral in Russia’s war, its military and economic ties with Russia have continued to deepen since the full-scale invasion was launched in 2022.
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) told Kyiv Post in July that more than 550 Chinese service members have trained at Russian military institutions, while over 180 Russian troops completed similar internships in China in November 2025 alone.
China was also the largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in August, at €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion), according to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air ( CREA ).
Cut off from Western technology by the European sanctions, Russia has increasingly turned to Chinese suppliers.
Chinese components, including turbo-jet engines, have helped Moscow build faster Shahed-type drones that are significantly harder for Ukraine to intercept due to their speed, able to reach 400-600 kilometers per hour (250-370 miles per hour).
On Oct. 16, The Insider reported that Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, a Chinese company, offered to supply nearly $2.9 million worth of communications equipment for attack drones, potentially helping Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operate deeper inside Ukraine.
The offer included 500 mesh modems to a factory in Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone.
Days prior, Zelensky warned that Beijing is assisting Russia’s efforts in building their own domestic Starlink rival, “ Rassvet .” The system, still under development, could strengthen military communications, reconnaissance capabilities, and long-range drone operations.
“It is a pity that China is not on our side in this war – politically. It is not even about weapons,” Zelensky said on Sept. 17, noting that Beijing has enough influence to push Putin to the negotiating table , but chooses not to.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: China Maritime Report #59: Be Focused, Be Humble, Be Happy: Career Progression, Organization, and Training of PLAN Submariners
body:
Led by the political commissar with the commanding officer serving as deputy, party committees are responsible for major decision-making, maintaining party control, training, and general leadership aboard People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) submarines. While Chinese sources extoll this collective leadership model, it is unclear how this command structure influences decision-making efficacy in practice.
PLAN political officers play a critical role in the leadership and decision making on PLAN submarines, but reportedly lack understanding of submarine operations. Despite attempts to improve the operational competency of political officers, this likely remains a problem for the PLAN submarine force.
The diverse PLAN submarine fleet and its increasingly ambitious operations require a high degree of technical competency within the submarine force. Recent reforms to the career structure of technical officers can be seen as efforts to retain increasingly needed technical expertise in the PLA, in part to meet this requirement.
According to PLA media reporting, the PLAN has made progress in expanding educational and career opportunities for NCOs, while enhancing their professionalization and technical competence with updated policies aimed at recruiting more college educated NCOs.
PLAN submarines’ apparent lack of a dedicated “supply department” may pose challenges to the submarine force’s ability to become a true “far seas protection” force. The PLAN is attempting to address this via technology investments at Shore Service Departments.
The U.S. submarine force uses lessons learned from incidents and accidents not only to enhance operations but also as a training tool. In contrast, the PLA treats accidents and near misses primarily as opportunities to promote the importance of political commissars in military decision making, while prioritizing party loyalty and propaganda value over genuine learning. While public discussions in Chinese media about submarine accidents and incidents are scarce, those that do exist reveal a clear focus on using such events for political messaging.
The PLAN submarine force has invested in simulators and training systems to enable its crews to exercise operational skills and maintain qualifications. In recent years, this has included more advanced technologies including virtual reality systems that permit some levels of training without as much physical infrastructure.

title: Some of Ukraine’s artillery soldiers were TikTokers yesterday, ComBat Vision says. Their new plugin teaches them to aim
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine receives Western weapons, but the code that teaches soldiers to aim them is increasingly its own. Developers of the Ukrainian battlefield reconnaissance and coordination system ComBat Vision have released a new plugin that turns the abstract math of artillery fire into a visual tool, letting crews simulate firing and learn to adjust it, the team says . The developers built the tool around a problem they name plainly: the quality of specialists entering the military is falling rapidly. “Artillery soldiers are sometimes yesterday’s TikTokers or "tanks" players,” the team explain, so the plugin makes firing and aiming as visual as possible to teach indirect fire quickly. On screen, it draws a round’s flight path from the weapon’s firing tables and the dispersion ellipse for that gun and munition, warns of obstacles on the calculated trajectory, and simulates the shell after the shot with a training error added. It then shows real or simulated bursts, averages the correction across a series of hits, and lets the user enter corrections, including by voice, and watch the result. The plugin draws its ballistics from MyGun, an app by Yaroslav Sherstiuk that automates ballistic and fire calculations for artillery. ComBat Vision itself coordinates troops and shares object data, integrating with optical sensors such as drones, ground robots and security cameras to fix targets in space. From a single app to a platform with a plugin store ComBat Vision’s bigger move is becoming a platform rather than a single app. The developers say they will open a plugin store within a week, where units can download the new artillery feature and others, such as repeater-coverage calculations and remote control of minefields. The team has announced plans to open it, not results from using it, so its payoff, letting one platform add new tools without building a separate system each time, is a claim to watch rather than a proven gain.
