title: Don't throw it all away: Caching an immediate-mode UI
body:
How Blick’s UI Painter keeps the pixels it has already rendered, combines shapes and opacity groups, and saves work behind an immediate-mode UI.
One common criticism of immediate-mode UI is that it repeats work. The application reconstructs its description of the interface each frame, even though much of the interface may be unchanged. The apparent tradeoff is simplicity of the programming model at the cost of repeated work.
I would like to show that this is not necessarily the case.
One straightforward rebuttal is that modern computers are really fast. If rebuilding the UI takes a millisecond at most, how much should we care?
And if you really dislike the idea of repeating work, then the simplest solution I can think of is to put your application to sleep when nothing is happening. This is what all immediate-mode desktop apps that I know of already do and is something that presumably suffices in many cases. It is also very easy to implement.
The story could end there as far as I am concerned, but things become less clear when we consider power usage. You may want your application to run nicely on laptops, phones, and tablets without draining the battery more than necessary. Furthermore, modern displays tend to have high resolutions and high refresh rates, which exacerbate this problem. A blinking cursor, a moving playhead, or an animated control can prevent the application from sleeping and keep the interface updating while almost everything else stays unchanged.
At the same time, we want room to make visual design choices: translucent panels, animated controls, and dense layouts should all be things the renderer can accommodate.
For Blick, we have a dense interface that contains thousands of such elements, both big and small. Rendering it shares the machine with media processing and other applications.
The basic approach we ended up with is to attach a cache to the rendering side of that system. The UI can describe the whole interface again while the renderer retains the pixels it has already produced and repaints only the parts whose rendering inputs changed.
Reconstructing the UI and repainting its pixels are separate kinds of work. An immediate-mode frontend can coexist with a renderer that remembers its previous output.
That is what I would like to showcase here.
We have some measurements to go with that. In a short scripted light-editing test on an unplugged M3 MacBook Pro, the macOS CPU and GPU power estimates together were about 20% lower with caching. I will get into what we can conclude from it below.
This post focuses on the current Metal backend where specific measurements or examples are required. But all the same things apply to our other backends as well: how the cache works, and how a small rendering language interpreted on the GPU makes it possible.
Imagine hovering over a button in a window. The button changes its color to indicate that it is hovered and clickable. Nothing else in the window changes. We may rebuild the UI tree and emit a stream of drawing commands for the whole window based on that tree, but most of those commands still describe the same things in the same places. It would be nice to keep the pixels we already have for those parts.
To do this, the renderer, or the painter as we like to call it, splits the window into tiles and finds the commands that can affect each one. We calculate a hash from those commands, including their order, and compare it with the hash from the previous frame. If it matches, we keep the pixels. Otherwise, we paint that tile again.
The nice thing about doing this in the renderer is that the UI system doesn't have to keep a separate list of changed widgets for it. We can work out what needs repainting from the drawing commands, even if the UI tree itself was rebuilt. And we can do it entirely on the GPU!
Of course, rebuilding the tree, doing layout, and producing commands still cost something. Checking for changes also takes work. What matters is how those costs compare with the work we avoid. The measurements later in this post give us one concrete example.
Let's first look at what we give the painter to work with.
By the time a command reaches the painter, layout has already happened. We know where the shapes go, what colors they have, where they should be clipped, and which textures they use.
The painter doesn't need to know what a popup menu, a timeline, or an audio clip is. The application and UI system take care of that. The commands it understands are fairly basic:
In the Metal backend, each GPU command takes up 64 bytes. They all have the same size, and the shader reads the fields it needs for the particular operation.
I think of this as a small rendering language because some commands affect how we process the ones that follow. We can begin a group of shapes, for example, or start collecting drawing operations that should share one opacity value. I will get into both of those in a moment.
So the shader looks a bit like a small interpreter. It walks through the commands and keeps a little state between them. The operations it knows about are all built into the shader.
This also gives us some room to play with how the UI looks. We can build a shape from several pieces and outline the result, or fade a whole popup together. Those choices are expressed in the same command stream that we split into tile lists and check for changes. Let’s look at how we process that stream, and then at what these operations let us draw.
We could simply run through every command for every pixel, but that would be a lot of unnecessary work. Most shapes only cover a small part of the window. We first want to find the commands that could matter at a particular location.
This is where the tiles come in. We divide the output into a grid and process it using ordinary compute shaders. These tiles are just part of our own organization of the work.
In a preprocessing pass, we work out the area each command can affect and record which coarse regions it overlaps. We store this in bitsets, where a set bit means that a command might matter in that region. Each fine tile then checks the candidates from its coarse region and collects the ones whose bounds overlap it.
We have to keep the drawing order intact while doing this. With alpha blending, swapping two shapes can change the result. We want each tile to end up with a shorter list of commands that still produces the right image for that region.
One detail that is easy to miss is that group boundaries need bounds too. A command that begins a group doesn't draw anything by itself, but leaving it out of a tile's list would change what happens to the shapes that follow. We need to include it wherever the group matters.
Similarly, a glow or shadow can reach beyond the shape that produced it. Its bounds have to include that extra area, or we will miss pixels that need painting.
Once we have a tile's list, each pixel walks through it from front to back.
For an analytic shape, we evaluate a distance function at the pixel's position. This tells us where the pixel is relative to the shape's boundary, which we use to work out edge coverage, fills, and outlines. For textured shapes, we also sample the image or coverage data and blend the result into the pixel.
Going from front to back has a useful property: once the result is fully opaque, anything behind it can no longer contribute. We can stop there, as long as we aren't inside a group or opacity operation that still needs finishing.
The shader keeps the color and opacity it has accumulated so far in local state. So we get to control both how we combine the shapes and when we have done enough work for a pixel.
Suppose we build an icon from a few overlapping shapes and want to put an outline around it. Outlining each shape separately would also draw the boundaries inside the icon. What we usually want is one outline around the combined shape.
This is what shape groups are for. Inside a group, we combine the shapes' distance values. When we reach the end, we apply the fill and outline to the combined result.
The UI can therefore assemble these visuals from existing shapes without us writing a special shader for each one. We can also use the group's geometry to draw a glow, inner glow, or shadow. Where we put those operations in the command stream determines how they blend with everything else.
There is a small catch here: combining distance functions doesn't necessarily leave us with an exact signed distance everywhere. Smooth blends in particular need some care when we use the result to draw an outline.
But the basic idea is quite convenient. We can change the shapes that make up an object and then give the whole thing a common appearance, using operations the painter already understands.
Another case where drawing everything independently doesn't quite work is fading a popup. Suppose it has an opaque background and opaque text, and we want the whole popup at 50% opacity. We need to draw the text over the background first, then fade the combined result.
If we just give both elements 50% opacity, the background shows through the text. Where they overlap, the combined opacity is 75%. That is a different image from the one we wanted.
We handle this with what we call alpha barriers. When we enter one, the painter saves the result it has accumulated so far and starts a separate result for the popup. At the end, it applies the popup's opacity and combines the two. From the UI side, we only need to specify the fade at the root of that subtree. Credit goes to Anton Mikhailov for giving us this idea.
All of this happens in the pixel's local shader state. We don't need to allocate a separate offscreen texture for the popup.
At the moment, we only support one active alpha barrier at a time, so they can't be nested. This also keeps the amount of state we carry around per pixel small.
Blick has some things to draw that need more than shapes and colors. Audio waveforms and video gradients, for example, need access to media data. If we put all of that directly into the painter, it would have to know more and more about the application.
In the Metal backend, we draw these in a separate effects pass and store the results in atlas textures. The painter then gets ordinary textured drawing commands for them. Glyphs also reach the painter as coverage in an atlas, although how we generate that coverage is a topic of its own.
This lets us work on application effects without teaching the painter about their data. As far as the painter is concerned, it just needs to sample the resulting texture and blend it with the other shapes.
We do have to distinguish between keeping space in an atlas and keeping the image stored there. Just because the allocation still exists doesn't mean its contents are up to date. The effects code tracks whether the content has been rendered and includes content revisions in the cache inputs where needed.
After binning, we have a list of the commands that matter to each tile. We can use that same list to decide whether we need to paint it again at all.
That includes the operations we just looked at. A combined shape or a faded popup still comes down to commands and their inputs. Changing a group’s outline or a popup’s opacity needs to invalidate the affected tiles, just like changing a rectangle’s color. If those inputs stay the same, we can keep the finished pixels, including all that compositing work.
The GPU calculates a hash from the tile's commands in drawing order. If it matches the hash from the previous frame, we leave that part of the UI texture alone. Otherwise, we append the tile to a list of work to do.
The GPU also produces the count used to dispatch the paint pass. This means we can paint the changed tiles without first sending the list back to the CPU.
We hash the command contents and their order. We are not comparing pixels to pixels. Different commands that happen to produce identical pixels can in theory cause us to repaint a tile unnecessarily.
A rectangle can also stay in exactly the same place while the image inside it changes. We have to include texture-content changes and animation in the invalidation logic too. Just checking the geometry would miss those.
Currently, we can skip work at two levels. First, we check whether the commands and their dependencies have changed, whether any effects need rendering, and whether the cache was explicitly invalidated. If none of those require work, we can skip the painter entirely. When it does run, the tile hashes still let us skip painting unchanged regions.
There is also a fairly straightforward way to check whether we are keeping pixels that should have changed. We could replay the same UI interactions with caching enabled and disabled, capture the results at matching points, and compare the images. With the same inputs and animation times, both should produce the same image. The uncached renderer would give us a useful reference for catching stale pixels after things like scrolling, resizing, or changing a texture. We haven't automated those checks yet, but having that reference makes the caching behavior easier to test.
This is the part I find useful for immediate-mode UI. We can describe the interface again and still keep much of what the renderer did last time. Layout, command generation, preprocessing, and presentation have their own costs, but we don't have to repaint everything just because we rebuilt the UI.
Of course, all of this comes with some overhead. We are doing extra work to find out which work we can avoid.
Binning and hashing take GPU time before we even start painting. Scrolling or animating large parts of the interface can change many tiles at once. If we have lots of translucent elements stacked on top of each other, we also get fewer opportunities to stop processing a pixel early. And the effects atlases need storage, tracking, and rendering work of their own.
Our tile lists currently have a fixed capacity too. That limits how many commands can overlap in one place, including group and barrier commands. It is a constraint on what this implementation can handle, which matters alongside how fast it runs.
To keep the bookkeeping reasonably small, we use SIMD-group operations to build the tile lists cooperatively, with temporary results in threadgroup memory. Compact commands and indices also help with how much data we need to move around. Whether that effort pays for itself still depends on what we are drawing.
To put some numbers behind this, we ran a scripted light-editing session on my M3 Pro MacBook Pro, unplugged, with the cache enabled and then with full repainting forced. It mixed pauses with playback, scrubbing, moving clips, and editing titles. Both versions could sleep when nothing was happening. The difference was whether we reused pixels when the application did update.
Across two paired comparisons, macOS estimated average CPU + GPU power at 0.304 W with caching and 0.380 W with forced repainting , about 20% lower . Both pairs favored caching. These estimates cover the machine’s CPU and GPU, including other processes; they aren’t a measurement of the whole laptop or Blick alone.¹
For the whole laptop, the cumulative battery telemetry suggests 3.44 W with caching versus 3.99 W with forced repainting , about 14% less power . Assuming 60 Wh of usable battery energy, that works out to about 2.4 extra hours if we kept doing this light-editing workload: roughly 17.4 hours instead of 15.1. That is a preliminary projection from a short test, rather than a measured battery rundown.
We also painted roughly 94% fewer tiles and spent 87% less GPU time in the painter . That is a substantial amount of painting we avoided while running the same editing sequence.
For me, this is useful evidence that the cache makes a practical difference even when both versions can idle. Longer measurements should help establish how well the battery-life projection holds up.
This design came from putting a few existing ideas together. I would like to give credit to the people whose work helped us get here.
rxi's Cached Software Rendering describes the caching idea very directly: collect drawing commands, hash them into a grid, and redraw the regions whose hashes changed. The application can describe everything again without having to track dirty regions itself. It is written about a software renderer, but the useful part for us was that separation between describing the UI and deciding which pixels need repainting.
Gareth Thomas's Compute-Based GPU Particle Systems , presented at GDC 2014 while at AMD, showed how tiled compute rendering could handle lots of overlapping, alpha-blended particles. The GPU Particles sample includes the implementation. Particles might seem a bit far removed from UI, but the rendering problem has something in common: lots of shapes layered over the same pixels. This was an important inspiration for doing the painting and blending ourselves in a compute shader.
Wessel Mast's UIPainter: Tile-Based UI Rendering in One Draw Call , presented in 2024, brought tiled rendering and signed distance fields together for Guerrilla's Decima editor UI. That was the other major piece: use a spatial grid to narrow down which shapes each pixel needs to evaluate.
Our approach combines these ideas on the GPU. The tiles give us both a way to make painting cheaper and a way to decide whether painting is needed at all. And, as mentioned in the popup example, Anton Mikhailov gave us the idea for alpha barriers, letting us apply group opacity within the pixel's local shader state.
The idea I hope is useful beyond Blick is fairly simple: you can put a rendering cache behind an immediate-mode UI. Rebuilding the description doesn't mean we have to throw away the pixels we already produced.
In our case, the tile lists help in two ways. They give each pixel fewer commands to process, and they give us something to hash when deciding whether to keep the previous result. When we do need to paint, going from front to back also lets us stop once the remaining shapes can't contribute.
That gives us a way to address some of the repeated work while keeping the immediate-mode programming model. The short light-editing experiment supports a CPU/GPU power benefit on this MacBook. I would still like to explore heavier workloads and other hardware to see how far that carries, and where the bookkeeping stops paying for itself.
I also like the flexibility this gives us when building the UI. Shape groups let us assemble visuals from smaller pieces, and alpha barriers let us fade a collection of elements together. The command stream describes how to draw them; the tile lists tell us where those commands matter; and the cache lets us keep the result when the inputs haven’t changed.
¹ Measurement note. Tested October 18, 2026 on an unplugged M3 Pro MacBook Pro at 60 Hz, roughly 50% brightness, and a 2400 × 1500 framebuffer. Four four-minute trials formed two paired comparisons, with both modes allowed to idle. CPU/GPU estimates use powermetrics over each trial's middle two minutes; painter work totals cover the full trials. This is a small, synthetic light-editing test.
Whole-laptop power uses cumulative AppleSmartBattery telemetry whose accuracy we have not independently validated. The battery figures remain preliminary, and runtime assumes 60 Wh of usable energy rather than a measured rundown.

title: BETA Becomes First Company to Secure Landmark FAA Authorization to Conduct Flight Operations with Prospective Customers in Electric VTOL Aircraft
body:
– First-of-its-kind authorization for an electric VTOL follows BETA’s earlier CTOL approval and reflects the operational and safety record BETA has built across both aircraft which have flown more than 250,000 nautical miles combined –
– BETA’s A250 is now authorized to conduct flight operations with operators and key stakeholders under a Special Airworthiness Certificate for market surveys –
– BETA’s A250 completes first flight under new FAA authorization on October 20, 2026 –
BETA Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: BETA) (“BETA”), an aerospace and defense company, today announced that the Federal Aviation Administration (“FAA”) has awarded its ALIA VTOL (“A250”) aircraft a Special Airworthiness Certificate for market surveys, marking the first such authorization granted to an electric vertical takeoff and landing (“VTOL”) aircraft.
“This authorization brings vertical flight closer to the people and places that will put it to work, building on BETA’s track record of industry firsts. We completed the first crewed electric VTOL transition flight in 2024, we were first to receive market survey authorization for our conventional takeoff and landing aircraft (“CTOL”), and now we’re first with our VTOL,” said Kyle Clark, founder and chief executive officer of BETA. “Operators can now experience the VTOL firsthand and begin planning how it fits into their businesses, from connecting communities to moving people and goods at a lower cost. This is an important step toward commercial adoption, and we’re grateful to the FAA for developing the regulatory framework that makes these operations possible.”
BETA’s A250 is an all-electric VTOL aircraft designed to operate from locations with or without runway access. Built with a simple, efficient design, the VTOL delivers lower operating costs, higher reliability, and industry-leading range and payload. The VTOL shares a common architecture and core technology foundation with BETA’s ALIA CTOL aircraft; the same propulsion systems, flight control computers, batteries and charging systems, allowing flight experience, manufacturing investment, and operational learning to support both platforms. This stable configuration and simplicity of design across CTOL and VTOL align with the FAA’s standards of safety.
The aircraft has dual pilot controls and is designed to be able to carry up to five passengers and more than 1,200 pounds of cargo, supporting missions across cargo and logistics, medical transportation, defense, and passenger operations.
“Incredible things are happening in aviation thanks to President Trump and his commitment to innovation. The FAA’s special airworthiness certification of BETA’s A250 aircraft is another critical step towards enabling the future of flight in America,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “I want to thank our incredible safety team at the FAA for their hard work and congratulate BETA on reaching this milestone. From bringing the next generation of aircraft online to modernizing our nation’s air traffic control system – we are delivering generational wins for the flying public at record speed.”
The authorization, issued under Part 21 of the FAA’s regulations, enables BETA to conduct flights with operators and key stakeholders, allowing them to experience the A250’s capabilities firsthand and building the confidence and familiarity that drive market adoption. The approval also expands the geographic scope of BETA’s operations, providing greater flexibility to demonstrate the capabilities of electric vertical flight across a wider range of operating conditions, subject to applicable FAA limitations.
“The FAA is committed to working with American innovators to safely integrate these new aircraft into our national airspace, while maintaining the rigorous safety standards that have made the United States a global leader in aviation,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.
BETA’s A250 completed its first flight under the new authorization on October 20, 2026. In its first flight under the market survey authorization, the ALIA VTOL took off vertically from Plattsburgh International Airport (PBG) in New York, transitioned to wing borne flight and landed vertically at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport (BTV) in Vermont, covering 34 nautical miles in 20 minutes.
As it works toward full type certification and commercial operations, BETA continues to expand real-world flight operations, build relationships and validate its technology across a growing range of applications.
BETA (NYSE: BETA) is an aerospace and defense company designing, manufacturing and selling high-performance electric aircraft, advanced electric propulsion systems, components and charging systems to top operators worldwide. BETA’s intentional approach to developing the enabling technologies necessary to electrify aviation unlocks lucrative aftermarket revenue opportunity over the life of each aircraft. These highly scalable enabling technologies allow BETA to serve a customer base across cargo and logistics, defense, passenger and medical end markets and unlock cost-effective and safe missions. Visit www.beta.team for more information about BETA and its products.

title: Deepmind founder Hassabis shortens AGI timeline from five to two to three years
body:
Demis Hassabis, Google Deepmind founder and Nobel laureate in chemistry, now believes AGI could arrive within two to three years. He defines AGI as a system matching the full cognitive range of the human brain.
That timeline keeps shrinking. Earlier this year , he said three to five years. "It's going to happen soon. My estimate keeps moving closer to the present," he told the Wall Street Journal . His litmus test is the "Einstein test": Could a system trained only on pre-1901 knowledge reproduce Einstein's 1905 papers?
Hassabis has compared AGI's impact to "10 times the industrial revolution at 10 times the speed." Since stepping down from Google DeepMind , he's focused on Google's drug discovery AI spin-off Isomorphic Labs . On safety, he recently pitched an industry-funded oversight board under government control to vet models before release. Bad regulation, he warns, is worse than none. Ad Ad

title: Ghost Shark Uncrewed Submarine Shown Launching Aerial Drones For The First Time
body: New footage of Australia’s Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous underwater vehicle (XL-AUV) provides the first look at how the vehicle launches aerial drones, while also revealing a pair of deployable masts not previously seen on the platform. The video comes soon after we got a glimpse of some of the payloads that the Royal Australian Navy plans to integrate on the new uncrewed submarine, as you can read more about in our coverage here . "Ghost Shark has teeth now." – @PatConroy1 , Australia's Minister for Defence Industry. The @ausgov and @Australian_Navy confirmed the payloads that our Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous submarine carries: sea mines, logistics caches, and air-launched effects for ISR and strike.… pic.twitter.com/IALPFpOf4V — Anduril Industries (@anduriltech) October 21, 2026 Published by manufacturer Anduril, the footage shows a Ghost Shark surfacing before doors on the top of its hull slide open. A launcher consisting of 12 angled tubes then emerges from a drone sub. Another launcher is seen in the other upper payload bay, but is not raised in the video. While it appears to be of the same type, the second launcher could also have a different arrangement of tubes. While the 12-tube ALTIUS aerial drone launcher on the left is seen elevating, the launcher on the right remains lowered. Anduril/screencap The footage subsequently cuts to an ALTIUS-type drone being launched from one of the tubes, with Ghost Shark itself remaining surfaced. A Ghost Shark launches an ALTIUS aerial drone from a raised 12-tube launcher. Anduril/screencap The sequence provides a much more concrete look at the aerial-drone deployment concept — or one of them — than the photographs released previously, which offered the first public view inside Ghost Shark’s side payload bay. The Australian government has said the vehicle is being developed for missions including persistent intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR) and strike, but the precise configuration and operational capabilities of its weapons and how they are launched had not previously been disclosed. The video does not identify which ALTIUS variant is being launched. However, Ghost Shark has previously been displayed at the Altus factory in Australia alongside derivatives of the ALTIUS-600 family. This includes the ALTIUS-600 for ISR, as well as the ALTIUS-600M, which is designed for strike missions. You can read more about this family of drones here . As we noted before , unarmed variants of the ALTIUS-600 are designed to be optionally expendable, and can be reused, although in many scenarios that isn’t possible. In terms of capabilities, the ALTIUS-600 has a maximum range of around 275 miles and can remain airborne for at least four hours, according to Anduril. Examples of the Anduril ALTIUS-600 displayed during a press conference at the Anduril Australia factory in Sydney, New South Wales. Australian Department of Defense Ghost Shark can clearly deploy a substantial number of aerial drones — two dozen in this case – in a single sortie, enabling swarms to be launched far from an adversary’s coastline. Depending on the drones carried and how they are employed, such a swarm could provide broad-area surveillance, wreak havoc on enemy air defenses via electronic warfare, or attack targets. The concept could also have value below the threshold of open conflict. A mass launch of relatively inexpensive drones could be used to probe or stimulate an adversary’s air defenses, prompting them to reveal their locations, signatures and operating procedures for collection by other intelligence assets or even some of the drones themselves. There is a precedent for exactly this going back to the early Cold War years, which you can read all about here . Ghost Shark could carry these capabilities deep into contested waters clandestinely without putting a crew at risk, unleashing their payload even at standoff distances or right next to the shore to give the drones maximum penetration and loitering time over target, depend on the risk profile. At the same time, while the 12-tube launchers fit neatly into Ghost Shark’s hull architecture, the modular nature of the design means that the same space can accommodate many other payloads, which might include alternative types of aerial drones. This could be fewer larger, more capable types, or far more plentiful smaller, less capable ones. The other notable development in the video is the appearance of two deployable masts. Their presence is particularly interesting given Anduril’s emphasis on designing uncrewed underwater vehicles without the kinds of protruding mast arrangements associated with traditional submarine designs. On UUVs, masts like these are generally used to support sensors, communications, and propulsion systems. Looking aft, with the two masts raised. Anduril/screencap “We don’t have big masts running down the backbone of our vehicle that a lot of other designs do that then preclude the ability for the payloads to come out in different directions… of the payload module itself,” Dr. Shane Arnott, Senior Vice President for Engineering at Anduril and the company’s maritime lead, told TWZ back in 2024. “So we have… in effect, unlimited flexibility in this design, just the way that we’ve configured the vehicle and the payload bay itself could be almost anything within a size configuration that you can dream up,” Arnott added. “We haven’t encountered a crazy idea yet from a customer that … we can’t fit.” The first Ghost Shark for the Royal Australian Navy. In this earlier view, the retractable masts are not visible. Australian Department of Defense The larger mast that lies flat is actually a fairly traditional one for large UUVs. It lies along the centerline of the hull when stowed, between the upper payload bays. It then deploys upward in an arm-like motion and carries an antenna. The smaller mast is located farther aft and rises vertically from its own housing. Potentially, the tall mast supports a line-of-sight datalink to the drones, while the other being a satcom array, such as one connected to Starlink/Starshield, sends drone feed to controllers anywhere in the world. It’s also worth noting that Ghost Shark could just launch the drones and send them on their missions autonomously, without needing to stay surfaced at all. Other arrangements could exist, as well, such as Ghost Shark launching a dozen drones and one larger one capable of carrying its own satcom terminal. This would allow direct control of the drones by operators anywhere in the world without Ghost Shark remaining present near the surface. Ghost Shark also has a lower-profile swept-back sail on top of its nose section, not visible in the video. Overall, the vessel would retain a very small signature above the waterline while connected to the drones, making it hard to detect by radar and electro-optical imaging systems. Ghost Shark submerged, with its reflection seen on the surface. This provides a good view of the retracted masts and how they fit neatly with the closed upper payload doors. Anduril/screencap The new video follows the recent disclosure of three payload concepts for the Royal Australian Navy’s Ghost Shark: the deployment of up to 12 sea mines in a mission, the placement of supply caches on the seabed, and the launch of aerial drones. Those capabilities expand the vehicle beyond conventional underwater surveillance into a broader range of undersea warfare missions. The mine-delivery option could support operations in strategically important maritime areas, while seabed caches could provide a means of positioning equipment and supplies for later retrieval. The aerial-drone capability, as seen in the new video, would allow Ghost Shark to extend surveillance beyond the reach of its own sensors or potentially deliver strike effects without exposing crewed platforms to the same risks. Having 12 ALTIUS drones ready to launch (and potentially the same number in the adjacent upper payload bay) would allow multiple missions to be undertaken. The modular design is central to Ghost Shark. As we have discussed , the payload section can be configured using different hull sections and mission-specific systems, allowing the same underlying vehicle design to accommodate different requirements. The newly revealed launcher provides a first look at how at least one of those payload concepts may be implemented in practice. A rendering of a Ghost Shark in Royal Australian Navy service. Australian Department of Defense Australia has committed substantial resources to autonomous and uncrewed undersea warfare capabilities, with a planned fleet of Australian-designed and built Ghost Shark vehicles serving alongside the Speartooth large uncrewed underwater vehicle (LUUV) and the BlueBottle uncrewed surface vessel (USV). The Ghost Shark program is also part of the broader AUKUS effort to develop advanced maritime technologies alongside the United Kingdom and the United States. The new footage provides a clearer picture of the practical design choices behind that effort. Most notably, how the underwater vehicle can operationalize its aerial drone launching capability and the quantity of those systems it could potentially deploy very quickly before slipping back below the waves. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Ghost Shark Uncrewed Submarine Shown Launching Aerial Drones For The First Time appeared first on TWZ .

title: Russian lawmakers approve four new deputy prime ministers and a transport minister in Mikhail Mishustin’s Cabinet reshuffle
body: The State Duma has approved all of Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin’s nominees for a government reshuffle. Anton Siluanov will become deputy prime minister while remaining finance minister. Oleg Kozhemyako, the governor of Primorsky Krai, will become deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to the Far East, replacing Yury Trutnev. Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin will become deputy prime minister overseeing transport. Dmitry Yadrov, the head of Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, will become transport minister. Irina Okladnikova, the first deputy finance minister, will become deputy prime minister and government chief of staff, replacing Dmitry Grigorenko. Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin announced the Russian government reshuffle on October 19. Vladimir Putin backed the proposal. Experts say Siluanov’s new role and the appointment of his first deputy at the Finance Ministry, Irina Okladnikova, point to Siluanov’s growing influence. Dmitry Grigorenko, whom Okladnikova will replace, is considered one of the officials closest to Mishustin. title: Inside a Ukrainian Minefield Rescue | Drone Footage & Exclusive Interviews
body:
Two Ukrainian soldiers are wounded by a mine blast in an open field. With mines around them and enemy drones overhead, soldiers from Ukraine’s Khartiia Brigade rush to help.
In exclusive interviews with Kyiv Post, combat medic “Osa” and platoon commander “Kamaro” recount the rescue, reaching their wounded comrades, carrying them across the minefield and making urgent decisions under the threat of attack.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Drone footage provided by the brigade captures the evacuation from above. Their firsthand accounts reveal what the camera could not: the fear, physical strain and fight to keep their comrades alive.

title: Russian scientist convicted of treason refuses food and water over alleged abuse in detention
body: Valery Kachin, a geodesist from Birobidzhan who was sentenced in January 2025 to 14 years in a penal colony for treason, has begun a dry hunger strike at Pretrial Detention Center No. 1 in Izhevsk, the human rights group Department One (Pervy Otdel) reported. In a letter from the detention center, Kachin, 39, said he had stopped eating and drinking after staff tormented and physically assaulted him. He said he has been held continuously in a punishment cell: After an initial seven days, he was given another 10 days, followed by two consecutive 15-day terms. He said staff force him to raise and lower a heavy bed by himself, even though he is not required to do so. He said staff also conduct nighttime inspections and confiscate personal belongings from his cell. “This morning, after we traded insults, they forced me to the floor. I bruised my face on the floor, and my elbows and knees are scraped. I started a hunger strike this morning — no water or food. Tell everyone,” he wrote, according to Pervy Otdel. Kachin is 182 centimeters (about 6 feet) tall and weighs just 60 kilograms (132 pounds), the group said. Kachin previously began a dry hunger strike in September 2025 at Penal Colony No. 8, known as Khokhryaki, in Udmurtia. He went on that strike after spending 60 days in a punishment cell. He said that while there, he was unable to keep to the vegan diet he has followed for 14 years. He had received food assistance from Vegan Peredachki (Vegan Care Packages), an initiative whose volunteers arrange vegan meals for political prisoners, but prisoners in punishment cells cannot receive care packages. Kachin’s case became public in December 2022. On January 27, 2025, the Birobidzhan City Court sentenced him to 14 years in a high-security prison. He was then transferred to a penal colony in Udmurtia. Kachin last worked as a junior researcher at the Bastak Nature Reserve in Birobidzhan. The news outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti reported that he had used social media to voice support for Alexei Navalny and the protests in Belarus and to speak out against the war in Ukraine. title: In Oslo, US pushes Zelenskyy toward deal with Russia again. Day later, in same city, Norway discusses arming Ukraine with more NASAMS missiles
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); As Washington leans on Ukraine to make a deal with Russia amid its diesel agreement ahead of the US elections, its European partners are meeting to keep it armed against deadly weapons. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he met Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik in Oslo on 21 October to discuss more NASAMS air defenses, a day after meeting US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in the same city. Washington has spent the past two weeks easing pressure on Russia and leaning on Kyiv, with a diesel deal, throttled Starlink, and talk of cutting intelligence, while Ukraine’s European partners move in the other direction. Russia pounds Ukrainian cities almost nightly, and the Norwegian-made NASAMS is one of the systems holding that barrage off critical infrastructure. Kongsberg opened an office in Ukraine in 2025. Its NASAMS uses the AIM-120 AMRAAM missile built by the US defense giant RTX, the same firm behind the Patriot launchers that are Ukraine’s only means of downing Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles. The same missile is also used in F-16s. “They effectively protect our people and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks virtually every day,” Zelenskyy said. He added that Ukraine is counting on additional defense support packages next month. A European shield Ukraine wants tested this year The visit also advanced a joint missile-defense project. Norway is actively involved in FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile program that Ukraine is helping to build. “There are already first results in creating individual elements of the system. Today we determined where we can and must speed up to reach testing by the end of this year,” Zelenskyy said. FREYJA now draws in 10 countries and is built around an interceptor missile designed to stop ballistic threats, a capability Europe largely lacks against Russia’s fastest weapons. A push for satellites as Starlink falters Zelenskyy also raised satellite communications amid the scandal over speed limitations on Elon Musk’s military Starlink service that disrupted a series of front-line missions. “We discussed in detail the start of work on new satellite-communication capabilities for our soldiers,” the president said, adding that Kyiv would bring in partners able to support them. The push comes after SpaceX throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use. Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps said the connection began dropping as drones moved at speed, negatively affecting their missions. title: Autonomous underwater systems added to Elbit Systems portfolio through acquisition
body:
VANCOUVER, Canada. Elbit Systems acquired Canada-based International Submarine Engineering (ISE), a manufacturer of autonomous underwater vehicles and remotely operated maritime systems, the company announced in a statement.
ISE, headquartered in the Vancouver area, develops autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), robotic systems, and computer control equipment, according to the statement. The company has operated in the subsea robotics industry for more than 50 years, supplying over 250 underwater vehicles to customers in more than 20 countries, Elbit Systems says.
The acquisition adds underwater vehicle technologies to Elbit Systems' existing naval portfolio, which includes uncrewed surface vessels, command-and-control (C2) systems, sonar, electro-optical equipment, communications systems, and electronic warfare technologies, the statement reads.
Elbit Systems intends to use ISE's technology to expand its capabilities in underwater intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), mine countermeasures (MCM), and anti-submarine warfare (ASW), according to the company.

title: 29 Russian Troops Captured, 108 Eliminated, 1,100+ Targets Hit: Ukraine’s HUR Summarizes Sumy Operation
body:
Ukraine’s military intelligence special forces cleared more than 600 hectares (1,480 acres) of forest of Russian troops during a seven-week operation in the Sumy region, thwarting Russian offensive plans.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence ( HUR ) announced the operation on Telegram on Oct. 20, saying fighters from the “GROUP 10” unit of its Department of Active Operations captured 29 Russian soldiers, neutralized 108 others and struck more than 1,100 targets.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The primary objective has been achieved!” HUR said, adding that the operation prevented Russian forces from cutting off logistical routes.
The operation lasted approximately seven weeks and consisted of two phases, according to the report. Forty special forces personnel took part in active combat operations.
During the operation, HUR operatives also destroyed Russian drone command posts, artillery systems, vehicles and fortifications. After clearing the forest, the special forces handed the positions over to Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
A video released alongside the report shows footage from the operation, including Ukrainian troops taking Russian soldiers prisoner. Kyiv Post has been unable to independently verify when or where the footage was filmed.
The operation comes amid reports of increased Russian activity along Ukraine’s northern border.
On Oct. 21, Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service, said Russian sabotage and reconnaissance groups (DRG) had become more active over the previous several weeks, primarily in the Sumy region and also along the border in Chernihiv region.
Ukrainian forces are deploying anti-sabotage reserves and technical equipment to detect the groups and prevent them from carrying out their plans, Demchenko said.
He also reported a slight increase in attacks by Russian infantry groups in Sumy, particularly in the Shostka and Konotop districts. However, the intensity of Russian troop deployments in the region remains below that in the Kharkiv region, he added.
“If Russia manages to secure additional resources – primarily in terms of manpower – we should expect that attacks within the Sumy region could also intensify,” Demchenko said.
In late September, Demchenko had also warned that Russian forces were repeatedly attempting to expand their zone of control near Ukrainian defensive positions in the Shostka and Konotop districts and the Yunakivka community.

title: Rocket-armed uncrewed aircraft intercepts multiple drones in U.S. tests
body:
EGLIN, Florida. A modified TRV-150 uncrewed aerial system (UAS) from BAE Systems subsidiary Malloy Aeronautics intercepted multiple one-way attack drones during tests in Florida, the company announced in a statement
The aircraft used a three-pod launcher carrying BAE Systems' laser-guided rockets to engage several airborne targets during a single flight without landing or reloading, the statement reads. The tests took place Sept. 21-25 at Eglin Air Force Base as part of a U.S. Office of the Under Secretary for Research and Engineering experimentation exercise.
Maryland-based SURVICE Engineering adapted the T-150 platform to meet U.S. Army requirements, while BAE Systems' FalconWorks division developed and integrated the rocket modification kit, the company says.
The trials expanded on a July 2025 test in which an adapted T-150 fired a precision munition, according to the statement.
The T-150 has served in a logistics role with British forces, including carrying supplies between ships during a Royal Navy Carrier Strike Group deployment to the Indo-Pacific, the company says. BAE Systems and its partners plan to examine the platform's counter-drone use at sea.

title: Iran's Baloch minority want Israeli strikes to continue until regime falls, activist tells 'Post'
body: The Islamic regime in Iran is paying and blackmailing people to manufacture displays of support for Tehran in Sistan and Baluchestan province. It is pursuing the same policy among minority communities across Iran, a Baloch human rights activist in hiding told The Jerusalem Post late Tuesday night.Identified only as “B” for security reasons, the activist has spent a decade in an Iranian prison over allegations he was tied to militia groups.Through translation, B described the dire conditions facing the Baloch community since the revolution, from the psychological toll of repeated executions to extreme poverty in a region rich in oil and minerals. He claimed that across Sistan and Baluchestan, a vast province accounting for approximately 10% of Iran's landmass, not a single Baloch family had been spared the loss of at least one of its members to the regime, either through shootings or executions.According to Iran Human Rights, a nongovernmental organization that monitors executions, at least 108 Baloch individuals were executed in Iran in 2024, accounting for 11% of all recorded executions, despite the minority making up an estimated 2% to 6% of the country's population. A report submitted to the UN Universal Periodic Review by several human rights organizations also found that Baloch people accounted for 29% of the 154 individuals executed in Iran between 2010 and 2023.Although almost all Baloch are Muslim, the majority belong to Sunni or Zikri communities, which the regime views as heretical, B explained. He added that Tehran brands the Baloch and other minority groups as collaborators with Israel because they focus on human rights abuses committed in front of them rather than on a Jewish state more than 1,500 miles away.'Israelis should be able to live a simple life'“They tell members of the armed groups that the Baloch are enemies of the government, asking them, 'Why are you not fighting Israel? Why do you have no problem with Israel? Why do you fight us?' But Baloch people do not want to fight Israel or harbor hostility toward Israelis,” he said. “Most Baloch are religious Sunnis, and unlike the IRGC, which spreads hatred of Israel every day, they do not promote that kind of hatred. They believe Israelis should be able to live a simple life alongside Palestinians.”Discrimination also limits the Baloch community's economic opportunities. B noted that Iran's Selection Law and other forms of discrimination prevent many Baloch from advancing in society, leaving some with few options but to smuggle subsidized fuel across borders to earn a living. Many have been burned to death by regime security forces, he said, adding that the forces knowingly opened fire on vehicles carrying the fuel.Using the case of Ya'qub Mehrnahad as an example, a young blogger hanged in 2008 after a closed-door trial widely condemned as unfair, B said the Baloch people were denied justice at even the most basic level.“He was just having a small protest about the regime, and he got executed,” B said. “They punish and torture people, forcing them to say on television whatever the regime wants them to say. The person is being punished or tortured, and they film them making statements they are being forced to make, then broadcast the footage on television. There is no court or proper judgment. They just arrest people, and this is still happening today.”Reflecting on his own years in prison, B said he had seen multiple minors and individuals being held without charge.Describing a reality in which people cannot afford food, and children must attend schools without shoes, classrooms, chairs or tables, he said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had not worsened conditions for his community. B said the supplies imported to Iran had never been meant for his people and that it was better to continue the blockade than risk supplying the regime.Love and respect for all Abrahamic religions “Every penny that comes through this Strait of Hormuz goes to the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC. Even when it comes to medicine and other supplies, they go to the Houthis and the Lebanese people. Not even one person benefits from the Strait of Hormuz, so it should be closed. It is better anyway because if it gets closed and the regime comes under pressure, maybe we can get this regime to go. Any benefit it gets from the Strait of Hormuz or anywhere else allows it to rebuild from within and grow stronger to beat the people, stop them from protesting, and prevent the regime from falling. It will do anything for that.”After signaling his own curiosity about how Israelis view the Baloch people, B said he and his community were happy when Israel began striking the regime and hoped the attacks would continue.“People were incredibly happy about this war. I could hear how happy they were. They were saying the war should not stop and expressing their love for Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump for carrying it out,” he said. “They were sending Trump messages of support for waging this war against the regime… I think Iranians love Netanyahu. They strongly support this war, and some have even been praying for it to continue, saying it should not stop until the regime falls and is replaced.”B noted that he was an observant Muslim, but he had love and respect for all Abrahamic people, insisting that once the regime was gone, they would be able to live in peace together.“We understand you. You are people who deserve to live in peace. We don't think you are bad people or that you should die. That is how the regime thinks, not us. We share the same enemy, and we understand each other's situation,” he said. “We have the right to life and peace. You and I are human beings, and even other living creatures have the right to life. We believe in one God, who created us all, and we are no different from anyone else. We deserve to live in peace. No one has the right to tell us that we do not deserve to live.”

title: Moscow court fines blogger 30,000 rubles for joke that presented Russia’s 2020 Telegram unblocking announcement (now effectively rolled back) as current news
body: A magistrate’s court in Moscow’s Tagansky district fined blogger Yekaterina Kuznetsova 30,000 rubles for an administrative offense involving abuse of media freedom under Part 9 of Article 13.15 of Russia’s Code of Administrative Offenses, the news outlets Ostorozhno, Novosti and Mediazona reported. The citation stemmed from a June 2026 post on Kuznetsova’s Telegram channel, Ne marginalny kontent, which has 15,000 subscribers. She shared a news item about Telegram being unblocked, writing, “Friends, looks like I’ve got some good news,” followed by a statement from Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, about fully unblocking the messaging app in the summer of 2020. Kuznetsova soon received a notice from Roskomnadzor demanding that she delete the post for spreading false information on a matter of public importance. Roskomnadzor concluded that Kuznetsova “presents old, accurate information as fresh, current news.” The regulator said the post could mislead readers and lead to widespread public disorder. Internet blocking in Russia Telegram is one of the last messaging apps in Russia that the state doesn’t control. Did the Kremlin just block it for good? title: Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Announces First-Ever Special Airworthiness Market Survey Certificate for eVTOL Aircraft
body:
‘Another critical step towards enabling the future of flight in America’
LAS VEGAS, NV – U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today announced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a first-of-its-kind Special Airworthiness Market Survey Certificate to BETA Technologies to conduct flight operations with its ALIA eVTOL aircraft (A250). This marks the Trump Administration’s latest move to unleash American innovation in our skies and unlock the future of flight in America.
In March, Secretary Duffy unveiled the eIPP program to begin testing advanced air mobility aircraft and their real-world applications. The eight selected projects span 28 states and partner with leading aircraft manufacturers, operators, and state partners, including:
After careful review by FAA safety experts, BETA’s A250 aircraft is now authorized to conduct flight operations with operators and participants for the purpose of conducting market surveys. The certificate also expands the geographic scope of BETA’s operations, allowing the aircraft to fly in more environments and gather more data.
The safe integration of next-generation Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) aircraft into the national airspace is essential to ensuring the U.S. leads the way in aviation innovation. AAM has the potential to reshape how Americans live, work, and connect by enhancing rural and urban transportation, strengthening cargo operations, and advancing both medical and military transportation. This certification takes the industry one step closer to that reality.
“Incredible things are happening in aviation thanks to President Trump and his commitment to innovation. The FAA’s special airworthiness certification of BETA’s A250 aircraft is another critical step towards enabling the future of flight in America,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “I want to thank our incredible safety team at the FAA for their hard work and congratulate BETA on reaching this milestone. From bringing the next generation of aircraft online to modernizing our nation’s air traffic control system – we are delivering generational wins for the flying public at record speed.”
“The FAA is committed to working with American innovators to safely integrate these new aircraft into our national airspace, while maintaining the rigorous safety standards that have made the United States a global leader in aviation,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.
“This authorization brings vertical flight closer to the people and places that will put it to work, building on BETA’s track record of industry firsts. We completed the first crewed eVTOL transition flight in 2024, were first to receive market survey authorization for our CTOL, and now we’re first with our VTOL,” said BETA Technologies Founder and CEO Kyle Clark. “Operators can now experience the A250 firsthand and begin planning how it fits into their businesses, from connecting communities to moving people and goods at a lower cost. That’s an important step toward commercial adoption, and we’re grateful to the FAA for developing the regulatory framework that makes these operations possible.”
Secretary Duffy will discuss the announcement later today at the National Business Aviation Association (NBAA) convention in Las Vegas, where he will also highlight the Department’s incredible progress in transforming the national airspace for the better. Thanks to $12.5 billion from the Working Families Tax Cut Act, the Department is modernizing America’s air traffic control system with new telecommunications lines, new radios and radars, and electronic flight strips—with all 13 modernization workstreams on track.
The eIPP is a first-of-its-kind initiative outlined in President Trump’s Unleashing Drone Dominance Executive Order . It creates one of the world’s largest real-world testing environments for next-generation aircraft with the potential to create jobs, connect communities, and strengthen American leadership in aviation.
Last year, Secretary Duffy and the FAA launched the nation’s first-ever advanced air mobility (AAM) strategy to unlock the future of flight. The Strategy and accompanying action plan outline 40 recommendations to safely and efficiently support AAM operations.

title: Putin ‘Ready’ for Three-Way Ukraine Talks in November, Kremlin Says
body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff that Moscow was ready in principle to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the US around mid-November, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Ushakov said Putin conveyed that position during their meeting in St. Petersburg. The proposed discussions would focus on postwar security arrangements.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations,” Ushakov told journalists, according to Interfax Russia.
The aide added that Moscow’s main proposed topic was establishing a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the fighting ends.
Ushakov also said Witkoff indicated that US President Donald Trump would welcome Russia’s willingness to return to negotiations. The Kremlin aide provided that description of the envoy’s response.
The announcement set out Moscow’s position and a proposed timeframe, rather than a jointly announced agreement among the three countries on when negotiations would take place.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said it is open to direct talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky, but it has demanded that the Ukrainian leader come to Moscow , effectively derailing the proposals.
The Kremlin’s statement followed Witkoff’s arrival in St. Petersburg with proposals discussed with Ukrainian and European leaders.
During Wednesday’s meeting, the US envoy said he had brought documents outlining possible approaches to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. He urged Putin to consider restarting negotiations involving representatives of all three countries, including technical working groups.
Witkoff described the preceding discussions in Oslo as productive and said they could move toward a ceasefire. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin would review the proposals.
The visit marked the US envoys’ first trip to Russia since Sept. 5, when Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Putin and senior Russian officials for three hours before traveling to Kyiv.
Before Wednesday’s meeting, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow would listen to US proposals but ruled out political concessions.
Security guarantees were also central to Zelensky’s talks with Witkoff and Nordic leaders in Norway on Tuesday, Oct. 20.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Witkoff would take proposals developed during the Oslo discussions to Russia’s leadership. The talks covered Ukraine’s security, territorial questions, sanctions and postwar prosperity.
Zelensky said a draft document included several types of guarantees, which Kyiv would present to the Russian side before assessing Putin’s response.
The Ukrainian president also confirmed that US intelligence sharing for early warnings of Russian attacks had resumed after a week of interruptions.
He said he expected progress within 48 hours on Patriot interceptors, intelligence cooperation and restrictions affecting Starlink terminals. Those issues formed part of the broader discussions over Ukraine’s ability to defend itself while diplomacy continued.
The proposed Russia-US-Ukraine format comes as Zelensky has rejected any attempt to negotiate Ukraine’s future without Kyiv.
Speaking in Oslo, he responded to reports of a possible separate meeting involving Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelensky said those leaders could hold their own discussions, but any negotiations on Ukraine’s future require Ukrainian participation.
He distinguished that potential summit from the three-way meeting he had proposed involving the US, Ukraine and Russia.
The Ukrainian president said the security proposals discussed in Oslo included arrangements resembling NATO’s Article 5 collective defense commitment. He emphasized that Ukraine needed strong guarantees after the war ends, and Kyiv was awaiting feedback from Witkoff’s discussions in Russia.
Støre likewise reaffirmed that decisions about Ukraine’s future could not be made without Ukraine’s involvement.

title: UAV Platform Propulsion Choice at High Thrust: T-MOTOR’s 24S Strategy and the A-Series Modular Propulsion Logic
body:
Does higher thrust really require a higher voltage platform?
A common engineering instinct says yes. But the real threshold is current, not thrust.
Industry engineering practice suggests that switching to a higher voltage platform becomes necessary when peak motor current reaches around 300A. T-MOTOR’s product definition on the 24S platform pushes single-unit thrust to the 84kg class (up to, under test conditions) while maintaining the stability and predictability of the electromagnetic design. The U15XXL, for example, has a maximum current of 165.52A — still short of that 300A threshold.
This means T-MOTOR raised the thrust ceiling within the mature 24S platform through electromagnetic optimization and material upgrades, rather than being forced into a high-voltage architecture rebuild. From a propulsion manufacturer’s perspective, the 24S strategy is more pragmatic: maximize thrust within a proven platform and fully release its potential, instead of jumping early into a high-voltage ecosystem whose supply chain is not yet mature.
The U15XXL reaches up to 84kg thrust, with a recommended thrust of 33.8kg, covering mainstream sub-100kg cargo platforms. For scenarios that genuinely need higher thrust — firefighting tethered systems, cargo eVTOL- T-MOTOR also offers mature solutions.
If the 24S strategy answers “how to push single-unit thrust higher,” the A-Series answers a different question: what can a propulsion manufacturer offer when integrators don’t want to match the propulsion system themselves?
The A-Series is T-MOTOR’s system-level response: 32 models, standard and coaxial configurations, three voltage platforms (14S/18S/24S), with recommended thrust covering up to 75kg. Underneath is MEPT (Modular Electric Propulsion Technology) — motor, ESC, and propeller pre-assembled into a plug-and-play module.
The core engineering logic of MEPT is not “packaging” but the completeness of factory calibration. The A-Series has undergone 2,000 hours of endurance aging, strength and fatigue simulation of key components, magneto-thermal coupling simulation, and cyclic cooling validation. The value of this test data: after receiving the module, integrators can use it as a reference for airworthiness or reliability assessment, reducing repetitive testing rather than starting from scratch.
On reliability, the differentiation of the A-Series lies not in the “variety” of monitoring features but in the systematic nature of its test data. Its reliability evidence chain includes: 2,000-hour endurance aging, 800+ hours of flight testing, -20~55°C temperature testing, IPX6 protection, and strength/fatigue simulation. This covers reliability across the full lifecycle, not just real-time monitoring during a single mission. Series and MEPT’s “depth of calibration.
The group standard “General Specification for Reliability of Hybrid Power Systems for Medium and Large UAVs” explicitly requires failure mode and effects analysis, key components adapting to operating condition changes within the mission cycle, and consideration of component aging effects on reliability.
This signals a shift: reliability data for propulsion manufacturers is moving from “marketing selling point” to “compliance threshold.” Those who can provide systematic, traceable, full-lifecycle test evidence will widen the gap with most manufacturers in this round of raising the bar.
For integrators, choosing a propulsion system is no longer just about thrust parameters — it’s about choosing a reliability evidence base that can be argued and referenced. That is exactly the direction T-MOTOR is betting on with both its 24S platform strategy and the A-Series modules.

title: ‘We Need to Move On’: Zelensky Won’t Wait in Oslo for Witkoff After Putin Meeting
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday he would not wait in Oslo for US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff to return from talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“I am not waiting for Witkoff in Oslo. We need to move on. We need to return to Ukraine,” Zelensky told Poland’s PAP news agency while visiting the Norwegian capital.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Zelensky said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre would receive an update on the outcome of Witkoff’s meeting with Putin, adding that Kyiv is in constant contact with Oslo.
“We shall see what the results are. Jonas is set to meet with the American special envoy. We remain in constant contact,” Zelensky said.
Earlier, Støre said Witkoff would stop in Oslo after meeting Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday to brief him on the talks.
Witkoff traveled to St. Petersburg to present the Kremlin with peace proposals discussed in Oslo on Tuesday. The proposals reportedly concern postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Kyiv’s future relationship with NATO.
In Oslo, Zelensky held talks with Witkoff , Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Støre. He also spoke remotely with Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.
Before noon on Wednesday, Zelensky also met with Norwegian Parliament President Masud Gharahkhani and leaders of several political parties.
The diplomatic meetings come as Washington seeks progress toward ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanist” during a meeting in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, even as Russian attacks continued to kill civilians across Ukraine.
Witkoff thanked the Kremlin leader for releasing US teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom Washington considered wrongfully detained, and presented proposals aimed at securing a ceasefire.
The praise contrasted with UN findings documenting mounting civilian casualties. At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in Ukraine in September, according to UN monitors.
In an update published Oct. 16, the UN said Russian attacks continued to cause mass casualties in October, alongside renewed strikes on electricity and heating infrastructure ahead of winter.
Witkoff said he had brought documents outlining possible approaches to a peace settlement and urged Putin to consider resuming negotiations involving the US, Ukraine and Russia, potentially with technical working groups.
Meanwhile, Russian media are circulating a statement by Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, who said the possibility of resuming trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, the US and Russia was “specifically discussed” during Witkoff’s meeting with Putin.
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, prepared to resume the aforementioned trilateral talks around Nov. 10, focusing on a key issue: establishing a security framework for Russia and Ukraine following the end of the conflict,” Ushakov said.
Earlier, Zelensky said Kyiv and Washington had agreed on proposals to end the war during their meeting in Norway, including security guarantees for Ukraine.
He also confirmed that intelligence sharing with the US had resumed and said progress on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions could come within 48 hours.
However, Trump later said Ukraine “has to want to make a deal,” claiming Washington and Europe had spent “a fortune” on Kyiv and that Europe was tired of the war.
Kyiv has repeatedly denied obstructing peace efforts, pointing to its ceasefire proposals and Zelensky’s offer of direct talks with Putin.
In September, 51 countries urged Moscow to accept an immediate truce at the UN General Assembly, but Russia rejected proposals to pause the war, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov saying the Kremlin would not suspend hostilities even during potential negotiations.

title: Proposed ASTM Standard Will Aid Unmanned Aircraft Industry
body:
Practice Will Help to Incorporate Human Factors into UAS Ground Control Systems.
ASTM International’s unmanned aircraft systems committee ( F38 ) is developing a proposed standard that will provide a minimum set of requirements for proper human factors when designing a ground control station for unmanned aircraft. The human factors discipline evaluates how end users interact with their systems, ensuring understanding, efficiency, and safety.
According to ASTM member Scott Scheff, the primary subject of the proposed standard is how remote pilots in command (RPICs) work with unmanned systems through ground control systems.
“We are looking to ensure the user interfaces, use of color, alerts, display formatting, controls, RPIC performance, including situation awareness and workload are all considered and designed in accordance with the various standards and resources available today,” says Scheff.
Scheff notes that human factors standards for ground control station design have historically been spread across multiple documents, including, but not limited to, ASTM standards. While larger companies working with agencies such as the U.S. Federal Aviation Agency (FAA) had a good handle on human factors requirements, this wasn’t always true for smaller entities.
“After working with small and large companies for more than a decade, the F38 committee found that there was a gap in understanding how to implement human factors standards for ground control design,” says Scheff. “Some didn’t know where to look, other didn’t know how to read and interpret the standards. The proposed standard will be designed to help manufacturers understand not only what good human factors are, but how best to incorporate human factors into their ground control station designs.”
Smaller UAS designers, developers, and manufacturers will be able to use the proposed standard ( WK90326 ) as a single document where they can obtain all necessary requirements for UAS ground control systems. According to Scheff, the proposed standard will include not only what information is needed, but also how that information should be used by those who need it.
ASTM welcomes participation in the development of its standards. Become a member at www.astm.org/JOIN .

title: European Parliament Vice President Declares Hunger Strike in Solidarity With Oleshky Residents
body:
European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno declared a hunger strike on Tuesday, Oct. 20 in protest over the humanitarian catastrophe Russia’s occupation has created in Oleshky, where thousands of civilians have been facing starvation for months.
Picierno, who also leads Spazio Pubblico – a reformist, pro-European Italian political movement, announced the strike in an interview with Italian newspaper La Repubblica . She said it was a response to Pope Leo XIV’s appeal for a truce in the town, located in the Kherson region, and hoped other leaders would join her.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Words are not enough, we must also put our bodies on the line to save the Ukrainians of Oleshky,” Picierno told La Repubblica, calling the fast “a gesture of anger and hope.”
Responding to growing calls in Italy for fewer weapons deliveries to Ukraine and increased diplomacy, she described her hunger strike as a “diplomatic and nonviolent initiative,” adding that “diplomacy without defense has another name: surrender.”
Oleshky is located on the left bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) southeast of Kherson city. It has been under Russian occupation since the opening days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Picierno called the town a symbol “of the inhumanity of the murderer who sits in the Kremlin,” pointing to Russian President Vladimir Putin who, according to senior Ukrainian authorities, recently ordered Russia’s military to abandon previous constraints and intensify attacks on civilian sites.
According to her estimates, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
Her figure matches that of Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha but differs from the estimates of Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian parliament commissioner for human rights, who has said about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements. In his view, up to 2,000 people could remain in Oleshky itself.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
What we do know is that the town’s residents hadn’t received any food or medicine deliveries for months, forcing some to to barter for basic goods. Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said on July 10 that no vehicles had entered or left the town since May 26.
The town’s only pharmacy has also reportedly run out of essential medications months ago, while overall medical care has been significantly complicated due to power cuts and lack of fuel as the city remains isolated.
Residents also cannot access their bank accounts nor withdraw cash as that would require leaving the town – which is nearly impossible.
“Those who stay risk starving to death; those who try to flee risk stepping on a mine,” Picierno said, echoing previous warnings of Ukrainian authorities who have been appealing to international organizations for months to help secure an evacuation corridor for the town and provide much needed additional humanitarian access.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Sybiha said .
In a statement on Sept. 16, Lubinets said that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” Lubinets said, adding that his office had received 176 appeals regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, and had already verified at least 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Putin on Oct. 16, in what marked the second phone call between the two, following their first conversation on June 4, 2025 that also focused on the war in Ukraine.
The pope had expressed his deep concern about the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, urging the Russian president to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
He also called for a safe evacuation of the civilians.
While the Kremlin backed Vatican’s initiative and agreed to cooperate, it again pinned the blame for the crisis on Ukraine, despite Kyiv’s repeated appeals to Russian authorities and international partners to secure humanitarian access to the town.
The pontiff then spoke to President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire . He expressed hope for a cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow which would allow for the desperately needed food and medical supplies to reach trapped civilians.
“We are working to help our people there. We are preparing decisions,” Zelensky said , confirming the conversation.
As of Oct. 19, Kyiv and Moscow are now in daily contact over a possible evacuation , Lubinets told Espreso TV, confirming that the Russian side had taken up all proposals previously submitted by Ukraine.
“I cannot disclose many details, but I will say this: In my view, we have made significant progress,” Lubinets said, while acknowledging that difficult issues remain.
No evacuation date has so far been announced.
Picierno urged that the talks be concluded without further delay. “The negotiation must be closed immediately,” she said, “food and medicine must be let in, and those who want to leave must be let out.”
